### Quadratic formula

In [elementary algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_algebra), the **quadratic formula** is a [closed-form expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed-form_expression) describing the solutions of a [quadratic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_equation). Other ways of solving quadratic equations, such as [completing the square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completing_the_square), yield the same solutions.

Given a general quadratic equation of the form $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, with $x$ representing an unknown, and [coefficients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient) $a$, $b$, and $c$ representing known [real](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number) or [complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_number) numbers with $a \neq 0$, the values of $x$ satisfying the equation, called the [*roots*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_of_a_function) or *zeros*, can be found using the quadratic formula,

$$
x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} }{2a},
$$

where the [plus-minus symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plus%E2%80%93minus_sign) "$\pm$" indicates that the equation has two roots.[^399] Written separately, these are:

$$
x_1 = \frac{-b + \sqrt {b^2 - 4ac} }{2a}, \qquad x_2 = \frac{-b - \sqrt {b^2 - 4ac} }{2a}.
$$

The quantity $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ is known as the [discriminant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant) of the quadratic equation.[^400] If the coefficients $a$, $b$, and $c$ are real numbers then when $\Delta > 0$, the equation has two distinct real roots; when $\Delta = 0$, the equation has one [repeated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repeated_root) real root; and when $\Delta < 0$, the equation has *no* real roots but has two distinct complex roots, which are [complex conjugates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_conjugate) of each other.

Geometrically, the roots represent the $x$ values at which the [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_of_a_function) of the [quadratic function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_function) $y = ax^2 + bx + c$, a [parabola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parabola), crosses the $x$-axis: the graph's $x$-intercepts.[^401] The quadratic formula can also be used to identify the parabola's [axis of symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_of_symmetry).[^402]

#### Derivation by completing the square

The standard way to derive the quadratic formula is to apply the method of [completing the square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Completing_the_square) to the generic quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$.[^403][^404][^405][^406] The idea is to transform the equation into the form $(x + k)^2 = s$ for some expressions $k$ and $s$ written in terms of the coefficients; take the [square root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_root) of both sides; and then isolate $x$.

We start by dividing the equation by the quadratic coefficient $a$, which is allowed because $a$ is non-zero. Afterwards, we subtract the constant term $c/a$ to isolate it on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned} ax^{2\vphantom|} + bx + c &= 0 \\[3mu] x^2 + \frac{b}{a} x + \frac{c}{a} &= 0 \\[3mu] x^2 + \frac{b}{a} x &= -\frac{c}{a}. \end{aligned}
$$

The left-hand side is now of the form $x^2 + 2kx$, and we can "complete the square" by adding a constant $k^2$ to obtain a squared binomial $x^2 + 2kx + k^2 = {}$$(x + k)^2$. In this example we add $(b / 2a)^2$ to both sides so that the left-hand side can be factored (see the figure):

$$
\begin{aligned} x^2 + 2\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)x + \left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 &= -\frac{c}{a}+\left( \frac{b}{2a} \right)^2 \\[5mu] \left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 &= \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2} . \end{aligned}
$$

Because the left-hand side is now a perfect square, we can easily take the square root of both sides:

$$
x + \frac{b}{2a} = \pm\frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} }{2a}.
$$

Finally, subtracting $b/2a$ from both sides to isolate $x$ produces the quadratic formula:

$$
x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} }{2a} .
$$

#### Equivalent formulations

The quadratic formula can equivalently be written using various alternative expressions, for instance

$$
x = -\frac{b}{2a} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2-\frac{c}{a} },
$$

which can be derived by first dividing a quadratic equation by $2a$, resulting in $\tfrac12 x^2 + \tfrac{b}{2a}x + \tfrac{c}{2a} = 0$, then substituting the new coefficients into the standard quadratic formula. Because this variant allows re-use of the intermediately calculated quantity $\tfrac{b}{2a}$, it can slightly reduce the arithmetic involved.

##### Square root in the denominator

A lesser known quadratic formula, first mentioned by [Giulio Fagnano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giulio_Carlo_de'_Toschi_di_Fagnano),[^407] describes the same roots via an equation with the square root in the denominator (assuming $c \neq 0$):

$$
x= \frac{2c}{-b \mp \sqrt {b^2 - 4ac} }.
$$

Here the [minus-plus symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minus%E2%80%93plus_symbol) "$\mp$" indicates that the two roots of the quadratic equation, in the same order as the standard quadratic formula, are

$$
x_1 = \frac{2c}{-b - \sqrt {b^2 - 4ac} }, \qquad x_2 = \frac{2c}{-b + \sqrt {b^2 - 4ac} }.
$$

This variant has been jokingly called the "citardauq" formula ("quadratic" spelled backwards).[^408]

When $-b$ has the opposite sign as either $+\sqrt {b^2 - 4ac}$ or $-\sqrt {b^2 - 4ac}$, subtraction can cause [catastrophic cancellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catastrophic_cancellation), resulting in poor accuracy in numerical calculations; choosing between the version of the quadratic formula with the square root in the numerator or denominator depending on the sign of $b$ can avoid this problem. See [§ Numerical calculation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_formula) below.

This version of the quadratic formula is used in [Muller's method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muller's_method) for finding the roots of general functions. It can be derived from the standard formula from the identity $x_1 x_2 = c/a$, one of [Vieta's formulas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vieta's_formulas). Alternately, it can be derived by dividing each side of the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ by $x^2$ to get $cx^{-2} + bx^{-1} + a = 0$, applying the standard formula to find the two roots $x^{-1}\!$, and then taking the reciprocal to find the roots $x$ of the original equation.

#### Other derivations

Any generic method or algorithm for solving quadratic equations can be applied to an equation with symbolic coefficients and used to derive some closed-form expression equivalent to the quadratic formula. Alternative methods are sometimes simpler than completing the square, and may offer interesting insight into other areas of mathematics.

##### Completing the square by Śrīdhara's method

Instead of dividing by $a$ to isolate $x^2\!$, it can be slightly simpler to multiply by $4a$ instead to produce $(2ax)^2\!$, which allows us to complete the square without need for fractions. Then the steps of the derivation are:[^409]

1.  Multiply each side by $4a$.
2.  Add $b^2 - 4ac$ to both sides to complete the square.
3.  Take the square root of both sides.
4.  Isolate $x$.

Applying this method to a generic quadratic equation with symbolic coefficients yields the quadratic formula:

$$
\begin{aligned} ax^2 + bx + c &= 0 \\[3mu] 4 a^2 x^2 + 4abx + 4ac &= 0 \\[3mu] 4 a^2 x^2 + 4abx + b^2 &= b^2 - 4ac \\[3mu] (2ax + b)^2 &= b^2 - 4ac \\[3mu] 2ax + b &= \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} \\[5mu] x &= \dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac } }{2a}. \vphantom\bigg) \end{aligned}
$$

This method for completing the square is ancient and was known to the 8th-9th century Indian mathematician [Śrīdhara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%9Ar%C4%ABdhara).[^410] Compared with the modern standard method for completing the square, this alternate method avoids fractions until the last step and hence does not require a rearrangement after step 3 to obtain a common denominator in the right side.[^409]

##### By substitution

Another derivation uses a [change of variables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Change_of_variables) to eliminate the linear term. Then the equation takes the form $u^2 = s$ in terms of a new variable $u$ and some constant expression $s$, whose roots are then $u = \pm \sqrt s$.

By substituting $x = u - \tfrac{b}{2a}$ into $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$, expanding the products and combining [like terms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Like_terms), and then solving for $u^2\!$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned} a\left(u-\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 + b\left(u-\frac{b}{2a}\right) + c &=0 \\[5mu] a\left(u^2-\frac{b}{a}u+\frac{b^2}{4a^2}\right) + b\left(u-\frac{b}{2a}\right) + c &= 0 \\[5mu] au^2 - bu + \frac{b^2}{4a} + bu - \frac{b^2}{2a}+c &= 0 \\[5mu] au^2 + \frac{4ac - b^2}{4a} &= 0 \\[5mu] u^2 &= \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{4a^2}. \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, after taking a square root of both sides and substituting the resulting expression for $u$ back into $x = u - \tfrac{b}{2a},$ the familiar quadratic formula emerges:

$$
x = \frac{-b\pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} }{2a}.
$$

##### By using algebraic identities

The following method was used by many historical mathematicians:[^411]

Let the roots of the quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ be $\alpha$ and $\beta$. The derivation starts from an identity for the square of a difference (valid for any two complex numbers), of which we can take the square root on both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned} (\alpha - \beta)^2 &= (\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4 \alpha\beta \\[3mu] \alpha - \beta &= \pm\sqrt{(\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4 \alpha\beta} . \end{aligned}
$$

Since the coefficient $a \neq 0$, we can divide the quadratic equation by $a$ to obtain a [monic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monic_polynomial) polynomial with the same roots. Namely,

$$
x^2 + \frac{b}{a}x + \frac{c}{a} = (x - \alpha)(x - \beta) = x^2 - (\alpha + \beta)x + \alpha\beta .
$$

This implies that the sum $\alpha + \beta = -\tfrac ba$ and the product $\alpha\beta = \tfrac ca$. Thus the identity can be rewritten:

$$
\alpha - \beta = \pm\sqrt{\left(-\frac{b}{a}\right)^2-4\frac{c}{a} } = \pm\frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} }{a} .
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned} \alpha &= \tfrac12(\alpha + \beta) + \tfrac12(\alpha - \beta) = -\frac{b}{2a} \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} }{2a}, \\[10mu] \beta &= \tfrac12(\alpha + \beta) - \tfrac12(\alpha - \beta) = -\frac{b}{2a} \mp \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} }{2a}. \end{aligned}
$$

The two possibilities for each of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the same two roots in opposite order, so we can combine them into the standard quadratic equation:

$$
x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} }{2a} .
$$

##### By Lagrange resolvents

An alternative way of deriving the quadratic formula is via the method of [Lagrange resolvents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagrange_resolvents),[^412] which is an early part of [Galois theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_theory).[^413] This method can be generalized to give the roots of [cubic polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_polynomial) and [quartic polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartic_polynomial), and leads to Galois theory, which allows one to understand the solution of algebraic equations of any degree in terms of the [symmetry group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetry_group) of their roots, the [Galois group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galois_group).

This approach focuses on the roots themselves rather than algebraically rearranging the original equation. Given a monic quadratic polynomial $x^2 + px + q$ assume that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the two roots. So the polynomial factors as

$$
\begin{aligned} x^2+px+q &= (x-\alpha)(x-\beta) \\[3mu] &= x^2-(\alpha+\beta)x+\alpha\beta \end{aligned}
$$

which implies $p = -(\alpha + \beta)$ and $q = \alpha\beta$.

Since multiplication and addition are both [commutative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutative_property), exchanging the roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$ will not change the coefficients $p$ and $q$: one can say that $p$ and $q$ are [symmetric polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_polynomials) in $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Specifically, they are the [elementary symmetric polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_symmetric_polynomials) - any symmetric polynomial in $\alpha$ and $\beta$ can be expressed in terms of $\alpha + \beta$ and $\alpha\beta$ instead.

The Galois theory approach to analyzing and solving polynomials is to ask whether, given coefficients of a polynomial each of which is a symmetric function in the roots, one can "break" the symmetry and thereby recover the roots. Using this approach, solving a polynomial of degree $n$ is related to the ways of rearranging ("[permuting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation)") $n$ terms, called the [symmetric group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symmetric_group) on $n$ letters and denoted $S_n$. For the quadratic polynomial, the only ways to rearrange two roots are to either leave them be or to [transpose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transposition_%28mathematics%29) them, so solving a quadratic polynomial is simple.

To find the roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$, consider their sum and difference:

$$
r_1 = \alpha + \beta, \quad r_2 = \alpha - \beta .
$$

These are called the *Lagrange resolvents* of the polynomial, from which the roots can be recovered as

$$
\alpha = \tfrac12 (r_1 + r_2), \quad \beta = \tfrac12(r_1 - r_2).
$$

Because $r_1 = \alpha + \beta$ is a symmetric function in $\alpha$ and $\beta$, it can be expressed in terms of $p$ and $q,$ specifically $r_1 = -p$ as described above. However, $r_2 = \alpha - \beta$ is not symmetric, since exchanging $\alpha$ and $\beta$ yields the [additive inverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Additive_inverse) $-r_2 = \beta - \alpha$. So $r_2$ cannot be expressed in terms of the symmetric polynomials. However, its square $r_2^2 = (\alpha - \beta)^2$ *is* symmetric in the roots, expressible in terms of $p$ and $q$. Specifically $r_2^2 = (\alpha - \beta)^2 = {}$$(\alpha + \beta)^2 - 4\alpha\beta = {}$$p^2 - 4q$, which implies $r_2 = \pm \sqrt{p^2 - 4q}$. Taking the positive root "breaks" the symmetry, resulting in

$$
r_1 = -p, \qquad r_2 = {\sqrt{p^2 - 4q} }
$$

from which the roots $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are recovered as

$$
x = \tfrac12(r_1 \pm r_2) = \tfrac{1}{2} \bigl({-p} \pm {\sqrt{p^2 - 4q} }\,\bigr)
$$

which is the quadratic formula for a monic polynomial.

Substituting $p = b/a$, $q = c/a$ yields the usual expression for an arbitrary quadratic polynomial. The resolvents can be recognized as

$$
\tfrac12 r_1 = -\tfrac12p = -\frac{b}{2a}, \qquad r_2^2 = p_2 - 4q = \frac{b^2 - 4ac}{a^2},
$$

respectively the vertex and the discriminant of the monic polynomial.

A similar but more complicated method works for [cubic equations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_equation), which have three resolvents and a quadratic equation (the "resolving polynomial") relating $r_2$ and $r_3$, which one can solve by the quadratic equation, and similarly for a [quartic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartic_equation) ([degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_of_a_polynomial) 4), whose resolving polynomial is a cubic, which can in turn be solved.[^412] The same method for a [quintic equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintic_equation) yields a polynomial of degree 24, which does not simplify the problem, and, in fact, solutions to quintic equations in general cannot be expressed using only roots.

#### Numerical calculation

The quadratic formula is exactly correct when performed using the idealized arithmetic of [real numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_number), but when approximate arithmetic is used instead, for example pen-and-paper arithmetic carried out to a fixed number of decimal places or the [floating-point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic) binary arithmetic available on computers, the limitations of the number representation can lead to substantially inaccurate results unless great care is taken in the implementation. Specific difficulties include [catastrophic cancellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catastrophic_cancellation) in computing the sum $-b \pm \sqrt\Delta$ if $b \approx \pm \sqrt\Delta$; catastrophic calculation in computing the discriminant $\Delta = b^2 - 4ac$ itself in cases where $b^2 \approx 4ac$; degeneration of the formula when $a$, $b$, or $c$ is represented as zero or infinite; and possible [overflow or underflow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_arithmetic) when multiplying or dividing extremely large or small numbers, even in cases where the roots can be accurately represented.[^414][^415]

Catastrophic cancellation occurs when two numbers which are approximately equal are subtracted. While each of the numbers may independently be representable to a certain number of digits of precision, the identical leading digits of each number cancel, resulting in a difference of lower relative precision. When $b \approx \sqrt \Delta$, evaluation of $-b + \sqrt \Delta$ causes catastrophic cancellation, as does the evaluation of $-b - \sqrt \Delta$ when $b \approx -\sqrt\Delta$. When using the standard quadratic formula, calculating one of the two roots always involves addition, which preserves the working precision of the intermediate calculations, while calculating the other root involves subtraction, which compromises it. Therefore, naïvely following the standard quadratic formula often yields one result with less relative precision than expected. Unfortunately, introductory algebra textbooks typically do not address this problem, even though it causes students to obtain inaccurate results in other school subjects such as introductory chemistry.[^416]

For example, if trying to solve the equation $x^2 - 1634x + 2 = 0$ using a pocket calculator, the result of the quadratic formula $x = 817 \pm \sqrt{667\,487}$ might be approximately calculated as:[^417]

$$
\begin{aligned} x_1 &= 817 + 816.998\,776\,0 &&= 1.633\,998\,776 \times 10^3, \\ x_2 &= 817 - 816.998\,776\,0 &&= 1.224 \times 10^{-3}. \end{aligned}
$$

Even though the calculator used ten decimal digits of precision for each step, calculating the difference between two approximately equal numbers has yielded a result for $x_2$ with only four correct digits.

One way to recover an accurate result is to use the identity $x_1 x_2 = c/a$. In this example $x_2$ can be calculated as $x_2 = 2 / x_1 = {}$$1.223\,991\,125 \times 10^{-3}\!$, which is correct to the full ten digits. Another more or less equivalent approach is to use the version of the quadratic formula with the square root in the denominator to calculate one of the roots (see [§ Square root in the denominator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_formula) above).

Practical computer implementations of the solution of quadratic equations commonly choose which formula to use for each root depending on the sign of $b$.[^418]

These methods do not prevent possible overflow or underflow of the floating-point exponent in computing $b^2$ or $4ac$, which can lead to numerically representable roots not being computed accurately. A more robust but computationally expensive strategy is to start with the substitution $x = -u \sgn(b)\sqrt{\vert c\vert} \big/\! \sqrt{\vert a\vert}$, turning the quadratic equation into

$$
u^2 - 2 \frac{|b|}{2\sqrt{|a|}\sqrt{|c|} }u + \sgn(c) = 0,
$$

where $\sgn$ is the [sign function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sign_function). Letting $d = \vert b\vert\big/2\sqrt{\vert a\vert}\sqrt{\vert c\vert}$, this equation has the form $u^2 - 2du \pm 1 = 0$, for which one solution is $u_1 = d + \sqrt{d^2 \mp 1}$ and the other solution is $u_2 = \pm1 / u_1$. The roots of the original equation are then $x_1 = -\sgn(b)\bigl(\sqrt{\vert c\vert} \big/\!\sqrt{\vert a\vert}~\!\bigr) u_1$ and $x_2 = -\sgn(b)\bigl(\sqrt{\vert c\vert} \big/\!\sqrt{\vert a\vert}~\!\bigr) u_2$.[^419][^420]

With additional complication the expense and extra rounding of the square roots can be avoided by approximating them as [powers of two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_of_two), while still avoiding exponent overflow for representable roots.[^415]

#### Historical development

The earliest methods for solving quadratic equations were geometric. Babylonian cuneiform tablets contain problems reducible to solving quadratic equations.[^421] The Egyptian [Berlin Papyrus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Papyrus_6619), dating back to the [Middle Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Kingdom_of_Egypt) (2050 BC to 1650 BC), contains the solution to a two-term quadratic equation.[^422]

The Greek mathematician [Euclid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid) (circa 300 BC) used geometric methods to solve quadratic equations in Book 2 of his *[Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's_Elements)*, an influential mathematical treatise[^423] Rules for quadratic equations appear in the Chinese *[The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nine_Chapters_on_the_Mathematical_Art)* circa 200 BC.[^424][^425] In his work *[Arithmetica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetica)*, the Greek mathematician [Diophantus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diophantus) (circa 250 AD) solved quadratic equations with a method more recognizably algebraic than the [geometric algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_algebra) of Euclid.[^423] His solution gives only one root, even when both roots are positive.[^426]

The [Indian mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_mathematics) [Brahmagupta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahmagupta) included a generic method for finding one root of a quadratic equation in his treatise *[Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Br%C4%81hmasphu%E1%B9%ADasiddh%C4%81nta)* (circa 628 AD), written out in words in the style of that time.[^427][^428] His solution of the quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx = c$ was as follows: "To the absolute number multiplied by four times the \[coefficient of the\] square, add the square of the \[coefficient of the\] middle term; the square root of the same, less the \[coefficient of the\] middle term, being divided by twice the \[coefficient of the\] square is the value."[^429] In modern notation, this can be written $x = \bigl(\sqrt{c \cdot 4a + b^2} - b\bigr) \big/ 2a$. The Indian mathematician [Śrīdhara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%9Ar%C4%ABdhara) (8th-9th century) came up with a similar algorithm for solving quadratic equations in a now-lost work on algebra quoted by [Bhāskara II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bh%C4%81skara_II).[^430] The modern quadratic formula is sometimes called *Sridharacharya's formula* in India and *Bhaskara's formula* in Brazil.[^431]

The 9th-century Persian mathematician [Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mu%E1%B8%A5ammad_ibn_M%C5%ABs%C4%81_al-Khw%C4%81rizm%C4%AB) solved quadratic equations algebraically.[^432] The quadratic formula covering all cases was first obtained by [Simon Stevin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Stevin) in 1594.[^433] In 1637 [René Descartes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Descartes) published *[La Géométrie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_G%C3%A9om%C3%A9trie)* containing special cases of the quadratic formula in the form we know today.[^434]

#### Geometric significance

In terms of coordinate geometry, an axis-aligned parabola is a curve whose $(x, y)$-coordinates are the [graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graph_of_a_function) of a second-degree polynomial, of the form $y = ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are real-valued constant coefficients with $a \neq 0$.

Geometrically, the quadratic formula defines the points $(x, 0)$ on the graph, where the parabola crosses the $x$-axis. Furthermore, it can be separated into two terms,

$$
x = \frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac } }{2a} = -\frac{b}{2a} \pm \frac{\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac} }{2a}.
$$

The first term describes the [axis of symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_of_symmetry), the line $x = -\tfrac{b}{2a}$. The second term, $\sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}\big/ 2a$, gives the distance the roots are away from the axis of symmetry.

If the parabola's vertex is on the $x$-axis, then the corresponding equation has a single repeated root on the line of symmetry, and this distance term is zero; algebraically, the discriminant $b^2 - 4ac = 0$.

If the discriminant is positive, then the vertex is not on the $x$-axis but the parabola opens in the direction of the $x$-axis, crossing it twice, so the corresponding equation has two real roots. If the discriminant is negative, then the parabola opens in the opposite direction, never crossing the $x$-axis, and the equation has no real roots; in this case the two complex-valued roots will be [complex conjugates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_conjugate) whose real part is the $x$ value of the axis of symmetry.

#### Dimensional analysis

If the constants $a$, $b$, and/or $c$ are not [unitless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitless) then the quantities $x$ and $\tfrac ba$ must have the same units, because the terms $ax^2$ and $bx$ agree on their units. By the same logic, the coefficient $c$ must have the same units as $\tfrac{b^2}{a}$, irrespective of the units of $x$. This can be a powerful tool for verifying that a quadratic expression of [physical quantities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_quantities) has been set up correctly.

### Lists of integrals

[Integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral) is the basic operation in [integral calculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_calculus). While [differentiation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derivative) has straightforward [rules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiation_rules) by which the derivative of a complicated [function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Function_%28mathematics%29) can be found by differentiating its simpler component functions, integration does not, so tables of known integrals are often useful. This page lists some of the most common [antiderivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiderivative).

#### Historical development of integrals

A compilation of a list of integrals (Integraltafeln) and techniques of integral calculus was published by the German mathematician Meier Hirsch (also spelled Meyer Hirsch) in 1810.[^435] These tables were republished in the United Kingdom in 1823. More extensive tables were compiled in 1858 by the Dutch mathematician [David Bierens de Haan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bierens_de_Haan) for his *[Tables d'intégrales définies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tables_d'int%C3%A9grales_d%C3%A9finies)*, supplemented by *[Supplément aux tables d'intégrales définies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suppl%C3%A9ment_aux_tables_d'int%C3%A9grales_d%C3%A9finies)* in ca. 1864. A new edition was published in 1867 under the title *[Nouvelles tables d'intégrales définies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nouvelles_tables_d'int%C3%A9grales_d%C3%A9finies)*.

These tables, which contain mainly integrals of elementary functions, remained in use until the middle of the 20th century. They were then replaced by the much more extensive tables of [Gradshteyn and Ryzhik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradshteyn_and_Ryzhik). In Gradshteyn and Ryzhik, integrals originating from the book by Bierens de Haan are denoted by BI.

Not all [closed-form expressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed-form_expression) have closed-form antiderivatives; this study forms the subject of [differential Galois theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_Galois_theory), which was initially developed by [Joseph Liouville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Liouville) in the 1830s and 1840s, leading to [Liouville's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liouville's_theorem_%28differential_algebra%29) which classifies which expressions have closed-form antiderivatives. A simple example of a function without a closed-form antiderivative is *e*^(−x2), whose antiderivative is (up to constants) the [error function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_function).

Since 1968 there is the [Risch algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risch_algorithm) for determining indefinite integrals that can be expressed in term of [elementary functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_function), typically using a [computer algebra system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_algebra_system). Integrals that cannot be expressed using elementary functions can be manipulated symbolically using general functions such as the [Meijer G-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meijer_G-function).

#### Lists of integrals

More detail may be found on the following pages for the **lists of integrals**:

- [List of integrals of rational functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_integrals_of_rational_functions)
- [List of integrals of irrational algebraic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_integrals_of_irrational_algebraic_functions)
- [List of integrals of trigonometric functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_integrals_of_trigonometric_functions)
- [List of integrals of inverse trigonometric functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_integrals_of_inverse_trigonometric_functions)
- [List of integrals of hyperbolic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_integrals_of_hyperbolic_functions)
- [List of integrals of inverse hyperbolic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_integrals_of_inverse_hyperbolic_functions)
- [List of integrals of exponential functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_integrals_of_exponential_functions)
- [List of integrals of logarithmic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_integrals_of_logarithmic_functions)
- [List of integrals of Gaussian functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_integrals_of_Gaussian_functions)

[Gradshteyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izrail_Solomonovich_Gradshteyn), [Ryzhik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iosif_Moiseevich_Ryzhik), [Geronimus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Veniaminovich_Geronimus), [Tseytlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michail_Yulyevich_Tseytlin), Jeffrey, Zwillinger, and [Moll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Hugo_Moll)'s (GR) *[Table of Integrals, Series, and Products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_of_Integrals,_Series,_and_Products)* contains a large collection of results. An even larger, multivolume table is the *Integrals and Series* by [Prudnikov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatoli_Prudnikov), [Brychkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuri_Aleksandrovich_Brychkov), and [Marichev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleg_Igorevich_Marichev) (with volumes 1-3 listing integrals and series of [elementary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_function) and [special functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_functions), volume 4-5 are tables of [Laplace transforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_transform)). More compact collections can be found in e.g. Brychkov, Marichev, Prudnikov's *Tables of Indefinite Integrals*, or as chapters in Zwillinger's *CRC Standard Mathematical Tables and Formulae* or [Bronshtein and Semendyayev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronshtein_and_Semendyayev)'s *[Guide Book to Mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Guide_Book_to_Mathematics)*, *[Handbook of Mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handbook_of_Mathematics)* or *[Users' Guide to Mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Users'_Guide_to_Mathematics)*, and other mathematical handbooks.

Other useful resources include [Abramowitz and Stegun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abramowitz_and_Stegun) and the [Bateman Manuscript Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bateman_Manuscript_Project). Both works contain many identities concerning specific integrals, which are organized with the most relevant topic instead of being collected into a separate table. Two volumes of the Bateman Manuscript are specific to integral transforms.

There are several web sites which have tables of integrals and integrals on demand. [Wolfram Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfram_Alpha) can show results, and for some simpler expressions, also the intermediate steps of the integration. [Wolfram Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfram_Research) also operates another online service, the Mathematica Online Integrator.

#### Integrals of simple functions

*C* is used for an [arbitrary constant of integration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbitrary_constant_of_integration) that can only be determined if something about the value of the integral at some point is known. Thus, each function has an infinite number of [antiderivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiderivative).

These formulas only state in another form the assertions in the [table of derivatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Table_of_derivatives).

##### Integrals with a singularity

When there is a [singularity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singularity_%28mathematics%29) in the function being integrated such that the antiderivative becomes undefined at some point (the singularity), then *C* does not need to be the same on both sides of the singularity. The forms below normally assume the [Cauchy principal value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy_principal_value) around a singularity in the value of *C*, but this is not necessary in general. For instance, in

$$
\int {1 \over x}\,dx = \ln \left|x \right| + C
$$

there is a singularity at 0 and the [antiderivative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiderivative) becomes infinite there. If the integral above were to be used to compute a definite integral between −1 and 1, one would get the wrong answer 0. This however is the Cauchy principal value of the integral around the singularity. If the integration is done in the complex plane the result depends on the path around the origin, in this case the singularity contributes −*i*π when using a path above the origin and *i*π for a path below the origin. A function on the real line could use a completely different value of *C* on either side of the origin as in:[^436]

$$
\int {1 \over x}\,dx = \ln|x| + \begin{cases} A & \text{if }x>0; \\ B & \text{if }x < 0. \end{cases}
$$

##### Rational functions

- $\int a\,dx = ax + C$

The following function has a non-integrable singularity at 0 for *n* ≤ −1:

- $\int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1} }{n+1} + C \qquad\text{(for } n\neq -1\text{)}$ ([Cavalieri's quadrature formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalieri's_quadrature_formula))
- $\int (ax + b)^n \, dx= \frac{(ax + b)^{n+1} }{a(n + 1)} + C \qquad\text{(for } n\neq -1\text{)}$
- $\int {1 \over x}\,dx = \ln \left|x \right| + C$
  - More generally,[^437]$\int {1 \over x}\,dx = \begin{cases} \ln \left|x \right| + C^- & x < 0\\ \ln \left|x \right| + C^+ & x > 0 \end{cases}$
- $\int\frac{c}{ax + b} \, dx= \frac{c}{a}\ln\left|ax + b\right| + C$

##### Exponential functions

- $\int e^{ax}\,dx = \frac{1}{a}e^{ax} + C$
- $\int f'(x)e^{f(x)}\,dx = e^{f(x)} + C$
- $\int a^x\,dx = \frac{a^x}{\ln a} + C$
- $\int{e^{x}\left( f\left( x \right) + f'\left( x \right) \right)\,dx} = e^{x}f\left( x \right) + C$
- $\int {e^{x}\left( f\left( x \right) - \left( - 1 \right)^{n}\frac{d^{n}f\left( x \right)}{dx^{n} } \right)\,dx} = e^{x}\sum_{k = 1}^{n}{\left( - 1 \right)^{k - 1}\frac{d^{k - 1}f\left( x \right)}{dx^{k - 1} } } + C$(if $n$ is a positive integer)
- $\int {e^{- x}\left( f\left( x \right) - \frac{d^{n}f\left( x \right)}{dx^{n} } \right)\, dx} = - e^{- x}\sum_{k = 1}^{n}\frac{d^{k - 1}f\left( x \right)}{dx^{k - 1} } + C$(if $n$ is a positive integer)

##### Logarithms

- $\int \ln x\,dx = x \ln x - x + C = x (\ln x - 1) + C$
- $\int \log_a x\,dx = x\log_a x - \frac{x}{\ln a} + C = \frac{x}{\ln a} (\ln x - 1) + C$

##### Trigonometric functions

- $\int \sin x \, dx = -\cos x + C$
- $\int \cos x\, dx = \sin x + C$
- $\int \tan x \, dx = \ln\left| \sec x \right| + C = -\ln\left| \cos x \right| + C$
- $\int \cot x \, dx = -\ln\left| \csc x \right| + C = \ln\left| \sin x \right| + C$
- $\int \sec x \, dx = \ln\left| \sec x + \tan x\right| + C = \ln\left| \tan\left(\dfrac{x}{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \right| + C$
  - (See [Integral of the secant function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_of_the_secant_function). This result was a well-known conjecture in the 17th century.)
- $\int \csc x \, dx = -\ln\left| \csc x + \cot x\right| + C = \ln\left| \csc x - \cot x\right| + C = \ln\left| \tan \frac{x}{2} \right| + C$
- $\int \sec^2 x \, dx = \tan x + C$
- $\int \csc^2 x \, dx = -\cot x + C$
- $\int \sec x \, \tan x \, dx = \sec x + C$
- $\int \csc x \, \cot x \, dx = -\csc x + C$
- $\int \sin^2 x \, dx = \frac{1}{2}\left(x - \frac{\sin 2x}{2} \right) + C = \frac{1}{2}(x - \sin x\cos x ) + C$
- $\int \cos^2 x \, dx = \frac{1}{2}\left(x + \frac{\sin 2x}{2} \right) + C = \frac{1}{2}(x + \sin x\cos x ) + C$
- $\int \tan^2 x \, dx = \tan x - x + C$
- $\int \cot^2 x \, dx = -\cot x - x + C$
- $\int \sec^3 x \, dx = \frac{1}{2}(\sec x \tan x + \ln\left|\sec x + \tan x\right|) + C$
  - (See [integral of secant cubed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integral_of_secant_cubed).)
- $\int \csc^3 x \, dx = \frac{1}{2}(-\csc x \cot x + \ln\left|\csc x - \cot x\right|) + C = \frac{1}{2}\left(\ln\left|\tan\frac{x}{2}\right| - \csc x \cot x \right) + C$
- $\int \sin^n x \, dx = - \frac{\sin^{n-1} x \cos x}{n} + \frac{n-1}{n} \int \sin^{n-2} x \, dx$
- $\int \cos^n x \, dx = \frac{\cos^{n-1} x \sin x}{n} + \frac{n-1}{n} \int \cos^{n-2}{x} \, dx$

##### Inverse trigonometric functions

- $\int \arcsin{x} \, dx = x \arcsin{x} + \sqrt{1 - x^2} + C , \text{ for } \vert x \vert \le 1$
- $\int \arccos{x} \, dx = x \arccos{x} - \sqrt{1 - x^2} + C , \text{ for } \vert x \vert \le 1$
- $\int \arctan{x} \, dx = x \arctan{x} - \frac{1}{2} \ln { \vert 1 + x^2 \vert } + C , \text{ for all real } x$
- $\int \arccot{x} \, dx = x \arccot{x} + \frac{1}{2} \ln { \vert 1 + x^2 \vert } + C , \text{ for all real } x$
- $\int \arcsec{x} \, dx = x \arcsec{x} - \ln \left\vert x \, \left( 1 + \sqrt{ 1 - x^{-2} } \, \right) \right\vert + C , \text{ for } \vert x \vert \ge 1$
- $\int \arccsc{x} \, dx = x \arccsc{x} + \ln \left\vert x \, \left( 1 + \sqrt{ 1 - x^{-2} } \, \right) \right\vert + C , \text{ for } \vert x \vert \ge 1$

##### Hyperbolic functions

- $\int \sinh x \, dx = \cosh x + C$
- $\int \cosh x \, dx = \sinh x + C$
- $\int \tanh x \, dx = \ln(\cosh x) + C$
- $\int \coth x \, dx = \ln \left| \sinh x \right| + C , \text{ for } x \neq 0$
- $\int \operatorname{sech} x \, dx = \arctan(\sinh x) + C$
- $\int \operatorname{csch}\,x \, dx = \ln\left|\operatorname{coth} x - \operatorname{csch} x\right| + C = \ln\left| \tanh {x \over2}\right| + C , \text{ for } x \neq 0$
- $\int \operatorname{sech}^2 x \, dx = \tanh x + C$
- $\int \operatorname{csch}^2 x \, dx = -\operatorname{coth}x + C$
- $\int \operatorname{sech}x \, \operatorname{tanh}x \, dx = -\operatorname{sech}x + C$
- $\int \operatorname{csch}x \, \operatorname{coth}x \, dx = -\operatorname{csch}x + C$

##### Inverse hyperbolic functions

- $\int \operatorname{arcsinh} \, x \, dx = x \, \operatorname{arcsinh} \, x - \sqrt{ x^2 + 1 } + C , \text{ for all real } x$
- $\int \operatorname{arccosh} \, x \, dx = x \, \operatorname{arccosh} \, x - \sqrt{ x^2 - 1 } + C , \text{ for } x \ge 1$
- $\int \operatorname{arctanh} \, x \, dx = x \, \operatorname{arctanh} \, x + \frac{\ln\left(\,1-x^2\right)}{2} + C , \text{ for } \vert x \vert < 1$
- $\int \operatorname{arccoth} \, x \, dx = x \, \operatorname{arccoth} \, x + \frac{\ln\left(x^2-1\right)}{2} + C , \text{ for } \vert x \vert > 1$
- $\int \operatorname{arcsech} \, x \, dx = x \, \operatorname{arcsech} \, x + \arcsin x + C , \text{ for } 0 < x \le 1$
- $\int \operatorname{arccsch} \, x \, dx = x \, \operatorname{arccsch} \, x + \left| \operatorname{arcsinh} \, x \right| + C , \text{ for } x \neq 0$

##### Products of functions proportional to their second derivatives

- $\int \cos ax\, e^{bx}\, dx = \frac{e^{bx} }{a^2+b^2}\left( a\sin ax + b\cos ax \right) + C$
- $\int \sin ax\, e^{bx}\, dx = \frac{e^{bx} }{a^2+b^2}\left( b\sin ax - a\cos ax \right) + C$
- $\int \cos ax\, \cosh bx\, dx = \frac{1}{a^2+b^2}\left( a\sin ax\, \cosh bx+ b\cos ax\, \sinh bx \right) + C$
- $\int \sin ax\, \cosh bx\, dx = \frac{1}{a^2+b^2}\left( b\sin ax\, \sinh bx- a\cos ax\, \cosh bx \right) + C$

##### Absolute-value functions

Let *f* be a [continuous function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_function), that has at most one [zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_of_a_function). If *f* has a zero, let *g* be the unique antiderivative of *f* that is zero at the root of *f*; otherwise, let *g* be any antiderivative of *f*. Then

$$
\int \left| f(x)\right|\,dx = \sgn(f(x))g(x)+C,
$$

where sgn(*x*) is the [sign function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sign_function), which takes the values −1, 0, 1 when *x* is respectively negative, zero or positive.

This can be proved by computing the derivative of the right-hand side of the formula, taking into account that the condition on *g* is here for insuring the continuity of the integral.

This gives the following formulas (where *a* ≠ 0), which are valid over any interval where *f* is continuous (over larger intervals, the constant C must be replaced by a [piecewise constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piecewise_constant) function):

- $\int \left| (ax + b)^n \right|\,dx = \sgn(ax + b) {(ax + b)^{n+1} \over a(n+1)} + C$when *n* is odd, and $n \neq -1$.
- $\int \left| \tan{ax} \right|\,dx = -\frac{1}{a}\sgn(\tan{ax}) \ln(\left|\cos{ax}\right|) + C$when $ax \in \left( n\pi - \frac{\pi}{2}, n\pi + \frac{\pi}{2} \right)$ for some integer *n*.
- $\int \left| \csc{ax} \right|\,dx = -\frac{1}{a}\sgn(\csc{ax}) \ln(\left| \csc{ax} + \cot{ax} \right|) + C$when $ax \in \left( n\pi, n\pi + \pi \right)$ for some integer *n*.
- $\int \left| \sec{ax} \right|\,dx = \frac{1}{a}\sgn(\sec{ax}) \ln(\left| \sec{ax} + \tan{ax} \right|) + C$when $ax \in \left( n\pi - \frac{\pi}{2}, n\pi + \frac{\pi}{2} \right)$ for some integer *n*.
- $\int \left| \cot{ax} \right|\,dx = \frac{1}{a}\sgn(\cot{ax}) \ln(\left|\sin{ax}\right|) + C$when $ax \in \left( n\pi, n\pi + \pi \right)$ for some integer *n*.

If the function *f* does not have any continuous antiderivative which takes the value zero at the zeros of *f* (this is the case for the sine and the cosine functions), then sgn(*f(x*)) ∫ *f(x*) *dx* is an antiderivative of *f* on every [interval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_%28mathematics%29) on which *f* is not zero, but may be discontinuous at the points where *f(x*) = 0. For having a continuous antiderivative, one has thus to add a well chosen [step function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Step_function). If we also use the fact that the absolute values of sine and cosine are periodic with period π, then we get:

- $\int \left| \sin{ax} \right|\,dx = {2 \over a} \left\lfloor \frac{ax}{\pi} \right\rfloor - {1 \over a} \cos{\left( ax - \left\lfloor \frac{ax}{\pi} \right\rfloor \pi \right)} + C$
- $\int \left|\cos {ax}\right|\,dx = {2 \over a} \left\lfloor \frac{ax}{\pi} + \frac12 \right\rfloor + {1 \over a} \sin{\left( ax - \left\lfloor \frac{ax}{\pi} + \frac12 \right\rfloor \pi \right)} + C$

##### Special functions

Ci, Si: [Trigonometric integrals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_integral), Ei: [Exponential integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_integral), li: [Logarithmic integral function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logarithmic_integral_function), erf: [Error function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_function)

- $\int \operatorname{Ci}(x) \, dx = x \operatorname{Ci}(x) - \sin x$
- $\int \operatorname{Si}(x) \, dx = x \operatorname{Si}(x) + \cos x$
- $\int \operatorname{Ei}(x) \, dx = x \operatorname{Ei}(x) - e^x$
- $\int \operatorname{li}(x) \, dx = x \operatorname{li}(x)-\operatorname{Ei}(2 \ln x)$
- $\int \frac{\operatorname{li}(x)}{x}\,dx = \ln x\, \operatorname{li}(x) -x$
- $\int \operatorname{erf}(x)\, dx = \frac{e^{-x^2} }{\sqrt{\pi } }+x \operatorname{erf}(x)$

#### Definite integrals lacking closed-form antiderivatives

There are some functions whose antiderivatives *cannot* be expressed in [closed form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closed-form_expression). However, the values of the definite integrals of some of these functions over some common intervals can be calculated. A few useful integrals are given below.

- $\int_0^\infty \sqrt{x}\,e^{-x}\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt \pi$ (see also [Gamma function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function))
- $\int_0^\infty e^{-a x^2}\,dx = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt \frac {\pi} {a}$ for *a* \> 0 (the [Gaussian integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_integral))
- $\int_0^\infty{x^2 e^{-a x^2}\,dx} = \frac{1}{4} \sqrt \frac {\pi} {a^3}$ for *a* \> 0
- $\int_0^\infty x^{2n} e^{-a x^2}\,dx = \frac{2n-1}{2a} \int_0^\infty x^{2(n-1)} e^{-a x^2}\,dx = \frac{(2n-1)!!}{2^{n+1} } \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{a^{2n+1} } } = \frac{(2n)!}{n! 2^{2n+1} } \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{a^{2n+1} } }$for *a* \> 0, *n* is a positive integer and !! is the [double factorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_factorial).
- $\int_0^\infty{x^3 e^{-a x^2}\,dx} = \frac{1}{2 a^2}$ when *a* \> 0
- $\int_0^\infty x^{2n+1} e^{-a x^2}\,dx = \frac {n} {a} \int_0^\infty x^{2n-1} e^{-a x^2}\,dx = \frac{n!}{2 a^{n+1} }$for *a* \> 0, *n* = 0, 1, 2, ....
- $\int_0^\infty x^n e^{-ax^b} dx = \frac{1}{b}\ a^{-\frac{n+1}{b} }\Gamma\left(\frac{n+1}{b}\right)$
- $\int_0^\infty \frac{x}{e^x-1}\,dx = \frac{\pi^2}{6}$ (see also [Bernoulli number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli_number))
- $\int_0^\infty \frac{x^2}{e^x-1}\,dx = 2\zeta(3) \approx 2.40$
- $\int_0^\infty \frac{x^3}{e^x-1}\,dx = \frac{\pi^4}{15}$ (used in the derivation of [Planck's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planck's_law) in physics)
- $\int_0^\infty \frac{x^n}{e^x-1}\,dx = \Gamma(n+1) \zeta(n+1)$ for $n > 0$ (see also [Riemann zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function))
- $\int_0^\infty \frac{\sin{x} }{x}\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2}$ (see [sinc function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinc_function) and the [Dirichlet integral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_integral))
- $\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin^2{x} }{x^2}\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2}$
- $\int_{0}^\frac{\pi}{2}\sin^n x\,dx=\int_{0}^\frac{\pi}{2}\cos^n x\,dx=\frac{(n-1)!!}{n!!} \times \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } n \text{ is odd} \\ \frac{\pi}{2} & \text{if } n \text{ is even.} \end{cases}$(if *n* is a positive integer and !! is the [double factorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_factorial)).
- $\int_{-\pi}^\pi \cos(\alpha x)\cos^n(\beta x) dx = \begin{cases} \frac{2 \pi}{2^n} \binom{n}{m} & |\alpha|= |\beta (2m-n)| \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$(for *α*, *β*, *m*, *n* integers with *β* ≠ 0 and *m*, *n* ≥ 0, see also [Binomial coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_coefficient))
- $\int_{-t}^t \sin^m(\alpha x) \cos^n(\beta x) dx = 0$(for *α*, *β* real, *n* a non-negative integer, and m an odd, positive integer; since the integrand is [odd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odd_function))
- $\int_{-\pi}^\pi \sin(\alpha x) \sin^n(\beta x) dx = \begin{cases} (-1)^{\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)} (-1)^m \frac{2 \pi}{2^n} \binom{n}{m} & n \text{ odd},\ \alpha = \beta (2m-n) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$(for *α*, *β*, *m*, *n* integers with *β* ≠ 0 and *m*, *n* ≥ 0, see also [Binomial coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_coefficient))
- $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos(\alpha x) \sin^n(\beta x) dx = \begin{cases} (-1)^{\left(\frac{n}{2}\right)} (-1)^m \frac{2 \pi}{2^n} \binom{n}{m} & n \text{ even},\ |\alpha| = |\beta (2m-n)| \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$(for *α*, *β*, *m*, *n* integers with *β* ≠ 0 and *m*, *n* ≥ 0, see also [Binomial coefficient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binomial_coefficient))
- $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(ax^2+bx+c)}\,dx = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{a} }\exp\left[\frac{b^2-4ac}{4a}\right]$(where exp\[*u*\] is the [exponential function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_function) *e*^(u), and *a* \> 0.)
- $\int_0^\infty x^{z-1}\,e^{-x}\,dx = \Gamma(z)$(where $\Gamma(z)$ is the [Gamma function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_function))
- $\int_0^1 \left(\ln\frac{1}{x}\right)^p\,dx = \Gamma(p+1)$
- $\int_0^1 x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1} dx = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}$(for Re(*α*) \> 0 and Re(*β*) \> 0, see [Beta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_function))
- $\int_0^{2 \pi} e^{x \cos \theta} d \theta = 2 \pi I_{0}(x)$ (where *I*₀(*x*) is the modified [Bessel function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessel_function) of the first kind)
- $\int_0^{2 \pi} e^{x \cos \theta + y \sin \theta} d \theta = 2 \pi I_{0} \left(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\right)$
- $\int_{-\infty}^\infty \left(1 + \frac{x^2}{\nu}\right)^{-\frac{\nu + 1}{2} }\,dx = \frac { \sqrt{\nu \pi} \ \Gamma\left(\frac{\nu}{2}\right)} {\Gamma\left(\frac{\nu + 1}{2}\right)}$(for *ν* \> 0 , this is related to the [probability density function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_density_function) of [Student's *t*-distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student's_t-distribution))

If the function *f* has [bounded variation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bounded_variation) on the interval \[*a,b*\], then the [method of exhaustion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_of_exhaustion) provides a formula for the integral:

$$
\int_a^b{f(x)\,dx} = (b - a) \sum\limits_{n = 1}^\infty {\sum\limits_{m = 1}^{2^n - 1} {\left( { - 1} \right)^{m + 1} } } 2^{ - n} f(a + m\left( {b - a} \right)2^{-n} ).
$$

The "[sophomore's dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophomore's_dream)":

$$
\begin{aligned} \int_0^1 x^{-x}\,dx &= \sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-n} &&(= 1.29128\,59970\,6266\dots)\\[6pt] \int_0^1 x^x \,dx &= -\sum_{n=1}^\infty (-n)^{-n} &&(= 0.78343\,05107\,1213\dots) \end{aligned}
$$

attributed to [Johann Bernoulli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Bernoulli).

[^436]: Serge Lang . *A First Course in Calculus*, 5th edition, p. 290
