- Tres Tetas Mountain or *El Chichión* in [Costa Grande of Guerrero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Grande_of_Guerrero)

##### Nicaragua

- [Ometepe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ometepe), in [Lake Nicaragua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nicaragua). Legend says that the island's volcanoes [Maderas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maderas) and [Concepción](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concepci%C3%B3n_%28Volcano%29) formed from the breasts of Ometepetl, a daughter of the Niquirano tribe.[^613]

- Cerro La Teta in [Las Guabas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Guabas)

- [Cerro Las Tetas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Las_Tetas) in [Salinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salinas,_Puerto_Rico)[^614]
- Tetas de Cerro Gordo in [San German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Germ%C3%A1n,_Puerto_Rico)

##### United States

- Bubble Mountains, in [Acadia National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acadia_National_Park), [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine).[^615]
- [Isanaklesh Peaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isanaklesh_Peaks), in [Maricopa County, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maricopa_County,_Arizona), formerly known as Squaw Tits.
- [Nippletop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nippletop), in the [Adirondack High Peaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adirondack_High_Peaks) of [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_%28state%29). During the later 19th century, it was euphemistically renamed "[Dial Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dial_Mountain)", a name now officially applied to another nearby peak.
- [Pilot Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_Mountain_%28North_Carolina%29), North Carolina. Referenced many times on *[The Andy Griffith Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Andy_Griffith_Show)* as Mt. Pilot. Andy spoke about a wonderful place to travel called "Pilot" by the locals.
- [Pinnacle Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinnacle_Mountain_%28Arkansas%29), [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas), near [Maumelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maumelle,_Arkansas). During the colonial and early American periods, the mountain was known as "Mamelle" mountain. "Mamelle" is a name commonly applied in the French-speaking parts of the world to a breast.[^616]
- [Rock Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_Mary), [Caddo County, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caddo_County,_Oklahoma).
- [Spanish Peaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Peaks), [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado), named Huajatolla by the [Ute Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ute_Indians), meaning "two breasts".[^617]
- Tetilla Peak, [Caja del Rio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caja_del_Rio), [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico). *Tetilla* is Spanish for "nipple".
- [Tatoosh Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatoosh_Peak) and [Tatoosh Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatoosh_Range), near [Mount Rainier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rainier) in [Washington State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_%28state%29). From the [Chinook Jargon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinook_Jargon) word for "breast".[^618]
- [Teton Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teton_Range). French-Canadian trappers named the Teton Mountains around 1820. The distinctive peaks appeared as *Les Trois Tétons* (The Three Breasts) as seen from the north;[^619][^587]
  - [Grand Teton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Teton),
  - [Middle Teton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Teton),
  - [South Teton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Teton).
- [Twin Peaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_Peaks_%28San_Francisco,_California%29), in [San Francisco, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco,_California). When the [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_people) [conquistadors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conquistadors) and settlers arrived at the beginning of the 18th century, they called the area "Los Pechos de la Chola" or "Breasts of the Indian Maiden" and devoted the area to ranching.[^620] When San Francisco passed under American control during the 19th century, it was renamed "Twin Peaks".
- Maggie's Peaks, just west of [Lake Tahoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Tahoe), California.
- [Uncanoonuc Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncanoonuc_Mountains), [Goffstown, New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goffstown,_New_Hampshire). From a Native American word for a woman's breasts.[^621]
- [Mollie's Nipple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollie's_Nipple) or Molly's Nipple is the name given to as many as seven peaks and some other geological features in [Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah).[^622]
- [Tunas Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunas_Peak) located in [Pecos County, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pecos_County,_Texas), west of [Bakersfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakersfield,_Texas).[^623]
- Betsy Bell and Mary Gray, two adjacent hills in [Staunton, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staunton,_Virginia).
- Little and Big House Mountain, two adjacent mountains in [Lexington, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexington,_Virginia), resemble breasts if viewed from Kerr's Creek.

### Gaet'ale Pond

**Gaet'ale Pond** is a small [hypersaline lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypersaline_lake) located near the [Dallol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallol_%28volcano%29) crater in the [Danakil Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danakil_Depression) ([Afar Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afar_Region), [Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia)). It is located over a [hot spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_spring) of tectonic origin and has no apparent inlet or outlet streams. The water of Gaet'ale Pond has a [salinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salinity) of 43%, making it the [saltiest water body on Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_bodies_of_water_by_salinity).[^629]

#### Location and origin

Gaet'ale Pond is the largest of a series of small ponds located approximately 4 kilometres (2.5 mi) southeast of [Dallol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallol,_Ethiopia) springs. It is crescent-shaped with a diameter of about 60 metres (200 ft).

According to residents of the nearby village of Ahmed'ela, an [earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthquake) in January 2005 reactivated a thermal spring and the pond was created.[^630] For this reason, its temperature of 50-55 °C (122-131 °F) is hotter than the environment.[^631]

#### Composition of the water

The salts in the water of Gaet'ale Pond are mainly composed by [calcium chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium_chloride) at 2.72 mol/kg and [magnesium chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnesium_chloride) at 1.43 mol/kg. It also contains small amounts of [Na⁺](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium_ion), [K⁺](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_ion) and [NO⁻\
₂](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrite) ions. The [total amount of dissolved solids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_dissolved_solids) content is 433 g/kg, or 43.3%. It also contains traces of [iron(III)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferric_ions) that form a complex with [chloride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cl%E2%81%BB), giving the water a characteristic yellow color.[^629]

Bubbles of odorless gas are emitted from the lake surface. It is likely volcanically-produced [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide). Bird and insect corpses have been found around the pond, and it has been proposed that the gas may be harmful for small animals or humans.[^631]

### Firefighting in Antarctica

**Firefighting in Antarctica** encompasses various organizations and procedures designed to [fight fires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firefighting) on the continent of [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica). Firefighting in Antarctica is complicated by the harsh conditions of the continent, the remoteness of the locations to be serviced, and the importance of protecting life-supporting shelter from immolation.

#### Conditions and considerations

Although there are no wildfires in Antarctica, fire represents a serious threat to human activity. Antarctica is the windiest place on earth, so there are often winds sufficient to quickly fan any flames. Due to the low temperatures, liquid water is often hard to obtain in large quantity.[^632]

Because of the harsh conditions, shelter is a necessity of life and significant loss of shelter to fire could be disastrous to the survival of a base's residents, exacerbated by the remoteness of the bases from outside aid. Because of this, bases in Antarctica are often designed to mitigate the devastation of a fire by being made up of a number of separate buildings with a significant distance between them.[^632]

In addition, many Antarctic bases have emergency supplies stored near to the base, but far enough away that even a large fire will not immolate them. If the base burns, the supplies are intended to be sufficient for base personnel to survive until help can arrive.[^632]

#### Antarctic Fire Department

The Antarctic Fire Department is based at [McMurdo Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMurdo_Station). It is the only full-time professional fire department in Antarctica, and the largest and best equipped.[^633]

The department maintains two fire stations at McMurdo, Station 1 and Station 2. Station 1 is located in central McMurdo and operates in the urban center of the base and is the AFD's headquarters. Station 2 is located at McMurdo International Airport and serves the station's airfields, Phoenix Airfield, Williams Field and the Ice Runway.[^634] As of 2025, the Station 1 fleet consisted of two [fire engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_engine), a water tender, an ambulance, a rescue vehicle, and a SCAT (Self Contained Attack Truck) firefighting vehicle. The Station 2 fleet consisted of an ambulance and seven ARFF (Aircraft Rescue Fire Fighting) vehicles, which are fully tracked to handle the deeper snowcover that surrounds the runways. Station 2 apparatus is distributed and dispatched to different airfields depending on the current flight activity.[^635]

During the Antarctic summer (October-February), McMurdo's population is at its highest with between 1,200 and 1,400 people living there.[^636] During this time, as of 2025, the Antarctic Fire Department maintains a staff of about 55, split between Station 1, Station 2, and Station 3 at the South Pole (see below). In the winter (February-August), McMurdo's resident population declines about 200 or less and the Antarctic Fire Department staffing decreases to a much smaller complement.[^637]

As well as fires and fire alarms, the department handles medical calls, hazmat spills, odor investigations, assists, dive emergencies, and other tasks as needed (including herding seals and penguins off runways for incoming flights). Department dispatchers monitor all off-base foot travel, and all off-base vehicle movements during [extreme weather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_weather).[^633][^638]

#### Southernmost Fire Department

The Southernmost Fire Department serves the American [South Pole Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Pole_Station).[^639]

Firefighting at South Pole Station was long the responsibility of a volunteer fire brigade, staffed by station personnel, who receive one week of training. Because of the cold climate, dry chemicals rather than water are usually used to extinguish fires.[^639][^640]

In the twenty-first century, a professional contingent of a few firefighters of the Antarctic Fire Department, designated as Station 3, was added to the station for the summer months. Their equipment is a tractor that pulls two modules on sleds, each containing 500 pounds (230 kg) of dry chemical and 600 pounds (270 kg) of foam.[^639]

#### Other fire departments

Other research stations in Antarctica, such as [Vostok Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vostok_Station) (Russia), [Scott Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Base) (New Zealand), and [Terra Nova Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zucchelli_Station) (Italy) are protected by part-time fire brigades.[^633]

#### Fires in Antarctica

The first known fire in Antarctica was during the British [Southern Cross Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Cross_Expedition) of 1898-1900, when a candle set fire to a hut and nearly burned it down, which would have been disastrous to the expedition.[^632][^641]

The British [Hope Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Bay,_Antarctica) Station was completely destroyed by fire in 1948. Two of the three staff were killed, the lone survivor lived alone in a tent for sixteen days until rescued.[^632]

On August 3, 1960, a fire whipped by strong winds struck the Soviet [Mirny Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirny_Station), killing eight.[^642][^643] Another fire on June 21, 2020 there damaged several labs, but no one was injured.[^644]

On April 12, 1984, the Argentine leader of the [Almirante Brown Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almirante_Brown_Base) burned the entire base down on purpose to [avoid having to stay the winter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter-over_syndrome). There were no injuries and personnel were evacuated by a United States Navy ship.[^632]

The [Comandante Ferraz Antarctic Station fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comandante_Ferraz_Antarctic_Station_fire) at Brazil's [Comandante Ferraz Antarctic Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comandante_Ferraz_Antarctic_Station) on February 25, 2012, destroyed much of the station, and materials and equipment used for research. Two people were killed and another injured.[^645]

On October 5, 2008, a building at the Russian [Progress Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progress_Station) burned down, with one person being killed and two seriously injured, and radio contact with the outside world being lost for a few days.[^632][^646]

### Diomede Islands

The **Diomede Islands** (/ˌdaɪ.əˈmiːdiː/; [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language): острова́ Диоми́да, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Russian): *ostrova Diomida*), also known in Russia as **Gvozdev Islands** ([Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language): острова́ Гво́здева, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Russian): *ostrova Gvozdeva*), consist of two rocky, [mesa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesa)-like islands. One is the [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia) island of [Big Diomede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Diomede) (part of [Chukotka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chukotka_Autonomous_Okrug)). The other is the U.S. island of [Little Diomede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Diomede_Island) (part of [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska)). The Diomede Islands are located in the middle of the [Bering Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bering_Strait) between mainland Alaska and [Siberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberia). At their closest points, the two islands are approximately 2.4 miles (3.8 km) away from each other.[^647]

Because they are separated by the [International Date Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Date_Line), Big Diomede is almost a day ahead of Little Diomede; due to locally defined time zones, Big Diomede is 21 hours ahead of Little Diomede (20 in summer).[^648] Because of this, the islands are sometimes called **Tomorrow Island** (Big Diomede) and **Yesterday Island** (Little Diomede).[^647][^649]

#### Etymology

The islands are named for the Greek [Saint Diomedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Diomedes); Danish-born Russian navigator [Vitus Bering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitus_Bering) sighted the Diomede Islands on 16 August ([O.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_calendar), 27 August [N.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar)) 1728, the day on which the [Russian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Orthodox_Church) celebrates the memory of the saint.[^650]

#### Location

The islands are separated by an international border, which also defines the [International Date Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Date_Line) in that area, about 1.2 miles (2 km) from each island, at 168°58'37"W. The two islands are about 2.4 miles (3.8 km) apart at their closest points.[^647]

Big Diomede Island is the easternmost point of Russia.[^651]

The Diomede Islands are often mentioned as likely intermediate stops for the hypothetical bridge or tunnel ([Bering Strait crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bering_Strait_crossing)) spanning the [Bering Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bering_Strait).[^652]

An ice bridge usually spans the distance between the two islands in winter.[^653]

#### History

The islands were once mountaintops in the central portion of the land mass known as the [Bering land bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bering_land_bridge).[^654]

The first European to reach the Bering Strait was the Russian explorer [Semyon Dezhnev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semyon_Dezhnev) in 1648. He reported two islands whose natives had bone lip ornaments, but it is not certain that these were the Diomedes. Danish navigator Vitus Bering discovered the Diomede Islands while leading a Russian expedition on 16 August (O.S., 26 August N.S.) 1728, the day when the Russian Orthodox Church celebrates the memory of the martyr St. Diomede (hence, the name of the islands).[^650] In 1732, a Russian [geodesist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geodesy), [Mikhail Gvozdev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Gvozdev), determined the longitude and latitude of the two islands.[^655]

The text of the 1867 treaty between the United States and Russia, which finalized the [Alaska Purchase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska_Purchase), uses the islands to designate the boundary between the two nations: the border separates "equidistantly Krusenstern Island, or Ignaluk, from Ratmanov Island, or Nunarbuk, and heads northward infinitely until it disappears completely in the Arctic Ocean".

During the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War), that gap constituted the border between the United States and the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union), and became known as the "[Ice Curtain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bering_Strait)". In 1987, however, [Lynne Cox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynne_Cox) swam from one island to the other and was congratulated by both [Mikhail Gorbachev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Gorbachev) and [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan) for her feat.[^656]

In the summer of 1995, British television actor and documentary presenter [Michael Palin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Palin) started his counterclockwise circumnavigation of the [Pacific Rim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Rim), encompassing 18 countries, on [Little Diomede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Diomede) Island, as part of the BBC series *[Full Circle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_Circle_with_Michael_Palin)*.[^657] He intended to set foot on it again at the end of his eight-month trek but could not because of rough seas.

After establishing a military base there in 1948, the Soviet government relocated the indigenous population of Big Diomede Island to mainland Russia.[^658] The island is now inhabited only by military units.[^659] Little Diomede had an [Inupiat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inupiat_people) population of 170,[^660] which had declined to 115 at the [2010 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_Census), entirely in the village site of [Diomede, Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diomede,_Alaska) on the west side of the island, though the island as a whole comprises the city of Diomede. This village has a school, a post office, and a store. Some residents are famous for their [ivory carving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory_carving). When weather permits, commercial air contact is maintained with the island as part of the [US Essential Air Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essential_Air_Service).

### Kamuning Footbridge

The **Kamuning Footbridge**, officially the **Scout Borromeo-NIA South Road Footbridge** and also known as the **EDSA-Kamuning Footbridge**, was a [steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_bridge) pedestrian [footbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footbridge) spanning [EDSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EDSA) in [Quezon City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quezon_City), Philippines.

Constructed by the [Metropolitan Manila Development Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Manila_Development_Authority) (MMDA) in October 2018, the footbridge is 9 meters (30 ft) high, located near [Manuel L. Quezon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_L._Quezon_University), the [National Irrigation Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Irrigation_Administration) Complex, and the [GMA-Kamuning station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GMA%E2%80%93Kamuning_station). It connects Scout Borromeo Street in Barangay [South Triangle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Triangle) to NIA South Road in Barangay [Pinyahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyahan), spanning both [EDSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EDSA) and the [MRT-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MRT_Line_3_%28Metro_Manila%29)'s [at-grade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_%28road%29) tracks. Its steep height and appearance has gained public attention, with many online comments remarking that it is inconvenient to use and discriminates against [people with disabilities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disability), [senior citizens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_age), [children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child), and those who suffer from [vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo). As a result, it was mockingly nicknamed as "**Mount Kamuning**" and a "stairway to heaven" by both the public and local media, leading to mock "hiking" stunts and being the subject of online ridicule.[^661][^662]

The MMDA defended the design, stating it was necessary to discourage jaywalking and alleged robberies in the area, and "only intended for able-bodied pedestrians". Suggestions to rectify the issue by installing elevators or escalators were raised but not addressed due to budget constraints.[^663][^664]

The footbridge is planned to be demolished and rebuilt following a directive from President [Bongbong Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos) in June 2025 to have the [Department of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Transportation_%28Philippines%29) (DOTr) replace the footbridge with a design more accessible and convenient to road users and commuters.[^665] The new Kamuning footbridge and busway concourse were opened to the public on March 5, 2026, with the closure and demolition of the old footbridge being underway.[^666]

#### History

Construction on the footbridge began in 2018. While it was being constructed, photos of the half-built footbridge went viral online in November 2018, as people criticized the footbridge's steep height and appearance, raising concerns on how it would be inconvenient for people with disabilities, senior citizens, and [pregnant women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pregnancy). The footbridge has a maximum clearance height of 9 meters (30 ft) high and has a project cost of ₱10 million[^663] and was constructed by the BF Corporation owned by former [MMDA chairperson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairperson_of_the_Metropolitan_Manila_Development_Authority) [Bayani Fernando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayani_Fernando).[^664]

In response, MMDA general manager Jojo Garcia stated that the project was designed to prevent [jaywalking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaywalking) along EDSA and reduce incidents of [robbery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robbery) in the area. He defended the footbridge by describing it as intended for "able-bodied pedestrians seeking to cross the road quickly and safely" and claimed that the footbridge provides "maximum comfort for pedestrians".[^662]

Garcia also addressed concerns about the steep height of the structure, explaining that it is located at a portion where the MRT-3 run near [ground level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersection_%28road%29), necessitating a gap of stating that it is located at a segment where the MRT-3 is near ground level and that the footbridge must maintain a [clearance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clearance_%28civil_engineering%29) of 3 to 4 meters (9.8 to 13.1 ft) above the MRT-3 tracks.[^662] He added that the decision to construct the footbridge out of metal was because it was "easier to construct" and "cheaper".[^664][^663] MMDA spokesperson Celine Pialago further defended the project, calling it as the agency's "best compromise" to discourage "reckless or lazy" pedestrian behavior, emphasizing that the MMDA is prioritizing public safety over convenience.[^662]

Following the initial backlash, the MMDA added landing areas for pedestrians to rest while climbing the footbridge.[^667] The MMDA also considered installing elevators and escalators to address concerns about the footbridge's steepness. However, Garcia stated that there was no available budget for such features.[^664]

On [April Fools' Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_Fools'_Day) in 2019, two individuals dressed up as [mountain climbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering) with hiking gear and backpacks and gave a satirical account of the "hike" to the media. One of them also recounted that the footbridge vibrates whenever MRT-3 trains pass below it.[^661]

In January 2022, Dirk Janssen, the [consul general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consul_%28representative%29) of the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands) in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco) posted an old photo of the footbridge on [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter), criticizing it with the caption: "*No hay mejor manera de dejar claro a los peatones que no importan*" (transl. There is no better way to make it clear to pedestrians that they don’t matter.)[^668]

In January 2025, a hiking app satirically listed "Mount Kamuning" and "Mount Shaw Boulevard" as peaks, describing the former as the "urban [Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest) of EDSA" and a "high-altitude reminder of the uphill battle for a more [pedestrian-friendly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walkability) city".[^669]

In June 2025, following a visit to [GMA-Kamuning station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GMA%E2%80%93Kamuning_station), Philippine president [Bongbong Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos) ordered the [Department of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Transportation_%28Philippines%29) (DOTr) to demolish and replace the footbridge to be more accessible and convenient to road users and commuters. The DOTr has bared plans to build a much lower footbridge that will use elevators and provide direct access to the Kamuning stop of the [EDSA Carousel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EDSA_Carousel).[^665] The new footbridge was opened on March 5, 2026.[^666]

### Japan National Route 339

**National Route 339** (国道339号, *Kokudō Sanbyaku san-jukyūgō*) is a [national highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_highways_of_Japan) of [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan) that traverses the western side of [Aomori Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aomori_Prefecture), traveling south to north. The 108.4-kilometer (67.4 mi) highway begins as a concurrent route with [National Route 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_National_Route_7) in central [Hirosaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirosaki), it then leaves National Route 7 in [Fujisaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujisaki,_Aomori) and travels north through the municipalities of [Itayanagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itayanagi,_Aomori), [Tsuruta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsuruta,_Aomori), [Goshogawara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goshogawara), and [Nakadomari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakadomari) before ending at an intersection with [National Route 280](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_National_Route_280) in [Sotogahama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sotogahama). In a unique feature, a 0.4-kilometer-long (0.25 mi) section of the route on [Cape Tappi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Tappi) is a staircase.

#### Route description

National Route 339 begins as a concurrent route with [National Route 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_National_Route_7) in central [Hirosaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hirosaki), northeast of [Undōkōenmae Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Und%C5%8Dk%C5%8Denmae_Station_%28Aomori%29). Shortly after, the highway has an interchange with [National Routes 102](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_National_Route_102), [394](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_National_Route_394), and Aomori Route 109. After passing through the city and entering the town of [Fujisaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujisaki,_Aomori), it leaves National Route 7 and turns northwest, paralleling the downstream path of the [Iwaki River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwaki_River). In [Itayanagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itayanagi,_Aomori), the route curves to the north again, heading directly towards central [Goshogawara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goshogawara). After entering Goshogawara, the highway intersects [National Route 101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_National_Route_101). The two highways parallel one another in central Goshogawara before diverging, Route 101 turns west and Route 339 curves northeast. North of the central district of Goshogawara, the highway connects to the [Tsugaru Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsugaru_Expressway), a [limited-access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited-access) bypass of the city, at Goshogawara-kita Interchange.

Continuing north, the highway begins its journey across to the [Tsugaru Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsugaru_Peninsula) to [Cape Tappi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Tappi) at its northern tip. In the former town of [Kanagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanagi,_Aomori), the highway draws closer to the parallel [Tsugaru Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsugaru_Railway). They parallel one another, crossing out of Goshogawara, until they reach central [Nakadomari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakadomari), where the railway terminates while the highway continues north out of the town. Upon leaving Nakadomari the first time, the highway re-enters Goshogawara and curves northwest along the northern shore of [Lake Jūsan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_J%C5%ABsan). Eventually the route arrives at the [Sea of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_of_Japan) coast of the peninsula, it curves north here and eventually enters Nakadomari once again. As the highway approaches Cape Tappi, it winds its way across the western [Tsugaru Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsugaru_Mountains) into the former town of [Minmaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minmaya,_Aomori) (now part of [Sotogahama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sotogahama)); due to the sharp curves and rapid changes in elevation, this section of the highway is closed during the winter when weather conditions would make the feature impassable.[^670] At Cape Tappi, a 338.2-meter-long (1,110 ft) section of the highway is a staircase made up of 362 stairs, the only one of its kind among the national highways of Japan. This section of the highway is open only to pedestrian traffic and is subject to closure in the winter.[^671] After the staircase section ends, the highway continues southeast away from the cape along the coast of the [Tsugaru Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsugaru_Strait). The route terminates at an intersection with [National Route 280](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_National_Route_280), just short of Sotogahama's border with [Imabetsu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imabetsu).[^672]

#### History

The staircase at Cape Tappi was built as a joint effort between local people and the [Japan Self-Defense Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_Self-Defense_Forces). When the national government was looking for local roads to incorporate into the planned National Route 339, the stairs were left in place and designated as part of the proposed highway because a normal road would be too steep and narrow.[^673] National Route 339 was established by the [Cabinet of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_Japan) in 1975 along the stairway and other local roads between Hirosaki and then-extant Minamaya (now part of Sotogahama).[^674] On 18 July 2018, a 1.5-kilometer (0.93 mi) section of the highway was realigned just north of central Goshogawara as a measure to improve its level of safety and its access to the Tsugaru Expressway. This section is referred to as the Goshogawara-kita Bypass.[^675]

The route lies entirely within [Aomori Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aomori_Prefecture).

### Sobieto

**Sobieto** ([Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language): ソビエト) is an uninhabited [islet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islet) in [Wakayama Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wakayama_Prefecture), Japan. It is famous for its unusual name resembling the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union) ("[sobieto](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/sobieto)" means "Soviet" in Japanese) and the unknown origin of the name.[^676][^677]

#### Etymology

The origin of the name of the island is unknown and subject to debate. It is believed that the name "Sobieto" predates the foundation of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union) in 1922. According to locals, the islet was named "Sobieto" by the locals since ancient times. According to Kiyoshi Taniguchi, a local in the area, the name comes from the Japanese term in [Wakayama dialect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kish%C5%AB_dialect) for "towering shape".[^676][^678] It is also unknown why the islet's name was written in [katakana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katakana).[^679]

The islet was not officially named until 1 August 2014, when the Minister of State for Ocean Policy under former Japanese prime minister [Shinzo Abe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shinzo_Abe) officially named the 158 uninhabited islands from 22 prefectures in Japan, including Sobieto. The act was made as the basis for determining the scope of [Japan's territorial waters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclusive_economic_zone_of_Japan).[^678][^680]

#### Geography

Sobieto is a small uninhabited islet or [skerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skerry) about 1 kilometer (0.62 mi) off the coast off Mirozu (見老津[^681]), [Susami, Wakayama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susami,_Wakayama) in Japan. It is located south of [Kii Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kii_Peninsula), behind the island of Oki-no-Kuroshima, thus not visible on the coast. It is about 5 metres (16 ft) long, about 10 metres (33 ft) wide and about 5 metres (16 ft) high.[^676][^679][^682][^683]

The island can only be accessed by ferry from Mirozu port. It is used by fishermen in the area for [rock fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_fishing), although it is also known for being dangerous as waves can hit the fishermen because of its rough topography.[^679][^682]

#### In popular culture

The island is featured in an episode of the [NHK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NHK) program *Wabi Tabi* aired on 9 May 2016.[^684]

### 20 Fenchurch Street

[51°30′41″N 0°05′01″W / 51.51128°N 0.08353°W](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=20_Fenchurch_Street&params=51.51128_N_0.08353_W_)

**20 Fenchurch Street** is a commercial [skyscraper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyscraper) in London that takes its name from its address on [Fenchurch Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenchurch_Street), in the historic [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London) financial district. It has been [nicknamed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nicknames_for_London_skyscrapers) "**The Walkie-Talkie**" because of its distinctive shape, said to resemble a [walkie-talkie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walkie-talkie) handset.[^685] Construction was completed in spring 2014, and the three-floor "sky garden" was opened in January 2015.[^686] The 38-storey building is 160 m (525 ft) tall. Since July 2017, the building has been owned by [Lee Kum Kee Groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kum_Kee).

Designed by architect [Rafael Viñoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Vi%C3%B1oly) and costing over £200 million, 20 Fenchurch Street features a highly distinctive top-heavy form which appears to burst upward and outward. The entrance floor and 34 floors of office space are topped by a large viewing deck. A bar and restaurants are included on the 35th, 36th and 37th floors; these are, with restrictions, open to the public.[^687]

The tower was originally proposed at nearly 200 m (656 ft) tall but its design was scaled down after concerns about its visual impact on the nearby [St Paul's Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul's_Cathedral) and [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London). It was subsequently approved in 2006 with the revised height. Even after the height reduction there were continued concerns from heritage groups about its impact on the surrounding area. The Secretary of State for Communities and Local Government, [Ruth Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Kelly), called in the project for another [public inquiry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_inquiry)[^688] which, in 2007, ruled in the developers' favour and the building was granted full planning permission.[^689] In 2015 it was awarded the [Carbuncle Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbuncle_Cup) for the worst new building in the UK in the previous 12 months.[^690][^691]

#### Ownership

Previously owned by the Land Securities Group, the company posted a £95m loss in 2016.[^692] In July 2017, the Hong Kong food company [Lee Kum Kee Groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kum_Kee) agreed to purchase the building from [Land Securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Securities) and [Canary Wharf Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canary_Wharf_Group) for £1.3 billion.[^693] Savills Management Resources hold the contract to carry out all management of 20 Fenchurch Street.

#### Previous building

The previous building at 20 Fenchurch Street was 91 m (299 ft) tall with 25 storeys and was built in 1968 by [Land Securities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_Securities). The architect was [William H. Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_H._Rogers_%28architect%29).[^694]

The building was formerly occupied by [Dresdner Kleinwort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dresdner_Kleinwort) and was notable for being one of the first tall buildings in the City of London, and for its distinctive roof. It was one of the towers nearest to the [River Thames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Thames) when viewed from the southern end of [London Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Bridge).

In 2007, one of the upper floors was used in the drama series *[Party Animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_Animals_%28TV_series%29)*.

Demolition of the building was completed in 2008. Despite the top-down method of construction, it was not demolished from the bottom-up, as a temporary structure was built, allowing Keltbray, the demolition contractor, to demolish the building from the top down.[^695][^696]

#### Design

The new tower at 20 Fenchurch Street was designed by Uruguayan architect [Rafael Viñoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Vi%C3%B1oly).[^697]

The 'sky garden' at the top of the building was claimed by the developer to be London's highest public park, but since opening there have been debates about whether it can be described as a 'park', and whether it is truly 'public' given the access restrictions.[^698] The garden spans the top three floors, which are accessible by two express [lifts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elevator) and include a large viewing area, terrace, bar and two restaurants. Fourteen [double-deck lifts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-deck_elevator) (seven low-rise up to the 20th floor, seven high-rise above the 20th floor) serve the main office floors of the building.

The south side of the structure is ventilated externally to improve efficiency and decrease solar gain, whilst the east and west faces incorporate extensive solar shading. There is a southern entrance in addition to the main northern entrance set back from Fenchurch Street.

#### Construction

In January 2009, Canary Wharf Contractors began piling on the site of 20 Fenchurch Street. Piling and ground works were completed in June 2009.[^699]

In January 2011, work at the basement level of the tower began.[^700] By the end of October 2011, the building was rising above street-level. December 2011 saw the tower's core begin to rise.[^701][^702] The concrete core was topped out in March 2012 and by July the structural steelwork was under way around the core. Structural steelwork topped out in December 2012.[^703]

Fire protection was applied to the structural steelwork in December 2012, completing in March 2013. Cementitious spray was applied to the steelwork, which was supplied directly to the entire building using a purpose-built mixing and pumping station located on the ground floor.[^704]

The building completed to shell and floor in April 2014 and the first tenants began moving into the building from May 2014 prior to final completion in August of that year.[^705]

#### Criticisms

##### Carbuncle Award

The building won the [Carbuncle Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbuncle_Cup) in 2015, awarded by *[Building Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building_Design)* magazine to the worst new building in the UK during the previous year.[^690][^691][^706] The chairman of the jury that decided the prize, Thomas Lane, said "it is a challenge finding anyone who has something positive to say about this building", whilst a [town planner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Town_planner) at the nearby [Royal Town Planning Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Town_Planning_Institute) described the building as "a daily reminder never to let such a planning disaster ever happen again."[^691] Earlier in 2013, during a public inquiry, Paul Finch of the [Design Council CABE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_Council) said he regretted supporting the project, saying that the developers "made a mess of it" and were architects of their own misfortune.[^707][^708]

##### Solar glare problem

During the building's construction, it was discovered that for a period of up to two hours each day if the sun shines directly onto the building, it acts as a [concave mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curved_mirror) and focuses light onto the streets to the south.[^709] Spot temperature readings at street-level including up to 91 °C (196 °F)[^710] and 117 °C (243 °F) were observed[^711] during summer 2013: the reflection of a beam of light up to six times brighter than direct sunlight shined onto the streets below, damaging parked vehicles,[^712] including one on [Eastcheap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastcheap) whose owner was paid £946 by the developers for repairs to melted bodywork. Temperatures in direct line with the reflection became so high that *[City A.M.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_A.M.)* reporter [Jim Waterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Waterson) used the intense heat to [fry an egg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fried_egg) in a frying pan set down on the pavement.[^713] The reflection also burned or scorched the doormat of a shop in the affected area. The media responded by dubbing the building the "Walkie-Scorchie"[^714][^715][^716] and "Fryscraper".[^709][^717][^718]

In September 2013, the developers stated that the [City of London Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London_Corporation) had approved plans to erect temporary screening on the streets to prevent similar incidents, and that they were also "evaluating longer-term solutions to ensure the issue cannot recur in future".[^709][^719] In 2014, a permanent awning was installed on the south side of the higher floors of the tower.[^720]

The building's architect, [Rafael Viñoly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Vi%C3%B1oly), also designed the [Vdara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vdara) hotel in Las Vegas which has a similar sunlight reflection problem that some employees called the "Vdara death ray".[^721] The glass has since been covered with a non-reflective film.[^722]

In an interview with *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian)*, Viñoly said that horizontal [louvre windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre_window) on the south side that had been intended to prevent this problem were removed at some point during the planning process. While he conceded that there had been "a lot of mistakes" with the building, he agreed with the building's developers that the sun was too high in the sky on that particular day. "\[I\] didn't realise it was going to be so hot", he said, suggesting that [global warming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming) was at fault. "When I first came to London years ago, it wasn't like this ... Now you have all these sunny days."[^722]

##### Sky garden

The Sky Garden, which was described as a large, free, public viewing space at the top of the building, was part of the justification for the [planners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_planner) allowing such a vast office block to be built on the edge of a [conservation area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_area). Computer visualisations shown to the planners included a glade of full-height trees, but the garden as constructed has a slope with ferns and succulents instead.[^723]

Free access to the public is provided in 60-minute slots, until 18:00 on weekdays or 21:00 on weekends & Bank Holidays, after which the garden is available only to paying customers of the catering facilities.[^723]

The Garden has been criticised for these restrictions, and for its extent and quality failing to meet pre-construction expectations. [Oliver Wainwright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Wainwright), architecture critic of *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian)*, described it as "a meagre pair of rockeries, in a space designed with all the finesse of a departure lounge".[^691]

The [City of London Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London_Corporation)'s former chief planner, Peter Rees, who approved the structure, said: "I think calling it a sky garden is perhaps misleading. If people \[are\] expecting to visit it as an alternative to [Kew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kew_Gardens), then they will be disappointed."[^724] In July 2015 it was reported that planners are to consider a landscape architect's alterations to the layout, following claims it is not consistent with illustrations submitted with the original planning application. The 'sky garden' was a key feature in sealing approval for the building, which is situated outside the main cluster of skyscrapers in the City.[^725]

##### Wind tunnel effect

In July 2015, the building was criticised for having an unexpected impact on wind strength at street-level. The [City of London Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London_Corporation) received an increased number of complaints about draughts around 20 Fenchurch Street following its completion.[^726] The Corporation's head of design, Gwyn Richards, said: "The wind outcome at street level experienced post-construction on a number of projects differs somewhat to the conditions we were expecting from the one outlined in the planning application wind assessments."[^727]

#### Tenancy

In June 2012 the insurer [Markel Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markel_Corporation) signed a tenancy agreement with the developers to move into 20 Fenchurch Street upon its completion. Markel, previously based on [Leadenhall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadenhall_Street), was the first confirmed tenant of the new tower and occupies the 25th to 27th floors.[^728]

Another insurance company, Kiln Group, announced in September 2012 that it had agreed to become the building's second tenant[^729] and Ascot Underwriting followed in November 2012.[^730] Other insurance companies that have taken space in the building include [RSA Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_Insurance_Group), [Tokio Marine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokio_Marine), [CNA Financial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNA_Financial), Allied World, [Liberty Mutual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Mutual)'s European operations, and Harry Townsend Corp.[^731]

International law firm [DWF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DWF_Group) is also a tenant, occupying the 32nd floor.[^732]

As of 2017, the ground floor is let for retail and the office space is fully let.[^693]

[CGI Inc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CGI_Inc.) the IT/business services group are a tenant.[^733]

### Buzludzha monument

The **Monument House of the Bulgarian Communist Party** ([Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_language): Дом паметник на БКП, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Bulgarian): *Dom pametnik na BKP*), also known as the **Buzludzha Monument** (/ˈbʊzlʊdʒə/), was built on [Buzludzha Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzludzha) in central [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria) by the Bulgarian communist government and inaugurated in 1981. It commemorated the events of 1891, when a group of socialists led by [Dimitar Blagoev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimitar_Blagoev) assembled secretly in the area to form an organized socialist movement that led to the founding of the [Bulgarian Social Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Social_Democratic_Party_%281891%29), a forerunner of the [Bulgarian Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Communist_Party), itself a forerunner of the current [Bulgarian Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Socialist_Party).

#### Construction

Construction of the monument began on 23 January 1974 under architect [Georgi Stoilov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgi_Stoilov), a former mayor of Sofia and co-founder of the Union of Architects in Bulgaria.[^734] The peak was leveled into a stable foundation using [TNT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNT), reducing the mountain's height from 1,441 metres (4,728 feet) to 1,432 metres (4,698 feet).[^734] Over 15,000 cubic metres of rock were removed in the process.[^734] The monument was built at a cost of 14,186,000 [leva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_lev), equivalent to US\$35 million in 2020.

The monument exemplifies the [futurist architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurist_architecture) common to many state-constructed communist buildings. All maintenance ended with the fall of communism in 1989, and the building remains closed to the public due to the hazards of the weakened structure.[^734] The Buzludzha Project has helped to begin work on the monument's preservation, with the eventual aim of creating an [interpretation center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpretation_centre) for Bulgarian history.[^735]

#### Mosaics

Inside the building, mosaics commemorating the history of the Bulgarian Communist Party cover approximately 937 square meters; 35 tons of cobalt glass were used in their manufacture. One-fifth of the mosaics have already been destroyed due to age, weather-related deterioration, and vandalism.

The largest mosaics were glorifying [Vladimir Lenin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Lenin) and [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx). The monument has a hall used for important celebrations of the Communist Party until the fall of communism in 1989. At the top of the monument’s hall, there was a star-shaped red window associated with communism. A corridor with 14 mosaics showed the labor of ordinary workers.[^736]

Mosaics on the outer ring of the monument were built with natural stones gathered from rivers across Bulgaria; these mosaics have mostly vanished due to [natural wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weathering).

The building's main ceiling mosaic features the communist [hammer and sickle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammer_and_sickle) encircled with a *[Communist Manifesto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Communist_Manifesto)* quote, "Proletarians of all countries, unite!"[^737]

#### Opening ceremony

The monument was opened on 23 August 1981.[^738] At the opening ceremony, Bulgarian communist leader [Todor Zhivkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todor_Zhivkov) announced:

> I am honoured to be in the historical position to open the House-Monument of the Bulgarian Communist Party, built in honour of the accomplishments of Dimitar Blagoev and his associates, who 90 years ago laid the foundations for the revolutionary Marxist Party in Bulgaria. Let the pathways leading here - to the legendary Buzludzha Peak, here in the Stara Planina where the first Marxists came to continue the work of sacred and pure love that was started by Bulgaria's socialist writers and philosophers - never fall into disrepair. Let generation after generation of socialist and communist Bulgaria come here, to bow down before the feats and the deeds of those who came before; those who lived on this land and gave everything they had to their nation. Let them feel that spirit that ennobles us and as we empathise with the ideas and dreams of our forefathers, so let us experience that same excitement today! Glory to Blagoev and his followers; those first disciples of Bulgarian socialism, who sowed the immortal seeds of today's Bulgarian Communist Party in the public soul!

#### In popular culture

The [Finnish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finland) [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music) band [Haloo Helsinki!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haloo_Helsinki!) shot the entirety of the [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video) for their 2014 single "Vihaan kyllästynyt" at the monument;[^739] the Dutch rock band [Kensington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kensington_%28band%29)'s 2015 "Riddles" music video was likewise entirely filmed on location there. The closing sequence of [Rita Ora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Ora)'s *[Bang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bang_%28Rita_Ora_and_Imanbek_EP%29)* [EP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_play) video was shot at the monument in early 2021.[^740]

The site was used as a filming location for the 2016 action movie *Mechanic: Resurrection*; special effects were added to show the structure next to a shoreline, with a [helipad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helipad) added to the top of the saucer building. The monument is visited by the main protagonist in the 2018 comedy film *[I Feel Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Feel_Good_%28film%29)*.

The 2019 opera *Frankenstein*[^741] by [Mark Grey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Grey) appears to take place inside the Buzludzha Monument.[^742]

#### Access

Buzludzha can be reached by two side roads from the [Shipka Pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipka_Pass),[^743] either a 16 km (10 mi) road from [Kazanlak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazanlak) in the south or a 12 km (7 mi) road from [Gabrovo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabrovo) on the north side of the mountain. The road in the south (Kazanlak) is in better condition than the other one as of October 2023.

#### Preservation

Multiple initiatives to preserve the monument had been undertaken throughout the years, most of them political and associated with the [Bulgarian Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Socialist_Party). In 2018, the monument was recognized by [Europa Nostra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_Nostra) as one of the seven most endangered heritage sites in Europe. The most recent preservation works started in 2019 under the Buzludzha Project Foundation, in collaboration with [ICOMOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Council_on_Monuments_and_Sites) Germany and the municipality of [Stara Zagora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stara_Zagora).[^744] Together they were able to secure a \$185,000 [Getty Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getty_Foundation) grant to establish a Conservation Management Plan for the monument.[^745] Early results indicated that the building could be preserved and used, leading to a second Getty grant in July 2020 to stabilize surviving mosaic panels. Conservation and preservation efforts are ongoing.[^746]

### Flannan Isles Lighthouse

**Flannan Isles Lighthouse** is a [lighthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse) near the highest point on Eilean Mòr, one of the [Flannan Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flannan_Isles) in the [Outer Hebrides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Hebrides) off the west coast of [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland). In 1900, its three keepers disappeared under mysterious circumstances.[^747]

#### History

The 23-metre (75 ft) lighthouse was designed by [David Alan Stevenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Alan_Stevenson) for the [Northern Lighthouse Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Lighthouse_Board) (NLB). Construction, between 1895 and 1899, was undertaken by George Lawson of [Rutherglen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutherglen) at a cost of £1,899 (equivalent to £216,000 in 2025) inclusive of the building, landing places, stairs, and railway tracks. All of the materials used had to be hauled up the 45-metre (148 ft) cliffs directly from supply boats. A further £3,526 (£401,000 in 2025) was spent on the shore station at [Breasclete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breasclete) on the [Isle of Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Lewis).[^748] The lighthouse was first lit on 7 December 1899.

A [cable-hauled railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_railway) was built to facilitate the transport of provisions up the steep gradients from the landing places. At that time, the light consumed twenty barrels of [paraffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerosene) a year. The cable was powered by a small steam engine in a shed adjoining the lighthouse. The rail line descended from the lighthouse in a westerly direction and then curved round to the south. In the approximate centre of the island it forked by means of a set of hand-operated [points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroad_switch) dubbed "Clapham Junction", in reference to a [railway junction in London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clapham_Junction_railway_station); one branch continued in its curvature to head eastwards to the east landing place, on the south-east corner of the island, thus forming a half-circle, while the other, slightly shorter, branch curved back to the west to serve the west landing, situated in a small inlet on the island's south coast. The final approaches to the landing stages were extremely steep. The cable was guided round the curves by pulleys set between the rails, and a line of posts set outside the inner rail prevented it from going too far astray should it jump off the pulleys. The cargo was carried in a small four-wheeled [bogie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogie).[^749]

In 1925, the lighthouse became one of the first Scottish lights to receive communications from the shore by [wireless telegraphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wireless_telegraphy).[^750] In the 1960s, the island's transport system was modernised. The railway was removed, leaving behind the concrete bed on which it had been laid to serve as a roadway for a "Gnat" - a three-wheeled, rubber-tyred cross-country vehicle powered by a 400-cubic-centimetre (24 cu in) [four-stroke engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-stroke_engine), built by Aimers McLean of [Galashiels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galashiels). This had a somewhat shorter working life than the railway, becoming redundant in its turn when the helipad was constructed.[^751]

On 28 September 1971, the lighthouse was automated. A reinforced concrete [helipad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helipad) was constructed at the same time to enable maintenance visits in heavy weather. The light is produced by burning [acetylene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acetylene) gas[^752] and has a range of 17 nautical miles (20 mi; 31 km). It is now monitored from the [Butt of Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butt_of_Lewis)[^752] and the shore station has been converted into flats.[^753]

In December 2025, [Western Isles Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Isles_Council) gave planning permission for the renovation and development of the shore station, which is a Grade B listed building. The plans involved creating exhibition space and offices on the ground floor, and two self-catering holiday flats on the first floor, with an additional self-catering unit in an adjacent building.[^754]

#### 1900 crew disappearance

The first record that something was abnormal on the Flannan Isles was on 15 December 1900 when the steamer *Archtor*, on a passage from [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia) to [Leith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leith), noted in its log that the light was not operational in poor weather conditions.[^747] When the ship docked in Leith on 18 December 1900, the sighting was passed on to the [Northern Lighthouse Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Lighthouse_Board).[^755] The relief vessel, the lighthouse tender *Hesperus*, was unable to sail from [Breasclete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breasclete), [Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Lewis), as planned on 20 December due to adverse weather; she did not reach the island until noon on 26 December.[^752] The lighthouse was manned by three men: James Ducat, Thomas Marshall and Donald McArthur, with a rotating fourth man spending time on shore.

On arrival, the crew of *Hesperus* and the relief keeper found that the [flagpole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagpole) had no flag, none of the usual provision boxes had been left on the landing stage for restocking and none of the lighthouse keepers were there to welcome them ashore. Jim Harvie, the captain of *Hesperus*, attempted to reach them by blowing the ship's whistle and firing a flare but was unsuccessful.[^756][^757]

A boat was launched and Joseph Moore, the relief keeper, was put ashore alone. He found the entrance gate to the compound and the main door both closed, the beds unmade and the clock unwound. Returning to the landing stage with this news, he then went back up to the lighthouse with *Hesperus*'s second mate and a seaman. A further search revealed that the lamps had been cleaned and refilled. A set of [oilskins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oilskin) was found, suggesting that one of the keepers had left the lighthouse without them. There was no sign of any of the keepers, neither inside the lighthouse nor anywhere on the island.[^752][^758]

Moore and three volunteer seamen were left on the island to attend the light and *Hesperus* returned to Lewis. Captain Harvie sent a telegram to the Northern Lighthouse Board dated 26 December 1900, stating:

> A dreadful accident has happened at the Flannans. The three keepers, Ducat, Marshall and the Occasional have disappeared from the Island... The clocks were stopped and other signs indicated that the accident must have happened about a week ago. Poor fellows they must have been blown over the cliffs or drowned trying to secure a crane.[^752][^758]

On Eilean Mòr the men scoured every corner of the island for clues as to the fate of the keepers. They found that everything was intact at the east landing but the west landing provided considerable evidence of damage caused by recent storms. A box at 33 metres (108 ft) above sea level had been broken and its contents strewn about; iron railings were bent over, the iron railway by the path was wrenched out of its concrete and a rock weighing more than a ton had been displaced. On top of the cliff, at more than 60 metres (200 ft) above sea level, [turf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sod) had been ripped away as far as 10 metres (33 ft) from the cliff edge.[^759]

##### Northern Lighthouse Board investigation

On 29 December 1900 Robert Muirhead, a Northern Lighthouse Board (NLB) superintendent, arrived to conduct the official investigation into the incident. Muirhead had originally recruited all three of the missing men and knew them personally.[^760][^761]

He examined the clothing left behind in the lighthouse and concluded that Ducat and Marshall had gone down to the western landing stage and that McArthur (the 'Occasional') had left the lighthouse during heavy rain in his shirt sleeves. He noted that whoever left the light last and unattended was in breach of NLB rules.[^752] He also noted that some of the damage to the west landing was "difficult to believe unless actually seen".[^762]

> From evidence which I was able to procure I was satisfied that the men had been on duty up till dinner time on Saturday the 15th of December, that they had gone down to secure a box in which the mooring ropes, landing ropes etc. were kept, and which was secured in a crevice in the rock about 110 feet \[34 metres\] above sea level, and that an extra large sea had rushed up the face of the rock, had gone above them, and coming down with immense force, had swept them completely away.[^763]

Ducat left a wife and four children; McArthur a wife and two children.[^762] The disappearances tarnished the lighthouse's reputation for many years after the incident.[^764]

##### Speculation and conjecture

No bodies were ever found, but there have been some mysterious sights resulting in "fascinated national speculation" in newspapers and periodicals of the era.[^765] Implausible stories ensued, such as that a sea serpent had carried the men away; that they had arranged for a ship to take them away and start new lives; that they had been abducted by foreign spies; or that they had met their fate through the malevolent presence of a boat filled with ghosts (the baleful influence of the "Phantom of the Seven Hunters" was widely suspected [locally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outer_Hebrides)).[^752] More than ten years later the events were still being commemorated and elaborated on. The 1912 ballad "[Flannan Isle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flannan_Isle)" by [Wilfrid Wilson Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilfrid_Wilson_Gibson) refers erroneously to an overturned chair and uneaten meal laid out on the table, indicating that the keepers had been suddenly disturbed.[^762]

> Yet, as we crowded through the door,\
> We only saw a table spread\
> For dinner, meat, and cheese and bread;\
> But, all untouch'd; and no-one there,\
> As though, when they sat down to eat,\
> Ere they could even taste,\
> Alarm had come, and they in haste\
> Had risen and left the bread and meat,\
> For at the table head a chair\
> Lay tumbled on the floor.[^766]

However, in a first-hand account made by Moore, the relief keeper, he stated that: "The kitchen utensils were all very clean, which is a sign that it must be after dinner some time they left."[^752]

##### Later theories and interpretations

Over time a story has developed of the existence of unusual log book entries. They supposedly have Marshall saying on 12 December that there were "severe winds the likes of which I have never seen before in twenty years". He also is said to have reported that Ducat had been "very quiet" and Donald McArthur had been crying. McArthur was a veteran mariner with a reputation for brawling, and thus it would be strange for him to be crying in response to a storm. Log entries on 13 December were said to have stated that the storm was still raging and that all three men had been praying. This was also puzzling, as all three men were experienced lighthouse keepers who knew they were in a secure structure 150 feet above sea level and should have known they were safe inside. Furthermore, there had been no reported storms in the area on the 12, 13 and 14 December. The final log entry is said to have been made on 15 December, stating "Storm ended, sea calm. God is over all." However, an investigation by [Mike Dash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Dash) for the *[Fortean Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortean_Times)* revealed that the logbooks were fictional, later additions to the story.[^760][^767]

Subsequent researchers have taken into account the geography of the islands.[^752] The coastline of Eilean Mòr is deeply indented with narrow gullies called [geos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geo_%28landscape%29). The west landing, which is situated in such a geo, terminates in a cave. In high seas or storms water would rush into the cave and then explode out again with considerable force. It was possible McArthur saw a series of large waves approaching the island and, knowing the likely danger to his colleagues, ran down to warn them only to be washed away as well in the violent [swell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swell_%28ocean%29).[^768] Recent research by James Love discovered that Marshall was previously fined five shillings when his equipment was washed away during a huge gale. It is likely, in seeking to avoid another fine, that he and Ducat tried to secure their equipment during a storm and were swept away as a result. The fate of McArthur, although he had been required to stay behind to man the lighthouse, can be guessed to be the same. Love speculates that McArthur probably tried to warn or help his colleagues and was swept away too.[^769] This theory also has the advantage of explaining the set of oilskins remaining indoors and McArthur's coat remaining on its peg,[^752][^770] although perhaps not the closed door and gate.[^771] Another theory is based on the first-hand experiences of Walter Aldebert, a keeper on the Flannans from 1953 to 1957. He believed one man may have been washed into the sea but then his companions, who were trying to rescue him, were washed away by more [rogue waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogue_wave).[^771]

A further proposal is based on the psychology of the keepers. Allegedly, McArthur was a volatile character; this may have led to a fight breaking out near the cliff edge by the West Landing that caused all three men to fall to their deaths.[^772]

#### In popular culture

- [Wilfrid Wilson Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilfrid_Wilson_Gibson)'s (1878-1962) poem "[Flannan Isle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flannan_Isle)" recounts the horror of the search party who find an empty lighthouse with no trace of "three men dead".
- British rock group [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_%28band%29) wrote and recorded "The Mystery of the Flannan Isle Lighthouse" in 1968. It was released in 1998 on *[Genesis Archive 1967-75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_Archive_1967%E2%80%9375)*.[^773]
- Fictional use of this premise was featured in the *[Doctor Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Who)* serial *[Horror of Fang Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horror_of_Fang_Rock)*.[^774]
- The mystery was inspiration for [Peter Maxwell Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Maxwell_Davies)'s 1979 [chamber opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamber_opera) *[The Lighthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lighthouse_%28opera%29)*.[^775]
- The 2018 film *[The Vanishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Vanishing_%282018_film%29)* is based on the event.[^776]
- The season 7 premiere of *[BuzzFeed Unsolved True Crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BuzzFeed_Unsolved)* on 21 October 2020 covers the disappearance.
- The Flannan Isles and the Lighthouse are featured in the 2021 [Mark Dawson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Dawson_%28writer%29) book *Never Let Me Down Again*.
- The disappearance initiates the events of [Natasha Pulley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natasha_Pulley)'s 2021 novel *The Kingdoms*.
- The video game *Dark Fall II: Lights Out* was partially inspired by this occurrence, and references both the *Doctor Who* episode and the Gibson poem listed above.
- The video game *Reverse: 1999* includes the Flannan Isles as a side story.
- Emma Stonex's book *The Lamplighters* is based on the events at the lighthouse.[^777]

### Kielce Bus Station

**Kielce Bus Station** ([Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_language): *Dworzec autobusowy w Kielcach*) is a [bus station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_station) in [Kielce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kielce), Poland. It is a [novelty architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_architecture) type of a building, shaped to resemble a [UFO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UFO).[^778] Opened in 1984, it was seen as one of the more modern bus stations of its kind in Poland at that particular time.[^779][^780]

The station is built upon a large roundabout of 89 meters in diameter providing room for 15 platforms each of 18 meters length (the largest legal length of a bus in Poland and most of Europe). An additional island increases the number of platforms by 3, also providing night-time operation when the main building is closed. The main building of circular shape with a dome is located in the center of the roundabout. It is accessed by two tunnels beneath the roundabout - this feature provides maximum safety as pedestrian and bus traffic never cross each other.

#### History

The building was constructed from 1975 to 1984,[^780] and opened on 20 July that year, two days before the 40th anniversary of the establishment of the [People's Republic of Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Poland).[^781] It was designed by Polish architect Edward Modrzejewski.[^781] The facility was seen as highly advanced in terms of its overall capacity,[^779] and quickly became a minor tourist attraction and one of the landmarks of Kielce.[^781] It was designed to accommodate 1,500 buses and the projected number[^779] of 24,000 passengers daily.[^782] The size of the complex is about 4 hectares (9.9 acres).[^783]

Recently the local government has declared the building to be a monument, and the [Świętokrzyskie Voivodeship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%9Awi%C4%99tokrzyskie_Voivodeship) monument curator has justified this decision by describing the building as [^780] "unique and novel example of People's Republic of Poland-era type of architecture" and "one of the most valuable architectural designs of the years of 1970s and 1980s in Poland, and a material document of this period".[^780]

The fortunes of the building decreased in the 1990s, as post-communist Poland saw a rise in private car ownership, and a decreased interest in public transit. The building, formerly owned by the [PKS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Przedsi%C4%99biorstwo_Komunikacji_Samochodowej) company, has been [privatized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privatization) in the early 2010s.[^781][^784] While the government authorities were interested in preserving the building, seen as an important landmark, its private owners were struggling to turn a profit out of it. As of the 21st century, the building became increasingly in need of renovation, and the owner, the PKS 2 company, was planning to replace it with a new construction at a different location, with the original building being heavily modified or replaced.[^780][^781][^783] A spokesman for the company has even declared that they are not willing to invest in renovating the building, and in fact are waiting for the building to collapse.[^781] This has caused criticism from individuals who see the building as part of modern Poland's cultural heritage, and demand that the design is not significantly altered.[^778][^785]

The city bought back the bus station at the end of March 2016.[^786] In September 2018, a major reconstruction project was started with the goal of almost completely rebuilding the station, but preserving the basic design and the distinctive shape of the building. The works are scheduled to finish in June 2020, with a planned cost of 68,7 million PLN, 9 million of which is to be provided by the city government (with the bulk of the rest of the funding coming from the European Union).[^787][^788]
