### Mount Athos

**Mount Athos**[^789] is a mountain on the **Athos peninsula** in northeastern [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece) directly on the [Aegean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegean_Sea). It is an important center of [Eastern Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodoxy) [monasticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monasticism).

The mountain and most of the Athos peninsula are governed as an [autonomous region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_administrative_division) in Greece by the [monastic community of Mount Athos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monastic_community_of_Mount_Athos), which is ecclesiastically under the direct jurisdiction of the [Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecumenical_Patriarchate_of_Constantinople). The remainder of the peninsula forms part of the [Aristotelis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotelis_%28municipality%29) municipality. By Greek law and by religious tradition, women are prohibited from entering the area governed by the monastic community.[^790]

Mount Athos has been inhabited since ancient times and is known for its long Christian presence and historical monastic traditions, which date back to at least the 9th century during the [Byzantine era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire). Because of its long history of religious importance, the well-preserved architecture of its monasteries, and the preservation of the natural environment of the peninsula, the monastic community of Mount Athos was inscribed on the [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO) [World Heritage List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_List) in 1988.[^791]

#### Names

In the [classical era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_Greece), Mount Athos was called *Athos* and the peninsula *Acté* (in Latin) or *Akté* ([Koine Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koine_Greek_language): Ἀκτή). In modern Greek, the mountain is *Oros Athos* ([Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language): Όρος Άθως) and the peninsula *Hersonisos tou Atho* (Χερσόνησος του Άθω), while the designation *Agio Oros* (Άγιο Όρος), translating to 'Holy Mountain', is also used.[^792]

Some languages of Orthodox tradition use names that translate to 'Holy Mountain', including [Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_language), [Macedonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonian_language) and [Serbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbian_language) (Света Гора, *Sveta Gora*),[^793] and [Georgian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_language) (მთაწმინდა, *mtats'minda*).[^794] However, not all languages spoken in the Eastern Orthodox world use this name: in the [East Slavic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Slavic_languages) ([Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language), [Ukrainian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_language), and [Belarusian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarusian_language)) it is simply called Афон (*Afon*, meaning 'Athos'), while in [Romanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_language) it is called 'Mount Athos' (*Muntele Athos* or *Muntele Atos*).[^795]

#### Geography

The peninsula, the easternmost "leg" of the larger [Chalkidiki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalkidiki) peninsula in central [Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Macedonia), protrudes 50 km (31 mi)[^796] into the [Aegean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegean_Sea) at a width of between 7 and 12 km (4.3 and 7.5 mi) and covers an area of 335.6 km² (130 sq mi). The actual Mount Athos has steep, densely forested slopes reaching up to 2,033 m (6,670 ft). The Athos peninsula, unlike [Sithonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sithonia) and [Kassandra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kassandra,_Chalkidiki), is a geological continuation of the [Rhodope Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodope_Mountains) of northern Greece and Bulgaria.[^797]

The surrounding seas, especially at the end of the peninsula, can be dangerous. In ancient Greek history, two fleet disasters in the area are recorded: Herodotus claimed that in 492 BC, [Darius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darius_the_Great), the king of [Persia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persia), lost 300 ships under general [Mardonius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mardonius_%28general%29).[^798] In 411 BC the [Spartans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparta) lost a fleet of 50 ships under the admiral Epicleas.[^799]

Mount Athos has an extensive [network of footpaths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footpaths_of_Mount_Athos), many of which date back to the [Byzantine period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_period). Many are typically not accessible to motor vehicle traffic.[^800]

#### Flora

Much of Mount Athos is covered with [mixed broadleaf deciduous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate_broadleaf_and_mixed_forests) and evergreen forests. Black pine (*[Pinus nigra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinus_nigra)*) forests are found at higher elevations. [Sclerophyllous scrub vegetation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegean_and_Western_Turkey_sclerophyllous_and_mixed_forests) is also found throughout Mount Athos. Typical forest trees are sweet chestnut (*[Castanea sativa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castanea_sativa)*), holm oak (*[Quercus ilex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quercus_ilex)*), kermes oak (*[Quercus coccifera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quercus_coccifera)*), Hungarian oak (*[Quercus frainetto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quercus_frainetto)*), oriental plane (*[Platanus orientalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platanus_orientalis)*), black pine (*[Pinus nigra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinus_nigra)*), and cedar (*[Calocedrus decurrens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calocedrus_decurrens)*). Other common plant species include the strawberry tree (*[Arbutus unedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbutus_unedo)* and *[Arbutus andrachne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbutus_andrachne)*), cypress (*[Cupressus sempervirens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupressus_sempervirens)*), laurel (*[Laurus nobilis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurus_nobilis)*), lentisk (*[Pistacia lentiscus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pistacia_lentiscus)*), phillyrea (*[Phillyrea latifolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillyrea_latifolia)*), wild olive (*[Olea europaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olea_europaea)*), and heather (*[Erica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erica_%28plant%29)* spp.).[^801] Deciduous trees that are primarily found alongside streams include [white willow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_willow), [laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_%28plant%29), [Oriental plane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oriental_plane), and [alder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alder) trees.[^802]

Aleppo pine (*[Pinus halepensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinus_halepensis)*) is more commonly found in the northern part of the peninsula. Broadleaf [maquis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maquis_shrubland) is found further south. Deciduous broadleaf forest dominated by [sweet chestnut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_chestnut) lies above the broadleaf maquis zone. There are also mixed forests consisting of deciduous oak trees, as well as [limes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilia), [aspen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspen), [hop hornbeam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hop_hornbeam), and [maple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maple). [Black pine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinus_nigra) and [stinking juniper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stinking_juniper) can be found at higher elevations. Some herbaceous plants with tubers and bulbs include [crocus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocus), [anemone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anemone), [cyclamen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclamen), and [fritillary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritillaria) species.[^803]

At least 35 plant species are endemic to Mount Athos, most of which are found in the area of the main summit in the south.[^804] *[Isatis tinctoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isatis_tinctoria)* ssp. *athoa*, a [woad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woad) subspecies, and *Viola athois* are named after Mount Athos.[^803]

Mount Athos is also home to 350 species of mushrooms.[^805][^806][^807][^808][^809]

#### Fauna

Mammals include the [grey wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey_wolf) (*Canis lupus*), [wild boar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_boar) (*Sus scrofa*), red fox (*[Vulpes vulpes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulpes_vulpes)*), jackal (*[Canis aureus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canis_aureus)*), European badger (*[Meles meles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meles_meles)*), beech marten (*[Martes foina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martes_foina)*), stoat (*[Mustela erminea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mustela_erminea)*), weasel (*[Mustela nivalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mustela_nivalis) vulgaris*), European hedgehog (*[Erinaceus concolor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erinaceus_concolor)*), shrews (*[Crocidura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocidura)* spp.), and Mediterranean monk seal (*[Monachus monachus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monachus_monachus)*).[^801] Other mammal species include [roe deer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe_deer), [hares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_hare), and [red squirrels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_squirrel).[^810]

Birds include the black stork (*[Ciconia nigra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciconia_nigra)*), short-toed snake-eagle (*[Circaetus gallicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circaetus_gallicus)*), golden eagle (*[Aquila chrysaetos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquila_chrysaetos)*), lesser kestrel (*[Falco naumanni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falco_naumanni)*), western capercaillie (*[Tetrao urogallus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrao_urogallus)*), Eurasian eagle-owl (*[Bubo bubo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubo_bubo)*), yelkouan shearwater (*[Puffinus yelkouan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puffinus_yelkouan)*), and Audouin's gull (*[Ichthyaetus audouinii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ichthyaetus_audouinii)*).[^811][^812] Other bird species include [swifts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swift_%28bird%29), [swallows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swallow_%28bird%29), [martins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_%28bird%29), [nightingales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightingale), and [hoopoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_hoopoe).[^810]

#### History

##### Antiquity

In [Greek mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mythology), [Athos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athos_%28mythology%29) is the name of one of the [Gigantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigantes) that challenged the [Greek gods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_gods) during the [Gigantomachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigantomachy). Athos threw a massive rock at [Poseidon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poseidon) which fell in the [Aegean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegean_Sea) and became Mount Athos.[^813][^814] According to another version of the story, Poseidon used the mountain to bury the defeated giant.[^815]

[Homer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer) mentions the mountain Athos in the [Iliad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iliad).[^816] [Herodotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herodotus) writes that during the Persian invasion of [Thrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrace) in 492 BC, the fleet of the Persian commander [Mardonius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mardonius_%28general%29) was wrecked with losses of 300 ships and 20,000 men, by a strong North wind while attempting to round the coast near Mount Athos.[^817] Herodotus also states that [Pelasgians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelasgians) from the island of [Lemnos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemnos) populated the peninsula, then called *Akte,* and names five cities thereon, [Sane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sane_%28Acte%29), [Kleonai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleonae_%28Athos%29) (Cleonae), [Thyssos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thyssos) (Thyssus), [Olophyxos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olophyxos) (Olophyxus), and [Akrothoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akrothoon) (Acrothoum).[^818] [Strabo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strabo) also mentions the cities of Dion (Dium) and Akrothoon.[^819] [Eretria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eretria) also established colonies on Akte. At least one other city was established in the Classical period: [Akanthos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acanthus_%28Greece%29) (Acanthus). Some of these cities minted their own coins.

The peninsula was on the invasion route of [Xerxes I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerxes_I), who spent three years[^820] excavating the [Xerxes Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerxes_Canal) across the isthmus to allow the passage of his invasion fleet in 483 BC. After the death of [Alexander the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great), the architect [Dinocrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinocrates) (Deinokrates) proposed carving the entire mountain into a statue of Alexander.

[Pliny the Elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Elder) stated in 77 AD that the inhabitants of Mount Athos could "live to their four hundredth year" due to the fact that they ate the skin of vipers.[^821]

The lack of historical accounts shrouds the history of the peninsula during the later ages. Archaeologists have not been able to determine the exact location of the cities reported by Strabo. It is believed that they must have been deserted when Athos's new inhabitants, the monks, started arriving sometime before the ninth century AD.[^822]

##### Early Christianity

According to the Athonite tradition, the [Blessed Virgin Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blessed_Virgin_Mary) was sailing accompanied by [John the Evangelist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_the_Evangelist) from [Joppa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaffa) to [Cyprus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprus) to visit [Lazarus of Bethany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazarus_of_Bethany). When the ship was blown off course to then-pagan Athos, it was forced to anchor near the port of Klement, close to the present monastery of Iviron. The Virgin walked ashore and, overwhelmed by the mountain's wonderful and wild natural beauty, she blessed it and asked her son [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus) for it to be her garden. A voice was heard saying, "Ἔστω ὁ τόπος οὗτος κλῆρος σὸς καὶ περιβόλαιον σὸν καὶ παράδεισος, ἔτι δὲ καὶ λιμὴν σωτήριος τῶν θελόντων σωθῆναι" ("Let this place be your inheritance and your garden, a paradise and a haven of salvation for those seeking to be saved"). From that moment, the mountain was consecrated as the garden of the Mother of God and was out of bounds to all other women.[^823][^824]

Historical documents on ancient Mount Athos history are very few. Monks have certainly been there since the fourth century, and possibly since the third. During [Constantine I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_I)'s reign (324-337) both Christians and followers of traditional Greek religion were living there.[^825]

During the reign of [Julian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_%28emperor%29) (361-363), the churches of Mount Athos were destroyed, and Christians hid in the woods and inaccessible places.[^826]

Later, during [Theodosius I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosius_I)'s reign (379-395), the temples of the traditional Greek religion were destroyed. The lexicographer [Hesychius of Alexandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hesychius_of_Alexandria) states that in the fifth century, there was still a temple and a statue of "[Zeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeus) Athonite".[^827]

After the [Islamic conquest of Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_conquest_of_Egypt) in the seventh century, many Orthodox monks from the Egyptian desert tried to find another calm place; some of them came to the Athos peninsula. An ancient document states that monks "built huts of wood with roofs of straw \[...\] and by collecting fruit from the wild trees were providing themselves improvised meals."[^828]

The biography of Saint Athanasius the Athonite describes the foundation of the first monastic community on Mount Athos.[^829]

##### Byzantine era and onwards

Monastic life on Mount Athos expanded significantly during the Byzantine period. In the 9th century the area began to attract hermits and ascetics seeking isolation for religious devotion. By the 10th century organized monastic communities had developed, and the Byzantine emperors granted privileges and protection to the monastic settlements.[^830]

A major milestone in the institutional organization of the monastic community occurred in 963, when the monk Athanasius the Athonite founded the [Great Lavra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lavra) monastery with the support of the Byzantine emperor [Nikephoros II Phokas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikephoros_II_Phokas). This foundation marked the transition from scattered hermitages to large cenobitic monasteries and became a model for later monastic institutions on the peninsula.[^831][^832]

Throughout the Byzantine era, Mount Athos received patronage from emperors and rulers across the Orthodox world, including those of the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire), the [Kingdom of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Georgia), and various Slavic states. Several monasteries representing different Orthodox traditions were established, contributing to the multicultural character of the monastic republic.[^833]

After the fall of Constantinople in 1453 and the expansion of the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire), the monasteries of Mount Athos continued to function under Ottoman rule. The monastic community retained a degree of autonomy and preserved its religious institutions, although it faced periods of economic hardship and political instability.[^830]

During the 19th century the monastic population increased and the peninsula experienced a revival, supported by donations from Orthodox countries such as [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia), [Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia), and [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania). In the 20th century Mount Athos was incorporated into the modern Greek state while maintaining its special autonomous status as a monastic community within [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece).[^834]

Today Mount Athos remains an important center of Eastern Orthodox monasticism and is recognized as a [UNESCO World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO_World_Heritage_Site).

##### Access

Access to Mount Athos is restricted and requires a special permit known as a *diamonitirion*. Entry is limited to male visitors and regulated by the monastic authorities in cooperation with the Greek state. Visitors typically arrive by boat from [Ouranoupoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouranoupoli), which serves as the main gateway to the monastic community.[^835]

### Saatse Boot

Saatse Boot (Estonia)Saatse Boot (Baltic states)Saatse Boot (European Union)

The **Saatse Boot** ([Estonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonian_language): *Saatse saabas*; [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language): Саатсеский сапог) is a boot-shaped area of [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia) territory of 115 hectares (1.15 km²; 280 acres; 0.44 sq mi) that extends through the road number 178 between the [Estonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonia) villages of [Lutepää](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lutep%C3%A4%C3%A4) and [Sesniki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesniki) (themselves between the larger settlement [Värska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A4rska) and village of [Saatse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saatse)) in [Setomaa Parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Setomaa_Parish). For many years, the boot was freely accessible to cross from and to Estonia, until the road was permanently closed by the [Estonian Police and Border Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_and_Border_Guard_Board) in 2025.[^836]

#### Background

The current [Estonian-Russian border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonia%E2%80%93Russia_border) was established in 1944 when about 3,000 km² of Estonian territory was transferred to the [Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_SFSR). Land transfers continued for the next decades. In 1957, the [Supreme Soviet of the Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Soviet_of_the_Soviet_Union) authorized small exchange of territories in the administrative border area south of Lake Peipus, forming the now Russian [semi-exclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enclave_and_exclave) of [Dubki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubki,_Pechorsky_District,_Pskov_Oblast) and the Saatse Boot.[^837]

During the [Soviet occupation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupation_of_the_Baltic_states), it was the boundary between two constituent republics of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union). Estonia [regained independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonian_restoration_of_Independence) in 1991 and since then the same border (officially referred to as 'line of control' by Estonia) has been the international border between the two countries. The border is oddly shaped because the land parcel belonged to a farm that was administratively part the village of [Gorodishche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorodishche,_Russia) (until 1944 Linnaste village in Estonian [Petseri County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petseri_County)'s Järvesuu Parish) located 1.5 km (0.9 mi) further east. The farmhouse in the boot has been abandoned since Estonia regained independence. Its last owner is said to live in Estonia. He was not allowed to turn off from the road starting and ending in Estonian territory, to the road leading to the farmhouse hundred metres from the road.[^838]

#### Värska-Saatse Road

The road between the settlements of Värska and Saatse went through the Saatse Boot for approximately 1 kilometre (0.62 mi). Until October 2025, motorists and bicyclists from the Estonian side were permitted to pass through the Russian portion without presenting to border control or needing a visa, as long as they did not stop until they re-entered Estonian territory. In the event a vehicle broke down, drivers were advised to remain in their vehicle, contact the Saatse border station and await further instructions. Passing through on foot or exiting the vehicle was forbidden.[^839] Warning signs in Estonian, Russian, and English were posted along the road to remind people.

##### Closure and future

In 2008, a new road connecting Sesniki to [Matsuri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matsuri,_Estonia) opened, making it possible to reach the aforementioned villages without necessarily passing through the 'boot'. This is however a 15 kilometres (9.3 mi) to 20 kilometres (12 mi) detour if going from Värska.

On May 22, 2024, Estonian Interior Minister [Lauri Läänemets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauri_L%C3%A4%C3%A4nemets) said Estonia planned to construct a border fence and a new, shorter detour road 4.7 kilometres (2.9 mi) in length around the Saatse Boot plus upgrades on 1.7 kilometres (1.1 mi) of existing roads for a total cost of about €4 million.[^840][^841] In early 2025, construction was halted after protected plant species were discovered in the area, forcing the government to conduct an environmental impact assessment.[^842]

On 10 October 2025, Estonian authorities temporarily closed the road after increased Russian activity in the region. On the next day Estonian media published images of 7 armed Russians wearing a mix of civilian and military clothing standing in the middle of the road on the Russian side.[^843][^844] A day before that a drone coming from Russia had violated Estonian airspace for 18 minutes in southeastern Estonia.[^845]

On 16 October 2025, the Estonian government decided to permanently close the Saatse Boot road based on the recommendation of the [Police and Border Guard Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_and_Border_Guard_Board).[^846] Concrete blocks were placed on the both ends of the roads on the Saatse Boot, closing off the 870 metres (2,850 ft) road section inside the boot. The same was done with the 27 metres (89 ft) long Lutepää Triangle road section.

In the interest of national security, it was also decided to forgo the environmental study in order to speed up construction of the new road, which was originally due to be completed following all planning, regulatory and procurement legal requirements in 2 years in autumn 2027.[^847] With accelerating certain steps in the process it was estimated the project can be finished a year earlier and with skipping further procedures the road can be built by early 2026.[^846][^836]

The construction of permanent border infrastructure was announced to begin immediately.[^848] Ninety metre temporary gravel by-pass of the Lutepää Triangle was finished 5 days later on 21 October.[^849][^850] The new permanent route will be 300-400 metres (980-1,310 ft) long, with land acquisition required.[^851]

Beside the longer Saatse Boot by-pass there is also a shorter route along a forest road which was widened for this purpose.[^851]

##### Proposed border swap

In the 2000s and 2010s, there were proposals to straighten out the boot to remove the border oddity.[^852] In one such proposal, the area of the boot was to be transferred to Estonia in exchange for two patches of land in [Värska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A4rska_Parish) and [Meremäe Parishes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merem%C3%A4e_Parish). A treaty was signed in 2005 by the foreign ministers of Estonia and Russia, and again in 2014 after renegotiations, but the agreements were never ratified.[^853] On May 22, 2024, Estonian Interior Minister Lauri Läänemets ruled out any land swaps with Russia for now.

##### Incidents

Despite the warning signs, people occasionally violated rules. Some tourists were caught getting out of their cars within the Boot to take photos of the Russian border posts, some of them not realising that in doing so they had already violated the rules. In 2017, according to the Estonian Police and Border Guard Board, ten violations were noted and one person was detained in the Boot.[^854]

### Vajdahunyad Castle

**Vajdahunyad Castle** ([Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_language): *Vajdahunyad vára*) is a [castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castle) in the [City Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Park_%28Budapest%29) of [Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest), Hungary.

#### History

The castle was designed by [Ignác Alpár](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ign%C3%A1c_Alp%C3%A1r) and built in 1896[^855] as part of the Millennial Exhibition, which celebrated the 1,000 years of Hungary since the [Hungarian Conquest of the Carpathian Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Conquest_of_the_Carpathian_Basin) in 895. Originally, it was made from cardboard and wood, but it became so popular that it was rebuilt from stone and brick between 1904 and 1908.

#### Description

The "castle" comprises an eclectic collage of multiple landmark buildings from different parts of the [Kingdom of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary), especially the [Hunyad Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunyad_Castle) in [Hunedoara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunedoara), Romania. As the castle contains parts of buildings from various time periods, it displays different [architectural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architectural) styles: [Romanesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanesque_architecture), [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_architecture), [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_architecture), and [Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_architecture). It is sited within Budapest City Park.

The statue by [Miklós Ligeti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikl%C3%B3s_Ligeti) of [Anonymus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anonymus_%28notary_of_B%C3%A9la_III%29), the unknown chronicler at the court of [King Béla III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_III_of_Hungary) (r 1172-96), known as *[Anonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anonymous_%28statue%29)*,[^856] is in the courtyard of the castle.[^857]

The external wall of the castle contains a bust of [Béla Lugosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9la_Lugosi), a Hungarian-American actor famous for portraying [Count Dracula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Dracula) in the original 1931 [film of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dracula_%281931_English-language_film%29).

As of 2015 the castle houses the Museum of Hungarian Agriculture, the biggest agricultural museum in Europe.[^858]

### Ciudad Mitad del Mundo

The **Ciudad Mitad del Mundo** (*Middle of the World City*) is a tract of land owned by the prefecture of the province of [Pichincha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pichincha_Province), [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador). It is located at San Antonio parish of the [canton of Quito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quito_%28canton%29), 26 kilometers (16 mi) north of the center of [Quito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quito). The grounds contain the **Monument to the Equator**, which highlights the exact location of the Equator (from which the country takes its name) and commemorates the eighteenth-century Franco-Spanish Geodesic Mission which fixed its approximate location; they also contain the **Museo Etnográfico Mitad del Mundo**, Ethnographic Museum Middle of the Earth, a museum about the indigenous people [ethnography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnography) of Ecuador.

The 30-meter-tall (98 ft) monument was constructed between 1979 and 1982 by Architect and Contractor Alfredo Fabián Páez with Carlos Mancheno President of Pichincha's Province Council to replace an older, smaller monument built by the Government of Ecuador under the direction of the geographer Luis Tufiño in 1936.[^859] It is made of [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron) and [concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete) and covered with cut and polished [andesite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andesite) stone. The monument was built to commemorate the first [Geodesic Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Geodesic_Mission) of the [French Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Academy_of_Sciences), led by [Louis Godin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Godin), [Pierre Bouguer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bouguer) and [Charles Marie de La Condamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Marie_de_La_Condamine), who, in the year 1736, conducted experiments to test the flattening at the poles of the characteristic shape of the Earth, by comparing the distance between a degree meridian in the equatorial zone to another level measured in Sweden.[^860] The older monument was moved seven kilometers (4.3 mi) to a small town near there called Calacalí.[^861]

The [UNASUR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNASUR) former headquarters is located in this place,[^862] but is now in disuse following Ecuador's withdrawal from the organization in 2019.[^863]

#### The French Geodesic Mission

The placement of the equatorial line was defined throughout a 1736 expedition called the [French Geodesic Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Geodesic_Mission). While such studies would later determine the exact measure and shape of the world, astronomers involved missed the possibility of encountering the remnants of highly sophisticated geographical achievements made on “Equatorial” territory for hundreds of years before their arrival. Throughout the time the astronomers attempted to measure the length of a degree of latitude on that part of the planet, a group of different sorts of ruins (built by the [Quitu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quitu_culture)-[Cara culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cara_culture)) were found nearby the territory where they thought the Equatorial line passed through. Years after that, it was brought to light that the "Geodesic Mission" had been wrong about the exact coordinates where the line passed through, the measurements had indeed proved the world was [oblate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spheroid) and not elongated (egg-shaped) at the poles, but their studies to define the placement of the equator were incorrect by 240 meters (790 ft). The [Catequilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catequilla) ruins found throughout the expedition between 1735 and 1745 were actually situated at latitude 0 ([0°0′0″N 78°25′43″W / 0.00000°N 78.42861°W](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Ciudad_Mitad_del_Mundo&params=0_0_0_N_78_25_43_W_)), or the exact position where the [Equatorial line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator) crosses.

In 1935, the Ecuadorean Government built a ten-meter-high (33 ft) monument to honor the French expedition under the guidance of local geographer Luis Gudiño. In 1972, that monument was replaced by a thirty-meter-high (98 ft) monument titled “Ciudad Mitad del Mundo” (Middle of the World City)).

#### Latitude discrepancy

Based on data obtained by Tufiño, it was believed that the equator passed through those two sites. However, according to readings based on the [World Geodetic System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Geodetic_System) WGS84, used in modern GPS systems and [GIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GIS) products, the equator actually lies about 240 metres (790 ft) north of the marked line.[^864]

Over the years, countless tourists have had their pictures taken straddling the line drawn down the center of the east-facing staircase and across the plaza.

The pyramidal monument, with each side facing a [cardinal direction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_direction) is topped by a globe which is 4.5 metres (15 ft) in diameter and weighs 5 tonnes (4.9 long tons; 5.5 short tons). Inside the monument is a small museum that displays a variety of indigenous items pertaining to [Ecuadorian culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_Ecuador): clothing, descriptions of the various ethnic groups, and examples of their activities.

Ciudad Mitad del Mundo contains other attractions such as a planetarium, a miniature model of Quito, and restaurants. On weekends, Ciudad Mitad del Mundo's Central Plaza hosts varied musical and cultural events for tourists. Also, there are diverse local handcraft stores and local food served at several cafés along a small colonial town.

#### Intiñan Solar Museum

200 metres (660 ft) northeast of the [Ethnographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnography) Museum Monument is a local private attraction, known as the Intiñan Solar Museum, reportedly built to mark the Equator, although modern measurements suggest that it no longer does.[^865]

Along with exhibitions of Ecuadoran culture, the museum professes to be a destination for natural science tourism.[^866] Tour guides and visitors demonstrate tricks which are supposedly possible only on the Equator, such as water flowing both counter-clockwise or clockwise down a drain due to the [Coriolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriolis_force) effect.[^867] However, the [Coriolis force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coriolis_force) has no effect on the apparent direction of draining water in household drains anywhere on Earth, as this is too small of a scale of motion to be affected by the larger-scale force.[^866] Another apparent trick performed here is balancing eggs on end.[^868] This is purportedly easier at the equator due to the claim of a relative maximum in the magnetic field at the equator. However, attempts to balance eggs work just as well anywhere else on Earth, and are not influenced by magnetism or the Coriolis force.[^866] Also, there is an apparent weakening of muscles due to low latitude.[^869] This is also linked to the claim that certain physical forces, including the Coriolis force, are significantly weakened at the equator. Many of the demonstrations and associated claims made by tour guides are inconsistent with each other.[^866][^870][^871]

### Plymouth, Montserrat

**Plymouth** is a [ghost town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_town) and the *[de jure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_jure)* capital of the island of [Montserrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montserrat), an [overseas territory of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Overseas_Territories) located in the [Leeward Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeward_Island) chain of the [Lesser Antilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesser_Antilles), West Indies. It is the only ghost town that is the capital of a political territory.

Constructed during the [Georgian era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgian_era) on historical lava deposits near the then long-inactive [Soufrière Hills volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soufri%C3%A8re_Hills_volcano), the town was evacuated in 1995 when the volcano resumed erupting. Plymouth was eventually abandoned permanently in 1997,[^872] after it was substantially buried by a series of [pyroclastic flows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyroclastic_flows) and [lahars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahar).

For centuries, it had been the only [port of entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_entry) to the island. A new capital is under construction at [Little Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Bay,_Montserrat),[^873] with nearby [Brades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brades) serving as the *[de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto)* capital for the time being.

#### History

##### St. Anthony's Church

After the establishment of the first European colony on the island of Montserrat in 1632, St. Anthony's Church was established in Plymouth in 1636.[^874] Although there is a [St. Anthony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Anthony_%28disambiguation%29) in Catholicism, it is believed that Governor Anthony Brisket, who went to England to secure funds to build the church, had the church named after himself.[^875] The church had to be rebuilt several times throughout its history due to damage from earthquakes and hurricanes. As of September 2021, the church is buried deep in the ash.

##### Hurricane Hugo

Montserrat was struck by [Hurricane Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Hugo) on 17 September 1989. The hurricane destroyed a 55-metre (180 ft) stone [jetty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jetty) in Plymouth's harbour.[^876] Many other buildings, including schools, health centres, and the recently constructed central hospital building, were rendered unusable by damage from the storm. Given that the hospital was the only one on the island, and damages were extensive enough that all patients had to be relocated, a survey conducted by engineers from the National Emergency Management Agency of [Trinidad and Tobago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad_and_Tobago) concluded that the hospital should undergo substantial redesign in order to ensure that its structural strength could withstand future storms.[^877]

##### Volcanic eruptions and abandonment

Beginning on 18 July 1995, a series of huge eruptions at the [Soufrière Hills volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soufri%C3%A8re_Hills_volcano), which had been inactive for centuries, sent ash falls across a wide area of southern Montserrat including the capital, Plymouth. It was soon clear that the town was in grave danger. On 21 August 1995, [tephra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tephra) fell on Plymouth, necessitating an evacuation that lasted until 3 September 1995. Following renewed volcanic activity, on 1 December 1995 residents were evacuated for the second time. This evacuation lasted for one month before residents were allowed back on 1 January 1996.[^878]

On 27 March 1996, a series of hot ash emissions and [pyroclastic flows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyroclastic_flow) began,[^879] marking the most dangerous period for the volcano up to that point. Areas nearest the volcano were immediately evacuated; as the volcanic activity continued to escalate, on 3 April 1996, Plymouth was evacuated for the third and final time.[^880] The island was divided into risk zones; during some periods, entry into Plymouth was prohibited,[^881] and at other times, it was allowed during daytime only to those with a means of rapid escape.[^882] The last time that access was legally allowed to Plymouth during daytime was 16 June 1997, with the exception of essential services.[^883][^884] On 25 June 1997, a further massive eruption produced [pyroclastic surges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyroclastic_surge) that killed 19 people and reached nearly to the island's airport on the eastern side of the island, which had remained open until that time.[^885][^886]

Between 4-8 August 1997, a further series of large eruptions destroyed approximately 80% of the town, burying it under 1.4 metres (4.6 ft) of ash. This hot material burned many of the buildings, making habitation nearly impossible for many of the residents.

The pyroclastic flows, lava, ash and other volcanic rock types were mostly compact, having a density similar to that of concrete. The removal of the overburden would have required the use of explosives, bulldozers and other resources too expensive for widespread use. It was anticipated that the soil underneath the hardened mud and lava would have been scorched and left completely non-[arable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arable_land) by the intense heat of the pyroclastic flows.

The government ordered the evacuation of Plymouth, with the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy) assisting by taking the population to safety. The entire southern half of the island was declared an [exclusion zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclusion_zone) because of the continuing volcanic activity at the Soufrière Hills. The government of the island was moved north to the town of [Brades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brades,_Montserrat), although Plymouth remains the *de jure* capital. As of 2013, a new port and capital are under construction at [Little Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Bay,_Montserrat), on the island's northwest coast. Daytime access to Plymouth has been permitted for some activities since about 2015, including sand and gravel extraction for construction projects.[^887]

The total destruction of Plymouth caused severe economic problems for the island of Montserrat. Plymouth had been by far the largest settlement on the island, with a population of around 4,000 inhabitants, and as such had been the site of almost all the island's shops and services, in addition to having been its seat of government.

Some of the lost facilities were subsequently rebuilt elsewhere on Montserrat, but this did not prevent emigration. Between 1995 and 2000, two-thirds of the island's total population was forced to flee, many of whom settled in the United Kingdom, leaving fewer than 1,200 people resident on the island as of 1997. The population figure has risen to nearly 5,000 by 2016.

#### Geography

Plymouth is situated on the lower southwest slope of the [Soufrière Hills Volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soufri%C3%A8re_Hills_Volcano). It is well within the volcanic exclusion zone, which is considered wholly uninhabitable.

##### Climate

Plymouth has a [hot semiarid climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_semiarid_climate) ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification): *BSh*).

#### Transport

The airport serving the island of Montserrat, [W. H. Bramble Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._H._Bramble_Airport), was shut down completely by 1997 and subsequently destroyed as it was buried in volcanic ash. A new airport, [John A. Osborne Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Osborne_Airport), opened in 2005 at Gerald's, near [Brades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brades) in the north of the island.[^889]

#### Education

In the pre-1997 period, it was served by Plymouth Primary School,[^890] and Plymouth Junior Secondary School.[^891]

### Borscht Belt

The **Borscht Belt**, or **Yiddish Alps**, is a region of the U.S. state of [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_%28state%29) that had [summer resorts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_resort) catering to [American Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Jews) vacationers, especially residents of [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City).[^892] The resorts, most later defunct, were located in the southern foothills of the [Catskill Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catskill_Mountains) in parts of [Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sullivan_County,_New_York) and [Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster_County,_New_York) counties, bordering the northern edges of the [New York metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_metropolitan_area).

A 2019 review of the history is more specific: "in its heyday, as many as 500 resorts catered to guests of various incomes."[^893] These resorts, as well as the Borscht Belt [bungalow colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bungalow), were a popular vacation spot for [New York City Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Jews) from the 1920s through the 1960s.[^894] By the late 1950s, many began closing, with most gone by the 1970s, but some major resorts continued to operate, a few into the 2010s.

#### Name

The name comes from [borscht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borscht), a soup of [Ukrainian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_cuisine) origin, made with [beets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beetroot) as the main ingredient, giving it a deep reddish-purple color,[^895] that is popular in many Central and Eastern European countries and brought by [Ashkenazi Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi_Jew) and [Slavic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slav) immigrants to the United States. The alliterative name was coined by [Abel Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Green), editor of [*Variety*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28magazine%29) starting in 1933, and is a play on existing colloquial names for other American regions, such as the [Bible Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_Belt) and [Rust Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_Belt).[^896] An alternate name, the *Yiddish Alps*,[^897] was used by [Larry King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_King) and is satirical: a classic example of borscht belt humor.

#### History

After the expansion of the railway system including the tracks [Ontario and Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_and_Western_Railroad) as well as the [Ulster and Delaware Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster_and_Delaware_Railroad),[^893] the area of the [Catskill Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catskill_Mountains) became a tourist destination because of the beauty of the landscape, which impressed the painters of [American Romanticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River_School), and because of the rising popularity of [fly fishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly_fishing) in its [trout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trout)-rich rivers. As New York City streets would bake in the summer and air-conditioning was not yet available, people flocked to the Catskills.

In the early 1900s, some hotels' and resorts' advertisements refused to accept Jews and indicated "No Hebrews or [Consumptives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis)" in their ads.[^898] This discrimination led to a need for alternative lodging that would readily accept Jewish families as guests. Visits to the area by Jewish families were already underway "as early as the 1890s ... [Tannersville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tannersville,_New_York) ... was 'a great resort of our Israelite breathren \[*[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic)*\]' ... from the 1920s on \[there were\] hundreds of hotels."[^899] The larger hotels provided "Friday night and holiday services as well as kosher cooking", thus supporting religious families to take a vacation in accordance to their customs.[^900]

##### Rise

Borscht Belt hotels, bungalow colonies, summer camps, and *kuchaleyns* (kuch-alein, literally: "Cook it yourself",[^901] a [Yiddish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yiddish_language) name for self-catered boarding houses)[^902] flourished. The bungalows usually included "a kitchen/living room/dinette, one bedroom, and a screened porch" with entertainment at the communal center, called the casino, being simple: bingo or a movie.[^903] The *kuchaleyns* were often visited by lower middle-class and working-class Jewish New Yorkers. Because of the many Jewish guests, this area was nicknamed the *[Yiddish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yiddish) [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps)* or *[Solomon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon) County*, a [malapropism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malapropism) of [Sullivan County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sullivan_County,_New_York), by many people who visited there.[^904]

A sufficient choice of Jewish cuisine was an important feature of the hotels in the Borscht Belt, and "too much was not enough" developed as a notion. [Jonathan Sarna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Sarna) wrote: "To understand the emphasis on food, one has to understand hunger. Immigrants had memories of hunger, and in the Catskills, the food seemed limitless."[^905][^906] The singles scene was also important; many hotels hired young male college students[^907] to attract single girls of a similar age. One book on the era contended that "the Catskills became one great marriage broker."[^908]

Borscht Belt resorts stood in towns such as [Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty,_New_York), [Fallsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallsburg,_New_York), [Mamakating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mamakating,_New_York), [Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thompson,_New_York), [Bethel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethel,_New_York) and [Rockland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockland,_New_York) in Sullivan County as well as [Wawarsing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wawarsing,_New_York) and [Rochester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_Ulster_County,_New_York) in Ulster County. Such resorts included Avon Lodge, Brickman's, [Brown's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brown's_Hotel_%28Catskills%29), Butler Lodge, [The Concord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Resort_Hotel), [Grossinger's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grossinger's), Granit, the Heiden Hotel, Irvington, [Kutsher's Hotel and Country Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kutsher's_Hotel), the [Nevele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevele_Grand_Hotel), Friar Tuck Inn, the Laurels Hotel and Country Club, the Pines Resort, [Raleigh Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raleigh_Hotel_%28South_Fallsburg,_New_York%29), the Overlook, the Tamarack Lodge, Shady Nook Hotel and Country Club, Stevensville, Stier's Hotel, and the Windsor. Some of these hotels originated from farms that Jewish immigrants had established in the early part of the 20th century.[^909]

Two of the larger hotels in High View, just north of [Bloomingburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomingburg,_New_York), were the [Shawanga Lodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawanga_Lodge) and the Overlook. One of the high points of Shawanga Lodge's existence came in 1959 when it was the site of a conference of scientists researching [laser beams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser_beams). The conference marked the start of serious research into lasers.[^910] The hotel burned to the ground in 1973.[^911] The Overlook, which offered rooms in the main building as well as bungalows, spiced up with entertainment, was operated by the Schrier family.[^893]

##### Decline

The Borscht Belt reached its peak in the 1950s and 60s with over 500 resorts, 50,000 bungalows, and 1,000 rooming houses.[^912] By the late 1960s, the start of a decline was apparent. "Railways began cutting service to the area, the popularity of air travel increased, and a younger generation of Jewish-Americans chose other leisure destinations."[^913] A secondary factor was that "anti-Semitism declined, so Jews could go other places."[^914] Official Sullivan County historian John Conway blames the decline on "the three ‘A’s: air conditioning, assimilation, and airfare".[^915]

Access to the area improved with the opening of the [George Washington Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington_Bridge) and upgrade of old travel routes such as old [New York State Route 17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Route_17). On the other hand, passenger train access ended with the September 1953 termination of passenger trains on the [Ontario and Western Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_and_Western_Railway) mainline from [Roscoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscoe,_New_York) at the northern edge of Sullivan County, through the Borscht Belt, to [Weehawken, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weehawken,_New_Jersey).[^916] A 1940 vacation travel guide published by the railroad listed hundreds of establishments that were situated at or near the railway's stations.[^917]

In 1941, the [New York Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Central) ceased running passenger trains on its Catskill Mountain Branch.[^918] The area suffered as a travel destination in the late 1950s and especially by the 1960s. Another source confirms that "cheap air travel suddenly allowed a new generation to visit more exotic and warmer destinations."[^919] More women remained in the workforce after marriage and could not take off for the entire summer to relocate to the Catskills.[^920]

A *[Times of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Times_of_Israel)* article specifies that "the bungalow colonies were the first to go under, followed by the smaller hotels. The glitziest ones hung on the longest" with some continuing to operate in the 1980s and even in the 1990s.[^905] Bungalow colonies fell into disrepair or many of the nicer ones have been converted into a [housing co-op](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housing_cooperative).[^921] The [Concord Resort Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Resort_Hotel), which outlasted most other resorts, went bankrupt in 1997 but survived until 1998 and was subsequently demolished for a possible casino site.[^893] By the early 1960s, some 25 to 30 percent of [Grossinger's Catskill Resort Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grossinger's_Catskill_Resort_Hotel) visitors were not Jewish;[^893] nevertheless it closed in 1986.[^922]

The Stevensville Hotel in [Swan Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swan_Lake,_New_York) was located on the shores of an artificial reservoir of the West Branch [Mongaup River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongaup_River) which had fed a [tannery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tannery) since the 1840s.[^923] It was commissioned in 1924 and managed by the Dinnerstein and Friehling families[^924] until around 1990.[^925] It reopened as *Swan Lake Resort Hotel*[^926] in 1999, offering Asian cuisine plus tennis and golf facilities and survived until 2007.[^927] In 2015, the ultra-Orthodox[^928] Congregation Iched Anash bought the property for \$2.2 million[^929] and began to operate the *[Satmar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satmar) Boys Camp*, a religious summer school ([yeshiva gedolah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeshiva_gedolah)).[^930]

In 1987, [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City) mayor [Ed Koch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Koch) proposed buying the Gibber Hotel in Kiamesha Lake to house the homeless. The idea was opposed by local officials[^931] and the hotel instead became the religious school Yeshiva Viznitz.[^932]

The Granit Hotel and Country Club, located in Kerhonkson, boasted many amenities, including a golf course. It closed in 2015 and was renovated and turned into the Hudson Valley Resort and Spa, which closed in 2018. The property was sold in May 2019 to Hudson Valley Holding Co. LLC. The company did not announce its plans for the hotel.[^933]

#### 21st century

As of the 2010s, the region was a summer home for many [Orthodox Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodox_Jewish) families.[^934] Some of the hotels have been converted into [rehab centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rehab_center), [meditation centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditation_center) or Orthodox Jewish hotels and resorts.[^935] The former Homowack Lodge in [Phillipsport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillipsport,_New_York) was converted into a summer camp for [Hasidic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasidic) girls. Officials of the state Department of Health ordered the property evacuated in July 2009, citing health and safety violations. The camp owners initially resisted, but left for good that August.[^936][^937] The property was unoccupied for many years and the main lodge burned down in 2023.[^938] The Flagler Hotel, Nemerson, Schenk's and Windsor Hotels in South Fallsburg, and the Stevensville Hotel in Swan Lake, were converted into Jewish religious summer camps.

In [Fleischmanns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleischmanns,_New_York), Oppenheimer's Regis Hotel serves an Orthodox clientele in a building dating back to the heyday of the Borscht Belt.[^939]

In 1984, the Catskills division of [Hatzalah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatzalah) was founded which covers the Borscht Belt and served the needs of a growing Orthodox clientele. As of 2020 a volunteer force of 450 rescue workers and paramedics is operating a fleet of 18 ambulances. Although financially independent from the other chapters, it cooperates in day-to-day business with Central Hatzalah of NYC as the 17. neighborhood and with State Forces (police, forest rangers, emergency medical services, fire departments).[^940][^941][^942][^943]

Many [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism) and [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism) retreat centers have been constructed on the land or in the restored buildings of former camps or resorts to serve adherents in New York City, the establishment of which has then drawn even more [temples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple) and centers to the area. This led to the coining of the nicknames "[Buddha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddha) Belt," "[Bhajan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhajan) Belt" and "Buddhist Belt" to refer to the area's revival.[^944][^945][^946]

Despite the region's decline as a [cultural epicenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_center), a handful of traveling acts, such as the [Doox of Yale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Duke's_Men_of_Yale), a [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University) [acappella group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acappella_%28group%29), continued to regularly tour the Borscht Belt as recently as 2015.[^947]

On August 7, 2025, the Yamim Ba’im music festival, starring Orthodox Israeli superstar [Ishay Ribo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ishay_Ribo), took place at [Bethel Woods Center for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethel_Woods_Center_for_the_Arts), the same site as the [1969 Woodstock Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodstock).[^948]

Between 2013 and 2018, the decaying state of the abandoned resorts was captured by several [ruins photographers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruins_photography):[^949][^950][^919][^951]

- [Grossinger's Catskill Resort Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grossinger's_Catskill_Resort_Hotel); the Grossinger's complex partially was demolished in 2018 and a new owner planned to build a hotel, homes and other amenities. A remaining structure on the property was destroyed by fire in August 2022.[^952][^953]
- [Kutsher's Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kutsher's_Hotel) and Country Club; a wellness club was built on the site and opened in June 2018.[^954][^955] The original Kutcher's nightclub is all that remains of the original hotel. The Kutcher's Hotel front electric sign was donated to the Sullivan County Historical Museum.
- The Pines Hotel closed in 1998. The dilapidated main building and surrounding structures remained in a state of decay until it was destroyed in a fire in June 2023.[^956] The Pines Hotel golf course has been converted into a Jewish religious summer camp.[^957]
- The former Gilbert's Hotel and Brickman Hotel are now part of the Siddha Yoga SYDA complex. A gift shop remains open at the sites, which are not in current active use.
- [Nevele Grand Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevele_Grand_Hotel)
- The Vegetarian Hotel
- White Lake Mansion House
- Homowack Lodge
- Lesser Lodge
- Tamarack Lodge
- [Concord Resort Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord_Resort_Hotel). In February 2018, [Resorts World Catskills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resorts_World_Catskills) opened on the site of the old hotel.
- [Shawanga Lodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawanga_Lodge)

##### Current status

By the 2020s, the Hasidic presence in the Catskills had grown into a substantial year-round phenomenon. Families from Brooklyn and other New York City Orthodox communities had increasingly settled permanently in towns such as South Fallsburg, Kiamesha Lake, Monticello, and Woodbourne, drawn by affordable real estate and proximity to established kosher infrastructure including synagogues, schools, and kosher stores and restaurants.[^958] The [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic) accelerated this trend, as remote schooling and work-from-home arrangements enabled many summer residents to remain in their bungalows and summer homes beyond the traditional season.[^959] During the summer months, Sullivan County's population swells dramatically due to the influx of Hasidic families, who largely stay in private kosher rental homes and bungalow colonies rather than the grand hotels of the Borscht Belt era.[^960]

#### Comedic legacy

The tradition of Borscht Belt entertainment started in the early 20th century with the Paradise Garden Theatre constructed in [Hunter, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter,_New_York) by [Yiddish theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yiddish_theater) star [Boris Thomashefsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Thomashefsky).[^961] A cradle of American Jewish comedy since the 1920s, the Borscht Belt entertainment circuit has helped launch the careers of [many famous comedians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Borscht_Belt_comedians) and acted as a launchpad for those just starting out.[^962][^963][^964]

Many of these performers and writers had a rapid-fire, often self-deprecating style.[^965][^966][^967] Typical themes include:

- [Bad luck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luck): "I told the doctor I broke my leg in two places. He told me to quit going to those places." ([Henny Youngman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henny_Youngman))
- [Puns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pun): "Sire, the peasants are revolting!" "You said it. They stink on ice." ([Harvey Korman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Korman) as Count de Monet and [Mel Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_Brooks) as [King Louis XVI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Louis_XVI), in *[History of the World Part I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_World_Part_I)*)
- Physical complaints and ailments (often relating to bowels and cramping): "My doctor said I was in terrible shape. I told him, 'I want a second opinion.' He said, 'All right, you're ugly too!'" ([Rodney Dangerfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodney_Dangerfield)); "I told my doctor, 'This morning when I got up and saw myself in the mirror, I looked awful! What's wrong with me?' He replied, 'I don't know, but your eyesight is perfect!'" (Dangerfield)
- [Aggravating relatives and nagging wives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinship): "My wife and I were happy for twenty years. Then we met." (Dangerfield); "Take my wife, please!" (Henny Youngman); "My wife drowned in the pool because she was wearing so much jewelry." ([Don Rickles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Rickles)); "My wife ain't too bright. One day our car got stolen. I said to her, 'Did you get a look at the guy?' She said, 'No, but I got the license number.'" (Dangerfield); "This morning the doorbell rang. I said 'Who is it?' She said 'It's the [Boston Strangler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Strangler).' I said 'It's for you dear!'" (Youngman)

#### Historical Marker Project

The Borscht Belt Historical Marker Project was founded by Marisa Scheinfeld, a noted Borscht Belt historical photographer, author, and Borscht Belt documentarian, in 2022.[^968] Scheinfeld had photographed the detritus of the former Borscht Belt hotels, bungalows, and historically important sites. She recognized the complete absence of any historical interpretive roadside markers documenting the sites of the former Borscht Belt.

The Borscht Belt Historical Marker Project initiated a unique program to place 20 vertical interpretive highway markers strategically sited to tell the story of the Borscht Belt and interpret the specific locations. The markers are enhanced with QR pegs for more in-depth explanations. A self-guided audio tour system is being developed.

The markers are double-sided with representative images. All carry an interpretive text about the specific area on one side and the following common text about the Borscht Belt on the other side: "From the 1920s through the early 1970s, the Borscht Belt was the preeminent summer resort destination for hundreds of thousands of predominantly East Coast American Jews. The exclusion of the Jewish community from existing establishments in the 1920s drove Jewish entrepreneurs to create over 500 resorts, 50,000 bungalows and 1,000 rooming houses in Sullivan County and parts of Ulster County. The Borscht Belt provided a sense of community for working and vacationing Jews. The era exerted a strong influence on American culture, particularly in the realm of entertainment, music, and sports. Some of the most well-known and influential people of the 20th century worked and vacationed in the area. Beginning around 1960, the Borscht Belt began a gradual demise due to many factors including the growth of suburbia, inexpensive airfare, and generational changes."[^969]

As of 2024, the Program has completed and sited nine markers in Sullivan County - Monticello, Mountain Dale, Swan Lake, Fallsburg, Kiamisha Lake, South Fallsburg, Hurleyville, Bethel, and Woodridge. Loch Sheldrake, Parksville, Livingston Manor, and Ellenville are being prepared for 2025. Six additional markers are planned for 2026. The Borscht Belt Historical Marker Project is funded by the Jewish American Society for Historic Preservation.[^970]

#### In popular culture

The Heiden Hotel in [South Fallsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Fallsburg) was the film location of the 1987 movie *[Sweet Lorraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_Lorraine_%28film%29)* starring [Maureen Stapleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maureen_Stapleton). It was destroyed by fire in May 2008 while no longer hosting guests.[^971]

In 1987, the movie *[Dirty Dancing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirty_Dancing)* replayed the heyday of the Borscht Belt in an upscale resort. The plot was inspired by the [screenwriter's experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleanor_Bergstein) as a teenager in the summertime community at [Grossinger's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grossinger's_Catskill_Resort_Hotel).[^972]

In the 1991 graphic novel *[Maus: A Survivor's Tale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maus)*, [Art Spiegelman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_Spiegelman)'s father Vladek spends the summer in a bungalow settlement in the Catskills and visits with his son at the nearby The Pines resort.[^973]

Pamela Gray wrote the 1999 film *[A Walk on the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Walk_on_the_Moon)* inspired by her experiences at Borscht Belt bungalow colonies between 1959 and 1971.[^974]

In the second season of the series *[The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Marvelous_Mrs._Maisel)* (2017-23), both the Weissman and Maisel families spend a summer vacation at Steiner's Resort in the Catskills, depicted by Scott's Family Resort on Oquaga Lake in [Deposit, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deposit,_New_York).[^975]

[Jason Reitman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Reitman)'s 2024 historical dramedy film, *[Saturday Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday_Night_%282024_film%29)*, depicts the chaos surrounding the 1975 telecast production hassles of [Lorne Michaels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorne_Michaels) ([Gabriel LaBelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_LaBelle)) and the ensemble cast during the [series premiere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live_season_1) of *[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live)*. In one scene, [Brad Garrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Garrett) plays an unidentified Borscht Belt stand-up comedian whose routine is bombing, but whose Borscht-esque humor is being transcribed by writer [Alan Zweibel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Zweibel) (portrayed by [Josh Brener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josh_Brener)).[^976]

Elyssa Friedland's 2021 novel, *Last Summer at the Golden Hotel*, tells the story of the Goldmans and the Weingolds and their beloved but dilapidated Golden Hotel, once the crown jewel of the Catskills.

### Donald J. Trump State Park

**Donald J. Trump State Park** is a 436-acre (1.8 km²) [state park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_park) in the towns of [Yorktown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorktown,_New_York) and [Putnam Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Putnam_Valley,_New_York) in [Westchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westchester_County,_New_York) and [Putnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Putnam_County,_New_York) counties, [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_%28state%29).

The park consists of property that was donated to New York State in 2006 by the [real estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_estate) developer [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump). Maintenance of the park was halted in 2010 due to budget constraints, and the park today is a "[passive park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passive_park)".[^977] Most of the buildings have been demolished; only a few foundations and the existing [tennis court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis_court) remain. Since 2015, there have been several calls to rename the park.

#### History

Trump purchased the property in 1998 with plans to build a \$10 million private golf course. Totalling \$2.5 million, it was purchased in two sections: Indian Hill for \$1.75 million and French Hill for \$750,000.[^978] The land contained significant wetlands, and development faced strict environmental restrictions and permitting requirements.[^979] He donated it in 2006[^980][^981] after he was unable to gain town approvals to develop the property.[^979] At that time, Trump claimed the parcel was worth \$100 million.[^978] He used the donation as a [tax write-off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_write-off).[^982] In the [press release](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Press_release) announcing the donation, Governor [George Pataki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki) praised the gift, and Trump said, "I have always loved the City and State of New York and this is my way of trying to give something back. I hope that these 436 acres of property will turn into one of the most beautiful parks anywhere in the world."[^978]

New York State announced the park's closure due to budget cuts in February 2010.[^983] It was questioned whether the closure was necessary since the operating budget for the park was only \$2,500 a year and it was maintained by workers from the nearby [Franklin D. Roosevelt State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt_State_Park).[^979] Although Trump threatened to somehow revoke his donation after the closure was announced,[^979] the land remains owned by the state of New York and controlled by its [Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Office_of_Parks,_Recreation_and_Historic_Preservation).[^984]

An attempt to convert a portion of the park's French Hill section for use as a dog park in 2010 revealed that at least one of the park's abandoned buildings contained [asbestos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asbestos).[^985] By 2012, the planned dog park remained on hold due to difficulties raising funds for fences and [asbestos abatement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asbestos_abatement).[^986]

The park is not listed at the New York State Office of Parks, Recreation and Historic Preservation park locator,[^987] although signs along the nearby [Taconic State Parkway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taconic_State_Parkway) direct visitors to Donald J. Trump State Park.[^988] During a 2015 visit by *[The Rachel Maddow Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rachel_Maddow_Show)*, there were no signs of any recent upkeep; instead, the publicly accessible land was found to contain crumbling [graffiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graffiti)-covered buildings, empty map kiosks, and weed-choked parking lots.[^989]

In 2017, an article on website *[The A.V. Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_A.V._Club)* framed the park as an "abandoned wasteland", with "muddy fields, overgrown tennis courts, and dilapidated buildings" and a swimming pool in disrepair.[^990]

Park access improvements including an asphalt driveway, gravel parking lot, entrance gates, wood fencing, and native tree and shrub plantings were noticed in 2020.[^991]

#### Geography

The park is divided into two sections, the 282-acre (1.1 km²) Indian Hill parcel in northern [Jefferson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Valley,_New_York) (part of the Town of Yorktown in Westchester County) and Putnam Valley (Putnam County), and the 154-acre (0.6 km²) French Hill parcel in southern [Yorktown Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorktown_Heights,_New_York), fully within the town of Yorktown. The parkland features a mix of continuous forest, open meadows, and several large wetlands. The Indian Hill section was formerly farmland but the farm houses and other buildings were all demolished by 2004.[^978] The headwaters of two streams, French Hill Brook and Dogwood Creek, originate in the French Hill section of the park.[^980]

#### Proposals to rename

In late 2015, State Senator [Daniel Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Squadron) introduced an "Anything but Trump Act" to change the park's name.[^992] Several suggestions for a name change were offered by elected officials. Assemblyman [Charles D. Lavine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_D._Lavine) suggested that the park be named for [Peter Salem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Salem), an African American who served in the [American Revolutionary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War) and is thought by some historians to have been Muslim,[^993] while the district's U.S. Representative [Sean Patrick Maloney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Patrick_Maloney) suggested that the park be named after folk singer [Pete Seeger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Seeger).[^994] In response, Trump suggested that New York State return the park's land to his ownership.[^995] Efforts to rename the park after Pete Seeger continued in early 2016 with a petition by activist group "People for the Pete Seeger State Park" on [Change.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Change.org).[^996]

In September 2017, [New York's 25th State Assembly district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York's_25th_State_Assembly_district) Representative [Nily Rozic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nily_Rozic), a [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_%28United_States%29), suggested renaming the park in honor of Heather Heyer, who died in [a vehicle-ramming attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlottesville_car_attack) while protesting the [Unite the Right rally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unite_the_Right_rally) in [Charlottesville, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlottesville,_Virginia). No renaming of the park has been undertaken and the proposal was largely ignored.[^997] Rozic, along with New York State Senator [Brad Hoylman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Hoylman), reintroduced legislation to rename the park in 2018 but it did not make it out of committee. They again introduced legislation in 2019 to rename the park.[^998]

After the [2021 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_United_States_Capitol_attack), there were renewed attempts to rename the park, and an online petition to rename it after [Sojourner Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sojourner_Truth) (a native of nearby [Ulster County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulster_County,_New_York)) gained over 160,000 signatures.[^999] New York Assemblywoman [Sandy Galef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Galef) argued that the state should move forward with changing the park's name, arguing that "Mr. Trump did not sign the appropriate documents with the state, rendering any claim of breach of contract moot." Galef called for the park to be renamed in honor of former New York Republican governor [George Pataki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Pataki), who grew up in the area. Galef wrote, "Monuments, landmarks, and parks can hold a symbolic meaning and in this case a park named for Donald J. Trump can only represent the division he has sought to create in our country over the past four years. This division has no place in our state. Motorists have complained about the Trump signs on the Taconic for years, and we must take a stand."[^1000] The effort to rename the park failed again in 2021 after not going up for a vote before state lawmakers during the legislative session.[^1001]
