### Interstate 180 (Wyoming)

**Interstate 180** (**I-180**) is a 1.12-mile-long (1.80 km) [expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limited-access_road) in the US state of [Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wyoming) between [I-80](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_80_in_Wyoming) and downtown [Cheyenne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne,_Wyoming).[^1002]

It is unusual for being one of the few [Interstate Highways](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Highway) that does not conform to [Interstate Highway standards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_Highway_standards). There is also no [control of access](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Controlled-access_highway) anywhere along its route. Other routes in [Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alaska) and [Puerto Rico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico) are similar in nature, as they are funded by Interstate dollars but do not conform to Interstate Highway standards.[^1003] The only [grade separations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grade_separation) are a [diamond interchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond_interchange) at its southern end (at a junction with I-80) and a pair of bridges that run over 1st Street and the [Union Pacific Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Pacific_Railroad) tracks. However, even the interchange with I-80 is a standard diamond with signalized intersections. There are five [traffic signals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_signal) along I-180.

I-180 is cosigned with [I-25 Business Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_25_Business_%28Cheyenne,_Wyoming%29) (I-25 BL), [US Highway 85](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_85_in_Wyoming) (US 85), and US 87 Business (US 87 Bus.), making it the only [concurrency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concurrency_%28road%29) of an Interstate, Interstate business route, US Highway, and US Highway business route.[^1004] It is also the only [auxiliary Interstate Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary_Interstate_Highway) in Wyoming.

#### Route description

I-180 begins at a [diamond interchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond_interchange) with [I-80](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_80_in_Wyoming) in [Cheyenne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne,_Wyoming), heading north [concurrently](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concurrency_%28road%29) with [I-25 BL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_25_Business_%28Cheyenne,_Wyoming%29)/[US 85](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_85_in_Wyoming)/[US 87 Bus.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_87_Business_%28Cheyenne,_Wyoming%29) on the four-lane [divided](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divided_highway) North Greeley Highway. South of this interchange, I-25 BL/US 85/US 87 Bus. continues along North Greeley Highway. From the southern terminus, I-180 passes over Deming Drive and passes local homes and businesses. The road curves northwesterly and intersects 5th Street at a traffic light. The highway passes under a pedestrian bridge at 7th Street before crossing 9th Street at a signalized intersection. Past 9th Street, the directions of I-180 split and pass over a large [Union Pacific Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Pacific_Railroad) yard. After this bridge, I-180 reaches its northern terminus at an at-grade signalized intersection with [I-80 BL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstate_80_Business_%28Cheyenne,_Wyoming%29)/[US 30](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Route_30_in_Wyoming). Past this intersection, I-25 BL/US 85/US 87 Bus. continues north on the [one-way pairing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-way_pair) of Warren Avenue northbound and Central Avenue southbound.[^1004][^1005]

#### History

I-180 was conceived in November 1967, when Wyoming requested it for a new spur route into Cheyenne.[^1006] The [American Association of State Highway Officials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Association_of_State_Highway_Officials) added it to the Interstate Highway System in June 1970. The original plan was to have a freeway along the same corridor, with a full freeway-to-freeway interchange at I-80, but the [Federal Highway Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Highway_Administration) (FHWA) rejected it in December 1970 due to high cost and access issues.[^1006] Wyoming revised the proposal to the current configuration in February 1971, and it was approved by the FHWA that March.[^1006] I-180 opened in June 1984, after six years of expressway upgrades.[^1004]

#### Major intersections

The entire route is in [Cheyenne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne,_Wyoming), [Laramie County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laramie_County,_Wyoming).

### Maharishi Vedic City, Iowa

**Maharishi Vedic City** (MVC) is a city in [Jefferson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_County,_Iowa), [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa), United States. The population was 277 at the time of the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_Census).[^1008] The city was incorporated in 2001 as "Vedic City" but then officially changed its name to "Maharishi Vedic City" five months later. It was the first city to incorporate in Iowa since 1982.[^1009] Maharishi Vedic City consists of approximately three square miles, located about four miles north of [Fairfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfield,_Iowa), the home of [Maharishi University of Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharishi_University_of_Management).[^1010]

The city plan and buildings are based on Maharishi Sthapatya Veda,[^1011][^1012] which is said to be an ancient system of architecture and design, revived by [Maharishi Mahesh Yogi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharishi_Mahesh_Yogi).[^1013] Its goals are to "protect, nourish, and satisfy everyone, upholding the different social, cultural, and religious traditions while maintaining the integrity and progress of the city as a whole".[^1014]

#### History

The concept of a "Vedic City" was conceived by the Maharishi,[^1012] and a real estate developer and several others began to actualize the vision for a [Vedic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedas) town in 1991. The first resolution of the city council proclaimed the constitution of the city to be the same as "the Constitution of the Universe, Total Natural Law, RK Veda".[^1014]

More than a dozen developers purchased 50 farms totaling 3,000 acres (12 km²), some 1,200 of which were designated for the town itself.[^1009] Together, they planned a city arranged in ten circles totaling about one square mile, along with paved roads, utilities, sewage and Internet. They then began the first phase of construction, which included two hotels, various houses and office buildings. After one year, 46 structures had been built and more than \$35 million spent on development.[^1015] Financial and infrastructure needs led the developers to seek formal designation as a city from the state, and after petitioning the Iowa City Development Board and holding a [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendum),[^1009] it was incorporated as Iowa's newest city on July 25, 2001, the first in Iowa since 1982.[^1016] Planners expected the city to have a population of over 1,000 by 2010, many of them transplants from nearby [Fairfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfield,_Iowa).[^1009] In the early stages of development, Vedic City set aside 50 acres as land for conservation and preservation. This acreage was then transformed from farmers' fields to native prairies, wetlands and forest.[^1017]

In 2002, a building known as "The Mansion" became a headquarters for the [Global Country of World Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Country_of_World_Peace) (GCWP).[^1018] The Mayor of MVC is Rogers Badgett.

According to city officials in 2004, "more than \$200 million of venture capital had been invested in Fairfield and Vedic City companies during the past 13 years".[^1019] By 2006, the city consisted of more than 200 buildings.[^1010]

In October 2011,[^1020][^1021] a television show titled "America's Most Unusual Town" aired on the [Oprah Winfrey Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oprah_Winfrey_Network) on March 25, 2012, and featured Winfrey's visit to Fairfield and Maharishi Vedic City.[^1022][^1023]

#### Organic economy

In November 2002, the [city council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_council) passed an [ordinance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_ordinance) banning the sale of non-[organic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_production) food within its borders.[^1024]

In 2003, the city began offering tours to the public and has several thousand visitors per year.[^1010][^1025] The city has an organic farm and sells produce to retail outlets such as the [Whole Foods Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market).[^1019] Maharishi Vedic City, and the nearby town of Fairfield, "receive federal grants from agencies including the Departments of Energy and Agriculture for developing renewable energy sources" and recycling programs.[^1019]

The city council voted to ban the use of synthetic pesticides and fertilizers within the city limits in April 2005, becoming the first all-organic city in the country.[^1010]

#### Geography

According to the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau), the city has a total area of 3.36 square miles (8.70 km²), all land.[^1026]

##### 2020 census

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_census) of 2020,[^1028] there were 277 people, 159 households, and 73 families residing in the city. The [population density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density) was 82.9 inhabitants per square mile (32.0/km²). There were 178 housing units at an average density of 53.3 per square mile (20.6/km²). The [racial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_and_ethnicity_in_the_United_States_census) makeup of the city was 84.5% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Americans), 5.4% [Black or African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans), 0.0% [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States), 5.1% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_Americans), 0.4% [Pacific Islander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Islander_Americans), 1.4% from other races and 3.2% from two or more races. [Hispanic or Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_and_Latino_Americans) people of any race comprised 2.2% of the population.

Of the 159 households, 10.1% of which had children under the age of 18 living with them, 32.1% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage) living together, 4.4% were cohabitating couples, 39.6% had a female householder with no spouse or partner present and 23.9% had a male householder with no spouse or partner present. 54.1% of all households were non-families. 49.1% of all households were made up of individuals, 28.3% had someone living alone who was 65 years old or older.

The median age in the city was 67.9 years. 6.5% of the residents were under the age of 20; 2.9% were between the ages of 20 and 24; 10.1% were from 25 and 44; 16.2% were from 45 and 64; and 64.3% were 65 years of age or older. The gender makeup of the city was 47.3% male and 52.7% female.

##### 2010 census

The [Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census_Bureau) has since done a recount for the 2010 census.[^1029]

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census)[^1030] of 2010, there were 259 people, 142 households, and 48 families residing in the city. The [population density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density) was 77.1 inhabitants per square mile (29.8/km²). There were 174 housing units at an average density of 51.8 per square mile (20.0/km²). The racial makeup of the city was 95.0% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_%28U.S._Census%29), 2.3% [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_%28U.S._Census%29), 1.5% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_%28U.S._Census%29), and 1.2% from two or more races. [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_%28U.S._Census%29) or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_%28U.S._Census%29) people of any race were 1.9% of the population.

There were 142 households, out of which 2.8% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 30.3% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage) living together, 2.1% had a female householder with no husband present, 1.4% had a male householder with no wife present, and 66.2% were non-families. 47.9% of all households were made up of individuals, and 7.7% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 1.74 and the average family size was 2.33.

The median age in the city was 57.8 years. 2.3% of residents were under the age of 18; 5.4% were between the ages of 18 and 24; 12.3% were from 25 to 44; 69.1% were from 45 to 64; and 10.8% were 65 years of age or older. The gender makeup of the city was 49.8% male and 50.2% female.

#### Features

Maharishi Vedic City utilizes a system of building called Maharishi Sthapatya Veda design architecture.[^1012] This ancient [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India) system of architecture and city planning is said to promote happiness, peace and prosperity for its occupants.[^1010][^1012] In Maharishi Sthapatya Veda, all structures are built according to precise Vedic proportions, with rooms placed according to the movement of the sun and entrances that face due east.[^1010][^1012] In addition, each building includes an interior, silent core called a "brahmasthan", a perimeter boundary called a "vastu fence" and a gold-colored roof fixture called a "kalash".[^1031][^1032]

One of the unique features of the city is an outdoor Vedic Observatory consisting of ten six-feet-tall, white, concrete-and-marble astronomical instruments arranged in a circle.[^1032] According to the observatory developer, Tim Fitz-Randolph, each instrument is precisely aligned with the sun, moon and stars, and could be used to calculate their actual movements and has the potential to create inner happiness and balance in the physiology.[^1009][^1032]

The city also owns and operates a 160-acre (0.65 km²) organic farm which includes a 1.2-acre (4,900 m²) greenhouse. A wind turbine provides electricity for the greenhouses and was paid for in part by a USDA renewable energy grant.[^1017] The farm distributes its "50 varieties of fruits and vegetables" locally as well as to restaurants in [Iowa City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_City), [Des Moines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Moines) and Chicago. The city has plans to expand the greenhouses to 70 acres (280,000 m²). The city does not have any streetlights or [utility poles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_poles) and its master plan includes only electric cars within the city limits. The city council has voted to provide its residents with "off-grid power" from wind and solar generated power.[^1032]

A Maharishi Ayur-Veda Spa Center and Hotel called "The Raj" is located in MVC on a 100-acre (0.40 km²) estate with gardens, lakes and nature trails. It offers a variety of treatments in accordance with the [Maharishi Vedic Approach to Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maharishi_Vedic_Approach_to_Health). The city also features the Rukmapura Park Hotel, a "25-room wood structure in the tradition of European country inns".[^1009][^1032]

The 2001 master plan includes two domes in the center of the city to serve as a venue for group practice of the Transcendental Meditation technique and the [TM-Sidhi program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TM-Sidhi_program), including [Yogic Flying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yogic_Flying). Residents subscribe to the theory and research that group practice of this technique "will create coherence for the whole country".[^1009] In 2006, a *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times)* reporter wrote that the city "displays all the architectural characteristics of a new exurban development: gaudy, over sized construction that has no stylistic relation to its environment."[^1033] A 2010 article reported that city officials were working with [Tom Doak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Doak) on the construction of a public golf course.[^1034]

#### Government

The city has a commitment to balance, [natural law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_law), and the principles of the [Vedas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedas), which are the [ancient sacred scriptures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_texts) of [Hinduism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism) written in [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit).[^1024] Maharishi Vedic City is administered by a five-person city council.[^1035]

### Northwest Angle

The **Northwest Angle**, known simply as **the Angle** by locals, and coextensive with **Angle Township**, is a [pene-exclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pene-exclave) of northern [Lake of the Woods County, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_of_the_Woods_County,_Minnesota).[^1036] Excluding surveying errors,[^1037] it is the only place in the contiguous United States north of the [49th parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/49th_parallel_north), which forms the border between the U.S. and [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada) from the Northwest Angle westward to the [Strait of Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strait_of_Georgia) (between the U.S. state of [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_%28state%29) and the Canadian province of [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia)). The land area of the Angle is separated from the rest of Minnesota by [Lake of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_of_the_Woods), but shares a land border with the Canadian province of [Manitoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoba).[^1036] It is one of [six non-island locations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada%E2%80%93United_States_border) in the 48 contiguous states that are [practical exclaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enclave_and_exclave) of the United States; three others are nearby in the vicinity of [Elm Point, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elm_Point,_Minnesota). The communities of [Oak Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Island_%28Minnesota%29), [Angle Inlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle_Inlet,_Minnesota) and [Penasse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penasse,_Minnesota) are in the Northwest Angle, as is the [Fort Saint Charles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Saint_Charles) archeological site.

Seventy percent of the land of the Angle is held in trust by the [Red Lake Indian Reservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Lake_Indian_Reservation) ([Ojibwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ojibwe_people)).[^1038]

The Angle is listed as one of several distinct [regions of Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_Minnesota), and is the smallest of those regions, with a total population of 149 at the [2020 United States Census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_Census),[^1039] up from 119 in 2010.[^1040] The area is mostly water and the land is mostly forest.

#### Origin

Angle Township was designated as territory of the United States because negotiators of the initial [Canada-U.S. border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada%E2%80%93United_States_border) misunderstood the geography of the area. [Benjamin Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin) and British representatives relied on the [Mitchell Map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitchell_Map) of colonial American geographer [John Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mitchell_%28geographer%29), which did not indicate the source of the [Mississippi River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River), thought to lie some distance to the northwest, or the true shape of [Lake of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_of_the_Woods), which was instead shown as roughly oval. The 1783 [Treaty of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_%281783%29) thus stated that the boundary between U.S. territory and the [British possessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_possessions) to the north would run "...through the Lake of the Woods to the [northwesternmost point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_point_of_the_Lake_of_the_Woods) thereof, and from thence on a due west course to the [river Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River)..."

But the source of the Mississippi River, [Lake Itasca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Itasca) (then unknown to European explorers), lies almost due south of Lake of the Woods, rather than north and west of it. Additionally, the irregular actual shape of the lake made the identification of its northwest corner difficult. By the time of the [Jay Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Treaty) of 1794, there was concern that the Mississippi did not go far enough north, and so as part of that treaty it was decided that a joint survey of the river would be conducted, and if it did not extend far enough north that new, "amicable negotiations" would be undertaken to set the boundary in accordance with the intent of the Treaty of Paris. In 1797, it was confirmed when [David Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Thompson_%28explorer%29), an explorer, located the most northerly source of the Mississippi a few miles north of Bemidji, which is south of Lake of the Woods.[^1041]

When the [Treaty of Ghent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Ghent) was signed in 1814, it again tried to settle the boundary, this time by creating a commission that would settle on the northwestern point of the Lake of the Woods. The British had suggested setting the boundary to run west from Lake Superior to Lake Itasca, the headwaters of the Mississippi, but the Americans were unwilling to cede any land at that point. As part of the negotiations over that treaty, both parties agreed to revisit the boundary west from the Lake of the Woods.[^1041]

By the time [Richard Rush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Rush) became the U.S. secretary of state in 1817, settlers were beginning to move to the lands west of the Lake of the Woods and both sides saw a need to settle the boundary west of the 1783 line. In the [Anglo-American Convention of 1818](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-American_Convention_of_1818), the error regarding the Mississippi River was corrected by having the boundary continue due north or south (“as the case may be”) from the northwest point of the lake (which had still not been determined) to the [49th parallel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/49th_parallel_north) and then due west along the parallel.

To determine the northwesternmost point of the lake a survey team was sent in 1822, but they failed to come to an answer. Another survey team, led by David Thompson in 1824, mapped the lake and found four possibilities for the northwesternmost point, but did not conclusively declare one location.[^1042] In 1825, a German astronomer in British service, Johann Ludwig Tiarks, surveyed the lake. Tiarks identified two possibilities for the northwesternmost point on the lake, based on Thompson's maps: the Angle Inlet and Rat Portage. To determine which point was the most northwestern, he drew a line from each point in the southwest-northeast direction. If the line intersected the lake at any point, it was not the most northwestern point. Tiarks determined that the only such line that did not intersect the lake was at the edge of a pond on the Angle Inlet.[^1042] A 1940 academic study documents this point as being in the vicinity of [49°23′24″N 95°09′11″W / 49.39°N 95.153°W](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Northwest_Angle&params=49.39_N_95.153_W_) ([NAD83](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAD83)).[^1043]

The [Webster-Ashburton Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webster%E2%80%93Ashburton_Treaty) of 1842 reaffirmed this border and established the exact location of the northwesternmost point of the lake. The placement of the northwestern corner and shape of the lake meant that this north-south line cut off a section of U.S. territory to its east, now known as the Northwest Angle.

#### Geography

According to the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau), Angle Township has a total area of 596.3 square miles (1,544 km²), of which 123.09 square miles (318.8 km²) is land and 473.2 square miles (1,226 km²) (79.36%) is water. The land includes several islands, including [Oak Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_Island_%28Minnesota%29), and two small capes that are below (south of) the [49th parallel north](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/49th_parallel_north) in the extreme southwest part of the township, one of which is known as [Elm Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elm_Point,_Minnesota), south of the southeast corner of [Manitoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoba), and not far from the northeast corner of [Roseau County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseau_County,_Minnesota). Of the [2000 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census,_2000) population of 152, there were 118 living on the mainland, and 34 persons on the islands in [Lake of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_of_the_Woods). All of the populated islands are north of the 49th parallel.

The mainland portion of the township north of the 49th parallel has an area of 116.632 square miles (302.08 km²). The total land area of all islands is 6.303 square miles (16.32 km²), and the two capes total 100 acres (0.16 sq mi; 40.47 ha). The township has the last [one-room public school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-room_school) in the state.

[Elm Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elm_Point,_Minnesota), in Lake of the Woods County, is a small cape southwest of the Northwest Angle. It borders Canada and is, together with a similar smaller cape to the west, separated by land from the continental United States.

##### Access

The Angle is accessible from the rest of Minnesota by one of two ways:

- The Angle can be reached without crossing the international border by crossing the [Lake of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_of_the_Woods). This can be done by boat when the lake is free of ice, by [ice road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_road) in the winter or by flying over it in a plane. No automobile ferries currently operate on the lake, so vehicles coming from the rest of Minnesota cannot reach the Angle without crossing the border except in winter. While the ice is forming in late autumn and breaking up in the spring, the lake's surface cannot be crossed safely - at these times domestic access to the Angle is possible only by air. In January 2021, local U.S. interests opened a 22-mile (35 km) toll road across the ice, at a round-trip charge of US\$120 to \$145, because the Canadian border was closed by [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic) restrictions. It was again opened, and lengthened to 37 miles (60 km) of road, in January 2022, and the toll set at \$250.[^1044]
- To reach the Angle by land, travelers take [Minnesota State Highway 313](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_State_Highway_313) northbound ([Warroad, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warroad,_Minnesota), to [Sprague, Manitoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprague,_Manitoba)) across the [Warroad-Sprague Border Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warroad-Sprague_Border_Crossing)[^1045] connecting to [Manitoba Highway 12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoba_Highway_12) at the border, then to [Provincial Road 308](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoba_Provincial_Road_308), to [Provincial Road 525](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manitoba_Provincial_Road_525), then finally crossing back into the United States in the Northwest Angle south of [Angle Inlet, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle_Inlet,_Minnesota) (Angle Inlet Township). The distance from Warroad or [Roseau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseau,_Minnesota) to the Angle proper is approximately 63 miles (101 km) through Minnesota and Manitoba back to the Angle's U.S. border. It is approximately 10 miles (16 km) from the actual border (intersection of Manitoba 525 and NWA Road Dawson) to the rural developments of the Northwest Angle.

The border crossing is unstaffed. Travelers using the single gravel road into the Angle are instructed to use an iPad kiosk at Jim's Corner,[^1036][^1046] Young's Bay Marina, or Carlson's Landing to contact [U.S. Customs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Customs_and_Border_Protection). Exiting the Angle, travelers use a telephone at the same locations to contact [Canadian Customs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_Border_Services_Agency) to make their declarations. After checking in via either direction, travelers are provided a case number to reference in the event they are questioned.

#### Political issues

Because of laws restricting fishing, some residents of the Northwest Angle suggested leaving the United States and joining Canada in 1997.[^1036] The following year, then-U.S. representative [Collin Peterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Peterson) of Minnesota proposed legislation to allow the residents of the Northwest Angle, which was part of his district, to vote on seceding from the United States and joining Canada. This angered the leaders of [Red Lake Indian Reservation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Lake_Indian_Reservation), which holds most of the Northwest Angle's land.[^1047][^1048] The incident resulted in fishing regulations being better synchronized across these waters.[^1049]

#### Demographics

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census)[^1050] of 2010, there were 119 people, 66 households, and 37 families residing in the Angle. There were 404 housing units. The racial makeup of the township was 99.2% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_and_ethnicity_in_the_United_States_Census). [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_and_ethnicity_in_the_United_States_Census) or [Alaska Native](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_and_ethnicity_in_the_United_States_Census) of any race were 0.8% of the population.

Out of the 66 households, 10.9% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 54.5% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage) living together, 0% had a female householder with no husband present, and 43.9% were non-families. 37.9% of all households were made up of individuals, and 3% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 1.80, and the average family size was 2.32.

In the Angle the age distribution is 10.1% under the age of 18, 0.8% from 18 to 24, 10.1% from 25 to 44, 51.3% from 45 to 64, and 27.6% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 50 years. For every 100 females, there were 120.3 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 124.1 males.

The median income for a household in the township was \$28,500, and the median income for a family was \$31,250. Males had a median income of \$28,500 versus \$21,250 for females. The [per capita income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita_income) for the township was \$13,932. About 13.3% of families and 12.3% of the population were below the [poverty line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_line), including none of those under the age of 18 or 65 and older.

#### Climate

According to the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification) system, the Northwest Angle has a Warm-summer, [Humid continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate) (*Dfb*). *Dfb* climates are characterized by at least one month having an average mean temperature ≤ 32.0 °F (0.0 °C), at least four months with an average mean temperature ≥ 50.0 °F (10.0 °C), all months with an average mean temperature \< 71.6 °F (22.0 °C) and no significant precipitation difference between seasons. Although most summer days are comfortably humid in the Northwest Angle, episodes of heat and high humidity can occur with [heat index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_index) values \> 90 °F (32 °C). The Northwest Angle weather station is one of the newer ones, as it only began keeping records in 1981, in contrast with nearby [International Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Falls) which has been keeping records for over a century. Since 1981, the highest air temperature was 96.8 °F (36.0 °C) on July 5, 1988, and the highest daily average mean [dew point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dew_point) was 73.1 °F (22.8 °C) on August 4, 2001. Since 1981, the wettest calendar day was 4.11 inches (104 mm) on June 9, 2002. During the winter months, the average annual extreme minimum air temperature is −38.0 °F (−38.9 °C),[^1051] putting it in hardiness zone 3a. Since 1981, the coldest air temperature was −47.3 °F (−44.1 °C) on February 2, 2002. Episodes of extreme cold and wind can occur with [wind chill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_chill) values under −55 °F (−48 °C). The average annual snowfall total (Sep-May) is between 48 inches (122 cm) and 54 inches (137 cm).

#### Ecology

According to the [A. W. Kuchler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._W._Kuchler) U.S. [potential natural vegetation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potential_natural_vegetation) types, the Northwest Angle would have a dominant vegetation type of Great Lakes [Spruce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spruce)/[Fir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fir) (*93*) with a dominant vegetation form of Northern [Conifer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conifer) Forest (*22*).[^1053] The [plant hardiness zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plant_hardiness_zone) is 3a with an average annual extreme minimum air temperature of −38.0 °F (−38.9 °C).[^1051] The spring bloom typically peaks in mid-May and fall color usually peaks in late September.

#### Representation in other media

- [Ernie Pyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernie_Pyle) wrote several columns about the Northwest Angle and its residents, which were collected in *[Home Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Country_%28book%29)* (1947), published posthumously.
- The American writer [Tim O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_O'Brien_%28author%29) set his bestselling novel *[In the Lake of the Woods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Lake_of_the_Woods)* (1994) in the Angle. His short story "On the Rainy River" is also set there.
- [William Kent Krueger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kent_Krueger)'s novel *Northwest Angle* (2011) is set in the area.
- The [Danny Orlis series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Orlis_series) of books, a Christian fiction series for youth, were largely set in the Northwest Angle.

### Sam Kee Building

The **Sam Kee Building** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters): 三記號大樓), also known as the **Jack Chow Insurance Building**, is a two-storey commercial building in [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver), British Columbia, Canada, located near the entrance to [the city's Chinatown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinatown,_Vancouver). It is noted for its narrow depth, which varies by floor. The ground floor is 4 feet 11 inches (1.50 m) wide, while the upper floor spans 6 feet (1.8 m) because of its overhanging bay windows. Additionally, a basement extends under the sidewalk adjacent to the storefront. This discrepancy has led to a dispute with the [Skinny Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skinny_Building) in [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh), Pennsylvania, over which commercial building is more narrow, as the Skinny Building has a consistent depth of 5 feet 2 inches (1.57 m). Nonetheless, the Sam Kee Building is recognized by *[Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records)* as the narrowest commercial building in the world and by *[Ripley's Believe It or Not!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripley's_Believe_It_or_Not!)* as the world's thinnest building.

The building was constructed as a [spite house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spite_house) in 1913, in defiance of [Vancouver City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver_City_Council)'s decision to [expropriate without compensation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminent_domain) a lot belonging to local [business magnate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_magnate) Chang Toy, also known as "Sam Kee". Located at the corner of Carrall Street and Pender Street, the depth of the original lot was reduced from roughly 30 feet (9.1 m) to 6 feet (1.8 m) for the widening of the latter street. Chang bet a business associate that he could construct a building on the land that remained and the Sam Kee Building was completed a year later. It originally consisted of a ground floor housing retail shops, an upper floor housing residential and organizational units, and a basement containing [public baths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_bathing).

Local businessman Jack Chow purchased the Sam Kee Building in 1985 and restored the property the following year. The building has since become a tourist attraction, although an insurance business still operates on the ground floor. It is considered a cultural heritage site by the municipal government and is listed in the [Canadian Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Register_of_Historic_Places).

#### Architecture

The Sam Kee Building is a [steel-framed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel_frame), two-storey building with an unusually narrow depth.[^1054][^1055][^1056] Its ground-floor depth measures 4 feet 11 inches (1.50 m).[^1057] Its upper-floor depth is wider at 6 feet (1.8 m) due to its overhanging bay windows.[^1057] Bay windows were a common Western feature of late 19th-century and early 20th-century Chinatown structures (the Sam Kee Building was built in 1913) because they increased interior floor space.[^1057][^1058] The building also has a basement that extends 10 feet (3.0 m) under the sidewalk of Pender Street.[^1057] The three floors are connected by glass staircases, which the municipal government disapproves of because they are a potential fire hazard.[^1056]

##### Dispute with Vancouver City Council

Local historians have described the Sam Kee Building as a "[spite house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spite_house)", a building constructed or modified to anger neighbours or other stakeholders.[^1054][^1059] The municipal government previously charged the building's owner - the Sam Kee Company and later Jack Chow Insurance - annual encroachment fees for the airspace used by the protruding windows and the under-street area used by the basement.[^1060]

In November 1996, [Vancouver City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver_City_Council) voted to retroactively reduce the encroachment fees, but Jack Chow Insurance responded by refusing to pay the fees and applied for them to be waived altogether. In support of their application, the company cited the building's heritage value and status as a tourist attraction and *[Guinness World Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records)* holder.[^1061] City council voted to waive the [CA\$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_dollar)2,500 fee for the basement in November 1998 and the CA\$260 fee for the windows in December.[^1060][^1061][^1062] Rod Chow, son of Jack Chow, described the latter decision as "the moral support of \[city\] council" being given to the building and the hopeful end of an "85-year feud".[^1060] Before their final vote on the matter, city council acknowledged the main argument against the waiver, that because Jack Chow Insurance was "us\[ing\] the encroachment space to generate revenue", a waiver would therefore be against "the principles of equity amongst similar uses ... for commercial activities on city property".[^1061]

#### History

Vancouver's Chinatown was home to the largest [Chinese community in Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Canadians) during the early 1900s, with 3,559 residents listed in the [1911 national census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1911_Canadian_census).[^1063] The [Vancouver Asiatic Exclusion League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asiatic_Exclusion_League), an all-European [lobbyist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobbying) group opposed to immigration from Asia, was established in 1907 with the goal of expelling Asians from the city.[^1064] In 1912, the league convinced Vancouver City Council to widen Pender Street, the [main street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_street) of Chinatown at the time, in order to render Chinese-owned lots on the street unsuitable for commercial use.[^1064][^1065] One such lot, located at the corner of Carrall Street and Pender Street, was owned by local businessman Chang Toy (陳才; 1857-1921), known in the [European community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Canadians) as "Sam Kee" (三記).[^1054][^1055][^1066][^1067]

Chang purchased the original, standard-sized lot for his primary business, the Sam Kee Company, in 1903.[^1068] The original lot was a [trapezoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trapezoid) measuring 30 by 88.71 by 30.94 by 96.04 feet (9.14 m × 27.04 m × 9.43 m × 29.27 m).[^1069] Its southern and eastern sides were slightly longer than its northern and western sides, respectively.[^1069] By 1907, the Sam Kee Company had become one of the four main firms operating in Chinatown. It operated an extensive import-export business that involved members of the [Anglo-European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Canadians) business establishment.[^1066]

In 1912, Vancouver City Council [expropriated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eminent_domain) most of the lot without compensating Chang. The width of the lot was reduced from roughly 30 feet (9.1 m) to 6 feet (1.8 m), making conventional commercial use of the remaining frontage impractical.[^1055][^1068] However, Chang bet a business associate that he could nonetheless construct a building on what remained of his lot.[^1054]

Chang hired architects Kennerly Bryan and William C. F. Gillam, eponymous partners of the Bryan & Gillam firm, to design a building for his narrow lot.[^1055][^1064][^1070] On March 27, 1913, a building permit was issued for a building "6.19 feet in width, 96.04 feet in length".[^1071] The Sam Kee Building was completed later that year and reportedly cost CA\$8,000.[^1072] For half a century, the Sam Kee Building saw mixed commercial-residential use. Retail shops were located on the ground floor, while the upper floor housed units for residential and organizational use.[^1055] The basement contained public baths.[^1073]

Local businessman Jack Wing Chow (周永職; 1930-2021) purchased the Sam Kee Building in 1985.[^1074][^1054][^1075] Chow hired architect Soren Rasmussen to restore the building, and the renovations, which cost CA\$250,000, were completed in 1986.[^1060][^1073] Reinforced glass blocks were built into the sidewalk in front of the building, with the approval of Vancouver City Council.[^1060] During nighttime, lights in the basement illuminate the sidewalk above, marking the entrance to Chinatown.[^1056][^1060] Chow later received numerous heritage awards for his restoration initiative.[^1076]

At present, the ground floor is used for insurance sales by Jack Chow Insurance, while the upper floor and basement are used primarily for tourism purposes. Most of the decorations and furniture inside the building are either "skinny or mini" to match the building's self-given title of "skinniest building in the world".[^1056] In 2013, the building was given a million-dollar renovation. The project was financed by Jack Chow's retirement funds and a CA\$100,000 grant from the municipal government.[^1077] A glass window wicket was installed in 2016, allowing customers to be served on the sidewalk in front of the building and doubling the building's business capacity.[^1054]

#### Recognition

The Sam Kee Building holds the *[Guinness World Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records)* for the narrowest commercial building in the world.[^1054][^1078] *[Ripley's Believe it or Not!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ripley's_Believe_it_or_Not!)*, meanwhile, recognizes it as the world's thinnest building.[^1079] The ownership of these titles has been challenged by the owners of the [Skinny Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skinny_Building) in [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh), Pennsylvania, United States. The Skinny Building has a depth of 5 feet 2 inches (1.57 m) on all its floors, while the depth of the Sam Kee Building varies by floor, with the lower floor's depth measuring 4 feet 11 inches (1.50 m) but the upper floor's measuring 6 feet (1.8 m).[^1057][^1079]

The municipal government formally recognized the Sam Kee Building as a cultural heritage site on January 14, 2003.[^1055] It is listed number 2814 in the [Canadian Register of Historic Places](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Register_of_Historic_Places).[^1055] Vancouver City Council's Chinatown Legacy Stewardship Group described the Sam Kee Building as a "key part of Chinatown's cultural heritage" and Jack Chow Insurance as a "legacy business".[^1054]

The Sam Kee Building was one of two winners of the People's Choice Award for the 2017 Vancouver Heritage Awards, the other being the Mah Society Building. The award's description of the Sam Kee Building is as follows:[^1080]

> Fully restored and revitalized, the thinnest building in the world, and a Chinatown landmark and architectural marvel, its rehabilitation was part of the celebration of its centennial. This included its distinctive gold embellished columns, the prominent '1913' on its parapet, its continuous bay-windows, its block-long illuminated glass sidewalk, and iconic twinkling neon sign for the public to enjoy.

### Zilwaukee, Michigan

**Zilwaukee** is a city in [Saginaw County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saginaw_County) in the [U.S. state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._state) of [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan). The [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census) places the population at 1,534. The city is adjacent to and was created from [Zilwaukee Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zilwaukee_Township). It is the home of the [Zilwaukee Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zilwaukee_Bridge).

#### History

Zilwaukee was founded in 1848 when [Daniel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Johnson_%28Michigan_politician%29) and Solomon Johnson, two brothers from [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City), built a saw mill there.

The provenance of the town's name is unknown, but local legends hold that it was a deliberate attempt to attract immigrants who thought they were heading for the larger [Milwaukee, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee,_Wisconsin).[^1081]

#### Geography

According to the [United States Census Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Census_Bureau), the city has a total area of 2.37 square miles (6.14 km²), of which 2.21 square miles (5.72 km²) is land and 0.16 square miles (0.41 km²) is water.[^1082]

##### 2020 census

As of the [2020 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_census), Zilwaukee had a population of 1,534. The median age was 45.7 years. 18.1% of residents were under the age of 18 and 20.8% of residents were 65 years of age or older. For every 100 females there were 101.0 males, and for every 100 females age 18 and over there were 97.6 males age 18 and over.[^1084][^1085]

100.0% of residents lived in urban areas, while 0.0% lived in rural areas.[^1086]

There were 685 households in Zilwaukee, of which 22.5% had children under the age of 18 living in them. Of all households, 45.1% were married-couple households, 19.6% were households with a male householder and no spouse or partner present, and 26.0% were households with a female householder and no spouse or partner present. About 30.8% of all households were made up of individuals and 12.9% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older.[^1084]

There were 721 housing units, of which 5.0% were vacant. The homeowner vacancy rate was 0.6% and the rental vacancy rate was 6.0%.[^1084]

##### 2010 census

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census)[^1087] of 2010, there were 1,658 people, 671 households, and 442 families living in the city. The [population density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density) was 750.2 inhabitants per square mile (289.7/km²). There were 723 housing units at an average density of 327.1 per square mile (126.3/km²). The racial makeup of the city was 92.3% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_%28U.S._Census%29), 3.7% [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_%28U.S._Census%29), 0.5% [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_%28U.S._Census%29), 0.3% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_%28U.S._Census%29), 1.6% from [other races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_%28U.S._Census%29), and 1.6% from two or more races. [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_%28U.S._Census%29) or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_%28U.S._Census%29) of any race were 7.7% of the population.

There were 671 households, of which 30.4% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 50.1% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage) living together, 10.7% had a female householder with no husband present, 5.1% had a male householder with no wife present, and 34.1% were non-families. 27.3% of all households were made up of individuals, and 12.2% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.47 and the average family size was 2.97.

The median age in the city was 40 years. 22.1% of residents were under the age of 18; 9.8% were between the ages of 18 and 24; 25.8% were from 25 to 44; 25.6% were from 45 to 64; and 16.6% were 65 years of age or older. The gender makeup of the city was 49.8% male and 50.2% female.

##### 2000 census

As of the [census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census) of 2000,[^1088] there were 1,799 people, 711 households, and 509 families living in the city. The population density was 810.7 inhabitants per square mile (313.0/km²). There were 729 housing units at an average density of 328.5 per square mile (126.8/km²). The racial makeup of the city was 93.94% [White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_%28U.S._Census%29), 1.78% [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American_%28U.S._Census%29), 0.44% [Native American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_%28U.S._Census%29), 0.50% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_%28U.S._Census%29), 2.61% from [other races](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_%28United_States_Census%29), and 0.72% from two or more races. [Hispanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispanic_%28U.S._Census%29) or [Latino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_%28U.S._Census%29) of any race were 6.23% of the population.

There were 711 households, out of which 28.1% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 57.8% were [married couples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage) living together, 10.4% had a female householder with no husband present, and 28.3% were non-families. 22.9% of all households were made up of individuals, and 9.1% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.53 and the average family size was 2.98.

In the city, the population was spread out, with 23.5% under the age of 18, 6.7% from 18 to 24, 31.2% from 25 to 44, 24.5% from 45 to 64, and 14.2% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 37 years. For every 100 females, there were 95.3 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 93.7 males.

The [per capita income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita_income) for the city was \$19,491. About 5.7% of families and 6.4% of the population were below the [poverty line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_line), including 10.4% of those under age 18 and 5.8% of those age 65 or over.

### Montague Street Bridge

The **Montague Street Bridge** is a [railway bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_bridge) in [South Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Melbourne), Australia, an [inner suburb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_suburb) of [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne,_Australia). The bridge is located at 83 Montague Street, between Woodgate Street and Gladstone Lane.

The bridge has a very low height clearance of 3 metres or 9 feet 10 inches, and despite prominent signage warning tall vehicles not to approach, drivers who miscalculate the height of their vehicles frequently collide with and sometimes become wedged under the bridge. Frequent [bridge strikes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_strike) have made the bridge a local landmark and the subject of much humorous media discussion.

#### History

Construction firm [Johns & Waygood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_&_Waygood) was contracted to build the bridge in 1914[^1091] as part of the infrastructure of the [Port Melbourne railway line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Melbourne_railway_line). [Montague Railway Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montague_railway_station) was located just south of the bridge and mainly served workers at nearby factories.

Flooding on Montague Street was a perennial problem; in 1916, the area around the bridge was under a foot of water and pedestrians could not approach it.[^1092] In 1934, South Melbourne council raised the underlying street level by about two feet, thus reducing the clearance height of the bridge.[^1093]

The last passenger train ran to Montague station on 10 October 1987 after it was announced that the line would be converted to [light rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_rail). The replacement light rail line was officially opened on 18 December 1987.[^1094] Currently the bridge carries trams along [route 109](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_tram_route_109) between Box Hill and Port Melbourne.

The bridge has a long history of vehicle collisions. In 2016 'Patrick' from Epping, a caller to [Jon Faine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Faine)'s ABC radio program, reported having witnessed a vehicle hit the bridge in 1929, aged seven. "I was there … and a truck got stuck under that bridge," he recalled. "I said to them, 'why don't you let his tyres down?'," adding that inflatable tyres were only new at the time.[^1095]

Meanwhile, 'Tony' from Blackburn, who managed the South Melbourne branch of a vehicle hire business during the 1970s, recalled that five or six trucks from his branch would hit the bridge each year. "How long does it take to get something done?" Tony rhetorically asked Faine.[^1095]

#### Notable crashes

On 22 February 2016, a 3.6-metre-high (12 ft) passenger bus carrying attendees of a conference at the nearby [Melbourne Convention and Exhibition Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Convention_and_Exhibition_Centre) attempted to drive under the bridge and hit it at 56 km/h (35 mph). The impact peeled back the roof of the bus to the fifth row of seats. The driver, Jack Aston, was seriously injured, along with four women and two men, who suffered injuries including head and spinal fractures, broken collarbones and facial lacerations.[^1096] Aston was convicted of negligently causing serious injury and sentenced to five years' imprisonment, but was released in 2019 after serving 10 months of the sentence when the charges were downgraded on appeal.[^1097]

Another bus owned by the same company had previously crashed into the bridge in March 2006, but the company did not have a policy to tell its drivers to avoid the area.[^1098]

On 20 June 2018, dashcam footage captured the moment a truck slammed into the bridge.[^1099]

#### Official responses

Following the February 2016 bus crash Victorian Premier [Daniel Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Andrews) posted on [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook) that the bridge "is fearless. It is formidable … It remains undefeated". The Victorian Government estimated that year that each collision caused \$100,000 worth of costs to the Victorian economy due to the resulting traffic delays. In addition, the cost of emergency services callouts and repairing the bridge after each collision is approximately \$30,000.[^1100]

In June 2016, the Victorian state government installed two warning [gantries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gantry_%28road_sign%29) on the two main approaches to the bridge on Normanby Road and City Road. Black and yellow paddles hang from the gantries to the height of the bridge; if any of the paddles hit a vehicle as it drives under the gantry, this will warn the driver to divert their course to avoid hitting the bridge. Additional signage has been installed in surrounding streets, providing a total of 26 advanced warning signs about the bridge.[^1101] Following these works Premier Andrews noted that "if anyone manages to get stuck under this thing after that, well, I give up".[^1100]

Since the installation of the gantries, over a dozen more vehicles crashed into the bridge - including a truck carrying sheets of glass on 13 June 2018.[^1102]

On 21 May 2025, the Victorian Government announced it would implement a speed limit reduction from 60km/h to 40km/h on a stretch of Montague Street about 170 metres long on either side of the bridge.[^1103] A 40km/h speed limit already applies before and after school hours.

The aim of the speed reduction is to give drivers more time to consider their vehicle's height and brake before reaching the bridge, and to reduce the severity of the damage to vehicles that continue to hit it. Within days of the speed limit reduction taking affect, the bridge was struck twice in consecutive days.[^1104][^1105]

The Victorian Government considers it to be unfeasible to modify or remove the bridge. Raising it would disrupt the tram network. Lowering the road is also not possible due to electricity cables as well as water and gas pipes that are located below it. Lowering the road could also cause flooding during heavy rain.[^1100]

#### In the media

Tom Waller is the founder of the website *[How Many Days Since Montague Street Bridge Has Been Hit](https://howmanydayssincemontaguestreetbridgehasbeenhit.com/)*, which tracks each "championship title bout" between the bridge and its vehicular opponents. The website has been operating since February 2016 and invites crowdsourced reports of new crashes.

The bridge is also a popular topic for local TV, radio and news media, which note the frequency with which the bridge is hit. In June 2017, the *[Herald Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herald_Sun)* reported, "Montague St bridge hit by truck once again", noting that "Melbourne's most-hit bridge has claimed another victim after it was struck by a truck yet again this afternoon … the third time the bridge has been hit in as many weeks."[^1106]

Other media reports strike a more jocular tone: in February 2018, youth website Pedestrian.tv reported, "After 8 Months Dormant, The Awful Montague Street Bridge Has Awoken To Feed".[^1107]

The bridge has its own Twitter account and Facebook page, both of which are written in the first person, as if by the bridge itself.

David Cosma has written a comedic song, 'Montague St Bridge', which includes the lyrics "Is it low?/Is it too low?/I don't know!/But I think I'm gonna go anyway."[^1108]

#### Similar bridges

The **Napier Street Bridge**, located in [Footscray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footscray,_Victoria), in Melbourne's western suburbs, has a four-metre clearance and is similarly prone to vehicle crashes. Like the Montague Street Bridge, it has its own Twitter account.

The **[Bayswater Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayswater_Bridge,_Perth)** in Perth had a [clearance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structure_gauge) of 3.8 metres (12 ft 6 in), and catalogues the crashes on a website modelled on the Montague Street Bridge website. The bridge was struck eight times in 2018. It was demolished in April 2023 and replaced by a new, higher bridge as part of a rebuild of the adjacent [Bayswater railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayswater_railway_station,_Perth).[^1109][^1110]

The **[11 foot 8 Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk_Southern%E2%80%93Gregson_Street_Overpass)** (3.56 m), (formally known as the Norfolk Southern-Gregson Street Overpass, and nicknamed "The Can-Opener"), is a railway bridge in [Durham, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham,_North_Carolina), US, that averages one crash a month. In October 2019, the bridge was raised 8 inches (0.20 m) to 12 feet 4 inches (3.76 m) but accidents continue.

The **"Fools Bridge"** in Sofia Street, [Saint Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg), Russia, also has its own humorous Twitter account. As of 2 February 2018, 140 vehicles had become stuck under the bridge.

### Whangamōmona

**Whangamōmona** is a township in the [Stratford District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratford,_New_Zealand) and [Manawatū-Whanganui Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manawat%C5%AB%E2%80%93Whanganui) of [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand). It lies on [State Highway 43](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_State_Highway_43), the "Forgotten World Highway", 65 kilometres (40 mi) north-east of Stratford and 55 kilometres (34 mi) south-west of [Ōhura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%8Chura). By rail it is 61 kilometres (38 mi) from Stratford on the [Stratford-Okahukura railway line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratford%E2%80%93Okahukura_Line).[^1111]

#### Demographics

Whangamōmona statistical area covers 689.60 km² (266.26 sq mi)[^1112] and had an estimated population of 170 as of June 2025,[^1113] with a population density of 0.25 people per km².

**Historical population**

| Year                     | Pop. | ±% p.a. |
|--------------------------|------|---------|
| 2006                     | 168  |,        |
| 2013                     | 150  | −1.61%  |
| 2018                     | 126  | −3.43%  |
| 2023                     | 159  | +4.76%  |
| Source: [^1114][^1115] |      |         |

Whangamōmona had a population of 159 in the [2023 New Zealand census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_New_Zealand_census), an increase of 33 people (26.2%) since the [2018 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_New_Zealand_census), and an increase of 9 people (6.0%) since the [2013 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_New_Zealand_census). There were 90 males and 69 females in 66 dwellings.[^1116] 1.9% of people identified as [LGBTIQ+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ). The median age was 44.4 years (compared with 38.1 years nationally). There were 33 people (20.8%) aged under 15 years, 18 (11.3%) aged 15 to 29, 75 (47.2%) aged 30 to 64, and 33 (20.8%) aged 65 or older.[^1114]

People could identify as more than one ethnicity. The results were 92.5% [European](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_New_Zealanders) ([Pākehā](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C4%81keh%C4%81)), 20.8% [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_people), 5.7% [Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_New_Zealanders), and 5.7% other, which includes people giving their ethnicity as "New Zealander". English was spoken by 98.1%, and Māori by 3.8%. The percentage of people born overseas was 11.3, compared with 28.8% nationally.[^1114]

Religious affiliations were 26.4% [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_New_Zealand), and 1.9% other religions. People who answered that they had [no religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreligion_in_New_Zealand) were 60.4%, and 9.4% of people did not answer the census question.[^1114]

Of those at least 15 years old, 12 (9.5%) people had a bachelor's or higher degree, 75 (59.5%) had a post-high school certificate or diploma, and 42 (33.3%) people exclusively held high school qualifications. The median income was \$22,700, compared with \$41,500 nationally. 6 people (4.8%) earned over \$100,000 compared to 12.1% nationally. The employment status of those at least 15 was 60 (47.6%) full-time, 15 (11.9%) part-time, and 12 (9.5%) unemployed.[^1114]

#### History

The first European settlers arrived in 1895, with the town proper established two years later.[^1117] Growth of the town was seriously affected by the deaths of 51 men (including some from the smaller nearby settlements of Kohuratahi and Tahora)[^1118] in the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I) and a major flood in 1924.[^1117] The town recovered with arrival of the railway line in 1933 and electrification in 1959, but its population declined in subsequent decades.[^1117] The school closed in 1979, followed nine years later by the post office.[^1117]

In July 2020, the name of the locality was officially gazetted as Whangamōmona by the [New Zealand Geographic Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Geographic_Board).[^1119]

#### Republic Day

As part of the [1989 local government reforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_local_government_reforms) Whangamomona was included in the [Manawatu-Wanganui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manawat%C5%AB-Whanganui) Region since the [Whangamōmona River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whangam%C5%8Dmona_River) is a tributary of the [Whanganui River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whanganui_River). Residents objected, as they preferred to become part of the [Taranaki Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taranaki_Region), and on 1 November 1989, they responded by declaring themselves the "Republic of Whangamomona" at the first Republic Day. Though the move began as a pointed protest, the town continued to hold a celebratory Republic Day once a year, during which a vote for president was held. The day has become a local festival day, and attracts visitors from throughout the North Island. In 2001, the celebration became biennial, held in January to take advantage of the summer weather.[^1120][^1121]

### Pope Donus II

**Pope Donus II** is an apocryphal [pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope) who allegedly held the title briefly between [Benedict VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_VI) and [Benedict VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_VII) sometime during the 970s. The creation is likely due to papal catalogues accidentally confusing the title *domnus* for a proper name caused by the later addition of some [antipopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antipope) into papal listings. His existence had been documented since at least the 15th century, and he was considered a pope by the Vatican for more than 200 years until the timeline was corrected in 1947. Despite his fictitious record, the nonexistent pope had been praised for honorable conduct.

#### History

Donus II was likely invented by later papal catalogues that listed him between [Benedict VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_VI) and [Benedict VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_VII). Benedict VI was likely listed prior to the phrase *Domnus de Sutri*, as he had been the [bishop of Sutri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Sutri). Later editions had added antipope [Boniface VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boniface_VII) and his years of reign into the same timeline directly after the mention of Benedict VI, which would have listed *Domnus de Sutri* independently alongside the year 974, which had been previously accredited to Benedict VI. Later editors would have read the phrase as the name of a pope, and then shortened the name to just *Domnus*, giving the impression of a Pope Domnus (also written as Domnus, Donus, or Bonus) who held the title in 974.[^1122] He was given the suffix of II as a [Pope Donus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Donus) already had held position between 676 and 678.[^1123]

Fanciful illustrations of Donus II have existed since at least the 15th century.[^1124] One example is a portrait (known as a *clipei*) in a gallery of Popes located at the [Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica_of_Saint_Paul_Outside_the_Walls).[^1125] The portraits of Popes at Saint Paul dates back to the 400s with the installation of the first 40.[^1125][^1126] The gallery was not continuously maintained, evident as the list was only expanded during rare periods of renovation.[^1126] In 1748, Pietro Piazza was commissioned to remake 158 portraits and to create a gallery that visualized the Vatican's claim of an uninterrupted line of popes since [Saint Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Peter). Many of the portraits did not reflect the actual likenesses of the popes and were fictionalized, as accurate depictions of individual popes was not the primary goal. Piazza worked on the *clipei* of popes from Stephen III of the 8th century to Benedict XIV of the 18th century, which would have included the fictional Donus II.[^1127][^1126]

In the 18th century, the mosaic gallery was used by [Giovanni Marangoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Marangoni) to create an official papal roster. For more than two hundred years, Donus II was considered a legitimate pope by the [Holy See](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_See). Although the list was known to be flawed, it was not formally audited until 1947. In addition to confirming the nonexistence of Donus II, the audit revealed that [Popes Cletus and Anacletus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Anacletus) were the same person, discovered Popes [Boniface VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Boniface_VI) and [Leo VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Leo_VIII), and corrected various details concerning dozens of other popes.[^1125]

Despite his accidental creation, egregious accounts of Donus II have been recorded. A book by [Alexis-François Artaud de Montor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis-Fran%C3%A7ois_Artaud_de_Montor) states that he was Roman, elected in 972 due to involvement by the [counts of Tusculum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counts_of_Tusculum), and "governed three months with great integrity" before dying on 19 December 972 and being interred at the [Vatican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vatican_City).[^1128] Other specifics of his alleged reign vary, such as being between 5 April 974 and October 975, or, according to [William à Beckett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_%C3%A0_Beckett), that he was "never charged with any injustice or dishonourable action." \[*[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic)*\][^1129][^1130] Regardless of the dates of his alleged papacy, no contemporary sources mention Donus II nor are any of his acts as pope recorded.[^1122]

### Glass delusion

**Glass delusion** is an external manifestation of a [psychiatric disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatric_disorder) recorded in Europe mainly in the late [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages) and [early modern period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_period) (15th to 17th centuries).[^1131] People feared that they were made of [glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass) "and therefore likely to shatter into pieces".

#### Delusion

In the 16th and 17th centuries in Europe, [glass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass) became a valuable commodity. It was regarded as a magical [alchemical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alchemical) object.[^1132] Associated with fragility and luxury, glass influenced the way noblemen of early Europe perceived their esteemed positions in society. This fixation on a novel material contributed to the manifestation of the delusion. [Edward Shorter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Shorter_%28historian%29), a historian of psychiatry from the [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto), attributes the rise of the delusion in 17th-century Europe to the novelty of glass, stating that "throughout history, the inventive [unconscious mind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unconscious_mind) has pegged its delusions on to new materials and technological advances of the age."[^1133] There is also a social explanation: copycat delusions spread by [social contagion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_contagion). The cases clustered among literate men, scholars, nobles, physicians, the people reading the medical case literature, and literary and historic accounts.[^1134]

Concentration of the glass delusion among wealthy and educated social classes allowed modern scholars to associate it with a wider and better described disorder of [melancholy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melancholia).[^1132]

#### Contemporary accounts

[Tommaso Garzoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommaso_Garzoni) documented a man who tried to throw himself into a glazier’s furnace and emerge as an *inghistara*, a long-necked jug without a handle.[^1134]

[Robert Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Burton)'s *[The Anatomy of Melancholy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Anatomy_of_Melancholy)* (1621) touches on the subject in the commentary as one of many related manifestations[^1135] of the same anxiety:

> Fear of devils, death, that they shall be so sick, of some such or such disease, ready to tremble at every object, they shall die themselves forthwith, or that some of their dear friends or near allies are certainly dead; imminent danger, loss, disgrace still torment others; that they are all glass, and therefore will suffer no man to come near them; that they are all [cork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cork_%28material%29), as light as feathers; others as heavy as lead; some are afraid their heads will fall off their shoulders, that they have frogs in their bellies, Etc.[^1136]

[Miguel de Cervantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel_de_Cervantes) based one of his short novels, *The Glass Graduate* ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language): *[El licenciado Vidriera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_licenciado_Vidriera)*, 1613), on the delusion of the title subject, an aspiring young lawyer named Tomás Rodaja.[^1137] The protagonist of the story falls into a grave depression after being bedridden for six months subsequent to being poisoned with a purportedly [aphrodisiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphrodisiac) potion. He claims that, being of glass, his perceptions are clearer than those of men of flesh and demonstrates by offering witty comments. After two years of illness, Rodaja is cured by a monk; no details of the cure are provided except that the monk is allegedly a [miracle-maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deus_ex_machina).

The Dutch poet [Constantijn Huygens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantijn_Huygens) (whose contemporary [Caspar Barlaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caspar_Barlaeus) experienced the glass delusion[^1138]) wrote in *Costly Folly* (1622) of its subject:[^1132]

> He fears everything that moves in his vicinity... the chair will be the death for him; he trembles at the bed, fearful that one will break his bum, the other smash his head.

French philosopher [René Descartes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Descartes) wrote *[Meditations on First Philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meditations_on_First_Philosophy)* (1641), using the glass delusion as an example of an [insane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insane) person whose perceived knowledge of the world differs from the majority.[^1139] In *[An Essay Concerning Human Understanding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Essay_Concerning_Human_Understanding)* (Book II, Chapter XI, 13) when proposing his celebrated model of madness, [John Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Locke) also refers to the glass delusion.[^1140]

In modern times, the glass delusion has not completely disappeared, and there are still isolated cases today. "Surveys of modern psychiatric institutions have only revealed two specific (uncorroborated) cases of the glass delusion. Foulché-Delbosc reports finding one Glass Man in a Paris [asylum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bic%C3%AAtre_Hospital), and a woman who thought she was a potsherd was recorded at an asylum in [Merenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merenberg)." Andy Lameijn, a psychiatrist from the Netherlands, reported in 2015 that he had a male patient suffering from the delusion in [Leiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leiden).[^1133]

German alchemist [Johann Joachim Becher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Joachim_Becher) had a fascination with glass delusion. In *[Physica Subterranea](https://archive.org/details/johjoachimibecch00bech)* (1669), he claimed to have discovered a way of turning dead human bodies into glass.[^1141]

#### Notable cases

##### Charles VI of France

King [Charles VI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VI_of_France) was afflicted by the glass delusion in his twenties. He wore clothing that was reinforced with iron rods and did not allow his advisors to come near him due to his fear that his body would accidentally shatter. He may have been the first known case of glass delusion.[^1131] Earlier, he had survived the traumatic event of the *[Bal des ardents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bal_des_ardents)*, when his costume, and those of his companions, caught fire. He had also furiously attacked his courtiers, out of fear of traitors, while riding to war; later, he forgot that he had done so.[^1134]

##### Princess Alexandra of Bavaria

[Princess Alexandra of Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Alexandra_of_Bavaria) believed that she had swallowed a glass piano as a child. She was convinced that the object remained inside her body from that point on, fearful that it might shatter and puncture her organs.[^1142]

##### Georgios Hatzianestis

[Georgios Hatzianestis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgios_Hatzianestis), a Greek military officer, was commander of the [Army of Asia Minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_of_Asia_Minor) during the [Greco-Turkish War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Turkish_War_%281919%E2%80%931922%29) in 1922. He failed to adequately respond to the [Great Offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Offensive) that turned the war in the Turks' favour because he believed that his legs were made of glass and could shatter if he moved. For his failure, he was tried as an anti-[Venizelist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venizelist) in the [Trial of the Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_the_Six) (the only military leader to be so prosecuted) and was executed for [high treason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_treason).[^1143]
