### Eggnog riot

The **eggnog riot**, sometimes known as the **grog mutiny** or the **Christmas 1826 cadet mutiny**, was a [riot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riot) that took place at the [United States Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy) in [West Point, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Point,_New_York), on 24-25 December 1826. It was caused by a drunken [Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas) party in the north barracks of the academy. Two days prior to the incident, a large quantity of [whiskey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whiskey) was smuggled into the academy to make [eggnog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eggnog) for the party, giving the riot its name. As described by Albert E. Church, who was absent on Christmas leave and missed the happenings but later became a math professor at the academy, "A large number of the cadets got on a spree, and became excessively riotous, setting all officers at defiance and even, with a drawn sword, chasing one to his room-throwing missiles through the halls, breaking windows and the railings of the stairs, &c. The scene, as described to me two days afterwards, was fit for Bedlam."[^1144]

The riot eventually involved more than one-third of the cadets by the time it ceased on Christmas morning. A subsequent investigation by academy officials resulted in the implication of 70 cadets and the [court-martialing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court-martial) of 20 of them along with one [enlisted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlisted_rank) soldier. Among the participants in the riot, though he was not court-martialed, was future [Confederate States president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Confederate_States_of_America) [Jefferson Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Davis).

#### Background

The large number of small dairy farms in America in the early 19th century made milk, cream, and eggnog more accessible to the American public.[^1145] [George Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Washington) drank eggnog that contained not only [rum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rum), but also significant amounts of [sherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherry), [brandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandy), and whiskey.[^1145]

In 1817, [Sylvanus Thayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvanus_Thayer) took command at the United States Military Academy.[^1146] By 1826, the academy had 36 men serving as faculty and staff with four recognized departments - [mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematics), engineering, [natural philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_philosophy) (now [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics),[^1147] [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemistry), and [life sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_sciences)[^1148]), and [military tactics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_tactics).[^1149][^1150]

Alcohol possession at the academy was prohibited along with [drunkenness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drunkenness) and [intoxication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Substance_intoxication), both of which could lead to [expulsion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expulsion_%28academia%29).[^1151] Tobacco use and gambling could lead to [demerits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_discipline), minor [incarceration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incarceration), or a loss of privileges.[^1151] By 1826, concern had been raised that drinking was starting to get out of hand among the 260 cadets at the academy.[^1152][^1153] The cadets were informed that, due to the alcohol prohibition on the site, their Christmas eggnog would be alcohol-free, prompting the decision to smuggle liquor into the academy.[^1154]

#### Timeline of events

##### 22 December 1826

###### 20:50-22:15

At Martin's Tavern, cadets William R. Burnley ([Alabama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alabama)), Alexander J. Center (New York), and Samuel Alexander Roberts (Alabama) almost got into a fight with the proprietors of another tavern concerning getting whiskey back to West Point. [Private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_%28rank%29) James Dougan, the duty security guard, agreed to let the three cadets take a boat across the Hudson to [smuggle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smuggle) the whiskey. The cadets planned to purchase one-half US gallon (1.9 L) of whiskey as an alcohol base for the eggnog party that would take place in the North [Barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barracks) two nights later.[^1155] Phillip St. George ([Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia)) was the 24-hour duty cadet guard of the day.[^1156] Burnley, Center, and Roberts successfully obtained two US gallons (7.6 L) of whiskey, smuggling them into North Barracks room No. 33.[^1145][^1157] Cadet T. M. Lewis ([Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky)) also returned with one US gallon (3.8 L) of rum from Benny's Tavern to North Barracks room No. 5.[^1158]

##### 23 December 1826

###### 07:00

Thayer met with George Bomford (New York) and [Robert E. Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_E._Lee) (Virginia). Bomford was questioned about his parental correspondence by Thayer while Lee questioned Thayer about [trigonometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometry) problems for [artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery) gunnery.[^1159] Classes and barracks [inspections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspections) continued as usual that day.[^1160]

###### 17:45

A Christmas party took place at Thayer's residence at which wine was served. Reverend Charles McIlvane, the academy chaplain, was among the attendees. During the party, a conversation ensued between Thayer and [Major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_%28United_States%29) [William J. Worth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_J._Worth), the [Commandant of Cadets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_commandants_of_cadets_of_the_United_States_Military_Academy), about Jefferson Davis's ([Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi)) disciplinary problems.[^1161] Entertainment was provided by the West Point [band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marching_band).[^1162] The party ended at 21:30.[^1151]

###### 18:00

Four cadets, Walter B. Guion (Mississippi), Davis, John Stocker ([Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania)), and David Farrelly (Pennsylvania), met at [Benny Havens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benny_Havens)' tavern. Most of the discussion was about everyday life among the cadets. They left before academy [quartermaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartermaster) Aeneas Mackay arrived.[^1163]

Meanwhile, at the North Barracks, cadets were planning the party. Preparations included stealing bits and pieces of food during their visits to the [mess hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cafeteria).[^1164] During this time, cadets residing in the South Barracks found out about the North Barracks' planned Christmas party.[^1165][^1166]

##### 24-25 December 1826

###### 22:00-04:15

Nathaniel Eaton ([Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts)) was the cadet in charge of the external post of the North Barracks.[^1167] [Captain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_%28United_States_O-3%29) [Ethan Allen Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethan_A._Hitchcock_%28general%29), a faculty member in military tactics, was also stationed in the North Barracks. Eaton and Hitchcock met and discussed the smuggled [liquor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquor) in the North Barracks.[^1168]

The eggnog party started among nine cadets in North Barracks room No. 28. Numerous cadets appeared as the party progressed, while another party began in room No. 5, mentioned by seven cadets including Davis. Farrelly went again to North's or Havens' and returned with another gallon of whiskey early on Christmas morning.[^1145][^1150][^1169]

Cadet Charles Whipple ([Michigan Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_Territory)), the [division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_%28military%29) superintendent during the first part of the incident, went to North Barracks room No. 5 at 02:00 after hearing a commotion, interrupting a round of singing among eight cadets, including Davis. Whipple returned to his room after a verbal exchange with Davis and the other cadets.[^1170] Hitchcock made another patrol around the barracks at 03:00.[^1171] Lieutenant William A. Thornton was asleep while the events unfolded.[^1171]

By 04:00, voices from the floor above Hitchcock were loud enough to cause the faculty member to investigate room No. 28, where Hitchcock knocked on the door and found six cadets drunk from the eggnog, as well as two others sleeping on a bed. Hitchcock ordered two of the cadets back to their rooms. After they left, Hitchcock woke the two sleeping cadets and ordered them to leave as well. Then he confronted cadet James W.M. "Weems" Berrien ([Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_%28U.S._state%29)), who responded with equal force. Hitchcock gave a stern lecture to the residents of the room for possessing alcohol on the premises. The captain left the room at 04:15.[^1172] Berrien began verbalizing his rage toward Hitchcock, which led William D.C. "Billy" Murdock ([District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia)) to lead an effort to organize a riot against Hitchcock.[^1173]

##### 25 December 1826

###### 04:30-06:05

Hitchcock went down to his room to sleep. Three times he heard knocks on the door only to find no one there. After finding another cadet drunk, Hitchcock saw Davis head over to room No. 5 where thirteen cadets were partying. Davis, seeing Hitchcock's arrival, warned the other cadets. The captain entered the room, ordering one of the cadets to open up another cadet's [footlocker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footlocker_%28luggage%29), but the cadet refused. Hitchcock ordered no more disorder, left the room, and started looking for Thornton around 04:50.[^1145][^1150][^1174]

Meanwhile, Thornton had strolled the North Barracks between 21:00 on the 24th and 02:00 on Christmas Day observing the ongoing partying, before going to sleep at 02:00. He was awakened by loud yells and, once out of his room, was attacked by two cadets. Thornton then put cadet William P.N. Fitzgerald (New York) under arrest for brandishing a weapon. Fitzgerald retreated from Thornton, then told two cadets in room No. 29 about the arrest.

At this point, noises erupted from the South Barracks which distracted Thornton. While going to investigate that commotion, Thornton was knocked out by Roberts, who had been ejected from room No. 28 by Hitchcock earlier that evening.[^1175]

Davis was asleep, but other cadets went looking for Hitchcock. Three other cadets were discovered by cadet James G. Overton ([Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee)), a relief sentinel and not involved in the parties, and questioned about their actions. They gave a drunken explanation about needing drums and a [fife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fife_%28musical_instrument%29). At around 05:00, Hitchcock found another inebriated cadet wandering the academy.[^1176] By this point, several window panes had been broken. Hitchcock returned to the room where he was staying, No. 8. Several cadets then attacked his door, Guion drawing his [pistol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pistol) and firing a shot into the room. Hitchcock opened the door and yelled at the cadets to stop. The captain then began arresting cadets.[^1177]

Hitchcock ordered Eaton to find Worth's headquarters. Overton asked Hitchcock to find Thayer and Hitchcock replied "No, Mr. Overton. Fetch the com \[Commandant Worth\] here." Several of the drunken cadets thought Hitchcock had stated the [bombardiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardier_%28rank%29) would be the ones to quell the riot, using heavy weapons, causing several cadets who were not drunk to take up arms in defense of the North Barracks. Thayer had been awoken at 05:00 by the sound of drums. He ordered his aide, Patrick Murphy, to get Major Worth because of what he could hear going on in the North Barracks.[^1178]

Hitchcock continued restoring order in the North Barracks, getting into a fight with cadet Walter Otey (Virginia).[^1179] Thornton awoke from the [stairway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stairway) where he had been knocked out and returned to his room. Hitchcock greeted him in his room at 05:45.[^1180] By 06:00, other cadets who were not drinking were also involved in restoring order.[^1181] The main rioters were attempting to recruit other cadets, but with no success.[^1182]

Overton could not find Cadet Eaton, who was checking the South Barracks, but did find Major Worth. Hitchcock met Worth and told him what had transpired. By this time, Thayer's aide had arrived in the North Barracks' guardroom. The Second Artillery had arrived at the North Barracks by the time of [reveille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reveille) at 06:05.[^1183]

###### 06:05-18:30

Reveille sounded at 06:05, along with gunfire, the sound of glass breaking, [profanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profanity) by cadets, cries of pain, and threats to academy officials.[^1145][^1184] North Barracks residents who were not drunk from the eggnog were appalled by the damaged property.[^1185] Cadets in the South Barracks were well rested, while other cadets in the North Barracks were disheveled. Some of the cadets remained in their rooms drinking, although some appeared in [parade formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_parade) despite being drunk.[^1186] Worth met with superintendent Thayer after the first formation to discuss what had happened in the North Barracks the previous evening.[^1187] Thayer instructed Worth to get the officers into the North Barracks and restore order.[^1188]

Captain Mackay, academy quartermaster, took down details of the damages to the property at North Barracks so repairs could take place in the following days.[^1189] Many cadets who were drunk made it to [company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_%28military_unit%29) [roll call](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/roll%20call) at 06:20, though they were subdued. The mutiny officially ended when Cadet Captain James A.J. Bradford (Kentucky) called the corps to attention and dismissed them from the mess hall after breakfast. [Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Point_Cadet_Chapel) formation took place after breakfast, followed by two hours of service, with most of the drunk cadets still recovering.[^1190]

Thayer was advised by Worth regarding the events at North Barracks. Captain Hitchcock and Lieutenant Thornton were bruised, while several cadets suffered minor injuries, and Fitzgerald suffered a hand injury. Worth told Thayer that between fifty and ninety cadets had been involved in the mutiny.[^1191] Later that day, Thayer met with [Gouverneur Kemble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gouverneur_Kemble), an [ordnance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery) manufacturer in [Cold Spring, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_Spring,_New_York), to discuss different items, including the events at West Point. Kemble asked Thayer what he would do about the misconduct, to which Thayer replied he did not know.[^1192]

##### 26 December 1826

###### 07:00-08:00

A faculty and staff meeting took place, with all but Captain Thomas C. Legate of the 2nd Artillery A Battery and a few [assistant professors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professors_in_the_United_States) in attendance. Thayer informed them that [Major General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_General_%28United_States%29) [Alexander Macomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Macomb_%28American_general%29), [Chief of Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_of_Engineers) and [inspector general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspector_general) of the academy, had been told of the riot, and that he was awaiting orders from Macomb. The superintendent also informed the attendees that an inquiry would take place during semester finals in January 1827, so some of the cadets would face simultaneous examinations and inquiry.[^1193]

Cadet Battalion Order 98 was read at formation and posted at several prominent locations at the academy. Twenty-two cadets were placed under [house arrest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_arrest) until further notice; among them was Davis, who had been reported as a malefactor by Hitchcock and Thornton.[^1166][^1194]

##### 6 January 1827

Thayer reviewed Order 49, dated 30 December 1826 and signed by Chief of Engineers Macomb, ordering a court of inquiry to be assembled as soon as possible to investigate the Christmas riots. No deadline was given by the War Department in Washington, DC, though the academy was expected to get it done as soon as possible. Major Worth was president of the inquiry, with Lieutenant Henry H. Gird acting as secretary ([court reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_reporter)), and two other faculty and staff to be selected by Thayer for court duties. If the inquiry determined that further disciplinary action was necessary, Thayer was empowered to [court-martial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courts-martial_in_the_United_States) any cadet or other military personnel.[^1195] Worth elected Hitchcock and Lieutenant William Bryant to the court, despite Hitchcock's involvement in controlling the riots in North Barracks.[^1196]

##### 7 January 1827

In the midst of the academy exams, Gird informed the cadets of the court of inquiry, which was to begin the next day.[^1197]

##### 8-22 January 1827

The inquiry included testimony from 167 witnesses. MacKay stated US\$168.83 (roughly \$5,380.27 in 2024)[^1198] worth of damages had occurred. Thayer testified that he never ordered the bombardiers, the Second Artillery, to police the barracks.[^1199] The academic board recommended James W. Hamilton (at-large) be discharged for bad conduct and five others, all fourth classmen ([freshman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freshman) or [plebes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plebs)), were dismissed for lack of aptitude in certain academic disciplines or bad conduct. Several other cadets also were dismissed.[^1166][^1200] A final report was presented to Thayer on 19 January 1827, which Thayer and Worth met to discuss after dinner that evening.

Following testimony, the inquiry determined that seventy cadets had been involved in the riots. Thayer picked the worst offenders (those who smuggled the whiskey, the cadets who incited the riots, and several others) for prosecution at court-martial.[^1150][^1201]

##### 24 January - 8 March 1827

In 1819, [Attorney General of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attorney_General_of_the_United_States) [William Wirt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wirt_%28Attorney_General%29) had opined that "the Corps ... form part of the land forces of the United States..." and its members were thus subject to [military law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_law) and trials by court-martial. Wirt's opinion was supported by [United States Secretary of War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_War) [John C. Calhoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Calhoun) and President of the United States [James Monroe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Monroe).[^1202]

Nineteenth-century American military justice was founded in the [American Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution). The [sentences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentence_%28law%29) were reviewed by the secretary of war, the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress), and the president. A general court consisted of between five and thirteen officers serving as [jurors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jury) and [magistrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magistrate). The accused was his own lawyer, prepared his own defense, and could plead guilty to one or more charges against him while contesting other charges.[^1203]

Trials were held from 08:00 to 15:00 daily or during daylight hours, whichever was later. A standard trial began with the charges being read, the [defendant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defendant) giving his plea, and opening statements by the prosecution and defense attorneys. Witness testimony then began, followed by closing statements given by the prosecution and defense attorneys, and the jury's decision. If the verdict was guilty, the defendant was then sentenced.[^1203]

The twenty cases were divided into three parts by the war department for administrative convenience.[^1203] The court-martial trials were held in succession without break from 26 January, with Lieutenant Gird serving as trial [judge advocate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judge_advocate).[^1204]

During the progression of the trials, Davis was released from house arrest along with two other cadets.[^1166][^1205] Cadet Humphreys was arrested on 27 January.[^1205] Gird stayed as trial judge advocate until 8 March, when he asked to be released; he was replaced by Lieutenant [William H. C. Bartlett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_H._C._Bartlett).[^1206]

##### 9 March - 3 May 1827

Bartlett started his duties on 9 March at 10:00,[^1207] and the trials concluded on 16 March.[^1208] Thayer forwarded the records to General Maccomb and Secretary of War [James Barbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Barbour) in late March; Barbour then sent the information to President [John Quincy Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Quincy_Adams).[^1209] Adams read the findings, and adjusted some of the verdicts for the cadets. The case was closed on 3 May.[^1210]

### Eduard Bloch

**Eduard Bloch** (30 January 1872 - 1 June 1945) was an Austrian physician practicing in [Linz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linz). Born to a [Jewish family of Czechoslovak origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_the_Czech_lands),[^1235] Bloch was the family doctor of [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler) and [his family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_of_Hitler) until 1907. Bloch oversaw the treatment of Hitler's mother, [Klara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klara_Hitler), when she was dying of [breast cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breast_cancer), charging the family very little, to sometimes nothing, for her treatment.

Following the German [annexation of Austria in 1938](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anschluss),[^1236] Hitler described him as an *Edeljude* ('noble Jew'), and bestowed [Gestapo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gestapo) protection on him in the midst of *[Kristallnacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristallnacht)* and the escalation of [anti-Jewish sentiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Jewish_sentiment) in Germany.[^1237] Hitler allowed Bloch to emigrate to the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States), where he lived until his death in 1945, succumbing to [stomach cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stomach_cancer).[^1238]

#### Biography

Eduard Bloch was born on 30 January 1872 in Podhrad, [Bohemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemia), [Austria-Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria-Hungary) (present-day [Hluboká nad Vltavou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hlubok%C3%A1_nad_Vltavou), Czech Republic).[^1239] He studied medicine in [Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague) at [Charles University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_University) and then served as a [medical officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physician) in the Austrian army.[^1238] He was stationed in Linz from 1899 until his discharge in 1901, at which point he opened a private practice there. His practice was in the [baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque) house at 12 Landstrasse, where he also lived with his family: his wife, Emilie ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name) Kafka) and their daughter Trude, born in 1903. According to Linz's future mayor [Ernst Koref](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Koref), Bloch was held in high regard, particularly among the lower and indigent social classes.

##### Hitler's family doctor

The first member of the Hitler family Bloch saw was Adolf. In 1904, Adolf Hitler had become seriously ill and was bedridden due to a serious lung ailment. Due to this, he was allowed to abandon his school career and return home. However, after checking Hitler's files, Bloch later maintained that he had treated the young man for only minor ailments - [cold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_cold) or [tonsillitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonsillitis) - and that Hitler had been neither robust nor sickly. He also stated that Hitler did not have any illness whatsoever, let alone a lung disease.[^1240]

In 1907, Hitler's mother, [Klara Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klara_Hitler), was diagnosed with [breast cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breast_cancer). She died on 21 December after intense suffering involving daily medication with [iodoform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iodoform), a foul-smelling and painful corrosive treatment typically used at the time and administered by Bloch. Because of the poor economic situation of the Hitler family, Bloch charged reduced prices, sometimes taking no fee at all. This showed in 1908, when Hitler wrote Bloch a [postcard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postcard) assuring him of his gratitude and reverence, which he expressed with handmade gifts.

##### Emigration

After [Germany's annexation of Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anschluss) in March 1938 (*Anschluss*), life became harder for Austrian Jews. After Bloch's medical practice was closed on 1 October 1938, his daughter and son-in-law emigrated overseas. The 66-year-old Bloch then wrote a letter to Hitler asking for help and was as a consequence put under special protection by the [Gestapo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gestapo). He was the only Jew in Linz with this status. Bloch stayed in his house with his wife undisturbed until the formalities for his [emigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emigration) from the Third Reich and [immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration) to the United States were completed. Without any interference from the authorities, they were able to sell their family home at market value, highly unusual with the distress sales of emigrating Jews at the time and Nazi expropriation of Jewish assets through the [Reich Flight Tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reich_Flight_Tax). Moreover, the Blochs were allowed to take the equivalent of 16 [ℛ︁ℳ︁](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reichsmark), equivalent to [€](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro)71 in 2021, out of the country; the usual amount allowed to Jews was a mere 10 ℛ︁ℳ︁,[^1241] equivalent to €44 in 2021.

In 1940, Bloch immigrated to the US and settled in the [Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronx), [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City) but was no longer able to practice medicine because his medical degree from [Austria-Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria-Hungary) was [not recognised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissolution_of_Austria-Hungary).

##### Death

He died of [stomach cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stomach_cancer) in 1945 at age 73, barely a month after Hitler's death.[^1242][^1243]

### Killing baby Hitler

**Killing baby Hitler** is a [thought experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thought_experiment) in [ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethics) and [theoretical physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theoretical_physics) which poses the question of using backwards [time travel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_travel) to assassinate an infant [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler). It presents an [ethical dilemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethical_dilemma) in both the action and its consequences, as well as a [temporal paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temporal_paradox) in the logical consistency of time. Killing baby Hitler first became a [literary trope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trope_%28literature%29) of [science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction) during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II) and has since been used to explore these ethical and [metaphysical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaphysics) debates.

Ethical debates on the problem of killing baby Hitler can demonstrate the outlook of various moral philosophies: [utilitarianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utilitarianism) holds that killing baby Hitler is justified, as the potential benefits outweigh the potential costs; [deontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deontology) holds that killing baby Hitler is unjustified, as [infanticide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infanticide) is always wrong; and [consequentialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequentialism) may question what the consequences of killing baby Hitler might be, holding that the unforeseen future consequences of such an act make it difficult to judge its morality. It is also used to raise the question of [nature versus nurture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_versus_nurture), whether changing the society that baby Hitler grew up in might be preferable to killing baby Hitler.

Metaphysical debates about the possibility of killing baby Hitler have been used to discuss different [philosophies of time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy_of_space_and_time): the [B-theory of time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-theory_of_time) considers killing baby Hitler to be impossible due to its inherent temporal paradox, while theories of [multiple time dimensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_time_dimensions) leave room for the past to be changed by killing baby Hitler.

Public debate around the question of killing baby Hitler reached its height in late 2015, after *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times)* published a poll asking its readers the question. Advocates of killing baby Hitler included Florida governor [Jeb Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bush) and film actor [Tom Hanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Hanks), while comedian [Stephen Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Colbert) and pundit [Ben Shapiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Shapiro) were counted among the opponents of the policy.

#### Literary trope

Killing baby Hitler is a common literary trope of [contemporary science fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_science_fiction),[^1244] usually depicting a [time traveler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_travel) going back to the 1890s to assassinate an infant Hitler before he can start [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II) and perpetrate the [Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust).[^1245] Stories of this kind date as far back as World War II itself, with publications in *[Weird Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weird_Tales)* (1941)[^1246] and *[Astounding Science Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_Science_Fiction_and_Fact)* (1942) including the trope.[^1247]

Stories in the sub-genre detail a variety of different consequences for killing baby Hitler.[^1248] In his 1995 short story "Dieu porte-t-il des lunettes noires?" (English: "Does God Wear Dark Glasses?"), [Maurice G. Dantec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_G._Dantec) presents an ethical dilemma in travelling through time to kill baby Hitler.[^1249] In his 1996 novel *[Making History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Making_History_%28novel%29)*, [Stephen Fry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Fry) depicts a history student travelling back in time and rendering [Alois Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alois_Hitler) infertile. But in the place of Adolf Hitler, a different and more effective Nazi dictator takes power, defeats the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union) with nuclear weapons, conquers Europe and exterminates the Jewish people.[^1250] In [Selden Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selden_Edwards)' 2008 novel *[The Little Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Little_Book_%28Edwards_novel%29)*, the protagonists find themselves back in 1890s [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna) and decide to assassinate a young Hitler, but find themselves unable to kill an "innocent boy", despite knowing what he would grow up to become.[^1251] In a 2015 short story, American humourist [Alexandra Petri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandra_Petri) depicted Hitler being abducted and raised well by a kindly time traveler.[^1252] In a [post-credits scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-credits_scene) of the 2018 film *[Deadpool 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadpool_2)*, the titular character goes back in time to kill baby Hitler, but the outcome is not shown.[^1253] In the [extended cut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_cut), the film shows [Deadpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wade_Wilson_%28film_character%29) realising he can not do it and changing baby Hitler's [diaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diaper).[^1254]

In order to avoid the "Hitler-murder paradox", some science fiction stories follow the [Novikov self-consistency principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novikov_self-consistency_principle), which holds that if time travel is possible, then changing the past cannot meaningfully alter the future. In the 1977 novella *[The Primal Solution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Primal_Solution)*, an elderly [Holocaust survivor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocaust_survivors) travels through time and attempts to kill a young Hitler, but he survives and is set down the path of [antisemitism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism) by the experience.[^1250] In a 2002 episode of *[The Twilight Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twilight_Zone_%282002_TV_series%29)*, "Cradle of Darkness", a woman travels through time and kills baby Hitler,[^1255] but another baby is adopted by Hitler's mother and grows up to do all the same things as Hitler.[^1250] An earlier episode of *The Twilight Zone*, "[No Time Like the Past](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Time_Like_the_Past)" (1963), depicts a time traveler failing to assassinate Hitler, in keeping with the self-consistency principle.[^1256] In [Juliusz Machulski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juliusz_Machulski)'s 2013 film *[AmbaSSada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambassada)*, the protagonists get transported back in time and meet Hitler due to a coincidence, only spontaneously deciding to kill him. As they had not travelled in time with the intention of killing Hitler, the "Hitler's Murder Paradox" is avoided and history is consequently altered.[^1257]

#### Ethical thought experiment

##### Consequentialist argument

According to [consequentialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequentialism), the morality of any given action is judged solely by its consequences.[^1255] Consequentialist ethics raises the dichotomy of immediate foreseeable consequences versus unforeseeable potential consequences; for example, in the story of Johann Kühberger saving a young Hitler from drowning, the immediate positive consequences of saving a person's life was the motivating factor, but it also resulted in the eventual negative consequences of Hitler's rise to power.[^1258] In a 2000 essay on consequentialism, British philosopher [James Lenman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Lenman) posited a German bandit in 100 BCE sparing the life of one of Hitler's distant ancestors. According to consequentialism, although the bandit sparing her life led to the unforeseeable future crimes of Hitler, he was not wrong to do so, as killing her could have led to even worse unforeseeable consequences.[^1250] Killing baby Hitler also raises the possibility of unforeseen consequences, including the commonly cited possibility that someone even worse than Hitler could rise to power in his place.[^1259] As the consequences of killing baby Hitler are not known, the problem lacks a clear solution.[^1250]

##### Deontological argument

According to [deontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deontology), the morality of an action is determined by certain [ethical values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_%28ethics_and_social_sciences%29), rather than by circumstances.[^1260] Even in the case that it would benefit the [common good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_good), deontology opposes killing out of the belief that all human beings have an "inalienable value".[^1261] Deontological ethics thus argues against killing baby Hitler, as it considers killing babies to always be wrong, irrespective of any potential consequences.[^1262]

##### Utilitarian argument

[Utilitarianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utilitarianism) is a moral philosophy that argues for the maximisation of happiness and the minimisation of suffering.[^1263] According to utilitarian ethics, killing baby Hitler is justified,[^1264] as it considers the potential benefits to be greater than the moral cost.[^1262] As Hitler was responsible for the suffering of millions of people, utilitarianism posits that killing one baby Hitler is justifiable in order to save millions of innocent lives.[^1265] In this way, the question of killing baby Hitler resembles the [trolley problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trolley_problem), which utilitarianism responds to similarly.[^1266] Arguments against the utilitarian response conclude that focusing on killing baby Hitler, without any guarantee of preventing future suffering, means that the only guaranteed outcome is that the time traveller would have committed the moral evil of [infanticide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infanticide).[^1267] American philosopher Janet Stemwedel therefore considers killing baby Hitler to be an unreliable means for maximising happiness. Stemwedel posits that applying utilitarian ethics to time travel favours [causation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causation_%28sociology%29) over human agency, disregarding the capacity for humans to choose different paths and change.[^1263]

##### Nature versus nurture

To Canadian psychologist [Julia Shaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Shaw_%28psychologist%29), the answer one gives to the baby Hitler question is telling of their view on [nature versus nurture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature_versus_nurture): people who would kill baby Hitler may have a [deterministic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinism) view of individual predisposition towards evil, while people that would not kill baby Hitler may place higher value on environmental factors of upbringing and social conditions.[^1268] In a psychoanalysis of Hitler's infancy, Austrian psychiatrist [Frederick Redlich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Redlich) found that he was "a fairly normal child" and showed few signs of the [genocidal intent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocidal_intent) or [dictatorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dictator) tendencies that would characterise his adulthood.[^1268] As there is no scientific explanation for Hitler's later actions based on his [genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetics), greater attention is often paid to Hitler's early childhood environment.[^1268] In a refutation of the [great man theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_man_theory),[^1269] it can be argued that killing baby Hitler would not eliminate this cultural environment, which would still result in other people growing up to pursue [far-right politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far-right_politics) and genocidal policies.[^1270] From this perspective, Janet Stemwedel argues that using time travel to change social conditions would be preferable to infanticide, as it would recognise that the responsibility for Hitler's actions lie not just with him, but also in the [collective responsibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_responsibility) of those that raised, followed and elected him.[^1263]

##### Limitations

The moral justification for killing baby Hitler usually rests on the question of whether a child can be held responsible for its future actions before having committed any [crimes against humanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimes_against_humanity) yet.[^1271] A follow-up question can then be posed regarding where the line ends for killing babies that would commit crimes against humanity.[^1272] The question of where the line ends was brought up by American activist [Shaun King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaun_King), who argued that the logic for killing baby Hitler could just as easily be applied to a newborn [Christopher Columbus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Columbus), infant [slave-owners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery) or a young [Dylann Roof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dylann_Roof).[^1273] Australian moral philosopher Matthew Beard likewise brought up the idea of babies [Pol Pot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pol_Pot) and [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin), arguing that a clear set of ethical principles would be needed to determine which historical babies deserve to be killed.[^1274]

#### In theoretical physics

The question of killing baby Hitler contains a version of the [grandfather paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temporal_paradox),[^1275] also known as the "Hitler's Murder Paradox".[^1257] According to the [B-theory of time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-theory_of_time),[^1276] if someone travelled back in time with the intention of killing baby Hitler, then their reason for travelling back in time would be eliminated. It is often concluded that as the past has already happened, alteration of the past is a logical impossibility.[^1277] As Hitler killed himself in 1945, it can also be inferred that no time traveler has killed baby Hitler.[^1278]

In contrast to the B-theory, models that adopt the [A-theory of time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-theory_of_time) avoid logical contradictions in the killing of baby Hitler by [considering time to be two-dimensional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_time_dimensions), where the first dimension is standard time (*t*(x)) and the second dimension is known as *hyper-time* (*Ht*(x)).[^1279] Theories that leave room for the past to be changed include hyper-[eternalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eternalism_%28philosophy_of_time%29), two-dimensional [presentism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophical_presentism) and hyper-presentism, which each demonstrate the possibility of killing baby Hitler in two-dimensional time.[^1280] In these temporal models, both the past and the future are held to be [mutable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutable); in changing the past by killing baby Hitler, the time traveller also changes the future.[^1281] Although it can also be debated whether such temporal models genuinely change the past, or if killing baby Hitler simply affects the past by causing a variation in hyper-time.[^1282]

If time travel caused creation of a parallel universe, killing baby Hitler would only create a [parallel universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Possible_world) without Hitler in it, and the original universe would continue existing and thus the suffering he caused in that timeline would not be alleviated by the time-traveling assassin. From this perspective, astrophysicist Brian Koberlein concluded that killing baby Hitler would be "inconsequential at best, and could be downright harmful", recommending that time travelers avoid such an activity and instead visit the 1980s.[^1283]

#### Public debate

In conversations about time travel, it is common to raise the subject of changing the past and specifically the question of killing baby Hitler,[^1284] in what is also known as "[Godwin's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godwin's_law) of time travel".[^1283] Public debate on the baby Hitler question was brought to prominence in October 2015, when a poll by *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times)* asked its readers if they would kill baby Hitler.[^1250] The poll received a plurality of affirmative responses:[^1285] 42% said they would kill baby Hitler, 30% said they would not and 28% were undecided.[^1286] The poll caused the hashtag \#babyhitler to begin trending on [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter), as the social media platform's users debated the subject.[^1251]

During the campaign for the [2016 Republican Party presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries), when the question of killing baby Hitler was posed by journalists of *[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost)* to Florida governor [Jeb Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Bush), he responded "Hell Yeah, I Would!".[^1287] While acknowledging the potential unknown consequences of such an action, he affirmed that he would still do it, saying "You gotta step up, man."[^1288] The issue of killing baby Hitler was also raised during that year's [Democratic Party presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries), with [New Hampshire primary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_New_Hampshire_Democratic_presidential_primary) [novelty candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_candidate) [Vermin Supreme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermin_Supreme) making it one of the four planks of his political platform.[^1289] American actor [Tom Hanks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Hanks) responded to the political debate by declaring that he would vote for a presidential candidate that supported killing baby Hitler.[^1290] When the question was posed to [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft)'s chatbot [Tay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tay_%28chatbot%29), it likewise replied that "of course" it would kill baby Hitler.[^1291]

In contrast, American comedian [Stephen Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Colbert) responded to the question by saying that he would not kill baby Hitler and would instead seek to raise him in a loving home.[^1292] In a 2018 interview with *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post)*, American actor [John C. Reilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_C._Reilly) responded similarly, calling for empathy with baby Hitler as an [apolitical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apoliticism) alternative.[^1293] That same year, English comedian [Ricky Gervais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Gervais) began telling jokes about the dilemma of killing baby Hitler.[^1294] At the [March for Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_for_Life_%28Washington,_D.C.%29) in 2019, American conservative pundit [Ben Shapiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Shapiro) argued against killing baby Hitler from an [anti-abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-abortion_movements) position, stating that "Baby Hitler was a baby."[^1295] His comments drew criticism and mockery from [liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States) commentators.[^1296] In response to his position on killing baby Hitler, three companies pulled their advertisements from Shapiro's podcast.[^1297]

### Radcliffe Line

The **Radcliffe Line** was the boundary demarcated by the two boundary commissions for the provinces of [Punjab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjab_Province_%28British_India%29) and [Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency) during the [Partition of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_India). It is named after [Cyril Radcliffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_Radcliffe,_1st_Viscount_Radcliffe), who, as the joint chairman of the two boundary commissions, had the ultimate responsibility to equitably divide 175,000 square miles (450,000 km²) of territory with 88 million people.[^1298]

The term "Radcliffe Line" is also sometimes used for the entire boundary between India and Pakistan. However, outside of Punjab and Bengal, the boundary is made of pre-existing provincial boundaries and had nothing to do with the Radcliffe commissions.

The demarcation line was published on 17 August 1947, two days after the independence of Pakistan and India. Today, the Punjab part of the line is part of the [India-Pakistan border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India%E2%80%93Pakistan_border) while the Bengal part of the line serves as the [Bangladesh-India border](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh%E2%80%93India_border).

#### Background

##### Events leading up to the Radcliffe Boundary Commissions

On 18 July 1947, the [Indian Independence Act 1947](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Independence_Act_1947) of the Parliament of the United Kingdom stipulated that British rule in India would come to an end just one month later, on 15 August 1947. The Act also stipulated the partition of the [Presidencies and provinces of British India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidencies_and_provinces_of_British_India) into two new sovereign [dominions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion): India and Pakistan.

Pakistan was intended as a Muslim homeland, while India remained [secular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secular). Muslim-majority British provinces in the northwest were to become the foundation of Pakistan. The provinces of [Baluchistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balochistan_%28Pakistan%29) (91.8% Muslim before partition) and [Sindh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sindh) (72.7%) and [North-West Frontier Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North-West_Frontier_Province) became entirely Pakistani territory. However, two provinces did not have an overwhelming Muslim majority, [Punjab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjab_Province_%28British_India%29) in the northwest (55.7% Muslim) and [Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_Presidency) in the northeast (54.4% Muslim).[^1299] After elaborate discussions, these two provinces ended up being partitioned between India and Pakistan.

The Punjab's population distribution was such that there was no line that could neatly divide the [Hindus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindus), [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslims), and [Sikhs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikhs). Likewise, no line could appease both the [Muslim League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-India_Muslim_League), headed by [Jinnah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Ali_Jinnah), and the [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_National_Congress) led by [Jawaharlal Nehru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru) and [Vallabhbhai Patel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vallabhbhai_Patel). Moreover, any division based on religious communities was sure to entail "cutting through road and rail communications, irrigation schemes, electric power systems and even individual landholdings."[^1300]

##### Prior ideas of partition

The idea of partitioning the provinces of Bengal and Punjab had been present since the beginning of the 20th century. Bengal had in fact been [partitioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_Bengal_%281905%29) by the then viceroy [Lord Curzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Curzon) in 1905, along with its adjoining regions. The resulting province of Eastern Bengal and Assam, with its capital at [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka), had a Muslim majority, while West Bengal, with its capital at [Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcutta), had a Hindu majority. However, this partition of Bengal was reversed in 1911 in an effort to mollify [Bengali nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_nationalism).[^1301]

Proposals for partitioning Punjab had been made starting in 1908. Its proponents included the Hindu leader [Bhai Parmanand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhai_Parmanand), Congress leader [Lala Lajpat Rai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lala_Lajpat_Rai), industrialist [G. D. Birla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G._D._Birla), and various Sikh leaders. After the 1940 [Lahore resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore_resolution) of the Muslim League demanding Pakistan, [B. R. Ambedkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._R._Ambedkar) wrote a 400-page tract titled *Thoughts on Pakistan.*[^1302] In the tract, he discussed the boundaries of Muslim and non-Muslim regions of Punjab and Bengal. His calculations showed a Muslim majority in 16 western districts of Punjab and non-Muslim majority in 13 eastern districts. In Bengal, he showed non-Muslim majority in 15 districts. He thought the Muslims could have no objection to redrawing provincial boundaries. If they did, "they \[did\] not understand the nature of their own demand".[^1303][^1304]

After the breakdown of the 1945 [Simla Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simla_Conference) of viceroy [Lord Wavell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Wavell,_1st_Earl_Wavell), the idea of Pakistan began to be contemplated seriously. Sir [Evan Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Meredith_Jenkins), the private secretary of the viceroy (later the governor of Punjab), wrote a memorandum titled "Pakistan and the Punjab", where he discussed the issues surrounding the partition of Punjab. [K. M. Panikkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K._M._Panikkar), then prime minister of the [Bikaner State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bikaner_State), sent a memorandum to the viceroy titled "Next Step in India", wherein he recommended that the principle of 'Muslim homeland' be conceded but territorial adjustments made to the two provinces to meet the claims of the Hindus and Sikhs. Based on these discussions, the viceroy sent a note on the "Pakistan theory" to the [Secretary of State for India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_India) .[^1305] The viceroy informed the Secretary of State that Jinnah envisaged the *full provinces* of Bengal and Punjab going to Pakistan with only minor adjustments, whereas Congress was expecting *almost half* of these provinces to remain in India. This essentially framed the problem of partition.[^1306]

The Secretary of State responded by directing Lord Wavell to send 'actual proposals for defining genuine Muslim areas'. The task fell on [V. P. Menon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._P._Menon), the Reforms Commissioner, and his colleague Sir [B. N. Rau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._N._Rau) in the Reforms Office. They prepared a note called "Demarcation of Pakistan Areas", where they included the three western divisions of Punjab ([Rawalpindi, Multan and Lahore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjab_Province_%28British_India%29)) in Pakistan, leaving two eastern divisions of Punjab in India ([Jullundur and Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punjab_Province_%28British_India%29)). However, they noted that this allocation would leave 2.2 million Sikhs in the Pakistan area and about 1.5 million in India. Excluding the [Amritsar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amritsar_district) and [Gurdaspur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurdaspur_district) districts of the Lahore Division from Pakistan would put a majority of Sikhs in India. (Amritsar had a non-Muslim majority and Gurdaspur a marginal Muslim majority.) To compensate for the exclusion of the Gurdaspur district, they included the entire [Dinajpur district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Dinajpur_district) in the eastern zone of Pakistan, which similarly had a marginal Muslim majority. After receiving comments from John Thorne, member of the Executive Council in charge of Home affairs, Wavell forwarded the proposal to the Secretary of State. He justified the exclusion of the Amritsar district because of its sacredness to the Sikhs and that of Gurdaspur district because it had to go with Amritsar for 'geographical reasons'.[^1307][^1308][^1309][^1310] The Secretary of State commended the proposal and forwarded it to the India and Burma Committee, saying, "I do not think that any better division than the one the Viceroy proposes is likely to be found".[^1311]

##### Sikh concerns

The Sikh leader [Master Tara Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_Tara_Singh) could see that any division of Punjab would leave the Sikhs divided between Pakistan and India. He espoused the doctrine of self-reliance, [opposed the partition of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_to_the_partition_of_India) and called for independence on the grounds that no single religious community should control Punjab.[^1312] Other Sikhs argued that just as Muslims feared Hindu domination the Sikhs also feared Muslim domination. Sikhs warned the British government that the morale of Sikh troops in the British Army would be affected if Pakistan was forced on them. [Giani Kartar Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyani_Kartar_Singh_Komal) drafted a scheme of a separate Sikh state if India was to be divided.[^1313]

During the Partition developments, Jinnah offered Sikhs to live in Pakistan with safeguards for their rights. Sikhs refused because they opposed the concept of Pakistan and also because they did not want to become a small minority within a Muslim majority. Vir Singh Bhatti distributed pamphlets for the creation of a separate Sikh state "[Khalistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khalistan_movement)".[^1314] Master Tara Singh wanted the right for an independent Khalistan to federate with either Hindustan or Pakistan. However, the Sikh state being proposed was for an area where neither religion was in absolute majority.[^1315] Negotiations for the independent Sikh state had commenced at the end of World War II and the British initially agreed but the Sikhs withdrew this demand after pressure from Indian nationalists.[^1316] The proposals of the Cabinet Mission Plan had seriously jolted the Sikhs because while both the Congress and League could be satisfied the Sikhs saw nothing in it for themselves, as they would be subjected to a Muslim majority. Master Tara Singh protested this to Pethic-Lawrence on 5 May. By early September the Sikh leaders accepted both the long term and interim proposals despite their earlier rejection.[^1315] The Sikhs attached themselves to the Indian state with the promise of religious and cultural autonomy.[^1316]

##### Final negotiations

In March 1946, the British government sent a [Cabinet Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1946_Cabinet_Mission_to_India) to India to find a solution to resolve the conflicting demands of Congress and the Muslim League. Congress agreed to allow Pakistan to be formed with 'genuine Muslim areas'. The Sikh leaders asked for a Sikh state with [Ambala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambala_Division), [Jalandher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jalandhar_Division), [Lahore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore_Division) Divisions with some districts from the [Multan Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multan_Division), which, however, did not meet the Cabinet delegates' agreement. In discussions with Jinnah, the Cabinet Mission offered either a 'smaller Pakistan' with all the Muslim-majority districts *except Gurdaspur* or a 'larger Pakistan' under the sovereignty of the Indian Union.[^1317] The Cabinet Mission came close to success with its proposal for an Indian Union under a federal scheme, but it fell apart in the end.[^1318][^1319]

In March 1947, [Lord Mountbatten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mountbatten) arrived in India as the next viceroy, with an explicit mandate to achieve the transfer of power before June 1948. Over ten days, Mountbatten obtained the agreement of Congress to the Pakistan demand except for the 13 eastern districts of Punjab (including Amritsar and Gurdaspur).[^1320] However, Jinnah held out. Through a series of six meetings with Mountbatten, he continued to maintain that his demand was for six full provinces. He "bitterly complained" that the Viceroy was ruining his Pakistan by cutting Punjab and Bengal in half as this would mean a 'moth-eaten Pakistan'.[^1321][^1322][^1323]

The Gurdaspur district remained a key contentious issue for the non-Muslims. Their members of the Punjab legislature made representations to Mountbatten's chief of staff [Lord Ismay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Ismay) as well as the Governor telling them that Gurdaspur was a "non-Muslim district". They contended that even if it had a marginal Muslim majority of 51%, which they believed to be erroneous, the Muslims paid only 35% of the land revenue in the district.[^1324]

In April, the Governor of Punjab [Evan Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Meredith_Jenkins) wrote a note to Mountbatten proposing that Punjab be divided along Muslim and non-Muslim majority districts and proposed that a Boundary Commission be set up consisting of two Muslim and two non-Muslim members recommended by the Punjab Legislative Assembly. He also proposed that a British judge of the High Court be appointed as the chairman of the commission.[^1325] Jinnah and the Muslim League continued to oppose the idea of partitioning the provinces, and the Sikhs were disturbed about the possibility of getting only 12 districts (without Gurdaspur). In this context, the Partition Plan of 3 June was announced with a notional partition showing 17 districts of Punjab in Pakistan and 12 districts in India, along with the establishment of a Boundary Commission to decide the final boundary. In Sialkoti's view, this was done mainly to placate the Sikhs.[^1326]

#### Process and key people

A crude border had already been drawn up by [Lord Wavell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Wavell,_1st_Earl_Wavell), the [Viceroy of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroy_of_India) prior to his replacement as Viceroy, in February 1947, by [Lord Louis Mountbatten.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Mountbatten,_1st_Earl_Mountbatten_of_Burma) In order to determine exactly which territories to assign to each country, in June 1947, Britain appointed [Sir Cyril Radcliffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Cyril_Radcliffe) to chair two boundary commissions, one for Bengal and one for Punjab.[^1327]

The commission was instructed to "demarcate the boundaries of the two parts of the Punjab on the basis of ascertaining the contiguous majority areas of Muslims and non-Muslims. In doing so, it will also take into account other factors."[^1328] Other factors were undefined, giving Radcliffe leeway, but included decisions regarding "natural boundaries, communications, watercourses and irrigation systems", as well as socio-political consideration.[^1329] Each commission also had four representatives, two from the [Indian National Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_National_Congress) and two from the [Muslim League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-India_Muslim_League). Given the deadlock between the interests of the two sides and their rancorous relationship, the final decision was essentially Radcliffe's.

After arriving in India on 8 July 1947, Radcliffe was given just five weeks to decide on a border.[^1327] He soon met with his fellow college alumnus Mountbatten and travelled to [Lahore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lahore) and [Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcutta) to meet with commission members, chiefly Nehru from the Congress and Jinnah, president of the Muslim League.[^1330] He objected to the short time frame, but all parties were insistent that the line be finished by the 15 August British withdrawal from India. Mountbatten had accepted the post as Viceroy on the condition of an early deadline.[^1331] The decision was completed just a couple of days before the withdrawal, but due to political considerations, not published until 17 August 1947, two days after the grant of independence to India and Pakistan.[^1327]

##### Members of the commissions

Each boundary commission consisted of five people: a chairman (Radcliffe), two members nominated by the Indian National Congress, and two members nominated by the Muslim League.[^1332]
