#### Lawsuit against Bears

Butkus's retirement came with four years remaining on a five-year contract with the Bears, which was to pay him \$115,000 per year through 1977. It came with a [no-cut, no-trade clause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_trade_clause), and was payable even if surgery was needed. The contract also promised necessary medical and hospital care which, according to Butkus, the Bears did not give him, causing irreparable damage to his knee. The Bears then told him he would not be paid if he could not play. Butkus sued the Bears' team doctor in May 1974, asking for \$600,000 in compensatory damages and \$1 million in punitive damages.[^1804][^1805] It was settled out of court when the Bears agreed to pay Butkus the full value of his contract. The episode caused a rift between Butkus and George Halas, and the two did not speak for the next five years.[^1806]

#### Profile and reputation

> Dick was an animal. I called him a maniac. A stone maniac. He was a well-conditioned animal, and every time he hit you, he tried to put you in the cemetery, not the hospital.[^1756]

 [Deacon Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deacon_Jones), Pro Football Hall of Fame defensive end

Standing 6 feet 3 inches (1.91 m) tall and weighing 245 pounds (111 kg), Butkus was a large linebacker for the era in which he played.[^1771] This size was a common trait in his family: all four of his brothers and his father were over six feet tall and weighed over 200 pounds. He was also diligent with his conditioning. In high school he would push a car up and down a street to strengthen his legs,[^1807] and in college he developed a routine of running at trees and dodging them to emulate avoiding blockers.[^1808] Despite his size, he had the speed and agility to make tackles from sideline to sideline and cover tight ends and running backs on pass plays.[^1809]

Hall of Famer [Bill George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_George_%28linebacker%29), whom Butkus succeeded as the Bears' middle linebacker, said: "The first time I saw Butkus, I started packing my gear. I knew my Bear days were numbered. There was no way that guy wasn't going to be great."[^1810]

Consistently cited as one of football's meanest, toughest, and most feared players, Butkus was renowned for his intimidating profile and style of play.[^1776][^1770] He was known to snarl at the opposition before plays.[^1811] Quarterbacks complained that Butkus bit them in pileups.[^1812] Lions tight end [Charlie Sanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Sanders) said Butkus poked him in the eyes through his face mask.[^1813] He once intercepted a pass from [Minnesota Vikings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Vikings) quarterback [Fran Tarkenton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran_Tarkenton) near the goal line, and instead of taking the ball into the end zone for an easy touchdown, he took aim at Tarkenton to run him over.[^1761] When asked by a reporter if he was as mean as the rumors suggested, Butkus replied, "I wouldn't ever go out to hurt anybody deliberately. Unless it was, you know, important, like a league game or something."[^1814]

Butkus played angry, often "manufacturing" things to make him mad, because he felt it gave him a competitive edge.[^1809][^1815] After the Bears lost to the Lions in their first matchup of 1969, Lions rookie running back [Altie Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altie_Taylor) told reporters that Butkus was overrated. The next time the teams played that season, Butkus chased Taylor out of bounds after a play and caused him to jump into the stands at [Wrigley Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrigley_Field).[^1816][^1817]

Butkus became most noted for his tackling ability, and the ferocity with which he tackled. He was named the most feared tackler of all time by the [NFL Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_Network) in 2009.[^1818] Once during practice, he hit a metal football sled so hard that he crumpled it and left a piece of it dangling.[^1810] Former Bears defensive end [Ed O'Bradovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_O'Bradovich) said: "Tackling wasn't good enough. Just to hit people wasn't good enough. He loved to crush people."[^1816] Butkus is credited with 1,020 tackles in his NFL career.[^1771][^1819][^1820]

Butkus recovered 27 fumbles in his career,[^1755] an NFL record at the time of his retirement.[^1771] One of his greatest strengths was his ability to rip the ball from a ball carrier's hands. Although not an official statistic at the time, it has been noted that Butkus would certainly be one of the all-time leaders in forced fumbles.[^1816][^1790]

Despite all Butkus did on defense, during his time with the Bears the team won 48 games, lost 74, and tied 4.[^1821]

#### Legacy and honors

*[USA Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USA_Today)* called Butkus the "gold standard by which other middle linebackers are measured."[^1757] Although not the creator of the middle linebacker position, which is credited to his predecessor [Bill George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_George_%28linebacker%29), Butkus is recognized as having defined the role.[^1756][^1819] He is also recognized for having set the benchmark for the success of Bears middle linebackers, which continued with [Mike Singletary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Singletary) and [Brian Urlacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Urlacher).[^1822] Hall of Fame running back [Earl Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_Campbell), known for his hard-hitting running style, cited Butkus as his hero growing up.[^1823]

After his university years, Butkus continued to receive recognition for his college career. He was inducted into the [College Football Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_Football_Hall_of_Fame) in 1983.[^1824] His No. 50 jersey is one of only two retired by the Illinois Fighting Illini football program, the other being the No. 77 of [Red Grange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Grange),[^1825] and he was an inaugural inductee into the Illinois Athletics Hall of Fame in 2016.[^1826] Butkus was named to the [Walter Camp Football Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Camp_Football_Foundation)'s All-Century Team in 1999, compiled to honor the best college players of the 20th century.[^1827] In November 2017, Illinois announced it would erect a statue of Butkus on campus to overlook a future football performance center.[^1828]

Butkus was elected to the [Pro Football Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_Football_Hall_of_Fame) in 1979, his first year of eligibility.[^1829] The Hall's voters also named him to the NFL's [1960s All-Decade Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League_1960s_All-Decade_Team) and [1970s All-Decade Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League_1970s_All-Decade_Team), deeming him one of the best players of both decades.[^1830] On October 31, 1994, the Bears [retired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retired_number) Butkus's No. 51 jersey along with Sayers's No. 40 jersey during a ceremony at Soldier Field.[^1831] In 2004, a sculpture featuring Butkus, Halas, and seven other former Bears greats was unveiled at Soldier Field.[^1806]

Butkus has been repeatedly ranked among the top players in NFL history, being named the ninth-best player in NFL history by *[The Sporting News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sporting_News)* in 1999,[^1832] the tenth-best by the [NFL Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_Network) in its *The Top 100: NFL's Greatest Players* series in 2010,[^1833] and the eighth-best by the *[New York Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Daily_News)* in 2014.[^1834] In 2017, NFL senior analyst [Gil Brandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gil_Brandt) ranked Butkus as the third greatest linebacker of all time, behind [Derrick Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derrick_Thomas) and [Lawrence Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Taylor).[^1835] He was also selected the 70th greatest athlete of the 20th century by [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN).[^1836] In 1994, he was named to the [NFL 75th Anniversary All-Time Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_75th_Anniversary_All-Time_Team), compiled to recognize the best players of the NFL's first 75 years as adjudged by NFL officials and media personnel.[^1837] In 2019, Butkus was named to the [NFL 100th Anniversary All-Time Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_100th_Anniversary_All-Time_Team).[^1838]

Butkus was ranked No. 1 on *[NFL Top 10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_Top_10): Most Feared Tacklers* when the episode aired in 2008.[^1839]

Honoring his contributions to Chicago sports, Butkus was inducted into the [Chicagoland Sports Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicagoland_Sports_Hall_of_Fame) in 2008.[^1840] On August 24, 2013, he was inducted into the National Lithuanian American Hall of Fame.[^1841] In 2018, Butkus was inducted as a laureate of [The Lincoln Academy of Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lincoln_Academy_of_Illinois) and awarded the Order of Lincoln, the state's highest honor, by the [Governor of Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Illinois).[^1842] In 2024, he was inducted into the National High School Football Hall of Fame.[^1843]

In 1985, the Downtown Athletic Club of [Orlando, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando,_Florida), created the [Butkus Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butkus_Award), which is given annually to the most outstanding linebacker at the high school, college, and professional levels as chosen by a nationwide panel of 51 coaches and sportswriters.[^1844] Butkus sued the Downtown Athletic Club for rights to the award in 2007, which it relinquished after a yearlong court battle. It has since been presented by the Butkus Foundation.[^1845]

As an homage, actor [Sylvester Stallone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvester_Stallone) named his pet [Bullmastiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullmastiff) *Butkus* after the dog ate a security blanket. He decided to name him after "possibly the fiercest football player in history".[^1846] The dog later starred alongside Stallone in the *[Rocky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_%28film_series%29)* film series.[^1756]

#### Film and television career

After his career as a player, Butkus became a celebrity endorser, broadcaster, and actor.[^1847][^1848] He appeared in films such as *[The Longest Yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Longest_Yard_%281974_film%29)* (1974),[^1849] *[Cry, Onion!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cry,_Onion!)* (1975),[^1850] *[Mother, Jugs & Speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother,_Jugs_&_Speed)* (1976),[^1851] *[Gus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gus_%281976_film%29)* (1976),[^1852] *[Superdome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superdome_%28film%29)* (1978),[^1852] *[Cracking Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cracking_Up_%281983_film%29)* (1983),[^1851] *[Johnny Dangerously](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Dangerously)* (1984),[^1851] *Hamburger: The Motion Picture* (1986),[^1851] *[The Stepford Children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stepford_Children)* (1987),[^1852] *[Spontaneous Combustion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spontaneous_Combustion_%28film%29)* (1990),[^1852] *Gremlins 2: The New Batch* (1990),[^1847][^1853] *[Necessary Roughness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necessary_Roughness_%28film%29)* (1991),[^1847] and *[Any Given Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Any_Given_Sunday)* (1999),[^1847] and as a regular character on TV shows such as *[Blue Thunder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Thunder_%28TV_series%29)*,[^1847] *[My Two Dads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Two_Dads)*,[^1847] *[MacGyver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacGyver_%281985_TV_series%29),*[^1847] and *[Hang Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hang_Time_%28TV_series%29)*,[^1847] as well as in a guest roles on *[Emergency!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency!)*, *[The Six Million Dollar Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Six_Million_Dollar_Man)*, *[Murder, She Wrote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder,_She_Wrote)* and *[Matlock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matlock_%281986_TV_series%29)*.[^1854] He portrayed himself in both the critically acclaimed TV movie *[Brian's Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian's_Song)* (1971)[^1855] and the 2002 comedy *[Teddy Bears' Picnic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teddy_Bears'_Picnic_%28film%29)*.[^1847] Butkus portrayed Officer Alvin Dimsky in *[Cass Malloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_Malloy)*,[^1856] the 1982 [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS) pilot for what later became the [syndicated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcast_syndication) situation comedy *[She's the Sheriff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/She's_the_Sheriff)*, and also made cameo appearances in episodes of several television shows.[^1847][^1848]

Butkus endorsed [Prestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AlliedSignal), a brand of [antifreeze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antifreeze), in a commercial during [Super Bowl IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_IV) in 1970. The ad marked the first highly successful celebrity endorsement in [Super Bowl advertising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_commercials).[^1857] Throughout the late 1970s and early 1980s, Butkus appeared alongside fellow former NFL star (and later *Blue Thunder* co-star) [Bubba Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubba_Smith) in a series of ads for [Miller Lite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller_Lite), which were released to high acclaim.[^1858] In 1985, he was a pitchman for [Echo Tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echo_Tools), a producer of outdoor power equipment.[^1859] In the 1990s, Butkus promoted the "Qwik-Cook Grill", a grill using newspaper as its main fuel.[^1860]

Butkus returned to the Bears as a color analyst on radio broadcasts in 1985, teaming with first-year play-by-play man [Wayne Larrivee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Larrivee) and former [St. Louis Cardinals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis_Cardinals_%28NFL%29) quarterback [Jim Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Hart_%28American_football%29). He was hired as the replacement for [Jimmy "The Greek" Snyder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_%22The_Greek%22_Snyder) on [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NFL_on_CBS)'s pregame show *[The NFL Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_NFL_Today)* in 1988,[^1861] serving as an analyst through 1989. He was named as head coach of the [XFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XFL_%282001%29)'s [Chicago Enforcers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Enforcers) franchise, but was replaced by coach [Ron Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Meyer) for the league's only season in 2001.[^1860] Instead, Butkus served as the league's director of competition and, during the second half of the season, a color commentator for the league's regional telecasts.[^1862]

In 2005, as part of the [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN) reality series *[Bound for Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bound_for_Glory_%28TV_series%29)*, Butkus served as head football coach of [Montour High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montour_High_School) in [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania).[^1863] He coached the team to a 1-6 record before departing with two games remaining in the season, saying he had fulfilled his contract for the show.[^1864]

#### Personal and later life

Butkus married his high school sweetheart, Helen Essenberg, in 1963, while they were students at the University of Illinois.[^1865][^1813] After retiring, Butkus moved to Florida, and later to [Malibu, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malibu,_California). He was an avid fan and frequent media image for the Bears.[^1770]

Butkus had three children: Ricky, Matt, and Nikki.[^1866] Matt played college football for the [USC Trojans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USC_Trojans_football) as a defensive lineman and joined his father in philanthropic activities.[^1867][^1868] Butkus's nephew [Luke Butkus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luke_Butkus) has been an assistant coach in the NFL for the Chicago Bears, [Seattle Seahawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Seahawks), and [Jacksonville Jaguars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacksonville_Jaguars); he also coached for the [University of Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Illinois), his alma mater, and as of 2023 is the offensive line coach for the [Green Bay Packers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Bay_Packers).[^1869][^1870] Butkus's grandson Ian Parish played [volleyball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volleyball_in_the_United_States) for the [UCLA Bruins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA_Bruins).[^1871]

Injuries sustained during Butkus's playing career compounded with time. He had his knee replaced with a metal unit. An [osteotomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteotomy) left him with one leg 1.5 inches shorter than the other, which affected his hips, back, and neck. Around 2002, nerve damage in his spine caused him to develop [foot drop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_drop). He lost strength in his hands, needing both to lift a coffee cup.[^1761] Still, Butkus maintained that football had a largely positive impact on his life, and that its benefits should not be overlooked.[^1872]

In August 2001, Butkus underwent quintuple [bypass surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_artery_bypass_surgery) to remove blockages in his arteries. After the surgery, he co-authored a book, *The OC Cure For Heart Disease*, with Lawrence J. Santora, the doctor who performed the procedure.[^1873]

Butkus died in his sleep at his home in [Malibu, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malibu,_California), on October 5, 2023, aged 80.[^1874] The cause of death was a stroke, with [atrial fibrillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atrial_fibrillation), [atherosclerosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atherosclerosis), and [hypercholesterolemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypercholesterolemia) listed as underlying causes.[^1875] He died hours before the Bears were scheduled to play a *[Thursday Night Football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thursday_Night_Football)* game against the [Washington Commanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Commanders). A moment of silence was held before the game.[^1876][^1877]

#### Philanthropy

Through The Butkus Foundation, Butkus supported many charitable causes. The foundation was formed to manage the receipt and disbursement of funds for his charitable causes. These include:

- The [Butkus Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butkus_Award), instituted in 1985, is one of the elite individual honors in football. The Butkus Foundation takes stewardship of the award recognizing athletic achievement and service to the community while honoring the nation's best high school, college, and professional linebackers. An independent selection committee comprises 51 people, including professional, college, and high school scouts, and sports journalists.[^1844]
- The Dick Butkus Center for Cardiovascular Wellness is a nonprofit organization in [Orange County, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange_County,_California), with a cardiac screening program that uses specialized testing to help identify those at risk of heart disease and [sudden cardiac death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudden_cardiac_death).[^1878] Butkus was on the field when [Chuck Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Hughes) collapsed and died of a heart attack during a game against the Lions in 1971.[^1879]
- The I Play Clean Campaign addresses [steroid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anabolic_steroid) use among high school athletes. The campaign educates and encourages athletes to train and eat well without resorting to performance-enhancing products.[^1880]

### Curtis Hidden Page

**Curtis Hidden Page** (April 4, 1870 - December 12, 1946) was a United States educator and writer.

#### Biography

Curtis Hidden Page was born in [Greenwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwood,_Missouri), Missouri.[^1881] He graduated from [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University), where in 1890 he became the first recipient of the [George B. Sohier Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_B._Sohier_Prize) for literature. He held teaching positions in French and English at [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University) (1893-1908), [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University) (1908-1909), [Northwestern University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_University) (professor of English literature, 1909-1911), and [Dartmouth College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_College) (professor of English literature, 1911-1946).[^1882]

Page was elected to the [New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hampshire) state legislature in 1933 and again in 1939.[^1882]

Compiler of anthologies of verse such as *British Poets of the Nineteenth Century* and *The Chief American Poets,*[^1881] Page also published verses, essays, and stories in numerous periodicals. In 1906, writing of his activities to his fellow Harvard alumni, he stated: "I have two volumes of verse nearly ready, but find little time to give to completing them and doubt if they will be published until after I am dead!"[^1883]

Page also translated many French works, including *A Voyage to the Moon*, by [Cyrano de Bergerac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrano_de_Bergerac_%28writer%29) and *The Man Who Married a Dumb Wife* by [Anatole France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatole_France). He published a well-regarded[^1884] translation of eight plays by [Molière](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moli%C3%A8re) in 1908; of these, *Tartuffe, or the Hypocrite* is available online from [Project Gutenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gutenberg).

He died in [Laconia, New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laconia,_New_Hampshire) on December 12, 1946.[^1885]

[*Who's Who in New York City and State*](https://books.google.com/books?id=xVUYAAAAMAAJ) (3rd ed.). New York: L.R. Hamersly. p. 1008. Retrieved May 11, 2025 - via Google Books.

University of Texas at Austin. Archived from [the original](http://research.hrc.utexas.edu:8080/hrcxtf/view?docId=ead/00426.xml) on March 1, 2012. Retrieved May 11, 2025.

### Pro-Life (politician)

**Pro-Life** (born **Marvin Thomas Richardson**; August 5, 1941) is an American [perennial candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perennial_candidate) and [strawberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strawberry) farmer known for his strong [opposition to abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_to_legal_abortion), which inspired him to legally change his name.[^1886] He lives in the unincorporated community of [Letha, Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letha,_Idaho).[^1887] He has made several unsuccessful runs for political office in Idaho[^1888] and has stated his intention to continue running for office until his death.[^1886][^1889] Pro-Life ran in the [2020 United States House of Representatives elections in Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_Idaho), receiving 2.2% of the vote, and was most recently the [Constitution Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Party_%28United_States%29) nominee in the [2022 Idaho lieutenant gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Idaho_lieutenant_gubernatorial_election), receiving 5.1%.

#### Early life and education

Born Marvin Thomas Richardson, Pro-Life was born in [Carbon County, Wyoming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_County,_Wyoming), to a [Latter Day Saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latter_Day_Saint) family. He played [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball) in high school and attended [Brigham Young University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_Young_University) on an [athletic scholarship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletic_scholarship) but was eventually cut from the varsity basketball team. He graduated from BYU in 1967 with a degree in [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science) after serving as an [LDS missionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missionary_%28LDS_Church%29) in [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California), and [Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada).[^1890]

Pro-Life has worked as an [organic farmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_farming) since 2002, mainly farming [strawberries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strawberry). He has previously worked as an [accountant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accountant), [coal miner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_mining), and salesman of [irrigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irrigation) equipment and [Caterpillar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caterpillar_Inc.) parts.[^1890]

#### Career

##### Campaigns

As Marvin Richardson, Pro-Life first ran for public office in 2004 when he challenged [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_%28United_States%29) [Kathy Skippen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Skippen) for a seat in the [Idaho House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idaho_House_of_Representatives). Skippen won 78% to 22%.[^1891]

Having [legally changed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Name_change) his middle name to "Pro-Life" in 2004,[^1890] Richardson filed for the [2006 Idaho governor's race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Idaho_gubernatorial_election) as Marvin Pro-Life Richardson.[^1886] The [Idaho Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_of_Idaho)'s office would not allow Richardson to appear on the ballot with his new middle name, although he could be listed as Marvin P. Richardson. Secretary of State [Ben Ysursa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Ysursa) said, "We've made it clear to him since March we were not going to put '[pro-life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-life)' on the ballot, and that's still our position. The ballot is not supposed to be a forum for political expression, it's supposed to be as neutral as it can be."[^1892] Richardson was invited to participate in the 2006 gubernatorial debate, but did not respond to his invitation in time.[^1893] Initially, Richardson was the [Constitution Party's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Party_%28United_States%29) candidate in the 2006 gubernatorial election,[^1894] but the [Constitution Party of Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Party_of_Idaho) disavowed him. That year, he had his name changed to simply "Pro-Life," but still appeared as Marvin Richardson on the ballot.[^1892] In the election, he received 1.62 percent of the vote, behind [Democrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_%28United_States%29) [Jerry Brady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Brady) and the winner, [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_%28United_States%29) [Butch Otter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butch_Otter).[^1895]

In 2008, Pro-Life ran as an independent for the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate) seat being vacated by [Larry Craig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Craig). That year, he was allowed to appear on the ballot as "Pro-Life." The executive director of an Idaho [anti-abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-abortion) group expressed concern that voters would mistake Pro-Life's name on the ballot for a position rather than a candidate.[^1896] Such fears led to a qualifier next to Pro-Life's name on the ballot: "(A person, formerly known as Marvin Richardson)."[^1897] He has appeared thus on all subsequent Idaho ballots. He received 1.34 percent of the votes in the race, behind [Libertarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libertarian_Party_%28United_States%29) Kent Marmon, independent [Rex Rammell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rex_Rammell), Democrat [Larry LaRocco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_LaRocco), and the winner, Republican [Jim Risch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Risch).[^1898]

In 2010, Pro-Life ran for governor for a second time.[^1899] He came in fifth in the race, behind Libertarian Ted Dunlap, independent Jana Kemp, Democrat [Keith Allred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_G._Allred), and the winner, Republican Butch Otter.[^1900]

Pro-Life was a candidate for [Idaho's 1st congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idaho's_1st_congressional_district) in the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress) in 2012.[^1901] He ran against incumbent Republican [Raúl Labrador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ra%C3%BAl_Labrador) and Democrat [Jimmy Farris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Farris). According to [OpenSecrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenSecrets), Pro-Life's 2012 campaign was entirely self-financed.[^1902] The incumbent won the race.[^1903]

Pro-Life ran a third campaign for [Governor of Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Idaho) in the [2014 gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Idaho_gubernatorial_election).[^1889][^1904]

Pro-Life ran for the [Senate again in 2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_Senate_election_in_Idaho).[^1905][^1906] He was defeated in the [Constitution Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_Party_%28United_States%29) primary on May 17, 2016 by Ray J. Writz.[^1907]

##### Political views

Pro-Life has said he believes that abortion is [murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder), and he supports charging doctors who perform abortions with murder.[^1896]

He opposed the [Troubled Asset Relief Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troubled_Asset_Relief_Program) as a candidate in 2008, citing concerns that its implementation would result in "a total fascist dictatorship run by the bankers."[^1908] He opposes war undertaken without a declaration of war by Congress;[^1901] he supports a [non-interventionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-interventionist) foreign policy and considers the wars in [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War), [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_%282001%E2%80%93present%29), and [Libya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libyan_Civil_War_%282011%29) to be unjust and unconstitutional.[^1909] He also opposes [public education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_education), which he considers to be [communist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communism).[^1886] After the [Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Hook_Elementary_School_shooting), he suggested allowing Idaho sheriffs to organize groups of armed volunteers to protect schools.[^1889]

#### Personal life

Pro-Life is a [vegetarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetarianism).[^1886] As Marvin Richardson, he married Jean Benson in 1964; they divorced in 1982.[^1890]

He has been married to Kirsten Faith since 1982. In 2006, she ran for the Idaho House of Representatives as the Constitution Party nominee against Republican [Steven Thayn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Thayn), receiving 3,026 votes (24.56%).[^1910] Pro-Life encouraged her to run for this position, despite their conviction that [women should not work outside the home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separate_spheres).[^1911]

Pro-Life has 15 children, seven from his previous wife, and eight from his current wife.[^1912]

Formerly a member of [the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints), Pro-Life left the church in 1998, because of his view that the church does not ascribe [personhood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personhood) to the unborn.[^1890]

### Hubert Blaine Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff Sr.

**Hubert Blaine Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff Sr.** (4 August 1914 - 24 October 1997; surname also given as **Wolfstern**,[^1917] **Wolfe + 666**,[^1918] **Wolfe+585**,[^1919] **Wolfe+590**,[^1920] and others) was a German-born American [typesetter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typesetting) who held the record for the longest [personal name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_name) ever used.

Hubert's world record name was made up from 27 names. Each of his 26 [given names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Given_name) starts with a different letter of the [English alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_alphabet) in alphabetical order; these are followed by a long single-word [last name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_name). The exact length and spelling of his name has been a subject of considerable confusion due in part to its various renderings over the years, many of which have typographical errors. One of the longest and most reliable published versions, with a 666-letter surname, follows:

> Adolph Blaine Charles David Earl Frederick Gerald Hubert Irvin John Kenneth Lloyd Martin Nero Oliver Paul Quincy Randolph Sherman Thomas Uncas Victor William Xerxes Yancy Zeus  Sr.[^1918][^1921]

The Guinness World Records verified the version as follows:

> Adolph Blaine Charles David Earl Frederick Gerald Hubert Irvin John Kenneth Lloyd Martin Nero Oliver Paul Quincy Randolph Sherman Thomas Uncas Victor William Xerxes Yancy Zeus .[^1922]

#### Biography

Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff was born in [Bergedorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergedorf_%28quarter%29) (now part of [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg)), Germany, as the son of Violet M. ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N%C3%A9e) Fleisher) and Edward R. Wolfstern.[^1923] He later emigrated to the United States, settling in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia).[^1919] His birthdate has been given as February 29, 1904,[^1919][^1923][^1924] but he was also reported to be age 47 in a 1964 wire story,[^1925] and Philadelphia County death records list a birthdate of August 4, 1914.[^1926] He became a typesetter according to [Bennett Cerf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennett_Cerf).[^1927]

His name first attracted attention when it appeared in the 1938 Philadelphia telephone directory on page 1292, column 3, line 17,[^1928] and in a court order of judge John Boyle of May 25, 1938: "*Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff, Jr., etc., vs. [Yellow Cab Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_Cab_Company)*, petition for compromise settlement granted", with speculation that the case was settled because "they couldn't pronounce it".[^1928]

A son, Hubert Blaine Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff Jr., was born in Philadelphia in 1952, and was able to pronounce his surname by age three.[^1929] Family letterhead used the form "Hubert Blaine Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff".[^1924]

When *[Philadelphia Inquirer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Inquirer)* journalist [Frank Brookhouser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Brookhouser) omitted the letter "u" in reporting a 1952 Philadelphia voter registration under the 35-letter version of the surname, Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff's prompt correction was carried by *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_%28magazine%29)*[^1930] and passed on to other outlets.[^1931] Philadelphia's business computers used an abbreviated form on the city's voting registration books; the utility company, however, when told he would not pay his bill unless his name was right, began spelling it properly, on three lines.[^1932] Brookhouser later responded by tributing the correctly spelled Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff as the exemplar Philadelphian named in the first sentence of his *Our Philadelphia*, comparing him to another local typesetter, [Benjamin Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin):

> Philadelphia, home of Hubert B. Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff, Sr., like Benjamin Franklin a typesetter, and 2,071,604 other residents according to the last official census in 1950, is the third largest city in the United States of America and the biggest small town in the world.[^1933]

The executive secretary-treasurer of the American Name Society also provided a 163-letter spelling of the surname: "*Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorffvoralternwarengewissenhaftschaferswessenschaftswarenwohlgefutternundsorgfaltigkeitbeschutzenvorangreifendurchihrraubgierigfiends*", stating that this was his "full name as given ... at birth on the envelope".[^1934] This spelling was reproduced verbatim by the *Maryland and Delaware Genealogist*.[^1935]

In 1964, a widely reprinted [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press) wire story reported that the [IBM 7074](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_7074) computer at the [John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Co.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hancock_Mutual_Life_Insurance_Co.) could process one million policies but refused to handle that of Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff, which was specially processed by hand.[^1925] He explained to reporter Norman Goldstein, "When somebody calls my name, I don't have any trouble finding out who they mean ... I don't like being part of the common herd."[^1925] The article includes a 666-letter version of the surname, though individual newspapers which ran it made numerous typographical errors, making it difficult to ascertain which renderings (if any) are correct.[^1918]

[Logologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logology_%28linguistics%29) [Dmitri Borgmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Borgmann) devoted several pages to the unusually long name in his 1965 book *[Language on Vacation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_on_Vacation)*. According to Borgmann, the name had never before appeared correctly and in full in any book, and its bearer himself usually signed his name as "Hubert B. Wolfe + 666, Sr.".[^1918][^1936] The long-form version reproduced in *Language on Vacation* is said to have come from Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff's 1963 [Christmas card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_card), and to be the form in which it was submitted to the Associated Press for publication.[^1918]

[Onomastician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onomastics) Elsdon C. Smith, writing in *Treasury of Name Lore*, provides a 161-letter version of the surname, "*Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorffvoralternwarengewissenhaftschaferswessenschafswarenwohlgefutternundsorgfalugkeitbeschutzenvorangreifendurchihrraubgierigfeinds*", but noted that its holder used only the 35-letter version in correspondence with him. Smith affirmed the personal name was the longest in the United States but implied that Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff was a publicity seeker for adopting it.[^1937]

Between 1975 and 1985, Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff appeared in the *[Guinness Book of World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_Book_of_World_Records)* as having the longest personal name, and was photographed for the book in front of a [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City) marquee displaying his name, once again misspelled.[^1938] He also made personal appearances in television shows based on the *Guinness Book*.[^1917][^1939] By 1983, only the 35-letter form of the name appeared in the book. Various editions claimed he had recently shortened his surname to "Wolfe+585, Senior"[^1919] or to "Wolfe+590, Senior". By the 1990 edition, the "longest name" category had disappeared altogether.[^1940] Since 2021, the name is present in category "Longest personal name".[^1922]

In 1983, *[The National Enquirer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_Enquirer)* reported that the winner of its competition to find America's longest name was SnowOwl Sor-Lokken (born 1979), whose [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_%28state%29) birth certificate gives her first name as a concatenation of *Snowowl* with a version of *wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff...* for a total length reported as 598 letters in the next edition of the *Guinness Book*.[^1941] Sor-Lokken's father said he wanted "to throw a monkey wrench into the government bureaucracy".[^1941] Her given-name length record was broken in 1984.[^1924][^1942]

Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff has also been catalogued by logologist [Gyles Brandreth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyles_Brandreth)[^1943] and by *The Book of Useless Information*.[^1944]

#### Origin and translation of surname

Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff claimed that his great-grandfather composed the surname in the 19th century, when German Jews, who had not previously used a second name, had to adopt one.[^1945] In some printings of the above-noted AP wire story, Wolfeschlegelsteinhausenbergerdorff himself provided the following explanation of his prodigious surname:[^1946]

> It tells a story of a wolf-killer, a resident of a stonehouse in a village, whose ancestors were conscientious shepherds whose sheep were well fed and carefully guarded against attack by ferocious enemies and whose ancestors 1,200,000 years before the first earth man, in a space ship made with tungsten and seven iridium motors and using light as a source of power, started a long journey across interstellar space, searching for a star around which was an inhabitable planet where they could establish a new race of intelligent mankind and where they would live long, happy lives and be free from attack by other intelligentsia from the outer space from whence they came.

[Dmitri Borgmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dmitri_Borgmann), a fellow emigrant from Germany, held that the 666-letter version of the surname was untranslatable due to its numerous grammatical and spelling errors, but offered his own paraphrase:[^1918]

> Ages ago, there were conscientious shepherds whose sheep were well tended and carefully protected against attack by their rapacious enemies. Twelve hundred thousand years ago there appeared before these first earthmen, at night, a spaceship powered by seven stone and iridium electric motors. It had originally been launched on its long trip into stellar space in the search for neighboring stars that might have planets revolving about them that were inhabitable and on which planets a new race of intelligent humanity might propagate itself and rejoice for life, without fear of attack by other intelligent beings from interstellar space.

The *New Dictionary of American Family Names* translates the 35-letter form as "a descendant of Wolfeschlegelstein (one who prepared wool for manufacture on a stone), of the house of [Bergerdorf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergedorf) (mountain village)";[^1947] the [Fairleigh Dickinson University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairleigh_Dickinson_University) Names Institute gives "wolf slayer who lives in the stone house in the mountain village".[^1948]

### Nobel disease

**Nobel disease** or **Nobelitis** is an informal term for the embrace of strange or scientifically unsound ideas by some [Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize) winners, usually later in life.[^1949][^1950][^1951] It has been argued that the effect results, in part, from a tendency for Nobel winners to feel empowered by the award to speak on topics outside their specific area of expertise,[^1952][^1953] although it is unknown whether Nobel Prize winners are more prone to this tendency than other individuals.[^1954] [Paul Nurse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Nurse), co-winner of the 2001 [Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine), warned later laureates against "believing you are expert in almost everything, and being prepared to express opinions about most issues with great confidence, sheltering behind the authority that the Nobel Prize can give you". Nurse also noted the media's role in reinforcing this tendency, observing that after receiving his Nobel Prize, journalists had begun to take him seriously when he commented on issues about which he knew little.[^1955]

#### Implications

While it remains unclear whether Nobel winners are statistically more prone to critical thinking errors than other scientists, the phenomenon provides an [existence proof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existence_proof) that being an authority in one field does not necessarily make one an authority in any other field, and, to the extent that winning a Nobel Prize serves as a proxy indicator of scientific brilliance and high general intelligence, such characteristics are not incompatible with irrationality.[^1956][^1954]

Nobel disease demonstrates that, for some prize winners, being universally hailed as correct appears to bolster the individual laureate's [confirmation bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confirmation_bias) more than it does their [skepticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skepticism).[^1957] [Milton Friedman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Friedman), winner of the [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences) in 1976, said this of the Nobel disease as it relates to his economic thinking towards an "antidote":[^1958]

> I myself have been asked my opinion on everything from a cure for the [common cold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_cold) to the market value of a letter signed by [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy). Needless to say the attention \[from receiving a Nobel prize\] is flattering, but also corrupting. Somehow we badly need an antidote for both the inflated attention granted a Nobel laureate in areas outside his competence and the inflated ego each of us is in danger of acquiring. My own field suggests one obvious antidote: competition through the establishment of many more awards. But a product that has been so successful is not easy to replace. Hence, I suspect that our inflated egos are safe for a good long time to come.[^1958]

#### Winners reported as examples

##### Phillip Lenard

[Phillip Lenard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillip_Lenard) won the 1905 [Nobel Prize in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics) for his work on cathode rays. He was a supporter of the Nazi party, and promoted the idea of [Deutsche Physik and Jewish physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Physik).[^1956]

##### Alexis Carrel

[Alexis Carrel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexis_Carrel), winner of the 1912 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the invention of the [perfusion pump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfusion_pump), became an advocate of [eugenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenic) policies in [Vichy France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France).[^1956]

##### Charles Richet

[Charles Richet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Richet) won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his research on [anaphylaxis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaphylaxis). He also believed in [extrasensory perception](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrasensory_perception), [paranormal activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranormal_activity), [dowsing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dowsing), and [ghosts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost).[^1954]

##### Linus Pauling

[Linus Pauling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linus_Pauling) won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on [chemical bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_bond) and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his peace activism. A decade before winning the first prize, he was diagnosed with [Bright's disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bright's_disease), which he treated in part by ingesting vitamin supplements, which he claimed dramatically improved his condition. He later espoused taking high doses of vitamin C to reduce the likelihood and severity of experiencing the common cold. Pauling himself consumed amounts of vitamin C on a daily basis that were more than 120 times the [recommended daily intake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommended_daily_intake). He further argued that megadoses of vitamin C have therapeutic value for treating [schizophrenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schizophrenia) and for prolonging cancer patients' lives. These claims are not supported by the best available science.[^1956][^1949][^1950]

##### William Shockley

[William Shockley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shockley), who shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics with [Walter Houser Brattain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Houser_Brattain) and [John Bardeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bardeen) for their invention of the [point-contact transistor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point-contact_transistor), believed in [racialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racialism) and [eugenics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenics).[^1952][^1956]

##### James Watson

[James Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Watson) was awarded the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, together with [Francis Crick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Crick) and [Maurice Wilkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Wilkins), "for their discoveries concerning the molecular structure of nucleic acids and its significance for information transfer in living material". Since at least 2000, Watson consistently and publicly claimed that black people are on average less intelligent than white people, and that exposure to sunlight in tropical regions and higher levels of melanin cause dark-skinned people to have a higher sex drive.[^1956][^1959][^1960]

##### Nikolaas Tinbergen

[Nikolaas Tinbergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolaas_Tinbergen) won the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning the organization and elicitation of individual and social behavior patterns in animals. During his Nobel acceptance speech, Tinbergen promoted the widely discredited[^1961] "[refrigerator mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrigerator_mother)" hypothesis of the causation of autism. In 1985, Tinbergen coauthored a book with his wife[^1962] that recommended the use of "[holding therapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holding_therapy)" for autism, a form of treatment that is empirically unsupported and that can be physically dangerous.[^1949][^1956]

##### Brian Josephson

[Brian Josephson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Josephson) won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1973 for his prediction of the [Josephson effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josephson_effect). Josephson has promoted a number of scientifically unsupported or discredited beliefs, including the [homeopathic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeopathic) notion that water can somehow "remember" the chemical properties of substances diluted within it (cf. [§ Luc Montagnier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_disease)); the view that [transcendental meditation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_meditation) is helpful for bringing unconscious traumatic memories into conscious awareness; and the possibility that humans can communicate with each other by [telepathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telepathy).[^1956]

##### Kary Mullis

[Kary Mullis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kary_Mullis) won the 1993 [Nobel Prize in Chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Chemistry) for development of the [polymerase chain reaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymerase_chain_reaction). Mullis [disagreed with the scientifically accepted view](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS_denialism) that [AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDS) is caused by [HIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV), claiming that the virus is barely detectable in people with the disease. He also expressed doubt in the evidence for human-caused [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change). In his autobiography, Mullis professed a belief in [astrology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astrology) and wrote about an encounter with a fluorescent, talking raccoon that he suggested might have been an [extraterrestrial alien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraterrestrial_alien).[^1952][^1956]

##### Louis J. Ignarro

[Louis J. Ignarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_J._Ignarro) was one of three winners of the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his research on [nitric oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitric_oxide) as a [signaling molecule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell_signaling) in the [cardiovascular system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circulatory_system), which led to the development of new medications to treat [cardiovascular disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiovascular_disease), as well as of [Viagra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viagra). In 2003, he became a consultant for [Herbalife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbalife) (which has been [investigated for various kinds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbalife) of [dishonesty about its products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regulation_of_food_and_dietary_supplements_by_the_U.S._Food_and_Drug_Administration)). As a member of their Scientific Advisory Board, he helped to promote dubious [dietary supplements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dietary_supplement). He studied the effects of his pet invention, Niteworks, on mice, and is known for saying, "What's good for mice is good for humans," an unverified statement.[^1956]

##### Luc Montagnier

[Luc Montagnier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luc_Montagnier) co-discovered [HIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV) in 1983, for which he won the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. In 2009, in a non-peer-reviewed paper in a journal that he had founded, Montagnier [claimed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_memory) that solutions containing the [DNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA) of [pathogenic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathogenic) bacteria and viruses could emit low frequency radio waves that induce surrounding water molecules to become arranged into "nanostructures". He suggested water could retain such properties even after the original solutions were massively diluted, to the point where the original DNA had effectively vanished, and that water could retain the "memory" of substances with which it had been in contact - claims that place his work in close alignment with the [pseudoscientific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoscientific) tenets of [homeopathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeopathy) (cf. [§ Brian Josephson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_disease)). He further claimed that DNA sequence information could be "teleported" to a separate test tube of purified water via these radio waves. He explained this in the framework of [quantum field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_field_theory).[^1963][^1950][^1964] He supported the scientifically discredited view that [vaccines cause autism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaccines_and_autism) and has claimed that antibiotics are of therapeutic value in the treatment of [autism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autism).[^1956] During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic), Montagnier promoted the idea that [SARS-CoV-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SARS-CoV-2) was [deliberately created and escaped from a laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lab_leak_theory),[^1965][^1966] a claim which has been rejected by other virologists.[^1967]

##### Other Nobelists

Scott O. Lilienfeld et al. list more examples of "Nobel laureates who held/hold weird ideas": [Pierre Curie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Curie), who participated in spiritual seances; [John William Strutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_William_Strutt), who "was fond of parapsychology"; [J. J. Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Thomson), who was interested in psychic phenomena; [Santiago Ramón y Cajal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santiago_Ram%C3%B3n_y_Cajal), who wrote a book "on hypnosis, spiritualism, and metaphysics"; [Wolfgang Pauli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Pauli), who, together with [Carl Jung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Jung), "developed the concept of [synchronicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synchronicity)"; [Egas Moniz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egas_Moniz), for his belief that [lobotomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobotomy) can treat mental illnesses; [Julian Schwinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Schwinger), for his work on [cold fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_fusion); [Ivar Giaever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivar_Giaever), for [global warming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_warming) skepticism; [Arthur Schawlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Schawlow), for his support of a subsequently debunked "technique of facilitated communication for autism"; and [Richard Smalley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Smalley), for promotion of anti-[evolutionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolution) ideas.[^1968]

### Deutsche Physik

***Deutsche Physik*** (German: \[ˈdɔʏtʃə fyˈziːk\], lit. "German Physics") or **Aryan Physics** ([German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language): *Arische Physik*) was a [nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalist) movement in the [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany) [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics) community in the early 1930s which had the support of many eminent physicists in Germany. The term appears in the title of a four-volume physics textbook by Nobel laureate [Philipp Lenard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philipp_Lenard) in the 1930s.

*Deutsche Physik* was opposed to the work of [Albert Einstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein), who was ethnically Jewish, and other modern theoretically-based physics, which was disparagingly labeled **Jewish Physics** ([German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language): ***Jüdische Physik***).

#### Origins

This movement began as an extension of a [German nationalistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_nationalism) movement in the physics community which went back to the [start of World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I) with Austria's [declaration of war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_war) on 28 July 1914. On 25 August 1914, during the German [Rape of Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape_of_Belgium), German troops used petrol to set fire to the library of the [Katholieke Universiteit Leuven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katholieke_Universiteit_Leuven).[^1969][^1970][^1971][^1972] The burning of the library led to a protest note which was signed by eight distinguished British scientists, namely [William Bragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Bragg), [William Crookes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Crookes), [Alexander Fleming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Fleming), [Horace Lamb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Lamb), [Oliver Lodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Lodge), [William Ramsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Ramsay), [Lord Rayleigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_William_Strutt,_3rd_Baron_Rayleigh), and [J. J. Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Thomson). In 1915, this led to a counter-reaction in the form of an "appeal" formulated by [Wilhelm Wien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Wien) and addressed to German physicists and scientific publishers, which was signed by sixteen German physicists, including [Arnold Sommerfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Sommerfeld) and [Johannes Stark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Stark). They claimed that German character had been misinterpreted and that attempts made over many years to reach an understanding between the two countries had obviously failed. Therefore, they opposed the use of the English language by German scientific authors, editors of books, and translators.[^1973] A number of German [physicists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physicist), including [Max Planck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Planck) and the especially passionate Philipp Lenard, a scientific rival of J. J. Thomson, had then [signed further "declarations"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifesto_of_the_Ninety-Three), so that gradually a "war of the minds"[^1974] broke out. On the German side it was suggested to avoid an unnecessary use of English language in scientific texts (concerning, e.g., the renaming of German-discovered phenomena with perceived English-derived names, such as "[X-ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-ray)" instead of "[Röntgen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_R%C3%B6ntgen) ray"). It was stressed, however, that this measure should not be misunderstood as a rejection of British scientific thought, ideas and stimulations.

After the war, the perceived affronts of the [Treaty of Versailles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Versailles) kept some of these nationalistic feelings running high, especially in Lenard, who had already complained about England in a small pamphlet at the beginning of the war.[^1975] When, on 26 January 1920, the former naval cadet Oltwig von Hirschfeld tried to assassinate German Finance minister [Matthias Erzberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthias_Erzberger), Lenard sent Hirschfeld a telegram of congratulation.[^1976] After the 1922 assassination of politician [Walther Rathenau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Rathenau), the government ordered flags flown at half mast on the day of his funeral, but Lenard ignored the order at his institute in [Heidelberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Heidelberg). Socialist students organized a demonstration against Lenard, who was taken into protective custody by state prosecutor Hugo Marx.[^1977]

During the early years of the twentieth century, [Albert Einstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Einstein)'s [theory of relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theory_of_relativity) caused bitter controversy within the worldwide physics community. There were many physicists, especially the "old guard", who were suspicious of the intuitive meanings of Einstein's theories, including Philipp Lenard, one of the authors of the Deutsche Physik volumes.[^1978] While the response to Einstein was based partly on his concepts being a radical break from earlier theories, there was also an anti-Jewish element to some of the criticism. The leading theoretician of the *Deutsche Physik* type of movement was [Rudolf Tomaschek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Tomaschek), who had re-edited the famous physics textbook *Grimsehl's Lehrbuch der Physik*. In that book, which consists of several volumes, the [Lorentz transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorentz_transformation) was accepted, as well as the [old quantum theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_quantum_theory). However, Einstein's interpretation of the Lorentz transformation was not mentioned, and Einstein's name was completely ignored. Many [classical physicists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_physics) resented Einstein's dismissal of the notion of a [luminiferous aether](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminiferous_aether), which had been a mainstay of their work for the majority of their productive lives. They were not convinced by the [empirical evidence for relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tests_of_general_relativity). They believed that the measurements of the [perihelion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perihelion) of [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_%28planet%29) and the null result of the [Michelson-Morley experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelson%E2%80%93Morley_experiment) might be explained in other ways, and the results of the [Eddington eclipse experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddington_experiment) were experimentally problematic enough to be dismissed as meaningless by the more devoted doubters. Many of them were very distinguished experimental physicists, and Lenard was himself a [Nobel laureate in Physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_in_Physics).[^1979]

#### Under the Third Reich

When the [Nazis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party) entered the political scene, Lenard quickly attempted to ally himself with them, joining the party at an early stage. With another Nobel laureate in Physics, [Johannes Stark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Stark), Lenard began a campaign to label Einstein's relativity as *Jewish physics*.

Lenard[^1980] and Stark benefited considerably from this Nazi support. Under the rallying cry that physics should be more "German" and "[Aryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryan_race)", Lenard and Stark embarked on a Nazi-endorsed plan to replace physicists at German universities with "Aryan physicists". By 1935, though, this campaign was superseded by the [Nuremberg Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuremberg_Laws) of 1935. There were no longer any Jewish physics professors in Germany, since under the Nuremberg Laws, Jews were not allowed to work in universities. Stark in particular also tried to install himself as the national authority on "German" physics under the principle of *[Gleichschaltung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gleichschaltung)* (literally, "coordination") applied to other professional disciplines. Under this Nazi-era paradigm, academic disciplines and professional fields followed a strictly linear [hierarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierarchy) created along ideological lines. In his 1938 paper, "The Pragmatic and the Dogmatic Spirit in Physics", Stark contrasted a "pragmatic spirit" driven by experimentation, against a "dogmatic spirit" dominated by theoretical frameworks. He claimed that pragmatic spirit was exhibited primarily by men of the Nordic race while physicists with dogmatic spirit were primarily Jewish.[^1981]

The figureheads of "Aryan physics" met with moderate success, but the support from the Nazi Party was not as great as Lenard and Stark would have preferred. They began to fall from influence after a long period of harassment of [quantum physicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_physics) [Werner Heisenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werner_Heisenberg), which included getting him labeled a "White Jew" in *[Das Schwarze Korps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Das_Schwarze_Korps)*. Heisenberg was an extremely eminent physicist, and the Nazis realized that they were better off with him rather than without, however "Jewish" his theory might be in the eyes of Stark and Lenard.[^1982] In an historic moment, Heisenberg's mother rang [Heinrich Himmler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinrich_Himmler)'s mother and asked her whether she would please tell the [SS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS) to give "Werner" a break. After beginning a full character evaluation, which Heisenberg both instigated and passed, Himmler forbade further attack on the physicist. Heisenberg would later employ his "Jewish physics" in the [German project to develop nuclear fission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_nuclear_weapons_program) for the purposes of [nuclear weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapons) or [nuclear energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_reactor) use. Himmler promised Heisenberg that after Germany won the war, the SS would finance a physics institute to be directed by Heisenberg.[^1983]

Lenard began to play less and less of a role, and soon Stark ran into even more difficulty, as other scientists and industrialists known for being exceptionally "Aryan" came to the defense of relativity and [quantum mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_mechanics). As historian Mark Walker puts it:[^1984]

> ... despite his best efforts, in the end his science was not accepted, supported, or used by the Third Reich. Stark spent a great deal of his time during the Third Reich fighting with bureaucrats within the Nazi state. Most of the Nazi leadership either never supported Lenard and Stark, or abandoned them in the course of the Third Reich.

#### Effect on the German nuclear program

It is occasionally put forth[^1985] that there is a great irony in the Nazis' labeling modern physics as "Jewish science", since it was exactly modern physics, and the work of many European exiles, which was used to create the [atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb). Even if the German government had not embraced Lenard and Stark's ideas, the German [antisemitic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism) agenda was enough by itself to destroy the Jewish scientific community in Germany. Furthermore, the [German nuclear weapons program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_nuclear_weapons_program) was never pursued with anywhere near the vigor of the [Manhattan Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Project) in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States), and for that reason would likely not have succeeded in any case.[^1986] The movement did not actually go as far as preventing the nuclear energy scientists from using quantum mechanics and relativity,[^1987] but the education of young scientists and engineers suffered, not only from the loss of the Jewish scientists but also from political appointments and other interference.

### Vortex tube

The **vortex tube**, also known as the **Ranque-Hilsch vortex tube**, is a [mechanical device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_device) that separates a compressed [gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas) into hot and cold streams. The gas emerging from the hot end can reach temperatures of 200 °C (390 °F), and the gas emerging from the cold end can reach −50 °C (−60 °F).[^1988] It has no [moving parts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moving_parts), but has poor energy efficiency.[^1989]

Pressurised gas is injected [tangentially](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tangential) into a *swirl chamber* near one end of a tube, leading to a rapid [rotation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotation), the first vortex, as it moves along the inner surface of the tube to the far end. A [conical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cone_%28geometry%29) [nozzle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nozzle) allows gas specifically from this outer layer to escape at that end through a valve. The remainder of the gas is forced to return in an inner vortex of reduced diameter within the outer vortex. Gas from the inner vortex transfers energy to the gas in the outer vortex, so the outer layer is hotter at the far end than it was initially. The gas in the central vortex is likewise cooler upon its return to the starting-point, where it is released from the tube.

#### Method of operation

To explain the temperature separation in a vortex tube, there are two main approaches:

##### Fundamental approach: the physics

This approach is based on first-principles physics alone and is not limited to vortex tubes only, but applies to moving gas in general. It shows that temperature separation in a moving gas is due only to [enthalpy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enthalpy) conservation in a moving [frame of reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frame_of_reference).

The thermal process in the vortex tube can be estimated in the following way:

The main physical phenomenon of the vortex tube is the temperature separation between the cold vortex core and the warm vortex periphery. The "vortex tube effect" is fully explained with the work equation of Euler,[^1990] also known as Euler's turbine equation, which can be written in its most general vectorial form as:[^1991]

$$
T - \frac{ \vec v \cdot \vec \omega \times \vec r}{c_p}=\text{const}
$$

,

where $T$ is the total, or [stagnation temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stagnation_temperature) of the rotating gas at radial position $\vec r$, the absolute gas velocity as observed from the stationary frame of reference is denoted with $\vec v$; the [angular velocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_velocity) of the system is $\vec \omega$ and $c_p$ is the isobaric heat capacity of the gas. This equation was published in 2012; it explains the fundamental operating principle of vortex tubes. The search for this explanation began in 1933 when the vortex tube was discovered and continued for more than 80 years.

The above equation is valid for an adiabatic turbine passage; it clearly shows that while gas moving towards the center is getting colder, the peripheral gas in the passage is "getting faster". Therefore, vortex cooling is due to angular propulsion. The more the gas cools by reaching the center, the more [rotational energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotational_energy) it delivers to the vortex and thus the vortex rotates even faster. This explanation stems directly from the law of energy conservation. Compressed gas at [room temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Room_temperature) is expanded in order to gain speed through a nozzle; it then climbs the centrifugal barrier of rotation during which energy is also lost. The lost energy is delivered to the vortex, which speeds its rotation. In a vortex tube, the cylindrical surrounding wall confines the flow at periphery and thus forces conversion of kinetic into [internal energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_energy), which produces hot air at the hot exit.

Therefore, the vortex tube is a rotorless [turboexpander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turboexpander).[^1992] It consists of a rotorless radial inflow turbine (cold end, center) and a rotorless [centrifugal compressor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centrifugal_compressor) (hot end, periphery). The work output of the turbine is converted into heat by the compressor at the hot end.

##### Phenomenological approach

This approach relies on observation and experimental data. It is specifically tailored to the geometrical shape of the vortex tube and the details of its flow and is designed to match the particular observables of the complex vortex tube flow, namely turbulence, acoustic phenomena, pressure fields, air velocities and many others. The earlier published models of the vortex tube are phenomenological. They are:

1.  Radial pressure difference: centrifugal compression and air expansion
2.  Radial transfer of [angular momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_momentum)
3.  Radial [acoustic streaming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acoustic_streaming) of energy
4.  Radial heat pumping

More on these models can be found in recent review articles on vortex tubes.[^1993][^1994]

The phenomenological models were developed at an earlier time when the turbine equation of Euler was not thoroughly analyzed; in the engineering literature, this equation is studied mostly to show the work output of a turbine; while temperature analysis is not performed since turbine cooling has more limited application unlike power generation, which is the main application of turbines. Phenomenological studies of the vortex tube in the past have been useful in presenting empirical data. However, due to the complexity of the vortex flow this empirical approach was able to show only aspects of the effect but was unable to explain its operating principle. Dedicated to empirical details, for a long time the empirical studies made the vortex tube effect appear enigmatic and its explanation - a matter of debate.

#### History

The vortex tube was invented in 1931 by French physicist [Georges J. Ranque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_J._Ranque).[^1995] He applied for patent in 1932 and obtained the same in 1934.[^1996] It was rediscovered by [Paul Dirac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Dirac) in 1934 while he was searching for a device to perform [isotope separation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotope_separation), leading to development of the [Helikon vortex separation process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helikon_vortex_separation_process).[^1997] German physicist Rudolf Hilsch improved the design and published a widely read paper in 1947 on the device, which he called a *Wirbelrohr* (literally, whirl pipe).[^1998] In 1954, Westley [^1999] published a comprehensive survey entitled "A bibliography and survey of the vortex tube", which included over 100 references. In 1951 Curley and McGree,[^2000] in 1956 Kalvinskas,[^2001] in 1964 Dobratz,[^2002] in 1972 Nash,[^2003] and in 1979 Hellyar [^2004] made important contribution to the RHVT literature by their extensive reviews on the vortex tube and its applications. From 1952 to 1963, C. Darby Fulton, Jr. obtained four U.S. patents relating to the development of the vortex tube.[^2005] In 1961, Fulton began manufacturing the vortex tube under the company name Fulton Cryogenics.[^2006] Fulton sold the company to Vortec, Inc.[^2006] The vortex tube was used to separate gas mixtures, oxygen and nitrogen, [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide) and helium, carbon dioxide and air in 1967 by Linderstrom-Lang.[^2007] [^2008] Vortex tubes also seem to work with liquids to some extent, as demonstrated by Hsueh and Swenson in a laboratory experiment where free body rotation occurs from the core and a thick boundary layer at the wall. Air is separated causing a cooler air stream coming out the exhaust hoping to chill as a refrigerator.[^2009] In 1988 R. T. Balmer applied liquid water as the working medium. It was found that when the inlet pressure is high, for instance 20-50 bar, the heat energy separation process exists in incompressible (liquids) vortex flow as well. Note that this separation is only due to heating; there is no longer cooling observed since cooling requires compressibility of the working fluid.

#### Efficiency

Vortex tubes have lower efficiency than traditional [air conditioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_conditioning) equipment.[^2010] They are commonly used for inexpensive spot cooling, when compressed air is available.

#### Applications

##### Current applications

Commercial vortex tubes are designed for industrial applications to produce a temperature drop of up to 71°C (128°F). With no moving parts, no electricity, and no refrigerant, a vortex tube can produce [refrigeration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrigeration) up to 1,800 W (6,000 BTU/h) using 100 standard cubic feet per minute (2.832 m³/min) of filtered compressed air at 100 psi (6.9 bar). They are the main technology used in cold air guns, enclosure coolers, and cooling vests.[^2011] A control valve in the hot air exhaust adjusts temperatures, flows and refrigeration over a wide range.[^2012][^2013]

Vortex tubes are used for cooling of cutting tools ([lathes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lathe) and [mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milling_machine), both manually-operated and [CNC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNC) machines) during machining. The vortex tube is well-matched to this application: machine shops generally already use compressed air, and a fast jet of cold air provides both cooling and removal of the chips produced by the tool. This eliminates or drastically reduces the need for liquid coolant, which is messy, expensive, and environmentally hazardous.
