### South-up map orientation

**South-up map orientation** is the [orientation of a map](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Map) with [south](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South) up, at the top of the map, west on the right, amounting to a 180-degree rotation of the map from the standard convention of north-up. Maps in this orientation are sometimes called **upside-down maps** or **reversed maps**.

#### Psychological significance

Research suggests that north-south positions on maps have psychological consequences. In general, north is associated with richer people, more expensive real estate, and higher altitude, while south is associated with poorer people, cheaper prices, and lower altitude (the "[north-south bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_North_and_Global_South)"). When participants were presented with south-up oriented maps, this north-south bias disappeared.[^2014]

Researchers posit that the observed association between map-position and goodness/badness (north=good; south=bad) is caused by the combination of

- the convention of consistently placing north at the top of maps, and
- a much more general association between vertical position and goodness/badness (up=good, down=bad), which has been documented in numerous contexts (e.g. power/status, profits/prices, affect/emotion, and even the divine).[^2015]

Common English idioms support the notion that many English speakers conflate or associate north with up and south with down (e.g. "heading up north", "down south", [Down Under](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_Under)), a conflation that can only be understood as learned by repeated exposure to a particular map-orientation convention (i.e. north put at the top of maps). Related idioms used in popular song lyrics provide further evidence for the pervasiveness of "north-south bias" among English speakers, in particular with regard to wealth. Examples include using "Uptown" to mean "high class or rich" (as in "[Uptown Girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uptown_Girl)" by [Billy Joel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Joel)), or using "Downtown" to convey lower socioeconomic status (as in "[Bad, Bad Leroy Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad,_Bad_Leroy_Brown)" by [Jim Croce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Croce)).[^2016]

#### Political use

Throughout history, [maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Map) have been made with varied orientations, and reversing the orientation of maps is technically very easy to do. As such, some cartographers maintain that the issue of south-up map orientation is itself trivial. More noteworthy than the technical matter of orientation, per se, is the history of explicitly using south-up map orientation as a political statement, that is, creating south-up oriented maps with the express rationale of reacting to the north-up oriented world maps that have dominated map publication during the modern age.

The history of south-up map orientation as political statement can be traced back to the early 1900s. In 1943, [Joaquín Torres García](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joaqu%C3%ADn_Torres_Garc%C3%ADa), a [Uruguayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguayans) modernist painter, created one of the first maps to make a political statement related to north-south map positions entitled "[América Invertida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Am%C3%A9rica_Invertida)". "Torres-García placed the South Pole at the top of the Earth, thereby suggesting a visual affirmation of the importance of the (South American) continent."[^2017][^2018]

##### McArthur's Universal Corrective Map of the World

In 1979, twenty-one year old Australian Stuart McArthur published "McArthur's Universal Corrective Map of the World". An inset on this map explains that he sought to confront "the perpetual onslaught of 'Down Under' jokes: implications from northern nations that the height of a country's prestige is determined by its equivalent spatial location on a conventional map of the world".[^2019] He had been drawing a map placing Australia at the visual centre of the page since he was 12 years old. At age 15, he was taunted as coming from Down Under as an exchange student. These experiences encouraged him to "correct" the world's map by placing [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia) at the top.[^2020]

#### In popular culture

South-up maps are commonly available as novelties or as sociopolitical statements, especially in Southern Hemisphere locales.[^2021] A south-up oriented world map appears in the episode "*[Somebody's Going to Emergency, Somebody's Going to Jail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somebody's_Going_to_Emergency,_Somebody's_Going_to_Jail)*" of *[The West Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_West_Wing)*, where issues of [cultural bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_bias) are discussed. The Argentine cartoon strip *[Mafalda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mafalda)* by [Quino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quino) once posed the question, "Why are we down?" American cartoonist [Leo Cullum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Cullum) published a cartoon in *[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker)* titled "*Happy Penguin Looking at Upside-Down Globe; Antarctica Is on Top*" (April 20, 1992).

The computer strategy game *[Neocolonialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neocolonialism_%28video_game%29)*, developed by Esther Alter, uses a south-up map. The developer stated that this choice was intended to "evoke \[*[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic)*\] discomfort" and to "exemplify the north-south dichotomy of the world, wherein the [Southern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere) is generally poorer than the [Northern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere)."[^2022]

### James Price (chemist)

**James Price** (1757[^2023] - 31 July 1783[^2024]), born **James Higginbotham**, was an English [chemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemist) and [alchemist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alchemy) who claimed to be able to turn [mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_%28element%29) into [silver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver) or [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold). When challenged to perform the conversion a second time in front of [credible witnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credible_witness), he instead killed himself by drinking [prussic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussic_acid) ([hydrogen cyanide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_cyanide)).

#### Early life

Born in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London) in 1757, his original surname was Higginbotham, but he changed it to Price following the wishes of a relative who had died and left him a legacy.[^2025] He attended [Oxford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University) and, although no records of his early education or his research at Oxford exist, had a successful career there. He became a [Master of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Arts_%28Oxbridge%29) in 1777 and the university made him a [Doctor of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine) in 1782, particularly for his work in the field of chemistry. In 1781, at the age of 24, he became a member of the [Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society).[^2026]

#### Work on transmutation

In the following year, he began working on the [transmutation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alchemy) of [base metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Base_metal) into [precious metals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precious_metal) and since 6 May 1782, after revealing his findings to a few of his friends, he hosted a series of public experiments at his laboratory in [Guildford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guildford). He claimed that he could produce precious metals by mixing [borax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borax), [nitre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitre), and a red or white powder of his own devising (which he called the powder of production) with fifty times its own weight in mercury and stirring the mixture in a [crucible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crucible) with an iron rod. Mixing in the red powder allegedly produced gold; the white powder, silver. He performed seven of the public demonstrations, the final one being on 25 May 1782, which were attended by peers, clergymen, lawyers, and chemists. Some of the gold that Price claimed was produced during the experiments was presented to King [George III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_III_of_the_United_Kingdom).[^2027]

#### Challenged by other Fellows

The Fellows of the Royal Society were less convinced, however, and asked him to repeat the experiments in the presence of some of the members of the society, which Price was reluctant to do. He claimed that his powders were exhausted and preparation of new samples would cost him time and money and be damaging to his health. He also protested that the cost of preparing the gold or silver by this method was not economical, as it cost £17 to make an [ounce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ounce) of gold, which was only valued at £4. The Royal Society insisted on the repetition of the experiments and reminded Price that, as a member, he was calling the honour of the society into question. Price rebuked them, claiming that his reputation and position in society should prevent any hint of suspicion from being cast upon the veracity of his claims, but he was eventually forced to submit.[^2028]

#### Events leading to suicide

In January 1783, Price returned to his laboratory in Guildford, ostensibly to start production of the miraculous powders. In fact, he set about the [distillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distillation) of [laurel water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurel_water) (which contained hydrogen cyanide, commonly known as prussic acid). He wrote his will at the same time, but it was another six months before he returned to London to invite members of the Royal Society to witness the experiment in his laboratory in Guildford.

Despite the claimed successes of his initial demonstrations and the furor they had caused, only three members turned up in Guildford on the appointed day. Although clearly disappointed by the poor turnout, Price welcomed the three men and then, stepping to one side, ended his life by drinking the flask of laurel water he had prepared. The three men immediately noticed a change in his appearance, but before they could do anything, Price had died of cyanide poisoning.[^2028]

### 229762 Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà

**229762 Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà** (provisional designation **2007 UK₁₂₆**) is a large [binary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_minor_planet) [trans-Neptunian object](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Neptunian_object) and dwarf planet candidate in the [scattered disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scattered_disc), located in the outermost region of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System).[^2029] It was discovered on 19 October 2007 by American astronomers [Megan Schwamb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Schwamb), [Michael Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_E._Brown), and [David Rabinowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_L._Rabinowitz) at the [Palomar Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palomar_Observatory) in California.[^2030]

Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà measures approximately 600 kilometers (400 miles) in diameter. This medium-sized TNO appears to be representative of a class of mid-sized objects under approximately 1000 km that have not collapsed into fully solid bodies. Its 100-kilometer [moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor-planet_moon) was discovered by [Keith Noll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Noll), Will Grundy, and colleagues with the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope) in 2008,[^2031][^2032][^2033][^2034] and named Gǃòʼé ǃHú.

#### History

##### Discovery

Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà was discovered on 19 October 2007 by American astronomers [Megan Schwamb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Schwamb), [Michael Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_E._Brown), and [David Rabinowitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_L._Rabinowitz) at the [Palomar Observatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palomar_Observatory) in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California).[^2030]

##### Numbering, naming and provisional designation

When the discovery of Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà was announced on 26 February 2008, the [Minor Planet Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_Planet_Center) (MPC) gave the object the [provisional designation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_designation) 2007 UK₁₂₆, which indicates its discovery date.[^2035] The MPC later gave it the [minor planet catalog number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_planet_number) of 229762 on 31 December 2009.[^2036] The [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union)'s Small Bodies Nomenclature Committee officially named the object Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà and its moon Gǃòʼé ǃHú on 6 April 2019.[^2037][^2038]

The name *Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà* is from the [Juǀʼhoansi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ju%C7%80%CA%BChoansi) ([ǃKung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C7%83Kung_people)) people of Namibia. In Juǀʼhoan mythology, G!kúnǁ'hòmdímà appears as an aardvark defending her people using *gǁámígǁàmì* spines,[^2039] hail, and her [oryx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemsbok) horn.[^2037] The name is composed of *gǃkún* 'aardvark', *ǁʼhòm mà* 'young woman' and the feminine suffix *dí*. The moon **Gǃòʼé ǃHú** is named after her horn; it means simply *gǃòʼé* 'oryx' *ǃhú* 'horn'.[^2040]

In the [Juǀʼhoan language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ju%C7%80%CA%BChoan_language), the primary and moon names are pronounced \[ᶢᵏǃ͡χʼṹ ᵑ̊ǁʰòmdí mà\] [](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/transcoded/3/3a/G%C7%83kun%C7%81%27homdima.ogg/G%C7%83kun%C7%81%27homdima.ogg.mp3)^(ⓘ) and \[ᶢǃòˀé ǃʰú\] [](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/transcoded/7/7f/G%C7%83o%27e_%C7%83Hu.ogg/G%C7%83o%27e_%C7%83Hu.ogg.mp3)^(ⓘ), respectively. Usually, when speaking English, the [click consonants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Click_consonant) in words from Juǀʼhoan and other San languages are simply ignored (much as *[Xhosa](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Xhosa)* is pronounced /ˈkoʊzə/ (*KOH-zə*) rather than \[ǁʰosa\]), resulting in /ˌɡuːnhoʊmˈdiːmə/ (*GOON-hohm-DEE-mə*) for *Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà* and /ˌɡoʊ.eɪˈhuː/ (*GOH-ay-HOO*) or /ˌɡoʊ.eɪˈkuː/ (*GOH-ay-KOO*) for *Gǃòʼé ǃHú*.

[ASCII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASCII) renderings of the names would be ⟨G!kun\|\|'homdima⟩ or ⟨G!kun//'homdima⟩ for the object and ⟨G!o'e !Hu⟩ or ⟨G!o'e!hu⟩ for the moon.[^2041]

The usage of [planetary symbols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_symbol) is now discouraged in astronomy by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union),[^2042] so Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà never received a symbol in the astronomical literature. There is no standard symbol for Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà used by astrologers either. An aardvark's head () has been used.[^2043]

#### Orbit and classification

##### Orbital characteristics and observations

Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà orbits the Sun at a distance of 37.5-107.9 [AU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_unit) once every 620 years and 2 months (226,517 days; [semi-major axis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-major_axis) of 72.72 AU). Its orbit has an [eccentricity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_eccentricity) of 0.48 and an [inclination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_inclination) of 23[°](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Degree_%28angle%29) with respect to the [ecliptic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecliptic).[^2044]

An eccentricity of 0.48 suggests that it was gravitationally [scattered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perturbation_%28astronomy%29) into its current eccentric orbit. It will come to [perihelion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apsis) in February 2046, and [mutual occultation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asteroid_occultation) events with its satellite will begin in late 2050 and last most of that decade.[^2037] It has a bright [absolute magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_magnitude) of 3.45,[^2045] and has been observed 178 times over 16 [oppositions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_%28planets%29) with [precovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precovery) images back to August 1982.[^2044]

##### Classification

Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà belongs to the scattered disc.[^2030] The scattered disc is a population of TNOs that have distant, eccentric, and inclined orbits that come close to [Neptune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptune) at [perihelion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perihelion).[^2046]

Scattered disc objects such as the dwarf planets [Eris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eris_%28dwarf_planet%29) and [Gonggong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonggong_%28dwarf_planet%29) and the large trans-Neptunian object [Chiminigagua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/532037_Chiminigagua), are strongly influenced by Neptune's [gravitational perturbations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_perturbations) and consequently experience [gravitational scattering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_scattering).[^2047]

Both the [Minor Planet Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_Planet_Center) (MPC) and *Johnston's Archive* classify Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà as a scattered disc object.[^2030][^2032][^2033]

#### Physical characteristics

##### Size, mass, density and shape

Stellar occultation events indicate that Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà has an effective (equivalent-sphere) diameter of 600-670 km, but is not spherical. Due to complications from its non-spherical shape, the rotational period cannot be definitely determined from current [light-curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_curve) data, which has an amplitude of Δm = 0.03 ± 0.01 mag, but the simplest solution is 11.05 hours.[^2048] It is almost certainly between that and 41 hours. The system mass is (1.36±0.03)×10²⁰ kg, about 2% that of Earth's moon and a bit more than Saturn's moon [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus). The geometric albedo of Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà is approximately 0.15, and its [bulk density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulk_density) is approximately 1 g/cm³.[^2037] The satellite Gǃòʼé ǃHú is unlikely to comprise more than 1% or so of the total.

##### Unlikely dwarf planet

Grundy et al. propose that the low density and albedo of Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà, combined with the fact that TNOs both larger and smaller - including comets - have a substantial fraction of rock in their composition, indicate that objects in the size range of 400-1000 km, such as Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà and [55637 Uni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/55637_Uni), retain a degree of porosity in their physical structure, having never collapsed and differentiated into planetary bodies like higher density or higher albedo (and thus presumably resurfaced) [Orcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orcus_%28dwarf_planet%29) and [Quaoar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaoar_%28dwarf_planet%29), or at best are only partially differentiated; such objects would never have been in hydrostatic equilibrium and would not be dwarf planets at present.[^2037]

##### Surface and spectra

In [visible light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visible_light), the surface of Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà appears moderately red ([color class IR or RR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Neptunian_object)) with a [geometric albedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_albedo) of about 0.15.[^2049] In [near-infrared](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near-infrared), however, its reflectance drops at longer [wavelengths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavelength), a characteristic more typical of bluer TNOs (color class BB or BR) than moderately red ones.[^2049] Because of this, Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà does not neatly fall within these four categories of TNO colors.[^2049] Rather, it shares its outlying colors with some TNOs, namely [(26375) 1999 DE9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%2826375%29_1999_DE9) and [145452 Ritona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/145452_Ritona).[^2050]

Near-infrared [spectroscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectroscopy) by the [James Webb Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Webb_Space_Telescope) (JWST) has shown that Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà's surface is composed of [water ice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice), [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide) (CO\
₂) ice, [carbon monoxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_monoxide) (CO) ice, and various [organic compounds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_compound) ([tholins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tholin)).[^2051][^2052] This composition is shared among [CO\
₂-type (aka "double-dip") TNOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Neptunian_spectral_types),[^2053] which are commonly found on dynamically excited orbits such as those in the scattered disc (where Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdíma resides).[^2051]

#### Satellite

Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà has one known satellite, **Gǃòʼé ǃHú**, which is one of the reddest known TNOs.[^2037] Size and mass can only be inferred. The magnitude difference between the two is 3.24±0.04 mag. This would correspond to a difference in diameter by a factor of 4.45±0.08, assuming the same albedo.[^2037] Red satellites often have lower albedos than their primaries, though it is not known if that is the case with this moon. Such uncertainties do not affect density calculations of Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà, as Gǃòʼé ǃHú has only about 1% the total volume, and therefore is less important than the uncertainties in Gǃkúnǁʼhòmdímà's diameter.[^2037]

### Seatbelt basalt

**Lunar Sample 15016**, better known as the "**Seatbelt Basalt**", is a [lunar sample](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_rock) discovered and collected on the [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15) mission in 1971 in the [Hadley-Apennine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadley-Apennine) region of the Moon. The rock is a 0.923 kg (2.03 lb) vesicular [olivine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivine) [basalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basalt).

It is so named because mission commander, [David Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Scott), noticed it on the surface while driving the [Lunar Roving Vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Roving_Vehicle) and stopped to collect it, but said to mission control that he was just fastening his seatbelt.[^2054] He did this because he assumed mission control would not give permission to stop for a sample collection due to time constraints.[^2055] This unplanned stop was later designated Geology Station 3, located about 125 metres (410 ft) west of [Rhysling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhysling_%28crater%29) crater.

This sample was collected from an area with abundant subdued craters between 0.1 and 1 metre (0.33 and 3.28 ft) in diameter. The sample is a very vesicular basalt, rounded by surface erosion. [Lithologically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithologically), it closely resembles samples 15535 and 15536, as well as a number of fragments in the rake samples from station 9A.[^2056]

The seatbelt basalt is currently stored at the [Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_Sample_Laboratory_Facility) at the [Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson_Space_Center). A piece of it is on display at the [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum) in Washington, DC.

#### Description

The seatbelt basalt is a highly-[vesicular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vesicular_texture), [olivine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivine)-normative, [basalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basalt) with [phenocrysts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenocryst) of zoned [pyroxene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyroxene) and olivine within a matrix of pyroxene and [plagioclase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plagioclase). The rock also contains [ilmenite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilmenite) and [ulvöspinel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulv%C3%B6spinel).

#### Age

The rock's [cosmic ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmic_ray) exposure age was discovered to be about 285 million years.[^2057] Another study determined the age to be 315 million years.[^2058]

The rock's age of formation has been estimated to be approximately 3.29 ± 0.05 billion years from [Rb-Sr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubidium%E2%80%93strontium_dating) [radiometric dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiometric_dating).[^2059]

### Auto-brewery syndrome

**Auto-brewery syndrome** (**ABS**) (also known as **gut fermentation syndrome** or **endogenous ethanol fermentation**) is an extremely rare and underdiagnosed medical condition characterized by the [fermentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermentation) of ingested carbohydrates in the gastrointestinal tract caused by bacteria or fungi.[^2060]

[Intoxicating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_intoxication) amounts of [ethanol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethanol) are produced through [endogenous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endogenous) fermentation within the [digestive system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digestive_system).[^2061] The organisms responsible for ABS include various yeasts and bacteria, including *[Saccharomyces cerevisiae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saccharomyces_cerevisiae)*, *[S. boulardii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saccharomyces_boulardii)*, *[Candida albicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candida_albicans)*, *[C. tropicalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candida_tropicalis)*, *[C. krusei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candida_krusei)*, *[C. glabrata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candida_glabrata)*, *[C. parapsilosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candida_parapsilosis)*, *[Kluyveromyces marxianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kluyveromyces_marxianus)*, *[Klebsiella pneumoniae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klebsiella_pneumoniae)*, and *[Enterococcus faecium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enterococcus_faecium)*.[^2060][^2062] These organisms undergo [lactic acid fermentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lactic_acid_fermentation) or mixed acid fermentation pathways to produce an ethanol end product.[^2063][^2064] The ethanol generated from these pathways is absorbed in the small intestine and stomach, raising [blood alcohol concentrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood-alcohol_concentration) and causing the effects of intoxication without the ingestion of [alcohol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_%28drug%29).[^2065]

Researchers suggest the underlying causes of ABS are related to prolonged [antibiotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antibiotic) use,[^2066] poor nutrition, and/or diets high in carbohydrates,[^2067] and to pre-existing conditions such as [diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diabetes) and genetic variations that result in improper liver enzyme activity.[^2066] Any of these conditions, alone or in combination, could cause ABS, and result in [dysbiosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysbiosis) of the microbiome.[^2068]

Other variants include urinary ABS and oral ABS, when fermentation occurs in the urinary bladder and mouth, rather than the gut.[^2066] Urinary ABS is asymptomatic and does not produce intoxicating effects because it occurs outside the digestive tract, therefore individuals who may have it are less likely to seek medical advice.[^2069] This condition still presents legal challenges, since [urinary tests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urine_test) are often used to confirm sobriety in cases of suspected drunk driving.[^2070]

Claims of endogenous fermentation have been attempted as a defense against drunk driving charges, some of which have been successful,[^2071] though the condition is so rare and under-researched they are currently not substantiated by available studies.[^2072]

#### Signs and symptoms

People with this condition typically experience signs of ethanol intoxication, including slurring of speech, incoordination, memory loss, and cognitive disturbances unusual for them.[^2073] Some report a fruity or foul smell from their breath.[^2074]

Acute symptoms associated with ABS may include blood alcohol content of 200 to 500 mg/dL. Mood changes and other neurological problems, including memory loss or [brain fog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain_fog) have also been reported.[^2074]

Chronic symptoms may include fatigue,[^2074] [liver cirrhosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liver_cirrhosis), [fatty-liver disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatty-liver_disease), and symptoms similar to [irritable bowel syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irritable_bowel_syndrome).[^2066] Secondary symptoms may include anxiety, depression, or relationship troubles.[^2066]

#### Risk factors

Certain clinical conditions such as [type 2 diabetes mellitus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_2_diabetes) and [liver cirrhosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirrhosis) have been identified as producing higher levels of endogenous ethanol.[^2070] Patients with [short bowel syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_bowel_syndrome), diabetes mellitus, [Crohn's disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crohn's_disease), liver cirrhosis, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, [gastroparesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastroparesis), and [immunocompromised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunocompromised) individuals may be at greater risk of developing ABS.[^2070]

An extensive history of a diet high in [ultra-processed food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra-processed_food) and use of antibiotics has been significantly associated with the disease.[^2066] Processed food is typically high in sugar, a type of carbohydrate, allowing the fermenting organisms to flourish.[^2075] Diet composition more broadly may influence ethanol production by altering the availability of fermentable substrate in the gut. Carbohydrate-rich diets provide fermentable sugars that can increase gut ethanol production by microorganisms, such as *[Saccharomyces cerevisiae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saccharomyces_cerevisiae)*. In contrast, ketogenic diets may limit ethanol production due to reduced substrate availability, while high-protein diets support more moderate levels of fermentation. These patterns are consistent with metabolic modeling of certain fermentative organisms, which predict increased ethanol production in high-glucose environments. It is believed antibiotics disrupt bacterial populations, allowing yeast species to proliferate and produce ethanol.[^2075]

#### Metabolic action

[Fermentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermentation) is a biochemical process during which yeast and certain bacteria convert sugars to ethanol and [carbon dioxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_dioxide), as well as other metabolic byproducts.[^2076] The fermentation pathway involves [pyruvate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyruvate) formed from yeast in the EMP pathway, while some bacteria obtain pyruvate through the ED pathway.[^2076] Pyruvate is then decarboxylated to [acetaldehyde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acetaldehyde) in a reaction involving the enzyme [pyruvate decarboxylase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyruvate_decarboxylase).[^2076] Reduction of acetaldehyde to ethanol produces [NAD⁺](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NAD+), which is catalyzed by [alcohol dehydrogenase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcohol_dehydrogenase) (ADH).[^2076] ADH removes alcohol from the body through a process called [first pass metabolism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_pass_metabolism).[^2077] However, if the rate of ethanol breakdown is less than the rate of production, intoxication ensues.[^2078]

#### Differential diagnosis

When considering diagnosis of auto-brewery syndrome, clinicians attempt to rule out other factors that can cause similar symptoms, including head injuries, [hypoglycemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypoglycemia), psychiatric disorders, [seizure disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seizure_disorders), and hidden drinking behaviors.[^2079][^2066]

#### Diagnosis

Diagnosis of ABS may take up to three weeks. Clinicians obtain a thorough patient history, blood work, and a physical exam to rule out other potential causes.[^2080] Patients seeking diagnoses can expect themselves and family members to be asked about the frequency and duration of symptoms, other medical diagnoses, and any reported drinking behavior.[^2066]

A 24-hour carbohydrate challenge test may be done to validate findings. To do this, patients consume 200g of carbohydrates and are periodically monitored for a rise in blood alcohol concentration. Patients are continually supervised to rule out the chance of alcohol consumption.[^2080][^2066]

Additional testing may include an upper and lower [endoscopy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endoscopy) to determine what bacterial and fungal cultures are present in the GI tract, and to test for sensitivity.[^2080]

#### Treatment

If patients present with signs and symptoms of acute alcohol poisoning, they will likely be treated according to specific protocols, ensuring the patient is in stable condition. This may include glucose monitoring and fluid administration with an [IV drip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IV_drip).[^2066]

Once someone is diagnosed with ABS, major lifestyle changes are recommended to protect the patient and reduce the occurrence and severity of symptoms. This may include adopting a diet low in carbohydrates (\<5 g / day),[^2066] consuming [probiotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probiotic) supplements, managing stress levels, and avoiding the use of antibiotics unless necessary.[^2066] A reduction or cessation from consuming ultra-processed foods is generally recommended.[^2081]

Patients are recommended to exercise caution before driving, especially after consuming carbohydrates, to reduce the chance of intoxicated driving.[^2060]

Some patients may benefit from antifungal medication including [fluconazole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluconazole) or [nystatin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nystatin),[^2075] though its effectiveness varies.[^2066] Often, probiotics are given concurrently to ensure proper species of bacteria recolonize the gut, and to prevent recolonization by the problematic microorganisms.[^2075]

[Fecal microbiota transplantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fecal_microbiota_transplantation) (FMT) is a new potential treatment for ABS, though additional research is required to establish its safety and effectiveness.[^2075]

#### History

Origins of ABS entered the medical literature in 1887 in the book, *Lectures on auto-intoxication in disease, or, Self-poisoning of the individual*,[^2082] by Charles Bouchard, a French physician. He first discussed intestinal microbial fermentation and harmful effects of absorbed fermentation products, but did not discuss the modern understanding of the condition itself.

ABS entered the medical lens in 1948, with the case of a 5-year-old African boy, when his stomach ruptured after consuming [sweet potatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_potatoes), suspected from immense gas produced from gut microorganisms. In an [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy) report, the clinician reported the penetrating odor of alcohol, despite the child never consuming any.[^2083]

In 1983, Japanese researchers described two case studies resembling symptoms of ABS and noted 37 additional reports with similar symptoms. However, the term auto-brewery syndrome was not yet mentioned.[^2084]

Throughout the late 20th century, the condition became more widely recognized with mounting case study publications and research on endogenous fermentation.

In the present, the condition is well-established, though often underdiagnosed due to its extreme rarity and resemblance to alcohol intoxication from consumption. Physicians may not include ABS in their [differential diagnosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_diagnosis) because it is unfamiliar or the presentation mimics signs of more common conditions.[^2070]

The condition has been depicted in popular media including on the television shows *[Grey's Anatomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grey's_Anatomy)* and [*The Good Doctor*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Good_Doctor_%28American_TV_series%29).[^2085] Mark Mongiardo started a TikTok channel in 2025 after controlling his condition with weeks of antifungal medication and a carb-free diet.[^2085]

#### Medicolegal

Auto-brewery syndrome presents a challenging situation in the field of forensic medicine. Numerous cases of driving under the influence (DUI) have been reported in individuals with ABS,[^2070] where individuals have claimed they had not consumed any alcohol. Since the disease is largely underdiagnosed, with most patients' [blood alcohol content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_alcohol_content) (BAC) rarely exceeding the normal limit, patients are often recommended to exercise caution when deciding to drive, and to closely monitor their carbohydrate intake.[^2070]

#### Case studies

In 2019, a 25-year-old man presented with symptoms consistent with alcohol intoxication, including dizziness, slurred speech and nausea. He had no prior alcoholic drinks but had a blood alcohol level of 0.3 g/dL. The patient was given 100 mg of the antifungal [fluconazole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluconazole) daily for 3 weeks, and his symptoms were resolved.[^2086]

In 2004, a 44-year-old male was treated with the antibiotics [clavulanic acid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavulanic_acid) and [amoxicillin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amoxicillin) for an unrelated condition. Eight days after being discharged, he returned to the emergency room with abdominal pain and belching and was in a state of confusion. An esophagogastroscopy showed the presence of *S. cerevisiae* and *C. albicans* in his gastric fluid, causing endogenous ethanol production.[^2087]

Reported in 2001, a 13-year-old girl with [short gut syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_gut_syndrome) suddenly developed symptoms of intoxication after eating "excess carbohydrates and juices". She had no access to alcohol any time the symptoms were present. Her small intestine was colonized by two organisms: *C. glabrata* and *S. cerevisiae*. She was treated with fluconazole and her symptoms resolved.[^2088]

A case of urinary fermentation of carbohydrates by endogenous microorganisms leading to urinary ethanol has been reported. This single reported case is associated with diabetes due to the presence of sugar in the urine for the yeast to ferment. The person did not develop symptoms of intoxication, but did test positive in the urine for alcohol. Fermentation may continue after the urine is expressed, resulting in it developing an odor resembling wine.[^2089][^2090]

Presentations at the [American College of Gastroenterology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_College_of_Gastroenterology)'s 2025 meeting included a case series of 22 patients[^2091] and another of 34 patients.[^2085]

### Hair-grooming syncope

**Hair-grooming syncope** (also known as **hair-combing syncope**) is a form of [syncope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncope_%28medicine%29) (a fainting disorder) associated with combing and brushing one's [hair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hair). It is most typically seen in children aged five to sixteen.

Hair-grooming syncope typically manifests as [presyncopal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncope_%28medicine%29) symptoms during hair combing, brushing, braiding, trimming, curling or blow drying.[^2092][^2093] These symptoms are followed by loss of consciousness and sometimes [convulsions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convulsions).[^2093] [Migraines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migraine), abdominal pain, "feeling funny" or blurred vision may also occur before or after episodes.[^2092][^2094] Possible causes of the condition include pain or nerve stimulation on the scalp (similar to parade-ground syncope), or compression of blood vessels or nerves resulting from neck [flexion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flexion) or [extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extension_%28kinesiology%29).[^2093] A 2009 study identified 111 [pediatric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pediatric) cases of hair-grooming syncope in the United States, almost three-quarters of which were in female patients; that study found that the condition is most associated with hair cutting in males and brushing in females.[^2095]

Hair-grooming syncope may be misdiagnosed as [epilepsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epilepsy), but is better described as a "paroxysmal non-epileptic event".[^2092] It may also be related to orthostatic [hypotension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypotension).[^2094] The condition is not associated with heart abnormalities.[^2096]

### Nitroglycerin (medication)

**Nitroglycerin**, also known as **glyceryl trinitrate** (**GTN**), is a [vasodilator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasodilator) used for [heart failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_failure), [high blood pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_blood_pressure), [anal fissures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anal_fissure), [painful periods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysmenorrhea), treating the pain from [esophageal spasm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esophageal_spasm), and to treat and prevent [chest pain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chest_pain) caused by [decreased blood flow to the heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_ischemia) ([angina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angina)) or due to the recreational use of [cocaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocaine).[^2097][^2098][^2099][^2100][^2101] This includes chest pain from a [heart attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myocardial_infarction).[^2097] It is taken [by mouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_administration), [under the tongue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sublingual_administration), [applied to the skin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transdermal) by [cream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ointment) or a [patch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transdermal_patch), as a spray, or by [injection into a vein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intravenous).[^2097][^2102]

Common side effects include [headache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headache) and [low blood pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_blood_pressure).[^2097] The low blood pressure can be severe.[^2097] It is unclear if use in [pregnancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pregnancy) is safe for the fetus.[^2097] It should not be used together with medications within the [PDE5 inhibitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PDE5_inhibitor) family such as [sildenafil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sildenafil) due to the risk of low blood pressure.[^2097] Nitroglycerin is in the [nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrate_%28pharmacology%29) family of medications.[^2097] While it is not entirely clear how it works, it is believed to function by [dilating blood vessels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasodilation).[^2097]

Nitroglycerin was written about as early as 1846[^2103][^2104] and came into medical use in 1878.[^2105][^2106][^2107] The drug nitroglycerin is a dilute form of the same chemical used as the explosive, [nitroglycerin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitroglycerin).[^2107] Dilution makes it non-explosive.[^2107] In 2023, it was the 207th most commonly prescribed medication in the United States, with more than 2 million prescriptions.[^2108][^2109]

#### Medical uses

Nitroglycerin is used for the treatment of angina, [acute myocardial infarction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acute_myocardial_infarction), severe [hypertension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertension), and acute [coronary artery spasms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_artery_spasm).[^2097][^2110] It may be administered [intravenously](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intravenous_therapy), as a [sublingual spray/tablet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sublingual_administration), or as a [patch applied to the skin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dermal_patch).

##### Angina

Nitroglycerin is useful in decreasing [angina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angina) attacks, perhaps more so than reversing angina once started, by supplementing blood concentrations of NO, also called [endothelium-derived relaxing factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endothelium-derived_relaxing_factor), before the structure of NO as the responsible agent was known. This led to the development of transdermal patches of nitroglycerin, providing 24-hour release.[^2111] However, the effectiveness of nitroglycerin is limited by development of tolerance/[tachyphylaxis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tachyphylaxis) within 2-3 weeks of sustained use. Continuous administration and absorption (such as provided by daily pills and especially skin patches) accelerate onset of tolerance and limit the usefulness of the agent. Thus, nitroglycerin works best when used only in short-term, pulse dosing. Indeed, studies show that a dosing regimen should include nitrate-free days, and in the case of transdermal patches (such as with Nitro-dur), which provide 10-12 hours daily of sustained release for at least 1 month[^2112] but don't yet have an established minimum time for nitrate-free windows, periods of 10-12 hours is sufficient for preventing tolerance build-up; therefore, an appropriate dosing schedule when used as patches (such as in the case with Nitro-dur) would include 12-14 hours of patch-on followed by a window of 10-12 hours of patch-off.[^2112]

Other forms of the drug are more effective for treatment of acute episodes of angina once they have started (while most forms are not due to the lack of rapid administration of the drug), and some are useful in the [prophylaxis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prophylaxis) of angina before activities which may precipitate an episode, like having [sexual intercourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_intercourse). Nitroglycerin when used as a spray can treat ongoing episodes with no more than three sprays in a 15-minute period and the same as prophylaxis of an angina attack.[^2113]

Nitroglycerin is useful for [myocardial infarction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myocardial_infarction) (heart attack) and [pulmonary edema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulmonary_edema), again working best if used quickly, within a few minutes of symptom onset.[^2114] It may also be given as a sublingual or buccal dose in the form of a tablet placed under the tongue or a spray into the mouth for the treatment of an angina attack.[^2115]

##### Other uses

Tentative evidence indicates efficacy of nitroglycerin in the treatment of various [tendinopathies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tendinopathy), both in pain management and acceleration of soft tissue repair.[^2116][^2117][^2118][^2119][^2120]

Nitroglycerin is also used in the treatment of [anal fissures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anal_fissure), though usually at a much lower concentration than that used for angina treatment.[^2098]

Nitroglycerin has been used to decrease pain associated with [dysmenorrhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysmenorrhea).[^2100]

Nitroglycerin was once researched for the prevention and treatment of [osteoporosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteoporosis); however, the researcher [Sophie Jamal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophie_Jamal) was found to have falsified the findings, sparking one of the largest [scientific misconduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_misconduct) cases in Canada.[^2121]

Nitroglycerin is also used to treat acute episodes of [esophageal spasms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esophageal_spasms), by increasing [nitric oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitric_oxide) (NO) levels it acts as a [smooth muscle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_muscle) relaxant which relaxes muscle cells and lowers pressure in the [lower esophageal sphincter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_esophageal_sphincter), reducing the intense, uncoordinated contractions in the esophagus and easing chest pain.[^2099] It is often used to treat esophageal spasms associated with [eosinophilic esophagitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eosinophilic_esophagitis) and [Gastroesophageal reflux disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gastroesophageal_reflux_disease) (GERD), although it appears to be less effective at treating spasms in those with GERD.[^2122][^2123] Nitroglycerin's effect at reducing lower esophageal pressure has also been found to be effective in helping to treat [esophageal food impaction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esophageal_food_bolus_obstruction) and foreign body obstructions in the [esophagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esophagus).[^2124][^2125][^2126]

##### Tolerance

After long-term use for chronic conditions, [nitrate tolerance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrate_tolerance), tolerance to agents such as nitroglycerin, may develop in a patient, reducing its effectiveness. Tolerance is defined as the loss of symptomatic and hemodynamic effects of nitroglycerin or the need for higher doses of the drug to achieve the same effects,[^2127] and was first described soon after the introduction of nitroglycerin in cardiovascular therapy.[^2128] Studies have shown that nitrate tolerance is associated with vascular abnormalities which have the potential to worsen patients' prognosis.[^2129][^2130] These include endothelial and autonomic dysfunction.[^2131] The mechanisms of nitrate tolerance have been investigated over the last 30 years, and several hypotheses to explain tolerance have been offered, including:

1.  plasma volume expansion
2.  impaired transformation of nitroglycerin into NO or related species
3.  counteraction of nitroglycerin vasodilation by neurohormonal activation[^2132]
4.  [oxidative stress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxidative_stress)[^2133]

#### Adverse events

Nitroglycerin can cause severe [hypotension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypotension), [reflex tachycardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflex_tachycardia), and severe headaches that necessitate [analgesic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analgesic) intervention for pain relief, the painful nature of which can have a marked negative effect on patient [compliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compliance_%28medicine%29).[^2134]

Nitroglycerin also can cause severe hypotension, [circulatory collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circulatory_collapse), and death if used together with [vasodilator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasodilation) drugs that are used for [erectile dysfunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erectile_dysfunction), such as [sildenafil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sildenafil), [tadalafil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadalafil), and [vardenafil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vardenafil).[^2135]

Nitroglycerin transdermal patches should be removed before [defibrillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defibrillation) due to the risk of explosion or burns, but investigations have concluded that nitroglycerin patch explosions during defibrillation were due to the [breakdown voltage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakdown_voltage) of the metal mesh in some patches.[^2136][^2137]

#### Mechanism of action

Nitroglycerin is a [prodrug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prodrug) which must be [denitrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denitration), with the [nitrite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrite) anion or a related species further [reduced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redox) to produce the active metabolite [nitric oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitric_oxide) (NO). Organic [nitrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrate) that undergo these two steps within the body are called [nitrovasodilators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrovasodilator), and the denitration and reduction occur via a variety of mechanisms. The mechanism by which such nitrates produce NO is widely disputed. It has been postulated that organic nitrates produce NO by reacting with [sulfhydryl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfhydryl) groups, while others believe that enzymes such as [glutathione *S*-transferases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glutathione_S-transferase), [cytochrome P450](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cytochrome_P450) (CYP), and [xanthine oxidoreductase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xanthine_oxidoreductase) are the primary source of nitroglycerin bioactivation.[^2138]

The NO produced by this process is a potent activator of [guanylyl cyclase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanylyl_cyclase) (GC) by [heme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heme)-dependent mechanisms; this activation results in formation of [cyclic guanosine monophosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclic_guanosine_monophosphate) (cGMP) from [guanosine triphosphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guanosine_triphosphate) (GTP). Among other roles, cGMP serves as a substrate for a [cGMP-dependent protein kinase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CGMP-dependent_protein_kinase) that activates [myosin light chain phosphatase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myosin_light_chain_phosphatase). Thus, production of NO from exogenous sources such as nitroglycerin increases the level of [cGMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclic_guanosine_monophosphate) within the cell, and stimulates [dephosphorylation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dephosphorylation) of [myosin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myosin_II), which initiates relaxation of smooth muscle cells in blood vessels.[^2139]

#### History

It was known almost from the time of the first synthesis of nitroglycerin by [Ascanio Sobrero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascanio_Sobrero) in 1846 that handling and tasting of [nitroglycerin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitroglycerin) could cause sudden intense [headaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headache),[^2103][^2104] which suggested a [vasodilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasodilation) effect.[^2140] [Constantine Hering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_Hering) developed a form of nitroglycerin in 1847 and advocated for its dosing as a treatment of a number of diseases; however, its use as a specific treatment for blood pressure and chest pain was not among these. This is primarily due to his deep rooted focus in [homeopathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeopathy).[^2141][^2142]

Following [Thomas Brunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Brunton)'s discovery that [amyl nitrite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amyl_nitrite) could be used to treat chest pain, [William Murrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Murrell_%28physician%29) experimented with the use of nitroglycerin to alleviate angina and reduce [blood pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_pressure), and showed that the accompanying headaches occurred as a result of [overdose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overdose). Murrell began treating patients with small doses of nitroglycerin in 1878, and the substance was widely adopted after he published his results in *[The Lancet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lancet)* in 1879.[^2105]

The medical establishment used the name "glyceryl trinitrate" or "trinitrin" to avoid alarming patients, because of a general awareness that nitroglycerin was explosive.[^2143][^2144]

Overdoses may generate [methemoglobinemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methemoglobinemia).[^2145]

#### Society and culture

##### Brand names

In the United States, the tablet form of nitroglycerin is marketed (brand name Nitrostat)[^2146] by [Viatris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viatris) after [Upjohn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upjohn) was spun off from [Pfizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pfizer).[^2147][^2148][^2149]

Nitroglycerin used for treatment of angina has multiple brand names depending on the mode of administration, such as Minitran, Nitro-Dur, Nitrolingual, Nitromist, and Nitro-Bid[^2150]. The brand name Nitro-bid is an ointment form of Nitroglycerin that is applied twice daily to the skin, hence the name, where "BID" indicates "twice daily" (B.I.D).[^2151]

### Water intoxication

**Water intoxication**, also known as **water poisoning**, **hyperhydration**, **overhydration**, or **water toxemia**, is a potentially fatal disturbance in [brain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain) functions that can result when the normal balance of [electrolytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolyte) in the body is pushed outside safe limits by excessive [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water) intake.

In normal circumstances, accidentally consuming too much water is exceptionally rare. Most deaths related to water intoxication in healthy individuals have resulted either from water-drinking [contests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Competition), in which individuals attempt to consume large amounts of water, or from long bouts of [exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exercise) during which excessive amounts of fluid were consumed.[^2152] In addition, [water cure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_cure_%28torture%29), a method of [torture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture) in which the victim is forced to consume excessive amounts of water, can cause water intoxication.[^2152] Excess [body water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_water) can also result from medical conditions or improper treatments, such as those causing [hyponatremia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyponatremia).

Although water is considered one of the least toxic chemical compounds, with an [LD₅₀](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median_lethal_dose) exceeding 90,000 mg/kg (90 g/kg) body weight in rats,[^2153] it can be considered a [poison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poison) when over-consumed in a brief period;[^2154] drinking six liters in three hours has caused the death of a human.[^2155]

#### Risk factors

##### Low body mass (infants)

It can be very easy for children under one year old (especially those under nine months) to absorb too much water. This is due to their small body mass; it is relatively easy for infants to take in a large amount of water relative to body mass and total body [sodium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sodium) stores.[^2156]

##### Endurance sports

[Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon) [runners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Running) are susceptible to water intoxication if they drink too much while running. This occurs when sodium levels drop below 135 mmol/L, which can happen when athletes consume large amounts of fluid. This has been noted to be the result of the encouragement of excessive fluid replacement by various guidelines. This has largely been identified in marathon runners as a dilutional [hyponatremia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyponatremia).[^2157] A study conducted on runners completing the 2002 [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon) found that thirteen percent finished the race with hyponatremia. The study concluded that the strongest predictor of hyponatremia was weight gain while racing (over-hydration), and hyponatremia was just as likely to occur in runners who chose sports drinks as those who chose water.[^2157]

##### Military training

Hyponatremia and other physical conditions associated with water intoxication are more often seen in those participating in military training. One US Army study found 17 trainees were admitted to a hospital over a year's period for water intoxication[^2158] while another found that three soldiers had died, leading to a recommendation that no more than 1-1.5 L of water should be consumed per hour of heavy sweating.[^2159]

##### Overexertion and heat stress

Any activity or situation that promotes heavy sweating can lead to water intoxication when water is consumed to replace lost fluids. People working in [extreme heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_wave) and/or humidity for long periods must take care to drink and eat in ways that help to maintain electrolyte balance. People using drugs such as [MDMA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MDMA) (often referred to colloquially as "Ecstasy") may overexert themselves, perspire heavily, feel increased thirst, and then drink large amounts of water to rehydrate, leading to electrolyte imbalance and water intoxication - this is compounded by MDMA use increasing the levels of [antidiuretic hormone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasopressin) (ADH), decreasing the amount of water lost through urination.[^2160] Even people who are resting quietly in extreme heat or humidity may run the risk of water intoxication if they drink large amounts of water over short periods for rehydration.[^2161]

##### Psychiatric conditions

[Psychogenic polydipsia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychogenic_polydipsia) is a psychiatric condition in which patients feel compelled to drink excessive quantities of water, thus putting them at risk of water intoxication. This condition can be especially dangerous if the patient also exhibits other psychiatric indications (as is often the case), as the caretakers might misinterpret the hyponatremic symptoms.[^2162]

##### Iatrogenic

When an unconscious person is being fed intravenously (for example, [total parenteral nutrition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_parenteral_nutrition)) or via a [nasogastric tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasogastric_tube), the fluids given must be carefully balanced in composition to match fluids and electrolytes lost. These fluids are typically [hypertonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonicity), and so water is often co-administered. If the electrolytes are not monitored (even in an ambulatory patient), either [hypernatremia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypernatremia) or hyponatremia may result.[^2163]

Some neurological/psychiatric medications ([oxcarbazepine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxcarbazepine), among others) have been found to cause hyponatremia in some patients.[^2164]

#### Pathophysiology

At the onset of this condition, fluid outside the cells has an [excessively low amount of solutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osmotic_concentration), such as sodium and other [electrolytes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrolyte), in comparison to the fluid inside the cells, causing the fluid to move into the cells to balance its [osmotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osmosis) concentration. This causes the cells to swell. The swelling increases [intracranial pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intracranial_pressure) in the brain, which leads to the first observable symptoms of water intoxication: headache, personality changes, changes in behavior, confusion, irritability, and [drowsiness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somnolence). These are sometimes followed by difficulty breathing during exertion, muscle weakness and pain, twitching, or cramping, nausea, vomiting, thirst, and a dulled ability to perceive and interpret sensory information. As the condition persists, papillary and vital signs may result including [bradycardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradycardia) and widened [pulse pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulse_pressure). The cells in the brain may swell to the point where blood flow is interrupted resulting in [cerebral edema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerebral_edema). Swollen brain cells may also apply [pressure to the brain stem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain_herniation) causing central nervous system dysfunction. Both cerebral edema and interference with the central nervous system are dangerous and could result in seizures, brain damage, coma, or death.[^2165]

#### Prevention

Water intoxication can be prevented if a person's intake of water does not grossly exceed their losses. Healthy kidneys can excrete approximately 800 millilitres to one litre of fluid water (0.84-1.04 quarts) per hour.[^2166] However, stress (from prolonged physical exertion), as well as disease states, can greatly reduce this amount.[^2166]

#### Treatment

Mild intoxication may remain asymptomatic and require only fluid restriction. In more severe cases, treatment consists of:

- [Diuretics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diuretic) to increase urination, which are most effective for excess blood volume.
- [Vasopressin receptor antagonists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasopressin_receptor_antagonist)

#### Notable cases

- 325 BC: [Alexander the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great) loses many companion travelers to excessive water intake during a march through the [Gedrosian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gedrosia) Desert.[^2167][^2168]
- 1097: During the [First Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Crusade), according to at least one chronicle, many Crusaders died after drinking too much from a river while marching to [Antioch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antioch).[^2169]
- 1991, [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol): Four years after his death, Warhol's family publicly accused the hospital where he had his [gallbladder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallbladder) removed of causing his death by water intoxication administered post-operatively. A claimed autopsy weight of 68 kg (150 lb), with his weight being 58 kg (128 lb) when admitted, was cited as evidence that too much fluid had been given.[^2170]
- 1995: [Leah Betts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leah_Betts), a British schoolgirl, died after drinking roughly 7 litres of water in less than 90 minutes. Though the media widely attributed her death solely to the [ecstasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MDMA) tablet she had taken at her 18th birthday party, an inquest determined her death was caused by water intoxication and [hyponatremia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyponatremia).[^2171]
- 2003: British actor [Anthony Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Andrews) survived a case of water intoxication. He was performing as Henry Higgins in a revival of the musical *[My Fair Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Fair_Lady)* at the time and consumed up to eight litres of water a day. He was unconscious and in intensive care for three days.[^2172][^2173]
- 2005: American college student Matthew Carrington died from water intoxication during a [Chi Tau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chi_Tau_%28local%29) [hazing ritual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazing_ritual) at [California State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University).[^2174] In response to Carrington's death, California passed [Matt's Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt's_Law), increasing penalties for hazing in the state, including [felony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felony) charges.[^2175]
- 2007: Jennifer Strange died after drinking nearly 2 US gallons (7.6 litres) of water in an attempt to win a [Wii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wii) game console.[^2176] The [KDND](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KDND) radio station's morning show, the *Morning Rave*, held an on-air contest entitled ["Hold Your Wee for a Wii,"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KDND) in which contestants were asked to drink as much water as they could without urinating. The DJs were made aware of the dangers but did not inform the contestants. KDND's parent company, Entercom Sacramento LLC, was subsequently ordered to pay \$16,577,118 in damages to Strange's family.[^2177][^2178]
