### Koro (disease)

**Koro** is a [culture-bound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture-bound_syndrome) delusional disorder in which individuals have an overpowering belief that their [sex organs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_organ) are retracting and will disappear, despite the lack of any true longstanding changes to the genitals.[^2179][^2180] Koro is also known as **shrinking penis**, and was listed in the *[Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagnostic_and_Statistical_Manual_of_Mental_Disorders)*.

The syndrome occurs worldwide, and [mass hysteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_hysteria) of genital-shrinkage anxiety has a history in [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa), [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia) and [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe).[^2181] In the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States) and Europe, the syndrome is commonly known as **genital retraction syndrome**.[^2182]

The condition can be diagnosed through psychological assessment, along with physical examination to rule out genuine disorders of the [genitalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_organ) that could be causing true retraction.[^2183][^2184]

The word was borrowed from [Malay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malay_language) and means the *head of a turtle* (or *tortoise*), referring to how it looks when they retract their heads into their shells.[^2185][^2186]

#### Signs and symptoms

Most patients report acute [anxiety attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_attack) due to perceived genital retraction and/or genital shrinkage, despite a lack of any objectively visible biological changes in the genitalia that are longstanding. "Longstanding" refers to changes that are sustained over a significant period of time and do not appear reversible, unlike the effect of cold temperatures on some genital regions that cause retraction. These changes may trigger a koro attack when observed, although the effects of cold temperatures are objectively reversible.[^2187]

According to literature, episodes usually last several hours, though the duration may be as long as two days.[^2185] There are cases in which koro symptoms persist for years in a chronic state, indicating a potential co-morbidity with [body dysmorphic disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_dysmorphic_disorder).[^2183][^2188] In addition to retraction, other symptoms include a perception of alteration of [penis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_penis) shape and loss of penile muscle tone. In cases when patients have no perception of retraction, some patients may complain of genital [paraesthesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraesthesia) or genital shortening.[^2189] Among females, the cardinal symptom is [nipple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nipple) retraction in the breast, generally into the [breast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breast) as a whole.[^2183]

Psychological components of koro [anxiety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anxiety) include fear of impending death, penile dissolution and loss of sexual power.[^2183][^2181] Feelings of impending death along with retraction and perceived [spermatorrhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spermatorrhea) has a strong cultural link with Chinese traditional beliefs. This is demonstrated by the fact that Asians generally believe koro symptoms are fatal, unlike most patients in the West.[^2183][^2190] Other ideational themes are intra-abdominal organ shrinkage, sex-change to [female](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woman) or [eunuch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunuch), non-specific physical danger, [urinary obstruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urinary_obstruction), [sterility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infertility), impending [madness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insanity), [spirit possession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirit_possession) and a feeling of being bewitched.[^2183]

Individuals with extreme anxiety and their family members may resort to physical methods to prevent the believed retraction of the penis. A man may perform manual or mechanical penile traction, or "anchoring" by a loop of string or some clamping device.[^2191] Similarly, a woman may be seen grabbing her own breast, pulling her nipple, or even having iron pins inserted into the nipple.[^2190] Physical injury may occur from these attempts.[^2183] These forceful attempts often lead to injuries, sometimes death.[^2192]

#### Causes

[Psychosexual conflicts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychosexual_development), personality factors, and cultural beliefs are considered as being of [etiological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etiological) significance to koro.[^2193] Sexual adjustment histories of non-Chinese individuals are often significant, such as [premorbid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premorbidity) sex inadequacy, [sexual promiscuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_promiscuity), guilt over [masturbation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masturbation), and [impotence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impotence).[^2194]

#### Diagnosis

Several criteria are typically used to make a [diagnosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagnosis) of koro. The primary criterion is a patient's report of genital (typically penile or female nipple) retraction despite a lack of objective physical evidence demonstrating retraction. This is accompanied by severe anxiety related to the retraction, [fear of death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_anxiety) as a result of retraction, and use of mechanical means to prevent retraction.[^2195] Cases that do not meet all the requirements are generally classified as koro-like symptoms or given a diagnosis of partial koro syndrome.[^2195] It has been argued that the criteria are sufficient but not necessary to make a diagnosis of koro.[^2183] Researchers have identified koro as a possible "cultural relative" of [body dysmorphic disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_dysmorphic_disorder). [DSM-IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DSM-IV) explains the process of [differential diagnosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_diagnosis) between these two disorders.[^2188]

##### History and physical examination

A medical, psychosexual and psychiatric history should be documented. The physician should explore the patient's concerns about appearance and body image (ruling out [body dysmorphic disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_dysmorphic_disorder)). Additionally, the physician should inquire about overall beliefs, personal values, and assumptions that the patient is making about his or her genitals. Given that koro is often an “attack” with a great deal of associated anxiety, the physician should ascertain the patient's emotional state along with the timeline from onset to the presentation at the examination.[^2196][^2197][^2198]

A physical examination should involve an assessment of overall health along with a detailed genital examination. In men, genital examination should be performed immediately after penile exposure, to avoid changes due to external temperature. The primary intent of the male exam is to exclude genuine penile anomalies such as [hypospadias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypospadias), [epispadias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epispadias) and [Peyronie's disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peyronie's_disease).[^2183][^2197] The presence of a significant suprapubic fat pad should be noted as well.[^2199] Careful measurements of flaccid length, stretched length and flaccid girth will also be useful. If male patients insist that their penis is shrinking and disappearing,[^2183] measurements after intracavernosal [alprostadil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alprostadil) may be used in the office to determine the true erect length and to diagnose any penile abnormalities in the erect state.[^2197] A physical examination should note any injuries inflicted by the patient in an effort to "prevent" retraction as further confirmation of koro.[^2183]

##### Classification

In [DSM-IV-TR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DSM-IV-TR), koro is listed as one of the entries in the Glossary of Culture-Bound Syndromes of Appendix I. The manual gives koro's definition as "a term, probably of Malaysian origin, that refers to an episode of sudden and intense anxiety that the [penis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_penis) (or, in females, the [vulva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulva) and [nipples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nipples)) will recede into the body and possibly cause death."[^2179] Attempts have been made by numerous authors to place koro into different classes. For example, koro may fit into the group of "specific culture-imposed [nosophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nosophobia)" (classification with cardinal sign),[^2200] "the genital retraction taxon" (classification with common factors between syndromes),[^2201] and the group with "culture-related beliefs as causes for the occurrence" (classification according to how the syndromes might be affected by cultural factors).[^2202]

Various authors have attempted to distinguish between complete and incomplete forms of koro, along with cultural and non-cultural forms.[^2193] Cultural forms are said to involve a cultural belief or myth which plays a role in the genesis and spread of the disease in the community. These are regarded as complete forms of koro, matching all the symptoms required for diagnosis without significant co-morbidity.[^2193][^2183] Differentiation into primary koro, a culture-bound expression, and secondary koro. Secondary koro is proposed to have co-morbidity with a [CNS disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_nervous_system_disease), another [psychiatric disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatric_disorder), or possible drug use.[^2183]

[Traditional Chinese medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_medicine) recognises koro as a sexual disease and classifies it into two categories, namely "cold conglomeration in [liver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liver)" and "depletion of [kidney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidney)'s [yang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yin_and_yang)".[^2203]

##### Differential diagnosis

Men who present with this complaint may have koro, but they may also be misinformed about normal genital size.[^2184] Additionally, they may have [penile dysmorphophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penile_dysmorphic_disorder).[^2204][^2205] Penile dysmorphophobia is related to [body dysmorphic disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_dysmorphic_disorder) (BDD), defined by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders-Fourth Edition (Text Revision) ([DSM-IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DSM-IV)-TR) as a condition marked by excessive preoccupation with an imaginary or minor defect in a facial feature or localized part of the body. BDD is different from koro. In koro, a patient is overcome with the belief that his penis is actively shrinking, and it may be in imminent danger of disappearing.[^2206] Clinical literature indicates that these two psychological conditions should be separated during [differential diagnosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_diagnosis).[^2184]

In addition to differentiating koro from [body dysmorphic disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_dysmorphic_disorder), physicians also recommend that [differential diagnosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differential_diagnosis) separates koro from physical urological abnormalities.[^2183][^2184][^2207] For example, one physical disorder that causes loss of penile size is [Peyronie's disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peyronie's_disease), where the [tunica albuginea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunica_albuginea_%28penis%29) develops scar tissue that prevents the full expansion of an erection and causes flaccid penis retraction.[^2208][^2209][^2210] Additionally, a [buried penis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buried_penis) is a normally developed penis, partially covered by the suprapubic fat which can be surgically removed.[^2184][^2199]

#### Treatment

In historical culture-bound cases, reassurance and talks on [sexual anatomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_anatomy) are given.[^2191] Patients are treated with [psychotherapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychotherapy) distributed according to symptoms and to etiologically significant points in the past. Prognosis appears to be better in cases with a previously functional personality, a short history and low frequency of attacks, and a relatively uncomplicated sexual life.[^2185]

For sporadic Western cases, careful diagnostic workup including searching for underlying sexual conflict is common. The choice of psychotherapeutic treatment is based on the psychiatric pathology found.[^2211]

##### Indigenous treatment

In China, traditional treatment based on the causes suggested by cultural beliefs are administered to the patient. Praying to gods and asking Taoist priests to perform exorcism is common. If a [fox spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huli_jing) is believed to be involved, people may hit [gongs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gong) or beat the person to drive it out. The person will receive a yang- or yin-augmenting Chinese medicine to try to balance the internal conditions, usually including herbs, pilose antler (stag of deer) or deer tail, and [tiger penis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_penis), [deer penis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deer_penis), or [fur seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_seal) penis. Other medicinal foods for therapy are pepper soup, ginger soup and [liquor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquor).[^2190]

#### Epidemiology

Among the Chinese, koro is confined to [South China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_and_southern_China) and the lower [Yangtze Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yangtze_Valley).[^2185] A 1992 study of self-report questionnaires suggests that in the epidemic area of China, individuals with koro are mostly [Han](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_Chinese), male, young, single, poorly educated and fearful of [supernatural forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural) and koro.[^2190]

The phenomenon is also found among overseas Chinese in [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia), especially [Malaysia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysia) and [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia), and less frequently among the [Malay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malay_%28ethnic_group%29) and [Indonesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_groups_in_Indonesia) inhabitants of the countries.[^2185] Though there are speculations that the occurrence of koro among people in Malaysia and Indonesia was the result of Chinese migrants, this cultural diffusion view is challenged since koro epidemics have been reported in [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand) and India, involving masses of non-Chinese people.[^2212]

Sporadic cases of koro among people with non-Southeast-Asian ethnicity have been reported across the globe, for example, [Nepali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_of_Nepal),[^2213] [Sudanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudanese_people),[^2214] [Jordanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Jordan),[^2215] [Tanzanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_Tanzania),[^2216] [Nigerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigerian_people),[^2217] [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people),[^2218] [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_people),[^2219][^2220][^2221] [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_of_the_United_States)[^2222][^2223] and [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians).[^2224][^2225] In most of the non-Chinese cases in the [Western Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Hemisphere), fear of genital shrinkage is reported but not all the other typical koro symptoms, such as fear of death, as in endemic countries.[^2226] The incomplete forms of koro are regarded as the non-cultural forms, while the complete form with acute anxiety is the classical culture-bound type.[^2193]

##### China

Local official records indicate genital retraction epidemics in [Hainan Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hainan_Island) and [Leizhou Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leizhou_Peninsula) in [Guangdong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangdong), China, as early as the late nineteenth century. There were a series of epidemic outbursts in 1948, 1955, 1966, and 1974, whenever there was social tension or impending disaster, followed by the last widespread episode in 1984-1985 and a much smaller outbreak in 1987. The 1984-1985 epidemics lasted for over a year and affected over 3,000 people in 16 cities and provinces. A mental health campaign was conducted for the epidemic and since then no further episodes of the epidemic has occurred in China. Improvement in local economic conditions, associated with a better quality of life, is suggested to contribute to the fading of the episodic occurrences of koro.[^2190][^2212]

##### Southeast Asia

A koro epidemic struck [Singapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singapore) in late October 1967 for about ten days. Newspapers initially reported that some people developed koro after eating the meat of pigs inoculated with a [vaccine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaccine) for [swine influenza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swine_influenza). Rumours relating eating pork and koro spread after a further report of an inoculated pig dying from penile retraction. The cases reported amounted to 97 in a single hospital unit within one day, at five days after the original news report. Government and medical officials alleviated the outbreak only by public announcements over television and in the newspapers.[^2227][^2228][^2229]

An epidemic outbreak in November 1976 in [Isan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isan), Thailand caused at least 350 cases, most of them Thai and males. Popular opinion and news media echoed the affected individuals' projection of viewing the epidemic as caused by Vietnamese food and tobacco poisoning in a hideous assault against the Thai people.[^2230][^2231] Another large-scale epidemic in Thailand occurred in 1982.[^2230]

##### India

In 1982, a koro epidemic episode in [Northeast India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_India) affected, in majority, poorly educated people from lower socio-economic strata. There was no evidence of significant premorbid or sexual psychopathology in most cases.[^2232]

Mass Koro epidemic was reported in Labour Camps in Kochi, Kerala in South India during August and September 2010 among migrant labour population from North and North-east India. Reportedly, the epidemic spread to about 100 individuals in 3 labour Camps within 2 weeks.

Mass Koro epidemic was reported in the state of [West Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bengal), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India) from July to December 2010, in the districts near southern part of [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India)-[Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh) border, affecting hundreds of people. It is called **Disco Rog** ([Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language): ডিস্কো রোগ) meaning weird disease or **Jhinjhinani Rog** ([Bengali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali_language): ঝিনঝিনানি রোগ) meaning tingling disease, in that region. Locals created some folk managements for this condition like partly submerging the patient in a pond and pulling and holding her nipples or his genital. It is reported and published in many newspapers like [Anandabazar Patrika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anandabazar_Patrika) at that time.

##### Africa

In the 1970s and early 1980s, newspapers reported incidents of genital shrinking in Western Nigeria. Since late 1996, a small-scale epidemic of genital shrinking was reported in West African nations. Affected individuals in the African outbreaks often interpreted the experience as genital theft, accusing someone with whom they had contact of "stealing" the organ and the spiritual essence, causing impotence. The perceived motive for theft was associated with local [occult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occult) belief, the [witchcraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witchcraft) of [juju](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juju), to feed the spiritual agency or to hold the genital for ransom. [Social representations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_representations) about juju constitute [consensual realities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensus_reality) that propose both a means and motivation for genital-shrinking experience.[^2195]

The epidemic began in [Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria) and [Cameroon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameroon), and spread to [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana), [Ivory Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory_Coast) and [Senegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senegal) by 1997.[^2195] Cases were reported in [Cotonou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotonou), [Benin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benin) where mobs attacked individuals accused of the penis theft and authorities ordered security forces to curb the violence, following the deaths of five people by [vigilantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigilante).[^2233] Later reports of outbreak suggest a spread beyond West Africa, including the coverage of episodes in [Khartoum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khartoum), [Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan) in September 2003; [Banjul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banjul), [Gambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gambia) in October 2003;[^2195] and [Kinshasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinshasa), [DR Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DR_Congo) in 2008.[^2234]

Comparing West African genital-shrinking epidemics with koro in Southeast Asia, the latter has symptoms centered on genital retraction (instead of shrinkage) and fear of death (which is absent in African cases).[^2195] A study analyzing the West African epidemics from 1997 to 2003 concluded that rather than [psychopathology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychopathology), the episodes were the product of normal psychological functioning in undisturbed individuals, who were influenced by the local cultural models or social representations.[^2195]

In 2025, rumors spread in the Central African Republic and Mali that certain people were stealing the penises of men who shook hands with them. A Russian-linked disinformation website attempted to capitalize on these beliefs by claiming that French intelligence services were using handshakes to steal African penises, then shipping the organs to France by boat in order to combat decreasing fertility rates in Europe. This claim was part of an ongoing effort by Russia to supplant French and Western influence in Africa.[^2235]

##### US and Europe

In the late Middle Ages in Europe, it was believed that men could lose their penises through magical attacks by witches.[^2181] The *[Malleus Maleficarum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malleus_Maleficarum)*, a fifteenth-century European manual for witchcraft investigations, relates stories of men claiming that their genitals had disappeared, being "hidden by the devil … so that they can be neither seen nor felt." They were said to have reappeared after the men had appeased the witches responsible.[^2236] Witches were said to store the removed genitals in birds' nests or in boxes, where "they move themselves like living members and eat oats and corn".[^2236]

At least three publications of the 1880s, from the US, Russia and England, reported genital retraction pathology, without using the Malay or Chinese term. Koro epidemics in China were first noticed in a French report in 1908 and descriptions of koro entered clinical books of western medicine in 1936. In the 1950s, koro is noted in [nosological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nosological) and diagnostic psychiatry.[^2230]

#### Society and culture

##### Chinese cultural beliefs

Most of the ancient literature concerning koro was related to Chinese ethnic groups. For example, koro (in its Chinese term of *shuk yang*, *shook yong* or *suo yang* (simplified Chinese: 缩阳; traditional Chinese: 縮陽)) is documented in the old medical book *New Collection of remedies of value* ([simplified Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters): 验方新篇; [traditional Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters): 驗方新篇) which was published in [Qing Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qing_Dynasty). The book described the condition as "[yin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yin_and_yang) type of [cold qi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qi) invasion" ([simplified Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters): 阴症伤寒; [traditional Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters): 陰症傷寒) which involved a sudden [seizure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seizure) during [sexual intercourse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_intercourse) with the penis retracting into the abdomen. It asserts that the patient will die if not treated with "[heaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_medicine)" drugs in time.[^2191]

Factors of cultural expectation in the genesis of koro can be built upon ideas of sex physiology in the [traditional Chinese medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_medicine), with free play of imagination which links fatality with genital retraction.[^2191]

In the ancient Chinese medical book *Zhong Zang Jing* ([simplified Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters): 中藏经; [traditional Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters): 中藏經), retraction of the penis with distension of the abdomen was described as a certain sign of death.[^2191] The [yin and yang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yin_and_yang) theory proposes that an unbalanced loss of the yang humour produces genital shrinkage.[^2185]

In [Taoism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taoism) and [traditional Chinese medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_medicine), frequent [ejaculation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejaculation) is regarded as detrimental to health, as [semen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semen) is considered to be related to a man's vital energy, and hence excessive depletion of semen may lead to illness or death. Some authors believe that the idea of death caused by the semen depletion resembles the idea of death caused by genital disappearance, although such linkage between koro and Taoism, which influences Chinese medicine to some degree, is only speculative.[^2190]

The popularity of [Chinese folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_folklore) also plays a role. The classic anthology of supernatural tales, *[Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strange_Stories_from_a_Chinese_Studio)*, describes a [fox spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huli_jing) which can make people weak physically and sexually and shrink their tissues. Belief in koro being caused by the fox ghost among the southern Chinese has been reported.[^2190]

##### Etymology and geographical background

The earliest Western reference to the term *koro* ("koro-koro") is found in a letter from Celebes (now Sulawesi) by Carl Wilhelm Maurus Schmidtmüller, published in 1849.[^2237] The name could be derived from a river, its surrounding valley, and a local tribe of the same name which is located at northwestern sector of [Sulawesi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulawesi), Indonesia.[^2238] The word is also used in [Makassarese language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makassarese_language), meaning "to shrink"; the full expression is *garring koro*.[^2183] Koro may also be derived from [Malay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaysian_language) term *Kura* which means "head of turtle"[^2238][^2190] or *keruk* which means "to shrink".[^2239] The term *shuk yang* (缩阳), adapted from Chinese, means "the shrinkage of penis".[^2190] The term *koro* is also known as *rok loo* (genital shrinkage disease) in [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand), *jinjinnia bemar* in [Assam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assam), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India), and *lanuk e laso* by the Bogoba tribe in [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines).[^2238]

### Legrand G. Capers

**Legrand G. Capers** (April 16, 1834 - December 2, 1877) was an American medical doctor, best known for his 1874 spurious [case report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_report) of bullet-mediated [impregnation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pregnancy) of a young woman.

#### Biography

Legrand Guerry Capers, Jr. was born on April 16, 1834, in [Charleston, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_South_Carolina), as the son of the merchant LeGrand G. Capers (1808-1868) and his first wife, Abigail Swift (1810-1846).[^2240] LeGrand G. Capers, Sr. served on Gen. [Worth's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_J._Worth) staff during the [Mexican-American War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War).[^2241]

LeGrand G. Capers, Jr. studied medicine as the assistant to his brother-in-law, Ebenezer Swift,[^2242] and graduated from [Jefferson Medical College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Medical_College).[^2243] Later he practised as ship physician on [Vanderbilt's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_Vanderbilt) steamers.

When the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War) broke out, Capers participated in the foundation of the Confederate Medical Department in Alabama. On July 19, 1861, he became assistant surgeon in the 4th Georgia Volunteer Infantry.[^2244] On October 30, 1863, he was promoted to chief surgeon in [Cutshaw's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilfred_Emory_Cutshaw) battalion.[^2245]

After the end of the war in 1865, Capers moved to [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans) and became demonstrator of anatomy in the [New Orleans School of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans_School_of_Medicine). He fell ill in October 1877 and died shortly after from [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis) on December 2. He is buried in [Vicksburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicksburg,_Mississippi).[^2245] Obituaries appeared in the *Transactions of the Mississippi State Medical Association*[^2246] and *American Medical Weekly*.[^2247]

#### "Bullet pregnancy"

The infamous case of "bullet pregnancy" was published in 1874 in The American Medical Weekly. Capers claimed that he witnessed this case eleven years before, while serving in the Confederate army:[^2248]

> On the 12th day of May, 1863, the battle of R. was fought. \[...\] Our men were fighting nobly, but pressed by superior numbers, had gradually fallen back to within one hundred and fifty yards of the house. My position being near my regiment, suddenly I beheld a noble, gallant young friend staggering closer, and then fall to the earth. In the same moment a piercing scream from the house reached my ear! I was soon by the side of the young man, and, upon examination, found a compound fracture, with extensive comminution of the left tibia; the ball having ricochetted from these parts, and, in its onward flight, passed through the scrotum, carrying away the left testicle. Scarcely had I finished dressing the wounds of this poor fellow, when the estimable matron came running to me in the greatest distress, begging me to go to one of her daughters, who, she informed me, had been badly wounded a few minutes before. Hastening to the house, I found that the eldest of the young ladies had indeed received a most serious wound. A [minnie ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnie_ball) had penetrated the left abdominal parietes, about midway between the umbilicus and anterior spinal process of the ilium, and was lost in the abdominal cavity, leaving a ragged wound behind. Believing there was little or no hope of her recovery, I had only time to prescribe an [anodyne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anodyne), when our army fell back, leaving both field and village in the hands of the enemy. \[...\] About six months after her recovery, the movements of our army brought me again to the village of R., and I was again sent for to see the young lady. She appeared in excellent health and spirits, but her abdomen had become enormously enlarged, so much so as to resemble pregnancy at the seventh or eighth month. Indeed, had I not known the family and the facts of the abdominal wound, I should have so pronounced the case. Under the above circumstances, I failed to give a positive diagnosis, determining to keep the case under surveillance. \[...\] Just two hundred and seventy-eight days from the date of the receipt of the wound by the minnie ball, I delivered this same young lady of a fine boy, weighing eight pounds. \[...\] About three weeks from the date of this remarkable birth, I was called to see the child, the grandmother insisting there was "something wrong about the genitals." Examination revealed an enlarged, swollen, sensitive scrotum, containing on the right side a hard, roughened substance, evidently foreign. I decided upon operating for its removal at once, and in so doing, extracted from the scrotum a minnie ball, mashed and battered as if it had met in its flight some hard, unyielding substance.

An editor's note in a subsequent issue of the journal revealed the case to be a joke:[^2249]

> DR. L.G. CAPERS, of Vicksburg, Miss., disclaims responsibility for the truth of that remarkable case of impregnation by a minnie ball, as reported in No. 19 of this Journal. He tells the story as it was told to him. He does not say it is untrue, but is disposed to appositely remember the truth of the old adage, that "accidents may happen in the best regulated families." The joke is, that the Doctor reported the case without any signature, but as the editor is indisposed to be made the victim of canards, and recognized the writing sent, he was unwilling to deprive the author of the contemplated fun, and allowed him to enjoy even more of this than was anticipated. The readers have enjoyed the story much, but not enough "to cut capers" after reading it.

### Mariam Nabatanzi

**Mariam Nabatanzi Babirye** (born c. 1980),[^2250] also known as **Maama Uganda** or **Mother Uganda**, is a Ugandan woman known for birthing 44 children, 38 of whom are still alive.[^2251][^2252] As of March 2025, her eldest children were 33 years old, and the youngest were eight years old.[^2251] In 2015, her husband abandoned the family, reportedly unable to support so many children.[^2253][^2254]

Born around 1980, Babirye first gave birth when she was 13 years old, having been forced into marriage the year before. By the age of 36, she had given birth to a total of 44 children, including three sets of [quadruplets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadruplets), four sets of [triplets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triplets), and six sets of [twins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin), for a total of fifteen births. The number of multiple births was caused by a rare genetic condition causing [hyperovulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovarian_hyperstimulation_syndrome) as a result of enlarged ovaries. In 2019, when Babirye was aged 40, she underwent a medical procedure to prevent any further pregnancies.[^2255]

#### Life and background

According to Babirye, her mother abandoned her family and five brothers three days following her birth.[^2256] When Babirye was seven years old and was away visiting a relative, her stepmother mixed cut glass into the food of her older siblings as a result of which all of them died.[^2256]

In 1993, a twelve year old Babirye was married off to a physically abusive 40 year old man, who was [polygamous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygamy) and already had multiple other wives.[^2255][^2257] Her father-in-law gave her family a piece of land to support themselves, and at the age of 13, she gave birth to twins, before giving birth to triplets two years later, and then a set of quadruplets a year and a half later.[^2255] She did not find this unusual, as multiple births were quite common in her family, saying:[^2255]

> My father gave birth to forty-five children with different women, and these all came in quintuplets, quadruples, twins and triplets.

 Mariam Nabatanzi

After her sixth delivery, she approached a doctor about having no more children and was told that "attempting to stop her from having another child would lead to her early death."[^2257] At age 23, she had given birth to 25 children but was advised to continue having children because "(her) ovary count was still high."[^2257]

In 2015, Babirye's husband abandoned the family, unable to provide for 42 children,[^2258] but not before leaving her pregnant with twins; he later on sold off the homestead where Babirye and her children were living. She and her children were hosted by her grandmother, but when her grandmother died, her relatives allowed her to remain in the homestead to house her children.[^2259] As of April 2023, she still owes a balance on that homestead before she can assume full ownership.[^2259]

According to Charles Kiggundu, a [gynecologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gynecologist) at the [Mulago National Specialised Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulago_National_Specialised_Hospital), after giving birth to her last set of twins via [cesarian section](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesarean_section), Babirye underwent [tubal ligation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tubal_ligation), preventing any further pregnancies.[^2255] One of the boys from that set of twins died in childbirth, being her most recent child to die.[^2258]

#### Living situation

Babirye and her household, comprising sixty-odd individuals, including her children, grandchildren and daughters-in-law, live in the village of [Kasawo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kasawo), located in the [Mukono district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mukono_District) of Central Uganda.[^2259] They are largely dependent on donors who donate food, beds and other necessities, but Babirye also works as a part-time tailor, [herbalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbal_medicine) and hairdresser.[^2259][^2260][^2261][^2262]

Babirye's household lives in a complex composed of five cement-block houses with corrugated iron roofs; the complex has seventeen rooms, fifteen of which are bedrooms and two are empty living and dining rooms.[^2259] Nine of the bedrooms are without any beds, and the other six bedrooms have a total of eight [bunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunk_bed) beds, four of which are not in usable condition. The other four beds accommodate a total of twenty-four children on mattresses.[^2250][^2259]

#### Plans

According to *The Uganda Times*, Babirye hopes to get [UGX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UGX) 5 million (about US\$1,400) to pay off the remaining balance on her family's living complex to her grandmother's relatives to take full ownership.[^2259]

She also hopes to acquire new iron sheets to replace the leaking roofs, twenty-five new bunk beds, and sixty-six new mattresses, so that each person has their own bed. Additionally, she plans to acquire some land for cultivating food and rearing animals with her family workforce, and to achieve financial security for her dependents, as well as starting a restaurant, a bridal salon, and an events management service to employ her children.[^2259]

### Coprolalia

**Coprolalia** (/ˌkɒprəˈleɪliə/ *KOP-rə-LAY-lee-ə*) is involuntary swearing or the involuntary utterance of obscene words or socially [inappropriate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inappropriate) and derogatory remarks. The word comes from the [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language) κόπρος (*kópros*), meaning "dung, [feces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feces)", and λαλιά (*laliā́*) "speech", from λαλεῖν (*laleîn*) "to talk".[^2263]

Coprolalia is an occasional characteristic of [tic disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tic_disorder), in particular [Tourette syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourette_syndrome), although it is not required for a diagnosis of Tourette's and only about 10% of individuals with Tourette's exhibit coprolalia.[^2264] It is not unique to tic disorders; it may also present itself as a [neurological disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurological_disorder).[^2265][^2266]

Coprolalia is one type of coprophenomenon. Other coprophenomena include the related symptoms of [copropraxia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copropraxia), involuntary actions such as performing obscene or forbidden gestures,[^2267] and [coprographia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coprographia), making obscene writings or drawings.[^2268]

#### Characteristics

Coprolalia encompasses the uncontrollable utterance of words and phrases that are culturally [taboo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taboo) or generally unsuitable for acceptable social use, when used out of context. The term is not used to describe contextual swearing. It is usually expressed out of social or emotional context, and may be spoken in a louder tone or different cadence or pitch than normal conversation. It can be a single word, or complex phrases. A person with coprolalia may repeat the word mentally rather than saying it out loud; these subvocalizations can be very distressing.[^2269]

Coprolalia is an occasional characteristic of [Tourette syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourette_syndrome), although it is not required for a diagnosis of Tourette's. Typically, symptoms of coprolalia follow the development of phonic or motor tics by four to seven years. The severity of symptoms tends to peak during adolescence and subside during adulthood.[^2270]  In Tourette syndrome, compulsive swearing can be uncontrollable and undesired by the person uttering the phrases. Involuntary outbursts, such as racial or ethnic slurs in the company of those most offended by such remarks, can be particularly embarrassing. The phrases uttered by a person with coprolalia do not necessarily reflect the thoughts or opinions of the person as they are unconsciously produced.[^2270]

It may occur after [traumatic brain injury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traumatic_brain_injury) such as stroke[^2266] and [encephalitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encephalitis);[^2266][^2271] in other neurological conditions such as [choreoacanthocytosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choreoacanthocytosis),[^2272] seizures,[^2273] and [Lesch-Nyhan syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesch%E2%80%93Nyhan_syndrome);[^2274] and rarely in persons with [dementia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dementia) or [obsessive-compulsive disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obsessive-compulsive_disorder) in the absence of [tics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tic).[^2266]

#### Brain regions implicated

The neural mechanisms underlying the presence of coprolalia alone are poorly understood. Current research is designed to locate the brain regions that are active during an involuntary tic. Individuals with Tourette Syndrome (TS) exhibit the symptoms of coprolalia, so researchers can study subjects with TS to deduce an etiology for phonic tics. Patterns of neural activity were tracked by using [Positron Emission Tomography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positron_Emission_Tomography) (PET) scans. The activity of the frontal [operculum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operculum_%28brain%29) and [Broca's area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broca's_area) (Brodmann's area 44 and 45), may be responsible for the initiation of these vocal tics. Both of these brain areas are responsible for planning and producing speech, which are active during coprolalic vocal tic episodes.[^2275]

[Limbic system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limbic_system) structures such as the [posterior cingulate cortex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posterior_cingulate_cortex) are also activated during coprolalic vocal tics. This region of the brain is responsible for emotional processing, so its increase in activation could reveal insights as to how taboo words may be organized differently than the [neurolinguistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurolinguistic) aspect of the brain.[^2276]

#### Prevalence in Tourette syndrome

Only about 10% of people with Tourette's exhibit coprolalia,[^2264] but it tends to attract more attention than any other symptom.[^2277]

There is a low number of [epidemiological studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidemiological_study) on Tourette syndrome due to [ascertainment bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascertainment_bias) affecting [clinical studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_trial). Studies on people with Tourette's often "came from tertiary referral samples, the sickest of the sick".[^2278] Further, the criteria for [Tourette's syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tourette's_syndrome) changed in 2000 when the impairment criterion was removed from the [DSM-IV-TR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DSM-IV-TR) for all tic disorders.[^2279] This resulted in an increase of diagnoses in milder cases. Additionally, many clinical studies suffer from small sample size. These factors combine to render older estimates of coprolalia occurrences outdated.

An international, multi-site database of 3,500 individuals with Tourette syndrome drawn from clinical samples found 14% of people with Tourette's accompanied by [comorbid conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comorbidity) had coprolalia, while only 6% of those with uncomplicated ("pure") Tourette's had coprolalia. The same study found that the chance of having coprolalia increased linearly with the number of comorbid conditions: individuals with four or five other conditions, in addition to tics, were four to six times more likely to have coprolalia than persons with only Tourette's.[^2280]

#### Management

[Botulinum toxin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botulinum_toxin) (botox) may be injected near the [vocal cords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_cords). This does not prevent the vocalizations, but the partial [paralysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paralysis) that results may help control the volume of any outbursts.[^2281][^2282][^2283] Botox injections result in more generalized relief of tics than the vocal relief expected.[^2284]

#### In deaf individuals

Coprolalia has also been documented in deaf individuals. Non-verbal phonic tics are referred to as "signing phonic tics" in deaf individuals. Coprolalia in signing individuals is characterized by uncontrollable fingerspelling of obscene and inappropriate words and phrases, the production of intercourse-related signs, flicking middle fingers, or compulsive repetition of signs.[^2285] Tourette syndrome is extremely understudied in the deaf community, often being misdiagnosed as [schizophrenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schizophrenia). Researchers are still studying the relationship between deafness and Tourette syndrome to combat misdiagnosis.[^2286]

#### Society and culture

The entertainment industry [often depicts those with Tourette syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Societal_and_cultural_aspects_of_Tourette_syndrome) as being social misfits whose only tic is coprolalia, which has furthered stigmatization and the public's misunderstanding of those with Tourette's.[^2287][^2288][^2289] The coprolalic symptoms of Tourette's are also fodder for radio and television talk shows.[^2290]

### Tanganyika laughter epidemic

The **Tanganyika laughter epidemic** of 1962 was an outbreak of [mass hysteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_hysteria) in or near the village of [Kashasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashasha) on the western coast of [Lake Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Victoria) in [Tanganyika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanganyika_%281961%E2%80%931964%29) (now part of [Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania)), near the border with Uganda.[^2291]

#### History

The laughter epidemic began on January 30, 1962, at a mission-run boarding school for girls in [Kashasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashasha). It started with three girls and spread throughout the school, affecting 95 of the 159 pupils, aged 12-18.[^2292][^2293] Symptoms lasted from a few hours to 16 days, averaging around 7 days.[^2294] The teaching staff were unaffected and reported that students were unable to concentrate on their lessons. The first outbreak in Kashasha lasted roughly 48 days. The school was forced to close on March 18, 1962.[^2295] When it reopened on May 21, a second phase of the outbreak affected an additional 57 pupils. The all-girl boarding school reclosed at the end of June.[^2294][^2293]

The epidemic spread to Nshamba of the [Muleba District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muleba_District), a village 55 miles west of [Bukoba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bukoba,_Tanzania), where several of the girls lived.[^2295] In April and May 1962, 217 mostly young villagers had laughing attacks over the course of 34 days. The Kashasha school was sued for allowing the children and their parents to transmit it to the surrounding area. In June, the laughing epidemic spread to Ramashenye girls' middle school, affecting 48 girls.[^2292] Additional schools and the Kanyangereka village were also affected to some degree.[^2295] The phenomenon died off 18 months after it started. All areas affected were within a 100-mile radius of Bukoba.[^2294] In all, 14 schools were shut down and 1,000 people were affected.[^2296]

#### Causes and symptoms

Symptoms[^2297] of the Tanganyika 'laughter epidemic' included laughter and crying, beside general restlessness and pain, as well as fainting, respiratory problems, and rashes. Many of the symptoms experienced were stress-induced due to various external factors. The stress and anxiety that provokes mass hysteria outbreaks are reactions to perceived threats, cultural transitions, instances of uncertainty, and social stressors.[^2294] Due to the majority of the population affected by this epidemic being young and adolescent children, the outbreak has been attributed to the young not having the appropriate coping skills to manage such stresses and anxieties. Coinciding with this, adolescents have a need for acceptance and are eager to blend into a group, making them vulnerable to influence contagion.[^2298]

#### External factors

Linguist Christian F. Hempelmann has theorized that the episode was stress-induced. In 1962, Tanganyika had just won its independence, he said, and students had reported feeling stressed because of higher expectations by teachers and parents. Mass Psychogenic Illness (MPI), he says, usually occurs in people without a lot of power. "MPI is a last resort for people of a low status. It's an easy way for them to express that something is wrong."[^2294]

Sociologist [Robert Bartholomew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bartholomew_%28sociologist%29) and psychiatrist [Simon Wessely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Wessely) both put forward a culture-specific epidemic hysteria hypothesis, pointing out that the occurrences in 1960s Africa were prevalent in missionary schools and Tanganyikan society was ruled by strict traditional elders, so the likelihood is the hysteria was a manifestation of the cultural dissonance between the "traditional conservatism" at home and the new ideas challenging those beliefs in school, which they termed "conversion reactions".[^2299]

#### Connected events

The laughter epidemic was one of three sequential behavioral epidemics that occurred in the vicinity of Lake Victoria.[^2294] These three major epidemics were classified as events of mass hysteria or mania. According to Benjamin H. Kagwa's observations in the East African Medical Journal, a notable characteristic is the prevalence of typical symptoms within specific ethnic groups, where the occurrence and propagation of comparable symptoms are aligned with tribal boundaries.[^2300] As with the hysteria epidemic in Tanganyika, these "manias" are attributed to the radically shifting culture that began to stray away from the traditional cultural beliefs of local tribes and communities.

"We must not, however, think for one moment that this is peculiar to Africans. There is much historical evidence to prove that emotional upheavals associated with hysteria occur whenever a people's cultural roots and beliefs become suddenly shattered" -Benjamin H. Kagwa[^2300]

**Correlating mass hysteria events [^2300]**

| Location | Start date | Type of "manias" | Symptoms |
|----|----|----|----|
| Bukoba, Tanganyika (now Tanzania) | January 1962 | laughter mania | laughter, crying, restlessness, pain, fainting, respiratory problems, rashes, and anxiety/stress |
| Kigezi, Uganda | July 1963 | running mania | running, chest pain, agitation, talkativeness, violence, anorexia, exhaustion, quietness, and depression |
| Mbale, Uganda | November 1963 | running mania | running, chest pain, agitation, talkativeness, violence, anorexia, exhaustion, quietness, and depression |

### Phagophobia

**Phagophobia** is a psychogenic [dysphagia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dysphagia), a fear of [swallowing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swallowing).[^2301] It is expressed in various swallowing complaints without any apparent physical reason detectable by physical inspection and laboratory analyses. An obsolete term for this condition is **choking phobia**,[^2302] but it was suggested that the latter term is confusing and it is necessary to distinguish the fear of swallowing (i.e., of the propulsion of [bolus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolus_%28digestion%29)) from [fear of choking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudodysphagia).[^2301]

Phagophobia is classified as a [specific phobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specific_phobia), and (according to [DSM-IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DSM-IV) classification) it belongs to the category of "other phobias". Phagophobia may lead to (and be confused with) [fear of eating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear_of_eating_%28disambiguation%29), and the subsequent [malnutrition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malnutrition) and [weight loss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weight_loss). In milder cases, a phagophobe eats only soft and liquid foods.[^2303]

### Common Surinam toad

The **common Surinam toad**, the **Suriname toad**, or **star-fingered toad** (***Pipa pipa***), is a fully-aquatic [species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species) of [frog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frog), in the family [Pipidae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipidae), with a widespread range across much of tropical [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America) and the island of [Trinidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad).[^2304] The females of this species are well-known for "incubating" their eggs on their backs, in honeycomb-like depressions directly within the skin, releasing fully-formed froglets after a period of 4-5 months. *Pipa pipa* is an [ambush predator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambush_predator), lying in-wait underwater for prey to inevitably wander too close, swiftly inhaling the unsuspecting creature using [suction feeding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suction_feeding). Additionally, the Surinam toad's rather flat body shape, combined with rather dark, dull coloration, serves as effective [camouflage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camouflage) in the murky waters they inhabit, mimicking a dead leaf or piece of rotting wood as they await their next meal.

#### Description

*P. pipa* is a strictly aquatic [frog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frog) and the largest member of its [genus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genus). The species has an exceptionally depressed body, almost entirely flat and with a broad, flat, triangular head, without a tongue.[^2305] The body is similar in appearance to a mottled brown leaf. The feet are broadly webbed with the front toes having small, star-like appendages. Males can grow up to 154 mm (6.1 in) long, whereas females can reach up to 171 mm (6.7 in). Females can be distinguished not only by their length but also by their ring-shaped [cloacas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloaca), visible when they are ready to breed.[^2306] The skin color is mostly light brown with some darker spots on the back, providing good camouflage[^2306][^2307] Nostrils are terminal, eyes very small, and the [tympanum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tympanum_%28anatomy%29) is missing. The limbs are in a laterally sprawled position in the plane of the body, and the fingertips are modified into four small lobes.[^2308] Absence of a tongue prevents the species from capturing prey with that organ like most other frogs, and instead suction capture is used.[^2309]

The skull is hyperossified and the cranial and postcranial bones are heavily modified compared to other anurans. While the eyes are relatively small and narrow, the species has a [lateral line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lateral_line) system and [neuromast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuromast) organs which are assumed to help it locate prey and predators.[^2305]

The Surinam toad lacks dermal [antimicrobial peptides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antimicrobial_peptides) that may inhibit disease agents such as [chytridiomycosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chytridiomycosis) and [Ranavirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranavirus), which could make it slightly more susceptible to disease.[^2310]

#### Habitat and distribution

The Surinam toad, despite its common name, is actually native to several South American countries; as well as [Suriname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suriname), it is known from [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil) (primarily the states of [Acre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acre_%28state%29), [Amazonas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazonas_%28Brazilian_state%29), [Mato Grosso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mato_Grosso), [Pará](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Par%C3%A1) and [Rondônia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rond%C3%B4nia)), [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia), [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia), [Ecuador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuador), [French Guiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Guiana), [Guyana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guyana), and [Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela), in tropical rainforest regions to the east of the [Andes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andes).[^2311] Additionally, a small population may be found in the southwestern corner of the island of [Trinidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad), just north of Venezuela across the [Columbus Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Channel).[^2304] *Pipa pipa* has the largest geographic distribution within its genus.[^2312] The Surinam toad inhabits warm, [acidic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH), murky and slow-moving to still waterways, including streams, backwaters, ponds and seasonal pools after localized [flooding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flood); these rich waters often have a low [pH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PH) due to a high concentration of organic matter and [tannins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tannin).[^2312]

The Surinam toad is so strongly adapted for an aquatic lifestyle that on land it is helpless and scarcely able to move.[^2313]

#### Diet

The species is an [omnivorous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnivore) ambush hunter. Its diet consists mostly of [invertebrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invertebrate), such as worms, insects, crustaceans and small fish.[^2306][^2314][^2315] Field caught *Pipa pipa* have been found with [erythrinid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythrinidae) fish species, other small *Pipa pipa*, [catfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catfish), [arthropods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthropod) and amphibian skin in their stomachs.[^2305] One study found that [Cyclopoida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclopoida) made up 67%, [Diptera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diptera) larvae 7.3%, and [Heteroptera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heteroptera) 6.3% of prey. The skin fragments that were found in their stomach are an indication that these frogs commit cannibalism or eat their own skin which is common among amphibians. Based on these results, *P. pipa* is an [ambush predator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambush_predator) that will opportunistically eat anything that falls into the water or that it may encounter when occasionally foraging on land.[^2316]

#### Feeding behavior

*P. pipa* employs a unique inertial [suction feeding mechanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquatic_feeding_mechanisms). The Surinam toad catches prey by [entraining](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/entrain) large volumes of water for ingestion and by limiting fish escape with its fingers. It uses bidirectional [suction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suction), a process the frog initiates by depressing its hyoid and retracting its clavicle.

The amount of entrained water the frog can ingest is related to its ability to actively increase its body volume. The frog's [buccopharyngeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buccopharyngeal_membrane) cavity (the cavity connecting the mouth and the pharynx) is very distensible and can expand substantially. It uses its entire trunk to rapidly enlarge the cavity, which expands into the lower end of the trunk. Its [visceral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visceral) organs,   the [hyoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyoid_bone) and [larynx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larynx), [heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart), [lungs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lung), [liver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liver), [esophagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esophagus), and [stomach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stomach),   are arranged so as to be capable of moving rearward by up to a third of the length of the body; this gives additional space for expansion of the buccopharyngeal cavity. Laboratory observations estimate *P. pipa* can achieve an increase in trunk volume of 1.5 times the resting volume. The rapid (in c. 12-24 milliseconds) expansion of the buccopharyngeal cavity results in negative pressure; this creates the suction which, in turn, entrains the water containing the prey. The fish are effectively siphoned into the expanded buccopharyngeal cavity, where it remains for a time, located centrally in the trunk of the frog, not the stomach. The siphoned water is released through the frog's partially open mouth, as its internal pressure returns to normal, while its forelimbs remain raised close to the mouth, guarding against the possibility of prey escape.[^2305]

The species may be the only [tetrapod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrapod) [vertebrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebrate) that can enlarge its entire trunk during suction feeding. Additionally, it has been found that *P. pipa* can modulate the timing of most elements of its prey capture process. For instance, it can asymmetrically or asynchronously move its jaw during the capture and manipulation of its prey.[^2305]

The forelimbs are used to "scoop" the prey into the mouth. Prior to capture of its prey, the forelimbs are held in a forward-flexed position so that each hand is positioned in front of the head. During prey capture, the forelimbs are extended and drawn towards the mouth. If the prey item is encountered during this movement, it is grabbed and pushed into the mouth. Otherwise it is sucked into the mouth without any use of the limbs. These frogs have a high degree of dexterity compared to other [pipid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipidae) species.[^2305]

#### Reproduction

The mating period of these frogs is during the fall and winter seasons. These frogs call usually during the morning and mid-afternoon hours.[^2317] Males of this species do not attract females with croaks, instead producing a sharp clicking sound by snapping the [hyoid bone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyoid_bone) in their throats.[^2318] The clicking sound resembles metallic noises. The average rate of these clicks is four clicks per second, consisting of blocks of 10 to 20 seconds per period.[^2317] Thereafter, the male will grab the front legs of the female in [amplexus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplexus), causing the cloaca and the skin of the female to swell.[^2319] The partners rise from the floor while in amplexus and flip through the water in arcs. The couple will swim around in the water until they have to swim to the surface to breathe. Afterwards, they will swim back down to the bottom of the water. There the male will lay on his back, with the female on top of him on her stomach.[^2320] During the amplexus, the female's back is gradually swelled to a puffy condition. The male and female [cloacae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloaca) are brought close together, and many eggs are transferred anteriorly to the female's swollen dorsal [epidermis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidermis).

The eggs, each around 6.5 mm (0.26 in) in diameter, then become implanted into the female's dorsal [epidermis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epidermis). During the first day the eggs on the female's back will sink into the skin and by evening will be set into the back of the female. Two days later, the yolks of most of the eggs are beneath the skin level and only parts of the jelly and outer membranes of the eggs are visible on the backs above. The coverings over the eggs will remain in the wild until the brood emerges.[^2317] The embryos develop through to the [tadpole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadpole) stage inside these pockets but do not emerge as tadpoles, instead remaining in their chambers until complete development to toadlet stage. The young toads grow a tail during their growth, but these will only be temporary because they will need the tail for inhaling oxygen. After 12 to 20 weeks, the young toads will hatch as small toads, looking identical to their parents. It takes a while for them to grow bigger since they are only 25 mm long when they are born. Once they have emerged from their mother's back, the toads begin a largely solitary life. After giving birth to the new toads, the mother slowly sheds the thin layer of skin used for birth and can begin the cycle again.[^2306][^2308]

##### Mating competition

When two males encounter each other during the [mating season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seasonal_breeder), there is a possibility that the two males will fight. The toads nearly press their snout to the chest or throat of the other male. During [the conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_conflict), both males make single clicks to each other, which resembles the sound that they normally use during breeding. If the toads have eye contact, they make a rapid series of these clicks. This process shows no visible movement of the vocal system. After some time, they will return to swimming, but will never lose contact with one another. One toad swims very closely above the other, touching his rival with only the front limbs. The fight between males may be long-lasting. Eventually, one of the males bites the other male and this is supposed to be the end of their encounter, although they do not always give up the fight. It may happen that the male that loses the battle does not give up and disturbs the [breeding pair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breeding_pair) itself, even during reproduction.[^2317]

#### Conservation

Although the species is classified as [Least Concern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Least_Concern) by the [IUCN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN), it is subject to habitat loss and habitat fragmentation caused by agricultural expansions.[^2321] Due to the deforestation and human encroachment on the Amazon rainforest, the species has been found in regions where it would not normally be encountered, such as terrestrial locations. This highlights the importance of preserving the endangered habitats that these frogs live in.[^2312][^2322]

#### Captivity

In the aquarium, the species prefers plants and rocks to hide behind. Low light conditions are required. Because the Surinam toad excretes high amounts of [ammonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammonia), water changes have to be frequent.[^2323]

#### Cultural significance

In a letter to Catherine Clarkson the poet [Samuel Taylor Coleridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Taylor_Coleridge) writes "I envy dear Southey's power of saying one thing at a time in short and close sentences, whereas my thoughts bustle along like a Surinam Toad, with little toads sprouting out of back, side, and belly, vegetating while it crawls".[^2324]

The Surinam toad is commonly cited as an example of a [trypophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trypophobia) trigger.[^2325]

### Lioconcha hieroglyphica

***Lioconcha hieroglyphica*** is a species of saltwater clam, a [marine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_%28ocean%29) [bivalve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bivalve) [mollusc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mollusc) in the family [Veneridae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veneridae), the venus clams.[^2326][^2327][^2328]

#### Description

The shell of *Lioconcha hieroglyphica* reaches a maximum length of about 42 mm. The shape of the shell is trigonal with a truncated posterior. The anterodorsal margin is acutely rounded. The linule is elongated and heart-shaped. It has tan to dark brown rod-like and angular markings, often with the appearance of [cuneiform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuneiform) or [hieroglyphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hieroglyph). The markings may be the result of a diffusion-mediated chemical [cellular automaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cellular_automaton), like *[Conus textile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conus_textile)'*s. The shell is white on the inside.[^2327]

It is sometimes confused with *[Lioconcha castrensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lioconcha_castrensis)*.[^2327]

#### Distribution

This species is found in the waters around [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii), the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines), and the [Marshall Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Islands).[^2326][^2327]

### Trout tickling

**Trout tickling** is the art of rubbing the underbelly of a [trout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trout) with fingers.[^2329] If done properly, the trout will go into a [trance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypnosis) after a minute or so, and can then easily be retrieved and thrown onto the nearest bit of dry land.[^2330]

#### History

Trout tickling has been evidently practiced for many centuries, if not since [time immemorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_immemorial). It is mentioned in Shakespeare's comedy *[Twelfth Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelfth_Night,_or_What_You_Will)*, where it is used as a metaphor for bamboozlement by Olivia's servant Maria, who is about to play a vengeful prank on the pompous steward, [Malvolio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malvolio):

> Close, in the name of jesting! Lie thou there,\
> for here comes the trout that must be caught with tickling.[^2331]

The technique was a common practice used by boys, [poachers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poaching) and working men in times of economic stress, particularly during the 1930s [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression) era.[^2332][^2333] Poachers using the method required no nets, rods or lines or any other incriminating equipment if apprehended by the [police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police) or [gamekeepers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamekeeper).

Thomas Martindale's 1901 book, *Sport, Indeed*, describes the method used on trout in the [River Wear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Wear) in [County Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_Durham):

> The fish are watched working their way up the shallows and rapids. When they come to the shelter of a ledge or a rock it is their nature to slide under it and rest. The poacher sees the edge of a fin or the moving tail, or maybe he sees neither; instinct, however, tells him a fish ought to be there, so he takes the water very slowly and carefully and stands up near the spot. He then kneels on one knee and passes his hand, turned with fingers up, deftly under the rock until it comes in contact with the fish's tail. Then he begins tickling with his forefinger, gradually running his hand along the fish's belly further and further toward the head until it is under the gills. Then comes a quick grasp, a struggle, and the prize is wrenched out of his natural element, stunned with a blow on the head, and landed in the pocket of the poacher.

In [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland) the technique is more often called "guddling" or sometimes "ginniling". The practice is currently illegal under most circumstances in [Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom).[^2334] A related method of catching [catfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catfish) by hand is called [noodling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noodling) in the United States.

#### In history and fiction

Trout tickling has an ancient history. [Aelian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudius_Aelianus), a [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks) writer of about 230 A.D., writes in his *[De Natura Animalium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Natura_Animalium)* (as published in England in 1565): "If men wade into the sea, when the water is low, end stroking the fish nestling in the pools, suddenly lay hands upon and secure them." While in [Francis Beaumont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Beaumont) and [John Fletcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fletcher_%28playwright%29)'s *[Rule a Wife and Have a Wife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_a_Wife_and_Have_a_Wife)*, a [ribald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribald) comedy dating from 1624, Estifania remarks "Here comes another trout that I must tickle, / And tickle daintily".

The technique is also mentioned in several of [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare)'s plays: in *[Twelfth Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelfth_Night)*, the servant Maria refers to the approach of the hated [Malvolio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malvolio), head of Olivia's household, with the words "for here comes the trout that must be caught with tickling" (Act 2, Scene 5). Maria and others are conspiring to trap Malvolio into acting foolishly by forging a love letter from Olivia.

Trout tickling is also mentioned in later works: [Mark Twain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Twain) wrote about catching [catfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catfish) in a similar manner while mentioning that [salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salmon) and certain other species can also be lured and caught in this way. [Arthur Ransome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Ransome)'s novel *[The Picts and the Martyrs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Picts_and_the_Martyrs)* contains a detailed description of the technique by a young boy from the English [Lake District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_District). It is also described as a [poaching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poaching) method in [Roald Dahl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roald_Dahl)'s classic novel *[Danny, the Champion of the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny,_the_Champion_of_the_World)*, in Linda Buckley-Archer's science fiction novel *[Gideon the Cutpurse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gideon_the_Cutpurse)*, in [Robert A. Heinlein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_A._Heinlein)'s fantasy novel *[Glory Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glory_Road)*, and in the video game *[Theme Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theme_Hospital)* as a hobby of many of the staff for hire. [Terry Pratchett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Pratchett)'s 2003 young adult novel *[The Wee Free Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wee_Free_Men)* opens with young Tiffany Aching amusing herself by tickling trout.

An interview conducted by CSV/BBC NI's Brian Morgan, Story of the Virgin Soldier, for the BBC's WW2 Peoples War project, reports how one soldier, Robert McIlroy, impressed his senior commanders by 'tickling trout' out of the river in order for fellow soldiers to eat.[^2335]

In the book *[The White Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tripods)* by John Christopher, one of the party members (Henry) attempts to tickle trout unsuccessfully in an attempt to forage food for the group.

In an episode of [The Waltons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Waltons) ("The Search", S. 4, E.15), Olivia, Jim Bob, and Elizabeth set out to visit a friend but become lost on Walton's Mountain, and while lost Jim Bob catches fish using this method which he had learned from Grandpa.

In an episode of [Auf Wiedersehen, Pet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auf_Wiedersehen,_Pet) ("Another Country", S. 2, E.4), Oz successfully tickles trout before being caught by a gamekeeper.

In an episode of [The Gentlemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gentlemen_%282024_TV_series%29) characters Lady Charlotte 'Charly' Horniman and Geoffrey Seacombe discuss her childhood and how she learned to tickle salmon.
