### My Friend Cayla

**My Friend Cayla** was a line of 18-inch (46 cm) dolls which used [speech recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speech_recognition) technology in conjunction with a smartphone app to recognize a child's speech and perform conversations with users. The doll used the internet to search what the user said, and then responded with data that it found online. My Friend Cayla was created by Bob Delprincipe, inventor of [Cindy Smart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cindy_Smart) and [Tekno the Robotic Puppy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tekno_the_Robotic_Puppy).

The doll generated much controversy due to its recording feature and internet connection, causing concerns that it was collecting information on children and that it could be hacked. This resulted in the doll being banned in [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany), since the German government considers it to be a [surveillance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveillance) device.[^2467]

#### Background

My Friend Cayla was distributed by Vivid in the United Kingdom.[^2468] Genesis was the distributor for users from the United States of America,[^2469][^2470] and the doll entered the US market in August 2015.[^2471]

#### Technology

Cayla functioned by sending microphone inputs to an app on an [iOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS) or [Android](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Android_%28operating_system%29) device via [Bluetooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluetooth). The app then parsed the speech into text and used keywords from the speech that it heard to search the Internet for a response.[^2472]

Cayla also had a "personality", with a database containing details of her family, pets, and interests, such as ballet.[^2473] The doll could be used by children to ask for help with homework,[^2474] and had a free Spanish language version.[^2471]

The creator of the doll, Bob Delprincipe, says "She's not a search engine, she's a seven-year-old girl. There are some things she just doesn't know." He argued that though there had been 'intelligent' toys before, there had never been an Internet-connected doll.[^2475]

#### Awards

The doll was named 2014 Innovative Toy of the Year by the London Toy Industry Association, and was a top 10 toy for all key European retailers that holiday season.[^2471] In 2015 My Friend Cayla won Most Wanted Dolls of 2015 from TTPM (Toys, Tots, Pets & More).[^2476]

#### Controversy

##### Hacking

Ken Munro of security firm Pen Test Partners claimed he hacked the doll, and demonstrated the hack in the [BBC World News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_World_News) Tech Tent program.[^2477][^2478] Tim Medin from Counter Hack also hacked the doll by simply using Bluetooth to use it as a remote speaker and microphone, which could be used to communicate with children.[^2479] Additionally, the official website for the doll claimed that it was incapable of using inappropriate language, as its software had a pre-set list of blocked words.[^2480] However, hackers were able to get it to say swears from the blocked list.[^2481]

Peter Magalhaes, general manager of Genesis, described the doll as "the subject of a tech prank."[^2482] The creator of the doll, Bob Delprincipe, said, "She's not a search engine, she's a seven-year-old girl. There are some things she just doesn't know."[^2475] This statement was criticized as an attempt to [anthropomorphize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropomorphism) the doll.[^2483]

##### Surveillance threat

Concerns were raised that Cayla could harvest personal data of children. The doll could allegedly learn family routines and remember when children were likely to be unattended.[^2484] It could also ask children to give away personal information, such as their parents' names and where they go to school.[^2485]

In February 2017 the German [Federal Network Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Network_Agency) notified parents that they were obliged to "destroy" any Cayla in their possession as it constitutes a concealed espionage device violating the German Telecommunications Act.[^2467][^2486] Keeping the doll can result in a large fine or two years in prison.[^2487] The agency also considers the Bluetooth device as insecure, allowing connections to Cayla's speaker and microphone within a 10 m (33 ft) radius.[^2467] One report claimed it had hacked the profiles of 508,000 children and 390,000 parents.[^2488]

The doll has also been criticised by the [Norwegian Consumer Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Consumer_Council) for allowing the use of the collected data from the child's speech for targeted advertisements and other commercial purposes and its sharing with third parties, as well as for hidden advertisements through the doll's positive statements about certain products and services.[^2489] For example, Cayla would often praise [Disney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company) movies, such as the then-recent [*Frozen*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frozen_%282013_film%29), and talk about visiting [Epcot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epcot) and [Disneyland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disneyland);[^2483] the provider of the app she ran on had a commercial partnership with Disney.[^2490][^2470]

In the United States, the [Electronic Privacy Information Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Privacy_Information_Center) filed a complaint about Cayla to the [Federal Trade Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Trade_Commission), believing the doll could violate the [Children's Online Privacy Protection Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children's_Online_Privacy_Protection_Act).[^2491] Senators [Mark Warner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Warner)[^2492] and [Edward J. Markey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Markey)[^2493] supported such investigations into the doll. The FTC considered an investigation,[^2494] but when Senator Warner reached out to the FTC via letter, they could not confirm or deny whether Genesis Toys had been investigated.[^2495] The controversy caused the toys to be removed from several American retailers, such as [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation) and [Toys "R" Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toys_%22R%22_Us), though Amazon continued to sell it for some time.[^2496]

#### Aftermath

The resulting controversy led to the doll's inclusion in the [Museum of Failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Failure) in [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden), where similar failed products and services which were either commercial failures or are controversial in their own right are on display.[^2497] The [Spy Museum Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spy_Museum_Berlin) also has a Cayla doll on display, the first toy in its collection of various espionage and surveillance devices. The doll was donated by a German mother who found the doll in her daughter's room after hearing about a government order to destroy the dolls following a ban on its sale and possession.[^2498][^2499]

Genesis, the toy's American manufacturer, seemingly went out of business following the controversy. The company's website has not been updated in years and no longer sells the doll.[^2500]

The controversy surrounding My Friend Cayla, as well as other [internet of things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_of_things) toys such as Hello [Barbie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbie), led to increased discussion over [European Union's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union) laws concerning advertising to children.[^2483] In the 2020s, with advent and popularity of toys powered by [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence), My Friend Cayla is sometimes brought up in discussions and criticisms of such "smart" toys.[^2501][^2502]

### Violence and Lego

[Lego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego) toys did not feature weapons or violence from their inception in 1949 until 1978. Subsequently, [The Lego Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lego_Group), the company that manufactures Legos, has stated that they maintain a goal of not producing products that promote violence in realistic daily-life scenarios, but allow for fantasy or imaginary violence. Academic research has shown that violence and weaponry has increased in Lego sets since the introduction of weapons in 1978, potentially to compete with the popularity of [action-figure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_figure) toys and [video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game).

#### Weaponry in Lego

The presence of Lego guns in the history of the company can be traced back to the immediate post-war years following [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II). Lego was still making wooden toys until 1947, when the company purchased a plastic injection moulding machine. From 1945 onwards, Lego began producing a wooden version of a toy pistol. The company then applied for a patent of the model in 1946. A plastic version of a rapid-firing pistol began to be manufactured in 1949.[^2503]

When Lego was first introduced in the United States through a deal with [Samsonite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samsonite) in 1962, the company's advertising rejected military themes, due to the increasing anxiety in the population over the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War). Lego products did not include dull green colours, unless used in trees and green base plates, in order to make it more difficult for children to build military vehicles. Lego advertising focused instead on creativity and free-thinking. A promotional Lego System Assortment 1968 UK catalogue stated, "A good toy is one which gives free reign \[sic\] to a child's natural creativity and does what he wants it to do."[^2504]

In 1978, Lego weapons were introduced into the [Lego Castle theme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego_Castle), which included a sword, a halberd and a lance.[^2505] Other Lego themes were released in later years which included weapon elements. In 1989, the [Lego Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego_Pirates) theme introduced handguns and cannons, and this trend continued with [Bionicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bionicle) sets in 2005 and 2006.

The increased presence of weaponry in Lego sets can be partly attributed to the popularity of movie-themed sets, such as [Lego *Star Wars*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lego_Star_Wars).[^2505] The *[Star Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Wars)* [films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Star_Wars_films) featured numerous weapons and parents raised concerns about its level of violence. When Lego won the *Star Wars* franchise and began to produce Lego *Star Wars* sets in 1999, parents complained that the company was abandoning its pacifist ideals. However, the [lightsabers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightsaber) and [blasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blaster_%28Star_Wars%29) produced in the sets were all fantasy weapons and clearly distinct from real weapons.[^2504]

The Lego Group has maintained its long-standing policy of avoiding the manufacture of realistic modern weaponry. In a 2010 Lego report, the company stated, "The basic aim is to avoid realistic weapons and military equipment that children may recognize from hot spots around the world and to refrain from showing violent or frightening situations when communicating about LEGO products. At the same time, the purpose is for the LEGO brand not to be associated with issues that glorify conflicts and unethical or harmful behavior".[^2505]

#### Academic research

In May 2016, researchers at the [University of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Canterbury) published a report in the scientific journal [PLOS One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PLOS_One),[^2506] which concluded that Lego had become "significantly more violent" after the research found that the violence of products highlighted in Lego catalogues had increased by 19 per cent every year from 1978 to 2014. The research also stated that almost 30 per cent of Lego sets included at least one weapon brick.[^2507] The researchers used the [Bricklink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bricklink) website, which catalogues every part used in every Lego set since 1949 and also examined 1,500 images from Lego catalogues since 1979. On balance, the report also noted, "It is unlikely that the LEGO company is the only toy manufacturer whose products have become increasingly violent; for instance, Oppel has already provided initial evidence that [Playmobil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playmobil) has followed a similar trajectory... The question remains, though, why violence has increased so much in general."[^2508][^2506] The research did not assess whether the increase had any influence on violent behaviour in children.[^2509]

Gary Cross, a professor of history at [Pennsylvania State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_State_University) remarked that Lego's expansion of weaponry in its products was the result of direct competition following a surge in the popularity of [action-figure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_figure) toys in the 1980s and also from video game companies, such as [Nintendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo) and [Sega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega). Lego's toy weapons may have simply been a symptom of the general rise of violence in pop-culture.[^2510]

After the publication of the University of Canterbury study, [The Lego Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lego_Group) stated that it makes a clear distinction between conflict and violence. Amanda Santorum, a brand manager at The Lego Group said, "we do not make products that promote or encourage violence. Weapon-like elements in a Lego set are part of a fantasy/imaginary setting, and not a realistic daily-life scenario."[^2510]

#### Custom-built weapons

Various custom builders of Lego, entrepreneurs and small companies have attempted to fill the gaps in the company's inventory of Lego weapons, often ignoring the company's ethos regarding Lego guns and modern military equipment. A British teenager named Jack Streat built a series of working Lego guns, including a replica [Lee-Enfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee%E2%80%93Enfield) bolt-action rifle.[^2511] He also produced a book titled, *LEGO Heavy Weapons*.[^2512] An [adult fan of Lego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Fan_of_Lego) (AFOL) named Will Chapman designed and cast his own non-functional toy guns using constructed aluminium moulds from a [CNC mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNC_milling) and [injection-molded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injection_molding) plastic from melted-down Lego bricks.[^2513]

### Toilet-related injuries and deaths

There have been many **toilet-related injuries and deaths** throughout history and in [urban legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_legend).

#### Accidental injuries

Infants and toddlers have fallen headfirst into toilet bowls and drowned. Safety devices exist to help prevent such accidents. It is highly unlikely for adults or teenagers to drown in toilets due to their larger body size.[^2514][^2515] Injuries to adults include bruised buttocks and tail bones, as well as dislocated hips that have resulted from unexpectedly sitting on the toilet bowl rim because the seat is up or loose. Injuries can also be caused by pinching due to splits in plastic seats and/or by splinters from wooden seats, or if the toilet itself collapses or shatters under the user's weight. Older high-tank cast-iron cisterns have been known to detach from the wall when the chain is pulled to flush, causing injuries to the user.[^2516] The 2000 [Ig Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ig_Nobel_Prize) in Public Health was awarded to three physicians from the [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow) [Western Infirmary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Infirmary) for a 1993 case report on wounds sustained to the [buttocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buttocks) due to collapsing toilets.[^2517] Furthermore, injuries are frequently sustained by people who stand on toilets to reach a height, then slip and fall. There are also instances of people slipping on a wet bathroom floor or from a bath and concussing themselves on the fixture.

Toilet-related injuries are surprisingly common, with some estimates ranging as high as 40,000 in the US every year.[^2518] In the past, this number would have been much higher, due to the material from which toilet paper was made. This was shown in a 1935 Northern Tissue advertisement, which depicted splinter-free toilet paper.[^2519] In 2012, 2.3 million toilets in the United States, and about 9,400 in Canada, were recalled due to faulty pressure-assist flush mechanisms which put users at risk of the fixture exploding.[^2520]

#### Injuries caused by animals

Animals also cause injuries. Some [black widow spiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latrodectus) prefer to spin their webs below the toilet seat due to the presence of insects that can inhabit and surround it. Therefore, several people have been bitten while using a toilet, particularly [outhouse toilets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outhouse). Although there is immediate pain at the bite site, these bites are rarely fatal.[^2521] The danger of spiders living beneath toilet seats is the subject of [Slim Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slim_Newton)'s comic 1972 country song "[The Redback on the Toilet Seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Redback_on_the_Toilet_Seat)".

It has been reported that in some cases [rats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rat) crawl up through toilet sewer pipes and emerge in the toilet bowl, so that toilet users may be at risk of having a rat bite their buttocks.[^2522] Many rat exterminators do not believe this, as pipes, at generally six inches (15 centimeters) wide, are too large for rats to climb and are also very slippery. Reports by janitors are always on the top floor, and could involve the rats on the roof, entering the soil pipe through the roof vent, lowering themselves into the pipe, and then into the toilet.[^2523]

In May 2016, an 11-foot snake, a [reticulated python](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reticulated_python), emerged from a [squat toilet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squat_toilet) and bit the man using it on his [penis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_penis) at his home in [Chachoengsao Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chachoengsao_Province), [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand). Both the victim and the python survived.[^2524][^2525]

#### Self-induced injury

Some instances of toilet-related deaths are attributed to the drop in blood pressure due to the [parasympathetic nervous system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasympathetic_nervous_system) during bowel movements. Existing circulatory issues may magnify this effect. It is further possible that people succumb on the toilet to chronic constipation, because the [Valsalva maneuver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valsalva_maneuver) is often dangerously used to aid in the expulsion of feces from the rectum during a bowel movement. According to Sharon Mantik Lewis, Margaret McLean Heitkemper, and Shannon Ruff Dirksen, the "Valsalva maneuver occurs during straining to pass a hardened stool. If defecation is suppressed over long periods, problems can occur, such as constipation or stool impaction. The Valsalva maneuver can facilitate defecation. This maneuver involves contraction of the chest muscles on a closed glottis with simultaneous contraction of the abdominal muscles."[^2526] This means that people can die while "straining at stool." In chapter 8 of their *Abdominal Emergencies*, David Cline and Latha Stead wrote that "autopsy studies continue to reveal missed bowel obstruction as an unexpected cause of death".[^2527]

A 2001 *[Sopranos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sopranos)* episode "[He is Risen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He_Is_Risen_%28The_Sopranos%29)" shows a fictional depiction of the risk, when the character [Gigi Cestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigi_Cestone) has a heart attack on the toilet of his social club while straining to defecate.[^2528]

#### Exploding toilets

In the [Victorian era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victorian_era), there was a perceived risk of toilets exploding. These scenarios typically include a flammable substance (either accidentally or deliberately) being introduced into the toilet water, and a lit match or cigarette igniting and exploding the toilet.[^2529] In 2014, Sloan's Flushmate pressure-assisted flushing system, which uses compressed air to force waste down the drain, was recalled after the company received reports of the air tank failing under pressure and shattering the porcelain.[^2530]

#### Historical deaths

- In 1945, the [German submarine *U-1206*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_submarine_U-1206) was sunk after a toilet accident resulted in seawater flooding into the hull, which created [chlorine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorine) gas upon contact with a battery and forced the submarine to resurface. At the surface, the sub was discovered and attacked by Allied forces, causing the sub's captain to scuttle the sub so Allied forces could not capture it. This case may not have been due to a malfunction, but rather the possibility that the pressurized flushing system in the U-boats, which was extremely complex and required a training course to operate, may not have been operated properly.[^2531]

- [Godfrey the Hunchback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godfrey_the_Hunchback), Duke of Lower Lorraine (an area roughly coinciding with the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands) and [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium)), was murdered in 1076 when staying in the Dutch city of [Vlaardingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vlaardingen). Supposedly, the assassin ensured which of the latrines, built and drained on the outer side of the wall according to medieval building style, belonged to the duke's sleeping room, and took a position underneath. Some sources claim that a sword was used for the assassination; others mention a sharp iron weapon, which could have been a sword, a spear, or a dagger. However, a spear seems to be the most practical choice. After being stabbed in the bottom, it took him several days to die from internal bleeding. The assassination was ordered by [Dirk V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirk_V), Count of [Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holland), and his ally [Robrecht the Frisian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_I,_Count_of_Flanders), Count of [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders).[^2532]
- The [Erfurt latrine disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erfurt_latrine_disaster) of 1184 caused the death of at least 60 people, most of them being nobles.
- [George II of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_II_of_Great_Britain) died on the toilet on October 25, 1760, from an [aortic dissection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aortic_dissection). According to [Horace Walpole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_Walpole)'s memoirs, King George "rose as usual at six, and drank his chocolate; for all his actions were invariably methodic. A quarter after seven he went into a little closet. His German *[valet de chambre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valet_de_chambre)* in waiting heard a noise, and running in, found the King dead on the floor." In falling, he had cut his face.[^2533]
- [Ioan P. Culianu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ioan_P._Culianu) was shot dead while on the toilet in the third-floor men's room of Swift Hall on the campus of the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago) on 21 May 1991, in a possibly politically motivated assassination. His killer has never been caught.[^2534]
- The [Abbasid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate) vizier [Al-Fadl ibn Sahl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Fadl_ibn_Sahl) was found dead mysteriously in a bathroom in [Sarakhs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarakhs) in [Northern Khorasan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarakhs_County). According to some rumors, the [Abbasid caliph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbasid_Caliphate) [al-Ma'mun ibn Harun ar-Rashid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Ma'mun) had ordered his assassination.[^2535]
- [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley) died when using the toilet.[^2536] "Most sources indicate that Elvis was likely sitting in the toilet area, partially nude, and reading when he collapsed."[^2537] According to Dylan Jones, "Elvis Presley died aged 42 on August 16th, 1977, in the bathroom of the star's own Graceland mansion in Memphis. Sitting on the toilet, he had toppled like a toy soldier and collapsed onto the floor, where he lay in a pool of his own vomit. His light blue pajamas were around his ankles."[^2538] In similar terms, Elvis biographer Joel Williamson writes, "For some reason, perhaps involving a reaction to the codeine and attempts to move his bowels, he experienced pain and fright while sitting on the toilet. Alarmed, he stood up, dropped the book he was reading, stumbled forward, and fell face down in the fetal position. He struggled weakly and drooled on the rug. Unable to breathe, he died."[^2539] This led to the common saying, "The King died on the throne".[^2540]

##### Possible occurrences

- [Duke Jing of Jin (Ju)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_Jing_of_Jin_%28Ju%29), ruler of the [State of Jin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jin_%28Chinese_state%29) during the [Spring and Autumn period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_and_Autumn_period) of ancient China, died after falling into a toilet pit in summer 581 BC.[^2541]
- [Edmund II of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_II_of_England) died of [natural causes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_causes) on November 30, 1016, though some report that he was stabbed in the bowels while attending the [outhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outhouse).[^2542]
- [Uesugi Kenshin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uesugi_Kenshin), a [warlord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warlord) in Japan, died on April 19, 1578, with some reports stating that he was [assassinated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination) on the toilet.[^2543]
- In 1928, [Ernest Hemingway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Hemingway) suffered a severe head injury in his Paris bathroom when he pulled a [skylight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skylight) down on his head thinking he was pulling on a toilet chain. This left him with a prominent forehead scar, which he carried for the rest of his life.[^2544]
- [Air Canada Flight 797](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Canada_Flight_797) was destroyed on June 2, 1983, with 23 fatalities after an in-flight fire began in or around the rear [lavatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_lavatory). Investigators were unable to determine the cause or exact point of origin for the fire.[^2545]
- Michael Anderson Godwin, a convicted murderer in South Carolina who had his sentence reduced from death by the [electric chair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_chair), sat on the metal toilet in his cell while fixing his television. When he bit one of the wires, the resultant electric shock killed him. Another convicted murderer, Laurence Baker in Pittsburgh, was electrocuted while listening to the television on homemade earphones while sitting on a metal toilet.[^2546]
- A collision between a disabled [Cessna 182](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cessna_182) and a row of [portable toilets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portable_toilet) on May 2, 2009, at Thun Field (south-east of [Tacoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacoma,_Washington)), despite an engine failure at 150 feet (46 m) altitude, ended without fatalities; the toilets "kind of cushioned things" for the 67-year-old pilot.[^2547]
- [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom) businessman and [Conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_%28UK%29) politician [Christopher Shale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Shale) was found dead in a [portable toilet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portable_toilet) at the [Glastonbury Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glastonbury_Festival) on June 26, 2011. It is suspected he died of a heart attack.[^2548]
- Aboard ships, the [head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_%28watercraft%29) (ship's toilet) and fittings associated with it are cited as one of the most common reasons for the sinking of tens of thousands of boats of all types and sizes.[^2549] Heads typically have through-hull [fittings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piping_and_plumbing_fitting) located below the water line to draw flush water and eliminate waste. Boats sink when fittings fail or the toilet back [siphons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siphon).[^2550]

#### Urban legends

[Urban legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_legend) have been reported regarding the dangers of using a toilet in a variety of situations. Several of them are questionable. These include some cases of the presence of venomous [spiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider)[^2551] but do not include the Australian redback spider, which has a reputation for hiding under toilet seats.[^2552] These recent fears have emerged from a series of hoax emails originating in the Blush Spider hoax, which began circulating the internet in 1999.[^2553] Spiders have also been reported to live under seats of airplanes. However, the cleaning chemicals used in the toilets would kill the spiders.[^2554]

In large cities like New York City, sewer rats often hold a mythical status due to their size and ferocity, resulting in tales of the rodents crawling up sewer pipes to attack an unwitting occupant. Of late, stories about [terrorists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorist) booby trapping the seat to [castrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castration) their targets have begun appearing.[^2555] Another myth is the risk of being sucked into an [aircraft lavatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_lavatory) as a result of vacuum pressure during a flight.[^2556]

### Tin foil hat

A **tin foil hat** is a [hat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hat) made from one or more sheets of [tin foil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin_foil) or [aluminium foil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_foil), or a piece of conventional headgear lined with foil, often worn in the belief or hope that it shields the [brain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_brain) from threats such as [electromagnetic fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_field), [mind control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brainwashing), and [mind reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telepathy). The notion of wearing homemade headgear for such protection has become a popular stereotype and byword for [paranoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranoia), [persecutory delusions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecutory_delusions), and belief in [pseudoscience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoscience) and [conspiracy theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conspiracy_theories).

"Tin foil" is a common [misnomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misnomer) for [aluminium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium) foil in English-speaking countries; packaging metal foil was formerly made out of [tin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin) before it was replaced with aluminium.[^2557]

#### Origin

A common delusion in schizophrenia is that others are influencing the sufferer's thoughts. [James Tilly Matthews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Tilly_Matthews) in 1797 complained of a machine he called an "Air Loom" influencing him, becoming one of the first documented cases. The common delusion was characterized in depth in the 1918 work '[On the Origin of the "Influencing Machine" in Schizophrenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Origin_of_the_%22Influencing_Machine%22_in_Schizophrenia)'. Some people - modernly called "Tin Foil Hatters" - have a belief that such hats prevent [mind control by governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mind_control_by_governments), spies, mobsters, corporations, extraterrestrial, or paranormal beings that employ [ESP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrasensory_perception) or the [microwave auditory effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microwave_auditory_effect). People in many countries who believe they are "[targeted individuals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_harassment)", subject to government, corporate, or criminal spying or harassment, have developed websites, conference calls, and support meetings to discuss their concerns, including the idea of protective headgear.[^2558]

An early allusion to an "insulative electrical contrivance encircling the head during thought" occurs in the unusual 1909 [non-fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fiction) publication *Atomic Consciousness*[^2559] by self-proclaimed "seer" John Palfrey (aka "James Bathurst") who believed such headgear was not effective for his "retention of thoughts and ideas" against a supposed "telepathic impactive impingement".[^2560] *Vice Magazine* writes that the tin foil hat in popular culture "can be traced back in a very weird and prescient short story written in 1927 by [Julian Huxley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Huxley)"[^2561] titled "[The Tissue-Culture King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tissue-Culture_King)," wherein the main character uses a metal hat to prevent being mind controlled by the villain scientist.[^2562][^2563] Over time the term *tin foil hat* has become associated with [paranoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paranoia) and [conspiracy theories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conspiracy_theory).[^2564]

#### Scientific analysis

[Effects of strong electromagnetic radiation on health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_radiation_and_health) have been documented for quite some time.[^2565][^2566] The efficiency of a metal enclosure in blocking electromagnetic radiation depends on the thickness of the foil, as dictated by the "[skin depth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skin_effect)" of the conductor for a particular wave frequency range of the radiation. For half-millimetre-thick aluminum foil, radiation above about 20 kHz (i.e., including both [AM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AM_band) and [FM bands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FM_band)) would be partially blocked, although aluminum foil is not sold in this thickness, so numerous layers of foil would be required to achieve this effect.[^2567]

[Allan H. Frey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_H._Frey) discovered in 1962 that the [microwave auditory effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microwave_auditory_effect) (i.e., the sounds induced by the reception of radio-frequency electromagnetic signals, heard as clicks and buzzes) can be blocked by a patch of [wire mesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wire_mesh) (rather than foil) placed above the [temporal lobe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temporal_lobe).[^2568][^2569] A [tongue-in-cheek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongue-in-cheek) experimental study by a group of MIT students in 2005 found that tin foil hats do shield their wearers from radio waves over most of the tested spectrum, but amplified certain frequencies, around 2.6 GHz and 1.2 GHz.[^2570][^2571]

#### In popular culture

Fans of the band [Devo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devo) was associated with tin foil hats, with the band sporting satirical "[Energy dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_dome)" hats they called [Orgone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orgone) collectors.[^2572]

In 1982, a police dispatcher shared a tale of recommending a tin foil hat to a caller who complained of invisible death rays.[^2573] That same year, the image of the paranoiac in protective tin foil hat was committed to film; in the resultant 1983 movie, titled *[Lovesick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovesick_%281983_film%29)*, Dudley Moore similarly plays a psychiatrist who, in one scene, wins the trust of a paranoid patient by providing him with tin foil headpiece as a protection against "sinster rays" that are "scrambling his brain".[^2574] Moore's psychiatrist character explains "Mr. Zuckerman ([David Strathairn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Strathairn)) feels that there are these sinister rays and voices beaming into his head from the top of the World Trade Center and scrambling his brains, with a result that he has been unable to secure other employment."[^2575]

Another news story told of tin foil used to "block out microwaves"[^2576], while a story on crack cocaine told of a paranoid user who wore a hat to protect from rays.[^2577][^2578]

In "Future Boy", a [1991 episode of *Quantum Leap*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantum_Leap_season_3), the hero must prevent the long-term psychiatric hospitalization of an eccentric ([Richard Herd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Herd)) who wears a foil hat in the shape of a [pyramid that "generates positive energy"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyramid_power). In 1999, discussion of [black helicopters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_helicopters) was dismissed with an allusion to tin foil hats,[^2579] while others began to speak of "lunatics" in tin-foil hats[^2580] or "sleeping under a railway bridge to keep the alien signals out of my brain".[^2581]

Tin foil hats have appeared in such films as *[Signs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signs_%282002_film%29)* (2002),[^2582] *Noroi: The Curse* (2005),[^2583] and *Futurama: Into the Wild Green Yonder* (2009).[^2584] The 2019 [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO) television series *[Watchmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchmen_%28TV_series%29)* features the character Wade Tillman/Looking Glass, a police officer who wears a mask made of reflective foil, and while off-duty, a cap lined in foil to protect his mind from alien psychic attacks.[^2585]

American comedy musician ["Weird Al" Yankovic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%22Weird_Al%22_Yankovic) referenced the concept in his 2014 song "[Foil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foil_%28song%29)," a parody of the song "[Royals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royals_%28song%29)" by [Lorde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorde). Yankovic begins the parody by discussing the merit of the use of aluminum foil for its uses for food preservation, before abruptly segueing into a discussion about various conspiracy theories and the necessity of protection using a tin foil hat.[^2586]

Several teachers in [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia)'s [Voronezh Oblast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voronezh_Oblast) reportedly posed in pictures with tin foil hats in 2024, due a prank by a Belarusian prankster Vladislav Bokhan, who posed as an official from [United Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Russia). He sent an "order" to local schools asking teachers to hold a "Helmet of the Fatherland" workshop, which contained instructions for making tin foil hats as a "patriotic campaign" and to "defend themselves from the irradiation from NATO satellites". The local branch of the Russian [Ministry of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Education_%28Russia%29) commended the teachers for demonstrating "patriotic spirit, strong dedication, and a creative approach to any task", despite it being a prank.[^2587][^2588]

### Cleckheaton Central railway station

**Cleckheaton Central railway station** was a railway station serving the [West Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Yorkshire) town of [Cleckheaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleckheaton), [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England), until it was closed in the [Beeching era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beeching_axe), which saw the closure of many minor lines and stations around the United Kingdom through the 1960s. It has the distinction of being the only British railway station to have been stolen.[^2589] It is one of two disused stations in Cleckheaton, the other being [Cleckheaton Spen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleckheaton_Spen_railway_station).

#### History

The station was originally constructed by the [Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire_and_Yorkshire_Railway), which was absorbed by the [LNWR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_and_North_Western_Railway) in 1922 and subsequently the [LMS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Midland_and_Scottish_Railway) in 1923 at [grouping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railways_Act_1921) and finally to [British Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail) on nationalisation. It served traffic from [Heckmondwike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heckmondwike), [Low Moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Moor_railway_station) (near [Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradford)) and [Mirfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirfield). The Mirfield line opened in 1848 and through to Low Moor in 1849.[^2590] The last passenger train working was the service from [Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradford) on 12 June 1965 arriving at Cleckheaton at 11:21 p.m.; the station closed to freight traffic some four years later.

In 1998, the remains of the station's railway bed were converted into part of the [Spen Valley Greenway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spen_Valley_Greenway), a greenway for people on horses, foot or bicycle.[^2591]

The land that the station once stood is now occupied by a series of garages, and the [car park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_park) of the local Tesco Superstore. As of July 2025, the site remains unmarked, with no mention of the station at its original location.

\

#### Theft case

The passenger station buildings were demolished by British Rail in February 1968 - but the stone-built island platform remained in situ for a few years more.

In 1972 a [Dewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewsbury) man appeared at [Wakefield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wakefield) [Crown Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Court) accused of stealing stone, timber, metal, track, chairs and even the [buffer stops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffer_stop) from the site; in the words of the prosecution counsel "what the case really comes to is that this man last August in effect stole Cleckheaton station".[^2589][^2592][^2593] In August 1971 [British Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail) had made a contract with another contractor who would clear the site and had the permission to sell and retain the proceeds from disposal of all materials and any scrap. However, on arrival, the firm discovered that the station and most of the material had already gone. It transpired that the defendant had been contracted by another company to clear the site. After he had been given an advanced sum to hire plant equipment, he had spent three weeks clearing the site. Subsequent efforts to trace the second firm failed. The court found the man not guilty deciding that he had been duped and left significantly out of pocket. The case is cited as an example of how the [Theft Act 1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theft_Act_1968) can be extended to cover goods forming part of a property.[^2594]

### Leata

The **Leata** was an [automobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automobile) manufactured by Stinebaugh Manufacturing Inc, founded by Donald E. Stinebaugh (1916-1992) with his son Leonard D. "Sonny" Stinebaugh (1946-2001) in [Post Falls, Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_Falls,_Idaho).

The first model produced in 1975 was a boxy [2-door sedan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2-door_sedan) powered by a [4-cylinder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4-cylinder) [Continental engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continental_engine), producing 50 [bhp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brake_horsepower) and giving the car a top speed of 112 kilometres per hour (70 mph), as well as [fuel economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuel_economy_in_automobiles) of 39-55 [miles per gallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miles_per_gallon).[^2595] The car sold for \$2895, and Stinebaugh claimed to have manufactured 23 of the cars & 4 flat bed truck by the end of March 1975. The company employed 15 workers, and Stinebaugh claimed that he was looking to produce between 1,000 and 1,500 cars a year.[^2595]

In 1977, a more modern-looking vehicle was launched, called the Cabalero. Stinebaugh named the car after his wife Hilda (Erickson) Stinebaugh, giving the car her nickname, Leata, a misunderstanding of *[litt](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/litt#Norwegian_Bokm%C3%A5l),* Norwegian for "little."

The Cabalero was powered by a 4-cylinder [General Motors LY-5 engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Motors_LS-based_small-block_engine),[^2595] and featured [power windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_windows), [power seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_seat) and [cruise control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruise_control), as well as baroque styling with custom fibreglass body panels, round headlights in square bezels, a rectangular "classic" grille, and heavily styled mudguards; Two models were made - a pickup or hatchback.[^2596]

Just 97 Leatas were made before the company closed down in late 1977.[^2597]

### Reduced-gravity aircraft

A **reduced-gravity aircraft** is a type of [fixed-wing aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed-wing_aircraft) that provides brief near-weightless environments for training [astronauts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut), conducting research, and making gravity-free movie shots.

Versions of such airplanes were operated by the [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA) Reduced Gravity Research Program,[^2598] and one is currently operated by the Human Spaceflight and Robotic Exploration Programmes of the European Space Agency. The unofficial nickname "**vomit comet**" became popular among those who experienced their operation.[^2599]

#### History

Parabolic flight as a way of simulating weightlessness was first proposed by the German aerospace engineer Fritz Haber and his brother, physicist [Heinz Haber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinz_Haber) in 1950.[^2600] Both had been brought to the US after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II) as part of [Operation Paperclip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Paperclip).[^2601] As well, [Shih-Chun Wang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shih-Chun_Wang) studied nausea in astronauts for [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA), which helped lead to the creation of the vomit comet.[^2602]

Parabolic flights are sometimes used to examine the effects of weightlessness on a living organism. While humans are by far the most common passengers, animals have occasionally been involved in experiments, including a notable experiment on how weightlessness affected a [domestic cat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_cat)'s [righting reflex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_righting_reflex)[^2603] and a [pigeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeon)'s attempts to navigate in a weightless state.[^2604]

#### Operating principles

The aircraft gives its occupants the sensation of weightlessness by following a [parabolic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parabola) flight path, which is the path that objects naturally follow while in [free fall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_fall).[^2605] The aircraft is used in this way to demonstrate to astronauts what it is like to [orbit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbit) the Earth. During this time the aircraft does not need to exert any [ground reaction force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ground_reaction_force) on its contents to keep them stationary relative to the aircraft, causing the sensation of weightlessness.

Initially, the aircraft climbs with a pitch angle of about 45 degrees. The sensation of weightlessness is achieved by reducing thrust and lowering the nose to maintain a neutral, or "zero lift", configuration such that the aircraft follows the same path that an object in free fall, with no air resistance, would follow. Engine thrust is used to exactly compensate for drag. Weightlessness begins at the point when the plane starts to follow this parabolic path, which is while the plane is ascending. It lasts through the rest of the ascent, and into the descent phase, until the aircraft must pull up, usually when it reaches a downward pitch angle of around 30 degrees. The aircraft then pulls back up to repeat the maneuver. During this pull-up, the forces felt are roughly twice that of gravity. This cycle can be repeated.[^2606]

This aircraft is used to train astronauts in zero-g maneuvers, giving them about 25 seconds of weightlessness out of 65 seconds of flight in each [parabola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parabola). During such training, the airplane typically flies about 40-60 parabolic manoeuvres. In about two thirds of the passengers, these flights produce [nausea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nausea) due to [airsickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airsickness),[^2607][^2608] giving the plane its nickname "vomit comet".

#### Operators

##### Canada

The [Canadian Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Space_Agency) and the [National Research Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Research_Council_%28Canada%29) have a [Falcon 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_20) used for microgravity research.[^2609] The small plane is normally not used for people to float freely and experience weightlessness; however, comedian [Rick Mercer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Mercer) did so for a segment of his [show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Mercer_Report).[^2610]

##### Ecuador

The first zero G plane to enter service in Latin America is a [T-39 Sabreliner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_Sabreliner) nicknamed *CONDOR*, operated for the [Ecuadorian Civilian Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuadorian_Civilian_Space_Agency) and the [Ecuadorian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecuadorian_Air_Force) since May 2008.[^2611] On June 19, 2008, this plane carried a seven-year-old boy, setting the Guinness world record for the youngest person to fly in microgravity.[^2612]

##### Europe

Since 1984, [ESA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Space_Agency) and the [CNES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNES) have flown reduced-gravity missions in a variety of aircraft, including NASA's KC-135, a [Caravelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sud_Aviation_Caravelle), an [Ilyushin Il-76MDK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilyushin_Il-76MDK), and an [Airbus A300](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_A300) known as the *Zero-G*. In 2014 the A300 was phased out in favor of a more modern [Airbus A310](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airbus_A310), also named *Zero-G*.[^2613] It is based at [Bordeaux-Mérignac airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A%C3%A9roport_de_Bordeaux_M%C3%A9rignac) in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France), operated by Novespace, and has also been flown from [Paris Le Bourget airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris%E2%80%93Le_Bourget_Airport) and [Dübendorf Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%BCbendorf_Air_Base) in Switzerland.[^2614] Since 1997 CNES subsidiary Novespace has handled the management of these flights.[^2615]

This A310 Zero G aircraft is used also to realize commercial flights for public passengers in partnership between operator Novespace and the Avico company, under Air Zero G brand.[^2616] The aircraft has also been used for cinema purposes, with [Tom Cruise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Cruise) and [Annabelle Wallis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annabelle_Wallis) filming for *[The Mummy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mummy_%282017_film%29)* in 2017.[^2617]

##### Russia

In Russia, commercial flights are offered on the [Ilyushin Il-76MDK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilyushin_Il-76MDK) jet; several U.S. companies book flights on these jets.[^2618]

The [Indian Air force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Air_Force) also used them to train the first batch of Indian Astronauts for the [Gaganyaan Project](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Human_Spaceflight_Programme) of [ISRO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISRO).[^2619]

##### United States

###### NASA

NASA flew zero gravity flights on various aircraft for many years. In 1959 [Project Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury) astronauts trained in a [C-131 Samaritan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-131_Samaritan) aircraft dubbed the "vomit comet".[^2620]

Twin [KC-135 Stratotankers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KC-135_Stratotanker) were used until December 2004 and later retired. One, a KC-135A registered N930NA (also known as NASA 930, formerly USAF serial no. 59-1481), flew more than 58,000 parabolas after NASA acquired it in 1973, before being retired in 1995. It is now on display at [Ellington Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellington_Field), near the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center). The other (N931NA or NASA 931, formerly AF serial no. 63-7998) was also used by [Universal Pictures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Pictures) and [Imagine Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_Entertainment) for filming scenes involving weightlessness in the movie *[Apollo 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_13_%28film%29)*; it made its final flight on October 29, 2004, and is permanently stored in the [Pima Air & Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pima_Air_&_Space_Museum) in Tucson, Arizona.

In 2005 NASA replaced these aircraft with a [McDonnell Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonnell_Douglas) [C-9B Skytrain II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonnell_Douglas_C-9) (N932NA) formerly owned by [KLM Royal Dutch Airlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KLM) and the [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy).[^2621]

NASA concluded the Reduced Gravity Research Program and ended operations in July 2014, due to aircraft technical problems. It is replaced with private company contracts.

As of 2015 NASA had a microgravity services contract with [Zero Gravity Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_Gravity_Corporation) (ZERO-G) and used its aircraft, G-FORCE ONE, a modified Boeing [727-200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/727-200).[^2622]

###### Other operators

In late 2004, the [Zero Gravity Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_Gravity_Corporation) became the first company in the United States to offer zero-g flights to the general public, using [Boeing 727](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_727) jets. Each flight consists of around 15 parabolas, including simulations of the gravity levels of the Moon and Mars, as well as complete weightlessness.[^2618]

In 2015, Integrated Spaceflight Services, began serving as the research and education integrator of the [National Research Council of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Research_Council_of_Canada) for the US market, offering comprehensive reduced-gravity services on a modified [Falcon 20](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falcon_20) aircraft.[^2623] ISS has flown annual microgravity research campaigns to evaluate space suits and other technologies with Project PoSSUM.[^2624]

Aurora Aerospace in [Oldsmar, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldsmar,_Florida) offers zero-g flights using a [Fuji/Rockwell Commander 700](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuji/Rockwell_Commander_700). It is also used to simulate the gravity of the Moon and Mars.[^2625]

#### Airsickness

According to former Reduced Gravity Research Program director John Yaniec, anxiety contributes most to passengers' airsickness. The stress on their bodies creates a sense of panic and therefore causes the passenger to vomit. Yaniec gives a rough estimate of passengers, that "one third \[become\] violently ill, the next third moderately ill, and the final third not at all." Vomiting is referred to as being "ill".[^2607]

[Scopolamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyoscine_hydrobromide) is often used as an [antiemetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antiemetic) during reduced-gravity-aircraft training.[^2626]

#### Use in media production

The 1995 film *[Apollo 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_13_%28film%29)* filmed many scenes aboard NASA's KC-135 parabolic aircraft.

In 2016, rock group [OK Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OK_Go) recorded a music video for their single "[Upside Down & Inside Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upside_Down_&_Inside_Out)" on a reduced-gravity aircraft, which involved acrobatic choreography created specifically for the zero-gravity environment. The production was done with the assistance of Russian cosmonauts.[^2627][^2628]

The adult entertainment production company [Private Media Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_Media_Group) has filmed a [pornographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pornography) movie called *[The Uranus Experiment: Part Two](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Uranus_Experiment)* where a zero-gravity intercourse scene was filmed aboard a reduced-gravity aircraft. The filming process was particularly difficult from a technical and logistical standpoint. Budget constraints allowed for only one 20-second shot, featuring the actors [Sylvia Saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvia_Saint) and Nick Lang.[^2629] [Berth Milton, Jr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berth_Milton,_Jr.), president and [CEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer) of Private Media Group, said in 2000 "You would not want to be afraid of flying, that's for sure!"[^2630]

The ZERO-G corporation was featured in the *[MythBusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MythBusters)* [NASA Moon Landing Conspiracy episode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MythBusters_%282008_season%29), in which it flew [Adam Savage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Savage) and [Jamie Hyneman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamie_Hyneman) on a custom flight path to replicate the Moon's gravity. This allowed Savage to replicate the footage of [Neil Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Armstrong) walking on the Moon, disarming [claims that the footage was forged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moon_landing_conspiracy_theories).

### Westray to Papa Westray flight

Loganair's **Westray to Papa Westray route** is the current shortest scheduled passenger flight in the world. Flights on the route are scheduled for one-and-a-half minutes[^2631], and actual flying time is closer to one minute. The record for the fastest flight is 53 seconds.[^2632][^2633] The route is flown by [Loganair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loganair), a Scottish [regional airline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_airline) that serves Scotland's [Highlands and Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highlands_and_Islands).

#### Background

With the completion of Papa Westray Airport's runway extension and removal of its stone walls in November 1967,[^2634] the route was inaugurated by Loganair on 4 December 1967, establishing the record for the world's shortest scheduled commercial flights.[^2635]

This route between the [Orkney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkney) islands of [Westray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westray) and [Papa Westray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papa_Westray) in northern Scotland is part of Orkney's [Inter-Islands air service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkney) which was launched in September 1967 with the initial connection of three of the Orkney islands.[^2636] An additional route connected a fourth island, Westray, in October,[^2636] and the addition of Papa Westray in December brought it up to five connected islands by the end of 1967.[^2635][^2637]

The [Orkney Islands Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkney_Islands_Council) operates the route as a subsidised [public service obligation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_service_obligation) and awards its operation, which along with the other routes connecting six of Orkney's islands forms Orkney's "Inter-Islands air service", through a public tendering process. The flights have been continuously operated by [Loganair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loganair) since their founding and in 2025 the contract was again awarded to Loganair for service through March 2029.[^2638][^2639][^2640]

#### Flights

Flights between Westray Airport and Papa Westray Airport operate daily: bi-directional on weekdays and uni-directional on weekends. On Saturdays only flights from Westray to Papa Westray are available, and on Sunday, only flights from Papa Westray to Westray are available.[^2641] The total distance covered by the flights is 1.7 miles (2.7 km), which is about the same length as the runway at [Edinburgh Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh_Airport).[^2633]

Stuart Linklater piloted the flight more than 12,000 times, more than any other pilot, before he retired in 2013. Linklater set the current record for the fastest flight between the islands at 53 seconds.[^2633][^2642]

##### Passengers

Many students and their teachers take these flights to study the 60 archaeological sites on Papa Westray, making up the majority of passengers. Occasionally health professionals are needed to assist one of the island's 90 residents, and patients will also take the flight from Papa Westray to medical facilities when needed. The flight has also become popular among tourists.[^2643]

As of 2024, the route sees an average of around 5000 passengers annually.[^2644]

##### Aircraft

Since its launch in 1967, Loganair continues to operate this flight with one of its two [Britten-Norman BN2B-26 Islander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britten-Norman_BN-2_Islander) aircraft. The Islander is a high-wing, twin piston engine, propeller-driven aircraft. It is flown by a single pilot, and there is seating for eight passengers in the passenger cabin. One additional seat usually remains empty next to the pilot.

Loganair's chief executive, Jim Cameron, described the Islander as "robust" and "well suited to the vagaries of Scottish weather".[^2645] Summarizing expert opinion of the Islander, Alastair Dalton of *[The Scotsman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Scotsman)* said the aircraft "had a good safety record and had proved versatile in operating from the shortest and roughest Highland runways".[^2646]

In 2018, Loganair was planning to introduce [electric aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_aircraft) to the Orkney Islands by 2021 due to the short distance between the islands that would make such flights possible.[^2647] However, as of 2024, the BN-2 Islander is still operating the routes.

##### Flight numbers

The flight times and numbers change daily and repeat with a weekly cycle. Loganair Flight 702 departs from [Westray Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westray_Airport) to [Papa Westray Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papa_Westray_Airport) on Monday morning, and Flight 705 returns to Westray that afternoon. On Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays, the flight number to Papa Westray is 709. The return flight number is 711. On Wednesday, Flight 714 goes to Papa Westray and the Flight 711 comes back to Westray. Flight 720 is the Saturday flight from Westray to Papa Westray, and on Sundays, Flight 726 is the return flight to Westray.[^2641]

##### The future of the route

In 2014, Orkney Islands Council (OIC) held [consultations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Isles_fixed_sea_link_connections) regarding building a number of fixed links between seven of the Orkney Islands. This would include a bridge between Westray and Papa Westray.[^2648] No such resulting actions were taken and in 2025 the OIC has said that these consultations were "exploratory in nature".[^2649][^2650]

In 2025, the Scottish Government National Islands Plan was formally drafted and presented to parliament which includes the proposals to increase the number of ferries and aircraft dedicated to increasing Inter Islands service capacity.[^2651] A third Britten-Norman Islander is now expected to brought into service (with updated timetables and potential increase to the Westray - Papa Westray flights) "by summer 2026".[^2652][^2653]

There is a passenger ferry service between the islands also, with several daily departures per direction. They are around 3 miles (5 km) and last around 25 minutes.[^2654] A car ferry usually runs twice a week.[^2655]

### Creeper and Reaper

**Creeper** was the first [computer worm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_worm), while **Reaper** was the first [antivirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antivirus) software, designed to eliminate Creeper.

#### Creeper

**Creeper** was an experimental computer program written by Bob Thomas at [BBN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBN_Technologies) in 1971.[^2656] Its original iteration was designed to move between [DEC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Equipment_Corporation) [PDP-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PDP-10) [mainframe computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainframe_computer) running the [TENEX operating system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TENEX_%28operating_system%29) using the [ARPANET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARPANET), with a later version by [Ray Tomlinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Tomlinson) designed to copy itself between computers rather than simply move.[^2657] This self-replicating version of Creeper is generally accepted to be the first [computer worm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_worm).[^2658][^2659][^2660] Creeper was a test created to demonstrate the possibility of a self-replicating computer program that could spread to other computers.

The program was not actively [malicious software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malware), as it caused no damage to data, the only effect being a message it output to the [teletype](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teleprinter) reading "I'M THE CREEPER : CATCH ME IF YOU CAN"[^2661][^2659][^2657]

##### Impact

Creeper had a minimal impact on the computers it infected. No more than 28 machines could have been infected, as that was the number of machines running the TENEX operating system on ARPANET.[^2662] The operators of the machines were also collaborators in the project, and Tomlinson needed permission to run the program on their machines. In an interview, Tomlinson also stated that there were no unintended effects from running the program.[^2662]

#### Reaper

**Reaper** was the first anti-virus software, designed to delete Creeper by moving across the [ARPANET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARPANET). It was created by Tomlinson in 1972.[^2657]

#### Cultural

The conflict between Creeper and Reaper served as inspiration for the [programming game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_game) *[Core War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Core_War)*,[^2657] while fictionalized versions of Reaper have been used as antagonists in the [anime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anime) *[Digimon Tamers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digimon_Tamers)*[^2663] and the [visual novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_novel) *Digital: A Love Story*.[^2664] A digital Creeper has also appeared in the [webcomic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webcomic) *Internet Explorer*, alongside the likewise personified [Morris Worm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_Worm).[^2665]

### PC LOAD LETTER

**PC LOAD LETTER** is a [printer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_printer) error message that has entered popular culture as a technology [meme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme) referring to a confusing or inappropriate [error message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_message). It is a real message that can be displayed by an [HP LaserJet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HP_LaserJet), and indicates the printer does not have the [US letter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_letter) sized paper needed to complete a particular print job. The message was mocked in the 1999 comedy film *[Office Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_Space)*.[^2666]

#### Message

The message is encountered when printing on older [HP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hewlett-Packard) [LaserJet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaserJet) printers such as the LaserJet II, III, and [4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HP_LaserJet_4) series. It means that the printer is trying to print a document that needs "[Letter size](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_%28paper_size%29)" (8½ × 11 in.) paper when no such paper is available.[^2667]

"PC" is an abbreviation for "paper cassette",[^2668] the tray which holds blank paper for the printer to use. These two-character codes are a legacy feature carried over from the first LaserJet printers, which could only use a two-character display for all printer status and error messages. "LOAD" is an instruction to refill the paper tray. "[LETTER](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_%28paper_size%29)" is the standard [paper size](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paper_size) used in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada) and some other nations. Thus, the message is instructing the user to refill the paper tray with letter-sized paper.[^2669]

Users are far more likely to think "PC" stands for "[personal computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computer)" than for "paper cassette", and "LETTER" with what is sent in physical or e-mail. In most countries, standard paper is [A4 size](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A4_%28paper_size%29), and users may not even know "LETTER" is a paper size.

#### Mitigation

The error can be dismissed (other than by filling the paper tray) by emptying the print queue and printer buffer or pressing "Shift+Continue"[^2670] and, in extreme cases, restarting the printer and repeating.

The [LaserJet 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LaserJet_5) introduced a "GO" button to override the warning message. Later LaserJet models feature number labels on paper trays and display a more easily understandable message: "TRAY 2 LOAD PLAIN LETTER".

#### Cultural references

> "PC LOAD LETTER? The fuck does that mean!?"

*,  Michael Bolton, *[Office Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_Space)* (1999)[^2671]*

The error message is mocked in the 1999 comedy film *[Office Space](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_Space)*, when employee Michael Bolton becomes frustrated as he does not know what it means.[^2671] Later in the film he and his coworkers are shown destroying the printer with a baseball bat.[^2672]

### Elvis operator

In certain [computer programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_programming) languages, the **Elvis operator**, often written **`?:`**, is a [binary operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_operator) that returns the first operand if its value is logically true (according to a language-dependent convention, in other words, a *[truthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truthy_%28computing%29)* value) or returns its second operand if the first operand is not true. That is, it is a [short-circuit `OR`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-circuit_evaluation), which returns its first truthy operand.

The syntax of the Elvis operator was inspired by the [ternary conditional operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ternary_conditional_operator), `? :`, since the Elvis operator expression `A ?: B` is approximately equivalent to the ternary conditional expression `A ? A : B`.

It is called the "Elvis operator" because the notation `?:`, when viewed sideways, resembles an [emoticon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emoticon) of [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley) with his [signature hairstyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompadour_%28hairstyle%29).[^2673]

A similar operator is the [null coalescing operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null_coalescing_operator), where the boolean truth(iness) check is replaced with a check for non-[null](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null_pointer) instead. This is usually written `??`, and can be seen in languages like [C#](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_Sharp_%28programming_language%29)[^2674] or [Dart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dart_%28programming_language%29).[^2675]

#### Alternative syntaxes

In several languages, such as [Common Lisp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Lisp), [Clojure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clojure), [Lua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lua_%28programming_language%29), [Object Pascal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object_Pascal), [Perl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perl), [Python](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_%28programming_language%29), [Ruby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby_%28programming_language%29), and [JavaScript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript), there is no need for the Elvis operator, because the language's [logical disjunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_disjunction) operator (typically `||` or `or`) is [short-circuiting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-circuit_evaluation) and returns its first operand if it would evaluate to a [truthy value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truthy_%28computing%29), and otherwise its second operand, which may be a truthy or falsy value (rather than a [Boolean *true* or *false* value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boolean_data_type), such as in C and C++). These semantics are identical to the Elvis operator.

#### Example

##### Boolean variant

In a language that supports the Elvis operator, something like this:

` x = f() ?: g() `

will set `x` equal to the result of `f()` if that result is truthy, and to the result of `g()` otherwise.

It is equivalent to this example, using the conditional ternary operator:

` x = f() ? f() : g() `

except that it does not evaluate `f()` twice if it yields truthy. Note the possibility of arbitrary behaviour if `f()` is not a state-independent function that always returns the same result.

##### Object reference variant

This code will result in a reference to an object that is guaranteed to not be null. Function `f()` returns an object reference instead of a boolean, and may return null, which is universally regarded as falsy:

` x = f() ?: "default value" `

#### Languages supporting the Elvis operator

- In GNU [C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_%28programming_language%29) and [C++](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C++) (that is: in C and C++ with [GCC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GNU_Compiler_Collection) extensions), the second operand of the ternary operator is optional.[^2676] This has been the case since at least GCC 2.95.3 (March 2001), and seems to be *the* original Elvis operator.[^2677]
- In [Apache Groovy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groovy_%28programming_language%29), the "Elvis operator" `?:` is documented as a distinct operator;[^2678] this feature was added in Groovy 1.5[^2679] (December 2007). Groovy, unlike GNU C and PHP, does *not* simply allow the second operand of ternary `?:` to be omitted; rather, binary `?:` must be written as a single operator, with no whitespace in between.
- In [PHP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PHP), it is possible to leave out the middle part of the ternary operator since PHP 5.3.[^2680] (June 2009).
- The [Fantom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantom_%28programming_language%29) programming language has the `?:` binary operator that compares its first operand with `null`.
- In [Kotlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kotlin_%28programming_language%29), the Elvis operator returns its left-hand side if it is not null, and its right-hand side otherwise.[^2681] A common pattern is to use it with `return`, like this: `val foo = bar() ?: return`
- In [Gosu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gosu_%28programming_language%29), the `?:` operator returns the right operand if the left is null as well.
- In [C#](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_Sharp_%28programming_language%29), the [null-conditional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe_navigation_operator) operator, `?.` is referred to as the "Elvis operator",[^2682] but it does not perform the same function. Instead, the [null-coalescing operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null-coalescing_operator) `??` does.
- In [ColdFusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ColdFusion) and [CFML](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CFML), the Elvis operator was introduced using the `?:` syntax.
- The [Xtend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xtend) programming language has an Elvis operator.[^2683]
- In Google's [Closure Templates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Closure_Tools), the Elvis operator is a [null coalescing operator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Null_coalescing_operator), equivalent to `isNonnull($a) ? $a : $b`.[^2684]
- In [Ballerina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballerina_%28programming_language%29), the Elvis operator `L ?: R` returns the value of `L` if it's not nil. Otherwise, return the value of `R`.[^2685]
- In [JavaScript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript), the nullish coalescing (`??`) operator is a logical operator that returns its right-hand side operand when its left-hand side operand is `null` or `undefined`, and otherwise returns its left-hand side operand.[^2686]
- In [Perl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perl) there is a logical short-circuiting disjunction `||` and a similar lower precedence `or`.[^2687] They differ from the *bitwise or* operator `|` which evaluates both operands without short-circuiting. There is also a corresponding assignment operator `||=` that evaluates its right-hand operand and assigns it to the left-operand unless the logical value of the left-operand is true. There is also a short-circuiting *defined-or* operator `//` which evaluates its right-operand and returns its value only if the left-operand is undefined. Finally, the corresponding assignment operator is `//=`. Similar *exclusive-or* operators are not *Elvis* operators as they do not short-circuit. Other short-circuiting operators are the *logical-and* ones `&&` and `and`, but their behavior is opposite that of the *Elvis* operator.

[^2673]: Joyce Farrell (February 7, 2013). *Java Programming*. Cengage Learning. p. 276. ISBN 978-1285081953. The new operator is called Elvis operator because it uses a question mark and a colon together (?:); if you view it sideways, it reminds you of Elvis Presley.

[^2674]: ["?? Operator"](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/operators/null-coalescing-operator). *C# Reference*. Microsoft. Retrieved December 5, 2018.
