### Your AI Slop Bores Me

**Your AI Slop Bores Me** (stylized in all lowercase and abbreviated as **YASBM**) is a [website](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Website) and [social experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_experiment) created by programmer Mihir Maroju.[^2688] Serving as a [parody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parody) of [large language models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_models) (LLMs) like [ChatGPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT) and [Claude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_%28language_model%29), all questions and image prompts posed by users are answered by other, randomly-selected human users of the site.[^2689]

As of March 2026, the site had reached 50 million hits and sustained approximately 16,000 concurrent users.[^2688]

#### Background and development

Maroju conceived the website in early 2026 out of frustration with the proliferation of [AI art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_art) and [AI slop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_slop) on the internet.[^2690]

After an initial launch with low traffic, the platform gained viral traction across [Tumblr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumblr), [Bluesky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bluesky), and [X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X_%28social_network%29) (formerly Twitter), eventually becoming a trending topic on X. This sudden influx of millions of visitors temporarily overwhelmed the site's infrastructure.[^2690] To manage the rapid growth, moderation challenges, and spam, Maroju expanded the project into a multi-person development team. The team subsequently established a code of conduct, implemented a moderation portal, and launched an official community [Discord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discord_%28software%29) server.[^2690]

#### Overview

The platform operates on a "credit economy" designed to ensure active participation. First-time users are granted 1 free credit. If a user's balance drops to 0, they automatically receive 2 credits every 10 minutes, up to a maximum cap of 6 credits.[^2690] Users must expend credits to submit prompts, which can either request text responses or digital sketches.

To replenish credits without waiting, users can choose to answer prompts submitted by others. When answering, the user is expected to "[larp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larp)" (live action roleplay) as an artificial intelligence under a strict 75-second time limit. Prompters can alternatively spend 2 credits to activate a "thinking mode," which grants the respondent an extended countdown of 150 seconds to complete their response.[^2691]

#### Reception

The site has garnered attention and praise from online communities for its subversion of internet automation. Writing for *[The Daily Dot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Dot)*, Rachel Kiley noted that "the best part about the game is that there's really no right or wrong way to do it. Humans aren't LLMs trained on copyrighted material and the whole of the free internet, but we do retain a certain amount of information... while also being capable of creativity."[^2692]

Chris Taylor of *[Mashable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashable)* described the application as "amateurish and charming."[^2693] Nicole Carpenter of *[Aftermath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aftermath_%28website%29)* wrote positively of the project, stating that the interface and human interactions reminded her of "the human touch of chaos."[^2694]

### Frozen Peas

***Frozen Peas*** is the colloquial term for a [blooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blooper) audio clip in which American actor and filmmaker [Orson Welles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orson_Welles) performs [narration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narration) for a series of British television advertisements for [Findus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Findus). The clip is also known informally as ***In July***, or ***Yes, Always***, based on several of Welles's complaints during the recording.

#### Background

The British Film Institute (BFI) database lists the titles "Findus: Lincolnshire (Peas)",[^2695] "Findus: Sweden"[^2696] and "Findus: Far West",[^2697] all dated 1970, and attributed to the [J. Walter Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Walter_Thompson) advertising agency.

[Jonathan Lynn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Lynn), who acted in Welles's film of *[The Merchant of Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Merchant_of_Venice_%281969_film%29)* made between 1969 and 1970, recalled being told about the recording session by Welles:

One night \[Welles\] told us about his voice over for Findus frozen peas. “An ad agency called and asked me to do a voice over. I said I would. Then they said would I please come in and audition. *'Audition?'* I said. 'Surely to God there’s someone in your little agency who knows what my voice sounds like?' Well, they said they knew my voice but it was for the client. So I went in. I wanted the money, I was trying to finish *[Chimes at Midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimes_at_Midnight)*. I auditioned and they offered me the part! Well, they asked me to go to some little basement studio in [Wardour Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wardour_Street) to record it. I demanded payment in advance. After I'd gotten the cheque I told them 'I can’t come to Wardour Street next week, I have to be in Paris.' I told them to bring their little tape-recorder and meet me at the [Georges Cinq Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Seasons_Hotel_George_V) next Wednesday at eleven am. So they flew over to Paris, came to the hotel at eleven - and were told that I had checked out the day before." He chortled happily. "I left them a message telling them to call me at the [Gritti Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Pisani_Gritti) in Venice. They did, and I told them to meet me there on Friday. When they got there I was gone - they found a message telling them to come to Vienna." Now he was laughing uproariously. "I made them chase me all around Europe with their shitty little tape recorder for ten days. They were sorry they made me audition."[^2698]

It is therefore possible that Welles recorded the session in Vienna, during the making of the *[Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_%28film%29)* segment of his unfinished *Orson's Bag* TV special.

Lynn’s second-hand story may be a recollection from the initial recording session with perhaps the same client (the director was heard to refer to a previous successful session). Also, the outtakes give many clues that they took place in a professional recording studio and not a hotel using a portable recorder. This also would better explain the client-mandated audition.

The BFI database also lists four more 1970 Findus advertisements with place names: "France",[^2699] "Highlands",[^2700] "Normandy[^2701] and "Shetland".[^2702] These may be part of the same series, and possibly also voiced by Welles.

##### Bootleg circulation

The original recording was made in 1970. The outtake/blooper reel was presumably spliced to circulate as a [bootleg recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootleg_recording), and nothing is known about who made it or their connection to Findus or J. Walter Thompson. The earliest record of the bootleg dates to 1979, when advertiser Peter Shillingford shared a copy with Welles, who enjoyed it.[^2703]

It is not known whether a complete recording of the session exists (since, for example, the "multiple takes" Welles alludes to are not contained on the circulated recording, and the recording transitions between different commercials). It is also not known whether film copies of the final advertisements exist in the BFI National Archive.

#### Summary

The recording begins with Welles reading the introduction to a script for a commercial for frozen peas.

> *"We know a remote farm in Lincolnshire, where Mrs. Buckley lives; every July, peas grow there..."*

Welles breaks from the script, expressing his dissatisfaction about the timing of the piece, as well as remarking that "it's so nice that you see a snow-covered field and say, "Every *July*, peas grow there...we're talking about 'em growing and she's picked 'em."

A director requests that he emphasize the word 'in' in the phrase "in July;" Welles claims this is impossible to do in a sensible fashion, claiming that the director isn't thinking.

> Why? That doesn't make any sense. Sorry. There's no known way of saying an English sentence in which you begin a sentence with 'in' and emphasize it. Get me a jury and show me how you can say "*in* July", and I'll go down on you. That's just idiotic, if you'll forgive me my saying so. That's just stupid, "*in* July"; I'd love to know how you emphasize 'in' in "In July"...impossible! Meaningless![^2704]

A director apologizes because the script actually said "Every July" rather than "in July", but Welles continues to complain that it was the other director ("your friend") who made the suggestion, and quips, "Too much directing around here."

From here, the recording transitions to a different commercial for fish fingers, apparently at either the same recording session, or for the same director:

> *"We know a certain fjord in Norway, near where the cod gather in great shoals. There, Jan St..."*

Welles struggles with the pronunciation of the fisherman's name, cursing under his breath. The director requests a different pacing, but Welles refuses.

> You don't know what I'm up against: because it's full of, of, of things that are only correct because they're grammatical but they're tough on the ear, you see; this is a very wearying one, it's unpleasant to read. Unrewarding.[^2705]

Welles attempts to finish the script but gets tangled around the words "crumb-crisp coating." The directors permit him to remove the word "crumb."

The recording moves on to yet another advertisement, for hamburgers, but not before Welles slips in a complaint.

> Here, under protest, is "beef burgers." *"We know a little place in the American far west, where Charlie Briggs chops up the finest prairie-fed beef and tastes..."* This is a lot of shit, you know that?

The directors ask for one more take, as they don't like the way he emphasizes "prairie-fed" over beef.

> But you can't emphasize 'beef'; that's like his wanting me to emphasize 'in' before 'July'! Come on, fellas, you're losing your heads! I wouldn't direct any living actor like this in Shakespeare, the way you do this! It's impossible![^2706]

The directors try to calm him down, but Welles insists he's giving it the right reading, to which a director responds, "For the moment." Welles continues to gripe about the number of takes he's made for these commercials, which he claims is twenty more than any other he's made.

> You're such pests...now, what is it you want? In your depths of your ignorance, what is it you want? Well, whatever it is you want, I can't deliver because I just don't see it.[^2707]

When the engineer attempts to give Welles some pointers, the actor reveals his frustration of being a performer, a "hired hand" on the commercial being given conflicting advice from different people in the booth.

> I take direction from one person...under protest, but from two I don't sit still.

The actual director continues to try to calm Welles down, but he storms out of the recording booth.

> This isn't worth it, no money is worth it!

#### Parodies

The tape has been [parodied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parody) many times, often when parodying Welles himself. In the [animated series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animated_series) *[Animaniacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animaniacs)*, an episode featuring [Pinky and the Brain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinky_and_the_Brain) titled "Yes, Always", featured a near-verbatim restaging (with vulgarities replaced by innocuous substitutes, e.g., "...and I'll make cheese for you" in place of "...and I'll go down on you"), with [Brain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinky_and_the_Brain) playing the part of Welles and [Pinky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinky_and_the_Brain) as the director.[^2708] Brain's voice actor, [Maurice LaMarche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_LaMarche), well known for his Welles impressions, would sometimes parody the "frozen peas" tape before recording sessions as a warm up, and parts of these warmup lines were incorporated into the cartoon's script.[^2709][^2710][^2711]

Another version portrayed in *[The Critic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Critic_%28TV_series%29)* features Welles, again voiced by LaMarche, whispering "Rosebud" à la *[Citizen Kane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citizen_Kane)* before the shot pans out to reveal Welles at a table, with a plate of Rosebud Frozen Peas he is advertising. After reading his lines, describing the peas as "full of country goodness and green pea-ness," he becomes disgusted and walks off, taking a handful of peas with him and eating them alongside a French fry stuck in his beard. In another episode, Welles, upset over having to read a [living will](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_will), begins endorsing for "Mrs. Pell's Fish Sticks" instead, eating them and declaring that "they're even better raw". He even appears later as a ghostly apparition to Margo Sherman to continue promoting and eating the fish sticks, declaring that "they're even better when you're dead".

Another parody of the tape appeared in a skit on the [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_in_Canada) sketch comedy show *[SCTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_City_Television)*, where Welles, played by [John Candy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Candy), is hired by [Liberace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberace), played by [Dave Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Thomas_%28actor%29), for a Christmas storytelling. Welles is frequently distracted by the TV crew and finally, he gets up and walks off (taking an entire roast turkey with him). Amongst Welles's complaints in this scene are three direct quotes from the "Frozen Peas" recording: "You don't know what I'm up against," "I wouldn't direct any living actor like this in Shakespeare," and "No money is worth this!"

Yet another animated example, once more portrayed by LaMarche comes from the 2010 *[Futurama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurama)* episode "[Lrrreconcilable Ndndifferences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lrrreconcilable_Ndndifferences)" for which he won an [Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Award). Welles (as a head in a jar) agrees to recreate his famous *[War of the Worlds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_War_of_the_Worlds_%281938_radio_drama%29)* broadcast for [Lrrr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_recurring_characters_in_Futurama), the Planet Express crew and a cheese log even when complaining on-air about obvious plot holes in the script.

The tape was referenced in the "Bishop" skit from *[Monty Python's Contractual Obligation Album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contractual_obligation_album)*, where it is mentioned that ["Bath and Wells"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_of_Bath_and_Wells) is busy "doing frozen peas for Nigel."[^2712]

[Will Ferrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Ferrell)'s bookend segments in the miniseries *[The Spoils of Babylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spoils_of_Babylon)*, as Eric Jonrosh (a Welles lookalike), feature Jonrosh breaking from the script frequently to complain of inane language and berate the unseen crew.

#### Other media

The experimental music group [Negativland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negativland) incorporated "frozen peas" in its entirety in the track "Jolly Green Giant", a collage also featuring sound effects and other archival recordings of commercials in production phase. The track appears on their 1998 EP *[Happy Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Heroes)*.

California punk band [Swingin' Utters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swingin'_Utters) released an album in 2011 entitled [Here, Under Protest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Here,_Under_Protest) and opens with a clip of Welles saying, "Here, under protest, is beef burgers".

### MacGuffin

In [fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiction), a **MacGuffin** (sometimes **McGuffin**) is an object, device, or event that is necessary to the plot and the motivation of the characters, but insignificant, unimportant, or irrelevant in itself.[^2713][^2714][^2715][^2716][^2717] Thus, the use of a MacGuffin in a narrative is a [plot device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plot_device). The term was originated by [Angus MacPhail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angus_MacPhail) for film,[^2714] adopted by [Alfred Hitchcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Hitchcock),[^2713][^2714][^2715][^2716][^2717] and later extended to a similar device in other fiction.[^2716]

The MacGuffin technique is common in films, especially [thrillers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thriller_film). Usually, the MacGuffin is revealed in the first [act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_%28theater%29), and thereafter declines in importance. It can reappear at the climax of the story but may actually be forgotten by the end of the story. Multiple MacGuffins are sometimes derisively identified as [plot coupons](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/plot%20coupon)[^2718][^2719], the characters "collect" the coupons to trade in for an ending.

#### History and use

The use of the MacGuffin plot technique predates *MacGuffin* as the name of the technique. The [Holy Grail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Grail) of [Arthurian legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matter_of_Britain) has been cited as an early example of a MacGuffin. The Holy Grail is the desired object that is essential to initiate and advance the plot, but the final disposition of the Grail is never revealed, suggesting that the object is not of significance in itself.[^2720] An even earlier example would be the [Golden Fleece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Fleece) of [Greek mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mythology), in the quest of [Jason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason) and the [Argonauts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argonauts); "the Fleece itself, the *raison d'être* of this entire epic geste, remains a complete \[...\] mystery. The full reason for its Grail-like desirability \[...\] is never explained."[^2721][^2722]

The World War I-era actress [Pearl White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_White) used the term "[weenie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weenie_%28design%29)" to identify whatever object (a roll of film, a rare coin, expensive diamonds, etc.) impelled the heroes and villains to pursue each other through the convoluted plots of *[The Perils of Pauline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Perils_of_Pauline_%281914_serial%29)* and the other silent film serials in which she starred.[^2723] In the 1930 detective novel *[The Maltese Falcon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Maltese_Falcon_%28novel%29)*, a small statuette provides both the book's title and its motive for intrigue.

The name MacGuffin was coined by the English screenwriter [Angus MacPhail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angus_MacPhail).[^2724] It has been posited that "'guff', as a word for anything trivial or worthless, may lie at the root".[^2725]

##### Alfred Hitchcock

Director and producer Alfred Hitchcock popularized the term MacGuffin and the technique with his 1935 film *[The 39 Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_39_Steps_%281935_film%29)*, in which the MacGuffin is some otherwise incidental military secrets.[^2726][^2727] Hitchcock explained the term MacGuffin in a 1939 lecture at Columbia University in New York City:

> It might be a Scottish name, taken from a story about two men on a train. One man says, "What's that package up there in the baggage rack?" And the other answers, "Oh, that's a MacGuffin." The first one asks, "What's a MacGuffin?" "Well," the other man says, "it's an apparatus for trapping lions in the Scottish Highlands." The first man says, "But there are no lions in the Scottish Highlands," and the other one answers, "Well then, that's no MacGuffin!" So you see that a MacGuffin is actually nothing at all.

In a 1966 interview with [François Truffaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Truffaut), Hitchcock explained the term using the same story.[^2728][^2729] He also related this anecdote in a television interview for [Richard Schickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Schickel)'s documentary *The Men Who Made the Movies*, and in an interview with [Dick Cavett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Cavett).[^2730]

The \$40,000 that [Marion Crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Crane) embezzles at the beginning of [Robert Bloch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bloch)'s *[Psycho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psycho_%28novel%29)*, popularised by [Hitchcock's 1960 movie of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psycho_%281960_film%29), are sometimes cited as an eminent example of MacGuffin, in that they don't play any role in the plot and the narration soon ceases to even mention the sum at all.[^2731] Hitchcock also said, "The MacGuffin is the thing that the spies are after, but the audience doesn't care."[^2732]

In [Mel Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_Brooks)'s parody of Hitchcock films, *[High Anxiety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Anxiety)* (1977), Brooks's character's hotel room is moved from the 2nd to the 17th floor at the request of "a Mr. MacGuffin", a recognition by name of Hitchcock's use of the device.[^2733]

##### George Lucas

In contrast to Hitchcock's view, [*Vanity Fair*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanity_Fair_%28magazine%29) reported that [George Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lucas) "believes that the audience should care about \[the MacGuffin\] almost as much as the dueling heroes and villains on-screen".[^2734] Lucas describes [R2-D2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R2-D2) as the MacGuffin of the [original *Star Wars* film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Wars_%28film%29),[^2735] and said that the [Ark of the Covenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ark_of_the_Covenant), the titular MacGuffin in *[Raiders of the Lost Ark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raiders_of_the_Lost_Ark)*, was an excellent example as opposed to the more obscure MacGuffin in *[Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Jones_and_the_Temple_of_Doom)* and the "feeble" MacGuffin in *[Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Jones_and_the_Last_Crusade)*.[^2734] The use of MacGuffins in [Indiana Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Jones) films later continued with the titular [crystal skull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_skull) in *[Kingdom of the Crystal Skull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Jones_and_the_Kingdom_of_the_Crystal_Skull)* and [Archimedes' Dial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_mechanism) in *[the Dial of Destiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Jones_and_the_Dial_of_Destiny)*.[^2734][^2736]

##### Yves Lavandier

Filmmaker and drama writing theorist [Yves Lavandier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Lavandier) suggests that a MacGuffin is a secret that motivates the villains.[^2737] *[North by Northwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_by_Northwest)*'s MacGuffin[^2738] is nothing that motivates the protagonist; Roger Thornhill's objective is to extricate himself from the predicament that the mistaken identity has created, and what matters to Vandamm and the [CIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency) is of little importance to Thornhill. A similar lack of motivating power applies to the MacGuffins of the 1930s films *[The Lady Vanishes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lady_Vanishes_%281938_film%29)*, *[The 39 Steps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_39_Steps_%281935_film%29)*, and *[Foreign Correspondent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Correspondent_%28film%29)*. In a broader sense, says Lavandier, a MacGuffin denotes any justification for the external conflict in a work.[^2737]

#### Further examples

The briefcase in *[Pulp Fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulp_Fiction)* (1994) motivates several of the characters during many of the film's major plot points, but its contents are never revealed.[^2739]

Similarly, the plot of the 1998 film *[Ronin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronin_%28film%29)* revolves around a case, the contents of which remain unknown. At the end of the film, it is said to have led to a historic peace agreement and an end to [the Troubles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Troubles) in Northern Ireland.[^2740]

George Lucas also used a MacGuffin in January 1975 in the second draft of *[Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Wars_%28film%29)*, at that time titled *Adventures of the Starkiller, Ep. I: The Star Wars*. Biographer Brian Jay Jones wrote that Lucas "decided that the Force could be intensified through the possession of a mystical Kiber Crystal \[*[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic)*\]," which Jones described as "Lucas's first, but by no means last, great MacGuffin".[^2741] By Lucas's fourth draft, completed January 1, 1976, Jones writes, Lucas "had wisely decided to remove the Kiber Crystal from the story altogether" during the process of "paring down subplots and characters, removing elements that either slowed things down or required too much backstory".[^2742] Decades later, beginning with *Star Wars: The Clone Wars*, the franchise reused the term (now spelled "[kyber crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyber_crystal)") in a non-MacGuffin context.

A similar usage was employed in [John Carpenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Carpenter)'s *[Escape from New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escape_from_New_York)*, where the protagonist [Snake Plissken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake_Plissken) is tasked with rescuing both the President of the United States and a cassette tape that will prevent a devastating war between the country and its enemies. While there are hints throughout the film, the contents of the tape are never revealed to the audience.[^2743]

### You (Time Person of the Year)

"**You**" was the official choice for *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_%28magazine%29)*'s [Person of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Person_of_the_Year) in 2006. The magazine set out to recognize the millions of people who anonymously contribute [user-generated content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User-generated_content) to websites such as [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube), [MySpace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MySpace), [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia) and other [wikis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikis), and the [multitudes of other websites featuring user contribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_2.0).[^2744][^2745]

While the status had been given before to inanimate objects, with the [personal computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computer) being the "Machine of the Year" for 1982,[^2746][^2745] as well as collections of people or an abstract representative of a movement, the choice of "You" attracted criticism from commentators in publications such as *[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic)* for being too much of a [pop culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_culture) [gimmick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gimmick).[^2747][^2745] A 2014 *[New York Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Daily_News)* article named the 2006 award as one of the ten most controversial "Person of the Year" moments in the history of *Time*.[^2745] The news magazine experienced generally successful sales.

#### Background

While most earlier choices for "Person of the Year" have been historically important individuals, many of them infamous rather than internationally popular ([Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler) was 1938's "Man of the Year", and [Ayatollah Khomeini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayatollah_Khomeini) won in 1979),[^2745][^2748] a few were inanimate. The [personal computer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computer) was the "Machine of the Year" for 1982,[^2746] while the "Endangered Earth" was the "Planet of the Year" for 1988.[^2749][^2745] Collections of people as well as a symbolic representative of multiple individuals had also won the award before; for example, "U.S. Scientists" were named "Men of the Year" in 1960.[^2748]

Similar media awards had already recognized the growing significance of [online community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_community) and user-generated content: "You!" was the first ranking choice in *[Business 2.0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_2.0)*'s list of "50 people who matter now" in July 2006;[^2750] while [ABC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_News_%28United_States%29) had listed [bloggers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blog) as "People of the Year" for 2006.[^2751]

#### Decision

In accordance with *Time*'s annual process, different [bureaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_bureau) suggested different candidates.[^2752] "You", or "the [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube) guys", was floated in November as a possible winner.[^2753] Readers' opinions were canvassed online.[^2752] The final decision was made by [managing editor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Managing_editor) [Richard Stengel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Stengel).

The decision was announced in *Time*'s December 25, 2006 issue.[^2744] The cover of the magazine featured an [iMac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMac) computer with a [reflective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflection_%28physics%29) [mylar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BoPET) pane appearing as the window of a [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube)-like video player, intended to reflect as online content the face of whoever picks up the magazine.[^2744] The time remaining indicator in the image indicates a total duration of "20:06," a visual pun connecting this ubiquitous bit of interface design to the year in which it gained ascendancy in *Time*'s view. Stories on the new user-driven media dynamic were provided by [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC) editor [Brian Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Williams)[^2754] and *Time* editors [Lev Grossman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lev_Grossman)[^2744] and [Richard Stengel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Stengel).[^2755] As Grossman describes, "It's about the many wrestling power from the few and helping one another for nothing and how that will not only change the world, but also change the way the world changes."

#### Criticism

The choice of "You" as Person of the Year was criticized for not mentioning important people that influenced the events of 2006. Paul Kedrosky called it an "incredible cop-out", and he also speculated that the selection marked "some sort of near-term market top for user-generated content".[^2756] Commentator Kevin Friedl noted that the award and cover design recalled the mirror viewed by the protagonist, the Dude, of *[The Big Lebowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Big_Lebowski)*, via which the viewer's reflection was framed as *Time*'s "Man of the Year".[^2757]

In December 2012, journalist David A. Graham wrote for *[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic)* that he thought *Time* had shown "a pattern of lackluster choices" and the overall promotional nature of the process shouldn't be treated as news, rather simply viewed as [marketing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marketing). He remarked, "Is anyone out there *not* sick of people ironically listing 'Time Person of the Year, 2006' in [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) bios, a reference to the gimmicky selection of 'You' that year?"[^2747]

The decision raised some criticism as it was described as ideological and even hypocritically political. Some weeks before the announcement, *Time* decided to ask the users in a poll, "Who Should Be Person of the Year?" After several weeks, the poll winner by a wide margin was [Hugo Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Ch%C3%A1vez), the president of [Venezuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venezuela), with 35% of the votes. The president of Iran, [Mahmoud Ahmadinejad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahmoud_Ahmadinejad), came in second. *Time* did not mention these results in the announcement of their "Person of the Year" and its critics claimed that *Time* discounted input from its [digital democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_democracy) among its readers. *Time* supporters argue that an online poll is not representative as it has no scientific value. The [hyperlink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Resource_Locator) to the online poll results has been removed.[^2758] A 2014 *[New York Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Daily_News)* article, which named the "You" naming as one of the ten most controversial "Person of the Year" moments in the history of *Time*, also remarked that "2006 had its fair share of newsmakers" while highlighting both Chávez and Ahmadinejad.[^2745]

### Corporate Memphis

**Corporate Memphis**, also known as ***Alegria***, is an [art style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_style) that features [minimalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimalism), flat elements, bright, solid colors, and [cartoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartoon)-like figures with disproportionate limbs and a lack of (smaller) details on larger figures. Named after the [Memphis Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Group), an Italian design group, the style became popular after [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook) introduced it in 2017 under the name *Alegria*. It has since been associated with corporate [Big Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Tech) in the late 2010s and early 2020s, having been used by companies such as [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google), [Slack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slack_%28software%29), and [WeTransfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WeTransfer). The style has received a polarized reception, with some designers criticizing it for its small color palette and describing it as lazy, while others have defended it on the basis of its depth and variety.

#### History

The term Corporate Memphis was coined by Mike Merrill.[^2759] The name originated from the title of an [Are.na](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Are.na) board that collected early examples, and is a reference to the [Memphis Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis_Group), a now-defunct 1980s Italian design group known for bright colors, childish patterns, and geometric shapes.[^2760]

The style dates to 2013, when [Apple Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc.) switched from [skeuomorphism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skeuomorphism) to flat design.[^2759] However, the modern-day style was created on [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook) in 2017 under the name *Alegria* by the media agency [Buck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buck_%28design_company%29).[^2761] The style became popular in the late 2010s and began to be referred to as "[globohomo](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/globohomo)" (global homogenization), Corporate Memphis, or "corporate tech style".[^2762] It began to trend in [editorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Editorial) illustration and especially the tech industry, which relied on simple, scalable illustrations to fill white space and add character to apps and web pages.[^2760]

#### Visual characteristics

The style is minimalist,[^2761] usually consisting of solid colors, cartoon-like figures, and flat elements. Its elements are distorted; arms are long and elastic,[^2759] while heads are small,[^2761] and torsos are disproportionate. Figures are abstract and often use bright colors, such as purple or blue skin, and are shown performing activities such as high-fiving, watering plants,[^2762] painting, and running. They can also be seen smiling.[^2760] A variant uses isometric projection.[^2759] Because of its flat elements, the style can be easily recreated, requiring less skill than skeuomorphic design.[^2761] While exaggerated proportions had gained prominence in western world by the early 20th century through [Modernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_art), such as in *[Les Demoiselles d'Avignon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Demoiselles_d'Avignon)* (1907) by [Pablo Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Picasso) and *[The Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance_%28Matisse%29)* (1910) by [Henri Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Matisse), this style became popular because of Facebook.[^2762]

#### Reception and use

When it was created in 2017, it was reported to be a success for Facebook, positioning it as a leader in modern design. Soon after, many companies aimed to replicate the style.[^2761] Image websites such as [Adobe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adobe_Inc.)'s art library, [Magnific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnific), and UnDraw have allowed users to adopt the style more easily. The style is used among startups, likely because it is cheaper than stock imagery. Smaller companies also use it to present themselves as "established tech companies". It is also present in [Big Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Tech), including property and financial technology companies. Writer Claire L. Evans wrote that the style makes Big Tech companies "look friendly, approachable, and concerned with human-level interaction and community - which is largely the opposite of what they really are". Companies such as [Slack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slack_%28software%29), [WeTransfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WeTransfer), [MoneyFarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MoneyFarm), and [Trainline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trainline) used the Corporate Memphis style, as did [Transport for London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transport_for_London).[^2759] [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google) featured a Corporate Memphis-styled video about Android in 2023.[^2763] *[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker)* has also used flat art designs by illustrators [Malika Favre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malika_Favre) and Olimpia Zagnoli,[^2762] including writer Sandra Siemens in her book *The Spoon*, which featured flat art illustrations by Bea Lozano.[^2764] [*Going Under*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Going_Under_%28video_game%29) (2020), a video game developed by [Aggro Crab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aggro_Crab), uses the Corporate Memphis art style, featuring minimalist and colorful characters,[^2765][^2766] as well as the new [Canadian passport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_passport) adopted in 2023.[^2767][^2768]

*[Wired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wired_%28magazine%29)* has reported that the style received criticism from graphic designers. Illustrator Jack Hurley described it as lazy, writing that it contains "simple shapes \[and\] untextured colours", while designer David Rudnick says that the style shows a universe made up of complementing elements where problems have already been resolved; he also criticized the small color palette and lack of depth.[^2759] Illustrator Julien Posture argues that criticism of the art style is rooted in larger anxieties about the creative industry under [capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism) and [neoliberalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoliberalism).[^2769] On the other hand, *[Creative Bloq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creative_Bloq)* had described it as "a pretty attractive design style".[^2770] *[Fast Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Company)* said that some scholars and illustrators liked the style, noting its depth and variety. Illustrator Julien Posture said that flat art style is often blamed for the issues the art industry has faced, while illustrator Michele Rosenthal, a self-described "flat-art apologist", defended the art style, despite saying that its distorted elements are associated with corporate styles.[^2762]

By 2022, *Fast Company* reported that companies had returned to 3D-like skeuomorphism.[^2762] *Creative Bloq* wrote that by 2023, its popularity had fallen due to its "uninspired design" and oversaturation, and that it had started to be "used as a form of parody".[^2761]

### Hellmouth

A **hellmouth** is a depiction of the entrance to [Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell) as the gaping mouth of a huge [monster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monster). Hellmouths are first present in [Anglo-Saxon art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxon_art) and often appear in scenes of the [Last Judgment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Judgment) and [Harrowing of Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrowing_of_Hell) in the late [medieval period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages) in Europe and at times, during the [Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance) and later. Hellmouths were used in polemical [popular prints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_print) after the [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation), when figures from the opposite side would be shown disappearing into the mouth.[^2771] A notable late appearance is in the two versions of a painting by [El Greco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Greco) of about 1578.[^2772] [Political cartoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_cartoon) showed [Napoleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_Bonaparte) leading his troops into a hell mouth.[^2773]

[Medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_theatre) and [early modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_period) theater incorporated hellmouths as [props](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theatrical_property) and [mechanical devices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_device) like [trapdoors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trapdoor) to give the audience a dramatic, vivid vision of an entrance to [Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell).[^2774][^2775]

A hellmouth was intended to remind a Christian audience of the danger of [damnation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damnation). Those shown entering, or already inside, are typically shown naked, their clothing not having survived the [general resurrection of the dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_resurrection) that is often part of the same image. Some, even if naked, wear headgear indicating their rank at the top of society, with the [papal tiara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_tiara), king's crown and [bishop's mitre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop's_mitre) the most common. Far rarer are indications of people being non-Christian, such as the [Jewish hat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_hat).[^2776]

#### History

According to art historian [Meyer Schapiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meyer_Schapiro), the oldest example of an animal-like hellmouth appears on an ivory carving of ca. 800 in the [Victoria and Albert Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_and_Albert_Museum). Schapiro notes most examples before the 12th century are English with many showing the [Harrowing of Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrowing_of_Hell), which appealed to Anglo-Saxon taste, as a successful military raid by Christ. Schapiro has speculated that the subject may have drawn from the pagan myth of the [Crack of Doom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crack_of_Doom), with the mouth that of the wolf-monster [Fenrir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenrir), slain by [Vidar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vidar), who is used as a symbol of Christ on the [Gosforth Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gosforth_Cross) and other pieces of [Anglo-Scandinavian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Scandinavian) art.[^2777] In the assimilation of Christianised [Viking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking) populations in northern England, pagan mythological imagery merged Christian ones, in [hogback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hogback_%28sculpture%29) grave markers for example.[^2778]

Satan himself is often shown sitting in Hell eating the damned. According to G. D. Schmidt this is a separate image, and a hellmouth should not be considered to be the mouth of Satan, although Hofmann is inclined to disagree with this.[^2779]

In the Anglo-Saxon [Vercelli Homilies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vercelli_Homilies) (4:46-48) Satan is likened to a [dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon) swallowing the damned:

> ... ne cumaþ þa næfre of þæra wyrma seaðe & of þæs dracan ceolan þe is Satan nemned.

Translation:

> \[they\] never come out of the pit of snakes and of the throat of the dragon which is called Satan.[^2779]

The whale-monster [Leviathan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leviathan) (translated from [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language), [Job](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Job) 41:1, "wreathed animal") has been equated with this description, although this is hard to confirm in the earliest appearances. However, in *[The Whale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Whale_%28poem%29)*, an [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English) poem from the [Exeter Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exeter_Book), the mouth of Hell is compared to a whale's mouth:

> The whale has another trick: when he is hungry, he opens his mouth and a sweet smell comes out. The fish are tricked by the smell and they enter into his mouth. Suddenly the whale's jaws close.
>
> Likewise, any man who lets himself be tricked by a sweet smell and led to sin will go into hell, opened by the devil, if he has followed the pleasures of the body and not those of the spirit. When the devil has brought them to hell, he clashes together the jaws, the gates of hell. No one can get out from them, just as no fish can escape from the mouth of the whale.[^2780]

Later in the Middle Ages, the classical [Cerberus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerberus) also became associated with the image.[^2781]

##### Later depictions

In general, hellmouths appear less frequently in Italy by the late 14th century. In Northern European works by [Hieronymous Bosch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hieronymous_Bosch) and his followers, where the wide interior of Hell is shown, a hellmouth is sometimes included. A hellmouth appears, swallowing a bishop, at bottom left in *The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse*, a famous [woodcut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodcut) by [Albrecht Dürer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albrecht_D%C3%BCrer) (c. 1497-98).

Greek painters were the exception to the decline in the depiction of hellmouth. Painters of the [Cretan School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretan_School) and the [Heptanese School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionian_school_%28painting%29) continued to depict variations of hellmouths in their Last Judgement imagery.[^2782][^2783] [Georgios Klontzas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgios_Klontzas) (1535-1608) created a significant amount of works depicting hellmouths, some include *[The Last Judgment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Judgment_%28Klontzas%29)* and *[The Last Judgement Triptych](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Judgement_Triptych_%28Klontzas%29)*. Other works featuring hellmouth were completed by [Frantzeskos Kavertzas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franghias_Kavertzas) in 1641 entitled *[The Last Judgment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Judgment_%28Kavertzas%29)* and [Leos Moskos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leos_Moskos) in 1653, entitled *[The Last Judgment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Judgment_%28Moskos%29)*.[^2784][^2783][^2782]

### Portland International Airport carpet

[Portland International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_International_Airport) (PDX) features an iconic carpet. Situated in [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon), United States, the [carpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpet) features geometric shapes on a [teal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teal) background, representing the intersection of the north and south runways seen by air traffic controllers from the airport's tower at night.

SRG Partnership designed the carpet in 1987, and it was installed throughout [Portland International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_International_Airport) in the early 1990s. In 2013, the [Port of Portland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Portland_%28Oregon%29) announced the carpet's replacement with a new pattern conceptualized by the Portland-based firm [Zimmer Gunsul Frasca Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZGF_Architects_LLP). Removal of the original carpet began in January 2015, with the airport recycling worn portions and making remaining pieces available for sale by local retail vendors. In February 2022, it was announced that the iconic carpet would be returning to a portion of the airport. After renovations to the main terminal were completed in 2024, the original design is once again in a section of the airport.[^2785][^2786] The renovated terminal opened on August 15, 2024.[^2787]

The carpet's design has proven popular, and its removal attracted attention on [social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media) from fans in the 2010s. The carpet has been referenced by Portland's NBA basketball team, the [Portland Trail Blazers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_Trail_Blazers). In 2015, point guard [Damian Lillard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damian_Lillard) released his first PDX carpet [colorway](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/colorway) on the [Adidas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adidas) D Lillard 1 sneaker.[^2788] In 2016, Lillard released the colorway on the D Lillard 2,[^2789] also inspired by the carpet. In November 2022, the Trail Blazers introduced their City Edition uniforms. The uniform pays homage to the airport carpet with a sash design that mimics the geometric pattern of the carpet.[^2790]

#### Background

To reduce the amount of noise created by people walking across hard terminal floors, the [Port of Portland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Portland_%28Oregon%29) contracted SRG Partnership to design new carpeting for [Portland International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_International_Airport) (PDX) in 1987. The SRG principal and co-designer of the carpet, Jon Schleuning, visited several airports before deciding what to create for the carpet at PDX. SRG steered away from the earth tones traditionally used by airports in the 1980s, incorporating blue and green into their design early on and hoping to evoke "northwest to the core".[^2791] Its pattern featured geometric shapes on a teal background,[^2792] an abstract depiction of the intersecting north and south runways seen by air traffic controllers from the airport's tower at night.[^2791][^2793][^2794] Several acres of the carpet were installed by the early 1990s.[^2791]

Over time, the carpet gained a cult following. Multiple social media accounts were dedicated to it and more than 20,000 pictures were posted to its official [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram) [hashtag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashtag), *\#pdxcarpet*.[^2793] Airport visitors often took pictures of their feet on the carpet.[^2794]

The original carpet design received a positive reception by Portland residents and airport visitors, eventually reaching "local icon" status.[^2793] Its pattern was used on a variety of products, including bicycle helmets, socks and T-shirts.[^2793] In 2013, *Portland Monthly* published "Ode on a Carpet", a poem inspired by [T. S. Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot)'s "[The Hollow Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hollow_Men)" (1925).[^2793][^2795] In September 2014, PDX installed an 11 ft × 16 ft (3.4 m × 4.9 m) collage made of the carpet.[^2793]

#### Replacement and return

A \$13 million replacement[^2796] of the airport's carpet was announced in 2013, sparking social media attention that was picked up by local and national media outlets.[^2794] The Port of Portland received a large number of comments from local residents who were concerned about the original carpet's future. Annie Linstrom, a spokesperson for the port district, confirmed they were investigating recycling options and considering giving away portions to locals as keepsakes.[^2791][^2793] She also said that the Port of Portland "understand\[s\] that people have an emotional connection to the carpet".[^2791] In December 2013, *[Portland Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_Monthly)* published a preview of the redesign, which was conceptualized by [Zimmer Gunsul Frasca Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZGF_Architects_LLP) of Portland. The magazine reported that the new design included "mood-enhancing colors and a new repeating pattern, while clearly preserving key elements" from the original carpet.[^2792] Linstrom said, "The Port hopes that travelers will grow to appreciate elements of the new carpet design over time, just as much as the old."[^2792]

In January 2015, removal of the nearly-30-year-old carpet began in front of a crowd of airport employees and media. The Port of Portland's chief operating officer said: "Normally we do these ribbon cuttings when we’re introducing a new thing, but it’s actually the reverse of that in removing the old carpet. We’re going to miss the carpet and we appreciate the community and the love of this carpet."[^2794] Any businesses that were able to receive, stockpile, and redistribute carpet could request 1,000 square yards (840 m²) from the Port of Portland.[^2793][^2794]

[^2792] According to [Oregon Public Broadcasting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Public_Broadcasting), the old and new carpet designs are similar in appearance "to the untrained, out-of-towner eye".[^2794] Installation was scheduled to continue through November 2015.[^2794] Local firm Hennebery Eddy Architects is overseeing its installation, having been contracted in June 2013 to select materials and manage logistics.[^2792] The new carpet is made of materials from recycled carpet and plastic bottles and jars.[^2793]

In February 2022, it was announced that the iconic carpet would be returning to the airport after the terminal was remodeled. On August 14, 2024, the remodeled terminal opened with the carpet featured in certain areas of the terminal.[^2797][^2798]
