### Tipu's Tiger

**Tipu's Tiger**, **Tippu's Tiger** or **Tipoo’s Tiger** is an 18th-century [automaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automaton) created for [Tipu Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipu_Sultan), the ruler of the [Kingdom of Mysore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Mysore) (present day [Karnataka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnataka)) in [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India). The carved and painted wood casing represents a [tiger mauling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger_attack) a near life-size British man. Mechanisms inside the tiger and the man's body make one hand of the man move, emit a wailing sound from his mouth and grunts from the tiger. In addition a flap on the side of the tiger folds down to reveal the keyboard of a small [pipe organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pipe_organ) with 18 notes.[^2799]

The automaton incorporates Tipu's emblem, the tiger, and expresses his hatred of his enemy, the British of the [East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company). It was taken from his [summer palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipu_Sultan's_Summer_Palace) when East India Company troops [stormed Tipu's capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Seringapatam) in 1799. The [Governor General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_India), [Lord Mornington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mornington), sent the tiger to Britain initially intending it to be an exhibit in the [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London). First exhibited to the London public in 1808 in [East India House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_House), then the offices of the East India Company in London, it was transferred to the [Victoria and Albert Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_and_Albert_Museum) in 1880.[^2800] It now forms part of the permanent exhibit on the "Imperial courts of South India".[^2801] From the moment it arrived in London to the present day, Tipu's Tiger has been a popular attraction to the public.

#### Background

Tipu's Tiger was originally made for [Tipu Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipu_Sultan) (also referred to as Tippoo Sahib, Tippoo Sultan and other epithets in nineteenth-century literature) in the Kingdom of Mysore (today in the Indian state of [Karnataka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnataka)) around 1795.[^2802] [Tipu Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipu_Sultan) used the tiger systematically as his emblem, employing tiger motifs on his weapons, on the uniforms of his soldiers, and in the decoration of his palaces.[^2803] His throne rested upon a probably similar life-size wooden tiger, covered in gold; like other valuable treasures it was broken up for the highly organised [prize fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prize_money) shared out among the British army.[^2804][^2805]

Tipu had inherited power from his father [Hyder Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyder_Ali), a Muslim soldier who had risen to become *dalwai* or commander-in-chief under the ruling Hindu [Wodeyar dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wodeyar_dynasty), but from 1760 was in effect the ruler of the kingdom. Hyder, after initially trying to ally with the British against the [Marathas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratha), had later become their firm enemy, as they represented the most effective obstacle to his expansion of his kingdom, and Tipu grew up with violently anti-British feelings.[^2806]

The tiger formed part of a specific group of large [caricature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caricature) images commissioned by Tipu showing European, often specifically British, figures being attacked by tigers or elephants, or being executed, tortured and humiliated and attacked in other ways. Many of these were painted by Tipu's orders on the external walls of houses in the main streets of Tipu's capital, [Seringapatam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seringapatam).[^2807] Tipu was in "[close co-operation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Indian_alliances)" with the French, who were at war with Britain and still had [a presence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_India) in South India, and some of the French craftsmen who visited Tipu's court probably contributed to the internal works of the tiger.[^2808]

It has been proposed[^2809] that the design was inspired by the death in 1792 of a son of General [Sir Hector Munro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Hector_Munro), who had commanded a division during [Sir Eyre Coote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyre_Coote_%28East_India_Company_officer%29)'s victory at the [Battle of Porto Novo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Porto_Novo) ([Parangipettai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parangipettai)) in 1781 when [Hyder Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyder_Ali), Tipu Sultan's father, was defeated with a loss of 10,000 men during the [Second Anglo-Mysore War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Mysore_War).[^2810] Hector Sutherland Munro, a 17-year-old East India Company Cadet on his way to Madras,[^2811] was attacked and killed by a tiger on 22 December 1792 while hunting with several companions on [Saugor Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagar_Island) in the [Bay of Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bay_of_Bengal) (still one of the last refuges of the [Bengal tiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal_tiger)).[^2812][^2813][^2814]

However a similar scene was depicted on the silver mount on a gun made for Tipu and dated 1787-88, five years before the incident. The [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art), which owns the [Staffordshire figure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staffordshire_figure) group illustrated, suggests that the continuing popularity of the subject into the 1820s was due to Tipu's automaton being on display in London.[^2815]

#### Description

Tipu's Tiger is notable as an example of early musical automata from India,[^2816] and also for the fact that it was especially constructed for Tipu Sultan.[^2800]

With overall dimensions for the object of 71.2 centimetres (28.0 in) high and 172 centimetres (68 in) long, the man at least is close to life-size.[^2802] The painted wooden shell forming both figures likely draws upon South Indian traditions of Hindu religious sculpture.[^2817] It is typically about half an inch thick, and now much reinforced on the inside following bomb damage in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II). There are many openings at the head end, formed to match the pattern of the inner part of the painted tiger stripes, which allow the sounds from the pipes within to be heard better, and the tiger is "obviously male". The top part of the tiger's body can be lifted off to inspect the mechanics by removing four screws. The construction of the human figure is similar but the wood is much thicker.[^2818] Examination and analysis by the V&A conservation department has determined that much of the current paint has been restored or overpainted.[^2819]

The human figure is clearly in European costume, but authorities differ as to whether it represents a soldier or civilian; the current text on the V&A website avoids specifying, other than describing the figure as "European".[^2820]

The operation of a crank handle powers several different mechanisms inside Tipu's Tiger. A set of bellows expels air through a pipe inside the man's throat, with its opening at his mouth. This produces a wailing sound, simulating the cries of distress of the victim. A mechanical link causes the man's left arm to rise and fall. This action alters the pitch of the 'wail pipe'. Another mechanism inside the tiger's head expels air through a single pipe with two tones. This produces a "regular grunting sound" simulating the roar of the tiger. Concealed behind a flap in the tiger's flank is the small ivory keyboard of a two-stop pipe organ in the tiger's body, allowing tunes to be played.[^2821]

The style of both shell and workings, and analysis of the metal content of the original brass pipes of the organ (many have been replaced), indicates that the tiger was of local manufacture. The presence of French artisans and French army engineers within Tipu's court has led many historians to suggest there was French input into the mechanism of this automaton.[^2809]

#### History

Tipu's Tiger was part of the extensive plunder from Tipu's palace captured in the fall of Seringapatam, in which Tipu died, on 4 May 1799, at the culmination of the [Fourth Anglo-Mysore War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Anglo-Mysore_War). An *[aide-de-camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aide-de-camp)* to the Governor-General of India, [Richard Wellesley, 1st Marquess Wellesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Wellesley,_1st_Marquess_Wellesley), wrote a memorandum describing the discovery of the object:[^2822][^2823]

> "In a room appropriated for musical instruments was found an article which merits particular notice, as another proof of the deep hate, and extreme loathing of Tippoo Saib towards the English. This piece of mechanism represents a royal Tyger in the act of devouring a prostrate European. There are some barrels in imitation of an Organ, within the body of the Tyger. The sounds produced by the Organ are intended to resemble the cries of a person in distress intermixed with the roar of a Tyger.[^2824] The machinery is so contrived that while the Organ is playing, the hand of the European is often lifted up, to express his helpless and deplorable condition. The whole of this design was executed by Order of Tippoo Sultaun. It is imagined that this memorial of the arrogance and barbarous cruelty of Tippoo Sultan may be thought deserving of a place in the Tower of London."

The earliest published drawing of Tipu's Tiger was the frontispiece for the book "A Review of the Origin, Progress and Result, of the Late Decisive War in Mysore with Notes" by [James Salmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Salmond_%28East_India_Company_officer%29), published in London in 1800. It preceded the move of the exhibit from India to England and had a separate preface titled "Description of the Frontispiece" which said:[^2825]

> "This drawing is taken from a piece of mechanism representing a royal tyger in the act of devouring a prostrate European. There are some barrels in imitation of an organ within the body of the tyger, and a row of keys of natural notes. The sounds produced by the organ are intended to resemble the cries of a person in distress, intermixed with the roar of a tyger. The machinery is so contrived, that while the organ is playing, the hand of the European is often lifted up to express his helpless and deplorable condition.
>
> The whole of this design is as large as life, and was executed by order of Tippoo Sultaun, who frequently amused himself with the sight of this emblematic triumph of the Khoodadaud, over the English, Sircar. The piece of machinery was found in a room of the palace at Seringapatam appropriated for the reception of musical instruments, and called the Rag Mehal.
>
> The original wooden figure from which the drawing is taken will be forwarded, by the ships of this season, to the Chairman of the Court of Directors, to be presented to his Majesty. It is imagined that this characteristic emblem of the ferocious animosity of Tippoo Sultaun against the British Nation may not be thought undeserving of a place in the Tower of London."

Unlike Tipu's throne, which also featured a large tiger, and many other treasures in the palace, the materials of Tipu's Tiger had no intrinsic value, which together with its striking iconography is what preserved it and brought it back to England essentially intact. The Directors of the [East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company) had at first intended to present the tiger to the Crown, with a view to it being displayed in the [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London), but then decided but to keep it for the company. After some time in store, during which period the first of many "misguided and wholly unjustified endeavours at "improving" the piece" from a musical point of view may have taken place, it was displayed in the reading-room of the East India Company Museum and Library at [East India House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_House) in [Leadenhall Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadenhall_Street), London from July 1808.[^2826][^2827]

It rapidly became a very popular exhibit, and the crank-handle controlling the wailing and grunting could apparently be freely turned by the public. The French author [Gustave Flaubert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustave_Flaubert) visited London in 1851 to see the [Great Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Exhibition), writes [Julian Barnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Barnes), but finding nothing of interest in [The Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crystal_Palace), visited the East India Company Museum where he was greatly enamoured by Tipu's Tiger.[^2828] By 1843 it was reported that "The machine or organ ... is getting much out of repair, and does not altogether realize the expectation of the visitor".[^2829] Eventually the crank-handle disappeared, to the great relief of students using the reading-room in which the tiger was displayed, and *[The Athenaeum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenaeum_%28British_magazine%29)* later reported that

> "These shrieks and growls were the constant plague of the student busy at work in the Library of the old India House, when the Leadenhall Street public, unremittingly, it appears, were bent on keeping up the performances of this barbarous machine. Luckily, a kind fate has deprived him of his handle, and stopped up, we are happy to think, some of his internal organs... and we do sincerely hope he will remain so, to be seen and admired, if necessary, but to be heard no more".[^2830]

When the East India Company was taken over by the Crown in 1858, the tiger was stored in [Fife House, Whitehall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fife_House,_Whitehall) until 1868, when it moved down the road to the new [India Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_Office), which occupied part of the building still used by today's [Foreign and Commonwealth Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Office). In 1874 it was moved to the India Museum in [South Kensington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Kensington), which was in 1879 dissolved, with the collection distributed between other museums; the V&A records the tiger as acquired in 1880. During World War II the tiger was badly damaged by a German bomb which brought down the roof above it, breaking the wooden casing into several hundred pieces, which were carefully pieced together after the war, so that by 1947 it was back on display. In 1955 it was exhibited in New York at the [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art) through the summer and spring.[^2831][^2832]

In recent times, Tipu's Tiger has formed an essential part of museum exhibitions exploring the historical interface between Eastern and Western civilisation, colonialism, ethnic histories and other subjects, one such being held at the Victoria and Albert Museum itself in autumn 2004 titled "Encounters:the meeting of Asia and Europe, 1500-1800".[^2833] In 1995, 'The Tiger and the Thistle' bi-centennial exhibition was held in Scotland on the topic of "Tipu Sultan and the Scots". The organ was considered too fragile to travel to Scotland for the exhibition. Instead, a full-sized replica made of fibreglass and painted by Derek Freeborn, was exhibited in its place. The replica itself also had an earlier Scottish association, having been made in 1986 for 'The Enterprising Scot' exhibition, which was held to commemorate the October 1985 merger of the [Royal Scottish Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Scottish_Museum) and the [National Museum of Antiquities of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Antiquities_of_Scotland) to form a new entity - the [National Museum of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Scotland).[^2802]

Today, Tipu's Tiger is a well known single work in the Victoria and Albert Museum. It is considered a "must-see" highlight for school children's visits to the Victoria and Albert Museum, and functions as an iconic representation of the museum, replicated in various forms of memorabilia in the museum shops including [postcards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postcard), model kits and stuffed toys.[^2834] Visitors can no longer operate the mechanism since the device is now kept in a glass case.

A small model of this toy is exhibited in [Tipu Sultan's wooden palace in Bangalore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipu_Sultan's_Summer_Palace).[^2835] Although other items associated with Tipu, including his sword, have recently been purchased and brought back to India by billionaire [Vijay Mallya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijay_Mallya),[^2836] Tipu's Tiger has not itself been the subject of an official repatriation request, presumably due to the ambiguity underlying Tipu's image in the eyes of Indians; his being an object of loathing in the eyes of some Indians while considered a hero by others.[^2837]

#### Symbolism

Tipu Sultan identified himself with tigers; his personal epithet was 'The Tiger of Mysore,' his soldiers were dressed in 'tyger' jackets, his personal symbol invoked a tiger's face through clever use of calligraphy and the tiger motif is visible on his throne, and other objects in his personal possession, including Tipu's Tiger.[^2838][^2839] Accordingly, as per Joseph Sramek, for Tipu the tiger striking down the European in the organ represented his symbolic triumph over the British.[^2840]

The British hunted tigers, not just to emulate the [Mughals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughals) and other local elites in this "royal" sport, but also as a symbolic defeat of Tipu Sultan and any other ruler who stood in the path of British domination.[^2840] The tiger motif was used in the "Seringapatam medal" which was awarded to those who participated in the 1799 campaign, where the British lion was depicted as overcoming a prostrate tiger, the tiger being the dynastic symbol of Tipu's line. The Seringapatam medal was issued in gold for the highest dignitaries who were associated with the campaign as well as select officers on general duty, silver for other dignitaries, field officers and other staff officers, in copper-[bronze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze) for the non-commissioned officers and in [tin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin) for the privates. On the reverse it had a frieze of the storming of the fort while the obverse showed, in the words of a nineteenth-century tome on medals, "the BRITISH LION subduing the TIGER, the emblem of the late Tippoo Sultan's government, with the period when it was effected and the following words 'ASAD ULLAH GHALIB', signifying the Lion of God is the conqueror, or the conquering Lion of God."[^2841]

In this manner, the iconography of this automaton was adopted and overturned by the British.[^2842] When Tipu's Tiger was displayed in London in the nineteenth century, British viewers of the time "characterised the tiger as a trophy and symbolic justification of British colonial rule".[^2843] Tipu's Tiger along with other trophies such as Tipu's sword, the throne of [Ranjit Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranjit_Singh), [Tantya Tope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tantya_Tope)'s *[kurta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurta)* and [Nana Saheb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nana_Saheb)'s betel-box which was made of brass, were all displayed as "memorabilia of the Mutiny".[^2844]

In one interpretation, the display of Tipu's Tiger in South Kensington, served to remind the visitor of the *[noblesse oblige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noblesse_oblige)* of the British Empire to bring civilisation to the barbaric lands of which Tipu was king.[^2845]

Tipu's Tiger is also notable as a literal image of a tiger killing a European, an important symbol in England at the time, and from about 1820 the "Death of Munro" became one of the scenes in the repertoire of [Staffordshire pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staffordshire_pottery) figurines.[^2810][^2813] Tiger-hunting in the [British Raj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj), is also considered to represent not just the political subjugation of India, but in addition, the triumph over India's environment.[^2840] The iconography persisted and during the [rebellion of 1857](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Rebellion_of_1857), [Punch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch_%28magazine%29) ran a political cartoon showing the Indian rebels as a tiger, attacking a victim in an identical pose to Tipu's Tiger, being defeated by the British forces shown by the larger figure of a lion.

> "Whether made for Tippoo himself or for some other Indian potentate a century and a half earlier, it is difficult to convey a more lively impression of the mingled ferocity and childish want of taste so characteristic of the majority of Asian princes than will be communicated at once by this truly barbarous piece of music."

*,  [The Penny Magazine of the Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_Magazine), 15 August 1835[^2846]*

It has been suggested that Tipu's Tiger also contributed indirectly to the development of a popular early-20th-century stereotype of China as the "Sleeping Lion". A recent study describes how this popular stereotype actually drew on Chinese reports about the tiger.[^2847]

Motives for collection of articles, such as Tipu's Tiger, are seen by literary historian Barrett Kalter as having a social and cultural context.[^2848] The collection of Western and [Indian art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_art) by Tipu Sultan is seen by Kalter as motivated by the need to display his wealth and legitimise his authority over his subjects who were predominantly Hindu and did not share his religion, viz. Islam.[^2848] In the case of the East India Company, collection of documents, artefacts and *objet's d'art*  from India helped develop the idea of a subjugated Indian populace in the minds of the British people, the thought being that the possession of such objects of a culture represented understanding of, dominance over, and mastery of that culture.[^2848]

#### As a musical instrument

In a detailed study published in 1987 of the tiger's musical and noise-making functions, Arthur W.J.G. Ord-Hume concluded that since coming to Britain, "the instrument has been ruthlessly reworked, and in doing so much of its original operating principles have been destroyed".[^2849] There are two ranks of pipes in the organ (as opposed to the wailing and grunting functions), each "comprising eighteen notes, \[which\] are nominally of 4ft pitch and are [unisons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unison) - i.e. corresponding pipes in each register make sounds of the same musical pitch. This is an unusual layout for a pipe organ although while selecting the two stops together results in more sound ... there is also detectable a slight beat between the pipes so creating a [celeste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voix_c%C3%A9leste) effect. ... it is considered likely that as so much work has been done ... this characteristic may be more an accident of tuning than an intentional feature".[^2850] The tiger's grunt is made by a single pipe in the tiger's head and the man's wail by a single pipe emerging at his mouth and connected to separate [bellows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellows) located in the man's chest, where they can be accessed by unbolting and lifting off the tiger. The grunt operates by cogs gradually raising the weighted "grunt-pipe" until it reaches a point where it slips down "to fall against its fixed lower-board or reservoir, discharging the air to form the grunting sound"[^2851] Today all the sound-making functions rely on the crank-handle to power them, though Ord-Hume believes this was not originally the case.[^2818]

Works on the noise-making functions included those made over several decades by the famous organ-building firm [Henry Willis & Sons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Willis_&_Sons), and Henry Willis III, who worked on the tiger in the 1950s, contributed an account to a monograph by Mildred Archer of the V&A. Ord-Hume is generally ready to exempt Willis work from his scathing comments on other drastic restorations, which "vandalism" is assumed to be by unknown earlier organ-builders.[^2852] There was a detailed account of the sound-making functions in *[The Penny Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Penny_Magazine)* in 1835, whose anonymous author evidently understood "things mechanical and organs in particular".[^2853] From this and Ord-Hume's own investigations, he concluded that the original operation of the man's "wail" had been intermittent, with a wail only being produced after every dozen or so grunts from the tiger above, but that at some date after 1835 the mechanism had been altered to make the wail continuous, and that the bellows for the wail had been replaced with smaller and weaker ones, and the operation of the moving arm altered.[^2818][^2854]

Puzzling features of the present instrument include the placing of the handle, which when turned is likely to obstruct a player of the keyboard.[^2855] Ord-Hume, using the 1835 account, concludes that originally the handle (which is a nineteenth-century British replacement, probably of a French original) only operated the grunt and wail, while the organ was operated by pulling a string or cord to work the original bellows, now replaced.[^2856][^2857] The keyboard, which is largely original, is "unique in construction", with "square ivory buttons" with round [lathe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lathe)-turned tops instead of conventional keys. Though the mechanical functioning of each button is "practical and convenient" they are spaced such that "it is almost impossible to stretch the hand to play an octave".[^2858][^2857] The buttons are marked with small black spots, differently placed but forming no apparent pattern in relation to the notes produced and corresponding to no known system of marking keys.[^2850][^2857] The two stop control knobs for the organ are located, "rather confusingly", a little below the tiger's testicles.[^2859] The instrument is now rarely played, but there is a V&A video of a recent performance.[^2857]

#### Derivative works

Tipu's Tiger has provided inspiration to poets, sculptors, artists and others from the nineteenth century to the present day.[^2860] The poet [John Keats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Keats) saw Tipu's Tiger at the museum in Leadenhall Street and worked it into his satirical verse of 1819, *The Cap and Bells*.[^2860] In the poem, a soothsayer visits the court of the Emperor Elfinan. He hears a strange noise and thinks the Emperor is snoring.[^2861]

"Replied the page: "that little buzzing noise….

Comes from a play-thing of the Emperor’s choice,

From a Man-Tiger-Organ, prettiest of his toys"

The French poet, [Auguste Barbier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Barbier), described the tiger and its workings and meditated on its meaning in his poem, *Le Joujou du Sultan* (The Plaything of the Sultan) published in 1837.[^2862][^2863] More recently, the American [Modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist) poet, [Marianne Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marianne_Moore) wrote in her 1967 poem *Tippoo's Tiger* about the workings of the automaton,[^2864] though in fact the tail was never movable:

"The infidel claimed Tipu's helmet and cuirasse

and a vast toy - a curious automaton

a man killed by a tiger; with organ pipes inside

from which blood-curdling cries merged with inhuman groans.

The tiger moved its tail as the man moved his arm."

*Die Seele* (The Souls), a work by painter [Jan Balet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Balet) (1913-2009), shows an angel trumpeting over a flower garden while a tiger devours a uniformed French soldier.[^2860] The Indian painter [M. F. Husain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._F._Husain) painted Tipu's Tiger in his characteristic style in 1986 titling the work as "Tipu Sultan's Tiger".[^2865] The sculptor [Dhruva Mistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhruva_Mistry), when a student at the [Royal College of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_College_of_Art), adjacent to the Victoria and Albert Museum, frequently passed Tipu's Tiger in its glass case and was inspired to make a fibre-glass and plastic sculpture *Tipu* in 1986.[^2860] The sculpture *Rabbit eating Astronaut* (2004) by the artist Bill Reid is a humorous *homage* to the tiger, the rabbit "chomping" when its tail is cranked round.[^2866]

The 2023 novel *Loot*[^2867] by [Tania James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tania_James) imagines the life of a young wood carver from Mysore who co-creates Tipu's Tiger, and years later goes on a quest for it at the English country estate of a British East India Company colonel who took it from Tipu's palace after his death.

### Comic book death

In the [comic book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comic_book) fan community, the apparent [death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death) and subsequent return of a long-running [character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_%28arts%29) is often called a **comic book death**. A comic book death is generally not taken seriously by readers and is rarely permanent or meaningful other than for story or thematic purposes. The term is usually not applied to characters who have the ability to return from the dead as an established power or ability, such as [Solomon Grundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon_Grundy_%28character%29) or [Ra's al Ghul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ra's_al_Ghul).

#### Context

Commenting on the impact and role of comic book character deaths, writer [Geoff Johns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoff_Johns) said: "Death in superhero comics is cyclical in its nature, and that's for a lot of reasons, whether they are story reasons, copyright reasons, or fan reasons".[^2868] The phenomenon of comic book death is particularly common for superhero characters. Writer [Danny Fingeroth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Fingeroth) suggests that the nature of superheroes requires that they be both ageless and [immortal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immortality).[^2869]

A common expression regarding comic book death was once "No one stays dead except [Bucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucky_Barnes), [Jason Todd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Todd), and [Uncle Ben](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle_Ben)",[^2870][^2871] referring to the seminal importance of those characters' deaths to the title character: [Captain America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_America)'s [sidekick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidekick) (retconned dead in 1964),[^2872] Batman's second [Robin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_%28character%29) (dead in 1988),[^2873][^2874] and [Spider-Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider-Man)'s uncle (dead since 1962),[^2875] respectively. This long-held tenet was broken in 2005, when Jason Todd returned to life as the [Red Hood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hood)[^2874] and Bucky was retconned to have survived the accident that seemingly killed him, and brought back as the [Winter Soldier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Soldier_%28comics%29) who had remained in the shadows for decades.[^2872] Uncle Ben also reappeared briefly thanks to Doctor Strange, as a way to reward to Peter Parker for helping stop Dormammu's revival, but he disappeared after speaking with Parker.[^2876]

Because death in American super-hero comics is so often temporary, readers rarely take the death of a character seriously; when a character dies, readers feel very little sense of loss, and are simply left wondering how long it will be before they return to life.[^2877][^2878][^2879][^2880]

#### Notable examples

Although several comic book deaths are well-known, two of the best-known are the 1980 "death" of [Jean Grey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Grey) in Marvel's "[Dark Phoenix Saga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dark_Phoenix_Saga)" and that of [Superman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superman) in [DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DC_Comics)'s highly publicized 1993 "[Death of Superman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Death_of_Superman)" storyline. There is one major distinction between the two, however: whereas it was never intended that Superman's death be permanent, but rather that he would return to life at the conclusion of the story,[^2881] Jean's passing was intended to be permanent, as the editor [Jim Shooter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Shooter) felt that would be the only satisfactory outcome given that she had committed mass murder.[^2882][^2883] Despite this, the story was [retconned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retroactive_continuity) a few years later to facilitate Jean's return, with the rationale, that the Phoenix was never Jean Grey to begin with, but an exact duplicate of her while Jean was actually cocooned underwater at the floor of the body of water where Phoenix emerged until she was found and recovered by the [Fantastic Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantastic_Four).

In 2007, the [death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Death_of_Captain_America) of [Captain America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_America) made real-world headlines[^2870][^2884][^2885][^2886][^2887][^2888] when he met his apparent end, but Steve Rogers returned in *Captain America: Reborn* two years later in 2009.[^2889][^2890]

[Planters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planters) cited comic book deaths (particularly those adapted in the [Marvel Cinematic Universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Cinematic_Universe)) as the inspiration for a storyline killing off its century-old mascot [Mr. Peanut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Peanut) in January 2020 and having him reborn as a baby the next month.[^2891]

An early [prime time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_time) television version of this plot trope is in the 1970s original superhero series *[The Six Million Dollar Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Six_Million_Dollar_Man)* after the 2-part episode "The Bionic Woman" produced spectacular ratings. With that unexpected success, the producers wanted to produce a [spin-off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinoff_%28media%29) series featuring the character despite the fact that [Jaime Sommers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaime_Sommers_%28The_Bionic_Woman%29) was killed off on the operating table from bionic rejection at the story's conclusion. To do so, a story in the next season, "Return of the Bionic Woman"! was produced where Steve Austin discovers that Jaime had been placed in [cryogenic freezing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryopreservation) at another doctor's insistence after she was declared dead, which allowed her medical condition to be successfully treated enough to revive her, albeit without her memory of Steve Austin.[^2892]

#### In-universe acknowledgement

> [Sasquatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasquatch_%28comics%29): Good guys do occasionally come back from the dead, though not as often as the bad guys...\
> [Talisman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talisman_%28Alpha_Flight%29): But that really only seems to happen to the big guns of the super hero biz, [Captain America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_America), the [Sub-Mariner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namor), people like them.

 *[Alpha Flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Flight_%28comic_book%29)* \#23, June 1985

> [The Thing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thing_%28Marvel_Comics%29): But I thought you X-Men always come back from the dead!

 *[Fantastic Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantastic_Four_%28comic_book%29)* \#395, December 1994

> [She-Hulk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/She-Hulk): (Handling Charles Xavier's will) I know this is a delicate question and one I would not normally have to ask, but you are the X-Men and you don't do normal ... To the best of your knowledge, is Xavier really dead? I only ask because we both know that "dead" and "dead dead"...

 *[Uncanny X-Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncanny_X-Men)* vol. 3 \#23 (September 2014)

Comic book characters themselves have made comments about the frequency of resurrections. [Professor X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professor_X) has commented "in mutant [heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heaven) there are no [pearly gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearly_gates), but instead [revolving doors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolving_door)".[^2893] When [Siryn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siryn) was made aware of [her father](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banshee_%28character%29)'s death, she refused to mourn him, giddily claiming that since her father has died as an [X-Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-Men), he was likely going to be soon resurrected, shocking her friends.[^2894] Her father is restored to life but is recruited by the [Apocalypse Twins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apocalypse_Twins) as part of their new [Horsemen of Apocalypse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horsemen_of_Apocalypse).[^2895]

Stating that he often pondered why superheroes return to life, [Reed Richards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mister_Fantastic) said "it's almost proof of [a higher power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-Above-All), of someone who needs us to live to stop what's coming. To fight the good fight".[^2896] The obituary writer of the in-universe newspaper the *[Daily Bugle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_Bugle)* bemoaned to reporter [Ben Urich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Urich) about how many retractions he has had to write after each resurrection of a superhero or [supervillain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supervillain).[^2897] In one issue of *[The Incredible Hercules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hercules_%28Marvel_Comics%29)*, there is a betting game for then deceased superheroes to return to life.[^2898]

### The Metric Marvels

***The Metric Marvels*** is a 1978-1979 series of seven animated educational [shorts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_film) featuring songs about [meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre), [liters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litre), [Celsius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celsius), and [grams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram), designed to teach [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States) children how to use the [metric system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_system). They were produced by Newall & Yohe, the same advertising agency which produced [ABC's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company) *[Schoolhouse Rock!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schoolhouse_Rock!)* series, and first aired on the [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC) television network in September 1978.[^2899] The spots were shown three times each Saturday during the children's programming block for the 1978-79 season.[^2900]

Voices for the *Metric Marvels* shorts include [Lynn Ahrens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn_Ahrens), [Bob Dorough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dorough), [Bob Kaliban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Kaliban), and [Paul Winchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Winchell).

#### Origins

On December 23, 1975, President [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford) signed the [Metric Conversion Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metric_Conversion_Act) into law; this act gave official sanction for the United States to convert to the metric system of measurement. At the time the United States mainly used the [U.S. Customary system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_customary_units). Ford's presidential successor, [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter), began to implement this law in earnest, helping to set up the [U.S. Metric Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Metric_Board) as a task force to determine when and how the U.S. would [convert to metric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metrication_in_the_United_States). The USMB suggested that the transition ought to be voluntary and gradual, taking place over at least a ten-year period.

As part of this gradual transition, the USMB sponsored a number of [public service announcements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_service_announcement) on radio and television. *The Metric Marvels* was one such television PSA, aired during NBC's Saturday morning cartoons. The shorts featured four animated metric superheroes: **Meter Man**, **Liter Leader**, **Super Celsius** and **Wonder Gram**.[^2901] Each superhero performed songs designed to teach children the difference between the old English system and the new metric system.

#### Episodes

1.  "**Meet Meter Man**" / Superhero Meter Man helps people convert length and distance to metric terms
2.  "**Mara-Mara-Marathon**" / The difference between miles and kilometers
3.  "**I'm Your Liter Leader**" / Superhero Liter Leader explains the difference between gallons and liters
4.  "**Eeny, Meeny, Miney Milliliters**" / Liter Leader uses recipes to explain milliliters
5.  "**Super Celsius**" / Superhero Super Celsius explains the Celsius temperature scale
6.  "**Wonder Gram**" / Superhero Wonder Gram expresses her weight in kilograms
7.  "**Wonder Baby**" / A young Wonder Gram converts pounds to kilograms

#### Legacy

The series shared the animation style, song quality and voice actors with the popular *Schoolhouse Rock!* on rival network [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company). Incoming NBC president [Fred Silverman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Silverman), formerly of ABC, may have thought to replicate the success of that show; Newall & Yohe also produced Saturday morning network IDs and the full-length *Drawing Power!* series for NBC. Despite this, the series was pulled from the air after a single seven-episode season. Being separated from *Schoolhouse Rock!* prevented the series from having an afterlife in [reruns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rerun). Moreover, at the time NBC was ranked third place in viewership among the three dominant television networks.

A deadline for metrication was never passed into United States federal law, and the push for metrication in the United States lost traction following the 1982 dissolution of the [United States Metric Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Metric_Board) under [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States) [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan). U.S. metrication is currently overseen by the [National Institute of Standards and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Institute_of_Standards_and_Technology), whose newer series *League of SI Superheroes* bears some similarities to *The Metric Marvels*, including a character named Meter Man with many similarities to the identically named character in the latter series.

#### Media

*The Metric Marvels* was released on VHS for educational buyers only in 1979 by Newell and Yohe, Inc.; Center for Humanities, Mount Kisco, NY. This release was in color and included one videocassette (approximately 17 min. 30 sec.) and seven teacher's guides, described as "seven 2+1⁄2 minute segments in which four animated superheroes explain the metric system" and carried the note "Previously issued as seven filmstrips by Xerox Films". The Xerox Films filmstrip release was described as "Elementary and junior high school, Filmstrip" and included seven 35 mm color filmstrips (approximately 200 frames), seven audiocassettes and five teacher's guides.[^2902] Xerox Films was a producer of films for schools and libraries, and was one of the 10 companies making up The Xerox Education Group at the time.[^2903]

### Year Hare Affair

***Year Hare Affair*** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language): 那年那兔那些事(儿); lit. 'Those stories of that rabbit that happened in those years')**[^2904]** is a Chinese [webcomic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webcomic) and media franchise by Lin Chao (林超), initially under the [pen name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pen_name) "逆光飞行" ([Pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin): *Nìguāng Fēixíng*, lit. "flight against the light"). The comic uses [anthropomorphic animals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropomorphic_character) as an [allegory for nations and sovereign states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_personification) to represent 20th and 21st century political, military, and diplomatic events.

#### Animation

*Year Hare Affair* was inspired by a lengthy post on a military web forum.[^2904]

Lin Chao created the animation.[^2905] It launched in 2015 and had its seventh season in 2025.[^2905]

#### Overview

The series uses anthropomorphic figures to depict China's history during and after the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War) period.[^2904] China is represented by a white rabbit, which the series portrays as peaceful and intelligent.[^2904] In the words of the series creator, the hare is "harmless to humans and animals alike."[^2905]

*Yare Hare Affair* conveys patriotic themes through metaphor and ideologically-vested euphemism.[^2905] The series calls on every hare to help "building China as a powerful nation".[^2905]

#### Characters

##### Factions and characters

| Nations / Sovereign states | Appearance | Reasons and source of the appearance |
|----|----|----|
| [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China) (or [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party)) | [Hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hare) | Hares are [herbivorous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbivorous) animals that are usually considered cute, docile and populous, as well as being "harmless to humans and animals alike" ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language): 人畜无害), but can still inflict nasty bites and kicks when irritated, representing the People's Republic of China's traditionally not so aggressive foreign policies, but can still pack a heavy punch when required. Another explanation for it is that the Chinese words for "[comrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comrade)" and "rabbit/hare" sound very similar when pronounced with a [Shanghainese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghainese) accent, as famously coined by [crosstalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiangsheng) comedian [Jiang Kun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiang_Kun_%28comedian%29) during the 1980s. The Hare normally prefers to act friendly and *[moe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moe_%28slang%29)* in front of others and is obsessed with working the fields harvesting [carrots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrot) and earning "small money", but when provoked into fighting often wields a [cleaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_chef's_knife) and a [brick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick) in each hand while emitting a hellish black [aura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aura_%28paranormal%29), and later learns to "plant [mushrooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mushroom_cloud)" and build "[water cabinets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanks_in_China)". When extremely enraged, the Hare dons a green [dinosaur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur) [suit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creature_suit), grabs a kitchen cleaver and a brick and becomes a [Godzilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godzilla)-like [monster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaiju) that [breathes fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire-breathing_monster). |

The Soviet bear has a symbol, the [hammer and sickle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hammer_and_sickle) of [Communism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communism), on his stomach, which later becomes more like a character, "父", meaning "father" in Chinese. |
| [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia) | Brown bear | To differentiate from Soviet Union, this bear has a character "大" ("big" in Chinese, or "eldest" when describing age order of siblings) on his stomach, meaning that he is the "eldest son" of the USSR. The hair refers to "毛子" ("hairy ones", referring to the comparatively higher [body hair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_hair) count in [Caucasians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caucasian_race)), a common [northern Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandarin_Chinese) nickname for [Russians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russians) (and all [East Slavs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Slavs) by extension). |
| [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine) | Brown bear | To differentiate from Russia, this bear has a number "2" on his stomach, meaning that he is the "second son" of the USSR. |
| [Belarus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus) | Brown bear | To differentiate from Russia, this bear has a number "3" on his stomach, meaning that he is the "third son" of the USSR. |
| [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan) | [Poussin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poussin_%28chicken%29) (insists on being addressed as [Crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crane_%28bird%29)) | The crane is an important symbol of Japanese culture, despite the [green pheasant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_pheasant) (who are [Galliformes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galliformes) while cranes are [Gruiformes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gruiformes)) being Japan’s official national bird. However, it is mocked and called [poussin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poussin_%28chicken%29) in canon. |

To differentiate with North Korea, a US-style [combat helmet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_helmet) is added to the appearance of South Korea. |
| [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea) | [Stick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaoli_bangzi) with a military skicap | To differentiate with South Korea, a Communist-style [red star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_star) cap is added to the appearance of North Korea. |

The Chinese characters for "update" (更) and "paste" (羹) are homophones both pronouncing *Gēng*, causing the series' fans to create a parodic [light poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_poetry): "if the Snake doesn't update, make \[him into\] a [snake paste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake_soup) ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language): 麻蛇不更麻蛇羹)." |

#### Video game

A [free-to-play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free-to-play) [strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategy_video_game) [role-playing video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Role-playing_video_game) based on the webcomic, was released on iOS and Android on 15 July 2015. The player controls one of three factions: Hare, Bald Eagle and Bear.[^2922] Another game called “Year Hare Affair: Burning Snow” was also released sometime later, and can currently be played on [itch.io](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Itch.io).[^2923] An [educational game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educational_game) about [Chinese history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_history) was also released and unlike the first two, this one can be played in its original format.[^2924]

#### Reception

Hare (Chinese: 我兔; lit. 'Our rabbit') is now used as [Internet slang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_slang) referring to China.[^2925]

##### Criticisms

The historical vision, provided in the first two seasons of *Year Hare Affair*, came under heavy criticism in an overview on the Russian website South China Insight, especially [Sino-Soviet relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Soviet_relations). Though it is admitted that relations with Russia "occupy a leading place" in reflecting of Chinese history, but with a "complete disregard for historical facts", such as Soviet involvement in the Chinese Communist Party's foundation and the [Red Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Army)'s [liberation of Manchuria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_invasion_of_Manchuria) from Japanese forces. It was also noted that the [Sino-Vietnamese War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Vietnamese_War) has been completely left out.[^2926]

Oiwan Lam of [Global Voices Online](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Voices_Online) finds [racism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism) in portraying African nations as hippopotamuses, which she considers "a lazy and stupid animal". In that regard, "China's aid for Africa has also been simplified as a last resort because 'the [first world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World) refused to play with us'".[^2927]

Some commentators argue that the webcomic and its animated adaptation oversimplify complex historical events, potentially promoting nationalist sentiment or stereotypes, especially in its depiction of countries such as Japan, South Korea, and the United States.[^2928] Critics have also pointed out instances where the series' satirical elements may reinforce negative stereotypes or historical grievances rather than fostering understanding.[^2929] Conversely, defenders of the series highlight its satirical and entertainment-focused intent, suggesting that it should not be interpreted as a historical documentary or a precise representation of historical facts, but rather as a creative work aimed at humor and satire.[^2930]

##### Ratings

The second and third season received 8.6 and 8.4 points out of 10 on [Douban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douban).[^2931]
