### Loudness war

The **loudness war** (or **loudness race**) is a trend of increasing audio levels in recorded music, which reduces audio fidelity and, according to many critics, listener enjoyment. Increasing [loudness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudness) was first reported as early as the 1940s, with respect to [mastering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastering_%28audio%29) practices for [7-inch singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7-inch_single).[^3318] The maximum [peak level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peak_level) of analog recordings such as these is limited by varying specifications of electronic equipment along the chain from source to listener, including [vinyl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinyl_record) and [cassette players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassette_player). The issue garnered renewed attention starting in the 1990s with the introduction of [digital signal processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_signal_processing) capable of producing further loudness increases.

With the advent of the [compact disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_disc) (CD), music is encoded to a [digital format](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_signal_%28signal_processing%29) with a clearly defined maximum peak amplitude. Once the maximum amplitude of a CD is reached, loudness can be increased still further through [signal processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal_processing) techniques such as [dynamic range compression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_range_compression) and [equalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equalization_%28audio%29). Engineers can apply an increasingly high ratio of compression to a recording until it peaks more frequently at the maximum amplitude, a technique colloquially known as *brickwalling*. In extreme cases, efforts to increase loudness can result in [clipping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clipping_%28audio%29) and other audible [distortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_distortion).[^3319] Modern recordings that use extreme dynamic range compression and other measures to increase loudness therefore can sacrifice sound quality to loudness. The competitive escalation of loudness has led music fans and members of the musical press to refer to the affected albums as "victims of the loudness war".[^3320]

#### History

While most critics trace the beginning of the loudness war to the introduction of the CD in the 1980s,[^3321] the practice of focusing on loudness in audio mastering had been documented before that;[^3322][^3323] when the [vinyl phonograph record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phonograph_record) was the primary released recording medium and when [7-inch singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_%28music%29) were played on [jukebox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jukebox) machines in clubs and bars. The so-called *wall of sound* (inspired by [Phil Spector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Spector)'s [Wall of Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_of_Sound) production technique) formula preceded the loudness war, but achieved its goal using a variety of techniques, such as instrument doubling and [reverberation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverberation), as well as [compression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_range_compression).[^3324][^3325]

Jukeboxes became popular in the 1940s and were often set to a predetermined level by the owner, so any record that was mastered louder than the others would stand out. Similarly, starting in the 1950s, producers would request louder 7-inch singles so that songs would stand out when auditioned by [program directors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Program_director) for radio stations.[^3318] In particular, many [Motown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motown) records pushed the limits of how loud records could be made; according to one of their engineers, they were "notorious for cutting some of the hottest 45s in the industry."[^3326] In the 1960s and 1970s, [compilation albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_album) of hits by multiple different artists became popular, and if artists and producers found their song was quieter than others on the compilation, they would insist that their song be [remastered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remaster) to be competitive.

Because of the limitations of the vinyl format, the ability to manipulate loudness was also limited. Attempts to achieve extreme loudness could render the medium unplayable. One example was the *hot* master of *[Led Zeppelin II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Led_Zeppelin_II)* by mastering engineer [Bob Ludwig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Ludwig) which caused some [cartridges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_cartridge) to mistrack; the album was recalled and issued with lower compression levels.[^3327] Digital media such as CDs remove these restrictions and as a result, increasing loudness levels have been a more severe issue in the CD era.[^3328] Modern computer-based digital audio effects processing allows mastering engineers to have greater direct control over the loudness of a song: for example, a *brick-wall limiter* can look ahead at an upcoming signal to limit its level.[^3329]

##### 1980s

The 1980s saw the advent of the CD, which allowed for higher [dynamic range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_range) than previous analog formats. This encouraged mastering engineers to make use of the potential of the then-new format, even though much of the industry was yet to know how to best optimize for the CD.[^3325] The common practice of mastering music for CD at the time involved matching the highest peak of a recording at, or close to, digital [full scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_scale), and referring to digital levels along the lines of more familiar analog [VU meters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VU_meter). When using VU meters, a certain point (usually -18[^3330] or −20 dB[^3331] below the disc's maximum amplitude) was used in the same way as the saturation point (signified as 0 dB) of analog recording, with several dB of the CD's recording level reserved for amplitude exceeding the saturation point (often referred to as the *red zone*, signified by a red bar in the meter display), because digital media cannot exceed 0 decibels relative to full scale ([dBFS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DBFS)).[^3331] The average [RMS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_mean_square) level of the average rock song during most of the decade was around −16.8 dBFS.[^3332]

##### 1990s

By the early 1990s, mastering engineers had learned how to optimize for the CD medium and the loudness war had not yet begun in earnest.[^3325] However, CDs with louder audio levels had already begun to surface, with the levels becoming more and more likely to bump up to the digital limit,[^3333] resulting in recordings where the peaks on an average rock or beat-heavy pop CD hovered near 0 dBFS,[^3334] but only occasionally reached it.[^3335]

The concept of making music releases *hotter* began to appeal to people within the industry, in part because of how noticeably louder some releases had become and also in part because the industry believed that customers preferred louder-sounding CDs, even though that may not have been true.[^3336] Engineers, musicians, and labels each developed their own ideas of how CDs could be made louder.[^3337] In 1994, the first digital brick-wall limiter with look-ahead (the [Waves L1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waves_Ltd)) was mass-produced; this feature, since then, has been commonly incorporated in digital mastering limiters and maximizers.[^3338] While the increase in CD loudness was gradual throughout the 1990s, some opted to push the format to the limit, such as on [Oasis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oasis_%28band%29)'s widely popular album *[(What's the Story) Morning Glory?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%28What's_the_Story%29_Morning_Glory?)*, whose RMS level averaged −8 dBFS on many of its tracks, a rare occurrence, especially in the year it was released (1995).[^3325] [Red Hot Chili Peppers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hot_Chili_Peppers)'s *[Californication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Californication_%28album%29)* (1999) represented another milestone, with prominent clipping occurring throughout the album.[^3337]

##### 2000s

By the early 2000s, the loudness war had become fairly widespread, especially with some remastered re-releases and greatest hits collections of older music. In 2008, loud mastering practices received mainstream media attention with the release of [Metallica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallica)'s *[Death Magnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_Magnetic)* album. The CD version of the album has a high average loudness that pushes peaks beyond the point of digital clipping, causing distortion. This was reported by customers and music industry professionals, and covered in multiple international publications, including *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone)*,[^3339] *[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal)*,[^3340] [BBC Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio),[^3341] *[Wired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wired_%28magazine%29)*,[^3342] and *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian)*.[^3343] [Ted Jensen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Jensen), a mastering engineer involved in the *Death Magnetic* recordings, criticized the approach employed during the production process.[^3320] When a version of the album without dynamic range compression was included in the [downloadable content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downloadable_content) for the video game *[Guitar Hero III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_Hero_III)*, copies of this version were actively sought out by those who had already purchased the official CD release. The *Guitar Hero* version of the album songs exhibit much higher dynamic range and less clipping than those on the CD release, as can be seen from the illustration.[^3344]

In late 2008, mastering engineer [Bob Ludwig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Ludwig) offered three versions of the [Guns N' Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guns_N'_Roses) album *[Chinese Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Democracy)* for approval to co-producers [Axl Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axl_Rose) and Caram Costanzo. They selected the one with the least compression. Ludwig wrote, "I was floored when I heard they decided to go with my full dynamics version and the loudness-for-loudness-sake versions be damned." Ludwig said the "fan and press backlash against the recent heavily compressed recordings finally set the context for someone to take a stand and return to putting music and dynamics above sheer level."[^3345]

##### 2010s

In March 2010, mastering engineer [Ian Shepherd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Shepherd) organised the first Dynamic Range Day,[^3346] a day of online activity intended to raise awareness of the issue and promote the idea that "Dynamic music sounds better". The day was a success and its follow-ups in the following years have built on this, gaining industry support from companies like [SSL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_State_Logic), [Bowers & Wilkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowers_&_Wilkins), [TC Electronic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TC_Electronic) and [Shure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shure) as well as engineers like [Bob Ludwig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Ludwig), Guy Massey and [Steve Lillywhite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Lillywhite).[^3347] Shepherd cited research showing there was no connection between sales and loudness, and that people preferred more dynamic music.[^3324][^3348] He also argued that file-based [loudness normalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudness_normalization) will eventually render the war irrelevant.[^3349]

One of the biggest albums of 2013 was [Daft Punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daft_Punk)'s *[Random Access Memories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_Access_Memories)*, with many reviews commenting on the album's great sound.[^3350][^3351] Mixing engineer [Mick Guzauski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Guzauski) deliberately chose to use less compression on the project, commenting "We never tried to make it loud and I think it sounds better for it."[^3352] In January 2014, the album won five Grammy Awards, including [Best Engineered Album (Non-Classical)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Engineered_Album,_Non-Classical).[^3353]

Analysis in the early 2010s suggested that the loudness trend may have peaked around 2005 and subsequently reduced, with a pronounced increase in [dynamic range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_range) (both overall and minimum) for albums since 2005.[^3354]

In 2013, mastering engineer [Bob Katz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Katz) predicted that the loudness war would be over by mid-2014, claiming that mandatory use of [Sound Check](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_Check_%28iTunes_feature%29) by Apple would lead to producers and mastering engineers to turn down the level of their songs to the standard level, or Apple will do it for them. He believed this would eventually result in producers and engineers making more dynamic masters to take account of this factor.[^3355][^3356][^3357]

[Earache Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earache_Records) reissued much of its catalog as part of its *Full Dynamic Range* series, intended to counteract the loudness war and ensure that fans hear the music as it was intended.[^3358]

##### 2020s

By the late 2010s/early 2020s, most major streaming services began [normalizing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_normalization) audio by default, which can be turned off if not wanted.[^3359] Target loudness for normalization varies by platform:

**Audio normalization per streaming service**

| Service | Loudness (measured in [LUFS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LUFS)) |
|----|----|
| [Amazon Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Music) | −13 LUFS[^3360] |
| [Apple Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music) | −16 LUFS[^3360] |
| [SoundCloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SoundCloud) | −14 LUFS[^3360] |
| [Spotify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spotify) | −14 LUFS, −11 and −19 available in premium[^3361][^3362] |
| [Tidal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tidal_%28streaming_service%29) | −14 (default) or −18 LUFS[^3363][^3360] |
| [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube) | −14 LUFS[^3364] |
| [YouTube Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube_Music) | −7 LUFS[^3365] |

Measured LUFS may further vary among streaming services due to differing measurement systems and adjustment algorithms. For example, Amazon, Tidal, and YouTube do not increase the volume of tracks.[^3360]

Some services do not normalize audio; [Bandcamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bandcamp) is an example.[^3360]

Despite the widespread adoption of loudness normalization, at least one critic has argued that the loudness war did not end but evolved. Mastering engineers have continued to master tracks for maximum loudness using aggressive compression combined with targeted equalization, rather than simple peak limiting, since a track is typically mastered assuming non-normalized playback even though most listeners now experience normalized audio.[^3366]

#### Radio broadcasting

When music is broadcast over radio, the station applies its own [signal processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_signal_processing), further reducing the dynamic range of the material to closely match levels of absolute amplitude, regardless of the original recording's loudness.[^3367]

Competition for listeners between radio stations has contributed to a loudness war in radio broadcasting.[^3368] Loudness jumps between television broadcast channels and between programmes within the same channel, and between programs and intervening adverts are a frequent source of audience complaints.[^3369] The [European Broadcasting Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Broadcasting_Union) has addressed this issue in the EBU PLOUD Group with publication of the [EBU R 128](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EBU_R_128) recommendation. In the U.S., legislators passed the [CALM act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CALM_act), which led to enforcement of the formerly voluntary [ATSC A/85](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATSC_A/85) standard for loudness management.

#### Criticism

In 2007, Suhas Sreedhar published an article about the loudness war in the engineering magazine *[IEEE Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_Spectrum)*. Sreedhar said that the greater possible dynamic range of CDs was being set aside in favor of maximizing loudness using digital technology. Sreedhar said that the over-compressed modern music was fatiguing, that it did not allow the music to *breathe*.[^3370]

The production practices associated with the loudness war have been condemned by recording industry professionals including [Alan Parsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Parsons) and [Geoff Emerick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoff_Emerick),[^3371] along with mastering engineers [Doug Sax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Sax), [Stephen Marcussen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Marcussen), and [Bob Katz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Katz).[^3326] Musician [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan) has also condemned the practice, saying, "You listen to these modern records, they're atrocious, they have sound all over them. There's no definition of nothing, no vocal, no nothing, just like, static."[^3372][^3373] Music critics have complained about excessive compression. The [Rick Rubin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Rubin)-produced albums *[Californication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Californication_%28album%29)* and *[Death Magnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_Magnetic)* have been criticised for loudness by *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian)*; the latter was also criticised by *[Audioholics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audioholics)*.[^3374][^3375] *[Stylus Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylus_Magazine)* said the former suffered from so much digital clipping that "even non-audiophile consumers complained about it".[^3325]

Opponents have called for immediate changes in the music industry regarding the level of loudness.[^3373] In August 2006, [Angelo Montrone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angelo_Montrone), the vice-president of [A&R](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A&R) for One Haven Music (a Sony Music company), in an open letter decrying the loudness war, claimed that mastering engineers are being forced against their will or are preemptively making releases louder to get the attention of industry heads.[^3328] Some bands are being petitioned by the public to re-release their music with less distortion.[^3371]

The nonprofit organization Turn Me Up! was created by [Charles Dye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dye), [John Ralston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Ralston_%28musician%29), and Allen Wagner in 2007 with the aim of certifying albums that contain a suitable level of dynamic range[^3376] and encourage the sale of quieter records by placing a Turn Me Up! sticker on certified albums.[^3377] As of 2019, the group has not produced an objective method for determining what will be certified.[^3378]

A hearing researcher at [House Ear Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Ear_Institute) is concerned that the loudness of new albums could possibly harm listeners' hearing, particularly that of children.[^3377] The [Journal of General Internal Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_General_Internal_Medicine) has published a paper suggesting increasing loudness may be a risk factor in hearing loss.[^3379][^3380]

A two-minute YouTube video addressing this issue by audio engineer Matt Mayfield[^3381] has been referenced by *[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal)*[^3382] and the *[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tribune)*.[^3383] Pro Sound Web quoted Mayfield, "When there is no quiet, there can be no loud."[^3384]

The book *Perfecting Sound Forever: An Aural History of Recorded Music*, by Greg Milner, presents the loudness war in radio and music production as a central theme.[^3337] The book *Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science*, by Bob Katz, includes chapters about the origins of the loudness war and another suggesting methods of combating the war.[^3332] These chapters are based on Katz's presentation at the 107th Audio Engineering Society Convention (1999) and subsequent *Audio Engineering Society Journal* publication (2000).[^3385]

#### Debate

In September 2011, Emmanuel Deruty wrote in *[Sound on Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sound_on_Sound)*, a recording industry magazine, that the loudness war has not led to a decrease in dynamic variability in modern music, possibly because the original digitally recorded source material of modern recordings is more dynamic than [analogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_signal) material. Deruty and Tardieu analyzed the *loudness range* (LRA) over a 45-year span of recordings and observed that the [crest factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crest_factor) of recorded music diminished significantly between 1985 and 2010, but the LRA remained relatively constant.[^3354] Deruty and Damien Tardieu criticized Sreedhar's methods in an AES paper, saying that Sreedhar had confused crest factor (peak to RMS) with [dynamics in the musical sense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_%28music%29) (pianissimo to fortissimo).[^3386]

This analysis was also challenged by [Ian Shepherd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Shepherd) and Bob Katz on the basis that the LRA was designed for assessing loudness variation within a track while the EBU R128 peak to loudness ratio (PLR) is a measure of the peak level of a track relative to a reference loudness level and is a more helpful metric than LRA in assessing overall perceived dynamic range. PLR measurements show a trend of reduced dynamic range throughout the 1990s.[^3387][^3388]

Debate continues regarding which measurement methods are most appropriate to evaluating the loudness war.[^3389][^3390][^3391]

### Uruguayan Invasion

The **Uruguayan Invasion** was a musical phenomenon of the 1960s similar to the [British Invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Invasion), with [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_roll) bands from [Uruguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruguay) gaining popularity in [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina).

#### History

Inspired by [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_rock) bands like [The Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles) and [The Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones), many young musicians in [Montevideo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo), Uruguay began to imitate their sounds. Two bands in particular, [Los Shakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Shakers) and [Los Mockers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Mockers) mirrored The Beatles and The Rolling Stones respectively.[^3406] Popular bands of the Uruguayan Invasion sang mostly in [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language).[^3406]

In the mid-1960s, as the British Invasion was at its height in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States), Uruguayan bands began a similar rise to fame in Argentina. Record labels began rapidly signing Uruguayan rock bands to promote in Argentina. Argentine television shows like *Escala Musical* were also a springboard for many of the bands' popularity.

Like the [British Invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Invasion), the Uruguayan Invasion had died down by the late 1960s, as it became more popular to record harder-hitting Spanish-language music. Spurred on by the band [Los Gatos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Gatos_%28band%29)'s 1967 hit record "[La Balsa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Balsa)", most bands began to record in [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language). With the coming of the [military dictatorship in 1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civic-military_dictatorship_of_Uruguay), the Uruguayan Invasion effectively ended.[^3406]

#### Uruguayan Invasion bands

- [Los Shakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Shakers)
- Los Malditos
- [Los Mockers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Mockers)
- Kano y Los Bulldogs

[^3406]: Zolov, Eric (25 July 2011). ["Shakers And Mockers: Uruguay's Place In Latin Rock History"](https://www.npr.org/sections/altlatino/2011/07/25/137627714/shakers-and-mockers-uruguays-place-in-latin-rock-history). *NPR*. Retrieved 5 September 2022.

### Plants used as musical instruments

**Live plants** have been **used as musical instruments**, especially in [electronic music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_music).

Live plants can be used as [electronic musical instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_musical_instrument) by running a weak electric current through them and by [amplifying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amplifier) the way the current is changed when the plants are touched, or by applying [contact microphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_microphone) and amplifying the projection and tone of the sounds produced when handling them.[^3407]

[John Cage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cage) composed *Child of Tree* (1975) and *Branches* (1976) for what he described as "amplified plant materials". Cage was a proponent of [chance music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chance_music) and felt that the organic nature of music without man-made instruments was very strong and influential. The percussion group [So Percussion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Percussion) gave a concert in 2007 featuring Cage's pieces, where percussionist "Jason Treuting played an amplified cactus, running his hand over the plant's unfriendly spikes to produce an alluring sound like a babbling brook."[^3408]

Another piece for amplified cactus is *Degrees of Separation* "Grandchild of Tree" by Paul Rudy which received mention at the Bourges International Competition for Electroacoustic Music in 2000.[^3409] Rudy mentions in his own program notes:[^3410]

> The idea for a cactus and tape work came about when I heard a performance of John Cage's *Child of Tree*. I was immediately taken with the sound of the cactus in particular. Taken from its natural environment and placed in the confined and groomed existence of a pot, amplified with a contact microphone, the cactus took on a completely new and interesting character...

A piece by [Mark Andre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Andre), *...zu Staub...* also features three amplified cacti alongside classical instruments.

In 2007, the French digital artist duo [Scenocosme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gr%C3%A9gory_Lasserre_&_Ana%C3%AFs_met_den_Ancxt) created a sound installation where visitors create sounds by touching the leaves of plants in pots hanging from the ceiling.[^3411]

### Kawaii metal

**Kawaii metal** (also known as **cute metal**, **J-pop metal,** or **kawaiicore**[^3412]) is a musical genre that blends elements of [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music) and [J-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J-pop) that was pioneered in Japan in the early 2010s. The genre combines both Eastern and Western influences that appeal to both cultures.[^3413] A typical kawaii metal composition combines the instrumentation found in various types of heavy metal music with J-pop [melodies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody) and a [Japanese idol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_idol) aesthetic. Kawaii metal's lyrical topics often contain [kawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kawaii) (cute, lovable, kidlike) themes.[^3414]

The Japanese girl group [Babymetal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babymetal) is often credited with the creation and success of kawaii metal.

#### History and characteristics

Japanese [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music) [idol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_idol) group [Babymetal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babymetal) are considered the inventors of the kawaii metal genre.[^3415][^3416] The concept of kawaii metal started with [Key “Kobametal” Kobayashi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobametal), the producer behind the group Babymetal. In an interview conducted by Billboard, Kobayashi explains that he was “just trying to do something no one had heard before”.[^3417] Kawaii metal gained international popularity in 2014, when the group Babymetal uploaded a song to Youtube called "[Gimme Chocolate!!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gimme_Chocolate!!)"[^3418] Angelica Wallingford of *City Times* opined that Babymetal's [eponymous debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babymetal_%28album%29) had pioneered the kawaii metal musical genre. Wallingford also defined the genre, and album, as a "mixture of varying genres including [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music), [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music), heavy metal, [electronic dance music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music), [industrial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Death_Metal) and [symphonic death metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphonic_death_metal)".[^3419] A guest contributor at *The Independent* believed that the genre was a derivative of [J-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J-pop) and various [extreme metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extreme_metal) genres, namely "[speed metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_metal), [power metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_metal), [black metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_metal), and [industrial metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_metal)".[^3420]

While discussing Babymetal, [*The Sydney Morning Herald*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sydney_Morning_Herald)'s Rob Nash stated that the genre consisted of "sugary pop melodies over [thrash metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrash_metal)". Nash also believed that the group's song "[Awadama Fever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal_Resistance)" exemplified the genre, with its "slabs of angry guitar and undanceably fast breakbeats, while the girls \[Babymetal\] squeak about 'bubble ball fever' and chewing gum".[^3421]

Babymetal has remained extremely popular. In 2019, Babymetal became the first Asian artists to top Billboard’s Top Rock Albums chart, with their third studio album, [Metal Galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metal_Galaxy).[^3422] Murray Stassen in *Music Week* commented that "Babymetal is, without a doubt, a genuine cross-genre musical phenomenon" and that, despite how the juxtaposition of metal and J-pop might not seem to make sense on paper: "\[Babymetal has\] proved that it can, and does work, and resistance to the Babymetal phenomenon is futile."[^3423]

Discussing Ladybeard, and Ladybaby, Jake Cleland of *The Sydney Morning Herald* defined the genre as "saccharine pop with his heavy metal [growling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_growl)".[^3424] Alex Weiss of [*Paper*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paper_%28magazine%29) defined the genre as "[hard rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock) with sugary sweet pop hooks". Weiss also used Babymetal's songs "[Karate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karate_%28Babymetal_song%29)" and "[Road of Resistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_of_Resistance)" as examples to explain the differing lyrical perspective between the kawaii metal and other metal genres, stating that kawaii metal songs "offer a perspective often missing from the [hyper-masculine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypermasculinity), aggressive lyrics usually present in most of the \[metal\] genre's hits".[^3425] Felix Clay of [Cracked.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cracked.com) also believed that the genre had less aggressive lyricism, citing the genre had lyrics about "pop music topics like kittens, chocolate, and fun".[^3426]

### Dave Blunts

**Davion Blessing** (born July 1, 2000), known professionally as **Dave Blunts**, is an American rapper, singer, and songwriter. He gained popularity in December 2024 after videos of him performing while using an [oxygen tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_tank)[^3427] went [viral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viral_video) and yielded public concern for his health.

Blunts began recording and releasing music in 2018. In 2024, he started uploading videos to [TikTok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TikTok), quickly gaining popularity. His 2024 song "The Cup" went viral on the platform. In June 2024, Blunts released his debut studio album, *Well Dude Here's My Thing*. His second studio album, *If I Could I Would*, was released in October.

In April 2025, Blunts released his third studio album, *You Can't Say That*. That same year, Blunts began working with American rapper [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West), writing the majority of his unreleased studio album, *[Cuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuck_%28album%29)*. Blunts has been reported as the sole songwriter for the album's three singles: "[WW3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WW3_%28Kanye_West_song%29)", "[Cousins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cousins_%28Kanye_West_song%29)", and "[Heil Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heil_Hitler_%28song%29)".[^3428] Blunts later cut ties with West in September 2025, alleging that he was coerced into writing the album's Nazi-related lyrics.

#### Early life

Davion Blessing was born in [Salt Lake City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_City), Utah[^3429] on July 1, 2000.[^3430] When he was around three years old, he moved to [Davenport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davenport,_Iowa), Iowa.[^3429] He has two sisters and one brother. Their father died when Blunts was eight. Blessing was raised in the Christian church, but as he grew up, he separated from Christianity. Later in life, he realized his separation and decided to do [Bible study](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_study_%28Christianity%29) with friends, though he clarified that he did not have time for it in July 2024.[^3431]

Blessing began recording and releasing music on [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook) in 2018. Due to the nature of his humor and the memes he frequently posted, his accounts were often banned. One of these accounts, registered under the name "Dave Blunts," later served as the origin of his stage name.[^3432][^3431]

#### Career

##### 2024: Initial virality

After contemplating quitting music in late 2023, Blunts began uploading videos to [TikTok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TikTok) in 2024, quickly gaining popularity. He released three projects between February and March, as well as the single "The Cup", which received support from rapper [Lil Yachty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Yachty).[^3433] Blunts later signed to the Los Angeles label Listen to the Kids. On June 28, 2024, he released his debut studio album, *Well Dude Here's My Thing*.[^3434] He released his second studio album, *If I Could I Would*, on October 18.[^3435]

In November 2024, Blunts performed at Juice Wrld Day, a concert commemorating late rapper [Juice Wrld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Wrld), while using an oxygen tank.[^3436] Videos of the performance went [viral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viral_video).[^3437][^3438] During the performance, he directed criticism towards rapper [Snoop Dogg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snoop_Dogg), who had previously insulted Blunts in an [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram) post.[^3437][^3439] Snoop Dogg later apologized for his comments.[^3434]

##### 2025: *You Can't Say That* and work with Kanye West

On an episode of Bradley Martyn's *Raw Talk* podcast posted to [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube) on December 17, 2024, Blunts announced that his upcoming third studio album would be titled *Exactly So Shut Up*.[^3440] Blunts supported the upcoming album on February 28, 2025, with the release of "First Day Out The Hospital," which later landed on *[Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_Networks)'s* list of the 20 best “First Day Out” songs.[^3441][^3442] The album was ultimately titled *You Can't Say That* and was released on April 18, 2025. On the album, Blunts raps about his health struggles, record deals, previous feuds with other artists, and former girlfriends.[^3443][^3444] In an Instagram post accompanying the album's announcement, Blunts complained about people who accused him of being too vulgar, saying that, "these are the harsh realities of my life and I'm not gonna [Kidzbopify](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidz_Bop) my lyrics because the shit I go through is not sunshine and rainbows."[^3443] The album received generally positive reception, with *[Vibe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibe_%28magazine%29)* praising the record for being "littered with moments that leave you with no choice but to sing and jam along".[^3444]

In February 2025, Blunts met fellow rapper [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West) through the latter's agent, and they started working on an album together.[^3445][^3446] According to West, he and Blunts spent hours talking each day, and Blunts wrote songs based on their conversations.[^3447] Blunts has been reported as the sole writer for West's unreleased album *[Cuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuck_%28album%29)*, starting after the former previewed the single "[WW3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WW3_%28Kanye_West_song%29)".[^3448][^3449] The album's second single, titled "[Cousins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cousins_%28Kanye_West_song%29)", was fully written by Blunts.[^3450] Blunts has denied that the album is antisemitic, describing it as being "about one man going between hurt, betrayal and pain".[^3449] He has also published several reference tracks created for *Cuck* online.[^3451]

#### Musical style

Blunts's musical style is characterized by shock value, self-deprecating lines, and personal experiences with exes.[^3444][^3452] He has stated that his favorite topics to rap about are "women, \[his\] friends, traumatic experiences, and controversial topics."[^3431] Blunts typically opens his songs with a vocal warm-up, singing "Yeah… yeah yeah yeah yeah".[^3453] His style has been compared to fellow rapper [Juice Wrld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juice_Wrld).[^3452] Blunts's music revolves around [edgy humor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgy_humor)[^3454] and has been categorized as [meme rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meme_rap).[^3452] [Popculture.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popculture.com) and *RapReviews* have accused Blunts of using homophobic lyrics.[^3455][^3456]

#### Health concerns

Blunts's Juice Wrld Day performance prompted widespread concern for his well-being due to his [morbidly obese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morbidly_obese) condition and being dependent on an [oxygen tank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxygen_tank) while on stage.[^3438][^3437] Blunts reportedly weighed over 600 pounds (270 kg) during this period, as mentioned in a September 2024 interview.[^3457][^3458] He suffered [heart failure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_failure) in 2023.[^3436] Blunts was hospitalized a week before his Juice Wrld Day performance,[^3459] although he later stated it was for a [checkup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checkup).[^3460]

On December 24, 2024, Blunts pledged to better his health, throwing away his signature purple tracksuit.[^3461] He suffered a case of [influenza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Influenza) shortly afterward, and was hospitalized again when his symptoms worsened. He later posted to X that he was "not giving up as long as you guys don't give up on me."[^3462][^3463][^3464]

##### Weight-loss

In March 2025, [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West) pledged to help Blunts lose weight by connecting him to his own [personal trainer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_trainer).[^3465] Blunts later thanked West for his action, writing on Instagram that it meant the world to him.[^3466] In June, Blunts worked out with AMP streamer [Agent 00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agent_00), who declared that the rapper would have "abs by November." He later posted photos of him with celebrity trainer Bradley Martin, captioning it "One Step At a Time". West congratulated Blunts on his progress, texting him that "Nobody can fuck with you. Best rapper on the planet." According to Blunts, he had lost over 200 pounds during his last hospitalization.[^3457]

Due to his health, Blunts announced that he would "\[take\] a brief hiatus from the internet, from music, and truly just focus on exercising, eating right and bettering myself. Not for the fans, not for the bitches, myself."[^3457]

#### Feuds

##### 50 Cent

In July 2025, Blunts started feuding with rapper [50 Cent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50_Cent) after the latter mocked West for showing up at [Sean Combs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Combs)' trial. 50 Cent had made other statements towards West in the same year, mainly in response to the song "Cousins".[^3467] Blunts began feuding with 50 Cent to defend West, with both exchanging posts about each other on social media. After 50 Cent said he would push Blunts "down the stairs" if he ever saw him, the latter previewed a [diss track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diss_track) aimed at the former, named "Hey Curtis" in reference to the rapper's legal name, on [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram). In the track, Blunts calls him an "actor" who does not "really want no drama", as well as accusing the mother of his children of going to Combs' [freak off parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diddy_parties).[^3468][^3469] Blunts also mocked 50 Cent's appearance in the 2011 film *[All Things Fall Apart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Things_Fall_Apart)*, writing it off in comparison to his own weight loss, as 50 Cent "lost all that weight for that weak ass movie and nobody watched that shit."[^3468] The song's [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video), previewed a few days before its release, parodies the video for 50 Cent's 2003 [promotional single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promotional_single) "[Many Men (Wish Death)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Many_Men_%28Wish_Death%29)", with Blunts working out while a trio of nurses examine him.[^3470] The diss track was officially released as a single on August 23, 2025.[^3471]

##### Kanye West

Despite working on the majority of *Cuck*, Blunts cut ties with West on September 13, 2025, via a text exchange where he urged West to "please find God."[^3472] Previously that same week, Blunts posted to Instagram that he would no longer collaborate with West, as he was "on my own path."[^3473] On September 17, [a diss track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tired_Of_Being_Groomed) aimed at West surfaced on social media, in which Blunts accuses West of [grooming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_grooming) him into Nazi ideology and forcing him to write antisemitic lyrics.[^3474] Blunts claimed in the song that he wrote the tracks on *Cuck* for millions of dollars despite not wanting "handouts" from West, and clarified that he did not support [incest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incest) despite writing "Cousins".[^3474][^3475] Three days later, Blunts previewed a new diss track alleging that West is "off his rocker" due to not taking medication for his [bipolar disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipolar_disorder), additionally calling him "gay" due to the events described on "Cousins".[^3476] Although West did not respond to any of Blunts's statements, longtime collaborator [Consequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequence_%28rapper%29) defended him by suggesting that Blunts only used West for fame via a [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) post.[^3477]
