### Sixto Rodriguez

**Sixto Diaz Rodríguez** (July 10, 1942 - August 8, 2023), mononymously known as **Rodríguez**, was an American musician from [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit), Michigan.

Though his career was initially met with little fanfare in the United States, he found success in [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia) (touring the country twice in his earlier career), and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand). Unbeknownst to him for decades, his music grew extremely successful and influential in South Africa, where he is believed to have sold more records than [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley).[^3633][^3634] Information about him was scarce, and it was incorrectly rumored there that he had died by suicide shortly after releasing his second album.[^3635]

In the 1990s, determined South African fans managed to find and contact Rodriguez, which led to an unexpected revival of his musical career. This was told in the 2012 [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award)-winning documentary film *[Searching for Sugar Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Searching_for_Sugar_Man)* and helped give Rodriguez a measure of fame in his home country. In May 2013, Rodriguez received an honorary [Doctor of Humane Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Humane_Letters) degree from his alma mater, [Wayne State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_State_University), in Detroit.[^3636]

Rodriguez lived in Detroit's historic [Woodbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodbridge,_Detroit) neighborhood, through which he is seen walking in *Searching for Sugar Man*.[^3637] He lived a simple life, possessing no telephone, and occasionally visited bars in the [Cass Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cass_Corridor) section of Detroit near Woodbridge and [Midtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midtown_Detroit), such as the Old Miami pub, where he performed live concerts for small local crowds.[^3638]

#### Biography

##### Early life

Sixto Diaz Rodriguez was born on July 10, 1942, in Detroit, Michigan. He was the sixth child of Mexican immigrant working-class parents Ramon and Maria Rodriguez. His mother died when he was three years old.[^3639] They had joined an influx of Mexicans who came to the [Midwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwestern_United_States) to work in Detroit's industries.[^3640] Mexican immigrants at that time faced both intense alienation and marginalization.[^3641][^3642] In most of his songs, Rodriguez takes a political stance on the difficulties that faced the [inner-city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_city) poor.[^3643]

Sixto Rodriguez studied philosophy at Wayne State University in Detroit, earning his bachelor’s degree in 1981.[^3644]

##### Recording career

In 1967, using the name "Rod Riguez" (given by his record label), he released a single, "I'll Slip Away", on the small Impact label. He did not record again for three years, until he signed with [Sussex Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex_Records), then an offshoot of [Buddah Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddah_Records). He used his preferred professional name, "Rodriguez", after that. He recorded two albums with Sussex, *[Cold Fact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_Fact)* in 1970 and *[Coming from Reality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_from_Reality)* in November 1971. However, both sold few copies in the U.S. and he was dropped by Sussex two weeks before Christmas 1971, and Sussex itself closed in 1975.[^3645] While *Searching for Sugar Man* implied that he was in the process of recording a third album when Sussex dropped him, in 2013 Rodriguez told *Rolling Stone* magazine that he unsuccessfully lobbied filmmakers to cut a reference to his unfinished third album. He told the magazine, "To me it distracted. It almost cheapened the film, like it was a promo film.… I’ve written about 30 songs, and that’s pretty much what the public has heard."[^3646]

Rodriguez quit his music career and in 1976 he purchased a derelict Detroit house in a government auction for \$50 (US\$283 in 2025 dollars[^3647]) in which he still lived as of 2013.[^3648] He worked in demolition and production line work, always earning a low income. He remained politically active and motivated to improve the lives of the city's working-class inhabitants and had run unsuccessfully several times for public office: for the [Detroit City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_City_Council) in 1989, for [Mayor of Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_Detroit) in 1981 and 1993 and for the [Michigan House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_House_of_Representatives) in 2000.[^3649]

In 2013, it was announced that Rodriguez was in discussions with [Steve Rowland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Rowland_%28record_producer%29), the producer of his *Coming From Reality* album. "I've written about thirty new songs," Rodriguez told *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone)* magazine. "He told me to send him a couple of tapes, so I'm gonna do that. I certainly want to look him up, because now he's full of ideas."[^3650]

##### International fame

Although Rodriguez remained relatively unknown in his home country, by the mid-1970s his albums were starting to gain significant airplay in Australia, [Botswana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botswana), New Zealand, [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe) and South Africa.[^3651][^3652]

When imported copies of his Sussex albums were sold out, an Australian record label, Blue Goose Music, bought the Australian rights to his recordings. Blue Goose released his two studio albums as well as a compilation album, *[At His Best](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodriguez_at_His_Best)*, that featured unreleased recordings from 1973 - "Can't Get Away", "I'll Slip Away" (a re-recording of his first single), and "Street Boy".[^3653]

*At His Best* went platinum in South Africa, which at one stage was the major disc-press source of his music to the rest of the world. Rodriguez was compared to contemporaries such as [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan) and [Cat Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_Stevens). Many of his songs carry anti-establishment themes, and therefore boosted anti-apartheid protest culture in South Africa[^3654] where his work influenced the music scene at the time and was also a considerable influence on a generation drafted, mostly unwillingly, to the then whites-only South African military. Reportedly, anti-apartheid activist [Steve Biko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Biko) was also a Rodriguez fan.[^3655]

Rodriguez was also successful in Australia and performed two concert tours across the country in 1979 and 1981 after Australian concert promoters had tracked him down in Detroit.[^3656] At his first performance in Sydney he reportedly mumbled in front of a big audience, "Eight years later ... and this happens. I don’t believe it." Rodriguez later stated that after his second tour in Australia he thought it was the highlight of his career, and that "not much happened after that. No calls or anything.”[^3657]

In 1991, both of his albums were released on CD in South Africa for the first time, which helped preserve his fame. However, few details of his life were known to his fans and it was rumored that he had killed himself during a concert in the 1970s.[^3658]

Despite his success abroad, Rodriguez's fame in South Africa had remained unknown to him until 1997 when his eldest daughter, Eva, came across a website dedicated to him.[^3659] After contacting the website and learning of his fame in the country, Rodriguez went on his first South African tour, playing six concerts before thousands of fans. A documentary, *Dead Men Don't Tour: Rodriguez in South Africa* was made in 1998. He also performed in Sweden before returning to South Africa in 2001 and 2005.[^3660]

In 1998, Rodriguez's signature song, "[Sugar Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_Man_%28song%29)", was covered by the South African rock band [Just Jinjer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Just_Jinger) (then spelled *Just Jinger*) and, later, by the Scottish singer-songwriter [Paolo Nutini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Nutini). In 2002, it was used by disc-jockey [David Holmes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Holmes_%28musician%29) to open his mix album, *Come Get It I Got It*, gaining Rodriguez more international airplay. "Sugar Man" had previously gained even more fame by having been sampled in the song "You're Da Man" in rapper [Nas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nas)'s 2001 album *[Stillmatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stillmatic)*.[^3661]

In April 2007 and 2010, he returned to Australia to play at the [East Coast Blues & Roots Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Coast_Blues_&_Roots_Music_Festival),[^3662] as well as sell out shows in [Adelaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide), [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne) and [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney). His song "Sugar Man" was featured in the 2006 film *[Candy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candy_%282006_film%29)*, starring [Heath Ledger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heath_Ledger).[^3663] Singer-songwriter [Ruarri Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruarri_Joseph) covered Rodriguez's song "Rich Folks Hoax" for his third studio album.[^3664] Irish singer-songwriter Darragh O'Dea mentions Rodriguez and references "Inner City Blues" in his 2020 single "Lost Dog Loyal".[^3665] Rodriguez continued to tour in various countries until his final show in 2021.[^3666]

Rodriguez's albums *Cold Fact* and *Coming from Reality* were re-released by [Light in the Attic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_in_the_Attic_Records) in 2009.[^3667] They were rereleased again on CD and vinyl in 2019 by [Universal Music Enterprises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Music_Enterprises), the current rights holder of the material.

In 2014, the French deep house and electro music producer [The Avener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Avener) released a new version of "Hate Street Dialogue" originally appearing on Rodriguez's album *Cold Fact*. The version by The Avener features Rodriguez's vocals. The release charted in France.[^3668]

##### *Searching for Sugar Man*

In January, 2012, the [Sundance Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundance_Film_Festival) hosted the premiere of the documentary film *Searching for Sugar Man*, by Swedish director [Malik Bendjelloul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malik_Bendjelloul), detailing the efforts of two South African fans to see if his rumored death was true and, if not, to discover what had become of him. The documentary, produced by Simon Chinn and John Battsek, went on to win the World Cinema Special Jury Prize and the Audience Award, World Cinema Documentary.[^3669]

*Sugar Man* played at other film festivals, including the [True/False Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/True/False_Film_Festival) in [Columbia, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia,_Missouri) and the summer [Traverse City Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traverse_City_Film_Festival) in Michigan, where Rodriguez and Bendjelloul appeared on stage with festival organizer, award-winning film director [Michael Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Moore).[^3670] The film opened in New York and Los Angeles on July 27, 2012, before a larger domestic cinematic run.[^3671] It was also screened as part of cinema programs in some European music festivals during the summer of 2012, including the [Way Out West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Way_Out_West_Festival) festival in August, where Rodriguez also performed. In November it won both the Audience Award and the Best Music Documentary Award at the [International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Documentary_Film_Festival_Amsterdam).[^3672]

The [*Searching for Sugar Man* soundtrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Searching_for_Sugar_Man_%28soundtrack%29) features a compilation of Rodriguez tracks from his albums *[Cold Fact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_Fact)* and *[Coming from Reality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_from_Reality)*, in addition to three previously unreleased songs from his third unfinished album. The album was released on July 24, 2012.[^3673] To allay possible concerns raised in the film about how Rodriguez was apparently cheated by his previous record label, the back cover bears the statement "Rodriguez receives royalties from the sale of this release."[^3674]

*Searching for Sugar Man* won the [BAFTA Award for Best Documentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BAFTA_Award_for_Best_Documentary) on February 10, 2013.[^3675]

On January 13, 2013, *Searching for Sugar Man* was nominated for and, on February 24, 2013, won the [Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Documentary_Feature) at the [85th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/85th_Academy_Awards).[^3676] Rodriguez declined to attend the award ceremony as he did not want to overshadow the filmmakers' achievement.[^3677] Upon accepting his award, Chinn remarked on such generosity, "That just about says everything about that man and his story that you want to know."[^3678] [Malik Bendjelloul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malik_Bendjelloul) also said on stage, "Thanks to one of the greatest singers ever, Rodriguez."[^3679]

##### Belated success in the United States and Europe

After the cinematic release of *Searching for Sugar Man* in 2012, Rodriguez experienced a flush of media exposure and fan interest in the United States, as well as Europe. He appeared as a musical guest on the *[Late Show with David Letterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Show_with_David_Letterman)* on August 14, 2012, performing "Crucify Your Mind",[^3680][^3681] and performed "Can't Get Away" on *[The Tonight Show with Jay Leno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tonight_Show_with_Jay_Leno)* on January 11, 2013.

Prominent news coverage included a mid-August 2012 [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN) feature story with an interview of Rodriguez discussing his life and career resurgence. On October 7, 2012, Rodriguez was featured on the U.S. television news program *[60 Minutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60_Minutes)*.[^3682] On November 18, 2012, Rodriguez was interviewed on the U.K. Sunday morning news program *[The Andrew Marr Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Andrew_Marr_Show)*, where he also played a short song over the closing credits. He performed on the BBC2 program *[Later... with Jools Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Later..._with_Jools_Holland)*[^3683] on November 16, 2012, and was interviewed by [Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jools_Holland).[^3684] Additionally, he performed on Internet web series shows such as *The Weekly Comet*.[^3685]

In addition to concerts in Australia, South Africa, and New Zealand,[^3686] Rodriguez's tour schedule for 2013 included his most highly attended U.S. concerts to date, such as the [Ann Arbor Folk Festival](https://www.annarbor.com/entertainment/rodriguez/) in January, a stint at the [Beacon Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beacon_Theatre_%28New_York_City%29) in New York City in April, and a spot at the 2014 [Sasquatch Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasquatch_Music_Festival) at [The Gorge Amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gorge_Amphitheatre), as well as other concerts in Europe.[^3666] He played on the Park Stage at the [Glastonbury Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glastonbury_Festival), U.K., in June 2013. On July 5, 2013, Rodriguez opened the [Montreux Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreux_Jazz) festival.[^3687] On August 10, 2013, he headlined at the Wilderness Festival in the U.K. In 2015, he opened for Brian Wilson's tour with Wilson, Al Jardine and Blondie Chaplin of the Beach Boys.[^3688]

Rodriguez received additional exposure in 2014 as the [Dave Matthews Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Matthews_Band) often covered "Sugar Man" in their summer tour.[^3689] Matthews would often preface the song with his experience as a fan of Rodriguez growing up in South Africa and his surprise at Rodriguez's lack of popularity in the United States.[^3690]

The film *Searching for Sugar Man* strongly implied that Rodriguez had been cheated out of royalties over the years, specifically by [Clarence Avant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_Avant). Rodriguez first expressed indifference to these "symbols of success" but then filed a lawsuit in 2013.[^3691] In 2022, the year before his death, the lawsuit was reported to have been settled with no amount disclosed.[^3692][^3693]

##### Later activity

In 2015, Craig Bartholomew Strydom and Stephen "Sugar" Segerman published a book entitled *Sugar Man: The Life, Death and Resurrection of Sixto Rodriguez*.[^3694] A review in *Business Day* called the book "probably one of the most unusual rock 'n roll stories out there".

Rodriguez headlined a tour in August 2018,[^3695] ending with a hometown show at Detroit's Garden Theater.[^3696] His final North American concert tour in late 2019/early 2020 culminated on February 20, 2020, at Nashville's City Winery.

Rodriguez and the process of his rediscovery was the subject of a 2022 episode of *Outlook* on the [BBC World Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_World_Service).[^3697]

#### Later life and death

He was first married to Rayma Rawa.

Since 1984, to Constance "Konny" Rodriguez née Koskos, and with them he had three daughters, Eva, Sandra and Regan.[^3698]

In March 2013, *Rolling Stone* wrote that Rodriguez was suffering from [glaucoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glaucoma) and was going blind. The disease had by then dramatically limited his vision and forced him to walk very slowly and often clutched to someone else's arm. They quoted Rodriguez as saying, "I'm still able to make out some people in the crowd at my shows".[^3657]

In August 2022, *[Le Monde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Monde)* reported that Rodriguez had become blind, and that he was still living in the same house in Detroit.[^3699]

In February 2023, Rodriguez suffered a stroke, then had surgery in March to repair stroke damage, followed by post-operative physical therapy.[^3700] Rodriguez's condition later worsened, and he was placed in hospice care.[^3701] He died on August 8, 2023, at the age of 81.[^3695][^3702][^3703][^3698] A concert celebrated his life on August 12, 2023, at Detroit's Majestic Theatre.[^3704]

Two Detroit area murals honor Rodriguez, one on a commercial building on Trumbull, across the street from his alma mater, Wayne State,[^3705] and another on the entire side of an apartment building at Vernor Highway and Sharon. Both were created while he was still alive.[^3706]

### Ya Ho Wha 13

**Ya Ho Wha 13**, otherwise known as **Ya Ho Wa 13** or **Yahowha 13**, is a [psychedelic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_rock) band fronted by [Father Yod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_Yod) (/joʊd/ *YOHD*), spiritual leader of a religious [commune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commune_%28intentional_community%29) called the [Source Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Source_Family), based in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles).

The band has released nine LPs of [psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music) music, which varied dramatically in style and quality. Some of the group's music featured tribal drums and distorted guitars or unrehearsed jam sessions, and others were relatively more conventional rock or folk music. Many of the musicians affiliated with Ya Ho Wa 13 were amateurs or obscure, but [Sky Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Saxon) was affiliated with the group for a period.[^3724]

#### Formation

In the early 1970s, members of The Source Family, who lived in the former [Harry Chandler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Chandler) mansion in [Los Feliz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Feliz,_Los_Angeles) in the [Hollywood Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_Hills), formed an improvisational, [psychedelic music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music) group.[^3725] Their name was inspired by the [Tetragramaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetragramaton), the four-letter name of God in Judaism. In 1973 they began recording LPs in a studio in a garage at the family's communal residence.

All the records made with Father Yod's participation were improvised, with no rehearsals or overdubs. Most were pressed in small runs of 500 to 1000 copies on the Higher Key label and sold to the public in [Father Yod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_Yod)'s [vegetarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetarian) restaurant.

Nine LPs were produced and released, but more than 65 albums were thought to have been recorded by the group and then lost over the years. The group's historian and archivist later found unreleased music tapes in the archives, and it was planned to remaster and release them through [Drag City Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drag_City_Records) of Chicago and the group's website.[^3726]

The band changed members and its name occasionally, from Father Yod and the Spirit of ’76 to Ya Ho Wha 13 to The Savage Sons of Ya Ho Wha, Yodship, and Fire Water Air. The key players were always the same: Djin Aquarian on guitar, Octavius Aquarian on drums, and Sunflower Aquarian on bass. Other family musicians were Lovely Aquarian, Zoroaster Aquarian, Hom Aquarian, Rhythm Aquarian, Pythias Aquarian, Aquariana Aquarian, Ahom Aquarian, and Electron Aquarian.

Father Yod does not appear on all album releases, but on those on which he participates, he handles lead vocals and percussion on a kettle drum. Yahowha 13 was Father Yod's signature band. He intended that its music and lyrics should continue his teaching after he was gone. [Sky Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Saxon) of [The Seeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Seeds) joined the Source Family in 1973 and also appeared on the band's recordings.

#### Discography

##### Father Yod and the Spirit of ‘76

- *Kohoutek* (1973)
- *Contraction* (1974)
- *Expansion* (1974)
- *All or Nothing at All* (1974)

Father Yod does not participate on *All or Nothing at All*, unlike the previous three albums released under this incarnation, in which his chanting and singing vocals are prominent.[^3727]

##### Ya Ho Wa 13

- *Ya Ho Wa 13* (1974), recorded at the Father House garage.
- *Savage Sons of Ya Ho Wa* (1974), recorded at the Father House garage.
- *Penetration: An Aquarian Symphony* (1974), recorded at the Father House garage, is the band's most popular recording and has been reissued several times.
- *I'm Gonna Take You Home* (1974), also called The Lovers, was recorded at the Father House garage.
- *To the Principles, For the Children* (1974), recorded at the Father House garage.
- *The Operetta* (1975), not released until the 2000s.

By the end of 1974, the Source Family had tried to move to [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii) but were met with hostility, which forced them to temporarily relocate to [Northern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_California) before eventually returning. This album was recorded during that time, and the tension is apparent. It has been described as “a more personalized, painfully vulnerable”[^3727] collection of songs. This long-lost final album of Ya Ho Wha with Father's participation was recently released by Swordfish Records. It was recorded in the spring of 1975, just after Ya Ho Wha's spontaneous visit to India, which culminated in his initiation in the [Great Pyramid of Giza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza) on [Easter Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easter_Sunday). He was en route to the US via France when the plane was rerouted due to a storm and forced to land in Cairo, Egypt. Upon arrival, the group (there were four traveling) hailed a taxi, and the taxi driver suggested they stay at his brother's house. The next morning at 4 am, they proceeded to the Great Pyramids. Upon arrival, they were greeted by a mysterious man who escorted them through the Great Pyramid. This LP represents the first recording Ya Ho Wha made after his "resurrection" in the Great Pyramid, and is also his last full collaboration with the band.[^3727]

- *Sonic Portation*, the first record release of the remaining members of YaHoWha13 in over 33 years through ProphaseMusic. The band released two more albums called 2013.

#### Music after Father's death

After [Father Yod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_Yod) / Ya Ho Wha's [hang-gliding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hang-gliding) accident and death in Hawaii in 1975, the original Yahowa 13 band dissolved, though many of the members continue to make music.

- *Golden Sunrise* (Fire Water Air, 1977), the first recording after [Father Yod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_Yod)'s death and the first featured appearance of [Sky Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Saxon) of [The Seeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Seeds).[^3728]
- *Yodship Suite* (1977) was a private pressing, and, except for Sky Saxon, the specific family members involved are unknown. The sound takes on a softer, less [acid rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_rock) tone with flutes and acoustic guitars, and most of the songs are [laments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lament) about Father's death.[^3728]
- *Yodship Suite, Part 3* (c. 1977), the last Ya Ho Wha-related album to be released. This poorly documented album features recordings from 1973 featuring the Spirit of '76 band, but with Sky Saxon on vocals instead of Father Yod. It's a one-sided LP with about 15 minutes of music, containing two different tracks spliced together. The music is considerably more aggressive than the preceding Yod Ship Suite. Only 2-3 copies of this album are known to exist.[^3729]

#### Legacy

Original LP pressings released under the various incarnations of Ya Ho Wha 13 have become collectible and can command high prices on the secondary market. *Contraction* and *Expansion* are among the better-known sought-after releases, while *All or Nothing at All* and *Yodship* are also considered particularly scarce.[^3730]

[Sky Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Saxon), singer of the seminal garage band [The Seeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Seeds) collaborated with Japanese label [Captain Trip Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Trip_Records) in 1998 to produce a deluxe 13-CD box set entitled *God and Hair*, including CD reissues of the original Source Family records and some unreleased material.[^3731] In 2002, The Source Foundation Corp LLC/Source.Org was created, and is currently not affiliated with the remaining members of YaHoWha13, nor involved with present musical endeavors.

Swordfish Records in the UK, in collaboration with The Source Foundation Corp LLC, remastered and released some of the Higher Key Record Catalog as both limited pressing LPs and CDs. This includes, *Penetration*, *I'm Going to Take You Home* (Lovers/Chariot), and *To the Principles for the Children*.[^3727] In the summer of 2009, Drag City Records released *Magnificence in the Memory*, rare cuts of YaHoWha13 from the archives of the Source Foundation.

In 2007, the three surviving members of YaHoWha13 (Sunflower, Octavius, and Djin) were invited by Isis Aquarian and Jodi Wille of Process to play in Los Angeles for their Source Book coming out event, the untold story of "Father Yod, Ya Ho Wha 13 and the Source Family". This was the first time they had played together in 33 years. This led to their first recording of *Sonic Portation* (Prophase Music). YaHoWha13 made several appearances in Los Angeles and San Francisco.

In 2009, Ya Ho Wha 13 played on the East Coast and in Canada. They are currently working on their new live/studio album, and appeared at [The South by SouthWest Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_by_Southwest_Music_Festival) in Austin, Texas, in spring of 2010 - playing with experimental psychedelic bands [The Acid Mothers Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid_Mothers_Temple) and [Plastic Crimewave Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_Crimewave).

### The Anacreontic Song

"**The Anacreontic Song**", also known by its [incipit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incipit) "**To Anacreon in Heaven**", was the official song of the [Anacreontic Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anacreontic_Society), an 18th-century gentlemen's club of amateur musicians in London. Composed by [John Stafford Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stafford_Smith), the tune was later used by several writers as a setting for their patriotic lyrics. These included two songs by [Francis Scott Key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Scott_Key), most famously his poem "Defence of Fort McHenry". The combination of Key's poem and Smith's composition became known as "[The Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Star-Spangled_Banner)", which was adopted as the official [national anthem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_anthem) of the United States of America in 1931.

#### Anacreontic Society

The Anacreontic Society was a [gentlemen's club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gentlemen's_club) of the kind that was popular in London in the late 18th century. In existence from approximately 1766 to 1792, the Society was dedicated to the ancient Greek poet [Anacreon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anacreon), who was renowned for his drinking songs and odes to love. Its members, who consisted mainly of wealthy men of high social rank, would meet on Wednesday evenings to combine musical appreciation with eating and drinking.

The Society met twelve times a year.[^3732] Each meeting began at half past seven with a lengthy concert, featuring "the best performers in London", who would be made honorary members of the Society.[^3732]

The Society came to an end after the [Duchess of Devonshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgiana_Cavendish,_Duchess_of_Devonshire) attended one of its meetings. Because "some of the comic songs \[were not\] exactly calculated for the entertainment of ladies, the singers were restrained; which displeasing many of the members, they resigned one after another; and a general meeting being called, the society was dissolved".[^3733] It is not clear exactly when this incident occurred, but in October 1792 it was reported that: "The Anacreontic Society meets no more; it has long been struggling with symptoms of internal decay."[^3734]

#### Original role of the song

An early reference to the Anacreontic Song is found in the long-unpublished journals of gentleman-composer [John Marsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Marsh_%28composer%29) (1752-1828). Writing of 11 December 1773, he recalls:

> Mr Bowen... invited me to accompany him on the Saturday following to a concert at the London Coffee House called the Anacreontic Meeting, which I of course readily accepted of & played with Mr Smith the leader after w'ch *\[sic\]* we sat down a pretty many of us to supper after which [catches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catch_%28music%29) & [glees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glee_%28music%29) were performed, in which a Mr Webster, a young man with a very fine bass voice much distinguish'd himself. The Anacreontic Song was also sung by him, in the last verse of which we stood hand in hand all round the table, this concert being in fact the origin of the Society held afterwards for many years at the Crown and Anchor.[^3735]

Another reference is found in the long-unpublished *Recollections* of Richard John Samuel Stevens (1757-1837). In this passage, Stevens is speaking of the year 1777:

> The Evening's entertainment began at seven o'clock, with a concert, chiefly of instrumental Music: it was not very uncommon to have some Vocal Music interspersed with the Instrumental. Mr. Sabattier was the Manager of this department, and generally stood behind the Person who was at the [Piano Forte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pianoforte). At ten o'clock the Instrumental Concert ended, when we retired to the Supper rooms. After Supper, having sung *[Non nobis Domine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_nobis)* we returned to the Concert Room, which in the mean time had been differently arranged. The President, then took his seat in the center of the elevated table, at the upper end of the room, supported on each side, by the various Vocal performers. After the *Anacreontic Song* had been sung, in the Chorus of the last verse of which all the Members, Visitors, and Performers joined, "hand in hand", we were entertained by the performance of various celebrated Catches, Glees, Songs, Duettos, and other Vocal, with some Rhetorical compositions, till twelve o'clock.[^3736]

Parke, writing in the early nineteenth century, recalls:

> After the concert an elegant supper was served up; and when the cloth was removed, the constitutional song, beginning, 'To Anacreon in Heaven,' was sung by the chairman or his deputy.[^3737]

The Anacreontic Song served as the "constitutional song" of the Society. After the initial concert and meal, the song would be sung to open the after-supper, more light-hearted part of proceedings. The verses, which are difficult to sing because of their wide range, would be sung by a solo singer, with the entire Society joining in the refrain.[^3738] Although it is often described as a "drinking song", Lichtenwanger states that "To Anacreon in Heaven" "was not a barroom ballad, a drinking ditty to be chorused with glasses swung in rhythm", but "convivial, ... in a special and stately way".[^3738]

#### Composition and authorship

##### Words

Early publications of the song ascribe its lyrics to the Society's president, Ralph Tomlinson. Tomlinson was baptised in [Plemstall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plemstall), Cheshire, in 1744; by 1766 he was a lawyer working in London. Tomlinson probably became president of the Society following the death of the previous president, George Bellas, in January 1776.[^3738] He died in March 1778 at the age of thirty-three.[^3739]

##### Music

While many early publications of the song attribute the words to Tomlinson, none name the creator of the music. The identity of the composer was a subject of controversy until the discovery, in the mid-twentieth century, of a passage in a then-unpublished manuscript of *Recollections* written by Richard John Samuel Stevens (1757-1837), a member of the Anacreontic Society. Writing of the year 1777, Stevens recalled:

> As I have mentioned the Anacreontic Society, it may not be improper to give some account of that Popular meeting. It was first held at the London Coffee House, on Ludgate Hill, but the room being found too small, it was removed to the Crown and Anchor Tavern in the Strand, then kept by one *Holloway.* The President was Ralph Tomlinson Esqre., very much of a Gentleman, and a sensible, sedate, quiet man: I believe that he was a Solicitor in Chancery. He wrote the Poetry of the *Anacreontic Song;* which Stafford Smith set to Music: this Song was sung by *Webster,* when I first attended the Society.[^3736]

In this passage, Stevens identified the composer as [John Stafford Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stafford_Smith) (1750-1836). Smith, the son of the organist of Gloucester Cathedral, was sent at a young age to sing in the [Chapel Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_Royal), and thereafter soon established himself in the capital. Like Stevens himself, Smith was a young professional musician active primarily in the chapels and churches of London. Smith was a published composer by 1772, subsequently winning two composition prizes from the London Catch Club in 1773.[^3740] Both Smith and Stevens were probably among the "honorary members" of the Anacreontic Society who played in its concerts without having to pay the subscription fee;[^3741] Smith is probably the "leader" identified by Marsh in his recollection of 1773 quoted above.

Smith outlived both Ralph Tomlinson and the Anacreontic Society by several decades before dying in 1836. During his lifetime, the melody of the song was set to other texts (most notably the "Defence of Fort McHenry" as discussed below) and became extremely popular. Despite this, Smith does not seem to have been eager to publicise the fact that he had composed the song. The best evidence we have for a claim of authorship occurs in his *Fifth Book of Canzonets* (1799),[^3742] which included an arrangement of the Anacreontic Song with the ambiguous notation "harmonized by the Author".[^3743][^3744]

It remains puzzling why Smith did not make more effort to associate himself with the song. Until the discovery of Stevens's *Recollections*, there was some controversy over whether Smith was in fact the composer.[^3745][^3746] However, no alternative story for the music's origins (whether as the work of a different composer or as a pre-existing tune) ever gained a consensus among historians. Lichtenwanger suggests that "\[p\]erhaps Smith composed the song for Tomlinson for money, for a flat fee, which meant yielding his legal rights in it to Tomlinson or the Society".[^3741]

##### Date

The date of the composition of the song is uncertain. It cannot predate the foundation of the Anacreontic Society (around 1766). Lichtenwanger suggests a composition date as late as 1776;[^3747] but if the Marsh journal is accurate then the song must have existed by December 1773.[^3748] The age of John Stafford Smith may also be of interest; Smith was in his mid-teens in 1766, while by 1773 he was in his early twenties and a published, prize-winning composer.

**Chronology of the Anacreontic Song**

#### Publication

The lyrics of the song were published in *The Vocal Magazine*, 1778, attributed to "Ralph Tomlinson, Esq.".[^3752] The music, along with the words, was published in *The Vocal Enchantress*, a collection published in 1783.[^3753] There are also various undated publications of the music which likely date to the early 1780s.[^3754] None of these publications name the composer of the music.

Particular interest attaches to the first Longman & Broderip edition of the music, published between 1777 and 1781.[^3751][^3755] This was likely the first publication of the music and the official edition from which others were copied. Broderip, a partner at the firm, is known to have attended meetings of the Society.[^3756]

#### Lyrics

The lyrics are "a good-natured takeoff on a bit of pseudoclassical mythology".[^3738] The following is taken from the first Longman and Broderip edition:[^3757]

**1**

To Anacreon in Heav'n, where he sat in full Glee,

A few Sons of Harmony sent a Petition,

That he their Inspirer and Patron would be;

When this answer arriv'd from the Jolly Old Grecian

"Voice, Fiddle, and Flute,

"no longer be mute,

"I'll lend you my Name and inspire you to boot,

"And, besides I'll instruct you, like me, to intwine

"The [Myrtle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myrtus) of [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_%28mythology%29) with [Bacchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacchus)'s Vine."

**2**

The news through [Olympus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Olympus) immediately flew;

When [Old Thunder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_%28mythology%29) pretended to give himself Airs.

"If these Mortals are suffer'd their Scheme to persue,

"The Devil a Goddess will stay above Stairs.

"Hark! already they cry,

"In transports of Joy,

"Away to the Sons of Anacreon we'll fly,[^3758]

"And there, with good Fellows, we'll learn to intwine

"The Myrtle of Venus with Bacchus's Vine.

**3**

"The [Yellow-Hair'd God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo) and his [nine fusty Maids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muse),

"From [Helicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Helicon)'s banks will incontinent flee,[^3759]

"[Idalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idalium) will boast but of tenantless Shades,

"And the [bi-forked Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Parnassus) a mere Desart will be

"My Thunder no fear on't,

"Shall soon do it's Errand,

"And dam'me! I'll swinge the Ringleaders, I warrant.

"I'll trim the young Dogs, for thus daring to twine

"The Myrtle of Venus with Bacchus's Vine."

**4**

[Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo) rose up, and said, "Pry'thee ne'er quarrel,

"Good King of the Gods, with my Vot'ries below:

"Your Thunder is useless", then shewing his Laurel,

Cry'd "*Sic evitabile fulmen*,[^3760] you know!

"Then over each head

"My Laurels I'll spread;

"So my Sons from your Crackers no Mischief shall dread,

"Whilst snug in their Club-Room, they jovially twine

"The Myrtle of Venus with Bacchus's Vine."

**5**

Next [Momus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momus) got up with his risible Phiz,

And swore with Apollo he'd chearfully join, 

"The full Tide of Harmony still shall be his,

"But the Song, and the Catch, and the Laugh shall be mine.

"Then, [Jove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_%28mythology%29), be not jealous

"Of these honest fellows."

Cry'd Jove, "We relent, since the Truth you now tell us;

"And swear by [Old Styx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styx), that they long shall intwine

"The Myrtle of Venus with Bacchus's Vine."

**6**

Ye Sons of Anacreon, then join Hand in Hand;

Preserve Unanimity, Friendship, and Love!

'Tis your's to support what's so happily plann'd;

You've the sanction of Gods, and the Fiat of Jove.

While thus we agree,

Our Toast let it be.

May our Club flourish happy, united, and free!

And long may the Sons of Anacreon intwine

The Myrtle of Venus with Bacchus's Vine.

##### Earlier version of the lyrics

In the first known version of the lyrics, as published in *The Vocal* magazine of 1778, there are two significant textual discrepancies from later publications.

- In the second verse, *A fig for Parnassus! To Rowley's we'll fly;* appears in place of *Away to the Sons of Anacreon we'll fly*
- In the third verse, *To the hill of old Lud will incontinent flee,* appears in place of *From Helicon's banks will incontinent flee,*

The two replaced lines refer to the Society's earlier meeting-place at the London Coffee-House, which was situated on Ludgate Hill and seems to have occupied the same premises as Rowley and Leech, a wine merchant.[^3750]

#### Subsequent history

The song, through its bawdy lyrics, gained popularity in London and elsewhere beyond the Anacreontic Society. New lyrics were also fashioned for it, including several patriotic titles in the United States. The most popular of these at the time was [Robert Treat Paine Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Treat_Paine_Jr.)'s "[Adams and Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adams_and_Liberty)"[^3761] (1798).

##### "The Star-Spangled Banner"

[Francis Scott Key](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Scott_Key) wrote "Defence of [Fort McHenry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_McHenry)" during the [War of 1812](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_1812), while detained on a British ship during the night of 13 September 1814, as the British forces bombarded the American fort. Key specifically wrote the lyrics with this familiar patriotic tune in mind, just as he had done with an earlier set of his lyrics, "When the Warrior Returns", in which he had made similar use of "star-spangled banner" imagery in praise of [Stephen Decatur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Decatur).[^3762] Later retitled "[The Star-Spangled Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Star-Spangled_Banner)", Key's lyrics, set to Stafford Smith's music, became a well-known and recognized patriotic song throughout the United States, and was officially designated as the U.S. national anthem on 3 March 1931.[^3763] The setting of new lyrics to an existing tune is called a [contrafactum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contrafactum).[^3764]

### Gloomy Sunday

"**Gloomy Sunday**" ([Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_language): *Szomorú Vasárnap*) is a song composed by Hungarian pianist and composer [Rezső Seress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rezs%C5%91_Seress) and published in 1933.

The original lyrics were titled "Vége a világnak" ("The World Is Ending") and were about despair caused by war, ending in a quiet prayer about people's sins. Poet [László Jávor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1szl%C3%B3_J%C3%A1vor) wrote his own lyrics to the song, titled "Szomorú vasárnap" ("Sad Sunday"), in which the protagonist wants to kill himself after his lover ends their relationship.[^3765] The latter lyrics ended up becoming more popular while the former were essentially forgotten. The song was first recorded in [Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_language) by pop singer [Pál Kalmár](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A1l_Kalm%C3%A1r) in 1935.

"Gloomy Sunday" was first recorded in English by [Hal Kemp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_Kemp) in 1936, with lyrics by [Sam M. Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_M._Lewis),[^3766] and was recorded the same year by [Paul Robeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Robeson), with lyrics by [Desmond Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Carter). It became well known throughout much of the [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language)-speaking world after the release of a version by [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz) and [swing music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_music) singer [Billie Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billie_Holiday) in 1941. Lewis' lyrics refer to suicide, and the record label described it as the "Hungarian Suicide Song". There is a recurring [urban legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_legend) which claims that many people have taken their own lives while listening to this song, particularly Hungarians.[^3767]

#### Writing and background

The song was composed by Rezső Seress while living in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris),[^3768] in an attempt to become established as a songwriter in late 1932.[^3769] The original musical composition was a piano melody in [C minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C_minor), with the lyrics being sung over it.[^3770] Seress wrote the song at the time of the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression) and increasing [fascist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism) influence in his native Hungary, although sources differ as to the degree to which his song was motivated by personal melancholy rather than concerns about the future of the world. The basis of Seress's lyrics is a reproach to the injustices of man, with a prayer to [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God) to have mercy on the modern world and the people who perpetrate evil.[^3771] There are some suggestions[^3772] that the words of "Vége a világnak" were in fact not written until [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II) itself and not [copyrighted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright) until 1946.

Seress initially had difficulty finding a publisher, mainly due to the unusually melancholy nature of the song. One potential publisher stated, "It is not that the song is sad, there is a sort of terrible compelling despair about it. I don't think it would do anyone any good to hear a song like that."[^3773]

The song was published as [sheet music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheet_music) in late 1933,[^3774] with lyrics by poet [László Jávor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1szl%C3%B3_J%C3%A1vor), who was inspired by a recent break-up with his fiancée.[^3769] According to most sources, Jávor rewrote the lyrics after the song's first publication, although he is sometimes described as the original writer of its words.[^3775] His lyrics contained no political sentiments, but rather were a lament for the death of a beloved and a pledge to meet with the lover again in the [afterlife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afterlife).[^3773][^3776][^3777] This version of the song became the best known, and most later rewritings are based around the idea of lost love.[^3778]

#### Urban legends

There have been several [urban legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_legend) regarding the song over the years, mostly involving it being allegedly connected with various numbers of suicides, and [radio networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_network) reacting by purportedly [banning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship) the song.[^3779] However, most of these claims are unsubstantiated.[^3780]

Press reports in the 1930s associated at least 100 suicides, both in Hungary and the United States, with "Gloomy Sunday",[^3767][^3769][^3781] but most of the deaths supposedly linked to it are difficult to verify. The urban legend appears to be, for the most part, simply an embellishment of the high number of Hungarian suicides that occurred in the decade when the song was composed due to other factors such as [famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famine) and [poverty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty). No studies have drawn a clear link between the song and suicide.[^3780]

On 11 January 1968, about 35 years after writing the song, Seress committed suicide.[^3782]

[The BBC banned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_songs_banned_by_the_BBC) [Billie Holiday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billie_Holiday)'s version of the song from being broadcast, as being detrimental to wartime morale, but allowed performances of instrumental versions.[^3767] In America, the version performed by [Paul Robeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Robeson) was prohibited on some radio stations and nightclubs.[^3783] However, there is little evidence of any other radio bans; the BBC's ban was lifted by 2002.[^3780]

#### Legacy

A cover of the song appeared on [the Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Associates_%28band%29)' second studio album *[Sulk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulk)*, released on 14 May 1982, and named 'Album of the Year' in *[Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody_Maker)* at the end of 1982.[^3791] Lead vocalist [Billy Mackenzie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Mackenzie) killed himself on 22 January 1997.

The song's lyrics are featured in the bridge of [the Dead Milkmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dead_Milkmen) song "(Theme from) Blood Orgy of the Atomic Fern", on the band's 1987 album *[Bucky Fellini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucky_Fellini)*.

A highly fictional version of the song's origin is at the heart of the 1999 German/Hungarian film *[Ein Lied von Liebe und Tod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ein_Lied_von_Liebe_und_Tod)* (*Gloomy Sunday - A Song of Love and Death*).

A cover of "Gloomy Sunday" is featured on track three of Venetian Snares's 2005 album *[Rossz Csillag Alatt Született](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rossz_Csillag_Alatt_Sz%C3%BCletett)*. It also samples Billie Holiday's vocals.[^3792][^3793]

The song inspired the 2006 movie *[The Kovak Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Kovak_Box)*, in which a writer is trapped on the island of [Mallorca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mallorca) with people who are injected with a microchip that causes them to take their own lives when they hear "Gloomy Sunday".[^3794] The song plays during the movie, sung by the actress Lucía Jiménez. A [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video) from the cover was released as part of the movie promotion. The song also features on the soundtrack of *Wristcutters: A Love Story* (2006), performed by Artie Shaw.[^3795]

### Ready 'n' Steady

"**Ready 'n' Steady**" is a song by American musicians Dennis Lucchesi and Jim Franks, recorded in 1979. The song appeared on *[Billboard's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_%28magazine%29)* [Bubbling Under the Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubbling_Under_Hot_100_Singles) chart for three weeks in June 1979, despite not being released as a record, and possibly not even receiving airplay. The song was credited to Lucchesi's first and middle initials, **D. A.**, which he had used as his stage name as a regional performer.[^3796]

For decades, the identity of D.A. was unknown. Further, no evidence of the song, nor any recording of it, could be found. This led many record collectors to consider the song a "phantom record" that possibly did not even exist. In 2016, researcher Paul Haney used copyright records to trace and find the recording, giving the song its first known public exposure.[^3797]

#### On the *Billboard* Bubbling Under chart

The June 16, 1979, issue of *[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_%28magazine%29)* listed 10 records on its [Bubbling Under Hot 100 Singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubbling_Under_Hot_100_Singles) chart, a chart which lists songs ranking just below entry onto the magazine's main chart, the [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100); the Bubbling Under rankings began with position number 101. One of these was "Ready 'n' Steady" by D.A., listed at the number 106 position (sixth among the ten Bubbling Under records).[^3798] The record, listed as being released on the Rascal label, moved up to number 103 on June 23,[^3799] then up to number 102 the following week before disappearing from the chart.[^3800]

#### Whitburn's research

American author and music historian [Joel Whitburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Whitburn), whose company, Record Research Inc., specializes in researching the *Billboard* charts, published various books containing chart data over the years. He collected thousands of records, including all of the 45s ever to hit the Hot 100 or Bubbling Under charts, all except "Ready 'n' Steady".

In a 1995 interview, Whitburn said he had never actually seen or heard the record. He added, "We think, we think, that it's a girl's rock group from Chicago. Punk group, we think, 1979. And we think that the Rascal label was out of a guy's home in Detroit." The Chicago female band [DA!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DA!_%28band%29) denied any link to the record, though Whitburn had suggested a connection.[^3801] Whitburn had found a small ad for a Rascal label located in Detroit in a punk rock publication, but by then the address was a boarded-up vacant house.[^3802] The entry in *Billboard* shows "Ready 'n' Steady" had a catalog number of 102; if there was a Rascal 101 released, it remains unknown to collectors.

In the fourth edition of Whitburn's *Bubbling Under the Hot 100* book, published in 2005, the entry for "D. A." was amended with a note stating, "The existence of this record and artist is in question", and quotes a price of \$150 as its value. In 2009, Whitburn published his latest *Top Pop Singles* book, which includes both Hot 100 and Bubbling Under singles, but D. A. was not listed at all. In an interview with the website CelebrityAccess, Whitburn noted he still had not been able to find "Ready 'n' Steady" and said, "I don't think it exists".[^3803] Whitburn also thought the song's listing on the chart could have been a [copyright trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fictitious_entry) by *Billboard*.[^3797]

The 2002 16th edition of Jerry Osbourne's *Official Price Guide to Records* listed the record, with a value of \$75-125, along with an unnamed LP on the Frontline label, dated 1985 or 1986. This is actually the album *[Fearful Symmetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fearful_Symmetry_%28album%29)* by the Christian rock band [Daniel Amos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Amos), which sometimes used the abbreviation "D.A.".

#### Resurfacing

The [United States Copyright Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Copyright_Office) catalog contains a registration of a song titled "Ready & Steady" with authorship credited to D. A. Lucchesi and Jim Franks; it was registered on September 16, 1986, with a creation date of 1979.[^3804] **Dennis Armand "D. A." Lucchesi** (June 5, 1945 - August 18, 2005) was an American [mortgage broker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mortgage_broker) and part-time musician from California who performed locally as "D. A. and the Dukes."[^3796][^3797]

In 2016, further investigation into this copyright registration by Paul Haney, of Record Research Inc., led to co-author Jim Franks, who provided Haney with a recording of the song. According to Haney, the song was recorded by [Steve Cropper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Cropper), but never released. As for how it appeared on the charts without any records for sales or airplay, according to Haney, a [record promoter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_promotion) with a major label took an interest in the band and somehow managed to get the song listed on the *Billboard* chart; this makes "Ready 'n' Steady" the only song ever to appear on any *Billboard* listing without actually being released. The Rascal label, at that time, existed only on paper and was owned by a relative of one of the band members; in 1984, Rascal (based in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles)) would issue a few independent singles, though nothing by D.A.[^3797]

"Ready 'n' Steady" was most likely never played on radio until Haney appeared on the *Crap from the Past* radio show on [KFAI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KFAI) in [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis), Minnesota, on July 8, 2016, during which the recording was aired.[^3797]

On May 19, 2017, *[Crap from the Past](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KFAI)* did a phone interview with Jim Franks.[^3805] He stated that the personnel for the song was:

- Dennis Lucchesi - lead vocals
- Jim Franks - guitar
- Ira Walker - bass
- Stu Blank - piano
- Dean Revelo - drums
- Meredith Lucchesi - background vocals
- 2 unknown female background singers

### You Suffer

"**You Suffer**" is a song by English [grindcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grindcore) band [Napalm Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napalm_Death), released on the band's debut studio album, *[Scum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scum_%28Napalm_Death_album%29)* (1987). The song was written by [Nicholas Bullen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Bullen), [Justin Broadrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Broadrick), and [Mick Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Harris) during the March 1986 demo sessions for *[From Enslavement to Obliteration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From_Enslavement_to_Obliteration)*. In March 2023, *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone)* ranked the song at number 72 on their "100 Greatest Heavy Metal Songs of All Time" list.[^3806]

#### Background and influence

The official four-word lyrics to the song are: "You suffer, but why?". [Justin Broadrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin_Broadrick) said about the song:

> "You Suffer" was largely a comedy thing, one-second song... it's ridiculous, but it was hilarious. We played that song in front of 30 local kids, like, every weekend. We played that song 30 times. It was hilarious.[^3807]

[Nicholas Bullen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Bullen), writer of the song's four-word lyrics, said that the brevity of "You Suffer" was inspired by Wehrmacht's 1985 song "E!".[^3808] "You Suffer" would become an influence on the "noisecore" micro-genre, inspiring many bands such as [Sore Throat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sore_Throat_%28grindcore_band%29), 7 Minutes of Nausea, Deche-Charge, [Anal Cunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anal_Cunt), and others to release full-length recordings of exclusively "microsong" content.[^3809] Swedish progressive metal band [Opeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opeth) and Finnish gothic metal band [HIM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIM_%28Finnish_band%29) have both covered the song live.[^3810][^3811] The song was featured in season 5, episode 3 ("Chief Operating Officer") of the HBO comedy show [Silicon Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_Valley_%28TV_series%29). In the episode, the song acts as Bertram Gilfoyle's alarm to indicate that Bitcoin's value dipped below a certain threshold, making it not worth to mine, thus requiring Gilfoyle to alter his mining rig.[^3809]

#### Release

In 1989, "You Suffer" appeared on one side of a 7" single given away free with copies of a compilation album entitled *Grindcrusher*. The song on the other side, "Mega-Armageddon Death Part 3" by the [Electro Hippies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electro_Hippies), also lasts approximately one second, making the disc the shortest single ever released. Each side features one groove at the outer edge of the disc containing the music, with the rest of the surface containing etched writing and cartoons.[^3812]

To coincide with the release of the *Scum* [DualDisc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DualDisc) in March 2007, a music video produced by Earache Records was released for the song.[^3813] The video shows a girl jumping up and down with fake blood/gunshot effects overlaid on the footage.

### Everyday Chemistry

***Everyday Chemistry*** is a [remix album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remix_album) that was made available as a free digital download on 9 September 2009. The album was released along with a story of anonymous authorship.[^3814] It [mashes up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashup_%28music%29) various songs from [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles)' individual solo careers, including tracks from 27 albums. The album portrays itself as being taken from an alternative universe in which the Beatles had not [broken up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakup_of_the_Beatles).[^3815][^3816]

#### Context

On 9 September 2009, a website with the URL thebeatlesneverbrokeup.com was created. This date coincided with an official Beatles anniversary campaign, including the [2009 remasters box set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles_Box_Set), an [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Records)-shaped USB drive containing the remasters, and *The Beatles: Rock Band*.[^3817] The website includes a download link to the entire album on [MP3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MP3).

The website was accompanied by a fictional short story (purporting to be true) written by an anonymous person under the pen name "James Richards" (a pseudonym drawn from the legal first names of [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney) and [Ringo Starr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ringo_Starr), the two surviving Beatles, who were born James Paul McCartney and Richard Starkey respectively).

In the story, Richards describes driving through the [Del Puerto Canyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Del_Puerto_Canyon) road in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California), when he had to pull over to let his dog use the restroom. The dog begins to chase a rabbit, leading to Richards knocking himself unconscious after tripping into a rabbit hole.

He wakes up with a bandage on his head in the home of a man named Jonas. Jonas tells Richards that he found him 20 feet away (despite the location being bare beforehand), and Richards realises he has woken up in a [parallel universe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiverse). In this universe, ketchup is purple, [cassette tapes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassette_tape) are more common than the [compact disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_disc), and the Beatles never broke up. Jonas shows Richards his tape collection, with most of them being ones he recorded. Some of them are tapes of new Beatles albums, with one of them being *Everyday Chemistry*.

Jonas and Richards both discuss their enjoyment of the Beatles, and just before leaving the parallel universe and travelling back to his own, Richards steals the tape of *Everyday Chemistry*, despite being told by Jonas to never take anything from another dimension.[^3818]

Richards explains why the album sounds like mashups of the Beatles' solo work, stating that "even though in the alternate universe The Beatles hadn't broken up, that didn't mean their future music ideas disappeared".[^3819]

The website also included photographs of the cassette tape and the location in which Richards claimed to have gone unconscious.

#### Album artwork

*Everyday Chemistry* was not given official artwork. Instead, photographs of the cassette tape were used for the cover. The first photograph (which appears on the main page of the website) includes the cassette's case, with the album title & [track list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_listing) being written on [ruled paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruled_paper). The other photograph (which has been used on the MP3 download of the album) is the tape itself, which is a [General Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Electric) 60-minute cassette tape. This photograph is unique as it doesn't match with the photographs that appear on the website.

Because of the lack of an official album artwork, fans would take it upon themselves to create their own. The most popular interpretation would include an art piece created in circa 1967 by Michael Leonard of what the Beatles would look like at the age of 64, an art piece inspired from the song "[When I'm Sixty Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_I'm_Sixty-Four)".[^3820]

#### Critical reception

Despite the criticism of Richards' story, *Everyday Chemistry* has been met with praise for its mixing, production and mashup choices.[^3821]
