### Self-Portrait (1969 film)

***Self-Portrait*** was a 1969 film made by the artist [Yoko Ono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoko_Ono). Premiering at the [Institute of Contemporary Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Contemporary_Arts) in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London) on 10 September 1969, the 42-minute film consisted of a single shot of her husband [John Lennon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lennon)'s semi-erect penis.

#### Background

On March 20, 1969, John Lennon and Yoko Ono married after ten months of dating. Yoko made several films in cooperation with Lennon. One of these films is *Self-Portrait*, which was released in 1969. It was a film that showed John Lennon's penis for 42 minutes. This proved to be too unconventional for audiences; the film was never reshown following its initial screening.

#### Synopsis

*Self-Portrait* is one long shot of John Lennon's semi-erect penis. As in Ono's *One: Fluxfilm No. 14* (aka *Match*) (1966) film, [slow motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slow_motion) is used to extend the sense of time. At the end of *Self-Portrait*, a drop of semen comes out of Lennon's penis. Lennon would later state in an interview about the film that the semen drop was accidental, and that the original idea was for his penis to rise and fall.

Ono had intended to film audience members reacting to *Self-Portrait*. This footage was intended to be part of another variation (a split-screen presentation, like in [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol)'s 1966 film *[Chelsea Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_Girls)*) of *Self-Portrait*, in which the crowd's reactions would be projected alongside the image of Lennon's penis. However, the recording equipment failed to record anything of the audience.[^4065] It is assumed this was a lighting issue, because in the summer of 1968, a hidden camera successfully secretly filmed the public reaction to John Lennon's "You Are Here" art exhibition[^4066] and also worked as part of the *[Plastic Ono Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_Ono_Band)* [multimedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multimedia) sculpture presented in absentia by Lennon and Ono at the [Apple Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Records) launch party for [The Plastic Ono Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Plastic_Ono_Band)'s record single "[Give Peace a Chance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Give_Peace_a_Chance)" held at the [Chelsea Town Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_Town_Hall) on July 3, 1969.[^4067]

#### Critical response

In 2009, renowned film critic [Philip French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_French), who was one of the few people to have seen *Self-Portrait*, would go on to describe his opinion of the film stating:

> "One film had the camera simply staring at Lennon's penis. Lasting some 40 minutes (it seemed like an eternity), it focused upon the unaided tumescence and detumescence of his member, reaching some sort of climax with a pearl-like drop of semen. The film, then jocularly known as "John Lennon's John Thomas" is actually called *Self Portrait*. The item listed in Yoko's filmography as *Erection* is in fact about John watching a hotel being built. John and Yoko were in the cinema, and during the performance there was a door open to the left of the screen with a sharp red light directed towards the auditorium. No one enquired about this, but it was later revealed Yoko had installed equipment to film the critics' reaction to John's comings and goings. The audience was to be one half of a split-screen feature: John showing his all, the critics responding to it frame by frame. Fortunately or unfortunately Yoko's apparatus recorded nothing. Sighs of relief all around. Otherwise that Film Critics' Circle might now be part of a permanent installation projected on the wall of Liverpool's John Lennon International Airport."[^4068]

#### Release

The film was premiered at the [Institute of Contemporary Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Contemporary_Arts) ICA in London in 1969, alongside two other films, *Rape* and *Folding*. Ono's films *Two Virgins*, *Smile* and *Honeymoon* were also shown at the ICA on the same night.[^4069][^4070]

Ono said in a 1970 interview with the film critic [Philip French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_French) that "the critics wouldn't touch it".[^4069]

### Woo In-hee

**Woo In-hee** ([Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_language): 우인희; c. 1940-1981) was a North Korean actress and a mistress of [Kim Jong Il](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Jong_Il).

Having reached stardom in the 1960s and 1970s, Woo, renowned for her beauty, acted in dozens of films.[^4071] She married Yoo Ho-sun, a famed film director, but she was involved in affairs outside of her marriage. In the late 1970s, she became a secret mistress of Kim Jong Il. After Woo began an affair with another man, Kim had her publicly executed in front of 6,000 people.

#### Early life

Woo In-hee was born in [Kaesong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaesong). Though her exact date of birth remains unknown, it is believed to be in the late 1930s or early 1940s. She worked during the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War). Already a dancer, she was later taken to [Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang) to become an actress and was dubbed the most beautiful woman in North Korea ever since.[^4072]

#### Career

After just one year in Pyongyang, Woo In-hee was given the main part in *The Tale of Chunhyang*,[^4073] earning her instant stardom.[^4072] She would go on to act in dozens of successful films.[^4074] In *The Girl from Diamond Mountain*, for instance, Woo acted the role of a woman spanning her whole life from her youth to advanced age.[^4072] Woo earned dozens of awards and had the prestigious title of People's Actress conferred upon her. Her feats attracted the personal interest and attention of [Kim Jong Il](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Jong_Il). As a gesture of confidence, she was given an extraordinary permission to travel abroad to [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovakia) and study acting there.[^4075] Woo's career flourished during the 1960s and 1970s.[^4076]

#### Personal life

##### Marriage to Yoo Ho-sun

Upon returning from Czechoslovakia, Woo In-hee married Yoo Ho-sun, one of North Korea's most gifted directors. The couple had three sons.[^4075][^4076] Woo, however, started affairs with various other men in the 1970s, which ruined her reputation.[^4077] Her first extramarital relationship was with a member of her camera crew. Others were also involved in the film industry.[^4075] By the end of the 1970s, rumors had spread to the point that her colleagues confronted her directly. They accused her of adultery during a [mutual criticism session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_criticism_session), but Woo reacted with defiance,[^4078] pointing out that her accusers were in fact men who had begun affairs with her and thus adulterers themselves. Her career was ruined as she was stripped of her title of People's Actress and instead of acting was made to tend to the boiler of the film studio for a year, a dangerous job with 12-hour shifts. In 1979, however, she was suddenly allowed to return to acting, and was even given some lead roles.[^4079]

##### Affair with Kim Jong Il

Woo started an affair with [Kim Jong Il](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Jong_Il). It is not known for certain when they began their courtship,[^4079] other than it took place sometime in the late 1970s.[^4076] At the time, *[Unsung Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unsung_Heroes)* was being filmed and her husband Yoo Ho-sun acted in the film.[^4080] It is possible that Kim and Woo had courted for years before Woo's fall from grace, or that her ruin made it possible for Kim to initiate a relationship in exchange for allowing her to return to acting.[^4079] Kim had a fellow actor follow her around and report on her activities.[^4081] The relationship was top secret and was being kept from everyone including Yoo.[^4082]

After Kim, Woo fell in love with a young [Zainichi Korean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zainichi_Korean) who had come to North Korea to work at a radio station.[^4083] Woo met him and he overcame her initial reluctance. The couple could not meet in public, so they met driving around for hours in the man's [Mercedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz). In the winter of 1980, after such a joyride, they were found in the car suffering from [carbon monoxide poisoning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_monoxide_poisoning) caused by the engine left running with windows shut to keep the cold out. The man had died and Woo had to spend two weeks at a hospital recovering. While interrogated over the death, she mentioned Kim Jong Il.[^4081]

#### Execution

Kim Jong Il had Woo executed for talking about her secret relationship with the Zainichi man.[^4084] In 1981,[^4085] Woo was told she was free to go,[^4086] but was instead taken to the [Kang Kon Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kang_Kon_Military_Academy) shooting grounds just north of Pyongyang.[^4087] She was tied to a post and shot in front of 6,000 people.[^4088] Twelve gunmen each fired 10 rounds from their [AK-47s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47), mutilating her body beyond recognition. Woo's husband was forced to watch the execution.[^4084] Kim nullified Woo and Yoo's marriage and forced the latter to finish *Unsung Heroes*.[^4080]

Woo's name and image were [purged from magazines and film catalogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damnatio_memoriae). She was edited out of films she had performed in, rendering their plots incomprehensible. Although the 6,000 witnesses to her execution were told not to talk about what they had seen,[^4084] the incident is widely known in North Korea.[^4076] A [South Korean TV drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_drama), *[Until the Azalea Blooms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Until_the_Azalea_Blooms)*, portrays her life. The show was banned in North Korea, but has nevertheless circulated in the country and people have been punished for watching it.[^4089]

#### Filmography

- *The Story of a Detachment Commander* (1966) (한 지대장의 이야기)[^4072]
- *The Town where We Live* (우리가 사는 고장)[^4072]

### Chris Rock-Will Smith slapping incident

During the [94th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/94th_Academy_Awards) on March 27, 2022, actor [Will Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Smith) walked onstage and [slapped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slapping_%28strike%29) comedian [Chris Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Rock) across the face during Rock's presentation for [Best Documentary Feature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Documentary_Feature_Film). The slap was in response to an unscripted joke Rock made about Smith's wife [Jada Pinkett Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jada_Pinkett_Smith)'s shaved head, a result of [alopecia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alopecia). Rock said that he "can't wait to see" Pinkett Smith in a sequel to the film *[G.I. Jane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G.I._Jane)* (1997), in which [Demi Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demi_Moore)'s titular character has a shaved head. After slapping Rock, Smith returned to his seat and shouted profanity at Rock, who briefly responded before completing his presentation without further interruption.

Later that evening, Smith won [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor) for his role in *[King Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Richard_%28film%29)*. In his acceptance speech, he apologized to the [Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences) (AMPAS) and other nominees, but not to Rock. The next day, he issued an apology to Rock and the AMPAS through social media. Smith resigned his Academy membership on April 1, facing a potential suspension or expulsion, and was banned from attending AMPAS events for 10 years.

Live television broadcasts in the United States mostly muted the incident due to [federal censorship laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_the_United_States). However, uncensored international footage went viral on social media; an excerpt from the Australian broadcast became one of the most-viewed online videos in the first 24 hours. The incident received worldwide attention and largely overshadowed the rest of the ceremony. Reactions to the incident were polarized, with most expressing disapproval of Smith's actions.

#### Background

[Jada Pinkett Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jada_Pinkett_Smith) (born Pinkett) is an American actress who rose to fame in 1991 for her role in the television show *[A Different World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Different_World)*. In 1994, she met [Will Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Smith) on the set of Smith's television show *[The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fresh_Prince_of_Bel-Air)*. The pair married in 1997, and she changed her name to Jada Pinkett Smith.[^4090][^4091]

Pinkett Smith and comedian [Chris Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Rock) had a long history of interactions.[^4092] The pair worked together on the [*Madagascar* films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar_%28franchise%29).[^4092] In 1997, in an interview on his late-night talk show *[The Chris Rock Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Chris_Rock_Show)*, he had commented on her participation in the [Million Woman March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Million_Woman_March).[^4093] Rock had previously hosted the awards twice, including [in 2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/88th_Academy_Awards), which several actors (including Pinkett Smith) boycotted due to the [lack of African-American nominees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/88th_Academy_Awards). Rock joked in his opening monologue, "Jada boycotting the Oscars is like me boycotting [Rihanna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rihanna)'s panties. I wasn't invited."[^4094][^4095][^4096]

In 2018, on her talk show *[Red Table Talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Table_Talk)*, Pinkett Smith revealed she had been experiencing [hair loss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hair_loss), potentially because of stress.[^4097] She was diagnosed with [alopecia areata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alopecia_areata) and in July 2021, she started completely shaving her head.[^4098][^4099]

By February 8, 2022, Will Smith had been nominated for an Academy Award for his acting in the film *[King Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Richard_%28film%29)*.[^4100] The [Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Motion_Picture_Arts_and_Sciences) announced Rock as one of the presenters of [94th Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/94th_Academy_Awards), taking place on March 27, 2022.[^4101]

#### Incident

Rock announced the nominees for [Best Documentary Feature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Documentary_Feature), performing a brief monologue largely read from a [teleprompter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teleprompter) script. Smith and Pinkett Smith were seated together near the front of the audience. Rock made an unscripted comment about Pinkett Smith's shaved head, comparing her to the titular character in the 1997 film *[G.I. Jane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G.I._Jane)*.[^4102]

> **Chris Rock**: Jada, I love you. *G.I. Jane 2*, can't wait to see it, all right?

Much of the audience, including Smith, laughed, while Pinkett Smith rolled her eyes in annoyance. Just as Rock was about to continue his speech, he noticed Smith rising from his seat, and jokingly addressed him as "Richard" in reference to Smith's portrayal of the [titular character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Williams_%28tennis_coach%29) in *King Richard*.

> **Rock**: It's, that was a, that was a nice one! Okay, I'm out here, uh oh, Richard! *\[laughs\]*

As Rock continued to laugh, Smith walked across the stage, slapped Rock across the left cheek, then turned around and walked back to his seat. Many in the audience initially thought that the attack was scripted; physical violence was incongruous with the calm, positive persona that Smith had maintained throughout his career.[^4103] When Smith began shouting at Rock, however, the audience realized that his outburst was genuine.[^4104][^4105]

> **Rock**: Oh, wow! Wow! Will Smith just smacked the shit out of me. *\[audience laughs\]* Thi, 
>
> **Will Smith**: *\[shouting from the audience\]* Keep my wife's name out your fucking mouth!
>
> *\[audience gasps\]*
>
> **Rock**: Wow, dude!
>
> **Smith**: Yes.
>
> **Rock**: It was a *G.I. Jane* joke.
>
> **Smith**: *\[slower; voice rising\]* Keep my wife's name out your fucking mouth!
>
> **Rock**: I'm going to, okay? Oh, I could, oh, okay. That was a... greatest night in the history of television, okay. *\[audience laughs\]* Okay. So we are here... to, uh... give a documentary out, to give an Oscar out for best documentary.[^4106][^4107]

Smith's expletives were censored by audio muting during the live broadcast in many countries.[^4104][^4108][^4109][^4110] The audience expected an explanation for the incident, but the show did not use hosts from this point on.[^4104]

##### Photograph

Photojournalist Brian Snyder, working for [Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters) in the photographer pool in the projection booth, photographed Smith striking Rock.[^4111] This photo quickly [went viral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Went_viral), was featured in news stories, and was adapted into [Internet memes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme).[^4105] He was unaware of the photo's cultural impact until after the ceremony, as his photos are automatically sent to his editors.[^4111] He was profiled by multiple media outlets,[^4112][^4113][^4114] including photography outlet *PetaPixel*.[^4115] Another described him as "The One Winner In The Will Smith vs. Chris Rock 'Smackdown'", speculating that "Surely, Snyder will now win the most coveted and prestigious photojournalism award, the [World Press Photo of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Press_Photo_of_the_Year), thanks to his photo that captured the moment Smith hit Rock, as his photo has been used by every publication under the sun."[^4116]

##### Uncensored viewership

In the United States, broadcaster [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company) muted Rock's and Smith's expletives due to [federal censorship laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_the_United_States). However, many international broadcasters chose not to, and uncensored recordings of the event went viral on social media.[^4117] The uncensored footage from the Australian broadcast on the [Seven Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Network) was posted by *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian)* on [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube)[^4106] and received more than 50 million views within 24 hours.[^4118]

##### Additional videos

Additional smartphone footage was published on March 31 from an audience member's perspective of the Smiths' table. This seems to show the reaction of Pinkett Smith during and after the joke, as unamused and rolling her eyes during the joke but then seeming to laugh when Rock commented, "Will Smith just smacked the shit out of me".[^4119]

#### Aftermath

##### Initial response

Immediately after the incident, Rock continued his presentation for Best Documentary Feature, which was awarded to the crew of *[Summer of Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_of_Soul)*. Smith continued to participate in the ceremony and subsequent celebrations. Some in attendance were surprised that no actions were taken; others wondered whether Smith would be allowed to stay.[^4120] Within forty minutes, Smith was presented the award for [Best Actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actor) for his portrayal of [Richard Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Williams_%28tennis_coach%29) in *[King Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Richard_%28film%29)*. He focused his emotional speech on divine justification and his need to protect those around him: "Love will make you do crazy things", he said, and apologized to the Academy, the other nominees, and to Richard's daughters [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_Williams) and [Serena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serena_Williams), who were in attendance.[^4121] However, he did not extend an apology to Chris Rock until the next day. The live audience gave Smith two [standing ovations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_ovation).[^4122][^4123] [Anthony Hopkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Hopkins), who then presented the [Academy Award for Best Actress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Actress), directly addressed Smith's behavior and Best Actor speech within his own speech, stating, "Will Smith said it all. What more can be said? Let's have peace and love and quiet."[^4124]

According to the Academy, Smith was asked to leave the ceremony but refused.[^4125] However, others who were present in the hall denied that Smith was ever asked to leave, either directly or through a representative. Backstage disagreement ensued between members of the Academy's leadership and ceremony producer [Will Packer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Packer) on whether Smith should be allowed to stay, which led to no action being taken.[^4126] *[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_%28magazine%29)* reported that Packer "was the key to Smith remaining in his seat".[^4126] Packer opposed suggestions to remove Smith from the theater because he did not believe that Rock would agree.[^4127]

After the ceremony, award winners were advised to only answer questions about their work and nothing else.[^4104] [LAPD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Police_Department) officers met with Packer, who later recalled that they were prepared to arrest Smith on charges of [battery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_%28crime%29). Rock repeatedly declined to press charges.[^4128][^4129] Early the next morning, Smith's son [Jaden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaden_Smith) tweeted, "And that's how we do it!" The tweet sparked mixed reactions, with many celebrities expressing strong disapproval.[^4130] In the first of many consequences for Smith, [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix) canceled a planned sequel to Smith's 2017 [urban fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_fantasy) [action film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_film) *[Bright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bright_%28film%29)*, mainly due to the negative publicity of Smith's altercation.[^4131]

##### Public apologies

Following public backlash, Smith issued a formal apology on [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram) and [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook) the next day.[^4132] He referred to his behavior as "unacceptable" and "inexcusable", directly addressing Rock: "I would like to publicly apologize to you, Chris. I was out of line and I was wrong. I am embarrassed and my actions were not indicative of the man I want to be. There is no place for violence in a world of love and kindness."[^4132][^4133][^4134]

Three days after the incident, Rock briefly mentioned the subject for the first time at a comedy show, saying that he was still processing it, but promised to talk about it in the future.[^4135] He said that Smith had not contacted him personally, nor had they spoken since the ceremony.[^4136] Claims on social media that Rock had apologized were debunked by fact-checkers.[^4137][^4138]

Smith posted a [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube) video on July 29 in which he addressed the incident and apologized to Rock, Rock's mother, Rock's brother [Tony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Rock), [Questlove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Questlove), the other Oscar winners, and his wife Jada saying he was "deeply remorseful" for his actions.[^4139]

##### Formal Academy review

The next day, March 28, the Academy's 42-member Board of Governors announced a formal review of the incident, scheduled for March 30.[^4140][^4141][^4142] AMPAS President [David Rubin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Rubin_%28casting_director%29) and CEO [Dawn Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_Hudson) announced this in an email to Academy members.[^4143][^4144] The following day, Smith initiated a six-minute [Zoom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoom_%28software%29) call with Rubin and Hudson, apologizing for his actions. The call was not mentioned at the review and the Board of Governors were not aware of the conversation when discussing disciplinary procedures. They charged Smith with "violations of the Academy's standards of conduct, including inappropriate physical contact, abusive or threatening behavior, and compromising the integrity of the Academy." The Academy said, "While we would like to clarify that Mr. Smith was asked to leave the ceremony and refused, we also recognize we could have handled the situation differently." Smith was invited to provide a written response within a fifteen-day period, after which the Board of Governors would vote on whether "suspension, expulsion or other sanctions under the Academy's standards of conduct" would be applied. Numerous Academy members said that AMPAS should, at the very least, suspend his membership, citing the organization's standards of conduct implemented eight weeks after [Harvey Weinstein's acts of sexual abuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Weinstein_sexual_abuse_cases) were exposed.[^4145] When the board learned of Smith's apology call, one of the participants stated the lack of transparency to the board was suspicious and showed lack of leadership.[^4146]

The Academy had never expelled a member prior to 2004, when the Board of Governors voted unanimously to expel actor [Carmine Caridi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmine_Caridi) for sharing promotional copies of films that were later mass-distributed.[^4147] Subsequently, the Academy expelled [Harvey Weinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Weinstein), [Roman Polanski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Polanski), [Bill Cosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Cosby), and cinematographer Adam Kimmel for sexual crimes.[^4148]

##### Resignation and ban

Smith preemptively resigned on April 1, 2022. AMPAS told him that he was likely to be expelled for a decade or more.[^4149][^4150] AMPAS announced it would continue disciplinary proceedings for violations of the Academy's Standards of Conduct.[^4151] Their next disciplinary meeting, scheduled for April 18, was intended to decide upon the issues unaddressed by Smith's resignation, including allowing him to retain his Best Actor Oscar for *King Richard*, allowing him to be invited by other members to future Academy Awards ceremonies, and allowing his nomination for future consideration while no longer a voting member of the Academy.[^4152][^4153] *Variety* reported that Smith's other professional membership at [SAG-AFTRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAG-AFTRA) would be informed of the AMPAS disciplinary review outcome.[^4152] The meeting was then moved earlier, to April 8;[^4154][^4155] Rubin wrote that "Following Mr. Smith's resignation of his Academy membership on Friday, April 1, suspension or expulsion are no longer a possibility and the legally prescribed timetable no longer applies. It is in the best interest of all involved for this to be handled in a timely fashion."[^4156]

At the April 8, 2022 meeting, Smith was banned from attending the Oscars or any other Academy event for 10 years.[^4157][^4158] NBC News obtained a letter signed by David Rubin and Dawn Hudson, revealing the Board of Governors' decision effective that day, of a ten-year ban where Smith "shall not be permitted to attend any Academy events or programs, in person or virtually, including but not limited to the Academy Awards".[^4159][^4160] Smith issued a succinct statement: "I accept and respect the Academy's decision."[^4161]

##### Smith film delayed

In June 2020, it was announced that Smith starred in *[Emancipation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emancipation_%282022_film%29)*, directed by [Antoine Fuqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Fuqua), in which he portrays [Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_%28enslaved_man%29), a runaway slave who outsmarts hunters and the Louisiana swamp on a journey to the [Union army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_army).[^4162] [Apple Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Studios) paid an estimated \$120 million for the rights to the film, outbidding several other studios.[^4163] However, by May 2022, the film's release was delayed to 2023, due to production issues, the controversy over Smith slapping Chris Rock, and an overcrowded film release schedule from Apple Studios.[^4164] The film was eventually released in select theaters on December 2, 2022 before being released on [Apple TV+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_TV+) on December 9, 2022.[^4165] Receiving mixed reviews from critics, the film earned a low-end \$3,000 to \$4,000 per location in its limited theatrical run.[^4165]

##### Later responses

Smith appeared as a guest on the November 29, 2022 episode of *[The Daily Show with Trevor Noah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Show_with_Trevor_Noah)* for his first public interview since the incident. After discussing Smith's upcoming film role in *Emancipation*, [Trevor Noah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Noah) questioned Smith about his reflections since the incident. Smith responded by saying, "That was a horrific night, as you could imagine. There's many nuances and complexities to it, but at the end of the day, I just lost it. I guess what I would say is you just never know what someone's going through."[^4166] Chris Rock spoke out about Smith for the first time in his Netflix [stand-up comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand-up_comedy) special *Selective Outrage* in March 2023, making numerous jokes about the incident.[^4167]

In October 2023, Jada Pinkett Smith's memoir *Worthy* was released. In it she revealed that she and her husband had been separated since 2016. She described the revelation as "weight off my shoulders". Of the incident at the Oscars, she said "it's so interesting how such an intense event can bring you closer together."[^4168] She said in a 2023 *[Parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parade_%28magazine%29)* interview, "That was a moment that I feel like we recognized once again... oh snap, we are just made for this journey together."[^4169][^4170]

#### Reactions

An opinion poll from [YouGov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouGov) conducted the day after the ceremony found that 61% of Americans said that Smith's actions were unacceptable and 22% said they were acceptable.[^4171] The [Federal Communications Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Communications_Commission), which regulates U.S. broadcasting, received 66 complaints about the incident.[^4172]

[SAG-AFTRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAG-AFTRA), the labor union representing film and television actors, issued a statement condemning Smith's behavior: "Violence or physical abuse in the workplace is never appropriate and the union condemns any such conduct. The incident involving Will Smith and Chris Rock at last night's Academy Awards was unacceptable. We have been in contact with the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and ABC about this incident and will work to ensure this behavior is appropriately addressed."[^4173][^4174]

##### Crew of *Summer of Soul*

Musician [Questlove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Questlove) and film producers David Dinerstein, [Robert Fyvolent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Fyvolent), and [Joseph Patel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Patel) were on stage immediately after the incident to accept the Best Documentary Feature award for *[Summer of Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_of_Soul)*, and some commenters opined that this award had been overshadowed by the incident.[^4175][^4176][^4177] The distracted audience searched [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) for information on Rock and Smith.[^4104] Gabrielle Ulubay of *[Marie Claire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Claire)* wrote that *Summer of Soul* "deserved to have its moment, and Questlove's touching speech and tribute to his parents deserved to have our full attention, but instead, the world kept its mind on Will Smith and Chris Rock and its eyes on Twitter."[^4178]

Questlove was asked about the incident by a reporter in a backstage press conference immediately after leaving the stage, and declined, "I'm not talking about that tonight, this is about the [Harlem Cultural Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem_Cultural_Festival)."[^4179] On *[The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tonight_Show_Starring_Jimmy_Fallon)* the next night, Questlove said he did not notice the slap in the moment because he was using [Transcendental Meditation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendental_Meditation) to curb his anxiety before the winner was called, and did not realize what had happened until "maybe three seconds before I spoke words".[^4180][^4181]

##### Comedians

The incident both provided fodder for on-stage comedians and elicited serious reactions for off-stage ones. Many comedians, including [George Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Wallace_%28American_comedian%29) and [Kathy Griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Griffin), spoke out about how the incident had worried them about potential future confrontations, and that they might be more careful about the topics of jokes going forward.[^4182][^4183] [Howie Mandel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howie_Mandel) connected the Rock and [Dave Chappelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Chappelle) incidents, stating, "That \[slap\] opened the floodgates. You saw what happened at the Academy Awards, and I thought that ... violence triggers violence, and I think this is the beginning of the end for comedy."[^4184]

In a *[CBS Mornings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Mornings)* interview where comedic actor [Jim Carrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Carrey) was asked about the incident, he stated, "You do not have the right to walk up on stage and smack somebody in the face because they said words,"[^4185] and that he would have sued Smith for \$200 million if he were in Rock's position, saying, "That video is going to be there forever. It's going to be ubiquitous. That insult is going to last a very long time." He further criticized the moral integrity of the [Hollywood film industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood_film_industry) for giving Smith standing ovations when receiving his Best Actor award, calling them "spineless en masse".[^4186]

Comedic actor [Cedric the Entertainer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedric_the_Entertainer) said in jest at an Oscars after-party that if he were assaulted during a [stand-up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand-up_comedy) routine for joking about someone's wife, he would defend himself.[^4187] Comedian [James Corden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Corden) commended Rock for "keeping the show moving" and criticized Smith for not taking a joke; he poked fun at the incident on *[The Late Late Show with James Corden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Late_Late_Show_with_James_Corden)* by performing a parody of the song "[We Don't Talk About Bruno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We_Don't_Talk_About_Bruno)" about Pinkett Smith.[^4188] Amy Schumer claimed she was traumatized by the incident, and criticized Smith while referring to him as "[Ali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_%282001_film%29)". She also criticized the control the AMPAS had over the ceremony, contrasting how she was restricted from joking about [Halyna Hutchins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halyna_Hutchins)'s death in the [*Rust* shooting incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rust_shooting_incident) against Smith's ability to "just come up and \[slap\] someone".[^4189]

Comedian [Gilbert Gottfried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilbert_Gottfried)'s final post on social media before his death on April 12 was supportive toward Rock, asking "Which is the worst crime? Chris Rock being physically assaulted or Chris Rock telling a joke?"[^4190] Late-night talk show hosts [Stephen Colbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Colbert), [Jimmy Kimmel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Kimmel), [Jimmy Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Fallon), [James Corden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Corden), [Bill Maher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher), [Andy Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Cohen), [Seth Meyers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seth_Meyers), and [Amber Ruffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amber_Ruffin) all condemned Smith's actions in their monologues.[^4191][^4192][^4193]

The [Laugh Factory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laugh_Factory) expressed its support of the [First Amendment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution) for comedians in the wake of the incident, and comedy clubs around the United States, including [Stand Up NY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand_Up_NY) and [Carolines on Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolines_on_Broadway), announced that they would be increasing security measures. The president of the Laugh Factory said he had noticed an increase of aggression among patrons since the businesses reopened after the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic) shutdowns.[^4194] The owner of the [Comedy Cellar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Cellar), however, expressed doubts that the attack would inspire copycats.[^4195][^4196]

[Bill Maher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Maher) commented "Alopecia is not [leukemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leukemia). We all struggle with our hair."[^4197] [Ricky Gervais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Gervais) held similar opinions, remarking sarcastically, "I'm fat and balding. I should get fucking [benefits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disability_benefits)."[^4198] During the [next Academy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/95th_Academy_Awards), host Jimmy Kimmel joked that in case of unexpected violence, his attacker would be "allowed to stay at the ceremony", "win Best Actor", and "spend the night partying while listening to '[Gettin' Jiggy wit It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gettin'_Jiggy_wit_It)' at the afterparty". At the conclusion of the telecast, a board parodying workplace "days without incident" signs displayed "Number of Oscars telecast without incident", and Kimmel raised the counter to "1".[^4199]

Five weeks after the incident, [Dave Chappelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Chappelle) was performing [stand-up comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand-up_comedy), where he was tackled onstage by an armed audience member.[^4200] Chris Rock suddenly joined him onstage to joke, "Was that Will Smith?"[^4201]

##### Politicians

Politicians worldwide publicly discussed or took a position on the incident.[^4202][^4203][^4204] Australian Prime Minister [Scott Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Morrison), reflecting on his own marriage, said that he "can understand" the reason for Smith's actions, but "that's not how you roll".[^4205] In Canada, Alberta premier [Jason Kenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Kenney) drew criticism for using a meme of the incident to express his position on [green energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_energy) policies.[^4206] The [New Zealand National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party) used a meme of the incident to criticize the [New Zealand Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party) on Facebook, but it was swiftly deleted and disavowed by leader [Christopher Luxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Luxon).[^4207] [Rishi Sunak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rishi_Sunak), British [Chancellor of the Exchequer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_of_the_Exchequer) at the time, compared himself to Will Smith, having recently had his wife [Akshata Murty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akshata_Murty) criticized over owning shares in a tech company based in Russia, but humorously remarked "At least I didn't get up and slap anybody".[^4208]

In the United States, [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_%28United_States%29) representatives [Ayanna Pressley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayanna_Pressley) and [Jamaal Bowman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaal_Bowman) tweeted in support of Smith, both of which were later deleted. Pressley, who has been diagnosed with alopecia areata, said that the condition is "not a line in a joke". Pressley also tweeted in defense of Smith, saying "Shout out to all the husbands who defend their wives living with alopecia in the face of daily ignorance & insults." and added "Women with baldies are for real men only ... boys need not apply." The tweet was later deleted.[^4203][^4209] Several [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_%28United_States%29) representatives, including [Marjorie Taylor Greene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marjorie_Taylor_Greene), also voiced support for Smith's actions,[^4202] and Representative [Andy Biggs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Biggs) used the incident to create [anti-Biden memes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Let's_Go_Brandon).[^4210]

##### Accusations of staging

Some commentators suspected the altercation was a [publicity stunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publicity_stunt), due in part to waning viewership numbers for recent years. David Griner from *[Adweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adweek)* tweeted: "A slow walk up, an open hand slap, no stagger, slow walk back with no scuffle and no security personnel stepping in? Feels absolutely staged for publicity," and several others agreed.[^4211] Rumors of the slap being staged were fueled by a version of the image that was digitally manipulated to create the illusion that Rock was wearing a cheek pad, which was then debunked.[^4212][^4213] Academy sources confirmed that the incident was not planned and that Rock's joke was ad-libbed.[^4214]

##### Views on criminality

The [LAPD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Police_Department) reported that Rock did not wish to file a police report. Former Los Angeles County prosecutor Alan Jackson believed that charges would not be pursued so long as Rock did not participate.[^4215]

However, former federal prosecutor Neama Rahmani explained that the idea of "pressing charges" is a legal misconception, and that the choice was ultimately up to the office of Los Angeles City Attorney [Mike Feuer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Feuer).[^4216] Criminal defense lawyer Alison Triessl echoed these sentiments, saying, "I would \[be\] surprised if the city attorney does not seriously consider \[charges\] because it was so public ... Are they sending the wrong message if they don't prosecute him? \[...\] It sends a message that you can commit a crime and you won't be punished. This was a very wrong message."[^4217] Chief legal analyst Aron Solomon of Esquire Digital, wrote, "It is clear that what happened at the Oscars was an assault under the California statutory definition." Tarek Fatah wrote in *[The Toronto Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Toronto_Sun)*, "Of the two men in the discussion, only one of them broke the law at the Oscars and got away with it because the LAPD stood back and let it happen ... Only when Will Smith is charged with assault and battery will it show that justice is blind". Jody Armour, a law professor at the [University of Southern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southern_California), argued, "If Smith is not charged, it could imperil the justice system's credibility".[^4217][^4218]

Other legal experts argued against charges. Alan Jackson said, "To be arrested on a misdemeanor, it has to happen in front of the authorities, or conversely the person against whom the crime was allegedly committed has to file a formal complaint with police". [Loyola Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loyola_Law_School) professor and former federal prosecutor Laurie Levenson said that the case was not serious enough to merit being treated as a priority; defense attorney and former prosecutor [Michael Cardoza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Cardoza) agreed, saying that though Smith's actions did constitute a crime, "it's not significant enough to clog our courts".[^4219] Defense attorney Lou Shapiro argued that Smith was not being given any special treatment by not being arrested, stating, "On a simple battery with no injury, LAPD is not deviating from the norm on this one. Unless it's a domestic violence case, they're more likely not going to use resources on it, because if the victim is not going to pursue charges, then who are we protecting at this point?"[^4220] Experts consulted by the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press) agreed that Smith would be unlikely to face charges at all.[^4215]

##### Memes

The public's reaction eventually morphed from shock to satire and [meme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meme). Media outlets referred to the altercation, from the [shot heard round the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shot_heard_round_the_world), as "the slap heard around the world".[^4104][^4108][^4109][^4110] Others referred to it as "[Slapgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_-gate_scandals_and_controversies)".[^4221][^4222][^4223] A few journalists preferred "The Slappening".[^4224][^4225][^4226] Countless [Internet memes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme) and parodies were created from the photo and video, a notable amount referencing their roles in [DreamWorks Animation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DreamWorks_Animation)'s movies *[Shark Tale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shark_Tale)* (2004) and *[Madagascar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madagascar_%282005_film%29)* (2005): Smith as Oscar in the former and Pinkett Smith and Rock as Gloria and Marty in the latter.[^4105][^4227][^4228] The photo was integrated into a mural by [Eme Freethinker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eme_Freethinker) on a remaining section of the [Berlin Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Wall) in [Mauerpark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauerpark).[^4229]

*[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live)*'s *[Weekend Update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weekend_Update)* discussed the way the Academy handled the incident, with [Colin Jost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Jost) quipping, "So now we just ask the victim right after they get hit in the head? 'Hey, are you cool if the guy who just attacked you hangs around for a while? You don't want to make him mad again.'"[^4230]

#### Analysis

##### Potential causes

[Monica Hesse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monica_Hesse), author and columnist for *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post)*, characterized the act of violence as a misguided attempt at [chivalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivalry).[^4231] *[Glamour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glamour_%28magazine%29)* magazine's Ateh Jewel characterized it as "a chivalrous act loaded with [toxic masculinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toxic_masculinity)".[^4232] [Duke University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_University) James B. Duke Distinguished Professor of African and African American Studies, [Mark Anthony Neal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Anthony_Neal), commented that the incident reflected upon societal values related to perceptions of race and African American [masculinity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masculinity) in American media.[^4233]

[Monash University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monash_University) professor at the School of Education Culture and Society, Steven Roberts, agreed that the incident belonged within the larger context of toxic masculinity. Roberts concluded that this was "another timely reminder that we need to invest in and promote forms of masculinity that are premised on democratic gender relations that centre on empathy and care".[^4234] University of Southern California professor and executive director of the USC Race and Equity Center, Shaun Harper, further elaborated on the incident as an example of toxic masculinity, emphasizing, "Will Smith is 53 years old, which confirms that toxic masculinity is not about immaturity. It is not a thing that men naturally grow out of. Some of us embody aspects of it our entire lives. Understanding what it is and how it shows up in our attitudes and behaviors might just save us from inflicting harm on ourselves and others."[^4235]

[Harvard Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Medical_School) psychologist Anna Precht supposed, "In a cooler, calmer moment, \[Smith\] would acknowledge that a joke is not actually a threat."[^4236] Author [Bernardine Evaristo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernardine_Evaristo) lamented that, with so few African American winners of Academy Awards, Will Smith "resorts to violence instead of utilizing the power of words".[^4237]

In a collaborative academic analysis of the incident, Monash University professors Steven Zech, Beatriz Gallo Cordoba, Lucas Walsh, and Matteo Bonotti, concluded, "Violence (also a form of incivility) is unacceptable, but civility, and when and how to enact it, is complicated. Sometimes it may be better to be impolite and not smile, if we want to promote change."[^4238]

Chris Rock and others widely speculated that Smith's assault was influenced by his possibly lingering agitation about his wife's previous and intense four-year extramarital affair with their son's friend [August Alsina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Alsina), who is 21 years her junior.[^4239][^4240] The Smiths unanimously concluded that theirs is a "bad marriage for life".[^4241][^4242]

##### Comparisons with historic Academy incidents

In a column for *[Glamour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glamour_%28magazine%29)* magazine, Jenny Singer contrasted the cases of Smith and French-Polish director [Roman Polanski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Polanski). Polanski has been a fugitive from American justice since 1978, after fleeing the country just hours before he was due to be sentenced for [drugging and raping a thirteen-year-old girl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Polanski_sexual_abuse_case). Singer observed that the Academy did not expel Polanski until forty years later, in the wake of the [MeToo movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MeToo_movement); and that, until his expulsion, the acting fraternity in Hollywood enthusiastically supported the director, including a standing ovation at the [2003 ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/75th_Academy_Awards) upon winning [Best Director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Director) for *[The Pianist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pianist_%282002_film%29)* (2002). By contrast, Smith was banned after only two weeks.[^4243]

Writing for *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian)*, Tayo Bero also described the treatment of Smith as "inequality in plain sight", and noted that the Academy took no action over the furor at the [1973 ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/45th_Academy_Awards) where [John Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wayne) allegedly had to be restrained by six security guards to prevent him from assaulting [Sacheen Littlefeather](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacheen_Littlefeather), an activist for [Native American civil rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_American_civil_rights).[^4244] However, a 2022 investigation found that Wayne's alleged behavior was an urban legend and had never happened.[^4245]

##### Financial impact

[Olin Business School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olin_Business_School) at the [Washington University in St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_University_in_St._Louis) professors Tim Solberg and [Glenn MacDonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_MacDonald) agreed that it was unlikely the incident would have significant financial impacts on the earnings power of either Smith or Rock, but could have negative impacts for the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences organization. Solberg said, "The Academy itself may suffer damage if it does not take action. ... The two stars have their followings and the audience is segmented. They will probably not have a drop in earnings as a result. In that sense, their brand is not harmed financially." MacDonald agreed, observing, "In entertainment, they often say there is no such thing as bad publicity." Solberg noted there could be a financial impact to Smith if the major film studios took action: "While financially, the stars have their brand and their following, unless a studio boycotts or the public cancels Will Smith, a major box office star making money for the company, due to the public show of violence, he will maintain his financial draw even if his brand is tarnished."[^4246]

Rock seemed to financially benefit from the incident when his comedy tour sold out. One secondary ticket seller had a 641% increase in the following days, and some tickets were auctioned for more than US\$1,700.[^4247]

### IKEA Heights

***IKEA Heights*** is a 2009 [comedic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy) [melodrama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodrama) [web series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_series) created by Dave Seger, Paul Bartunek, Delbert Shoopman, Spencer Strauss, and Tom Kauffman for [Channel 101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Channel_101). A [spoof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parody) of [soap operas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soap_opera), the series was [filmed covertly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla_filmmaking) inside the [IKEA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IKEA) store in [Burbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burbank,_California), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California).[^4248] *IKEA Heights* stars [Randall Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randall_Park), [Whitney Avalon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Avalon), and [Matt Braunger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Braunger).

*[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly)*'s Whitney Pastorek wrote that the series "is so brilliant and awesome that its glories can really only be diminished by additional words."[^4249]

Madeleine Löwenborg-Frick, a spokesperson for IKEA's Canadian branch, said of the series, "Absolutely, we think it's funny. We see the humour in it and we approach our own marketing with a similar tongue-in-cheek humour. But unauthorized filming in our stores isn't a good thing. There's proper channels that people who want to film in our stores can go through."[^4250]

#### Premise

The series is set in the sketchy town IKEA Heights, and focuses on different mysteries and crimes that impact the residents. These include murders caused by being smothered by pillows, and a zombie invasion.

### Susunu! Denpa Shōnen

***Susunu! Denpa Shōnen*** (進ぬ！電波少年) is a Japanese [reality television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reality_television) show which aired from January 11, 1998, to September 29, 2002, on the [Nippon TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihon_TV) network, and online from October 2009.

#### Description

The title means "Do not proceed! Crazy youth". "[Denpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denpa)" literally means *[radio waves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_wave)*, but colloquially also refers to crazy people, about instances of mentally insane people claiming to be controlled by radio waves.[^4251] The title is also a pun; the predecessor of the show was called *Susume! Denpa Shōnen* (lit. *Onward! Crazy Youth*). To depict that the show had indeed moved onward, one of the [characters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiragana) of the title was changed from the "me" (め) to "nu" (ぬ), approximately meaning *Do not proceed!*.

The show is known for the extreme situations the participants were placed in. It gained high ratings, spawned a sister show, ***Raiha Shōnen*** (雷波少年), and was controversial due to the [sadistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadomasochism) challenges and rule changes made by the television producers if they felt the participants were doing too well. The show also received criticism for some of the show segments being staged.[^4252]

The participants were usually unknown comedians who were ready to do anything to get famous. Upon application, they were chosen randomly and were not told what the objective of their challenge was. Some of the challengers became more or less famous, while some remained relatively unknown.

The program's initial cancellation was related to a government crackdown on "torture"-themed shows,[^4253] but has seen a revival on the [World Wide Web](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Wide_Web) from October 2009 on the streaming website *Number Two Nihon Television* (第2日本テレビ). Its first new "challenger" for the webcast was [comedian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owarai) [Yoshio Kojima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshio_Kojima).[^4254]

#### Major challenges

In the four-year course of the original program, participants completed about 20 challenges.

Amongst the best known are:

- [**Denpa Shōnen teki Kenshō Seikatsu**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasubi) (電波少年的懸賞生活; lit. "Denpa Shōnen's Prize Life"), probably the best known challenge of the show. Starting in January 1998, [Nasubi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasubi), a young comedian, was forced to live for 15 months naked in an apartment in Japan and later [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea) only on prizes won in sweepstakes.[^4255]
- **Denpa Shōnen teki Mujintō Dasshutsu** (電波少年的無人島脱出; lit. "Denpa Shōnen's Desert Island Escape") and the **Swam** series. Two comedians were put on a desert island, with no food nor clue about where they were, and were only told that their ordeal would finish if they built a raft and reached Tokyo. After their escape from the desert island, which took them four months, they were given a swan-shaped [pedalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedalo) and were told to reach Tokyo with it, and then go with the same pedalo from India to Indonesia.
- **Denpa Shōnen teki Afurika Yūroppa Tairiku Ōdan Hitchihaiku no tabi** (電波少年的アフリカ・ヨーロッパ大陸縦断ヒッチハイクの旅; lit. "Denpa Shōnen's Vertical Africa-Europe Continental Hitchhike"). A comedian named Takashi Itō and a [radio DJ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_DJ) from [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong) named Tse Chiu-Yan hitchhiked from the [Cape of Good Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_of_Good_Hope) in South Africa to [North Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Cape_%28Norway%29) in Norway. The two contestants were forbidden to use their travel money and thus faced starvation, dehydration and harsh weather conditions. At one point in the challenge, Itō collapsed in the [Sahara Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahara_Desert) and was airlifted to a local hospital for treatment.
- **Denpa Shōnen teki Penanto Rēsu** (電波少年的ペナントレース; lit. "Denpa Shōnen's Pennant Race"). This segment tested the loyalties of diehard fans of the [Central League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_League) teams - the [Yomiuri Giants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomiuri_Giants), the [Hanshin Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanshin_Tigers), and the [Chunichi Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chunichi_Dragons). The contestants would be confined to a single room with a TV that only showed their team's baseball games. Their faces would also be hidden from public view. If their team won, they got to eat dinner and a small portion of their face would be revealed to the audience. If their team lost, they would get no food and the lights would turn off, leaving them in darkness until the next day's game. If the contestant's favorite team went on a win streak, the quality of the food they could eat would increase as well as gain public exposure and popularity due to their entire face being shown on TV until their team finally lost. A losing streak would mean that a contestant could go days in the dark without food. At the end of the season, the contestant would win an overall prize depending on how their team placed.

#### *Denpa Shōnen International*

***Denpa Shōnen International*** was the special of the program with location shootings outside Japan, aired mainly on holidays or reorganizational periods of TV programs.

[Kunihiro Matsumura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunihiro_Matsumura), [Akiko Matsumoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akiko_Matsumoto), and other guests performers attempted to visit foreign celebrities to do challenges without appointments. Major challenges include:

- Sing the song *Ladybug Samba* to [Yasser Arafat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yasser_Arafat) of [Palestine Liberation Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palestine_Liberation_Organization).
- Meet foreign leaders and say "I hate you". Leaders that the programs ultimately succeed to meet were [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela) of South Africa and [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter) of the United States.
- Play [rock paper scissors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_paper_scissors) with [Vladimir Zhirinovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Zhirinovsky) of the [Liberal Democratic Party of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democratic_Party_of_Russia).
- Shave the beard of [Fidel Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro) of Cuba (failed).

Other challenges include:

- **Stop AIDS Campaign** (STOPエイズキャンペーン): [Tetsurō Degawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetsur%C5%8D_Degawa) went to [LGBT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT) Bars in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London), [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco), and [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney) with a hidden wireless microphone to distribute condoms. During one distribution event, Degawa signaled he was being sexually harassed by a man but the staff of the program did not step in to help him. The program that was ultimately aired has the audio recording of Degawa being sexually assaulted. Degawa later reflected this to be the "most horrific" location shoot ever in his life.[^4256][^4257]
- **Inherit the will of [Princess Diana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Diana)** (ダイアナ元妃の意思を継ぎたい): Matsumoto heads for the removal of landmines buried in Cambodia.
- **Matsumura Overseas Animal Confrontation Series** (松村海外動物対決シリーズ): Matsumura confronts various dangerous animals like a [lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion) (in Africa), a [bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear) (in Canada), a [crocodile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodile) (in Australia), a [mountain gorilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_gorilla) (in Africa), and [komodo dragon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komodo_dragon) (in Indonesia) with a [harisen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harisen).

### Turn-On

***Turn-On*** is an American [surreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surreal_humour) [sketch comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sketch_comedy) series created by [Digby Wolfe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digby_Wolfe) and [George Schlatter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Schlatter) that aired once on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company) on Wednesday, February 5, 1969. Only one episode was shown before [being pulled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_television_series_canceled_after_one_episode) from ABC's schedule, leaving another episode unaired. The show has since been considered one of the most infamous [flops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_television_series_notable_for_negative_reception) in TV history, with significantly low initial ratings and negative critical reception.

Schlatter and [Ed Friendly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Friendly), who had previously been the producers of *[Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowan_&_Martin's_Laugh-In)*, were contracted by [Bristol-Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol-Myers_Squibb) to develop the show, and provided it to [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company) for a projected 13-week run after it was rejected by [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC) and [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS). *Turn-On*'s sole broadcast episode replaced the Wednesday episode of *[Peyton Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peyton_Place_%28TV_series%29)* - a fact referenced on the show itself, where, in the opening, [Tim Conway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Conway) refers to the show as "Peyton Re-Place". Conway was the first episode's guest host, and also participated in certain sketches. Among the cast were [Teresa Graves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teresa_Graves) (who would join the *Laugh-In* cast that fall), [Hamilton Camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton_Camp), and [Chuck McCann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_McCann). The writing staff included [Albert Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Brooks). [Urban legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_legend) by Conway and Schlatter claimed *Turn-On* was cancelled *during* the episode by affiliates; while this did not happen, multiple stations protested to ABC after it aired, screened it at a later timeslot, or refused to air it altogether.

#### Premise

*Turn-On*'s premise was that it was "the first computerized TV show", according to its opening sequence; the show had no sets except for a clinical white backdrop, where sketches generated by an artificially intelligent computer would be acted out. Unlike the generally appealing humor of *Laugh-In*, *Turn-On* was oriented around [off-color humor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off-color_humor) and "focused almost exclusively on sex as a comedic subject",[^4258] using various rapid-fire jokes and risqué [skits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skits). Co-creator and production executive Digby Wolfe described it as a "visual, comedic, sensory assault involving [animation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animation), [videotape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Videotape), [stop-action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop-action) film, electronic distortion, [computer graphics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_graphics), even people."[^4259]

Sounds created with [Moog synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moog_synthesizer) were used in lieu of a [laugh track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laugh_track), representing the computer's laughter. The program was also filmed instead of presented live or on videotape; in a style of presentation that was novel for the time, several sketches and jokes were presented with the screen divided into four squares resembling [comic strip panels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comic_strip). The production credits of the episode were inserted at random intervals after the first commercial break, instead of conventionally at the beginning or end.

#### Reaction

When initially presented to CBS, a network official stated that *Turn-On* was "so fast with the cuts and chops that some of our people actually got physically disturbed by it."[^4260] Tim Conway has stated that *Turn-On* was [canceled midway through its only episode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_television_series_canceled_after_one_episode), so that the party that the cast and crew held for its premiere as the show aired across the United States also marked its cancellation.[^4261][^4262] A native of [Cleveland, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland), Conway later claimed that the Cleveland ABC affiliate, [WEWS-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WEWS-TV), replaced the show after the first commercial break and utilized an "emergency protocol" of a black screen with live organ music.[^4261]

Ten minutes into *Turn-On*, WEWS general manager Donald Perris called ABC's headquarters by telephone to notify them that they would no longer air the show[^4263] and sent to ABC president [Elton Rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_Rule)[^4264] an angry [telegram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegram_%28telegraphy%29): "If your naughty little boys have to write dirty words on the walls, please don't use our walls. *Turn-On* is turned off, as far as WEWS is concerned. You tried too hard."[^4265][^4266][^4267] After the program aired, a WEWS spokesman claimed that the station's [switchboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switchboard_operator) was "lit up" with protest calls, and Perris derided *Turn-On* as being "in excessive poor taste".[^4264] George Schlatter would later accuse Perris of actively lobbying other affiliates *prior* to the broadcast to force a network cancellation after objecting to it replacing *[Peyton Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peyton_Place_%28TV_series%29)* on the Wednesday night schedule.[^4268][^4269] However, Perris told *[The Cleveland Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cleveland_Press)* that neither he nor the station's then-current program director, Ernest Sindelar, had a chance to preview the show prior to broadcast, saying that:

> It was previewed by a member of our staff whose judgment is usually good. Last night it wasn't very good. The show shouldn't have gone on. It's all right to be racy, but this was just plain dirty. This was a hate show. Its spirit was dirty. I watched it at home and I felt very bad that it was on.[^4265]

At the same time, [WAKR-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WVPX-TV) in [Akron, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akron,_Ohio), the Cleveland market's other primary ABC affiliate, did not receive any negative phone calls but their general manager criticized the show's "questionable taste".[^4264]

Several stations in the eastern time zones refused to air *Turn-On* before its premiere, including [Memphis, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee)'s [WHBQ-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WHBQ-TV), which refused to air the series because the management felt that it was "not up to our broadcast standards for that time of evening". The station quickly replaced it with an episode of *[The Real McCoys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Real_McCoys)*.[^4270] After seeing the episode, several stations in the later western time zones decided not to broadcast the show at all, including [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon)'s [KATU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KATU_%28TV%29),[^4271] [Seattle, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle)'s [KOMO-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KOMO-TV), and [Denver, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver)'s [KBTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KUSA_%28TV%29). KATU's management stated their belief that certain portions of the program "are not in good taste and that these portions would be objectionable to a substantial and responsible part of the community."[^4271][^4272] Viewers of [Little Rock, Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Rock,_Arkansas)'s [KATV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KATV), which disliked the show but decided to air it, "jam\[med\] the station's switchboard" with complaints.[^4266] [Dallas, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas), ABC affiliate [WFAA-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WFAA) elected to air the show on the following Sunday night at 10:30 local time, to an overwhelmingly negative response.[^4273]

Both *The New York Times* and the Associated Press gave the show poor reviews,[^4266] as did Bill Barrett, who was the TV critic for the *Cleveland Press*. Barrett remarked that "it appears to have proven one point: a television program needs more than shock-and-sex content to be attractive. It has to have taste and style. *Turn-On* lacked it last night. For all its special effects of split screen, psycho lights and electronic throbbing, it was merely a half-hour of vulgar little snickers."[^4274] An ABC executive stated that "creatively, *Turn-On* didn't work". He compared the show negatively to the comedy of [Dean Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_Martin), *Laugh-In*, and the [Smothers Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smothers_Brothers), which the executive described as "absolutely beyond belief ... awfully [blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribaldry)", but were popular and less controversial because unlike *Turn-On*, "they're funny".[^4275]

#### Cancellation

On February 7, ABC announced that *Turn-On* would go on hiatus. Instead of the scheduled February 12 episode, the *ABC Wednesday Night Movie* (*[The Oscar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Oscar_%28film%29)*, itself an infamous flop) would start 30 minutes early.[^4276] This announcement came after the following week's *TV Guide* went to press; it published a listing for the scheduled February 12 episode, which would have starred [Robert Culp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Culp) and then-wife [France Nuyen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_Nuyen) as hosts.[^4266][^4259] Finally, on February 10, the show was formally canceled. By this time, WEWS, KBTV, and KATV all told ABC that they would not air the show again; with several other affiliates having already turned it down, it no longer made financial sense to air it.[^4266]

ABC received 369 calls of complaint during the show and 20 calls that supported it;[^4260] by comparison, the network received 1,800 protest calls several weeks earlier after preempting the *Wednesday Night Movie* for an address by [President Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon) introducing [his cabinet appointees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Richard_Nixon).[^4263] Network officials told sponsor [Bristol-Myers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol-Myers) that the show was unacceptable and Bristol-Myers ordered Schlatter and Friendly to end production.[^4260] Many assumed the show's title was itself an implicit reference to [Timothy Leary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Leary)'s pro-drug maxim, "[Turn on, tune in, drop out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turn_on,_tune_in,_drop_out)".

Schlatter's contract was bought out by ABC under the stipulation that *Turn-On* never be rerun.[^4277] The network eventually replaced *Turn-On* with a revival of *[The King Family Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_King_Family_Show)* focusing on the [Four King Cousins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_King_Cousins). The controversy led ABC to reject a pilot written by [Norman Lear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Lear), stating that the [lead character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Bunker) was "foul-mouthed, and bigoted", out of fear that it might anger its affiliates again. CBS liked the pilot, picked it up as *[All in the Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_in_the_Family)*, and began airing it during the 1970-71 midseason.[^4278][^4279] Schlatter, who returned to *Laugh-In*, had the writers on that show include jokes lampooning Cleveland after a directive from NBC to eliminate [ethnic jokes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_joke), largely due to on WEWS' handling of *Turn-On*; he later said, "What is funny about Cleveland? I don't know. I've never been to Cleveland."[^4277]

#### Legacy

After *Turn-On*'s cancellation, *[TV Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_Guide)* called the show "the biggest bomb of the season". It stated that both CBS and NBC had rejected the show due to its perceived lack of quality, and that its sexual content was an important reason why viewers rejected the show. The magazine quoted a source who lamented *Turn-On'*s lack of a regular host or interlocutor: "\[T\]here wasn't any sort of identification with the audience - just a bunch of strangers up there insulting everything you believe in."[^4280] Conway said in 2008 that *Turn-On* was "way ahead of its time. I'm not sure even if you saw it today that maybe that time has also passed."[^4261] Bart Andrews, in his 1980 book *The Worst TV Shows Ever*, stated that *Turn-On* was actually quite close to the original concept for *Laugh-In*. "It wasn't that it was a bad show, it was that it was an awkward show," concluded author [Harlan Ellison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlan_Ellison), a fan of [counter-cultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-culture) comedy and a TV critic for the *Los Angeles Free Press* in 1969.[^4277]

In 2002, *Turn-On* was ranked number 27 on *TV Guide's* 50 Worst TV Shows of All Time.[^4281] *What Were They Thinking?: The 100 Dumbest Events in Television History* ranked it at number 25.[^4282]

Both completed episodes are available for public viewing at the [Paley Center for Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paley_Center_for_Media).[^4283] They were also made available for viewing on YouTube on October 9, 2023.[^4284] On February 4, 2024, a third episode was released on YouTube, composed of unused footage from Conway's episode as well as footage from an episode guest-starring [Sebastian Cabot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastian_Cabot_%28actor%29) of *[Family Affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_Affair_%281966_TV_series%29)*.
