### Calculator (Nintendo Switch)

**Calculator** is a [software calculator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_calculator) released by Sabec for the [Nintendo Switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Switch), a [video game console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_console), in May 2021. It was widely criticized for its US\$10 price point and platform, with critics noting that better-suited devices featured free software with equivalent functionality. As an [Internet meme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme), Calculator became one of [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic)'s best-rated games for the Switch by user score. It was cited as an influence on subsequent [utility software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_software) releases on the [Nintendo eShop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_eShop).

#### Overview

Calculator replicates a [scientific calculator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_calculator), including methods to compute [elementary arithmetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_arithmetic), [trigonometric functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions), and [logarithms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logarithm).[^4285][^4286] It visually resembles [the calculator app](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calculator_%28Apple%29) bundled with [iOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOS) devices.[^4287] Calculator was developed by the British company Sabec for the [Nintendo Switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Switch), a [video game console](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_console).[^4288] Before it, the company had been known for releasing [utility software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility_software) and simple games for the platform.[^4288][^4289] These include a [piano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano), [drum set](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_set), and [guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar), as well as a [night vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_vision) app that uses the [Joy-Con](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy-Con)'s [infrared sensor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrared_sensor).[^4289][^4290] *[TouchArcade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TouchArcade)*'s Shaun Musgrave, who had regularly reported on Sabec's releases, regarded them as "over-priced, virtually useless software".[^4291] Calculator was first listed on the [Nintendo eShop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_eShop) on May 11, 2021, and released on May 12.[^4292] It was priced at US\$10 or £8.09.[^4293][^4294] Sabec advertised it as being suited for students and engineers.[^4295] The app was later rated for ages 3 and up by the [International Age Rating Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Age_Rating_Coalition) and then released in Japan on June 24 at ¥899.[^4286][^4288]

#### Reception

Calculator was the first Sabec app to [go viral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Go_viral).[^4296] It was widely criticized for its price point, which was more expensive than some physical calculators, while not offering more features than free alternatives for [smartphones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smartphone) and [personal computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_computer). Publications that criticized Calculator's [price-performance ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Price%E2%80%93performance_ratio) include *[CNET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNET)*,[^4292] *[Engadget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engadget)*,[^4295] *[Eurogamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurogamer)*,[^4294] *[GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot)*,[^4287] Gfinity,[^4285] *[Kotaku](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kotaku)*,[^4297] *[Nintendo Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Life)*,[^4298] and *[TechRadar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TechRadar)*.[^4293] Several critics questioned its usefulness, as there were devices better suited to use as calculators.[^4285][^4297] Musgrave considered it not to be the company's worst release and highlighted the comedic aspect of using a calculator on a gaming platform.[^4291] Henry Stockdale, in his review for Gfinity, noted that the app's [widescreen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widescreen) layout felt unnatural for a calculator.[^4285] Adam Vjestica, writing for *TechRadar*, considered Calculator proof of the faulty maintenance of the eShop, saying that "the bar is so low, that as long as a game works, it'll be allowed to slither onto the eShop, even if it stinks up the joint in the process". He believed that the number of low-quality releases, as well as the media coverage they attained, hampered the visibility of higher-quality [indie games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_game).[^4293]

Calculator became an [Internet meme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme). On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic), a [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator) for video games and other media, users [review-bombed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_bomb) the app with perfect 10/10 scores accompanied by humorous comments. This gave Calculator an average user score of 9.1/10 within days of its release, ranking it as the fifth-best Switch game by user score, on par with *[Monster Hunter Rise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monster_Hunter_Rise)*.[^4299][^4300] In [speedrunning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speedrunning), [SmallAnt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SmallAnt), a [video game streamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_streamer), set the record for counting to 1,000 using Calculator in 38 seconds.[^4301]

#### Legacy

Following the popularity of Calculator, Sabec released further non-game software on the eShop, including a [xylophone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xylophone),[^4296][^4302] a [handpan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handpan),[^4290] and Spy Alarm, which uses the Joy-Con's infrared sensor to [detect motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_detector).[^4303][^4304] The company also developed licensed games based on the British game show *[Bullseye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bullseye_%28British_game_show%29)* and the character [Popeye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popeye).[^4305][^4306][^4307] Calculator has been cited as an influence on other non-game products coming to the eShop, such as the [note-taking software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Note-taking_software) Notes released by Game Nacional in June 2021.[^4308][^4309][^4310] In August, it spawned the [multiplayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiplayer) game *Battle Calculator* by Blacksmith DoubleCircle, in which up to four players compete to compute a given number as quickly as possible.[^4311][^4312]

### Don't Buy This

***Don't Buy This*** (also known as ***Don't Buy This: Five of the Worst Games Ever***) is a [compilation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_compilation) of [video games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game) for the [ZX Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZX_Spectrum) released on 1 April 1985. As described on the box, it contains five of the poorest games submitted to publisher [Firebird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecomsoft). Instead of rejecting the submissions, they decided to mock the original developers by releasing them together and publicly brand it as "unoriginal" and "awful". Firebird even [disowned all their copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_domain) to the game and encouraged buyers to redistribute it at will.[^4313]

Reviews for the game were universally negative, with critics questioning how to critique the game due to its publicity being based on it being a collection of bad games. Despite the negative reception, the game was a commercial success.

#### Games

- ***Fido 1***: The player controls a dog named Fido to defeat moles and birds[^4313] to protect an area for several levels. Fido also needs to keep eating in order to stay alive. In the later levels, enemies such as a low flying canary and a cat which throws projectiles at you are added, but their attacks are very easy to avoid.
- ***Fido 2: Puppy Power***: Features similar gameplay as the original *Fido*, but Fido can now move up and down instead of just left and right. In addition to Fido being able to defeat enemies with its tail, used as an attack in the previous game, Fido can now shoot laser beams from its eyes in order to destroy other enemies and gain health.
- ***Fruit Machine***: The player controls an animated, low-resolution [slot machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slot_machine) with reels that spin rather slowly. The instructions sarcastically describe the game as a "mysterious, original new game \[that\] requires skill, timing, nerve and absolute concentration".[^4313] It also suggests that you should play the game in the middle of the night while also sleeping. A medley of short tunes plays when the player wins.
- ***Race Ace***: A [racing game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racing_video_game) where the player controls a light blue race car that can only turn 90 and 180-degree angles. The game is impossible to win, regardless of the speed setting of the player's car because the computer-controlled cars advance more quickly every time the player turns. The controls have the tendency to freeze if another car invades your space. On one screen, the game is erroneously titled "*Ace Racer*". There is evidence to suggest that *Race Ace* was first published as its own cassette in 1983, having been developed by Tony Rainbird, who co-created the Firebird label, as opposed to being a submitted [indie game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_game).[^4314]
- ***Weasel Willy***: A game where a purported [weasel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weasel), which in actuality has the appearance of a humanoid figure in-game, has to avoid trees that are completely green and its own large, uniform footprints. The trees spawn in random locations whenever a level starts, so the weasel may be blocked by trees, preventing the player from being able to play the level. The weasel may even start a level with a tree occupying the same space as it does, causing immediate loss of the level.[^4315]

#### Release

> The package contains a selection of the worst Spectrum games ever published in the world!

*,  James Leavey, Firebird's marketing manager on *Don't Buy This*.[^4316]*

*Don't Buy This* was published by [Telecomsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecomsoft) under the [Firebird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecomsoft) label. Firebird disowned the game upon release, with Firebird's marketing manager James Leavey claiming that the game "wasn't released, it just escaped!"[^4317] The publisher also encouraged copying the game, offering a chance to win a sticker or badge for people who wrote to the company about the game.[^4318] It was released on 1 April 1985 under Firebird's Silver Range for £2.50.[^4319] A sequel was in consideration, with the working titles of either *Don't Buy This 2*, *Don't Buy This Again*, or *Don't Buy This Either*.[^4314]

#### Reception

Reception

**Review scores**

| Publication | Score |
|----|----|
| *[Crash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crash_%28magazine%29)* | (39.333333)%[^4315][^4320] |
| *[Sinclair User](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinclair_User)* | 2/5[^4321] |
| *[Sinclair Programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinclair_Programs)* | 9%[^4322] |
| *[Your Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Your_Spectrum)* | 4/15[^4323] |

*[Your Spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Your_Spectrum)* wrote: "The games aren't that bad as do-it-yourself games but, they won't provide that much fun."[^4323] *[Sinclair User](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinclair_User)* said it contained "five of the most uninspired games ever to disgrace the Spectrum."[^4321]

A reviewer for *[Computer and Video Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_and_Video_Games)* noted that the game was difficult to give a score due to it being publicised as being a collection of bad games, but declared it to be "good for a laugh".[^4324]

John Szczepaniak from *Hardcore Gaming 101* featured the game as part of their "Your Weekly [Kusoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kusoge)" column. Szczepaniak, while describing the games as "uninspired, dull and lazy", he did not consider them to be the worst games on the ZX Spectrum.[^4318] Despite the negative criticism towards the game, *[Retro Gamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retro_Gamer)* in 2005 reported that it was a commercial success.[^4319]

### I am Error

"**I am Error**" is a [quote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotation) from the [NES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Entertainment_System) [game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game) *Zelda II: The Adventure of Link*. The quote is spoken by a villager, apparently named Error, in the town of Ruto. In the original Japanese version of the game, the line is *Ore no na wa Erā da…* (オレノナハ エラー ダ…), which translates to "My name is Error…".

The unlikely character name is widely believed to have been a programmer's [in-joke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-joke), since the game also features a similar looking character named *Bagu* (バグ; lit. Bug), meaning [software bug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_bug). In computing, a bug is a flaw in the programming code that might lead to an error. Error and Bug are thus assumed to form a comical, in-universe parallel. In the English version, the name *Erā* was translated, but the name *Bagu* was not. Many gamers therefore missed the joke and variously believed the "I am Error" phrase to be a mistranslation, a misspelling, or an actual [error message](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_message).

The phrase has since become part of the [NES](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NES) folklore and became an early [Internet meme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme) around 2000. It has been referenced in a number of games, including *[Super Paper Mario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Paper_Mario)*, *[The Binding of Isaac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Binding_of_Isaac_%28video_game%29)*, *[Guacamelee!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guacamelee!)*, *[Pony Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pony_Island)*, and *[Terraria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terraria)*.

#### Origin

*Zelda II: The Adventure of Link* was released in Japan on 14 January 1987, and internationally in late 1988. The player controls [Link](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Link_%28The_Legend_of_Zelda%29), who travels through Hyrule in his quest to rescue [Princess Zelda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Zelda). Early in the game, Link arrives in the town of Ruto, where he can enter a house inhabited by a bearded man in purple attire. If the player approaches him, he announces: "I am Error".

Many puzzled gamers believed the cryptic phrase to be a textual mistake or a [glitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glitch) within the game, but it is actually neither. The line is a correct English translation of the original Japanese text *Ore no na wa Erā da…* (オレノナハ エラー ダ…), of which a more precise translation would be "My name is Error…".[^4325][^4326] Initially, the character does not say anything else. When the player advances to the harbor town of Mido, a man there advises Link to "Ask Error of Ruto about the Palace". If the player then goes back to Error, he provides Link with a clue about how to gain access to the Island Palace, the game's third dungeon.

While no official explanation from Nintendo exists regarding the origin of the *Erā*/Error character, his name is widely believed to have been an [in-joke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-joke) from the game's programmers. Aside from Error, the game also features a character named *Bagu* (バグ), meaning "[\[software\] bug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_bug)". In computing, a bug is an error in the programming code, leading to unintended results. *Bagu*/Bug lives near Error, residing in a house hidden in a forest south of Ruto. The two characters look identical, except that Error wears a purple tunic, while Bug's tunic is red. It is therefore assumed that one of the developers named one character Error and another one Bug, having the two men form a humorous thematic connection within the game's universe.[^4326][^4327] When the game was translated to English, the name *Erā* was correctly translated to Error, but the name *Bagu* was not translated to Bug, leading *[Official Nintendo Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Nintendo_Magazine)* to conclude: "In reality, then, *Bagu* is the mistake, because his name was translated wrongly and should have been Bug. So there".[^4328]

Translator [Clyde Mandelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clyde_Mandelin) wrote that the "I am Error" quote is often incorrectly believed to be a translation mistake, and is even considered "one of the biggest mistranslations of early Nintendo games", even though it is not actually a mistranslation.[^4326] Another incorrect notion about Error is that his name is a typo and should have been Errol.[^4329][^4330][^4331][^4332] The original Japanese text proves this wrong though. The reason for the phrase often being considered a translation or spelling mistake is likely because many early games from the 1980s and 90s, including [the first *Zelda* game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Legend_of_Zelda_%28video_game%29), were rife with mistranslations and poor English prose ('[Engrish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engrish)').[^4327] A well-known example of this is "[All your base are belong to us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_your_base_are_belong_to_us)" from *[Zero Wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero_Wing)* (1989).[^4333]

#### Legacy

Around 2000, "I am Error" became an early [Internet meme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme). According to [Ben Huh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Huh), founder of [Cheezburger Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Can_Has_Cheezburger?), the meme was inspired by the success of the "[All your base are belong to us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_your_base_are_belong_to_us)" meme, which inspired a number of memes based on '[Engrish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engrish)' quotes from old games, such as "A Winner is You" (from the NES game *[Pro Wrestling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_Wrestling_%28NES_video_game%29)*).[^4333] The "All your base" joke is believed to have sprung up in 1998 and surged in popularity in 2000-2001, giving some indication of when the "I am Error" meme must have originated.[^4334]

Despite being a minor [NPC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-player_character), Error has become part of the wider NES folklore and has been mentioned in several pieces of media. For example, *VideoGamer.com*'s Emily Gera included him in a list of the "oddest character names in games", describing him as "\[p\]ossibly one of the most well known minor characters of all time".[^4330] *[GamesRadar+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamesRadar+)* included his phrase in a list of the 40 most repeated quotes.[^4335] *[GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot)* mentioned the phrase in an article discussing poor translation in video games, incorrectly calling it a 'translation oddity'.[^4336] *[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN)* included it in their list of the worst in-game quotes at number two. The editor joked that the 'mystery' of Error "ranked up with [Sasquatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasquatch) and the [Loch Ness Monster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Ness_Monster)".[^4337] *[The Escapist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Escapist_%28magazine%29)*'s Brett Staebell called Error a "pioneer in game humorology", and used the quote as the subtitle for his article.[^4338] A *[Nintendo Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendo_Life)* review for *Castlevania II: Simon's Quest* noted that the game had a script similar to that of "I am Error", likening the game's garbled translation to the phrase.[^4339]

From approximately 2012 to 2015, the [404 page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/404_page) of nintendo.co.uk stated "I am Error", along with a picture of the character.[^4340] At [E3 2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Entertainment_Expo_2014), the Nintendo Treehouse's presentation of *[Super Smash Bros. for Wii U](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Smash_Bros._for_Wii_U)* displayed an error page based on the "I am Error" scene after experiencing technical difficulties.[^4341]

Nathan Altice wrote a book titled *I Am Error*, named after the character, which gives a technical history of the NES, focusing especially on the console's technical limitations and how they influenced its games. It was published in May 2015 by [MIT Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIT_Press).[^4327]

On day 2 of the Nintendo Treehouse presentation at [E3 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E3_2019), an "I am Error" technical difficulties screen was shown after the Treehouse was hit by a brief power outage within the South-Hall.[^4342][^4343]

A [Nintendocore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nintendocore) band named Iamerror existed from 2005 to 2009.[^4344][^4345][^4346]

##### Appearances in other video games

*[Super Paper Mario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Paper_Mario)* (2007) features a boss battle against a character named Fracktail, a robotic dragon. It is at one point hacked, which causes it to utter several confused lines, including "I am Error. Press any key to restart".[^4347] An achievement in *[Guacamelee!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guacamelee!)* (2013) was given the title "I Am Error".[^4348] *[Zeno Clash II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeno_Clash_II)* (2013) also features it as an achievement title.[^4349] The quote is featured in *Fossil Fighters: Champions* (2010).[^4350] Video game designer [Edmund McMillen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_McMillen) put references to the quote in two of his games: *[Time Fcuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Fcuk)* and *[The Binding of Isaac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Binding_of_Isaac_%28video_game%29)*.[^4351][^4352] In *[Splatoon 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splatoon_2)* (2017), Pearl says "I am Error" when her Team Retro loses the Splatfest to Marina's Team Modern.[^4353] In *[Cadence of Hyrule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cadence_of_Hyrule)* (2019), if the player finds a way to go out of bounds, they encounter a character in a house who says "I am Error". Talking to him again has him call himself "Error Houlihan", a reference to the Chris Houlihan room.[^4354]

### Oh Shit!

***Oh Shit!*** is a [*Pac-Man* clone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Pac-Man_clones) released in 1985 for the [MSX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MSX) developed by The ByteBusters and published by [Aackosoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aackosoft) under the *Classics* range of games; a range that consists of [clones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_clone) of arcade games. *Oh Shit!'s* level and art design is identical to that of *[Pac-Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pac-Man)*,[^4355][^4356][^4357][^4358], but features [digitized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digitization) speech; when the player loses a life, the [eponymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eponym) phrase "Oh Shit!" is said.[^4359][^4360][^4355]

*Oh Shit!* was twice republished with differing titles and cover art; in the United Kingdom as *Oh No!* due to the title being considered too [obscene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obscenity) for a video game,[^4356] and for the European re-release by Premium III Software Distribution as *Shit!*, of which uses cover art from the 1985 horror novel *The Howling III: Echoes* without permission.[^4361] For both renamed releases, the speech is changed accordingly.[^4356]

#### Gameplay

*Oh Shit!'s* gameplay is identical to that of *[Pac-Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pac-Man)*, down to the level design.[^4355][^4356] This was noted as a positive by reviewers who deemed it a faithful reproduction of the arcade original.[^4355][^4356] The [ghosts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghosts_%28Pac-Man%29) in *Oh Shit!* are named Joey, Paul, Willy, and Frankie.[^4359]

#### Development

*Oh Shit!* was coded by Steve Course.[^4359] The speech generation code was written by Ronald van der Putten,[^4359] and *Oh Shit!'s* speech was performed by Ronald van der Putten of The ByteBusters.[^4359]

*MSX Computing* states in their review that they received two copies of the game for their review, both the UK *Oh No!* version and the European *Oh Shit!* version, stating that the European version's name was "deigned unsuitable for the UK".[^4356] The MSX UK *Oh No!* version cost £2.99 in 1986.[^4356] The MSX version of *Oh Shit!* originally cost ƒ29.50 [Dutch Guilder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Guilder) in 1985, and was reduced to ƒ14.95 in 1987.[^4362] In 1988, the cassette release of *30 MSX Hits* was ƒ49.90, and the [floppy disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floppy_disk) release was ƒ79.90.[^4363][^4364]

#### Releases

The 1985 MSX release was published by Aackosoft, but later releases of the MSX version were released by different publishers; the European version of *Oh Shit!* was later published by Eaglesoft (an alternate label of Aackosoft), and *Oh Shit!* was published by Compulogical in [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain).[^4365] The UK release, *Oh No!*, was also published by Eaglesoft.[^4366] The European re-release, *Shit!*, was developed by Eurosoft and published by Premium III Software Distribution, notably using cover art from the 1985 horror novel *The Howling III: Echoes*, possibly without permission.[^4361] The original MSX version of *Oh Shit!* was made for compatibility with MSX 32K computers, and later re-releases offer MSX 64K compatibility. Unlike other Aackosoft titles in the *Classics* range, *Oh Shit!* is incompatible with MSX 16K computers.[^4355]

Aackosoft went [bankrupt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy) in 1988, after which *Shit!*, alongside other Aackosoft titles, were re-published by Premium III Software Distribution and developed by Eurosoft (a former label of Aackosoft) in the same year.[^4357] Premium III Software Distribution released the *30 MSX Hits* compilation in 1988, including *Oh Shit!* as part of its lineup.[^4357] According to Dutch gaming magazine *MSX-DOS Computer Magazine*, after Aackosoft went bankrupt in 1988, their [intellectual property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property) was transferred to a company called Methodic Solutions, and all previous MSX Aackosoft titles were re-published by Premium III Software Distribution and developed by Eurosoft, both separately and in a compilation titled *30 MSX Hits*.[^4357]

The 1988 *30 MSX Hits* compilation release of *Oh Shit!* offers [MSX2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MSX)[^4367] compatibility.[^4363][^4364] All MSX releases of *Oh Shit!*, *Shit!* and *Oh No!* are [cassette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassette_tape) releases, except for the *30 MSX Hits* release, which had both cassette and [floppy disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floppy_disk) releases.[^4363][^4364]

##### Version differences

*Oh Shit!* introduces the game's ghosts on the title screen using digitized speech stating "This is Joey, Paul, Willy and Frankie",[^4359] however the UK version *Oh No!* says "This is Joey, this is Paul, this is Willy, and this is Frankie".[^4356] "This is" has the same [enunciation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elocution) all four times it is said.[^4368] Unlike *Oh Shit!*, where "Oh Shit!" is said every time the player dies, in *Oh No!*, "Oh No!" is only said after the player has lost all their lives and gets a game over.[^4368][^4359]

#### Reception

Reception

**Review scores**

| Publication         | Score                            |
|---------------------|----------------------------------|
| *MSX Gids*          | 4.5/5 (*Oh Shit!* - MSX)[^4360] |
| *MSX Computing*     | 2/3 (*Oh No!* - MSX)[^4356]     |
| *MSX Club Magazine* | 9/10 (*Oh Shit!* - MSX)[^4358]  |

*Oh Shit!* was generally positively received by reviewers, who considered it to be a faithful reproduction of *Pac-Man*,[^4360][^4358] and several reviewers praised the addition of digitized speech.[^4363][^4355][^4356] *Oh Shit!* was predominantly reviewed in Dutch gaming magazines, as *Oh Shit!* was developed & originally published in the Netherlands.[^4360][^4355][^4357][^4363][^4364][^4358]

Dutch gaming magazine *MSX Gids* gave the MSX version of *Oh Shit!* an overall score of 4.5 out of five, rating graphics, game quality, and price five stars, but giving sound three stars. *MSX Gids* criticises *Oh Shit!'s* sound effects, stating that "The speech, which gets boring quickly, has been added at the expense of the original wokka-wokka sounds. Too bad."[^4360]

Dutch gaming magazine *MSX Computer Magazine* reviewed the MSX version of *Oh Shit!* alongside other Aackosoft titles based upon arcade titles, *Boom* (*[Galaxian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxian)*), *Scentipede* (*[Centipede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centipede_%28video_game%29)*), and *Hopper* (*[Frogger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frogger)*). *MSX Computer Magazine* praises *Oh Shit!'s* gameplay, calling *Oh Shit!* a "perfect reproduction of the original arcade game", and praising the inclusion of the 'coffee break' [cutscenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutscene) from the original *Pac-Man* that play as intermissions between levels. *MSX Computer Magazine* further notes *Oh Shit!'s* similarity to *Pac-Man*, stating that the levels are "identical to the arcade original", but expresses that *Oh Shit!* differentiates itself through the addition of speech. *MSX Computer Magazine* criticises *Oh Shit!'s* incompatibility with MSX 16Ks.[^4355]

*MSX Computer Magazine*, now named *MSX-DOS Computer Magazine*, reviewed the MSX version of *Shit!* alongside other arcade clones, particularly comparing it to another *Pac-Man* clone, *Maze Master*, stating that they prefer the original *Pac-Man* or *Shit!* over *Maze Master*. *MSX-DOS* expresses that they mourned Aackosoft's [bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy), stating that "*Shit!* used to be a favorite of mine, *Pac-Man* fan that I am, and with the loss of Aackosoft a good program was withdrawn from rotation", praising the game's re-publishing by Premium III Software. *MSX-DOS* criticises the shortening of the game's speech of "Oh Shit!" to just "Shit!", but still expresses that "Despite that, *Shit!* still always remains a sublime *Pac-Man*, too bad about the change of voice acting."[^4357]

*MSX-DOS Computer Magazine* reviewed the MSX version of *Oh Shit!* in 1988 as part of the compilation release *30 MSX Hits*, expressing that "*Oh Shit!* is a good *Pac-Man*-clone with a great name". *MSX-DOS Computer Magazine* notes *30 MSX Hits'* MSX2 compatibility, further expressing that not all MSX games offer this compatibility, stating "So you thought that any MSX program could be used on any MSX computer? As long as you don't try MSX2 software on MSX1 hardware? Well, everyone thought that, in the past. Before the MSX standard was well defined, game programmers sometimes did not adhere to that standard. There has been a lot of trouble with non-running games in the past."[^4363] *Oh Shit!'s* MSX2 compatibility was also noted by *MSX Club Magazine* in their review of *30 MSX Hits* in 1988.[^4364]

British gaming magazine *MSX Computing* gave the UK MSX version, *Oh No!*, an overall score of two out of three stars, noting its similarity to *Pac-Man*, stating that "*Pac-man* fans will love this game as it is based very much along the same lines." *MSX Computing* praises *Oh No!'s* digitized speech, expressing that "The speech is a really novel and fun feature and does much to enhance the game" and further noting *Oh No!* as "far superior" to similar games due to its speech capability. *MSX Computing* praises *Oh No!'s* gameplay, calling it "addictive" and "an easy game to play", further recommending it due to its low price of £2.99 in 1986.[^4356]

Dutch gaming magazine *MSX Club Magazine* reviewed the MSX version of *Oh Shit!* in 1986, giving it an overall score of 9/10, beginning their description of *Oh Shit!'s* gameplay by stating "You already know how to play it: it's Pac-Man." *MSX Club* called *Oh Shit!'s* graphics "not graphically amazing, but this doesn't hinder gameplay", and criticised *Oh Shit!'s* sound effects, stating that "Beyond the typical irritating *Pac-Man* sounds there's also speech present", and calls the death message of "Oh Shit!" "terrible shouting". *MSX Club* notes a difficulty curve in *Oh Shit!* as the game progresses, and praises the addition of cutscenes.[^4358]

### Sheng Long

**Sheng Long** is a character [hoax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoax) related to the *[Street Fighter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter)* series, created by *[Electronic Gaming Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_Gaming_Monthly)* as an [April Fools'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_Fools') prank in 1992. Conceived by editor Ken Williams due to a mistranslation suggesting the existence of a character named Sheng Long in [Capcom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capcom)'s [fighting game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_game), *[Street Fighter II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_II)*, the publication released an article describing a method to fight the character in the game. Despite intending it to be an obvious joke, many players took it seriously, and other publications reprinted the details as fact without verifying its legitimacy, causing the Sheng Long hoax to spread worldwide. As a result, the magazine later acknowledged it was indeed a hoax, though it revisited the concept for a similar joke in 1997. Claiming Sheng Long would appear in *[Street Fighter III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_III)*, they provided a backstory for the character and an appearance designed by editor Mike Vallas. Despite the article trailing off and being incomplete, it resulted in confusion between the North American and Japanese branches of Capcom, with the former calling the latter to ask why they had not been informed about the character.

As a character and a hoax, Sheng Long has been described as one of the most famous and well-known legends related to video gaming by publications such as *[UGO.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UGO.com)* and *[GameSpot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameSpot)*. Several publications have attributed the hoax with the creation of *Street Fighter* character [Akuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akuma_%28Street_Fighter%29), who was added to *[Super Street Fighter II Turbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Street_Fighter_II_Turbo)* as a secret [boss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boss_%28video_games%29) with several similarities to the original joke. Fan appeal for the character affected later Capcom titles, with public requests for the inclusion of Sheng Long in an actual video game leading to the consideration of his inclusion in the *Street Fighter: The Movie* video game and the appearance of the character [Gouken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gouken) as both a secret [boss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boss_%28video_games%29) and playable character in *[Street Fighter IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_IV)*. Capcom has also added in-game achievements referencing Sheng Long in *Street Fighter II* re-releases, and for the 25th anniversary of the hoax temporarily posted artwork and a profile for the character on their website, this time designed by Shigenori "Kiki" Kiwata. This version of the character was later reused for his appearance as a [non-player character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-player_character) in the World Tour mode of *[Street Fighter 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_6)*, acting as a high-difficulty optional [boss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boss_%28video_game%29).

#### Origin

The name Sheng Long comes from a mistranslated portion of the name of a [special move](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fighting_game) performed by the series' main character, [Ryu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryu_%28Street_Fighter%29); the characters *shō ryū* ([昇](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E6%98%87)[龍](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E9%BE%8D), *rising dragon*) from *Shōryūken* (昇龍拳), Ryu's flying uppercut, are *shēng lóng* in Chinese [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin). This was carried into one of Ryu's quotes to defeated opponents in the [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language) localization of the 1991 arcade game *Street Fighter II*, changing the [Japanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_language) quote "If you cannot overcome the Shoryuken, you cannot win!" (昇龍拳を破らぬ限り、お前に勝ち目はない！, *Shōryūken o yaburanu kagiri, omae ni kachime wa nai!*) to "You must defeat Sheng Long to stand a chance." As a result, players were given the impression that Ryu was referring to a person instead of the attack.[^4369]

The [Super Nintendo Entertainment System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Nintendo_Entertainment_System) (SNES) [port](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porting) of *Street Fighter II*, released shortly after the April Fools' prank, changed the translation to "*You must defeat my Dragon Punch to stand a chance.*"[^4369] However, the English instruction manual for the SNES *Street Fighter II* referred to "Master Sheng Long" as Ryu and [Ken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Masters)'s teacher.[^4370][^4371] Instruction manuals for later ports to the SNES and [Sega Mega Drive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sega_Mega_Drive) consoles replaced all references to Sheng Long by referring to Ryu and Ken as disciples of the "[Shotokan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shotokan) school of karate".[^4372][^4373] A character named [Gouken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gouken) was later introduced in Masaomi Kanzaki's 1993 [*Street Fighter II* manga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_II_%28manga%29) as Ryu and Ken's sensei[^4374] and was adapted into the series' backstory in *Super Street Fighter II Turbo*.[^4375]

##### Original April Fools' article

The mistranslation spawned rumors about the existence of a Sheng Long character in the game,[^4369] and players sent letters to [video game publications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_game_publications) attempting to confirm the character's existence.[^4376] *Electronic Gaming Monthly* editor Ken Williams, who was an avid *Street Fighter II* player, also took an interest in the rumor, feeling there had to be some secrets in the game due to his experiences with the first *Street Fighter* arcade game. Wanting to try the office's newly acquired [Adobe Photoshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adobe_Photoshop) software, he modified screenshots of the game to "create" a "secret boss" by combining [sprites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprite_%28computer_graphics%29) from different characters, using it as a way to let off steam due to the stresses of work. Pleased with the results he invited the other writers over, who enjoyed the humor and encouraged Williams to create a second screenshot of the character, with Ray Price suggesting to give the character a flaming fist version of Ryu's "Shoryuken" special attack. Unsure what to do with the screenshots at this point, and with their April issue approaching, they invited founding editor Steve Harris over and proposed using the images for an [April Fools' Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_Fools'_Day) prank article. Harris took one look and responded "Make it happen."[^4377]

As a result, in the April 1992 issue of the video game magazine, a method was "revealed" to reach Sheng Long in the arcade game. The article claimed that the character could be found if a player using Ryu did not let the character suffer any damage during the entire game. Upon reaching the final match against the game's boss [M. Bison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._Bison), the player had to avoid hitting Bison and being hit by him until the time limit expired, thus ending the round in a draw. After repeating this for ten consecutive rounds Sheng Long would then appear out of nowhere and throw Bison off of the edge screen and out of the way. The game's on-screen timer would then stop at 99 seconds, resulting in a "fight to the death" between Ryu and Sheng Long. As a character Sheng Long was stated to feature the special moves of all the fighters, such as [Chun-Li](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chun-Li)'s "Spinning Bird Kick" and [Sagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagat_%28Street_Fighter%29)'s "Tiger Shot", but inflict more damage. In addition, the character was supposedly faster than any other fighter in the game, negating the pause between projectile attacks. Other attacks mentioned included an air-based throw attack and the aforementioned "Shoryuken" covered in flames to represent his greater power.[^4376] The "ridiculous requirements" to encounter Sheng Long were intended to help cue readers in that the article was indeed a joke, however they felt they needed more to make that clear. Editor Martin Alessi suggested adding an "Honorable Mention" to "W.A. Stokins" ("waste tokens") of "Fuldigen, HA" ("fooled again, ha"). Williams felt that nobody would fall for the joke without being incredibly gullible.[^4377]

However, people did indeed try to find the character, with arcade owners sending complaints to the magazine that their machines were being broken: large amounts of quarters were being deposited by players, causing them to eventually get stuck. The magazine also received a large volume of hate mail by players themselves, who were complaining that the requirements were impossible.[^4377] Rival publication *[GamePro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamePro)* also received letters from players asking to verify the authenticity of Sheng Long, much to the chagrin of their editor Dan Amrich.[^4378] Compounding matters, publications from [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe), [Hong Kong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong) and other countries reprinted the trick without verifying it or asking *Electronic Gaming Monthly*'s permission causing the hoax to spread worldwide. [Capcom's North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Capcom_subsidiaries) branch also for a time changed their introductory message for their corporate line to address the hoax, instructing anyone calling about Sheng Long to call *Electronic Gaming Monthly*'s offices instead. Though Williams was unconcerned with the reaction due to only being known at the publication as "Sushi-X", the other writers were.[^4377] In their December issue of that year revealed, *Electronic Gaming Monthly* noted that it was a hoax, and were surprised at the worldwide coverage the joke received.[^4379]

##### April Fools' 1997

During the development of *Street Fighter III*, fans discussed the prospect of the character's inclusion in the new title.[^4369] By this point in time Capcom had introduced the backstory character [Gouken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gouken), who had been killed by his brother [Akuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akuma_%28Street_Fighter%29), a playable character added to later iterations of *Street Fighter II*. Taking advantage of this, *Electronic Gaming Monthly* perpetuated the hoax again in 1997 by claiming that Sheng Long was in the game, and provided character artwork depicting his appearance alongside new screenshots which were all [photoshopped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photoshopped) works by editor Mike Vallas.[^4377] Unlike the first article, they did not finish their explanation of how to reach him, ending the article with "To reach him, you will need at least six perfects and..." Additionally, the words "April Fools" were spelled out in the first letter of the first ten sentences of the article.[^4380]

The character's design was expanded on greatly in the article; Sheng Long was now stated to be the American [localization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language_localisation) name for the character Gouken. His profile listed in the article paralleled Gouken's, but instead of Akuma killing him he was knocked into a raging river. The result gave him a scar over his eye, and a desire to get revenge on his brother. To this end, he revived several "killing techniques" of his fighting style, which included an air version of Akuma's red "[Hadouken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadouken)" projectile attack that knocked his opponent down, a ground high-low projectile that could be used on the ground, an unblockable "Denjin-Shinryuu-Ken" super attack that would shock the opponent, an air rapid "Hadouken" super attack akin to a move used by [Ibuki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibuki_%28Street_Fighter%29), and a third super attack intended to be a stronger version of Akuma's "Shun Goku Satsu".[^4380] In a later issue, the staff reported that despite this being the second Sheng Long joke, it was convincing enough that Capcom of America called the company's headquarters in Japan asking why they had not been told that the character was in the game.[^4381]

#### Legacy

The April Fool's joke has seen significant discussion in media outlets since its debut, with *[IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN)* describing it as having the biggest impact of all of *Electronic Gaming Monthly*'s April Fools jokes,[^4382] while *[UGO.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UGO.com)* named it one of video gaming's greatest [urban legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_legend), noting its impact upon the series' success.[^4383] Capcom community manager Seth Killian described the hoax as "a part of gaming history", comparing Sheng Long to the [Konami Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konami_Code).[^4384] However, Tom Coulter of *[GamesRadar+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GamesRadar+)* listed it as one of the video game legends he never wanted to hear about again, stating that while it was a good prank at first, it had gone from "sly wink to the fans" to "[Borat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borat) t-shirt."[^4385]

The rumor is often credited with inspiring the creation of Akuma, a character who debuted as a hidden final boss in *Super Street Fighter II Turbo*, due to their similarities,[^4386] although Capcom has never confirmed nor denied this. As in the hoax, the process of fighting Akuma would require certain achievements met during the game, with Akuma interrupting the final match of the game between the player and M. Bison. "The similarity was nodded at in the [high-definition remake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Street_Fighter_II_Turbo_HD_Remix) of *Super Street Fighter II Turbo*, in which an [Xbox 360 Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360_Achievement) titled "Sheng Long is in Another Castle" could be earned for defeating Akuma in the game's arcade mode.[^4387] Despite the lack of direct confirmation from Capcom, the staff of *Electronic Gaming Monthly* felt the character was added in response to the hoax, with Williams stating that they were "flabergasted that something we did had an impact on the industry like that."[^4377]

##### *Street Fighter: The Movie*

Sheng Long is mentioned four times in the 1995 arcade game *Street Fighter: The Movie* in the endings for Ryu,[^4388] Ken,[^4389] and Akuma.[^4390] In each, he is stated as the master of Ryu and Ken, and Akuma's brother, but never stated as dead. Despite the repeated mention, Sheng Long does not appear in the game. On January 30, 2007, the game's designer, Alan Noon, appeared on Shoryuken.com's forum and discussed aspects of the game cut during development, among them a playable Sheng Long character.[^4391]

According to Noon, talk had circulated about adding extra characters that were not in the film. As the Sheng Long hoax and Akuma's debut in *Super Street Fighter II Turbo* were fairly recent at the time, the designers asked for [Capcom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capcom)'s permission to add both characters into the game. Capcom approved the addition of Akuma, but denied the inclusion of Sheng Long. However, Capcom later unexpectedly approved the addition of Sheng Long. Noon designed Sheng Long's appearance for the title, giving him black [gi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keikogi) pants and a long, green, padded/quilted, sleeveless Gi style top which was tied off with a black belt mandarin style, long white braided hair, [Fu Manchu moustache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fu_Manchu_moustache), a thick black ribbon over his eyes due to being blinded by Akuma and one hand taking the form of a dragon's claw, described as a result of his power being so advanced, that he began to physically manifest dragon like attributes. Capcom approved the design and Luis Mangubat, an artist from the development team (who would later work at [Midway Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midway_Games)), posed as Sheng Long. However, the character was left unfinished because of time constraints.[^4392]

##### *Street Fighter IV*

In an interview in the January 2008 Issue of *Electronic Gaming Monthly*, *Street Fighter IV* producer Yoshinori Ono stated "Let's just say that \[jokes\] that your magazine have reported in the past might find their way into the game as fan service." Executive editor Shane Bettenhausen took this to mean the appearance of Sheng Long in *Street Fighter IV*, though added that if the character did appear in the game, it would be Gouken.[^4393] When asked in a later interview by *[1UP.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1UP.com)* regarding the possibility of Sheng Long's appearance in the title, Ono replied "Are you coming to the [Tokyo Game Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo_Game_Show)? How about you ask me that question again then."[^4394] Capcom later revealed Gouken as a character in *Street Fighter IV*,[^4395] with Ono stating in an interview with *[Play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_%28US_magazine%29)* magazine that his inclusion in the title was in response to fans requesting Sheng Long's presence in the game.[^4396]

On the first of April 2008, Capcom announced Sheng Long as a "secret, unlock-able character" in their Japanese development blog for *Street Fighter IV* and later posted in their official US blog accompanied with a silhouette of the character.[^4397][^4398] The post took the tone of a Capcom representative trying to announce a character without giving away too many details, hinting that "Sheng Long is Ryu's..." then holding back and saying to wait for an official character announcement. In a similar fashion to the original joke, the post lists the method to unlock him as requiring the player to win every round as Ryu without taking any damage whatsoever and then perform his "Shoryuken" move during the final boss fight. Reception to the joke the third time was negative[^4399] and included criticism from *1UP.com*.[^4400] The following day, the Japanese website confirmed that it was indeed a joke and explained the origin of Sheng Long while adding "Sheng-Long is still now and always will be, truly a character of legend."[^4369][^4384]

##### *Street Fighter 6*

In March 2017, 25 years after the original hoax was published, Capcom gave Sheng Long a joke profile in the Shadaloo Combat Research Institute part of their Capcom Fighters Network website, which showcased artwork and profiles for every character related to the *Street Fighter* series. Satirizing the Sheng Long rumor, it states that he became a living legend, appears after consecutive draw games, his moves are impossible to counterattack and always register as counter hits and that anyone that sees him will die after 24 hours.[^4401] Drawn by Shigenori "kiki" Kiwata,[^4402] the artwork resembles his appearance in *Electronic Gaming Monthly*'s *Street Fighter III* April Fools article, except instead of long hair and a beard this version sports a long mohawk and a mustache forked upwards, while his biography stated he stands 6 ft 1 in (185 cm) tall. A small note at the bottom of the page stated it would be deleted after 48 hours, and shortly after it was completely removed.[^4401]

Sheng Long appears as a non-playable character in the "World Tour" mode of *[Street Fighter 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_6)* whom players fight atop the SiRN building at night after completing the game. Using Ryu's fighting style, he has been described as one of the mode's hardest opponents.[^4403][^4404]

#### Other Media

#### Comics

- Sheng Long would later make an appearance in the 1993 [Malibu Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_%28Malibu_Comics%29) as Ryu and Ken's master, where he is poisoned by an evil clone of Ryu created by the comic's villain.[^4405]
- A Hong Kong [manhua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhua) based on *Street Fighter II* by Jademan Comics even altered their story to include the character in response.[^4406]
- In *Street Fighter Origins: Sagat* (2023), a graphic novel written by Chris Sarracini with art by Joe Ng and published by [Udon Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Udon_Entertainment), Sheng Long falsely assumes the identity of the legendary master [Gen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gen_%28Street_Fighter%29) in an attempt to gain notoriety. The plan, however, has an unexpected outcome: while maintaining the charade, he ends up crossing paths with the real Gen, who reveals the secret move and defeats the imposter.[^4405]

### Venetian Blinds (video game)

***Venetian Blinds*** is a [simulation video game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simulation_video_game) developed by [Activision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activision) co-founders [David Crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Crane_%28programmer%29) and [Bob Whitehead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Whitehead) for the [Atari 2600](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atari_2600). The game simulates the raising and lowering of [Venetian blinds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venetian_blinds) on a window, and was facetiously presented as a [technology demonstration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_demonstration) of Whitehead's graphical programming technique of the same name, although it does not use the technique.[^4407]

*Venetian Blinds* was created as a [tongue-in-cheek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongue-in-cheek) [in-joke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-joke) in 1982 relating to a then-ongoing lawsuit between Activision and [Atari, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atari,_Inc.) about the use of Whitehead's technique. The game was only shown internally and to people familiar with the lawsuit, and was not released publicly until 2003, as part of *[Activision Anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activision_Anthology)* for [Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Windows), [macOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacOS), and [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance). It was later released as a standalone title in 2010 through the [Game Room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Room) service for Windows, [Xbox 360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360), and [Windows Phone 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows_Phone_7).

#### Gameplay

The player controls grey [Venetian blinds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venetian_blinds) on an olive window in a brown room. The blinds can be raised and lowered by pressing the [joystick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atari_CX40_joystick) up and down. When the blinds are raised, they reveal a detailed sunset behind a green valley. In the bottom-left corner of the screen is the Activision logo, a feature of most Activision games of the era.[^4407][^4408][^4409]

#### Development

The Venetian blinds technique was created by American video game developer [Bob Whitehead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Whitehead) while working for [Atari, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atari,_Inc.), for the game *[Video Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_Chess)*. The technique was created to circumvent the Atari 2600's hardware limitations, which prevented it from rendering more than six unique [sprites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprite_%28computer_graphics%29) simultaneously on a single horizontal [scan line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scan_line). Though some Atari 2600 games used techniques such as alternating sprite flickering or hiding different sprites per frame to create the illusion of multiple moving sprites at once, these often irritated players or displayed improperly in videos with certain frame rates.[^4407] The Venetian blinds technique drew every other horizontal[^4410] line of a sprite, which "left you with sprites that looked like they had stripes". This allowed developers to get around the limitation by offsetting every second sprite vertically, lining up rows of pixels with rows of empty space. Its name comes from its resemblance to Venetian blinds.[^4407] In *Video Chess*, the technique is used to simulate up to eight [chess pieces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess_piece) on the same row using only four sprites.[^4409]

[Activision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activision) was formed in 1979 by Whitehead, [David Crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Crane_%28programmer%29), [Larry Kaplan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Kaplan), and [Alan Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Miller_%28game_designer%29). These developers had left Atari over low pay, lack of recognition, and Atari's policy of not crediting game developers to ensure they did not get scouted by rival companies and to reduce their leverage in contract negotiations.[^4407] The releases of several successful Atari 2600 games by Activision in 1980, such as *[Boxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boxing_%281980_video_game%29)*, *Bridge*, *Checkers*, *[Dragster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragster_%28video_game%29)*, and *[Fishing Derby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fishing_Derby)*, prompted Atari to attempt to tarnish Activision's reputation, first through [attack ads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_ad) and then, by the end of 1980, a lawsuit alleging Whitehead, Crane, Kaplan, and Miller had violated [non-disclosure agreements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-disclosure_agreement) and stolen [trade secrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_secret), including the Venetian blinds technique, despite Activision having then not published any games using said technique.[^4407][^4411] Atari was reportedly not expecting to win the lawsuit, but was merely using it as a [scare tactic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scare_tactic) to pressure Activision into leaving the video game industry, dissuade others from doing business with them, or otherwise hinder them with costly legal proceedings.[^4407][^4408]

Although the Activision team members were aware they had not actually stolen anything from Atari, morale still plummeted as a result of the lawsuit. In response, Crane and Whitehead developed *Venetian Blinds* as an in-joke. Crane said that the sunset in the window was a new and unique innovation.[^4407]

Activision brought *Venetian Blinds* to the 1982 [Consumer Electronics Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_Electronics_Show) at [McCormick Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McCormick_Place) in Chicago, but it was not on public display. Crane privately displayed the demo to people familiar with the lawsuit, and asked them, "Is this what Atari means by the Venetian Blind Technique?"[^4407][^4408] It is often claimed that these people were Atari's lawyers,[^4409][^4411] but this is a rumor stemming from a misreporting of events by the Atari history [fansite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fansite) *AtariProtos*, which had first revealed the existence of *Venetian Blinds* on the internet on October 18, 2002, per information from an Activision employee.[^4407][^4408]

Atari and Activision eventually dropped the lawsuit in 1982 under unclear circumstances, most likely an out-of-court settlement, with Activision agreeing to pay royalties to Atari but otherwise legitimizing the [third-party development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third-party_development) model.[^4407][^4412][^4413]

#### Release

*Venetian Blinds* was not intended for public release and, aside from private displays of the game at the 1982 Consumer Electronics Show, was otherwise unknown to the public. The sunset technique used in *Venetian Blinds* was eventually reused in Activision's *[Barnstorming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnstorming_%28video_game%29)*.[^4407]

*Venetian Blinds* was first officially released to the public in late 2003, when it was included as part of the [Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Windows), [macOS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacOS), and [Game Boy Advance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Boy_Advance) ports of *[Activision Anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Activision_Anthology)*. These ports include Crane's information on the game's background.[^4407][^4408]

On January 2, 2005, Thomas Jentzsch and Matt Reichert released the binary for *Venetian Blinds* online as a free download through Atari fansite *AtariAge*. The release included an early prototype of *[Freeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeway_%28video_game%29)* titled *Bloody Human Freeway*, featuring a human character instead of the final game's chicken, and two prototypes for unnamed, unreleased games.[^4414][^4415]

On December 22, 2010, *Venetian Blinds* was released through the [Game Room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_Room) service for Windows, the [Xbox 360](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_360), and [Windows Phone 7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows_Phone_7), as part of Game Pack 013.[^4407] It was added to [Xbox Game Pass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xbox_Game_Pass)’s [*Retro Classics*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retro_Classics) collection at launch in May 2025.[^4416]

#### Reception

*Bad Game Hall of Fame*, in an article about *Venetian Blinds*, considered it "a stretch to even call it a 'game'", but noted its historical importance. The article also criticized its inclusion on Game Room, and highlighted Activision allowing it to be sold as a sign that the company "became the very soulless husk they sought to spite so long ago".[^4407]

Tyler Treese of *[GameRevolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameRevolution)* deemed *Venetian Blinds* "one of gaming's greatest moments of pettiness" and categorized it as a "[diss game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diss_track)", commending its historical importance and rarity but calling its inclusion on Game Room "ridiculous".[^4409]

### Brain rot

In [Internet culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_culture), the term ***brain rot*** (often written as ***brainrot***) describes digital media deemed to be of low quality or value.[^4417][^4418] More broadly, the term refers to the harmful cognitive effects associated with excessive or disordered use of digital and social media, particularly [short-form content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-form_content),[^4419] [AI slop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_slop), and [doomscrolling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomscrolling).[^4420] Popularized by [Generation Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_Z) and [Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_Alpha) on social media, the term has since entered mainstream usage.[^4421] It was the *[Oxford English Dictionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_English_Dictionary)*'s 2024 "[Word of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_of_the_Year)".[^4418]

#### Origin and usage

According to [Oxford University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University_Press), the first recorded use of the term *brain rot* traces back to the 1854 book *[Walden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walden)* by [Henry David Thoreau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_David_Thoreau).[^4422][^4423][^4424] In that book, Thoreau reflected on materialism and argued that a tendency to prefer trivial ideas could weaken the mind, a harbinger for how the term would come to be used to describe the effects of disordered use of [digital content](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_content).[^4425] He asked:[^4426]

> While England endeavors to cure the [potato-rot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phytophthora_infestans), will not any endeavor to cure the brain-rot, which prevails so much more widely and fatally?

Thoreau was criticizing what he saw as a decline in intellectual standards, comparing it to the [effects of potato blight in 1840s Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_potato_failure), which had caused widespread crop failures.[^4421]

In 2007, *brain rot* was used by [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) users to describe [dating game shows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dating_game_show), video games, and "hanging out online".[^4427] Usage of the phrase increased online in the 2010s before spiking in popularity in 2020 on [Discord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discord), when it became an [Internet meme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme).[^4427] From 2023 to 2024, Oxford reported the term's usage increased by 230% in frequency per million words.[^4421][^4422]

As of 2024, it was used in the context of Generation Alpha's digital habits, with critics noting that the generation is "[excessively immersed in online culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extremely_online)",[^4428] underscoring the fact that by 2024, an estimated 79 percent of the world's population of 15-24 year olds used the internet.[^4429] The term *brain rot* has been associated with the tendency for young people to pepper their speech with Internet references[^4417] such as *skibidi* (referencing *[Skibidi Toilet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skibidi_Toilet)*), *[rizz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizz)* (charisma), *[gyatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyatt)* (buttocks), *[fanum tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanum_tax)* (taking food from another's meal), and *[sigma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigma_%28meme%29)* (solitary, masculine men).[^4430][^4422][^4431]

#### Analysis

In an article for *[Literary Hub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_Hub)*, Josh Abbey argued that the concept of brain rot had existed long before the phrase was coined, likening it to [William Wordsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wordsworth)'s criticism of "frantic novels" in 1800 and the criticisms of film and television by [Virginia Woolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Woolf) and [Aldous Huxley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldous_Huxley) in the 20th century.[^4432] Günseli Yalcinkaya compared brain rot to 20th century artistic and political movements such as [Dada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dada) for being "intentionally absurd, context-less and fast-paced", and noted how it can be used to push political messages.[^4433]

Alexander Serenko has attributed popularization of brain rot content to [supply and demand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supply_and_demand) factors. On the supply side, Serenko associates brain rot both with the business models of the major [social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media) platforms that rely on maintaining user attention, and the desire on the part of creators to monetize low-quality material for profit, increasingly with reliance on [generative AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_AI) (see [AI slop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_slop)). On the demand side, he links consumption of such material to users' psychological preference for low-effort, repetitive, rewarding activities. He sees typical features of brain rot content as being associated with emotional intensity, brevity, familiar characters, and references to cultural or societal themes, and ease of understanding.[^4434]

##### Mental health responses

Educational psychologists began utilizing the phrase *brain rot* in reviews of research into the relationships between cognitive decline, mental exhaustion, and excessive exposure to low-quality social media materials, arguing that research has demonstrated that brain rot leads to "emotional desensitization, cognitive overload, and a negative self-concept".[^4435] By 2024, mental health organizations had begun to use the term, offering suggestions for prevention and treatment. The [Newport Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_Academy_and_Newport_Institute), an organization dedicated to providing resources for young adults, suggested the following prevention techniques: "try limiting screen time, deleting distracting apps from your phone, and turning off unnecessary notifications".[^4436] Others have suggested resilience training, [AI literacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_literacy), and regular mental health assessments.[^4437] Those in higher education have also sought to promote responses to brain rot. Professor Dr. Sri Lestari from [Universitas Muhammadiyah Surakarta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universitas_Muhammadiyah_Surakarta) observed that although brain rot has not been classified as an official psychological disorder, she recommended instilling self-control at a young age and reducing screen time.[^4438]

#### Influence

The term *brain rot* was named [Oxford Word of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Word_of_the_Year) in 2024, beating other words like *[demure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demure)* and *[romantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_fantasy)*.[^4421][^4422] Its modern usage is defined by the *[Oxford University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University_Press)* as "the supposed deterioration of a person's mental or intellectual state, especially viewed as the result of overconsumption of material (now particularly online content) considered to be trivial or unchallenging".[^4421] Offering an explanation for the term, *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian)* journalist Siân Boyle provided commentary on the "brain rot" scholarship that purportedly identified links between excessive screen use and reduced memory capacity and reduced attention.[^4439] In the Spanish language periodical [*El País*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Pa%C3%ADs_%28Uruguay%29), Uruguayan journalist Facundo Macchi then similarly reviewed scholarship on the effects of excessive amounts of low-quality online materials, utilizing the disputed phrase "social media addiction" (rather than the scientifically accurate phrase [problematic social media use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Problematic_social_media_use)) to argue that the scholarship supported a link between so-called "junk content" and both shortened attention spans and weakened memory.[^4440]

In the same year, [millennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennial) Australian senator [Fatima Payman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatima_Payman) made headlines by making a short speech to the [Australian parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_parliament) using Generation Alpha slang. She introduced the speech as addressing "an oft-forgotten section of our society", referring to Generations Z and Alpha, and said that she would "render the remainder of my statement using language they're familiar with".[^4441] Using slang terms, Payman criticised the government's [plans to ban under-16s from social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_Safety_Amendment) and closed by saying that, "Though some of you cannot yet vote, I hope that, when you do, it will be in a more [goated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GOAT_%28sports_culture%29) Australia for a government with more aura. Skibidi!" The speech, written by a 21-year-old staff member, was labeled by some as an example of "brain rot" outside the online world.[^4442]

In the 2025 Jubilee of the World of Communications, *brain rot* was also used by [Pope Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Francis), the head of the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church), as he urged people to reduce their use of social media and avoid "*putrefazione cerebrale*".[^4443][^4444]

Taking a different approach, one researcher who interviewed Norwegian 16- and 17-year-olds about the term has argued that brain rot is best understood as a way that young people participate in social media, utilizing deliberately non-productive messaging as a means of resisting the pressures of productivity and self-optimization.[^4445]
