### Extremely online

An **extremely online**, **terminally online**,[^4446] or **chronically online**[^4447] person is someone who is closely and consistently engaged with the [Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet) and [Internet culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_culture).[^4448] People who are extremely online often believe that their own online activity, or what they see online, is important enough to the point where it interferes with their offline life.[^4449][^4450] Events and phenomena can themselves be extremely online;[^4449] while often used as a descriptive term, the phenomenon of extreme online usage has been described as "both a reformation of the delivery of ideas - shared through words and videos and [memes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme) and [GIFs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics_Interchange_Format) and [copypasta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copypasta) - and the ideas themselves".[^4450] The term "extremely online" or similar variants are sometimes used as [pejoratives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pejorative) and [insults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insult).

#### Criteria

While the term was in use as early as 2014, it gained popularity over the latter half of the 2010s in conjunction with the increasing prevalence and notability of Internet phenomena in all areas of life.[^4448] Extremely online people, according to *[The Daily Dot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Dot)*, are interested in topics "no normal, healthy person could possibly care about",[^4448] and have been analogized to "pop culture fandoms, just without the pop".[^4448] Extremely online phenomena such as fan culture and reaction GIFs have been described as "swallowing democracy" by journalists such as [Amanda Hess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Hess) in *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times)*,[^4451] who claimed that a "great convergence between politics and culture, values and aesthetics, citizenship and commercialism" had become "a dominant mode of experiencing politics".[^4451] *[Vulture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulture_%28website%29)* - formerly the [pop culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_culture) section of *[New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_%28magazine%29)* magazine, now a stand-alone website - has a section for articles tagged "extremely online".[^4452]

#### Historical background

In the 2010s, many categories and labels came into wide use from media outlets to describe Internet-mediated cultural trends, such as the [alt-right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alt-right), the [dirtbag left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirtbag_left), and [doomerism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomer).[^4453] These ideological categories are often defined by their close association with online discourse. For example, the term "alt-right" was added to the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press)' stylebook in 2016 to describe the "digital presence" of far-right ideologies,[^4454] the dirtbag left refers to a group of "underemployed and overly online millennials" who "have no time for the pieties of traditional political discourse",[^4455] and the [doomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomer)'s "blackpilled[^4456] despair"[^4453] is combined with spending "too much time on message boards in high school"[^4453] to produce an [eclectic](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/eclectic) "anti-socialism".[^4453]

Extreme onlineness transcends ideological boundaries. For example, right-wing figures like [Alex Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Jones)[^4457] and [Laura Loomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Loomer)[^4457] have been described as "extremely online", but so have those on the left like [Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria_Ocasio-Cortez)[^4458] and fans of the *[Chapo Trap House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapo_Trap_House)* podcast.[^4459][^4460] Extremely online phenomena can range from acts of offline violence (such as the [2019 Christchurch shootings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch_mosque_shootings)[^4461]) to "\[going\] on NPR to explain the [anti-capitalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-capitalist) [irony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irony) inherent in [kids eating Tide Pods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tide_pod_challenge)".[^4448]

United States President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump)'s [posts on social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_media_use_by_Donald_Trump) have been frequently cited as extremely online,[^4450] during both his presidency[^4462] and his [2020 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_2020_presidential_campaign); *[Vox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vox_%28website%29)* claimed his approach to re-election veered into being "Too Online",[^4450] and *[Reason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reason_%28magazine%29)* questioned whether the final presidential debate was "incomprehensible to [normies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normality_%28behavior%29)".[^4463] While individual people are often given the description, being extremely online has also been posited as an overall cultural phenomenon, applying to trends like lifestyle movements suffixed with "[-wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaporwave)" and "[-core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cottagecore)" based heavily on Internet media,[^4449] as well as an increasing expectation for [digital social researchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_research) to have an "online presence" to advance in their careers.[^4464]

#### Participants and media coverage

|     | **wint** (@dril) tweeted: |
|-----|---------------------------|

> who the fuck is scraeming 'LOG OFF' at my house. show yourself, coward. i will never log off

September 15, 2012[^4465]

One example of a phenomenon considered to be extremely online[^4448] is the "[wife guy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wife_guy)" (a guy who posts about his wife);[^4466] despite being a "stupid online thing"[^4467] which spent several years as a piece of Internet slang, in 2019 it became the subject of five articles in leading U.S. media outlets.[^4467]

Like many extremely online phrases and phenomena, the "wife guy" has been attributed in part to the in-character Twitter account [dril](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dril).[^4468] The account frequently parodies how people behave on the Internet, and has been widely cited as influential on online culture.[^4469][^4470] In one tweet, his character refuses to stop using the Internet, even when someone shouts outside his house that he should log off.[^4471]

Many of dril's other coinages have become ubiquitous parts of [Internet slang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_slang).[^4469] Throughout the 2010s, posters such as dril inspired commonly used terms like "corncobbing" (referring to someone losing an argument and failing to admit it);[^4472][^4473][^4474] while originally a piece of obscure Internet slang used on sites like Twitter, use of the term (and controversy over its misinterpretation) became a subject of reporting from traditional publications, with some noting[^4475] that keeping up with the rapid turnover of inside jokes, memes, and quotes online required daily attention to avoid embarrassment.[^4475][^4476]

[Twitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitch_%28service%29) has been described as "talk radio for the extremely online".[^4477] Another example of an event cited as extremely online is [No Nut November](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Nut_November).[^4478] Increasingly, researchers are expected to have more of an online presence, to advance in their careers, as networking and portfolios continue to transition to the digital world.[^4464]

In November 2020, an article in *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post)* criticized the [filter bubble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filter_bubble) theory of online discourse on the basis that it "overgeneralized" based on a "small subset of extremely online people".[^4479]

The [2021 storming of the United States Capitol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_storming_of_the_United_States_Capitol) was described as extremely online, with "pro-Trump internet personalities", such as [Baked Alaska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baked_Alaska_%28influencer%29),[^4480] and fans livestreaming and taking selfies.[^4481][^4482] People who have been described as extremely online include [Chrissy Teigen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrissy_Teigen),[^4483] [Jon Ossoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Ossoff),[^4484] and [Andrew Yang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Yang).[^4485] In contrast, [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden) has been cited as the antithesis of extremely online, *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times)* wrote in 2019 that he had "zero meme energy".[^4451][^4486][^4487]

### Joe Biden (The Onion)

**Joe Biden** (also known as "**Diamond Joe**" or "**Uncle Joe**") was a recurring fictionalized [characterization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Characterization) of American politician [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden) in satirical online newspaper *[The Onion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Onion).* Between 2009 and 2019, *The Onion* staff portrayed Biden as a [blue-collar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-collar_worker) "[average Joe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Average_Joe)", an affable "goofy uncle", a [muscle car](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscle_car) driver, an avid fan of 1980s [hair metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hair_metal), a raucous party animal, a shameless womanizer, a recidivist petty criminal, and a drug-dealing outlaw. The Biden character became one of *The Onion*'s most popular features during the [Obama presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Barack_Obama), garnering critical acclaim and a large readership.

*Onion* writer-editor Chad Nackers originated the newspaper's distinctive version of Biden, which its staff developed over the course of the real Biden's two terms as vice president. Nackers took inspiration from his upbringing in Midwestern Wisconsin and, more loosely, from aspects of Biden's personality and public face. Although *The Onion* had mentioned Biden's name as early as 2006, he was not treated as the primary subject of an item in the newspaper until [Obama's (and his) first inauguration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_inauguration_of_Barack_Obama) in January 2009. The first full-length treatment of the Biden character was a May 2009 article titled "Shirtless Biden Washes [Trans Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac_Firebird_Trans_Am) in [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House) Driveway". The character subsequently appeared in more than 50 *Onion* articles, as well as numerous videos and other media.

Despite the extreme differences between the fictional character and the real politician, *The Onion* was regarded as having a significant, mostly positive influence on Biden's public image. Commentators noted that the character likely reinforced public perceptions of Biden as a political figure with [populist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Populism) working-class appeal and a good-natured, easy-going disposition. The real Biden made several public comments noting his enjoyment of his characterization in *The Onion*. In 2016, [Mitch McConnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_McConnell) referenced the character on the Senate floor in a speech tributing the departing vice president amid the [presidential transition of Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidential_transition_of_Donald_Trump).

Early reception for the character was generally enthusiastic. As the [2020 Democratic primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries) and Biden's [2020 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_2020_presidential_campaign) got underway, *The Onion* attracted criticism for the character's detachment from reality and its distraction from the real Biden. Former *Onion* editor [Joe Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Garden) wrote a self-critical op-ed on the subject in May 2019. While Garden still felt the caricature had been funny, he expressed regret that it had failed to provide more meaningful commentary on the politician's record and what Garden found to be substantive shortcomings. After reviving the "Diamond Joe" version of Biden in its coverage of the [primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries) for one final article,[^4488] *The Onion* retired the character. Since mid-2019, the publication's parodies of Biden have drawn more closely from real-world developments.

#### Background

[Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden) is an American retired politician. A member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_%28United_States%29), Biden represented [Delaware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delaware) in the [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate) from 1973 to 2009. As the running mate of [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama), Biden was elected vice president of the United States in 2008 and 2012.[^4489] In his [third presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_2020_presidential_campaign), following previous efforts [in 1988](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_1988_presidential_campaign) and [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_2008_presidential_campaign), he was elected President of the United States in 2020. He served as the 46th [president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States) from 2021 to 2025.

*[The Onion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Onion)* is an American publication that [parodies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parody) traditional [newspapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newspaper) and [satirizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire) current events. Founded in 1988 in [Madison, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison,_Wisconsin) as a weekly satirical [print newspaper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsprint), it began [publishing online](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_newspaper) in 1996 and discontinued its print edition in 2013.[^4490] Articles in *The Onion* often lampoon real-world public figures and events using fictitious elements. *The Onion* had a few noteworthy instances of consistent characterizations over time prior to Biden, such as portrayals of [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton) and [Bob Dole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dole) in the 1990s.[^4491]

Chad Nackers, the writer who created the Biden character, joined *The Onion* in 1997. By 2017, he had been on staff longer than anyone else in the paper's history.[^4492]

#### Origin and development

Prior to becoming vice president in 2009, Biden was not heavily featured in *The Onion*. His few early appearances did not reflect the distinctive traits of the later character. The earliest mention of Biden was published in August 2006, during the early period of the [2008 Democratic Party presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries). With the headline "Critics Accuse Joe Biden of Running for President for Political Reasons", the article was based on a nonspecific premise that did not rely on any aspect of the real Biden's personality or career and, in principle, could have been written using any candidate as its subject.[^4493]

Even after Biden was [selected as Obama's running mate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Democratic_Party_vice_presidential_candidate_selection), he was only occasionally mentioned in *The Onion*. However, Nackers said that the candidate's public appearances as Obama's running mate, especially, in Nackers's words, the "[shit-eating grin](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/shit-eating%20grin) he had" at those appearances, began to provide a "spark" of inspiration for the character.[^4494] Nackers felt that Biden's easygoing persona struck a dramatic contrast with the more intense, sinister public perception of his predecessor [Dick Cheney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Cheney).[^4492] Asked about the genesis of the character, *The Onion*'s founding editor [Scott Dikkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Dikkers) said Biden had "this great inappropriate, older buddy wild child kind of vibe."[^4495] Nackers also drew inspiration from his own "strong connection to blue-collar life" and upbringing in [Appleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appleton,_Wisconsin), [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin). When writing Biden articles, Nackers would play music by bands like [Mötley Crüe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6tley_Cr%C3%BCe) and [White Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Lion) to evoke memories and details that could inform the character, a technique *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post)* compared to [method acting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Method_acting).[^4492]

The first appearance of the Biden character coincided with the [first inauguration of Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_inauguration_of_Barack_Obama) on January 20, 2009, when *The Onion* ran the headline "Joe Biden Shows Up to Inauguration With Ponytail" paired with a [manipulated image](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photo_manipulation) of Biden sporting a long blond [ponytail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ponytail), without an accompanying article.[^4496] The full-fledged character debuted on May 5, 2009, in the article "Shirtless Biden Washes Trans Am in White House Driveway".[^4497]

During Biden's first year in office, *The Onion* published a few articles that depicted him as a more traditional vice president, including a spoof on the [National Thanksgiving Turkey Presentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Thanksgiving_Turkey_Presentation) (titled "Biden Pardons Single Yam in Vice-Presidential Thanksgiving Ritual"),[^4498] but by 2010 the writing staff had settled on exclusively using Nackers's "virtually unrecognizable" take on the character. Soon, the newspaper's editors had so many jokes based on the character that there was a backlog of rejected pitches.[^4499]

#### Characterization

*The* *Onion*'s Biden is typically described as a [blue-collar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-collar_worker) [everyman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everyman) with a taste for partying and debauchery. Often referred to by the nickname "Diamond Joe", the character loves [hair metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glam_metal) and classic rock from the 1970s and 1980s. He drives a 1981 [Pontiac Firebird Trans Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontiac_Firebird_Trans_Am) and motorcycles. He also noticeably has [tattoos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tattoos).[^4500] According to *[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times)* journalist [Jeremy W. Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_W._Peters), the *Onion* staff wrote Biden in "one of two molds: Boozy and brash, or slick and over-sexed."[^4499] In 2013, the direction of the character took a turn in articles that depicted him as a criminal and [gang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gang) member; this arc deepened the following year, as Biden became a [drug dealer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illegal_drug_trade) and [user](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Substance_abuse), particularly of [cannabis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannabis_%28drug%29).[^4501] The character has an intense [bromance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromance) with Obama, although it is not necessarily reciprocated.[^4502]

*The* *Onion*'s Biden shares little in common with Biden's real life, career, or behavior; indeed, as [Dave Itzkoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Itzkoff) put it, the character shares little at all with "any version of established reality or fact."[^4503] For instance, while the *Onion*'s Biden is a binge drinker, the real Biden is a [teetotaler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teetotalism).[^4504] Unlike the *Onion* Biden's preference for the Trans Am, the real Biden said his car of choice is the [Chevrolet Corvette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevrolet_Corvette), to which Nackers responded, "So that's the thing, he is into a [muscle car](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscle_car) still."[^4505] The portrayal is almost entirely [apolitical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apolitical), especially compared to *The Onion*'s more pointed satirizing of other major political figures.[^4506] Joel Goldstein, a law professor and expert on vice-presidential history, said that a likely reason for *The Onion*'s divergent take on Biden is that the vice president holds an "awkward office" in a support role to the president's agenda, making it difficult to satirize in its own right.[^4505]

Most of the similarities between the two Bidens are in the broad outlines of their image and personality. In political terms, Biden's reputation as a liberal [populist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Populism) corresponds to the character's blue-collar life. *The Onion*'s Biden has much in common with Biden's image as a "goofy uncle" and his nickname "Uncle Joe".[^4507] A headline like "Biden Loses Control of [Butterfly Knife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butterfly_knife) during Commencement Speech" is an extreme exaggeration of some of Biden's perceived traits, like his "reported gaffes and generally casual demeanor."[^4508] [Mark Leibovich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Leibovich) said part of the character's plausibility stems from the contrast between Biden's image and those of his contemporaries, posing the [rhetorical questions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhetorical_question): "Would *The Onion* put a shirtless [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry) washing a Trans Am in the driveway of the State Department? [Speaker Boehner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boehner) wearing a ponytail at the Inauguration? [Harry Reid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Reid) getting banned for life from [Dave & Buster's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_&_Buster's) restaurants ('following dozens of complaints from wait staff and numerous incidents')?"[^4509] Brian Resnick, writing for *[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic)*, said both have a "[larger-than-life](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/larger%20than%20life)" quality.[^4510] In Nackers's view, the overlap where the "real personality converges with Diamond Joe" is that both have "a [heart of gold](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/heart%20of%20gold)".[^4492]

Compared to most comedic portrayals of Biden, *The Onion*'s was unconventional in its almost complete detachment from his real attributes.[^4505] Other comedians and satirists tended to portray Biden as a well-meaning [buffoon](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/buffoon) prone to [gaffes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_gaffe), exaggerating the politician's actual or perceived traits without making outlandish embellishments.[^4511] [Jim Downey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Downey_%28comedian%29), a comedian and longtime writer on *[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday_Night_Live)*, described the *Onion* parody as somewhat risky, because it implicitly relies on the audience's understanding of how dissimilar it is from the real Biden. For the humor to work, Downey said readers "have to know that it's completely wrong and arbitrary", but readers without an existing impression of Biden may believe that the parody is referencing some of his actual characteristics.[^4499] Similarly, the scholar Nicholas Holm said the character's humor comes from two things: the "sheer unlikeliness" of his traits, and the extreme contrast with "the gaffe-prone and folksy, but generally affable, public presentation of Biden."[^4501]

#### Notable appearances (2009-2017)

> "The 6 best *Onion* parodies of Joe Biden" (according to *[The Week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Week)*)
>
> 1.  "Biden Receives Lifetime Ban from [Dave & Buster's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_&_Buster's)"
> 2.  "Biden Says Life Better Than It Was 4 Years Ago But Nothing Can Touch Summer of '87"
> 3.  "Shirtless Biden Washes Trans Am in White House Driveway"
> 4.  "Joe Biden Hitchhikes to Democratic National Convention"
> 5.  "Biden to Cool His Heels in Mexico for a While"
> 6.  "Biden to Honor Fallen Soldiers by Jumping Motorcycle Over [Vietnam Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_Veterans_Memorial)"

*,  Samantha Rollins (January 18, 2013)[^4512]*

In his two terms as vice president between 2009 and 2017, Biden was the subject of more than 50 articles and multiple videos in *The Onion*.[^4501] The newspaper would sometimes publish multiple articles about Biden in quick succession, as they did for Biden's appearance at the [2016 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Democratic_National_Convention).[^4513]

One of the *Onion*'s [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) accounts, @OnionPolitics, live-tweeted the [October 11, 2012 vice presidential debate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_vice-presidential_debate,_2012) between Biden and Republican candidate [Paul Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Ryan).[^4514] The website ran four stories on Biden that day along with a manipulated image of Biden wearing his "lucky debate suit", which was a jacket similar to [Michael Jackson's *Thriller* jacket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jackson's_Thriller_jacket) that exposed his hairy chest.[^4515]

In January 2013, *The Onion* published the [e-book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-book) *President of Vice: The Autobiography of Joe Biden* as a [Kindle single](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindle_single) through [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_%28company%29)'s [Kindle Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindle_Store). The book, ostensibly an [autobiography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobiography), gives a fictionalized account of Biden's life in the character's voice. Most of the book's plot deviates completely from Biden's life story, there is, for example, a description of Biden [meeting God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theophany) during some "mystical-ass experiences" in the summer of 1987, but it also offers alternate retellings of real incidents, like Biden's role in [Robert Bork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bork)'s unsuccessful [Supreme Court nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Bork_Supreme_Court_nomination).[^4516] As part of the promotion for the book, *The Onion* participated in an AMA ("Ask Me Anything") on [Reddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit)'s [IAmA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki//r/IAmA) by responding in-character to user-submitted questions.[^4503]

On April 30, 2016, *The Onion* hosted a Biden-themed event to coincide with the [White House Correspondents' Dinner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Correspondents'_Dinner). Titled "Diamond Joe Biden's Badass Balls-to-the-Wall Fiesta", the event was hosted at the [Newseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newseum) in Washington, D.C.[^4517] The event featured an [ice sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_sculpture) of Biden riding a [Harley-Davidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harley-Davidson) motorcycle and a [string quartet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_quartet) playing renditions of hair-metal songs. Biden was invited to attend, but declined.[^4492] Sam Sanders at [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR) reported that it was the "most popular" of the several unofficial events orbiting that year's Correspondents' Dinner.[^4518]

In one of the last Biden articles before the [inauguration of Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_inauguration_of_Donald_Trump), titled "Biden Sadly Realizes This Could Be Last Time He Throws Lit Firecracker Into Press Conference", the character remarked that it was the "end of an era, man."[^4519]

After Biden left office, *The Onion* mostly dropped the popular character but found similar breakout success with its portrayal of [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump)'s sons, [Donald Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump_Jr.) and [Eric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Trump), who are depicted partaking in childish misadventures as the "Trump boys".[^4520] Meanwhile, *The Onion* has portrayed Biden's successor [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence) as stiff and uptight, which Nackers called a "weird reverse-Biden role".[^4520]

#### Popularity and reception

> ... Biden was a fucking blast.

*,  Chad Nackers, then-head writer for *The Onion* in 2017[^4521]*

Articles about Biden were some of the most-read articles on *The Onion*'s site of their time.[^4522] [Analytical measurements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_analytics) of [web traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_traffic) showed that, by November 2010, the first major Biden article ("Shirtless Biden Washes Trans Am") had accumulated more than 500,000 page views, while the video "Biden Criticized for Appearing in [Hennessy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hennessy) Ads" had been viewed 450,000 times. The site drew about 7.5 million unique visitors per month at that time, and as such the metrics for the Biden pieces were considered substantial.[^4499] Editor Will Tracy said Biden had been a "[breakout character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_breakout_characters)" and "fan favorite" during the Obama administration.[^4523]

The character has received widespread praise in the media. [Mike Pesca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pesca), host of the [podcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Podcast) *[The Gist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gist_%28podcast%29)*, said he considered the *Onion*'s Biden to be one of "the great comic characters of our day" alongside [Homer Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer_Simpson), [Gob Bluth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobias_F%C3%BCnke) and [Tobias Fünke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobias_F%C3%BCnke) of *[Arrested Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrested_Development)*, and [Selina Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selina_Meyer) of *[Veep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veep)*.[^4524] The month before the [2012 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_presidential_election), *[Slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate_%28magazine%29)* named the character as the best parody of Biden, topping the animated Biden on *[SuperNews!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SuperNews!)*, [Jason Sudeikis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Sudeikis)'s performances on *Saturday Night Live*, and Bill Barol's essay "My Name Is Joe Biden and I'll Be Your Server" in *[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker)*.[^4525] *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_%28magazine%29)* magazine ranked *The Onion*'s Biden at number 7 on a list of the top 10 political memes of 2012.[^4526] When *The Onion* discontinued its print edition in 2013, staffers at the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times)* named the Biden character among their favorite work published by *The Onion*.[^4527] [Marc Hogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Hogan) at *[Pitchfork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_%28website%29)* listed "The 20 Best *Onion* Articles About Music" and included "Biden Huddling With Closest Advisers on Whether to Spend 200 Bucks on [Scorpions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scorpions_%28band%29) Tickets".[^4528]

##### In light of allegations of Biden's inappropriate physical contact with women

After [Lucy Flores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_Flores) published an essay in 2019 alleging Biden had inappropriately kissed and touched her, there was renewed attention on other [allegations that Biden has made inappropriate physical contact with women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_sexual_assault_allegation).[^4529] In turn, the increased attention on the issue prompted critical reassessments of the *Onion*'s portrayal of Biden, particularly the character's interactions with women. [Antonia Noori Farzan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonia_Noori_Farzan) at *The Washington Post* said some of the older headlines about Biden and women, like "Biden Invokes Freedom of Information Act to Find Out When Woman Gets off Work" and "Biden Invites Nation's Women to Tax Code Discussion at Private Mountain Chalet", had "a sharper edge now that multiple women have said that Biden's close physical contact at public events made them feel uncomfortable."[^4530]

To some, *The Onion* had tacitly excused Biden's conduct or minimized the seriousness of inappropriate behavior toward women. *The New Yorker*'s Katy Waldman wrote that the *Onion*'s articles about Biden "made [hypermasculine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypermasculinity) tropes look not only unthreatening but delightful" and "were the satirical equivalent of petting the [Labrador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labrador_Retriever) on the head".[^4531] Gavin Fernando at *[The New Zealand Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Zealand_Herald)* noted Biden's tendency to touch women at public events had "rarely been criticised directly" in the media despite widespread awareness, highlighting an *Onion* story from 2009 that had "zoned in on his behavior towards women" yet all the while depicted him as "endearing and lovable."[^4532]

Conversely, other commentators felt that the *Onion*'s jokes had called attention to the issue of Biden's inappropriate behavior toward women without necessarily glorifying or excusing his behavior. Joe Berkowitz at *[Fast Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fast_Company)* wrote that "\[e\]ven the *Onion*, whose memification of the Veep ... helped shore up affection for \[him\], couldn't help commenting on his attitudes toward women from time to time."[^4533] [Maureen Callahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maureen_Callahan) at the *[New York Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Post)* said *The Onion* had "spoofed Biden's sleaziness as early as 2009", which she cited as proof that Biden's perceived inappropriate behavior had been in the public eye for a long time and would not be easy or morally acceptable to minimize or excuse.[^4534] [Matthew Yglesias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Yglesias) at *[Vox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vox_%28website%29)* said that the discussion about Biden and women had raised the "issue" of "what standard of conduct is acceptable for men in power" and that, on that topic, the overarching meaning of *The Onion*'s long-running "joke" about Biden had been that the vice president "really was an [old-school](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/old%20school#Adjective) presence in the Obama White House".[^4529]

#### Reactions from Biden and his staff

Biden publicly commented on the character on several occasions, generally indicating that he enjoyed the *Onion* articles about him. He also tended to express relief that the character was so radically different from his actual personality and poked fun at the *Onion* Biden's affinity for the Trans Am. Beyond his public comments, *Onion* staffers have said members of Biden's staff privately conveyed his enjoyment of the character to them.[^4535] Biden reacted with similar approval to most comedic portrayals of himself.[^4536]

Will Tracy, an associate editor at *The Onion*, told the *New York Times* in 2010 that the [Office of the Vice President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Vice_President_of_the_United_States) had sent the *Onion* staff an email with the message "Keep it up. He really likes it." Tracy commented, "Apparently he's a fan." Biden's office denied being aware of any communication between the Vice President and *The Onion*. When the *Times* reporter requested an interview with Biden to confirm Tracy's statement, [White House Press Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Press_Secretary) [Jay Carney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Carney) denied the request and replied, "Let me get this straight: You want to interview the vice president about stories about him in *The Onion?* Well, I'll give you credit for trying."[^4499]

In a 2011 video interview with [Yahoo! News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahoo!_News), Biden was asked about *The Onion* and said most of his acquaintances and even members of the press tended to think of him as "a little bit [square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square_%28slang%29)", but "now, I'm the philanderer. I think it's hilarious, the stuff they do on me."[^4537] He also said he was "flattered" that the character was "totally inconsistent with my personality."[^4538] At *[HuffPost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HuffPost)*, Ross Luippold said his interview answer "seemed alternately tickled and confused by the mockery."[^4539]

Later that year, *[Car and Driver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_and_Driver)* magazine asked Biden, "Sadly, we must ask about the *Onion* story. While shirtless, have you ever washed a 1981 Pontiac Trans Am in your driveway?" He replied, "You think I'd drive a Trans Am? I have been in my bathing suit in my driveway and not only washed my Goodwood-green 1967 Corvette but also [simonized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simoniz) it. At least the Onion should have had me washing a Trans Am [convertible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convertible). I love convertibles."[^4540]

[Eric Metaxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Metaxas) discussed the character with Biden at the 2012 [National Prayer Breakfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Prayer_Breakfast). Metaxas, who was the event's keynote speaker, was making small talk with Biden before his speech and asked the vice president if he was aware of the *Onion* pieces. According to Metaxas, Biden replied "yes, he had seen them, and he didn't mind them at all, because they were so obviously about someone who was completely different from what he was really like. ... Then he added, as a kind of [Q.E.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q.E.D.): 'For one thing, I hate \[Chevrolet\] [Camaros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevrolet_Camaro)!'"[^4541]

When Reddit hosted an AMA for the *Onion*'s Biden in January 2013, the @VP [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) account tweeted the following:

|     | **Office of VP Biden** (@VP) tweeted: |
|-----|---------------------------------------|

> Q for @reddit AMA with my @TheOnion pal: A Trans-Am? Ever look under the hood of a Corvette? \#imavetteguy -VP

January 18, 2013[^4542]

The signature "-VP" was used to credit the tweet to Biden personally, rather than a member of his staff.[^4543] A photo of Biden standing beside a Chevrolet Corvette was attached to the tweet. The presidential account retweeted it soon after it was posted.[^4509] The *Onion*'s Biden did not reply to the real one's tweet, but it did respond to a Reddit user's question about the Corvette: "I think there's some imposter out there spreading bad shit about me. I'll tell ya right now, whatever they say nothing can come between me and my Zam."[^4544]

In an April 2016 interview with [CNBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNBC), Biden said that he was "not comfortable with goofy Uncle Joe ... And by the way, the so-called goofy Uncle Joe, if you notice, I beat every Republican in every poll when they thought I was running \[in 2016\]. You notice that my favorability was higher than anybody that's running for office in either party."[^4545] While this was not a direct comment on *The Onion*, Biden's image as "goofy Uncle Joe" was closely associated with, and influenced by, *The Onion*.[^4546]

##### As a public relations strategy

According to several academic commentators, Biden engaged with comedic portrayals of himself as a [public relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_relations) strategy. Historian [Edward L. Widmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_L._Widmer) said Biden's public embrace of the *Onion* and other parodies helped to signal his sense of humor and show "a quality of humanity."[^4509] Joel Goldstein, a law professor at [Saint Louis University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Louis_University_%28United_States%29), said he believed Biden's reactions were likely sincere but, even if Biden actually disliked *The Onion*'s portrayal, "the worst mistake \[he\] could make is being offended by it".[^4505] In the journal *[Critical Studies in Media Communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Critical_Studies_in_Media_Communication)*, Don J. Waisanen and Amy B. Becker wrote that Biden responded approvingly to comedic portrayals that reinforced his "[folksy](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/folksy)" public image, which further cultivated that perception.[^4547]

#### Effect on Biden's image

> \[T\]he series is less concerned with naming and shaming comic flaws with the real Biden than it is with constructing an entirely independent self-sustaining comic persona. The humour of *The Onion*'s ongoing coverage of womanising, thrill-seeking, drug-dealing Biden is the result of a self-perpetuating internal logic of ever-increasing goofiness that is constantly moving away from any engagement with the political existence of the real Biden. By the time 'Biden Lines Up Sweet Summer Gig Installing Above-Ground Swimming Pools' \[in June 2016\], *The Onion* has moved so far away from the original political context that despite the highly politicised nature of its subject, the joke has no grounding in the political sphere, let alone a critical politics.

*,  Nicholas Holm, *Humour as Politics: The Political Aesthetics of Contemporary Comedy* (2017)[^4506]*

There is a general consensus that *The Onion* made an impact on Biden's public image. In 2014, Jonathan Bernstein at *[Bloomberg Opinion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomberg_News)* attributed Biden's image to a combination of *The Onion*'s character and the vice president's own actions and personality. "All veeps become ridiculous; the only question is how", Bernstein wrote, and "once the *Onion* came up with the image, it seemed to fit really well."[^4548]

Scholar Byron C. Wallace suggested *The Onion*'s patently absurd, often risqué characterization of Biden would be easily recognized as implausible by most readers and that, as such, their articles about Biden were presumptively less likely to be mistaken for real news than other, subtler satirical content.[^4549] On the other hand, the heightened contrast between the fiction and the real person has prompted concern that readers' impression of *The Onion*'s Biden could supplant their impression of the real Biden.[^4550] *The Onion* editor Tracy remarked in 2012: "My sense is that we've done so much on him that our vision for our version of Joe Biden has, in some way, seeped into the nation's consciousness \[and\] people think our character of Joe Biden is somehow him."[^4523] In a profile of Biden for *[The New Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Republic)*, George Blaustein asked:

> Has a satire ever so effectively overwritten the image of a politician? ... The full corpus of Diamond Joe amounts to a powerful and paradoxical new origin story. It is intriguing that this fantasy caricature of Biden makes him an endearing outlaw when the real Biden's political legacy includes the [1994 Crime Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Violent_Crime_Control_and_Law_Enforcement_Act), and the terrible scale of [mass incarceration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_incarceration) that followed from it.[^4489]

Nevertheless, it remains difficult to quantify *The Onion*'s impact on Biden's image, and so the precise extent of the newspaper's influence is unclear.[^4530] Jeremy Gordon at *[The Outline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Outline_%28website%29)* doubted the extent of *The Onion*'s effect on Biden's popularity, noting that the website's audience had decreased in the preceding years and that its audience skewed younger and more liberal than Biden's base of predominantly older, moderate Democrats.[^4551] Conversely, historian Christine Wenc has argued that *The Onion*'s dominance in its home state of Wisconsin helped Biden to win it as the third-closest state of the [2020 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election).[^4552]

##### In Internet culture

*The Onion*'s Biden became a popular [meme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme) and influenced perceptions of Biden in [Internet culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_culture), particularly during the Obama administration.[^4553] Seth Millstein at the women's magazine *[Bustle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bustle_%28magazine%29)* ranked *The Onion* character as the 13th best Biden meme (out of 15) and said it had "played an enormous role in shaping the public's perception of Biden."[^4554] Regarding Biden's chances of appealing to [Millennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millennials) voters in the 2020 Democratic presidential primaries, [Peter Hamby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Hamby) at *[Vanity Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanity_Fair_%28magazine%29)* wrote that Biden may be "old, but thanks to the *Onion* and his Uncle Joe persona, he's already optimized for meme culture."[^4555]

In addition to becoming a meme in its own right, *The Onion*'s Biden influenced other memes and online discourse about Biden, which frequently imagined him as a roguish goof paired with Obama as the more serious "[straight man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straight_man)".[^4556] A viral tweet from Twitter user @blippoblappo played off this dynamic:

|     | **blupman** (@blippoblappo) tweeted: |
|-----|--------------------------------------|

> REPORTER: Mr. President, what's your favorite [Wu Tang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wu-Tang_Clan) album?
>
> \
> \
> OBAMA: What kind of question is -\
> \
> \[biden grabs podium\]\
> \
>
> BIDEN: [LIQUID SWORDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liquid_Swords)

April 26, 2014[^4557]

Brian Feldman at *[New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_%28magazine%29)* magazine wrote that "Biden-joke pedants might point out that the butt-rock-loving Biden of the *Onion* would probably not be a Wu-Tang Clan fan," but @blippoblappo's tweet "nevertheless carries with it the same myth-making potency: an image that it feels more true than the actual truth."[^4558]

##### In the *Congressional Record*

The character entered the *[Congressional Record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Record)* on at least two occasions. During the [presidential transition of Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_presidential_transition_of_Donald_Trump), [Mitch McConnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_McConnell) referenced the character in a December 2016 speech to the Senate floor delivered in tribute to Biden. McConnell said, "When *The Onion* ran a mock photo of him washing a Trans Am in the White House driveway shirtless, America embraced it. And so did he."[^4559]

In June 2019, while giving testimony to the [House Intelligence Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Permanent_Select_Committee_on_Intelligence) on the topic of "[deepfake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepfake)" imagery, former FBI agent [Clint Watts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clint_Watts) discussed *The Onion*'s manipulated photo of Biden washing a car shirtless.[^4560] Some members of Congress later pointed to the *Onion* image as an example of potential problems with [moderating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moderation_system) deepfake imagery, namely, the difficulty of trying to distinguish between [satire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire) and [fake news](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fake_news).[^4561]

##### Criticism from former *Onion* editor

[Joe Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Garden), a former *Onion* writer and editor who left in 2012 after 19 years, publicly criticized the newspaper's portrayal of Biden in May 2019. After he tweeted some of his recent thoughts about the character, *[Vice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_%28magazine%29)* published a full op-ed by Garden titled "Area Man Regrets Helping Turn Joe Biden into a Meme".[^4562]

In the *Vice* piece, Garden wrote that he still believed the Biden pieces were funny in their light-hearted way. However, he had also come to believe they had failed as satire because "\[i\]nstead of viciously skewering a public figure who deserved scrutiny, we let him off easy".[^4563] In hindsight, he said, Biden's vocal approval of the character should have been a [red flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_flag_%28idiom%29) indicating that their satire was ineffective. He compared their work to Trump's appearance as the host of *Saturday Night Live* in 2015 and [Jimmy Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Fallon)'s interview with Trump on *[The Tonight Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tonight_Show_Starring_Jimmy_Fallon)* in 2016, both of which had been criticized as overly conciliatory treatments that downplayed what he felt were [inflammatory and racist aspects of Trump's messaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_views_of_Donald_Trump). Garden concluded:

> I don't believe *The Onion*'s Biden is solely responsible for this early popularity of real-life Biden. We were just one small link in a chain of institutions that didn't scrutinize Biden closely enough. I wish we had looked more at his actual career in politics, which includes [opposition to busing as a way to integrate schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_career_of_Joe_Biden) and support for predatory financial institutions, and tried to really puncture him, rather than just turning him into a clown. We helped make him more likable by inventing a version of Biden that never existed. ... As a guideline, if the people you're satirizing aren't mad, then you should dig deeper. I hope that my alma mater, and everyone else in comedy, follows this rule now that Diamond Joe is back.[^4563]

Garden's op-ed was discussed in *The Washington Post* and *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times)*.[^4564]

#### Retirement of the character (2019-present)

> You can't understand what the *Onion* is today without first understanding the extent to which the outlet feels haunted by the ghost of Joe Biden. Or, more accurately, 'Joe Biden'.

*,  Derek Robertson, *[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico)* (February 2020)[^4565]*

Shortly after Biden announced [his 2020 presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden_2020_presidential_campaign) in March 2019, the character briefly reemerged in a story titled "Biden Pulls Off Dusty Tarp Covering Old Campaign Motorcycle".[^4566] Since then, *The Onion* abandoned its formerly warm, fanciful characterization of Biden. Its subsequent satirical coverage of the candidate has become more critical and direct. Recent articles have tended to focus on real-world developments in the presidential race, such as his frequent [gaffes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_gaffe), and issues like public [concern over Biden's age and mental acuity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_and_health_concerns_about_Joe_Biden).[^4567]

Noting the turn, secondary sources have cited late-2019 *Onion* headlines like the following:

- "[Jill Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Biden) Urges Democratic Voters to Ignore Which Candidates Are Mentally Sharp Enough to Finish Complete Sentences for Good of Party" (described as "just brutal" in the conservative website *[Townhall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Townhall)*);[^4568]
- "'Help! Help! Who Am I? Where Am I? Who Are You People?' Says Biden in Embarrassing Campaign Gaffe" (described as "devastating" by liberal pundit [Amanda Marcotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Marcotte));[^4569]
- "Biden Declares Self Only Candidate Who Can Defeat [George Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush) in [1988 Election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_United_States_presidential_election)" (dubbed the "best evidence \[of\] bad news for Team Biden" in *[New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_%28magazine%29)* magazine).[^4570]

### NBACentel

**NBACentel** (sometimes spelled as **NBA Centel**, often referred to simply as **Centel**) is a [satirical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satirical) [sports journalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_journalism) account on [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter). A [parody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parody) of [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association) (NBA) [news aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_aggregator) page NBACentral, the Centel page often posts humorous or outlandish faux headlines regarding NBA teams, players, coaches, and personalities. Because of the account's near-identical appearance to NBACentral, many readers are fooled by the account's satirical headlines, mistaking them for genuine sports reporting. Professional NBA players and sports media figures have been tricked by the account, which has since been dubbed "getting Centel'd" a term made by famous NBA Player, Kevin Durant.

Despite explicitly labelling itself as a [parody account](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parody_account), NBACentel has been the subject of critique online due to its contribution towards monetized [disinformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disinformation) on social media. The account garnered further attention after it was abruptly [shadow-banned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow-banned) from [X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) on February 26, 2025, before being reinstated the following day. As of August 2026, Centel has over 800,000 followers on the platform.

#### History

NBACentel is an [X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) account directly parodying NBACentral, a basketball [news aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_aggregator) on the platform.[^4571] The account was opened in July 2022 under a different handle, and initially posted non-parody NBA content before pivoting to its NBACentel identity in 2023.[^4571] The owner of the account, an individual from [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto), Ontario, who remains anonymous, credits his inspiration primarily to "Ballsack Sports", another satirical account that has had fake quotes picked up and spread by legitimate news outlets.[^4571]

Media writers have suggested that X's incentive structure that allows for [monetization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetization) on posts by [X Premium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X_Premium) subscribers has led to the increase in accounts like that of NBACentel.[^4571][^4572]

In July 2023, shortly after NBACentel began posting satirical content, the page successfully fooled [Golden State Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_State_Warriors) forward [Draymond Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Draymond_Green) into responding to a fake quote attributed to retired [Hall of Famer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naismith_Basketball_Hall_of_Fame) [Kevin Garnett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Garnett) regarding an October 2022 altercation between Green and then-teammate [Jordan Poole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_Poole).[^4571][^4573] This prompted a response from Garnett, who pointed out NBACentel was a fake account and called for X CEO [Elon Musk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elon_Musk) to "fix it".[^4571] Other players and media members have since been fooled by or otherwise drawn attention to Centel's tweets, such as [Kevin Durant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Durant), [Stephen A. Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_A._Smith) and [Colin Cowherd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Cowherd).[^4573][^4574]

##### Notable faux stories

One of NBACentel's more notable posts was a story falsely credited to NBA freelance reporter [Brandon "Scoop B" Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandon_%22Scoop_B%22_Robinson), supposedly quoting [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers) forward [LeBron James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeBron_James) having stated: "It's crazy, I was bumping to '\[ [Mo Money Mo Problems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo_Money_Mo_Problems)\]' earlier today in the car and I had a weird feeling today was the day the [feds](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/feds#English) will catch [Diddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diddy)". Robinson stated that his contacts in the entertainment industry congratulated him on the supposed story.[^4571]

In October 2024, [Phoenix Suns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Suns) forward [Kevin Durant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Durant) referenced Centel in multiple tweets; in one, he replied to a profane X post directed towards him by user @JasonAWilkinson, who responded to a post by NBACentel which included a fake quote attributed to Durant. Durant then replied to Wilkinson, informing him "you got centel'd".[^4575][^4576][^4577] This exchange led to a [tweet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tweet_%28social_media%29) by the [Merriam-Webster Dictionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merriam-Webster_Dictionary) humorously acknowledging the word *centel'd* as a verb.[^4576] Around this time, the account had approximately 154,000 followers.[^4571] Durant also stated that he browses the comments on the account's posts "just to truly see how many dummies come online thinking that they have high [IQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IQ)".[^4578]

On November 11, NBACentel posted a fabricated quote from [Milwaukee Bucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee_Bucks) head coach [Doc Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers), humorously writing that Rivers "have \[*[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic)*\] informed the Bucks he'll start taking coaching 'seriously' now," after the team lost eight of its first 10 games to start the [2024-25 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024%E2%80%9325_Milwaukee_Bucks_season).[^4579][^4580] Following the post, the Bucks would go on to win nine of their next 10 games and win the [2024 NBA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_NBA_Cup) tournament.[^4580]

NBACentel "broke" a fictitious story on February 21, 2025, reporting that the [Dallas Mavericks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Mavericks) had banned fans wearing [Luka Dončić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luka_Don%C4%8Di%C4%87)'s jersey from entering the team's home arena, [American Airlines Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Airlines_Center).[^4581][^4582] This came after multiple legitimate instances of Mavericks fans being escorted out of home games for chanting or holding signs reading "Fire Nico", a negative response to Mavericks general manager [Nico Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nico_Harrison) [trading Dončić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luka_Don%C4%8Di%C4%87_trade) to the [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers) earlier in the month.[^4583][^4584] Centel's faux headline fooled Cowherd, who mentioned the fake story during [his show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Herd_with_Colin_Cowherd) on [Fox Sports 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Sports_1).[^4585][^4586]

##### X shadow ban

On the afternoon of February 26, 2025, posts from the @TheNBACentel profile page on X stopped loading, and posts from the account ceased.[^4587][^4588][^4589] It was initially unclear if the [shadow ban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_ban) on the account indicated a permanent suspension.[^4574][^4590] As the account appeared shut down, Centel received tribute posts on X from [Stephen A. Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_A._Smith) and the official accounts of various NBA teams, posting [hashtags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hashtags) such as \#RIPCentel and \#FreeCentel, and dedicating wins from that night's games in the account's honor.[^4587]

Though the NBACentel account was transparent in its parody,[^4572] it did not officially tag itself as a parody account on X, which was speculated by many users to be the reason for the account being shut down.[^4591] The owner of the "Ballsack Sports" account tweeted that "Centel has told me he just wants to be back and having fun with you guys. We're hoping this a temporary restriction on his account, and not a ban".[^4591] NBACentel continued to post on [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram),[^4574] and its X account was restored the following morning, on February 27.[^4592] The account had accumulated around 357,000 followers at the time of the temporary ban.[^4590]
