### Rickrolling

**Rickrolling**[^4593] is an [Internet meme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme) and [prank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prank) involving the unexpected appearance of the [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video) for the 1987 hit song "[Never Gonna Give You Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never_Gonna_Give_You_Up)", performed by the English singer [Rick Astley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Astley). The meme is a type of [bait and switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bait_and_switch) and commonly uses a disguised [hyperlink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperlink) that leads to the music video instead of what was expected. The meme has also extended to using the song's lyrics in unexpected contexts or singing it during public events. After the origin of the meme in 2007 and the height of its popularity in 2008, rickrolling has become a very long-lived meme. Astley has seen his performance career revitalised by the meme's popularity.

The meme grew out of a similar bait-and-switch trick called "duckrolling" that was popular on the website [4chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4chan) in 2006. Rickrolling originated on 15 May 2007, when 4chan user Shawn Cotter uploaded the "Never Gonna Give You Up" music video to [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube) and linked to it in place of the trailer for the video game *[Grand Theft Auto IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Theft_Auto_IV)*. It quickly became popular and spread to other Internet sites later that year.

The meme gained mainstream attention in 2008 through several events, beginning with a campaign by the hacker group [Anonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anonymous_%28group%29) to protest the [Church of Scientology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scientology) through rickrolling. Awareness of rickrolling increased after two events in April 2008: YouTube used the meme for its [April Fools' Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_Fools'_Day) event, and users of several websites voted for "Never Gonna Give You Up" in a poll for the [New York Mets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Mets)' rally song. The meme inspired videos remixing "Never Gonna Give You Up", including "BarackRoll", which combined the song with footage of United States presidential candidate [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama). Astley was initially hesitant about using the meme to further his career; he declined to appear at the [2008 MTV Europe Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_MTV_Europe_Music_Awards), in which an online vote had named him "Best Act Ever". He accepted the publicity by rickrolling the 2008 [Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's_Thanksgiving_Day_Parade), seen by millions of television viewers, with a surprise performance of the song on the *[Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foster's_Home_for_Imaginary_Friends)* float.

Use of rickrolling peaked in 2008, but it remained popular. Later perpetrators of the prank included United States Representative [Nancy Pelosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi) in 2009, members of the [Oregon Legislative Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Legislative_Assembly) in 2010, and the [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) account of the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House) in 2011. Anonymous again used rickrolling as a tactic against the [Islamic State of Iraq and Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State_of_Iraq_and_Syria) in 2015. The rock band [Foo Fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foo_Fighters) featured surprise appearances by Astley to rickroll audiences in 2017, having previously used the meme to protest the [Westboro Baptist Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westboro_Baptist_Church). The prank was also conducted by sports stadiums, including that of the [San Diego Padres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_Padres) in 2019. Rickrolling resurged in popularity during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic). By 2021, the official YouTube video of "Never Gonna Give You Up", one of several uploads used for rickrolling, had been viewed over one billion times.

#### History

##### Background

"[Never Gonna Give You Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never_Gonna_Give_You_Up)" is a song written by songwriting trio [Stock Aitken Waterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_Aitken_Waterman) and recorded by English singer [Rick Astley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Astley).[^4594] It appeared on his 1987 debut album *[Whenever You Need Somebody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whenever_You_Need_Somebody)*[^4595][^4596] and was released as a single on 27 July of that year.[^4594] It was a number-one hit on several charts,[^4594] including the [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100) in the US,[^4597] the [ARIA Charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARIA_Charts) in Australia,[^4596] and the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart),[^4594] becoming the most popular single of the year in the UK.[^4598] It is a [dance-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance-pop) song[^4596][^4599] with heavy use of [synthesizers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer),[^4594] [catchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catchy) music, and repetitive lyrics[^4600] sung in a [baritone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baritone) voice.[^4601] It begins with a distinctive drum riff[^4602][^4603] and a synthesizer melody,[^4604] followed by the lines, "We're no strangers to love / You know the rules and so do I".[^4605] The accompanying [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video), Astley's first, was made in a single week, and Astley brought his own outfits.[^4601][^4606] It features 21-year-old Astley[^4607] performing the song while awkwardly [dancing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing), wearing a [trenchcoat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trenchcoat) and a coiffed hairstyle,[^4594][^4597][^4606][^4608] alongside [backup dancers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backup_dancer) wearing [spandex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spandex)[^4609] and a [bartender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartender) doing [backflips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Backflip).[^4607]

The song faded from popularity, being a common song on the radio for only about a year.[^4610] It also received disapproval, with the television network [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1) listing it as one of the "50 Most Awesomely Bad Songs", and its style fell out of fashion.[^4594] The song's reputation was influenced by its 1980s-style composition, its unpolished music video, and a perceived incongruity between Astley's youthful appearance and his low-pitched vocals.[^4594][^4611] "Never Gonna Give You Up" was Astley's most successful song; it was one of two, alongside "[Together Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Together_Forever_%28Rick_Astley_song%29)", to reach number one on the *Billboard* chart.[^4612] Astley initially retired in 1994, at the age of 28,[^4594][^4595] as he wanted more time with his family.[^4602] He returned to touring in 2004[^4613] to mild success.[^4614]

[Internet memes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme) originated in the 1990s, when they mostly involved humorous images. Video-based memes, such as [viral videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viral_video), became popular in the 2000s as technology improved.[^4615] Many memes originated on the [imageboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imageboard) website [4chan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4chan), which was also the origin of the hacker group [Anonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anonymous_%28group%29).[^4605][^4608] On several websites, beginning in the late 1990s, users frequently posted [bait-and-switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bait-and-switch) links that [trolled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trolling) readers by redirecting them to unexpected targets. These links often led to [shock sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shock_site), which contained disturbing or graphic imagery.[^4616] Trolling and bait-and-switch humour were popular on 4chan.[^4594][^4616] Internet scholar Lee Knuttila wrote that bait-and-switch humour was a simple, fundamental element of the subculture of 4chan.[^4616] According to *[Know Your Meme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Know_Your_Meme)* editor-in-chief Don Caldwell, rickrolling was the first bait-and-switch meme to gain mainstream popularity.[^4611]

Pre-dating the first rickroll, in August 2005, the sitcom *[It's Always Sunny In Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Always_Sunny_In_Philadelphia)* featured "Never Gonna Give You Up". In the episode "[Charlie Has Cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Has_Cancer)", the character [Dennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Reynolds) sings along to the song in his car.[^4617] Another precursor of rickrolling occurred in 2006, when rural Michigan resident Erik Helwig called in to a local radio sports talk show and, instead of conversing with the DJs, played "Never Gonna Give You Up". Caldwell said there was no confirmation of whether it had inspired the 4chan use of the song, and Helwig said he did not claim to be the "founder" of the meme.[^4594] YouTuber Harrison Renshaw listed both Helwig and *It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia* as contributors to the popularity of the rickroll.[^4611]

##### Origin

The use of "Never Gonna Give You Up" for rickrolling originated on 4chan.[^4594] It was based on an earlier meme on the website known as "duckrolling", which originated in 2006. That year, the site's moderator, [Christopher "moot" Poole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Poole), implemented a [word filter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_filter) replacing the word *egg* with *duck* as a gag. On one thread, where *eggroll* had become *duckroll*, an anonymous user posted an [edited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photo_manipulation) image of a duck with wheels.[^4594][^4618][^4619] According to video game historian Kate Willært, this image had been created in April 2005 by [Gaming-Age Forums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NeoGAF) user Christian "ferricide" Nutt, inspired by a fellow user of the forums known as Duckroll.[^4620] The image caught on across 4chan, becoming the target of a [hyperlink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperlink) with an otherwise interesting title, with a user clicking through being said to be "duckrolled".[^4594][^4618]

In March 2007, [Rockstar Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockstar_Games) released the first trailer for the highly anticipated *[Grand Theft Auto IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Theft_Auto_IV)*. Viewership was so high that it crashed Rockstar's site. Several Internet users helped to post mirrors of the video on different sites, but one 4chan user linked to the "Never Gonna Give You Up" video on [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube) claiming to be the trailer, tricking numerous readers.[^4618] Under the YouTube username cotter548, he uploaded the video, titled "Rickroll'D", on 15 May.[^4602][^4616][^4621] The uploader was nineteen-year-old Shawn Cotter, a [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force) airman in South Korea;[^4602][^4606] he publicly revealed his identity in an "[ask me anything](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R/IAmA)" post on [Reddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit) in 2011,[^4602] describing himself as "the one who inadvertently became the biggest troll on the internet".[^4622] In a 2022 interview with [Vice Media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_Media), he said the reason of using "Never Gonna Give You Up" was because he had found an online list about songs that were popular in 1987, the year of his birth; he found the video funny and wanted it to be a meme.[^4606] Cotter is generally agreed to be the originator of the rickroll.[^4622]

The practice of rickrolling became popular within a few days[^4602] and replaced duckrolling with links pointing to Astley's video.[^4618] The term began showing up in Google search data the same month.[^4596] Rickrolling became popular on YouTube, with videos featuring people [lip-syncing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lip-syncing) to the song or rickrolling public events,[^4597] as well as [mashup videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashup_%28video%29).[^4607] Many videos used the phrase, "You've been RickRolled."[^4597] The trend contributed to sales of "Never Gonna Give You Up", beginning in late December 2007, it received over 1,000 downloads per week, reaching a peak of 2,500 in the week of 9 March 2008.[^4597] Participants in the meme were too young to remember the original song.[^4607]

Astley first became aware of rickrolling when he fell for the prank through a series of emails from a US-based friend during the early days of the phenomenon. Astley was on vacation and was confused until he called the friend, who explained the meme.[^4598][^4606][^4623]

##### Growth in 2008

###### Rickroll against Scientology and early mainstream coverage

The first rickroll to gain mainstream attention, in February 2008,[^4594][^4608] targeted the [Church of Scientology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Scientology), which had been aggressively trying to remove videos critical of the church. The group Anonymous, as part of their [Project Chanology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Chanology) to challenge these actions, protested at the Church's various headquarters by chanting "Never Gonna Give You Up" and playing it on [boomboxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boombox).[^4608] Several YouTube videos documented these events, including one in which the rickroller falsely described Astley as "some dead guy".[^4607] Members of Anonymous also created a website that [mimicked the URL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typosquatting) of a Scientologist website denouncing Anonymous, instead playing a rickroll.[^4608]

In March 2008, two employees of the athletics department of [Eastern Washington University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Washington_University), Pawl Fisher and Davin Perry, rickrolled a number of games by [the collegiate basketball team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Washington_Eagles_women's_basketball).[^4594] These performances had Perry dressing up as Astley from the video and lip-syncing to the music as a prank before the start of the game.[^4610] Fisher filmed and edited these into a YouTube video that made it appear as a single rickroll interrupting a game. After the video received millions of views, it was covered by local television station [KHQ-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KHQ-TV) as well as *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times)*. Fisher pranked *New York Times* reporter Evelyn Nussenbaum by claiming the video was a single, unedited rickroll; the newspaper published a retraction after KHQ reported that this was false.[^4594][^4624]

Popular blogs such as *[Gizmodo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gizmodo)*, *[Slashdot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slashdot)*, and *[Boing Boing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boing_Boing)* introduced the meme to larger audiences.[^4625] Various Youtube uploads of the music video collectively reached 25 million views by April 2008,[^4618] one of which, linked from the webpage yougotrickrolled.com, had 7 million views.[^4610] Internet users also created lists of rickroll URLs, [browser plugins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browser_plugin) that claimed to block rickrolls but actually caused them, and a [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia) article about the phenomenon.[^4608] As potential victims of rickrolling began to suspect links, pranksters began to hide rickrolls within more complex videos, such as edited versions of scenes from popular media.[^4626] The band [Radiohead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiohead) posted a rickroll claiming to be a download of their new album, *[In Rainbows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_Rainbows)*, in March 2008.[^4627]

Astley first publicly spoke about rickrolling in a March 2008 interview with the *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times)*, titled "Never Gonna Give You Up, Rick Astley", in which he said:[^4607]

> I think it's just one of those odd things where something gets picked up and people run with it. But that is what's brilliant about the Internet.[^4594][^4628]\
> ...\
> If this had happened around some kind of rock song, with a lyric that really meant something, a [Bruce Springsteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Springsteen) \[song\], "[God Bless America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_Bless_America)", or an anti-something kind of song, I could kind of understand that. But for something as, and I don't mean to belittle it, because I still think it's a great pop song, but it's a pop song, do you know what I mean? It doesn't have any kind of weight behind it, as such. But maybe that's the irony of it.[^4594][^4629]

 Rick Astley, *Los Angeles Times*, "Never Gonna Give You Up, Rick Astley"

Astley also said in the interview that he was not troubled by the phenomenon, stating that he found it "bizarre"[^4618] and "weird", since he had not performed much lately, but he found the interest funny.[^4607][^4630] The following month, a spokesperson for Astley's record label released a comment that stated, "I'm sorry, but he's done talking about Rickrolling".[^4618][^4631] Despite this, the meme revived his career, and he continued to be asked about it years later.[^4594] Astley overcame his initial annoyance about rickrolling after speaking with his daughter, who thought it was cool[^4612][^4632] and told him that the joke was not about him.[^4599][^4611]

###### April 2008 peak

In a 2008 [April Fools'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_Fools') joke, YouTube made all links to videos on the site's home page end up on the "Never Gonna Give You Up" music video.[^4609][^4633][^4634] The coordinators of the prank had contacted Astley's record label, [Sony BMG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_BMG),[^4635] which had made its music available on the website two years earlier; according to label executive Sam Gomez, Astley had liked the idea.[^4597] YouTube was one of several websites to independently pull such a prank that day,[^4618] along with *[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated)* and [LiveJournal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LiveJournal). On that day, the YouTube video received 6.6 million views and 43,000 comments, while the song became the 77th most popular listing on [Amazon Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Music).[^4597] April Fools' Day strongly contributed to the meme's popularity.[^4609]

The following week,[^4618] the [New York Mets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Mets) baseball team asked fans on the Internet to choose their [seventh-inning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventh-inning_stretch) rally song for the upcoming season. "Never Gonna Give You Up" received five million write-in votes, driven by websites like YouTube and news aggregators [Fark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fark) and [Digg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digg).[^4609][^4618][^4629][^4636] The team considered the online vote hijacked[^4636] and replaced it with an audience vote of the six most-voted songs during the first game of the season;[^4618][^4629] the audience booed in response to "Never Gonna Give You Up".[^4618][^4636]

Rickrolling gained further mainstream awareness after the Mets event, with a [SurveyUSA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SurveyUSA) poll the same month estimating that at least 18 million US adults had been rickrolled, based on a sample of 959.[^4594][^4637] [Google Trends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Trends) showed that the highest volume of searches about rickrolling occurred that month.[^4594][^4596] By this time, "Never Gonna Give You Up" became one of the biggest viral videos or memes,[^4609][^4629] with many online creators attempting to outdo other rickrolls.[^4636] As the meme received mainstream media coverage, some people within the online subculture considered it to be the end of rickrolling. For example, moot was quoted by *[FOX News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FOX_News)* as saying that he was "very surprised" at the prank's use by mainstream websites and that he expected the meme to fade soon.[^4618][^4638]

A [flash mob](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flash_mob) performed a rickroll at [Liverpool Street Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Street_Station), London, in April 2008.[^4639] Another flash mob performed a rickroll in [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore) the following month, organised by Facebook user Ryan Goff, which received coverage in *[The Baltimore Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Baltimore_Sun)*.[^4594]

###### Further recognition, "BarackRoll" videos, and Astley parade appearance

Videos adapting the rickroll meme were popular during the [2008 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election) between [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama) and [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain).[^4640] An August 2008 YouTube video by [Hugh Atkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Atkin), titled "BarackRoll", was a mashup consisting of footage of Obama dancing on *[The Ellen DeGeneres Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ellen_DeGeneres_Show)*, paired with words spoken by Obama spliced to match the lyrics of "Never Gonna Give You Up".[^4641] The video was acknowledged by *The Ellen DeGeneres Show* and by Astley,[^4594] who called it his favourite use of the meme.[^4613] Atkin also made a sequel titled, "John McCain Gets BarackRoll'd",[^4594] using footage of a speech by McCain, with "BarackRoll" edited onto a screen behind him while he stays silent. According to media scholar Carol Vernallis, the two "BarackRoll" videos reflect the popular conceptions of the two candidates: Obama is portrayed as a skilled singer who will "never give up", and a parallel is drawn between him and Astley as both appealed to both Black and White people, while McCain appears dull in contrast.[^4642] "BarackRoll" followed a format of "Never Gonna Give You Up" mashup videos that used the word "roll" in the title to transparently indicate the connection to rickrolling.[^4643] A similar video spliced clips from the series *[Mad Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad_Men)* to match the song.[^4601]

At the [2008 MTV Europe Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_MTV_Europe_Music_Awards) in November 2008, Astley was nominated for "[Best Act Ever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_Europe_Music_Award_for_Best_Act)" after the online nomination form was flooded with votes.[^4644] Despite not being on the original shortlist of nominees, Astley won with one hundred million votes, more than all other votes combined, effectively rickrolling the awards.[^4594][^4645] Astley chose not to attend the ceremony,[^4646] instead making a statement saying, "This is the first time I have been nominated for the EMAs and I would like to thank everyone who voted for me".[^4594][^4645] Astley stated in an interview that he felt the award was "daft", but noted that "MTV were thoroughly rickrolled".[^4647] An MTV executive also said, "We've been well and truly Rickrolled".[^4594][^4645]

By November 2008, the "Never Gonna Give You Up" video on YouTube had more than 20 million views.[^4646] Astley initially appeared indifferent to the newfound fame[^4594] and was wary of trying to promote himself using the popularity of the meme. However, he agreed to make an appearance at the 2008 [Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's_Thanksgiving_Day_Parade) because [Cartoon Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartoon_Network) offered him a considerable payment for his performance and because his friends in America urged him to accept.[^4595] Astley made a surprise appearance on a [float](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Float_%28parade%29) of the Cartoon Network show *[Foster's Home for Imaginary Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foster's_Home_for_Imaginary_Friends)*. After the puppets singing on the float were cut off by a [record scratch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_scratch),[^4622] Astley joined to lip-sync the song to the crowd and millions of television viewers,[^4646] with a puppet saying, "I love rickrolling!"[^4648] According to design scholar Ursula Murray Husted, viewers unfamiliar with rickrolling would have considered it an ordinary parade appearance before the term "rickroll" was spoken.[^4649] That performance was the largest rickroll yet.[^4646] It went viral on social media within minutes.[^4646] *[The Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Telegraph)* wrote that this appearance was "the pinnacle of Rickrolling" and "may have been the most widely-seen Rickroll ever".[^4594][^4646]

The Macy's parade made rickrolling more of a mainstream phenomenon and led many 4chan users to lose interest in it, feeling the joke had been exhausted.[^4650] It led to a wave of rickrolls outside of the Internet, including on radio and television.[^4651] Two weeks after the parade,[^4648] a user of the message board [I Love Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Love_Music_%28forum%29), Grady Gillian, rickrolled other users with a file that appeared to be a leak of the upcoming [Animal Collective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_Collective) album *[Merriweather Post Pavilion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merriweather_Post_Pavilion_%28album%29)* until played;[^4652] viewers responded with both praise and harassment.[^4653] When the [United States Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress) launched its YouTube account in January 2009, it posted a video of cats in the office of Representative [Nancy Pelosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi), which turned into a rickroll.[^4654] The video was intended to promote the channel[^4655] and was part of Pelosi's targeting of Internet users.[^4656][^4657] Also in 2009, students at the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology) conducted a rickroll by painting [sheet music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheet_music) on a university building.[^4598]

##### Enduring popularity

###### Post-peak usage

Rickrolling continued to be popular after its peak in 2008,[^4594] lasting much longer than other memes.[^4594][^4658] In 2009, Astley wrote about 4chan founder moot for *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_%28magazine%29)* magazine's annual *[Time 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100)* issue, thanking him for the rickrolling phenomenon.[^4659][^4660] Moot also acknowledged rickrolling in a 2010 [TED Talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TED_Talk), saying it had revived interest in Astley.[^4616] Although "Never Gonna Give You Up" had received hundreds of millions of views on YouTube as a result of the meme, one of the song's writers, [Pete Waterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Waterman), said in April 2009 that he had received only £11 (equivalent to £16 in 2025).[^4661][^4662] According to *[The Register](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Register)*, as of 2010, Astley had directly received only US\$12 (\$17 in 2025) in [performance royalties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performance_royalties) from YouTube; Astley did not compose the song and received only a performer's share of the sound recording copyright.[^4663]

> |----|----|----|
> | @whitehouse |  |  |
>
> Sorry to hear that. Fiscal policy is important, but can be dry sometimes. here's something more fun:
>
> https://tinyurl.com/y8ufsnp \#WHChat
>
> 27 July 2011[^4664]
>

> >
> > This WH correspondence briefing isn't nearly as entertaining as yesterday's. \#TCOT \#WHchat
> >
> > 27 July 2011[^4665]

After the cultural saturation of rickrolling, it continued to be recognised positively.[^4666] [University of Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oregon)-based [a cappella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_cappella) group On The Rocks posted a video of themselves singing "Never Gonna Give You Up" on the [New York City Subway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Subway) in March 2010; the video went viral and brought fame to the group.[^4594] The same month, members of the [Oregon state legislature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_Legislative_Assembly), spearheaded by [Jefferson Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jefferson_Smith_%28politician%29) of [the legislature's lower house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oregon_House_of_Representatives), slipped snippets of the song's lyrics into speeches they gave in 2011.[^4594] Smith stitched together a video compilation of these snippets into the full song, posted on April Fools' Day.[^4596][^4667][^4668] On 27 July 2011, the Twitter account of the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House), during a chat session run by staffer [Brian Deese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Deese), posted a rickroll link in response to a user who had criticised the dull tone of the session's posts.[^4594][^4601] The White House's rickroll contributed to the popularity of the meme.[^4669]

In 2015, members of Anonymous began rickrolling the [Islamic State of Iraq and Syria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_State_of_Iraq_and_Syria) (ISIS) by hacking into websites used to promote the group[^4670] and spamming related hashtags.[^4671] Reporter James Geddes wrote, "Until now, Rickrolling has generally been used as a harmless internet prank, but now it's being used in a war that has much bigger stakes," while reporter Corey Charlton wrote that the prank was "giving ISIS a taste of its own medicine", as the group used social media tactics to unexpectedly spread its propaganda.[^4670]

Rickrolls continued to occur years after the meme's popularity had declined. [Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple,_Inc.) rickrolled consumers in 2015 by showing them the song's lyrics when they viewed the [Apple Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Watch) help page.[^4594] At the [2016 Republican National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Republican_National_Convention), [Melania Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melania_Trump), campaigning for her husband [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump), said, "He will never, ever give up and ... never, ever let you down,"[^4672] which many viewers considered a rickroll.[^4603] Speaking with *[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker)*, Astley said he found it plausible that the rickroll was intentional.[^4598] Australia's [ABC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_News_%28Australia%29) later called this "the biggest political rickroll".[^4596]

The rock band [Foo Fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foo_Fighters) first performed a rickroll[^4623] at an August 2015 concert in [Kansas City, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri), using a truck to counterprotest a demonstration by the homophobic group [Westboro Baptist Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westboro_Baptist_Church).[^4601][^4669][^4673] This mirrored the tactic used by Anonymous against Scientology.[^4596] In 2017, the Foo Fighters brought Astley on stage to rickroll the audience of a concert at the [Summer Sonic Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Sonic_Festival) in Tokyo, mashing up "Never Gonna Give You Up" with "[Smells Like Teen Spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smells_Like_Teen_Spirit)".[^4622] As Astley recounted in his memoir, this performance had been unplanned as Astley, also performing at the festival, had been watching the Foo Fighters from backstage before being invited to join them.[^4623] The Foo Fighters brought Astley to rickroll a concert in London the same year.[^4594]

In April 2018, the creators of the television drama *[Westworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westworld_%28TV_series%29)*, participating in a Reddit discussion, released a video that purported to be a spoiler guide for the second season in advance, but instead featured lead actress [Evan Rachel Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Rachel_Wood) singing "Never Gonna Give You Up".[^4674] While responses from Reddit users were mostly positive,[^4675] the website *[Polygon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygon_%28website%29)* wrote, "*Westworld* has finally killed the Rickroll".[^4594][^4631] In the [post-credits scene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-credits_scene) of [Walt Disney Animation Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_Animation_Studios)' 2018 film *[Ralph Breaks the Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Breaks_the_Internet)*, a fake sneak peek of *[Frozen II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frozen_II)* suddenly switches to Ralph singing "Never Gonna Give You Up" and replicating Astley's music video.[^4676]

Rickrolls also became popular at sports games.[^4623] On 25 August 2019, the [Boston Red Sox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Red_Sox) and the [San Diego Padres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_Padres) played a [Major League Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball) game at [the Padres' stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petco_Park). During a mid-inning break, the Padres' scoreboard began to play "[Sweet Caroline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_Caroline)", a tradition at Red Sox home games, but as the song approached the chorus, the videoboard switched to "Never Gonna Give You Up".[^4622][^4677] On 13 October 2019, during a [Sunday Night NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Sunday_Night_Football) game between the [Pittsburgh Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers) and [Los Angeles Chargers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Chargers) at [the Chargers' stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dignity_Health_Sports_Park), the announcers played the beginning of the [Styx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Styx_%28band%29) song "[Renegade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renegade_%28Styx_song%29)", a standard at [the Steelers' stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heinz_Field), then switched to "Never Gonna Give You Up".[^4678][^4679]

###### 2020s resurgence

Rickrolling saw a significant resurgence online in the 2020s, during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic).[^4611] Replying to a [Reddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit) post by Astley in June 2020, a user, u/theMalleableDuck, claimed to have met Astley backstage when they were 12 years old, but instead posted a link to the song. Astley replied with a clapping emoji, implying that he had been tricked into clicking the link.[^4680][^4681] The thread became Reddit's most upvoted post of 2020.[^4681] In July 2021, the YouTube video for "Never Gonna Give You Up" reached [1 billion views](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most-viewed_YouTube_videos), becoming the fourth 1980s song to do so;[^4613][^4622] this had included 2.3 million views on the preceding April Fools' Day.[^4604][^4622][^4628] Astley responded in a Twitter video, "That is mind-blowing. The world is a wonderful and beautiful place, and I am very lucky."[^4612] He also celebrated the event by selling signed copies of the song on vinyl, which quickly sold out.[^4604]

In a 2021 episode of the sitcom *[Ted Lasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Lasso)*, "No Weddings and a Funeral", the character Rebecca prepares to give a eulogy but instead leads the attendees in singing "Never Gonna Give You Up", rickrolling them.[^4682] Activist [Greta Thunberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Thunberg) performed a rickroll during an October 2021 climate-action speech at the [Climate Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_Live) concert in Stockholm, in which she said, "We're no strangers to love", before being joined by another activist in singing and dancing to the song; Astley tweeted that the video was "fantastic".[^4683][^4684] Astley recreated the original video clip in a 2022 advertisement for the [California State Automobile Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Automobile_Association). Physical advertisements for the agency included QR codes to this video to rickroll the viewers.[^4685]

In February 2025, in response to demands for the release of [files related to the criminal investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epstein_list) of [Jeffrey Epstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeffrey_Epstein), the Twitter account of Republicans on the [House Judiciary Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_the_Judiciary) posted "#BREAKING: EPSTEIN FILES RELEASED" with a rickroll link. This post received a negative response from users, many of whom considered it inappropriate to joke about the subject,[^4686] including Republican politician [Anna Paulina Luna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Paulina_Luna) and right-wing activist [Laura Loomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Loomer).[^4654][^4687] The post was then deleted.[^4654][^4687]

In the final Class 12 mathematics exam of India's [Central Board of Secondary Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Board_of_Secondary_Education) held in March 2026, the QR code on the front of some students' question papers linked to a rickroll, while others simply got the letter A, leading to claims that the paper was tampered or leaked.[^4688][^4689][^4690] The examination board clarified that the papers were not compromised and that it would ensure that this would not happen again.[^4691]

#### Mechanism

##### Forms of humour

Rickrolling is a [bait-and-switch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bait-and-switch) joke in which the viewer clicks a link, expecting it to be something interesting, often involving sex, video games, or cats[^4692], but is instead brought to the song "Never Gonna Give You Up" or its video.[^4594][^4693][^4669] This creates a humorous [non-sequitur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-sequitur_%28literary_device%29).[^4605] Like many memes, rickrolling is [multimodal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multimodality) as it incorporates multiple elements, [hypertext](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertext) and a music video.[^4693] The music video is the part of the meme that is reproduced, while the fake target of the link is the part that varies.[^4694] In its original form, rickrolling simply involves the unaltered music video.[^4670] According to an analysis by informaticists Alexander O. Smith, Jasmina Tacheva, and Jeff Hemsley, images associated with the meme show little variation as the intention is to be recognised an obvious rickroll.[^4695]

Unlike forms of humour used in most memes, rickrolling is a [prank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prank) as it creates a situation that has a victim without serious harm. However, according to cultural scholars Joanna Nowotny and Julian Reidy, a rickroll is unlike a typical prank or [hoax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoax) as it is not directed toward a specific victim, while also being less physical than most pranks and less serious than most hoaxes. Nowotny and Reid further state that an online prank like rickrolling may occur spontaneously, as a physical prank cannot, and the nature of online spaces allows victims to respond, a typical feature of hoaxes but not pranks.[^4696]

Rickrolling, like the [Trollface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trollface), is a meme primarily used for [trolling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trolling); in contrast with other forms of trolling, it is fun rather than offensive.[^4697] According to information scholars Madelyn Sanfilippo, Pnina Fichman, and Shannon Yang, forms of trolling such as rickrolling can create humour out of a reference recognised by an [ingroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingroup), distinguishing it from non-trolling humour.[^4698] According to design scholar Ursula Murray Husted, members of the ingroup who recognise the meme respond positively to it and introduce it to newcomers by pranking them.[^4699]

As a meme that has had multiple waves of popularity for over a decade, rickrolling has evolved into various forms of humour that incorporate the same song.[^4658] The term has been extended to the act of playing the song to interrupt a public event, as was the case with the Scientology rickrolling[^4610], which gives the meme a spatial component.[^4700] Other videos inspired by rickrolling include mashups, [cover versions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_version), and [remixes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remix) of "Never Gonna Give You Up".[^4692] Rickrolling also entails a phrase-based meme with the use of the song's lyrics in creative contexts,[^4701] such as in a conversation.[^4702]

##### Hyperlinking

Several YouTube uploads of "Never Gonna Give You Up" are used for rickrolling.[^4703] Astley's official channel uploaded the music video on 24 October 2009,[^4704] its [URL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/URL) ending with the identifier "dQw4w9WgXcQ".[^4705] Computer scientists Benoit Baudry and Martin Monperrus called this "the canonical rickroll URL", being the first result for the YouTube search string `rick astley never gonna give you up`.[^4706] The oldest version of the video on YouTube was uploaded by Cotter when the meme began.[^4602] The website briefly removed this several times, including in February 2010 (which YouTube said was from the video being mistakenly reported),[^4661][^4639] May 2012 (caused by an [antivirus software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antivirus_software)),[^4616] and July 2014 (which the company did not explain);[^4621] in each case, it was restored within hours, but its removal received widespread online attention.[^4616] By 2014, the original, unofficial upload had 70 million views, while the official upload had 84 million.[^4616]

Many cases of rickrolling have occurred on forums and on social media platforms such as Twitter and [Vine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vine_%28service%29).[^4707] Another common way to rickroll is to use a [QR code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QR_code), as this hides the target until it is scanned. According to a study by Ada Lerner et al, users of the [Scan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scan_%28company%29) app scanned codes leading to the "dQw4w9WgXcQ" URL over 1,600 times between May 2013 and March 2014.[^4705] Authors of academic literature also include rickrolls, such as by placing them in footnotes.[^4708] Baudry and Monperrus documented such cases by searching [Google Scholar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Scholar) for "dQw4w9WgXcQ" in 2022, finding 24 instances in which an author appeared to include the URL with the intent to rickroll.[^4709]

#### Analysis and impact

The meme had a positive impact on Astley's career,[^4613] introducing a new group of fans to his music.[^4660] He said it caused him to like "Never Gonna Give You Up" after "15 years of not singing it".[^4614] He also said it played a role in the reestablishment of his music career, his 2016 album *[50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50_%28Rick_Astley_album%29)*, his first in over a decade, reached number one on the [UK Album Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Album_Chart).[^4623] In a 2016 interview with *[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone)*, Astley said of the meme, "It's done me a lot of good, probably. The thing is it's not personal to me, even though I know it is me and it's my name in the title of Rickrolling. It's that video that I'm in, it's that song that's mine, but it could have been anybody."[^4596][^4622][^4710] Quoted in the *[Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press)* in 2022, he said, "The video and the song have drifted off into the ether and become something else, and I'm ever so grateful for it."[^4599][^4613] After performing at [Glastonbury Festival 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glastonbury_Festival_2023), Astley said this would not have been possible "without my old songs and without the Rickrolling thing with its own little universe".[^4614] That year, *[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Observer)* writer Barbara Ellen stated that the meme gave Astley an image of being cool, unlike most late-career musicians.[^4613]

Writing for *[MEL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MEL_%28magazine%29)* magazine, Brian VanHooker attributed the use of the song to its "randomness" and its status as a decades-old hit.[^4594] Writing for *[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Yorker)*, Michael Schulman said these factors and the catchiness of the song contribute to the meme's "[Dadaist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dadaist) humor".[^4598] Rickrolling is less negative than other pranks;[^4611] unlike other media used in bait-and-switch humour, the song is inoffensive, allowing it to be used by many types of people in many situations as a friendly prank.[^4711][^4616] [Tumblr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumblr) user deluxetrashqueen wrote, "Honestly, Rick Rolling is the best practical joke ever. Like, there's nothing offensive or mean spirited about it. It's just like 'Oops you thought there would be something else here but it's "Never Gonna Give You Up".' which isn't even a bad song."[^4712] According to communication scholars [Ryan M. Milner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_M._Milner) and Whitney Phillips, rickrolling is a form of [Internet folklore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_folklore) based on a copyrighted work; as such, participants are an example of "poachers", as defined by [Michel de Certeau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michel_de_Certeau), whose cultures rely on the property of others.[^4616]

According to Milner, rickrolling is a meme that appeals to those within Internet culture but also uses elements that resonate with the general public, comparing it to [Doge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doge_%28meme%29), a meme incorporating a picture of a dog.[^4713] Writing for *[Mashable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashable)*, Chloe Bryan called rickrolling "universal" as it can easily be adapted to different contexts.[^4603] According to sociolinguist Danielle H. Heinrichs, some rickrolls blend humour with another genre, which she compares to the folkloric motif of the multifaceted [trickster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trickster).[^4708] Communication scholar Eric Harvey interprets rickrolling as making fun of the act of clicking a link for [instant gratification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant_gratification).[^4648] Cultural scholar Tracey Potts wrote, "it is easy to see pop culture as one giant rickroll, a cultural bait-and-switch where, regardless of what we select or click on, we end up back with more of the same".[^4672]

Blogger David Griner of *[Adfreak.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AdWeek)* said in 2008 that rickrolling was the "perfect example of a viral video because the definition of one is something that gets out and is uncontrollable".[^4609] *Mashable*'s Bryan wrote in 2017 that, although the rickroll is no longer popular, this works in favour of the prank as victims are less likely to expect it.[^4603] Caldwell of *Know Your Meme* said in 2020, "It seems like the volume of memes these days means that none of them have any longevity, but for Rickrolling, it's such an old meme that it's like an 'old-school' Internet reference. It's nostalgic."[^4594] Cotter expressed this sentiment in the description of his YouTube upload: "as long as trolls are still trolling, the Rick will never stop rolling".[^4596][^4616]

### Ted Cruz-Zodiac Killer meme

The **Ted Cruz-Zodiac Killer meme** is an [Internet meme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme) which originated in 2013 and gained popularity in 2015. The meme is a satirical [conspiracy theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conspiracy_theory) claiming that [United States senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_senator) [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz) is the real identity of the [Zodiac Killer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zodiac_Killer), despite Cruz being born on December 22, 1970, 14 months after the last confirmed Zodiac killing. Proponents of this meme generally do not believe that Cruz is the Zodiac Killer. According to [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR), the meme captures an unease with Cruz, "\[people\] think he's creepy. And they want to point that out, as clearly as they can."[^4714]

#### Origin and spread

> To be clear: the Zodiac Killer line is a joke. But it's a prolific joke, and one you can find printed on bumper stickers and a variety of black metal tees across the country. For Cruz, the Baptist senator for Texas and right-wing Republican presidential candidate, it's an unexpected foray into popular culture.

*,  Dylan Baddour of the *[Houston Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Chronicle)*, April 26, 2016[^4715]*

A 2016 investigation by Miles Klee of *[The Daily Dot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Daily_Dot)* found the first use of the meme to be by a [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) user in March 2013, as Cruz was speaking at the [Conservative Political Action Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Political_Action_Conference) and vowing to repeal the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act).[^4716][^4717] The actual Tweet was, "Alert: Ted Cruz is speaking!! His speech is titled: 'This Is The Zodiac Speaking'".[^4718] The meme was not repeated until November 2014, by another Twitter user writing about Cruz's proposal against [net neutrality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Net_neutrality_in_the_United_States).[^4717]

It continued in obscurity up to February 2016, when another Twitter user edited a picture of a Republican debate in order to include "Is Ted Cruz the Zodiac Killer?" in the interactive ticker at the bottom.[^4714] That month, "is ted cruz the zodiac killer" was the second highest suggestion in [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google)'s [autocomplete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocomplete) for "is ted", but by April it was not in the autocomplete at all.[^4714][^4719] [News.com.au](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News.com.au) writer Matthew Dunn suggested that Google was [censoring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_censorship) the search term, showing evidence that it accounted for 89% of total searches when compared to other terms in the autocomplete.[^4719]

In April 2016, the *[Houston Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Chronicle)* said the meme "has a following. A [Facebook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facebook) group named for the meme has more than 27,000 members. A Google search turns up 621,000 hits, including exploratory articles by some of the biggest news publications on the web".[^4715]

Cruz himself has jocularly alluded to the meme by [tweeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter) one of the Zodiac Killer's [cryptograms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptogram); first in October 2017 responding to a retweet from Senator [Ben Sasse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Sasse) referring to Cruz as "the son of the guy who killed Kennedy" (a reference to [a conspiracy theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_assassination_conspiracy_theories) involving [Rafael Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Cruz))[^4720] and then wishing a "Happy [Halloween](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween)" in 2018.[^4721][^4722] In December 2020, after the [340-character Zodiac cipher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zodiac_Killer) was cracked, Cruz retweeted an article about the cipher with the caption "uh oh".[^4723] In October 2026 Cruz [quote tweeted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quote_tweet) a post by DiscussingFilm about the announcement of [Marvel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Marvel_Cinematic_Universe_television_series_%28Marvel_Studios%29) television series *[Zodiac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zodiac_%28TV_series%29)* with the caption "Can't wait to watch it.".[^4724]

#### In popular culture

After the edited image showing the question on Google trended, the meme spread into popular culture.[^4714] *[GQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GQ_%28magazine%29)* and the *[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tribune)* have referenced the meme.[^4725][^4726] Books about Cruz being the Zodiac Killer, including romantic ones, were listed on [Amazon.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com).[^4717]

In February 2016, [Public Policy Polling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_Policy_Polling) asked registered voters in Florida ahead of the Republican primary if they believed Cruz to be the Zodiac Killer; 10% believed and 28% were not sure. The other 62% did not think he was.[^4727][^4728]

Comedian [Larry Wilmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Wilmore) made references to the meme in his April 2016 routine at the [White House Correspondents' Dinner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House_Correspondents'_Association), including a joke that Cruz was not campaigning to win the nomination, but to continue a murder spree.[^4729]

In October 2022, the satirical news outlet *[The Babylon Bee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Babylon_Bee)* produced a sketch as part of a series following the lives of two Californians who had moved to Texas. In the sketch titled "Episode 3 - The Church", two Californians are canvassing for [Beto O'Rourke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beto_O'Rourke) as part of the [2022 US midterm elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_elections) and Cruz answers the door. In response to the canvassers, Cruz states he is short on time having "letters to write" before closing the door and inadvertently dropping one of the letters. The canvassers quickly flee after seeing that the letter is printed with a cypher.[^4730] Ted Cruz plays himself in the video.[^4731]

#### Reception

Lindsey Martin, a Twitter user who helped circulate the meme, told NPR that she did so because it is "so obviously untrue ... if there was any way that it could possibly be true I would be scared to joke about it just because of the repercussions."[^4714] *[The Verge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Verge)* writer Kaitlyn Tiffany opined that some may consider the subject of the meme to be "distasteful and irresponsible, even dangerous".[^4717] [Leigh Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leigh_Alexander_%28journalist%29) considered its spread an example of the growing political engagement of youth, writing that in such memes, "the political figure is exaggerated, his context made grotesque or fantastical, just as in traditional [political cartooning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_cartooning)."[^4732] According to Julie Lozano, an employee at Houston [bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_%28establishment%29) Grand Prize who named a [cocktail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocktail) she created "Ted Cruz is the Zodiac Killer", the point of the meme is to "\[demonize\] his character".[^4715] [Heidi Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heidi_Cruz) responded to the meme by stating that she has "been married to him for 15 years, and I know pretty well who he is, so it doesn't bother me at all. There's a lot of garbage out there".[^4733]

### YouTube Poop

A **YouTube Poop** (shortened as **YTP**) is a type of [video mashup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_mashup) or [collage film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collage_film), created by remixing or editing pre-existing media sources. YouTube Poops originated around 2004, quickly becoming popular online.

YouTube Poops often incorporate [internet memes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_meme), [slang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slang), and [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music), carrying [subcultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subcultural) significance into a new video for [humorous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humour), [nonsensical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonsense), [random](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_humor), [vulgar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgar_humor), [satirical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire), obscene, absurd, profane, annoying, confusing, or dramatic purposes.[^4734]

#### History

##### Precursors and influences

YouTube Poop is a subset of [remix culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remix_culture),[^4735] in which existing ideas and media are modified and reinterpreted to create new art and media in various contexts.[^4736] Forms of remix culture have existed long before the internet, with DigitalTrends' Luke Dormehl listing the [cut-up technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cut-up_technique) of [William Burroughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Burroughs) and [sampling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_%28music%29) in [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop) as examples.[^4737] Dormehl also says that "aesthetically", YouTube Poop is similar to the "frenetic editing style" of [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV) in the 1980s, which featured "fast, non-linear cuts" that focused less on character or plot than on evoking a feeling.[^4737]

YouTube Poop also draws on elements from the [vidding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vidding) scene,[^4738] in which fans of a piece of media would create music videos using footage from the work.[^4739] Observers have also proposed influences from a more modern, internet-based practice similar to vidding, the [anime music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anime_music_video) (AMV) - particularly from more comedic variations of the AMV.[^4740]

##### Early history and "Golden Age"

The genre began in the early 2000s.[^4741] The first video to be regarded as a YouTube Poop is named "*The Adventures of Super Mario Bros. 3 REMIXED!!!*" (which has been renamed to "*I'D SAY HE'S HOT ON OUR TAIL*") by the creator SuperYoshi, uploaded onto SheezyArt[^4742] on December 22, 2004, preceding the creation of YouTube by a few months.[^4737] It remixes clips from the 1990 animated television series *[The Adventures of Super Mario Bros. 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Adventures_of_Super_Mario_Bros._3)* as a primary source,[^4737] using the video editing software [Windows Movie Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows_Movie_Maker).[^4743] Media scholar Randall Halle suggests that the name "[poop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feces)" as used to refer to videos like SuperYoshi's referred to the purported low quality of these early works.[^4743]

Throughout the mid-to-late 2000s, YouTube Poop (YTP) emerged as a dominant and highly influential genre of absurdist remix culture on YouTube, characterized by the frenetic editing of found footage to produce nonsensical or transgressive audiovisual collages.[^4744] YouTuber EmpLemon describes this era as being characterized by popular recurring memes and in-jokes in the community.[^4737] According to Halle, the 2010 video "jonathan swift returns from the dead to eat a cheese sandwich" has been cited as "a work that moved YTP towards artistry", with heavy use of video in video editing and other methods of distortion.[^4743]

##### Decline in popularity

The YouTube Poop genre declined in popularity during the late 2010s.[^4741] Popular creators such as [Schaffrillas Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schaffrillas_Productions) and EmpLemon switched their focus to other topics; in Schaffrillas' case, film analysis.[^4745] [eMarketer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMarketer) principal analyst Nicole Perrin speculated that the reason why the genre had "fallen to the wayside" was as part of a larger YouTube "shift to glossier, more corporate-friendly content."[^4746]

Luke Dormehl wrote in 2019 in relation to this loss of mainstream popularity that "as with every other corner of the internet", YTP had undergone fragmentization from a large single community with a shared set of sources into a series of sub-communities, each with their own preferred source material. However, this has also allowed each individual sub-community to develop its own set of convoluted "references-within-references" even further.[^4737] Additionally, YTP has followed the general YouTube trend of increasing professionalization and editing, with more sophisticated and larger amounts of [special effects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_effects) and elaborate writing.[^4737][^4747]

##### Legacy

YTP has had a significant influence on memes and Internet culture.[^4737] Many stylistic traits of YTP have entered the editing vocabulary of mainstream YouTubers, such as rapid editing, sound effects, and sudden drastic changes in volume for comedic effect.[^4747] Many mainstream YouTubers even hire YTP editors to edit their normal videos.[^4747]

#### Style and techniques

##### Structure, culture and subgenres

Some videos may involve completely or partially repurposing sources to create or convey an often self-aware story, while others follow a [non-linear narrative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-linear_narrative), and some may contain no storyline at all, instead regarded among the lines of [surreal humor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surreal_humour) and artistic experimentation.[^4738] To this degree, a YouTube Poop may even consist solely of an existing video, sometimes modified, repeated in a slowed or remixed loop.[^4748] Associate professor of [cultural anthropology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_anthropology) at [Kansas State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas_State_University) [Michael Wesch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Wesch) has defined YouTube Poops as "absurdist remixes that ape and mock the lowest technical and aesthetic standards of [remix culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remix_culture) to comment on remix culture itself".[^4749]

YTP can often be derivative in the sense that the work of one creator (or, within the community, *pooper*) is sometimes used as the underlying work for another video; this can be recirculated and lead to the creation of "YTP tennis" videos, named for how they exist in rounds where the original video accumulates edits and alterations. [Lawrence Lessig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Lessig), Professor of Law at [Harvard Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Law_School), compared this aspect to a form of [call and response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Call_and_response), here seen as being prominent within [remix culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remix_culture).[^4750]

A YTP "collab", or collaboration, is a common practice, and involves various creators joining to produce a single, sometimes very long, video.[^4743]

A subgenre of YouTube Poops is YouTube Poop music video (YTPMV), which involves clips from different forms of media remixed in a musical form, often in a fast-paced and editing-intensive manner.[^4740] Japanese online communities formed a type of YTPMV popular on [Niconico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niconico) called otoMADs (音MAD); these videos often use Niconico or Japanese pop culture references.[^4751]

##### Source material

While essentially any audiovisual media is "fair game" for source material,[^4746] some of the most common sources of YouTube Poops include [movies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film), [television shows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_program), [anime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anime), [cartoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartoon), [commercials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercials), or other YouTube videos.[^4752]

Among the most popular sources are 1990s cartoons, particularly critically disregarded ones such as *[Super Mario World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Mario_World_%28TV_series%29)* and *[Adventures of Sonic the Hedgehog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventures_of_Sonic_the_Hedgehog)*.[^4734][^4744][^4753] The work of children's poet [Michael Rosen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Rosen_%28author%29) has also been used.[^4754] These diverse media sources, from different time periods and styles, are often combined in YTPs.[^4755]

The [cutscenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cutscenes) from Nintendo games released on the [Philips CD-i](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philips_CD-i), most notably *[Hotel Mario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotel_Mario)*, *Link: The Faces of Evil and Zelda: The Wand of Gamelon*, which received mixed reception at the time of their release but have been retrospectively criticized for low-quality animation, voice acting, and scripts, are also frequently used, and have achieved more widespread notoriety as a result.[^4738]

##### Editing techniques

A typical YouTube Poop uses visual and auditory effects to alter the [underlying work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underlying_work), as well as rearrangement of individual clips.[^4738] The edits are often "abrupt and jarring", with lots of quick [cuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cut_%28transition%29) and time stretching leading to an "often-frenetic" pace.[^4752] Ruth Alexandra Moran interprets the style as producing "aesthetics of malfunction".[^4756]

The most common type of rearrangement is "sentence-mixing", a form of editing in which dialogue is rearranged or chopped up to form new, often humorous or vulgar dialogue.[^4737][^4741] One famous sentence-mix from the YouTube Poop "Robotnik Has a Viagra Overdose" by creator Stegblob takes a scene from an episode of *Adventures of Sonic the Hedgehog* titled "Boogey-Mania" in which [Doctor Robotnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Robotnik) accuses his henchmen of "snooping as usual" and cuts out everything but the second and third [syllable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syllable) to leave only the nonsensical word "pingas", which was construed to resemble the word "[penis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penis)". Over the years, "Pingas" has since become one of the biggest memes related to the *[Sonic the Hedgehog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_the_Hedgehog)* franchise in general and has been referenced in both the [Archie comic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_the_Hedgehog_%28Archie_Comics%29) and the *[Sonic Boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_Boom_%28TV_series%29)* television series.[^4744] In an interview, *[Sonic the Hedgehog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonic_the_Hedgehog_%28film%29)* co-star [James Marsden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Marsden) was asked a question about the word, in which he erroneously guessed that it was Doctor Robotnik's original catchphrase.[^4757]

Some techniques are more abrasive, like the "stutter loop", in which a short clip of video is repeated over and over.[^4737][^4741] An abrasive auditory trope is the sudden extreme increase in volume to shock the viewer, known as "ear-rape" or "earrape".[^4741][^4744][^4747]

#### Copyright and fair use

As YouTube Poop is a medium built on repurposing copyrighted media, it has been particularly vulnerable to copyright law.[^4737] YouTube Poops have often been subject to copyright claims on YouTube.[^4741] Political scientist and author Trajce Cvetkovski noted in 2013 that, despite [Viacom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viacom_%282005%E2%80%932019%29) filing a [copyright infringement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_infringement) [lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawsuit) against YouTube in 2007 explicitly concerning YouTube Poops, in particular "*The Sky Had a Weegee*" by Hurricoaster, which features scenes from the animated series *[SpongeBob SquarePants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpongeBob_SquarePants)* episode "[Shanghaied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghaied_%28SpongeBob_SquarePants%29)", it and many others have remained on YouTube.[^4758]

Copyright law in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom) allows people to use copyrighted material for the purposes of [parody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parody), [pastiche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastiche), and [caricature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caricature) without being seen as infringing on the copyright of the material.[^4759] Copyright owners are only able to sue the parodist if the work is perceived as communicating hateful or discriminative messages, and modifying the intended purpose of the copyright owner's material. If the case is then taken to court, judges are advised in jurisdictional terms to decide whether the video meets these criteria.[^4760]

### Cherry Sisters

The **Cherry Sisters** - **Addie** (1859-1942), **Effie** (1867-1944), **Ella** (1854-1934), **Lizzie** (1857-1936), and **Jessie Cherry** (1871-1903) - were five sisters from [Marion, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion,_Iowa) who formed a notorious [vaudeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaudeville) touring act in the late 19th century. They were also the plaintiffs in a landmark 1901 legal case heard by the [Iowa Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_Supreme_Court), *Cherry v. Des Moines Leader,* which was instrumental in establishing and confirming the right of the press to [fair comment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fair_comment).

The Cherry Sisters' vaudeville act, *Something Good, Something Sad,* was infamous for its poor quality and the vehement responses it elicited by audiences, who threw vegetables and disrupted performances. The sisters toured with the act for ten years, during which time they briefly appeared on Broadway. In 1898 they sued two Iowa newspapers for [libel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libel) after they printed a scathing review of *Something Good, Something Sad.* The case eventually went to the Iowa Supreme Court, which ruled in the newspapers' favor and set a precedent for the right to fair comment.

The Cherry Sisters' act dissolved after the sudden death of the youngest member of the group, Jessie, in 1903. The rest of the sisters went on to other ventures and opened a bakery, but died in modest circumstances.

#### Early life

The Cherry sisters were the daughters of Thomas Cherry and Laura Rawson. The family was composed of eight children: Ella, Elizabeth, Addie, Effie, and Jessie, their brother Nathan, and two additional siblings who died at young ages. Ella, the eldest, was born in 1854 in Massachusetts, but the remainder of the children were born in Iowa, and were raised on a farm in [Linn County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linn_County,_Iowa).[^4761]

#### Vaudeville career

The Cherry Sisters' vaudeville act was formed in the early 1890s, after the death of their parents and the disappearance of their brother Nathan. Originally all five sisters were involved; however, the eldest, Ella, retired from the stage before 1896, leaving her siblings to continue the act as a quartet.[^4762]

Addie Cherry described the Cherry sisters' work as "concerts,--literary entertainments."[^4763] Titled *Something Good, Something Sad,* their show featured songs, dances, skits, morality plays and essays authored and performed by the sisters. Some of their songs featured new lyrics set to traditional standards; others were completely original compositions. Musical accompaniment was provided for some numbers by Elizabeth and Jessie, who played the piano and bass drum. The material had strong patriotic and religious themes; in one scene, Jessie was suspended from a cross in an imitation of the [crucifixion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crucifixion_of_Jesus).[^4761][^4762][^4764][^4765]

The act was received politely by the sisters' neighbors in [Marion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion,_Iowa), but when it went on the road, it received overwhelmingly negative responses from the audiences to which it played. Spectators routinely laughed, heckled, catcalled, booed and threw vegetables at the sisters throughout the entire performance. In several instances the audience's violence reached dangerous proportions: in one incident in [Dubuque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubuque,_Iowa), a fire extinguisher was sprayed directly into one of the sisters' faces, and the show was stopped by the local marshals to prevent further harm. Eventually the sisters performed behind a wire mesh curtain to avoid being struck by projectiles from the audience, although they would later deny that this had ever been necessary.[^4761][^4762][^4764][^4766][^4767]

In 1896, the Cherry Sisters were brought to Broadway by [impresario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impresario) [Willie Hammerstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Hammerstein) in an attempt to attract attention to his floundering new venue, the [Olympia Music Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympia_Theatre_%28New_York%29).[^4768] His rationale, as given in an interview, was, "I've been putting on the best talent, and it hasn't gone over...I'm going to try the worst."[^4762] The theory was sound: *Something Good, Something Sad* saved Hammerstein from bankruptcy only twelve days after opening on November 16, and ran for six weeks, drawing audiences who were curious to see the act the *New York Times* referred to as "Four Freaks from Iowa".[^4765]

The *Times,* in their assessment of the sisters, considered the act "more pitiable than amusing" and noted "...the effects of poverty, ignorance, and isolation are much the same all over the world, and the Cherry sisters exhibited every one of them with a pathetic frankness that left no question as to their status or their character."[^4765]

The sisters were known for their rigid moral standpoints both on and off-stage. While living in New York during their run at the Olympia, they refused all invitations to parties and claimed that they would not visit [Coney Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coney_Island) because they did not want to see women in bathing costumes.[^4762]

##### *Cherry v. Des Moines Leader*

The Cherry Sisters' act was met with derision by the local press as well as audiences. In 1930, *Time* magazine noted, "In every town that the Cherry sisters played, it was an invariable custom for the editor of the local paper to review their act with a column and a half of humor, satire, parody and biting sarcasm."[^4764] In January 1893, Fred P. Davis, the city editor of the *Cedar Rapids Gazette,* reviewed their performance at Greene's Opera House, noting, "...their knowledge of the stage is worse than none at all." The sisters demanded a retraction, and the *Gazette* complied, allowing them to write it themselves. The Cherry sisters did not consider the retraction to be sufficient and accused Davis of libel. The complaint resulted in a light-hearted mock trial onstage at a Cherry Sisters' performance in March 1893.[^4761]

In 1898, the *Odebolt Chronicle* printed an extremely negative review of the Cherry sisters' act, titled "The Cherries Were Here". Critic and newspaper editor Billy Hamilton's piece described the sisters as being "three creatures surpassing the witches in [Macbeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macbeth) in general hideousness" and continued, "the mouths of their rancid features opened like caverns and sounds like the wailings of damned souls issued therefrom." The article was later reprinted in other newspapers around the state, including the *Des Moines Leader*.[^4769]

In response, the Cherry Sisters sued the *Chronicle* and the *Leader* for US \$15,000, claiming that the unflattering descriptions of their physical appearance presented in the article constituted acts of "false and malicious" libel.[^4770] The *Odebolt Chronicle* kept an ongoing log of the progress of the proceedings, which included a courtroom performance by the sisters, noting on April 27, 1899, "we had lots of fun out of the case".[^4771]

The Polk County Court decided in the newspapers' favor in 1899,[^4769] and the sisters appealed to the Iowa Supreme Court. The Court upheld the verdict, stating in their May 28, 1901 decision, "the editor of a newspaper has the right, if not the duty, of publishing, for the information of the public, fair and reasonable comments, however severe in terms, upon anything which is made by its owner a subject of public exhibition, as upon any other matter of public interest; of privileged communications, for which no action will lie without proof of actual malice...Surely, if one makes himself ridiculous in his public performances, he may be ridiculed by those whose duty or right it is to inform the public regarding the character of the performance."[^4763]

*Cherry v. Des Moines Leader* is considered to be a landmark decision confirming the right to fair comment and critical analysis in the press[^4772] and is still frequently held up as a precedent in contemporary court cases.[^4773]

##### Retirement and later life

After Jessie died from [typhoid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoid) in 1903 [^4761][^4767] the sisters retired for a short period. However, Addie and Effie continued to perform until the late 1930s, their final appearances taking place in their home town of Cedar Rapids in April 1938. In 1924 and 1926, Effie ran for mayor of Cedar Rapids on a reform platform, but was defeated both times.[^4774][^4775][^4776]

#### References in contemporary culture

The Cherry Sisters have been the subject of at least two contemporary theatrical productions: *Cherry Bomb,* a comedic musical play produced and performed by 1812 Productions in Philadelphia, and *Cherry Sisters Revisited,* a 2006 play by [Dan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_O'Brien_%28playwright%29).[^4777][^4778]

They are featured as forerunners of the [outsider music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outsider_music) genre in [Irwin Chusid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irwin_Chusid)'s book *[Songs in the Key of Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songs_in_the_Key_of_Z)*.

The story of the Cherry Sisters is featured as one of the segments in Season 4, Episode 11 of [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central)'s show *[Drunk History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drunk_History)*. The sisters were portrayed by [Jessie Ennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Ennis) (Ella), [Ashley Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashley_Johnson) (Elizabeth), [Andrea Savage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Savage) (Addie), [Mary Lynn Rajskub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Lynn_Rajskub) (Effie), and [Allison Tolman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allison_Tolman) (Jessie).

An advertisement for the Cherry Sisters is featured as one of the objects explored in Season 7, Episode 22 of *[Mysteries at the Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysteries_at_the_Museum)*.
