### 2014 Hiram vs. Mount St. Joseph women's basketball game

The **2014 Hiram vs. Mount St. Joseph women's basketball game**, billed as **Play for 22**,[^5050] was the first game of the 2014-15 NCAA basketball regular season. The [Division III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_III) game between [Hiram College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiram_College) and [Mount St. Joseph University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_St._Joseph_University) (MSJ) was originally intended to be played at the Hiram campus in [Hiram, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiram,_Ohio), on November 15, 2014.[^5051] However, the game was moved to November 2 to accommodate Lauren Hill, a Mount St. Joseph freshman who had been diagnosed with terminal brain cancer and wished to play in one college game before her death.[^5051] The game was also moved to [Cincinnati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati), initially to the MSJ campus in nearby [Delhi Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Township,_Ohio) and ultimately to [Cintas Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cintas_Center) on the campus of [Xavier University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xavier_University).[^5052]

#### Background

##### Lauren Hill

[Lauren Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauren_Hill_%28basketball%29) (October 1, 1995 - April 10, 2015) was born in [Greendale, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greendale,_Indiana).[^5053] and been a star basketball player at Lawrenceburg High School in [Lawrenceburg, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrenceburg,_Indiana), located about 30 miles (48 km) west of Cincinnati. On her 18th birthday in 2013, she committed to play at Mount St. Joseph.[^5051] However, as she was preparing for her senior season at Lawrenceburg High, she was noticing problems with her game. As she would tell a reporter from [WKRC-TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WKRC-TV) in Cincinnati in late 2014, "I wasn't keeping up with the other girls. My ball handling was sloppy so I just figured I was out of shape."[^5054] After further problems in the following weeks, she thought that she had suffered a concussion, and her family took her to [Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Children's_Hospital_Medical_Center). On November 20, 2013,[^5051] less than two months after committing to MSJ, she was diagnosed with [diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diffuse_intrinsic_pontine_glioma) (DIPG), a rare type of brain cancer that normally affects children age 5 to 7.[^5052] The cancer, which grows from the brain stem, is inoperable and is not considered survivable.[^5054]

Initially, Hill was given a best-case prognosis of two years to live. Her father recalled that immediately after the diagnosis, "I got weak, \[Lauren's mother\] Lisa got sick, and typical Lauren she wanted to know if she could still play basketball." She indeed continued to play in her senior season at Lawrenceburg High despite undergoing regular chemotherapy and radiation treatments, and as scheduled came to MSJ for the 2014-15 season. In September 2014, she had an [MRI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magnetic_resonance_imaging) that revealed that the tumor had grown; at that time, doctors told her and her family that she would probably die before the end of the year. Shortly after this diagnosis, she told new MSJ head coach[^5050] Dan Benjamin, "One game. I want to play one college game."[^5054] She also chose to spend her last months as an advocate for DIPG research, which had made little progress at the time.[^5052]

##### Buildup

After this news, the MSJ athletic department approached its counterpart at Hiram. The two teams had initially planned to open their respective seasons on November 15 at Hiram's Price Gymnsaium, but Hiram agreed to move the game to November 1 at MSJ if the [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association) would give permission.[^5054] This was needed because under NCAA rules, Division III schools cannot play regular-season games before November 15.[^5055] The NCAA ultimately granted the schools a waiver to play on November 2.[^5056]

The game was then scheduled to be held at the Mount St. Joseph campus. The school's arena, Harrington Center, has a capacity of 2,000,[^5057][^5058] and the typical attendance for a women's basketball game is about 100.[^5056] However, as news spread of Hill's story, the demand for tickets and media credentials was too great for MSJ to accommodate. At that time, Xavier University stepped in, offering MSJ free use of its arena, Cintas Center, with arena employees volunteering their time for the game.[^5056] Even with the move to the 10,250-seat venue, the game sold out in 30 minutes. The interest in the game also led [Fox Sports Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Sports_Ohio) to televise it live.[^5050]

The game would soon be billed as "Play for 22", after Hill's jersey number. The schools decided to turn the game into a charity fundraiser; Hill and her family chose The Cure Starts Now Foundation (TCSN), a charity devoted to DIPG research,[^5059] as the beneficiary.[^5050] The foundation would provide the funds from the event to Cincinnati Children's, where Hill had been undergoing treatment, which at the time was working on an international DIPG registry.[^5050] The fundraising efforts went beyond game proceeds; MSJ invited NCAA member schools to donate a \#22 jersey. Hill signed the donated jerseys, which would be auctioned off during the game and in the following days.[^5060] She raised US\$1 million for pediatric cancer research with a Cincinnati telethon for the foundation,[^5061] which then donated \$1 million to brain cancer research[^5062][^5063] and continues to grow and donated over \$4.7 million to medical research in 2015.[^5064]

Hill and Benjamin also created a charity challenge, modeled after the [ALS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amyotrophic_lateral_sclerosis) [Ice Bucket Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_Bucket_Challenge), known as "Layup4Lauren". Because her cancer caused dizziness and weakened her normally dominant right hand, she was forced to shoot primarily with her left hand. The challenge involves spinning in a complete circle three times, and then making a [layup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Layup) with one's non-dominant hand.[^5065]

#### The game

The game itself followed the theme of brain cancer awareness. MSJ had special gray uniforms made for the game, but Benjamin did not tell Hill until the team was in the locker room. Gray is recognized as a color for brain cancer awareness (similar to pink for breast cancer), signifying gray matter. During pregame warmups, Hiram wore "Play for 22" T-shirts with "MSJ" on the front.[^5052] Many local celebrities were in attendance, as were several national sports luminaries, among them [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball) women's coach [Pat Summitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Summitt), [Buffalo Bills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Bills) running back [Fred Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Jackson_%28running_back%29), and [WNBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_National_Basketball_Association) stars [Tamika Catchings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamika_Catchings), [Elena Delle Donne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elena_Delle_Donne), and [Skylar Diggins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skylar_Diggins).[^5056]

Hill started the game, and after MSJ won the opening tip,[^5050] they ran a play designed to get Hill a layup for the opening points of the game. The play had been practiced regularly, and the night before the game, MSJ's coaching staff had a dinner with their counterparts from Hiram at which both staffs discussed the play.[^5052] Hill made the left-handed layup, and the game was immediately stopped. Both teams gave Hill a standing ovation, she was presented with the game ball, and was then helped to the bench by her father.[^5052] Due to nausea caused by the medication she was taking to control some of the symptoms of her cancer, she spent most of the game on the bench.[^5056]

During halftime, Hill was presented with the [Pat Summitt Most Courageous Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USBWA_Most_Courageous_Award), given by the [United States Basketball Writers Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Basketball_Writers_Association), by Summitt herself.[^5056] The award was first presented in 1978, with separate men's and women's versions since 2010; the women's award has borne Summitt's name since 2012.[^5066] The women's version is normally presented during the [Women's Final Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Women's_Division_I_Basketball_Championship), but the USBWA decided to hand out the award at the game, presumably so that Hill could receive it in person.[^5067] Also during halftime, the NBA and WNBA teams that play in Hill's home state of Indiana, respectively the [Indiana Pacers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Pacers) and [Indiana Fever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Fever), jointly gave a \$5,000 check to TCSN.[^5056]

The game was closely fought until MSJ pulled away in the closing minutes. With the Lions having the ball with 30 seconds to play and a safe 9-point lead, Benjamin called a timeout and sent Hill back into the game.[^5056] They ran another play for Hill, this time for a right-handed layup, but she missed. One of her teammates rebounded the ball and passed it back to her for a second right-handed layup, which she made to close out the scoring in the Lions' 66-55 win.[^5056] After the game, MSJ announced that \$40,000 had been raised for TCSN.[^5056]

The attendance of 10,250 made the game the most-attended NCAA women's game in history that did not involve a [Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I) team. It more than doubled the previous Division III record of 4,395, set on January 7, 2009, by [Calvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Knights) when it hosted [Trine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trine_University),[^5068] and also exceeded the [Division II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_II) record of 7,543 set by [North Dakota State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota_State_Bison_women's_basketball) when it hosted [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota_Fighting_Hawks_women's_basketball) on February 23, 1996.[^5069]

#### Reactions

Hill's story resonated on social media, with basketball stars such as [LeBron James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LeBron_James) and [Candace Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candace_Parker) expressing their admiration for Hill's courage.[^5056] Delle Donne said, "When I read Lauren's story and heard about the game, nothing could keep me away. It's incredible what she's doing and how many people she's reached. To be her age and have the kind of perspective to think beyond herself, she's amazing."[^5056]

ESPN writer Alyssa Roenigk summed up the event:

> If thoughts and emotions produce energy and that energy can alter an atmosphere, if the power of smiles and hugs and "good afternoons" and "be wells" can build and build until all that positivity overflows to change the molecules of air within a basketball arena, then that is what happened inside the Cintas Center on Sunday. The building overflowed with positive vibes, and that emotion was infectious. This day was not about basketball. It was not about a game. This was a celebration of life and a community coming together to support one girl and two teams as they banded together to beat up on cancer.[^5052]

#### Later developments and legacy

The initially announced fundraising total of \$40,000 proved inaccurate. At a ceremony on November 19 at MSJ, Hill presented a check to TCSN for nearly \$59,000, representing only proceeds from the "Play for 22" game. By that time, funds raised from the game and other initiatives involving Hill, such as the Layup4Lauren challenge and the jersey auction, totaled over \$324,000.[^5070] Her ultimate goal was to raise at least \$1 million.[^5071]

Hill remained in good enough health to travel with the team to its next two games on November 21 and 22 in a tournament hosted by [Baldwin Wallace University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baldwin_Wallace_University), located [near](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berea,_Ohio) [Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland). She played briefly in MSJ's tournament opener, a 69-64 loss[^5072] to [Bethany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethany_College_%28West_Virginia%29), scoring two points on a right-handed layup.[^5073] Hill did not play in MSJ's second tournament game, a 77-68 win over [Buffalo State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_State_Bengals).[^5074] After her return from the tournament, she went to a Lawrenceburg High game on November 24 under the impression that she would only be supporting her alma mater. Instead, during a halftime ceremony, the school retired her \#22, and the city's mayor announced a [Lauren Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauren_Hill_%28basketball%29) Week.[^5075]

After Hill played in four games and made five layups,[^5076] Mount St. Joseph basketball coach Dan Benjamin announced that she would not play in future games but would like to stay on as an honorary coach.[^5077] On January 7, 2015, Hill served as an assistant coach for the team.[^5078]

Hill's family signed her up for hospice care on December 1, 2014.[^5079] A recent cutback in her steroids dosage, combined with further growth of her tumor, led to more severe symptoms.[^5080] Three days later, the [V Foundation for Cancer Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Valvano), founded by late college coach and broadcaster [Jim Valvano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Valvano) in 1993 during his own losing fight with cancer, donated \$100,000 to TCSN during halftime of the Jimmy V Women's Classic game between [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Connecticut_Huskies_women's_basketball_team) and [Notre Dame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish_women's_basketball_team). A statement from Hill, taped at her home, was shown during the presentation.[^5071] Despite her advancing cancer, she was able to leave hospice care to play in a third game on December 13, the Lions' first game of the season at the Harrington Center against [Franklin College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_College_%28Indiana%29). Hill started the game and scored the first two points before being substituted.[^5081][^5082] Hill again started and scored the first basket in the Lions' next game on December 16 against [Wooster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Wooster); the following day, her family announced on Facebook that she had played her last game. At that time, Benjamin sent an email to multiple media outlets stating that Hill would remain on MSJ's bench as an honorary coach as long as her health permitted.[^5083] On December 30, Hill's goal of raising \$1 million for TCSN had been surpassed.[^5084]

[Fox Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Sports_%28United_States%29) named Hill's first game as the top U.S. sports story of November 2014 in its end-of-year timeline,[^5085] and the game was named "[Best Moment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Moment_ESPY_Award)" at the [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_ESPY_Awards) [ESPY Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPY_Award).[^5086]

[Wheaties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheaties) honored Hill with her picture on its cereal box.[^5087]

On February 6, 2015, Hill was given an honorary [Doctorate of Humane Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctorate_of_Humane_Letters) degree by Mount St. Joseph University.[^5088]

On March 4, 2015, she was named to the all-conference first team in the [Heartland Collegiate Athletic Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heartland_Collegiate_Athletic_Conference). "This award is being presented to Lauren in recognition of her courage and outstanding leadership", said conference commissioner Chris Ragsdale.[^5076]

On April 5, 2015, she was given the [Pat Summitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Summitt) Courage Award.[^5089]

Hill died on April 10, 2015, at [Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Children's_Hospital_Medical_Center).[^5090][^5091] A public visitation and memorial service was held on April 13, 2015, at the Cintas Center with a private funeral and burial on April 15, 2015.[^5092]

In June 2015, Hill was honored with a brick in the courtyard of the [Indiana Basketball Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Basketball_Hall_of_Fame); the brick is inscribed with her name and the word "Hero".[^5093]

On July 15, 2015, Hill was honored with the "[Best Moment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Moment_ESPY_Award)" Award at the annual [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_ESPY_Awards) [ESPY Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPY_Awards). Her parents, Brent and Lisa Hill, accepted the award on her behalf.

On October 13, 2015, MSJ and Xavier announced the creation of the Lauren Hill Tipoff Classic, intended to be an annual season-opening basketball event. The inaugural event, held November 14, was preceded by the "2.2M for 22 in 22" telethon, which aired on three major Cincinnati TV stations for 22 hours. Before her death, Hill increased her fundraising goal to \$2.2 million (matching her number), and the telethon was intended to complete this goal. Immediately after the end of the telethon, a women's basketball doubleheader followed at Cintas Center. The opener saw [Xavier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015%E2%80%9316_Xavier_Musketeers_women's_basketball_team) defeat [Evansville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015%E2%80%9316_Evansville_Purple_Aces_women's_basketball_team) 65-57, followed by Hiram defeating MSJ 70-63. All paid spectators at the doubleheader received a [bobblehead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobblehead) of Hill scoring her first layup; a total of 5,000 were intended to be given away, but attendance was only 3,122.[^5094][^5095]

On June 11, 2016, Hill received the first "For the Love of the Game" award presented by the [Women's Basketball Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Basketball_Hall_of_Fame). This award is presented for showing outstanding courage and inspiration. Her college coach at Mount St. Josephs, Dan Benjamin received the award during the WBHOF Induction Ceremony in Knoxville, TN.

Hill's legacy was again remembered at the ceremony for the 2018 Summitt Award. Avery Marz, who had planned to start play at [Saint Joseph's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Joseph's_Hawks_women's_basketball) in 2014, suffered a stroke while moving into her dormitory room that August. One doctor who treated her told her she would never play again. After one of her rehab sessions, Marz returned home to watch coverage of the Hiram-MSJ game, including the Summitt Award ceremony. She eventually returned to the court for Saint Joseph's in 2017-18, and received the award in March 2018 with Hill's parents and Summitt's son [Tyler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyler_Summitt) in attendance. While accepting her award, Marz remarked, "I had time on my side, and she knew she did not. I knew if I was able to find just half the courage Lauren had, I'd be able to get back on the court." Hill's mother likened Marz to her daughter, telling the [Associated Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press), "I see of lot of her there. The tenacity and the drive to keep moving forward, to get herself back on the court -- that's exactly what Lauren did."[^5096]

### Game of three halves

The "**Game of three halves**" was a [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football) match played between [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunderland_A.F.C.) and [Derby County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_County_F.C.) on the opening day of the [1894-95 English football season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1894%E2%80%9395_in_English_football).

Derby had travelled to Sunderland on 1 September for their first round fixture in the new [First Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_First_Division) season, but as the nominated [referee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referee_%28association_football%29), [Tom Kirkham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Kirkham), was running late, the game started with a replacement referee, John Conqueror, in charge.

After 45 minutes play, with Sunderland leading 3-0, Kirkham arrived and, "to the surprise of everyone", ordered that the game be restarted from scratch.[^5097][^5098]

Two more halves followed, thus allowing three halves to be played, but the decision to start the match again did not help Derby. They conceded three further goals in the "second half" and five goals in the "third half" to officially lose the match 8-0.[^5099]

### Potato race

A **potato race** is one of several similar [racing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racing) events where contestants compete to collect a number of [potatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato) as quickly as possible. Participants may run on foot or be mounted on [horseback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horseback), depending on the style of race. It is not clear precisely when or where the potato race originated. Potato races of both types were most popular in Australia, England, Scotland, the United States of America and Wales. Potato races were commonly held at community events such as [county fairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_fair), [rodeos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodeo), [picnics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picnic), and [track and field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_and_field) meets from at least the middle of the 19th century until approximately the 1930s.

Potato races run on foot were generally considered events for children, and were often held in schools as playground games or part of physical education, or at local events such as fairs.

Mounted events were particularly prevalent in the [Southwestern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_United_States). Individual mounted events usually consisted of individuals competing to be the fastest at collecting potatoes along a structured course. Team-based events had no defined course, and were notable for their violence. Players were permitted almost every possible tactic for interfering with the opposing team, including dragging other riders off their horses.

Potato races, both on-foot and mounted, are occasionally still held at local gatherings or riding competitions today, although the violent mounted version has died out.

#### History

It is unclear precisely where and when the potato race was originally developed. It was mentioned by name without elaboration in newspaper reports of athletic events in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia), and [Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wales) as early as the 1860s.[^5100][^5101][^5102] The [state fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_fair) of [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin) advertised a potato race "that beats Base Ball all hollow" in 1869, although again there was no description of the rules.[^5103] In September 1871, newspapers in a number of US states reprinted a report from the *[Boston Advertiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Advertiser)* which detailed an on-foot potato race that had taken place in [East Wilton, New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilton,_New_Hampshire), with many remarking that such events were becoming fashionable.[^5104][^5105][^5106] The county fair of [Lycoming County, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lycoming_County,_Pennsylvania) listed an on-foot potato race on its program in September 1871, directly referencing these reports.[^5107][^5108] Official rules for potato racing were printed in the 1902 Official Handbook of the [Amateur Athletic Union of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_Athletic_Union).[^5109]

In 1902, *[The Courier-Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Courier-Journal)* of [Louisville, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisville,_Kentucky) described a mounted potato race that took place at the Louisville Horse Show, remarking on its violence and noting that it "made a big hit."[^5110] It was not until 1912 that newspapers reported potato racing as a mounted rodeo event, with advertisements for one large [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles) rodeo listing the potato race by name, although without elaboration on the rules.[^5111] A 1913 report in the [San Francisco Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Chronicle) clearly describes a team-based potato race taking place at a [Mardi Gras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mardi_Gras) celebration in [Salinas, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salinas,_California), calling it a "new riding stunt".[^5112]

By 1913, on-foot potato races were being referred to as old-fashioned.[^5113] A 1917 article in [Popular Mechanics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_Mechanics) magazine suggested racing to screw in a line of [lightbulbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightbulb) as a substitute for potato races.[^5114] The popularity of mounted potato races as rodeo events died out by the 1930s.[^5115]

Informal on-foot potato races for children are still featured as a means of entertainment at many local celebrations and events in the United States.[^5116][^5117] Mounted potato races are still used as a part of [equestrian gymkhana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymkhana_%28equestrian%29) events for youth today, albeit in a more structured and form that lacks the violence of the team-based rodeo version.[^5118]

#### Foot races

Potato races run on foot were commonly held for children as playground games and during [physical education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_education) classes in schools.[^5119][^5120] They were also featured at local events such as picnics or fairs, and still occasionally are today.[^5116][^5121] Potato races have also been used by researchers to measure physical performance in children.[^5122][^5123]

A number of lanes, one per runner, would be marked out. Potatoes would be placed at intervals along each lane, and a basket would be placed several feet behind the lane. Runners would race to retrieve potatoes one by one, returning each one to the basket before returning for the next. The winner was the first to collect all the potatoes in their lane.[^5119] In one variation, two runners competed to be the first to return fifty potatoes to their own basket, racing simultaneously to take the closest potato from a single line of one hundred potatoes rather than separate lanes.[^5124]

On-foot potato races have been likened to the [Zuni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zuni_people) game of *A-we-wō-po-pa-ne,* which involved collecting stones rather than potatoes.[^5125]

Writing in 1915, [feminist theorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminist_theory) [Charlotte Perkins Gilman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Perkins_Gilman) described seeing a [moving picture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film) of a potato race on ice, and remarked on the notable difference between the performance of men and women, which she attributed to the restrictive clothing worn by women at the time.[^5126]

#### Mounted

##### Individual competition

Potato races with mounted participants were historically geared toward adult participation. They were prominent in the [Southwestern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_United_States).[^5127] In mounted races, competitors used sharpened stakes to spear potatoes and bring them from one end of a course to another. These races were timed, and the racer whose basket was heaviest at the end was the winner.[^5115] One less common variation bore some similarities to the [blood sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_sport) of [rooster pulling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goose_pulling), but used potatoes rather than partially buried [roosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rooster). A line of potatoes was spaced out along a course, and a rider would ride by at a [loping pace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canter_and_gallop), leaning down from their horse and snatching the potatoes from the ground. Riders who failed to maintain speed, or missed a potato, would be disqualified. The fastest remaining rider was the winner.[^5115]

Mounted potato races have been staged with participants riding on vehicles rather than horses. The *[British Almanac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Almanac)* of 1897 mentions a bicycle-mounted potato race in an article describing bicycle gymkhana.[^5128] A large picnic in [Radford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radford,_Coventry), England, in 1908 featured a bicycle potato race whose riders were young women. It was described at the time as a "splendid exhibition".[^5129] In 1910, 5,000 spectators at the [Indianapolis Motor Speedway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis_Motor_Speedway) watched a sort of reverse potato race where passengers in [cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car) tried to throw potatoes from the vehicle into baskets placed along a track.[^5130] *[American Motorcyclist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Motorcyclist)* magazine reported that the First Annual Motorcycle Rodeo, held in 1970, featured a potato race with riders mounted on motorcycles.[^5131]

##### Team-based tournament

> Swinging their laths like swords and crashing into one another, potato racers at [Cassoday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassoday,_Kansas) left the hundred-yard course strewn with potatoes and an occasional horseman as spirits, and tempers, rose.

 Jim Hoy, *Plains Folk: A Commonplace of the Great Plains*, p. 126[^5115]

Around the turn of the 20th century some mounted potato races were run as competitions between teams attempting to fill a basket with potatoes. These events were not so much ordered races as they were free-for-alls, which could last as long as ten minutes.[^5110] They were notably chaotic, as riders were not confined to lanes, and the rules permitted competitors to use their stakes to knock potatoes off the stakes of the other teams.[^5115] Physical violence often ensued; the [autobiography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobiography) of [cowboy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowboy) Harry Arthur Gant describes one team race at a [Frontier Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontier_Days_%28rodeo%29) event in 1909 that became so violent that the judges were forced to halt the competition in the middle.[^5132] *The Courier-Journal* noted that violent tactics such as pulling riders off their horses were considered acceptable, and that "biting is about the only thing that is barred."[^5110]

Writing in *Plains Folk*, James Hoy remarked upon the similarity of these races to the [Central Asian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asia) sport of [buzkashi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzkashi), which also involves fiercely competitive riders attempting to bring items to a goal, albeit on a much larger scale than potato races.[^5115]

### Brites de Almeida

**Brites de Almeida**, known as the Baker of [Aljubarrota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aljubarrota) ([Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language): *Padeira de Aljubarrota*), is a legendary figure and [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_people) heroine whose name is associated with the victory of the Portuguese, against [Castilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_of_Castile) forces, at the [Battle of Aljubarrota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Aljubarrota) in 1385. The battle resulted in a decisive victory for the Portuguese, putting an end to Castilian ambitions to take over the Portuguese throne.[^5133]

#### The legend

Brites de Almeida is said to have been born in [Faro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faro,_Portugal), [Algarve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algarve), in 1350, to poor parents. According to the legend she had [six fingers on each hand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydactyly). After both of her parents died, she sold her few possessions and began to travel. There are many stories about her life after she left home in her twenties. One says that she became a [muleteer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muleteer) and that she killed a suitor in a fight. Another that she was on a boat attacked by [Algerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria) pirates who sold her as a slave to the Imperial Harem in Algiers, from which she escaped. It is also said that she travelled in Portugal disguised as a man. She ended up settling in Aljubarrota, where she became a bakery owner and married a local farmer. Her bread was supposed to be the best in the country.[^5133][^5134][^5135][^5136]

After their defeat in the Battle of Aljubarrota, the Castilian soldiers in flight were attacked and killed by the local inhabitants. According to the story, seven or eight of them found shelter at Brites' bakery, which was empty because she had gone out to help to kill the soldiers. On her return she found the door closed and suspected the presence of enemies. She found the men hiding in her baker's oven and killed them with a shovel. She then cooked them in the oven along with the bread.[^5133][^5134][^5135][^5136]

Although it is undeniable that the story was a legend, Brites de Almeida came to be celebrated by the Portuguese in their songs and traditional stories and her deeds have remained as a symbol of Portugal's independence.[^5134] She was commemorated in a 1927 Portuguese postage stamp.

[^5134]: ["Lenda da Padeira de Aljubarrota"](https://ncultura.pt/lenda-da-padeira-de-aljubarrota/). *Ncultura*. Retrieved 10 September 2020.

### Mari Lwyd

The **Mari Lwyd** (/meri lʊid/; [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_language): *Y Fari Lwyd*,[^5137] \[ə ˈvaːri ˈlʊi̯d\] [](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/e3/Y_Fari_Lwyd_-_Mari_Lwyd.wav/Y_Fari_Lwyd_-_Mari_Lwyd.wav.mp3)^(ⓘ)) is a [wassailing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wassailing) [folk custom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tradition) in South Wales. The tradition entails the use of an eponymous [hobby horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobby_horse) which is made from a horse's skull mounted on a pole and carried by an individual hidden under a sheet.

The custom was first recorded in 1800, with subsequent accounts of it being produced into the early twentieth century. According to these, the Mari Lwyd was a tradition performed at [Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas) time by groups of men who would accompany the horse on its travels around the local area, and although the makeup of such groups varied, they typically included an individual to carry the horse, a leader, and individuals dressed as stock characters such as [Punch and Judy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch_and_Judy). The men would carry the Mari Lwyd to local houses, where they would request entry through song. The householders would be expected to deny them entry, again through song, and the two sides would continue their responses to one another in this manner. If the householders eventually relented, the team would be permitted entry and given food and drink.

Although the custom was given various names, it was best known as the *Mari Lwyd*; the etymology of this term remains the subject of academic debate. The [folklorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folkloristics) [Iorwerth Peate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iorwerth_Peate) believed that the term meant "Holy Mary" and thus was a reference to [Mary, mother of Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary,_mother_of_Jesus), while the folklorist E. C. Cawte thought it more likely that the term had originally meant "Grey Mare", referring to the heads' equine appearance. Several earlier folklorists to examine the topic, such as Peate and Ellen Ettlinger, believed that the tradition had once been a pre-Christian religious rite, although scholarly support for this interpretation has declined amid a lack of supporting evidence. The absence of late medieval references to such practices and the geographic dispersal of the various British hooded animal traditions, among them the [Hoodening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoodening) of [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent), [the Broad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Broad_%28folk_custom%29) of the [Cotswolds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotswolds), and the [Old Ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Ball), [Old Tup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Tup), and [Old Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Horse) of northern England, have led to suggestions that they derive from the regionalised popularisation of the sixteenth and seventeenth-century fashion for hobby horses among the social elite.

Although the tradition declined in the early to mid-twentieth century, partly due to opposition from some local Christian clergy and changing social conditions, it was revived in new forms in the mid-to-latter part of the century. The tradition has also inspired various artistic depictions, appearing, for instance, in the work of the painter [Clive Hicks-Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Hicks-Jenkins) and the poet [Vernon Watkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_Watkins).

#### Description

The Mari Lwyd itself consists of a horse's skull that is decorated with ribbons and affixed to a pole; to the back of the skull is attached a white sheet, which drapes down to conceal both the pole and the individual carrying this device.[^5138] On occasion, the horse's head was represented not by a skull but was instead made from wood or even paper.[^5139] In some instances, the horse's jaw was able to open and close as a result of string or lever attached to it, and there are accounts of pieces of glass being affixed into the eye sockets of some examples, representing eyes.[^5140] An observer of the tradition as it was performed at [Llangynwyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llangynwyd) during the nineteenth century noted that preparation for the activity was a communal event, with many locals involving themselves in the decorating of the Mari Lwyd.[^5141]

The Mari Lwyd custom was performed during winter festivities, specifically around the dates of [Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas) and [New Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year).[^5142] However, the precise date on which the custom was performed varied between villages, and in a number of cases the custom was carried out for several consecutive nights.[^5143] There is a unique example provided by an account from [Gower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gower_Peninsula) in which the head was kept buried throughout the year, only being dug up for use during the Christmas season.[^5144]

The custom used to begin at dusk and often lasted late into the night.[^5145] The Mari Lwyd party consisted of four to seven men, who often had coloured ribbons and rosettes attached to their clothes and sometimes wore a broad sash around the waist.[^5146] There was usually a smartly dressed "Leader" who carried a staff, stick, or whip, and sometimes other stock characters, such as the "Merryman" who played music, and [Punch and Judy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch_and_Judy) (both played by men) with blackened faces; often brightly dressed, Punch carried a long metal [fire iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_iron) and Judy had a [besom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besom).[^5147]

> Wel dyma ni'n dwad (Well here we come)\
> Gy-feillion di-niwad (Innocent friends)\
> I ofyn am gennad (To ask leave)\
> I ofyn am gennad (To ask leave)\
> I ofyn am gennad i ganu (To ask leave to sing)

*,  A common opening to the *pwnco*.[^5148]*

The Mari Lwyd party would approach a house and sing a song in which they requested admittance. The inhabitants of the house would then offer excuses for why the team could not enter. The party would sing a second verse, and the debate between the two sides - known as the *pwnco* (a form of musical battle similar to [flyting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flyting)) - would continue until the house's inhabitants ran out of ideas, at which time they were obliged to allow the party entry and to provide them with [ale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ale) and food.[^5149] An account from [Nantgarw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nantgarw) described such a performance, in which the Punch and Judy characters would cause a noise, with Punch tapping the ground to the rhythm of the music and rapping on the door with a [poker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_iron), while Judy brushed the ground, house walls, and windows with a broom.[^5150] The householders had to make Punch promise that he would not touch their fireplace before he entered the building, otherwise it was the local custom that before he left he would rake out the fire with his poker.[^5151] In the case from Llangynwyd, however, there was no interplay between the householders and troupe, but rather the latter were typically granted entry automatically after singing the first verse of their song.[^5152]

Once inside, the entertainment continued with the Mari Lwyd running around neighing and snapping its jaws, creating havoc, frightening children (and perhaps even adults) while the Leader pretended to try to restrain it. The Merryman played music and entertained the householders.[^5145] The [folklorist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folkloristics) [Iorwerth Peate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iorwerth_Peate) believed that in recorded examples from [Glamorgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glamorgan) it was apparent that the Mari Lwyd custom had become "indistinguishable" from the practice of [wassailing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wassailing), although added that there were still some examples of wassailing that did not involve the Mari Lwyd.[^5153] He added that links between Mari Lwyd and wassailing were also apparent from recorded examples in other part of Wales, thus opining that Mari Lwyd represented a variant of the wider wassailing custom that was found throughout Britain.

#### Early development

##### Etymology

Although the custom was given various names, most recorded sources term this particular custom *Mari Lwyd*.[^5154] [Marie Trevelyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Trevelyan) states that the name *Marw Lwyd* had been used in many parts of Wales since the seventeenth century. She derived this name as "Grey Death", arguing that it was a symbol of "the dying or dead year".[^5155]

However, this etymology is heavy contested, Jones considered this to be a translation of "Blessed Mary", and thus a reference to the [Virgin Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Mary), mother of Jesus, a key religious figure in the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church), [Eastern Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church), and others.[^5156] Although translating it slightly differently, as "Holy Mary", Peate endorsed this viewpoint.[^5157] Although some of his acquaintances later suggested that the use of *Mari* for Mary was unknown in Wales prior to the [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation), he countered these criticisms with the observation that the term *Mari* was being used in reference to the Virgin in the mid-14th century *[Black Book of Carmarthen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Book_of_Carmarthen)*, thus attesting to its early usage in Welsh.[^5158] He nevertheless accepted that during the medieval period the term might have been restricted largely to poets, given that there is no evidence of its usage among the common dialect in this period.[^5159]

Given that *llwyd* is the usual word for "grey" in the Welsh language and that Welsh speakers would have been exposed to the English word "mare", an alternative suggestion considered by Peate was that the term *Mari Lwyd* had originally meant "Grey Mare".[^5160] This etymological explanation would have parallels with the name of a similar hooded horse tradition found in [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland) and the [Isle of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Man), which is known in [Irish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_language) as the *[Láir Bhán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1ir_Bh%C3%A1n)* and in [Manx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manx_language) as the *Laare Vane*, in both cases meaning "White Mare".[^5161] Initially believing that "there is much to be said for this suggestion",[^5159] Peate later embraced it fully.[^5162] Cawte similarly believed that "Grey Mare" was the most likely original meaning of the term, noting that the Mari Lwyd appeared to represent a horse and that similar [hobby horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobby_horse) customs in neighbouring England, such as the hoodening tradition of East Kent, also made reference to horses with their name.[^5139] Peate suggested that even if the term *Mari Lwyd* had originally referred to a "Grey Mare", it could still have come to be associated with Mary in popular folk culture following the Reformation, thus explaining why Mary is referred to in the lyrics of some surviving Welsh wassailing songs.[^5163]

A further suggestion is that *Mari Lwyd* derives from the English term *Merry Lude*, referring to a merry game.[^5164] Peate opposed this idea, arguing that if the latter was converted into Welsh then the result would be *merri-liwt* or *merri-liwd*.[^5165] Peate also dismissed the idea that had been suggested to him that the term *Mari* in this context had derived from *Morris*, a reference to [Morris dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_dance).[^5159] Another reason to doubt this idea is that there is no known historical link between the Mari Lwyd, which was found in South Wales, and the Morris dance, which was concentrated in the north of the country.[^5166]

In other recorded instances, the *Mari Lwyd* custom is given different names, with it being recorded as *y Wasail* "The Wassail" in parts of [Carmarthenshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmarthenshire).[^5167] In the first half of the 19th century it was recorded in [Pembrokeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pembrokeshire) under the name of *y March* "The Horse" and *y Gynfas-farch* "The Canvas Horse".[^5168] One account from [West Glamorgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Glamorgan) has the head termed the *aderyn bee* \[*bi*?\] *y llwyd*, meaning the "Grey Magpie",[^5169] although this may be due to an error on the part of the recorder, who could have confused the horse's head for the *aderyn pica llwyd*, an artificial bird in a tree that was carried by wassailers in the same area.[^5170]

Note that in modern Welsh, the *Mari Lwyd* is referred to with [definite article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Definite_article) *y*, which subsequently causes a [soft mutation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colloquial_Welsh_morphology) of *m* to *f* (Welsh pronunciation: \[v\]), rendering the form *y Fari Lwyd*.[^5171]

##### Origins

Positing the custom to be "the survival of some ancient popular rite or ceremony", in 1888 David Jones suggested that its origins were Christian, and that it had once been part of the festivities of the [Feast of the Ass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feast_of_the_Ass), a commemoration of the [flight into Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_into_Egypt) of Mary and [Saint Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Joseph) that was historically marked on 14 January. According to Jones' idea, the Mari Lwyd itself represented the donkey on which Mary rode during the story.[^5172]

Peate was of the opinion that the Mari Lwyd was "no doubt a survival of a pre-Christian tradition" that had once been spread across Britain and other parts of Europe, and which - having survived the [Christianisation of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romano-British_culture) - had been renamed *Mari Lwyd* in reference to the Virgin Mary during the Middle Ages.[^5157] He expressed the view that the original custom had been "horrific in origin and intention" and that from an early date it had been connected to wassailing.[^5173] Cawte concurred that it was "reasonable to accept" that the Mari Lwyd head had become attached to an independent wassailing tradition, but said that the connection to the Virgin Mary was unnecessary.[^5139] Pearce also suggested the possibility that in parts of Glamorgan and [Monmouthshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monmouthshire) the Mari Lwyd tradition came under the influence of [mystery plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mystery_play), thus explaining why later recorded examples from those counties contained characters known as "the Sergeant" and the "Merryman".[^5174]

The folklorist Trefor M. Owen also suggested that the Mari Lwyd was a practice "which probably had a religious (if pre-Christian) origin", adding that by the time it had been recorded, it had become "emptied of its religious content".[^5175] Also embracing Peate's suggestion of ancient origins, Ellen Ettlinger believed that the Mari Lwyd represented a "death horse", as symbolised by the white cloth worn by its carrier,[^5176] suggesting that it was originally employed in a pre-Christian ritual to mark the festival of [Samhain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samhain).[^5177] The folklorist [Christina Hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Hole) suggested that this "ancient character" was once "a bringer of fertility".[^5178] However, after 1970 the folkloric trend for interpreting such hobby horse traditions as pre-Christian survivals had ended, as scholars came to express greater caution about proposing origins for such customs.[^5179]

The Mari Lwyd was part of a wider "hooded animal" tradition that the folklorist E. C. Cawte identified as existing in different forms in various parts of Britain.[^5180] Features common to these customs were the use of a hobby horse, the performance at Christmas time, a song or spoken statement requesting payment, and the use of a team who included a man dressed in women's clothing.[^5181] A related example is the [hoodening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoodening) custom of [East Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Kent) in southeastern [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England).[^5182] In an area along the border between [Derbyshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derbyshire) and [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire), the [Old Tup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Tup) tradition featured groups knocking on doors around Christmas carrying a hobby horse that had a goat's head.[^5183] Hole drew parallels between hoodening and the Christmas Bull tradition recorded in [Dorset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorset) and [Gloucestershire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gloucestershire).[^5184] In south-west England, there are two extant hobby horse traditions, the Padstow ['Obby 'Oss festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'Obby_'Oss_festival) and [Minehead Hobby Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minehead_Hobby_Horse), which take place not at Christmas time but on [May Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_Day).[^5185] Although the origins of these traditions are not known with any certainty, the lack of any late medieval references to such practices may suggest that they emerged from the documented elite fashion for hobby horses in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.[^5186] In this, the hooded animal traditions may be comparable to England's [Morris dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morris_dance) tradition, which became a "nation-wide craze" in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries before evolving into "a set of sharply delineated regional traditions".[^5187]

#### Regional coverage

As late as 1909, [Marie Trevelyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Trevelyan) stated that the Mari Lwyd tradition at [Llandaff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llandaff) remained an annual event, while a tradition at [Trecynon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trecynon), [Aberdare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdare) continued into the twentieth century. However, she also records that by that time the Mari Lwyd of [Llantwit Major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llantwit_Major) (that would also visit several locations in the [Vale of Glamorgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vale_of_Glamorgan)) had become "sporadic" and was no longer an annual tradition.[^5155]

In mapping the distribution of Mari Lwyd appearances, Cawte noted that it was principally a custom associated with Glamorgan, with two-thirds of instances falling within that county.[^5188] The custom stretched east into the industrial valleys of Monmouthshire, with the most easterly account coming from [Monmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monmouth) itself; this account is also one of the earliest.[^5188] A number of examples were also found in [Carmarthenshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmarthenshire),[^5189] with a single example found in both [Brecknockshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brecknockshire) and [Ceredigion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceredigion).[^5190] There is a single record of the custom being performed in [North Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Wales), in an example from [Wrexham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrexham), which Cawte believed was the result of a Glamorgan man bringing the custom with him as he moved north.[^5189] Previously, Peate had cautioned that the comparative absence of recorded examples from Mid and North Wales was not proof that the Mari Lwyd custom had never been present in those areas.[^5157]

Cawte opined that there was "no clear reason" for the distribution of the Mari Lwyd custom, which cut through various local cultural features.[^5189] Those areas where it was found did not correlate with any distinction between English-speaking and Welsh-speaking areas in South Wales.[^5191] He acknowledged however that there was a "reasonable correspondence" between the areas in which the Mari Lwyd was recorded and the areas which were used for mineral production in the 14th century.[^5192] He therefore suggested the possibility that it might have been performed by coal and iron miners in western Glamorgan, Carmarthenshire, and western [Monmouthshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monmouthshire), and that from there it could have spread into those villages where goods were manufactured using those minerals.[^5192]

#### Recorded appearances

##### 18th and 19th centuries

The earliest published account of the Mari Lwyd appeared in 1800 in J. Evans' *A Tour through Part of North Wales, in the year 1798, and at Other Times*.[^5193] Although the book itself focused on North Wales, the chapter in which the passage was included discussed the language and customs of Wales more generally.[^5193] In this section, Evans related that:

A man on new year's day, dressing himself in blankets and other trappings, with a factitious head like a horse, and a party attending him, knocking for admittance, this obtained, he runs about the room with an uncommon frightful noise, which the company quit in real or pretended fright; they soon recover, and by reciting a verse of some [cowydd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cywydd), or, in default, paying a small gratuity, they gain admission.[^5194]

Evans returned to the custom in his 1804 work *Letters Written During a Tour Through South Wales, in the year 1803, and at Other Times*. Here he provided a clearer discussion than before, making it apparent that teams accompanying a man dressed as a horse or bull toured the local area from Christmas until after [Twelfth Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelfth_Night_%28holiday%29), and that they were given food or money to leave the householders alone.[^5195]

The Mari Lwyd next appeared in an 1819 account from [West Glamorgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Glamorgan), where the Mari Lwyd itself was termed an *Aderyn Bee y llwyd* (roughly "Grey Magpie") and was accompanied by "three or four partners in the profits of the expedition, who are by turns horse, groom, or attendants".[^5169]

It has been suggested that the [Welsh Methodist revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_Methodist_revival) contributed to the decline of both the Mari Lwyd and a number of other Welsh folk customs.[^5196] In 1802, the harpist [Edward Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Jones_%28Bardd_y_Brenin%29) of [Merionethshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merionethshire) published a book in which he lamented the destructive impact that Christian preachers were having on Welsh folk customs, which they were criticising as [sinful](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sin). In his view, "the consequence is, Wales, which was formerly one of the merriest and happiest countries in the World, is now becoming one of the dullest".[^5197] Reflecting such a view, in 1852 the Reverend William Roberts, a [Baptist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baptists) minister at [Blaenau Gwent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blaenau_Gwent), condemned the Mari Lwyd and other related customs as "a mixture of old Pagan and Popish ceremonies... I wish of this folly, and all similar follies, that they find no place anywhere apart from the museum of the historian and antiquary."[^5198]

Owen suggested that the custom's decline was also a result of changing social conditions in South Wales. He argued that the Mari Lwyd wassailing custom "gave an approved means of entering the houses of neighbours in a culture in which there were few public assemblies - at least in the heart of winter - in which the convivial spirit of the season could be released".[^5199] Further, he suggested that the gifts of food, drink, and sometimes money "no doubt helped to further the feeling of community among country folk while at the same time manifesting it".[^5199] He argued that the changing social conditions altered the ways that people in southern Wales celebrated Christmas, hence contributing to the folk custom's decline.[^5199]

##### 20th century revival

In a 1935 article on the subject of the Mari Lwyd, Peate stated that the tradition "is still met with; it is practised in the Cardiff district, Bridgend, Llangynwyd, Neath and other Glamorgan districts".[^5157] He highlighted an example from [Christmas Eve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas_Eve) 1934, in which a Mari Lwyd was observed performing alongside at least twelve singers in a chemist's shop in the [Mumbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbles), Swansea.[^5157] Ettlinger subsequently expressed the view that "Dr. Peate deserves the sincerest gratitude of all folk-lore students for having so valiantly penetrated the mysteries surrounding the Mari Lwyd."[^5200]

The historian [Ronald Hutton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Hutton) stated that the Mari Lwyd tradition appeared to have become defunct in the early 20th century.[^5201] In the middle of that century it was revived in [Llangynwyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llangynwyd).[^5201] In 1967, Lois Blake published a letter in the journal *[English Dance and Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Folk_Dance_and_Song_Society)* in which she noted that the Mari Lwyd appeared each Christmas Eve at the Barley Mow Inn at [Graig Penllyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penllyn,_Vale_of_Glamorgan), near [Cowbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowbridge), where a man named John Williams had kept the custom alive for the past sixty years.[^5202] Blake also explained that she believed that the custom was still performed at several villages in the [Maesteg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maesteg) area of Glamorgan.[^5202] During the 1970s, Hole commented that the tradition was still found in Glamorganshire and Carmarthenshire.[^5178]

During the 1980s, further revived forms of the Mari Lwyd tradition emerged in [Caerphilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caerphilly), [Llantrisant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llantrisant), and [St Fagans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Fagans), all of which are in the same borderland between Vale and mountains.[^5201] Commenting on the example of Llantrisant, which was inaugurated in 1980, Mick Tems noted that the custom had "re-established herself so strongly that there are complaints if she misses any of her regular calls".[^5203] He noted that in 1991 the Llantrisant Mari Lwyd was taken to [Yn Chruinnaght](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yn_Chruinnaght), a [Pan-Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Celticism) festival on the Isle of Man, and that it had also been taken to the [Lowender Peran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowender_Peran) festival at [Perranporth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perranporth) in [Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall).[^5204] Hutton believed that the custom re-emerged in the borderlands between Vale and the mountains in part because people in Glamorgan sought to reaffirm their sense of cultural identity during the termination of their traditional industries, and partly because the [Welsh Folk Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Wales) was located in the area.[^5201] More widely, he believed that the revival of the Mari Lwyd was in large part due to the "forces of local patriotism", noting that a similar situation had resulted in the resurrection of the hoodening tradition in East Kent.[^5148]

The Mari Llwyd is a feature in modern celebrations of the [Hen Galan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_New_Year) (English: Old New Year), such as those at [Cowbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowbridge), [Cwm Gwaun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cwm_Gwaun) and [Aberystwyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberystwyth).[^5205] The town council of Aberystwyth also organised "The World's Largest Mari Lwyd" for the Millennium celebrations in 2000.[^5206]

A mixture of the Mari Lwyd and Wassail customs occurs in the border town of [Chepstow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chepstow), South Wales, every January. A band of English Wassailers meet with the local Welsh [Border Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Morris) Side, The Widders, on [the bridge in the town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Wye_Bridge,_Chepstow).[^5207][^5208] In the 21st century, the revival of the custom has extended to [Abergavenny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abergavenny).[^5209]

#### In culture

> Mari Lwyd, Lwyd Mari\
> A sacred thing through the night they carry.\
> Betrayed are the living, betrayed the dead\
> All are confused by a horse's head.

*,  Vernon Watkins, "Ballad of the Mari Lwyd", lines 398-400*

The Mari Lwyd has prompted responses from the arts in Wales. In 1941 [Faber & Faber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faber_&_Faber) published *"Ballad of the Mari Lwyd and other poems*, then first book by poet [Vernon Watkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernon_Watkins). The [Archbishop of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury) [Rowan Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rowan_Williams) has written that the title ballad, "one of the outstanding poems of the century, draws together the folk-ritual of the New Year, the [Christian Eucharist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucharist), the uneasy frontier between living and dead, so as to present a model of what poetry itself is - frontier work between death and life, old year and new, bread and body."[^5210]

The Mari Lwyd was utilised by the artist [Clive Hicks-Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Hicks-Jenkins) in a series of drawings from around 2000 that focused on a metamorphosing horse/man as a nightmarish harbinger of his father's death.[^5211] Catriona Urquhart wrote a sequence of poems titled *The Mare's Tale* which were published alongside Hicks-Jenkins' images in 2001.[^5212] In her 1977 novel *[Silver on the Tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_on_the_Tree)*, the author [Susan Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Cooper) included an appearance from the Mari Lwyd.[^5213]

In [a 2024 episode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RuPaul's_Drag_Race_UK_series_6) of *[RuPaul's Drag Race UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RuPaul's_Drag_Race_UK)*, drag contestant Marmalade referenced the Mari Lwyd in her outfit as a means of representing her home town of [Pontyclun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontyclun).[^5214]

#### Related Welsh customs

In 1919, H. W. Evans recorded the existence of a similar custom which had existed in [Solva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solva), Pembrokeshire circa 1840, during his mother's childhood. He stated that this custom entailed the use of what he termed a "Mari Lwyd", furthermore providing a drawing of it using his mother's recollections as a basis, although was unaware of how this costume had been used.[^5215] According to Evans' description, this Mari Lwyd consisted of a sheet that had been sewn together along two adjacent sides to make a cone, which was then stuffed with hay and decorated with buttons for eyes and harvest gloves for ears, thus resembling an animal's snout. An individual could conceal themselves under the sheet and use a [hay fork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork) inserted into the hay to hold it up.[^5216] A similar custom appears in an account from 1897, in which an entity known as the *Bwca Llwyd* ("Grey Bogy") was described; it involved an imitation horse's head being made from canvas and stuffed with hay, being carried about using a hay fork on [All Hallow's Eve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Hallow's_Eve).[^5217]

Cawte also noted the example of other Welsh folk customs featuring the head of a horse, however he opined that these "so not seem to be closely related to the mari lwyd".[^5192] A horse's head was prepared in a manner akin to the Mari Lwyd for a spring festival known as the *mynwenta* or *pynwenta*, which took place in Pembrokeshire circa 1820. As part of this festival, young men and women gathered at a mill for a night's entertainment.[^5192] In the late nineteenth century, a tradition was recorded in North Wales that was known as "giving a skull", in which the skull of a horse or donkey was placed over the front door of a woman's house on [May Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_Day) as a sign of contempt.[^5192] In parts of Wales a horse's head - sometimes with horns attached - was featured as part of the *[charivari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charivari)* processions designed to shame those who were deemed to have behaved in an immoral manner.[^5218]
