### Hungarian Two-Tailed Dog Party

The **Hungarian Two-Tailed Dog Party** ([Hungarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_language): *Magyar Kétfarkú Kutya Párt* \[ˈmɒɟɒr ˈkeːtfɒrkuː ˈkucɒ ˈpaːrt\], **MKKP** \[ˈɛmkaːkaːpeː\]) is a [satirical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_frivolous_political_parties) [political party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_party) in [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary). It was founded in [Szeged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szeged) in 2006, but did not register as an official political party until 2014.

#### Political activity

##### 2006-2010 elections

All of the electoral candidates were called *Nagy István* (literally "Stephen Grand", the Hungarian equivalent of [generic names](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Placeholder_name) such as the English *John Smith*) during the 2006 national and local elections.[^5368]

The Two-Tailed Dog Party was not a registered political party until 2014, though it participated in the 2006 elections. The party platform promised eternal life, world peace, a one-day [workweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workweek_and_weekend), two [sunsets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunset) a day (in assorted colours), lower [gravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity), free [beer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer), and low taxes.[^5369] Other electoral pledges have included building a mountain on the [Great Hungarian Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hungarian_Plain). Party election posters were mostly in Szeged and featuring the candidate István Nagy, who is a two-tailed dog, with slogans such as "He's so cute, surely he isn't going to steal".

The party is on good terms with another joke party, the *Fourth Way*, which is led by two birds. However, there are some disagreements between them, since Fourth Way plans to abolish [bird flu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avian_influenza), which is opposed by the Two-tailed Dog Party on the principle of viral rights. On 20 June 2009, the MKKP held a "general" protest with approximately three hundred participants in front of the [Hungarian Central Statistical Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Central_Statistical_Office) (KSH) to demand "Tomorrow should be yesterday!", "Look stupid!" and "Disband!" etc., with a chant of "What do we want? Nothing! When do we want it? Never!".[^5370]

In 2010, the party announced their candidacy for mayor of Budapest with the main slogan "Let everything be better!".[^5371] Campaign slogans include "More everything, less nothing!", "Eternal life, free beer, tax-deduction!" and "We promise anything!".[^5372] In [Erzsébetváros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erzs%C3%A9betv%C3%A1ros) (District VII, Budapest), the mayoral candidate of the party was notable [stand-up comedian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand-up_comedian) Dániel Mogács, who has carried out a number of awareness-generating actions during the campaign period, including a surreal interview with television host [Olga Kálmán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olga_K%C3%A1lm%C3%A1n) ([ATV's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATV_%28Hungary%29) Straight Talk).[^5373] However, neither candidate was able to collect the appropriate number of recommendation slips to participate in the election.[^5374] According to its detailed economic program, MKKP intended to develop Szeged space station into an interplanetary spaceport, which would be used for [Pulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puli_dog)' export to [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaica). The program also contained environmental elements, such as patching the [ozone hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone_depletion) and the creation of new species to replace extinct ones. The party also proposed establishing trade relations with extraterrestrial life forms, and opening a Hungarian restaurant on [Mars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mars) to improve the country's image.[^5375]

##### 2014-2018 elections

The party spent most of 2013 trying to finish the official registration process, which new election law made compulsory, so it could start its campaign.[^5376] The registration was rejected in early 2014 on the grounds of the party's "flippancy".[^5377] In July 2014, the Supreme Court ruled that this was not a valid reason to reject the party, and the registration process should continue.[^5378] The MKKP was officially registered on 8 September 2014, only 16 minutes before the deadline for nomination of candidates for the [2014 local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Hungarian_local_elections), so the party was unable to participate in the election.[^5379]

In June 2015, the ruling [Third Orbán Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Orb%C3%A1n_Government) launched an anti-immigrant poster campaign during the intensifying [European migrant crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_migrant_crisis), with slogans such as "If you come to Hungary, you cannot take the Hungarians' jobs away!".[^5380] In response, the Two-Tailed Dog Party and the Vastagbőr blog ("Thick Skin") jointly called for an "anti-anti-immigration campaign", and collected more than 33 million HUF (ten times the expected amount) from supporters[^5381] to set up around 800 billboards parodying those of the government, with slogans in Hungarian and English such as "Sorry about our Prime Minister" and "Feel free to come to Hungary, we already work in England!".[^5382]

On 4 February 2016, Medián's poll for the first time registered support for the Hungarian Two-Tailed Dog Party, which suggested they would get 1% of the vote.[^5383]

The Hungarian Two-Tailed Dog Party was closely involved in the campaign during the [October 2016 migrant quota referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Hungarian_migrant_quota_referendum), mocking the government's anti-immigrant messages and phrases. In response to government posters which read "Did you know?" followed by claimed facts about immigration, the party spent €100,000 of voluntary donations from 4,000 people on posters with satirical slogans, such as "Did you know there's a war in Syria?", "Did you know one million Hungarians want to emigrate to Europe?", "Did you know? The perpetrators in most corruption cases are politicians" and "Did you know? During the Olympics, the biggest danger to Hungarian participants came from foreign competitors". Party leader Gergely Kovács told [BBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_News) that "... What we can do is appeal to the millions in Hungary who are upset by the government campaign. We want them to know they are not alone". The party asked people to cast invalid ballots in the referendum.[^5384] Eventually, 6% of the voters cast a spoiled ballot.[^5385]

Shortly before the referendum, the party made a mobile app available for download on its website. The app, called "Vote Invalidly", could be used to take a photo of the [spoilt votes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spoilt_vote) and publish it. MKKP received a fine of 832,000 Hungarian forints for releasing the app, because publishing a ballot paper is illegal (even though the app published them anonymously).[^5386] The fine was later reduced to 100,000 Hungarian forints by the decision of the [Curia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curia_of_Hungary), based on the argument that publishing ballot papers anonymously did not violate the secrecy of the voting, although it was a misuse of the ballot papers.[^5387]

##### 2018-2022 elections

The party officially took part in the [2018 parliamentary elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Hungarian_parliamentary_election) and got 1.73% of the total vote, but no seats. Because the party participated in the election, it became eligible to receive government funds, which it spends on the "[Rózsa Sándor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A1ndor_R%C3%B3zsa) State Fund Wasting Public Program".[^5388]

The party participated in the [2019 European Parliament election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_European_Parliament_election_in_Hungary). Despite an increase to 2.62% of the votes, it did not win a seat. Its campaign promises included building an [overpass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overpass) above the country for refugees, opening six [Nemzeti Dohánybolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nemzeti_Doh%C3%A1nybolt) stores outside Hungary, introducing mandatory [siesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siesta) and banning the [Eurovision Song Contest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurovision_Song_Contest).[^5389]

In the [2019 local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Hungarian_local_elections) the party ran in four districts of [Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest) ([II.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_district_of_Budapest), [XII.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hegyvid%C3%A9k), [XIV.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zugl%C3%B3), [XV.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15th_district_of_Budapest)) where they had elected one council member each.[^5390] They also formally or informally supported a handful of mayoral candidates, most notably in [Ferencváros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferencv%C3%A1ros) and [Szombathely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Szombathely). After the election, newly elected Ferencváros mayor Krisztina Baranyi appointed co-leader Zsuzsanna Döme as one of her deputy mayors.[^5391]

##### 2022-2026 elections

The party officially took part in the [2022 parliamentary elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Hungarian_parliamentary_election) and increased their vote share to 3.27% of the total vote, making them the fourth largest political block, but gained no seats because of the 5% threshold.

The party participated in the [2024 European parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_European_Parliament_election) election and the simultaneously held [2024 local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Hungarian_local_elections). In [District 12 of Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hegyvid%C3%A9k), party co-leader [Gergely Kovács](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gergely_Kov%C3%A1cs_%28politician%29) won 61% of the first preference votes in a [ranked-choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant-runoff_voting) opposition primary, the first the party has joined. Other main opposition parties are now expected not to field a candidate for mayor and half of the district seats for councilors are to be nominated exclusively by the Two-Tailed Dog Party, plus 2 seats. Kovács won the mayorship with 54% of the votes, and the party won 10 out of the 18 seats in the district council.[^5392]

In April 2025, the party held its largest demonstration to date, marching under the banner of 'illiberal pride' to protest changes the government made to the [right to assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_assembly).[^5393]

##### 2026 election

Ahead of the [2026 Hungarian parliamentary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Hungarian_parliamentary_election), MKKP confirmed that it would be running independently, after it had considered allying with [Péter Magyar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A9ter_Magyar)'s [Tisza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tisza_Party).[^5394] The MKKP's list in 2026 is led by the party's director, [Dávid Nagy](https://hu.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagy%20D%C3%A1vid%20%28politikus%29). The following four candidates, who are to take leadership positions, include several local politicians. The two leaders of the party are not going to run for national election.[^5395]

On 6 April 2026 an online [documentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Documentary) entitled "Az ebek ura" (lit. 'Lord of the Dogs') was released by journalist Vera Mérő; the documentary alleges [embezzlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embezzlement) of funds, [corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption) and internal purges of dissenting opinion.[^5396] The party leadership has denied the accusations and described the documentary as [character assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_assassination).[^5396]

In the election, the party ended up with only 0.82% of the vote, failing to secure a candidate seat; chairman Dávid Nagy announced his resignation immediately.[^5397] Due to not having reached 1% of the votes, the party has to pay back its 686 million forints (around \$2.2M) worth of campaign funding it received from the government. As they have spent the funding, they are attempting to cover it through donations.[^5398]

#### Street art and protest

Especially starting off, the party utilised street art and protest campaigns to get its message across.[^5399][^5400][^5401] This targeted various companies and public bodies, often highlighting poor infrastructure. For example, in 2009, party leader Gergely Kovács created a parody of the website Pecs2010.hu (the official site of [Pécs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P%C3%A9cs) as [Cultural Capital of Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Capital_of_Europe) in 2010), for which he was threatened with legal action, but the owners of the original site backed down after the case got publicity.[^5402] Local parties also undertake city beautification actions, such as renovating street benches.[^5403]

Increasingly during the latter half of the 2010s, the party began to run more campaigns and art stunts opposing the [authoritarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism) and [anti-immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-immigration) policies of the government led by [Viktor Orbán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Orb%C3%A1n).[^5404]

#### Party organisation

The MKKP is structured in a three-tier system: a national organisation, six national coordinators, and over 100 local organisations. Local authorities have relative autonomy.[^5403]

Anyone can join in with the activities of the party informally. Party membership is granted to actively participating activists, and acts as the most important decision-making body. For example, members elect the leadership and decide election candidates.[^5403]

### McGillicuddy Serious Party

The **McGillicuddy Serious Party** (**McGSP**) was a [satirical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire) [political party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_party) or [joke party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joke_party) in [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_New_Zealand) in the late 20th century. Between 1984 and 1999, it stood candidates in elections - one purpose being to make the political process more entertaining. The party's logo, the head of a [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval) [court jester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_jester), indicated the intention to critique current systems by poking fun at them.

The party stood candidates in the 1984, 1987, 1990, 1993, 1996 and 1999 general elections and the 1986, 1989, 1992, 1995 and 1998 Local Body elections;[^5405] along with local-body and [parliamentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary) [by-elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/By-election) and university [student association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_association) elections.[^5406]

It gained its highest number of votes in the last [first-past-the-post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-past-the-post_voting) (FPP) [general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_election) in [1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_general_election,_1993), when it stood candidates in 62 out of 99 electorates and received 11,714 votes, 0.61% of the vote.

#### Origins

The party was formed in 1984[^5407] in [Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilton,_New_Zealand) as the political arm of Clan McGillicuddy (established in 1978). Members of the Clan had stood as candidates in the 1983 local-body elections in the [Waikato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waikato),[^5407] and the party came together in time to contest the 1984 General Election. It had a strong Scottish theme, with the renaissance of a Jacobite monarchy being one of the party's main policy planks. Candidates included street performers, students, artists and members of musical groups such as the [Big Muffin Serious Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Muffin_Serious_Band).

#### Policies

The party selected its policies on the basis of their absurdity, but also how they tied into an over-arching grand plan. The features of this plan were: Funism (a doctrine of the most fun for the most people), The Great Leap Backwards (returning NZ to a medieval, subsistence, tribal economy) and replacing parliament with a McGillicuddy-style monarchy based on Jacobitism: a non-hereditary monarch would be appointed in a similar manner to that used to determine the [Dalai Lama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalai_Lama). The high number of NZers with (some) Scottish heritage was the reason given for creating a Jacobite renaissance in the south Pacific.[^5408] As time went on some McGillicuddies were influenced by Situationism. Another McGSP guiding principle was to do "Politics as Art and Art as Politics". MCGSP candidates, rallies and publicity stunts were characterised by the use of costume, hand-made props, live music and/or performance art.

Policies included:

- Free [dung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feces)
- Sending out intelligence agents around the world to wipe New Zealand off published maps, thus ensuring that no-one could invade the country.[^5409]
- Standing a dog for parliament in the Hobson seat in Northland. Her policies included the abolition of cars, and turning a meat-works into an organic flea-powder factory.[^5410]
- The abolition of money, replacing it with [chocolate fish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chocolate_fish) or with sand.
- The demolition of [The Beehive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beehive_%28building%29), [parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Parliament) buildings, and all other buildings on a last-up, first-down basis.[^5411]
- The diversion of aluminium production away from building US military aircraft and missiles to build giant space-mirrors to melt the polar icecaps and destroy all of the foolish greed-worshipping cities of man in one stroke, thereby returning man to the sea, which he should never have left in the first place (this the inspiration of the Admiral of the Highland Navy Aaron Franklin).
- Raising the [school leaving-age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/School_leaving_age) to 65 (after Parliament raised the school leaving-age by one unambitious year)[^5411]
- Full unemployment, or full employment through [slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery)[^5412]
- Using [beer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beer) as a National Defence strategy: leaving bottles of beer on all beaches, so that any invading army would abandon its attack and get drunk while the broken bottles would prevent the army advancing any further.
- Restricting the vote to [minors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_%28law%29): i.e., ONLY those under 18 years of age could vote (announced when Parliament lowered the voting age to 18 years, despite New Zealand reducing the voting age to 18 in 1974). The party ran its 1993 electoral advertisements during children's programming.
- Student loans for [Plunket Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plunket_Society) (or [Kindergarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kindergarten)) attendance: prior to the 1984 election, [David Lange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lange)'s [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party) promised to maintain free [tertiary education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertiary_education), but the Education Minister, [Phil Goff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Goff), introduced student fees when elected. [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party) education spokesman [Lockwood Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockwood_Smith) promised a return to free education if elected, but did not carry out this promise. Most party supporters, many of them students, felt displeased that both major political parties had deemed free tertiary education unsustainable, but had deliberately lied about their intentions to attract votes.
- Abandoning male [suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffrage): New Zealand, the first nation to achieve [women's suffrage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_suffrage) (in 1893), made a big deal of the centenary of this at the time of the 1993 election.
- Votes for trees: New Zealanders have a reputation as [environmentalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmentalism), and the [University of Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Auckland)'s ex-[Marxist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxist) law lecturer Klaus Bosselmann seriously advocated giving trees (and other bits of the environment) some legal standing. The party could not decide on whether native trees should have the option to vote in [Māori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C4%81ori_people) [electorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_district), whether male trees as well as female trees should vote, and on the status of shrubs.
- The demolition of the [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland) [CBD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_business_district) to create a giant [sundial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sundial), using the [Sky Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_Tower_%28Auckland%29) as the [gnomon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gnomon); or to protect the Sky Tower by placing a [condom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Condom) over it.
- Replacing the [Royal New Zealand Armoured Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_New_Zealand_Armoured_Corps) with Mounted Knights, claimed as more modern. The [New Zealand Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Army)'s outdated equipment became a constant source of quips and embarrassment in the 1990s, at the time [Queen Alexandra's Mounted Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Alexandra's_Mounted_Rifles) operated [FV101 Scorpions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FV101_Scorpion) and [M-113s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M113_armored_personnel_carrier).
- Building [dreadnoughts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreadnought) in the [Tamaki Estuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamaki_River): a reference to the [Royal New Zealand Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_New_Zealand_Navy)'s controversial purchase of [Anzac class frigates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anzac_class_frigate).
- An [All Whites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Whites) victory in the [Football World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_World_Cup): both the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party) and the [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party) used the [All Blacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Blacks)' victory in the [1987 Rugby World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Rugby_World_Cup) in their 1990 campaigning, the All Whites stood about as much chance of winning the Football World Cup as [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_national_rugby_union_team) have of winning the Rugby version.
- An indecent society: [Jim Bolger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Bolger)'s [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_National_Party) used the slogan "A Decent Society".
- A [potato famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato_famine_%28disambiguation%29): [Jim Bolger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Bolger)'s somewhat pock-marked countenance bore an unfortunate resemblance to a potato. Much to his displeasure, he became widely known as "[Spud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potato)"; the [Royal New Zealand Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_New_Zealand_Air_Force), with a typically [Kiwi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiwi_%28people%29) lack of reverence, christened his [Boeing 727](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_727) "[Spud One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spud_One)".
- Limiting the [speed of light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_of_light) to 100 km/h: 50 km/h in [Mt Roskill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Roskill,_New_Zealand), (Auckland's [Bible Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible_Belt)), because folks there preferred to stay less enlightened.
- Linking the [North Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Island) and [South Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Island) by bulldozing the [Southern Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Alps_%28New_Zealand%29) into [Cook Strait](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_Strait).[^5413]
- Post-natal [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion): making abortion illegal, but any mother could kill her child up to the age of 18, provided she did it with her own hands. The party designed this policy to offend all sides in the abortion debate. The [fundamentalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamentalist) [Christian Heritage Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Heritage_New_Zealand) used abortion as a major policy.[^5411]
- Mandatory [homosexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexuality) for 33% of the population, also devised to annoy the [fundamentalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamentalists).
- Free [castration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castration)
- Setting up a Frivolous Fraud Office to investigate any fraud deemed too silly for the [Serious Fraud Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serious_Fraud_Office_%28New_Zealand%29)
- [Air bags](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_bag) for the [New Zealand Stock Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Stock_Exchange) (following the 1987 [stock market crash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_market_crash))
- Replacing the [Queen's chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_chain) with [hemp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemp): the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party) had a policy of protecting and extending the Queen's chain (publicly accessible land bordering watercourses), forcing [farmers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmer) and [iwi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwi) to allow public access to waterways. Candidate Dominic Worthington proposed replacing the chain with more environmentally sound hemp; with the [Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_regnant), of course, replaced by [Prince Geoffie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Geoffie) the reluctant. Rather than limiting the chain to protecting [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water) in aqueous form, the King's hemp would also serve to hold together water in solid form, as in the [ice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice) in [glaciers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glacier) and in the [Ross Dependency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Dependency) (in particular, the [Ross Ice Shelf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Ice_Shelf), alleviating environmentalists' concerns that the ice shelf might collapse and raise [sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea)-levels). Ultimately, the policy envisaged that [technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology) would regress far enough for it to become feasible to [lasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lasso) water in gaseous form (i.e. [clouds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clouds)).[^5414]
- Fixing [accountants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accountant) in [concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete) and using them as [traffic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic) barriers, occasionally accompanied by a pledge to steal some of the [Monster Raving Loony Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Monster_Raving_Loony_Party)'s other policies as well, possibly a reference to political parties accusing each other of stealing policies, or possibly just silliness.
- Good weather (but only if voters behaved).[^5415]
- Full employment by carpeting the national highways: this would also save wear and tear on tyres
- Breaking its promises

Note: not all of the above were party-wide policies outlined in manifestoes - candidates had creative licence to come up with their own policies.

#### Peak and Decline

The party attracted a surprising level of support, and became one of the larger parties outside parliament. On a number of occasions, particularly following the introduction of the [mixed member proportional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_member_proportional) (MMP) electoral system, pundits predicted that the party might actually win parliamentary representation, but this never happened. When the major parties boycotted the [Tauranga by-election 1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tauranga_by-election_1993) in 1993, the party's candidate Greg Pittams, who appeared in nationwide newspapers during this campaign wearing his "emperor's new kilt" outfit, consisting of only a shirt and [sporran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sporran), finished second to [Winston Peters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Peters). Votes for the party presumably most often represented [protest votes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protest_vote), something that the party encouraged with one of its slogans: "If you want to waste your vote, vote for us."

In the [1996 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_general_election,_1996), the party put up 65 list candidates; 45 candidates stood as an electorate candidate.[^5416]

The introduction of MMP [Mixed Member Proportional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_Member_Proportional) representation at the 1996 election changed the political landscape: there were more smaller parties to vote for with more of a chance of getting into Parliament. The McGSP percentage of the vote fell. The [1999 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_general_election,_1999) campaign proved a disappointment. The party gained only 0.15% of the vote, a considerable drop. In addition to this, the increased reporting required from small parties under MMP changed the 'work to fun ratio'[^5417] of taking part in elections.

#### Disbandment and deregistration

Shortly after the 1999 election, the party disbanded and the [Electoral Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_Commission_%28New_Zealand%29) officially deregistered it as a political party.[^5418] Party leader [Graeme Cairns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graeme_Cairns) marked the event and did penance for the loss by placing himself in stocks in Garden Place in Hamilton in December 1999 as disgruntled party members pelted him with rotten fruit.[^5419]

#### McGillicuddy candidates

A number of former members went on to stand as candidates for "real" parties. Former MP and co-leader of the Green party, [Metiria Turei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metiria_Turei),[^5420] formerly held party membership, and was number 27 on the party list for the 1999 General Election.[^5421]

Other prominent candidates from this first generation of electioneering included founder and Party Leader [Graeme Cairns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graeme_Cairns), the "Laird of Hamilton"; Mark Servian; KT Julian, a long-time Party Deputy Leader; Adrian Holroyd; [Cecil G. Murgatroyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_G._Murgatroyd) (who subsequently stood against Australian Prime Minister [Bob Hawke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Hawke) under the [Imperial British Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_British_Conservative_Party) banner);[^5422] Sam Buchanan; Steve Richards; [Donna Demente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donna_Demente); and Penni Bousfield.

#### Younger pretenders

Some of the party's members became upset at the cancellation of their lifetime membership. In July 2005 a "McGillicuddy Serious Party" put out a press-release announcing plans to participate in the 2005 election, one initial policy involving replacing MPs with harmless jargon-generators.[^5423]

One candidate stood under the McGillicuddy Serious banner in the [2008 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_general_election,_2008): Steve Richards contested the [West Coast-Tasman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast-Tasman) electorate and received 259 votes.[^5424]

#### Current status

Despite the demise of the party, Clan McGillicuddy continued to hold regular public events for some time. A pacifist battle in [Oamaru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oamaru) on 31 December 2007 saw McGillicuddy "Martians" take on Alf's Imperial Army in an enactment of *[The War of the Worlds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_War_of_the_Worlds)*.[^5425] YouTube hosts a video of this battle.[^5426] On 31 December 2013, there was a pacifist battle in [Waitati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waitati) in which the McGillicuddies defended Castle Almond (the castle-like home of one their members) against an "attack" by the local Waitati Militia.[^5427]

### Catmando

**Catmando** (1995-2002; also spelled "**Cat Mandu**"[^5428]) was a cat named "joint leader" of Britain's [Official Monster Raving Loony Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Monster_Raving_Loony_Party) (OMRLP) from 1999 to 2002, along with his owner, party chairman [Howling Laud Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howling_Laud_Hope).[^5429] He died in 2002, serving as leader until his death.

#### Life and career

Following the 1999 death of the party's founder, [Screaming Lord Sutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screaming_Lord_Sutch), the OMRLP held a leadership election with [Alan "Howling Laud" Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_%22Howling_Laud%22_Hope) (who was then the party's chairman and deputy leader) and Catmando as the only two candidates. The vote was a tie, with Hope and Catmando each receiving 125 votes. Hope, as the party chairman, had the deciding vote, and decided that he and Catmando should serve as joint leaders.[^5430][^5431]

During Catmando's time as joint leader, the OMRLP saw its greatest electoral performance to date, fielding 15 candidates in the [2001 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_United_Kingdom_general_election). Catmando served as joint leader until his death as a result of a traffic accident in July 2002. Hope then became the party's sole leader.[^5432]

Following Catmando's death, the party proposed that there should be cat-crossings on all major roads.[^5433]

#### Name origins

Catmando was originally called "**Catman**". His name was changed after a customer at the Golden Lion (Hope's [pub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_house) and [guesthouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guesthouse) in [Ashburton, Devon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashburton,_Devon)) asked a music question that Hope could not answer; the customer commented: "I bet Catman do \[know the answer\]". Consequently, he became "**Catmando**".

The cat later moved with Hope to the Dog and Partridge public house in [Yateley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yateley), Hampshire. [Gurkhas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gurkha), stationed nearby at [Aldershot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldershot_Garrison), were intrigued by a name that sounded like the [Nepalese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal) capital [Kathmandu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathmandu); subsequently the cat became the subject of a front-page feature in the *[Nepali Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepali_Times)*. The "Cat Mandu" spelling became common through media misinterpretation, but Hope has confirmed that "Catmando" is the correct spelling.[^5428]

### Redskins Rule

The **Redskins Rule** was an observed longstanding coincidence between the [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League) (NFL) game results of the [Washington Redskins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Redskins), now known as the [Washington Commanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Commanders), and the results of subsequent [United States presidential elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_election). Briefly stated, when Washington won its last home game prior to the presidential election, the party of the prior popular vote winning party won the presidency; when Washington lost, the opposition party won. This coincidence was noted by many sports and political commentators, and held true for the first eighteen elections after the franchise first moved to Washington in 1937. The rule was first broken in 2012, and then again in 2016 and 2024.

#### History

The [Washington Commanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Commanders), formerly known as the Washington Redskins, are an [American football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football) team belonging to the [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League) (NFL). The rule, named the Redskins Rule, stated that if they won their last [home game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_%28sports%29) before the election, the incumbent party would win and that if they lost, the challenging party would win.[^5434] The rule was first noticed prior to the [2000 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_presidential_election) by Steve Hirdt, executive vice president of the [Elias Sports Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elias_Sports_Bureau).[^5435][^5436][^5437] That year, the Redskins would begin what would become a four-game losing streak with retrospect to the rule when they lost to the [Tennessee Titans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee_Titans). [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush) defeated [Al Gore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Gore) in the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Electoral_College), but lost the popular vote. This would cause problems for the original version of the rule after the 2004 election.[^5437]

In the [2004 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election), the Redskins lost their last home game before the presidential election, indicating that the [incumbent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incumbent) should have lost. However, President George W. Bush (the incumbent) went on to defeat [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry). Hirdt modified the rule by stating when the winner of the popular vote fails to win the election, the impact of the team's game on the subsequent election gets flipped.[^5438]

This changed the rule to be based on the year’s electoral vote outcome and the prior popular vote outcome, as if Washington wins and the party that won the prior popular vote wins the year’s electoral vote, the rule would be upheld, as it would if both lost. In the election in 2000, Gore won the popular vote while Bush won the electoral vote, and thereby the revised Redskins Rule was upheld for the 2004 election. In the [2008 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election), the Redskins lost to the [Pittsburgh Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Steelers), predicting a win for [U.S. Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate) from [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois) [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama) over U.S. Senator from [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona) [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain), because Bush won the popular vote in the previous election.[^5439]

Prior to the [2012 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_presidential_election), the Redskins lost against the [Carolina Panthers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolina_Panthers) on November 4. The Redskins Rule predicted an outright loss for incumbent Barack Obama against challenger [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney), or that Obama would win the popular vote but lose via the Electoral College.[^5440] However, Obama won the election with 332 [electoral votes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_votes) to Romney's 206,[^5441] held the advantage in the popular vote by more than 4.7 million votes, and the Redskins Rule did not hold in 2012.

In 2016, the Redskins played their last designated home game prior to the election on October 16, defeating the [Philadelphia Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Eagles) 27-20. This outcome predicted a victory for [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton) of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_%28United_States%29), which was in power. Clinton's loss to [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_%28United_States%29) challenger [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump) in the election meant that the Redskins Rule did not hold in 2016 despite Clinton winning the popular vote.

Before the 2020 season, the Redskins retired their longtime name following [the George Floyd protests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Floyd_protests), using the temporary name Washington Football Team for that season. They defeated the [Dallas Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas_Cowboys) 25-3 in their last home game prior to the election, which because of the rule being inverted due to the popular vote winner losing the previous election, predicted a victory for [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden) of the Democratic Party, which ended up correct.

The franchise adopted the name "Commanders" starting from the 2022 season. Their 2024 [Hail Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hail_Maryland) victory against the [Chicago Bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Bears) suggested a victory for [Kamala Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamala_Harris) against Donald Trump in the [2024 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election), although this was incorrect.[^5442]

The rule typically does not count the team's time playing in Boston (1932-1936). The team competed as the Boston Braves in 1932 when they won 19-6 over the [Staten Island Stapletons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island_Stapletons). This game does not conform to the rule, as [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt) defeated incumbent [Herbert Hoover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Hoover) in that [election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1932_United_States_presidential_election). However, in 1936, the first election year the team competed under its longtime nickname, they defeated the [Chicago Cardinals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Cardinals) and the incumbent, Roosevelt, went on to win re-election.

### The Wizard of New Zealand

**The Wizard of New Zealand** (born **Ian Brackenbury Channell**; 4 December 1932) is a British-born New Zealand educator, comedian, [illusionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illusionist), and politician. He is also known by his shorter name, **The Wizard**.

#### Life and career

##### England

The Wizard was born Ian Brackenbury Channell on 4 December 1932 in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London), England.[^5444] He was educated at [Framlingham College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framlingham_College), [Suffolk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffolk), and from 1945 to 1951 at [Bromley Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromley_Grammar_School) for Boys, now [Ravensbourne School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravensbourne_School,_Bromley). In 1951, he was called up for [national service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_in_the_United_Kingdom) in the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force). Although he initially trained to be a pilot, he was later transferred to navigator training in Canada and was subsequently posted as the [adjutant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjutant) at [RAF Duxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duxford_Aerodrome). He left the RAF in 1953 and became a sales representative for a paper merchant. In 1956, he married his girlfriend, Monica, and from 1958 spent two years teaching English in Iran. He then returned to England in order to attend the [University of Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Leeds) and graduated with a double honours degree in [psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychology) and sociology in 1963. While a student at Leeds, he represented the institution on the quiz show *[University Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Challenge)*, playing on a team against the University of Manchester during the show's inaugural episode in 1962.[^5445][^5446]

##### Australia

Shortly after his graduation in 1963, he was recruited by the [University of Western Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Western_Australia) Adult Education Board to run their community arts programme. In 1967, he became a teaching fellow at the newly opened School of Sociology at the [University of New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_New_South_Wales) in Sydney. He was required to study towards a PhD thesis, but was informally promised a lectureship once completed.[^5447]

During this time he created a direct action reform movement called Alf (Action for Love and Freedom) and implemented what he called "The Fun Revolution". In 1968, he separated from his wife and his thesis was terminated due to insufficient progress. As his position was dependent on the continuation of his studies, he was consequently dismissed as a teaching fellow. The next year he was appointed as "Wizard" (effectively an events officer) of the University of New South Wales. He would also take on another persona, when elected as dictator of the student union. In late 1969, he was made Wizard by the [World University Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_University_Service) of Australia and toured university campuses throughout 1970. He was able to persuade the [Melbourne University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_University) Union Activities Department to appoint him their unpaid "[Cosmologer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmologer), Living Work of Art and [Shaman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaman)" in 1971. The vice-chancellor gave him the use of the Old Pathology Lecture Theatre for his classes in synthetic cosmology and the director of the [National Gallery of Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Gallery_of_Victoria) accepted the offer of his live body as a living work of art. At this time, shocked when the student pacifist society sent money to the [Viet Cong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viet_Cong), he founded [Alf's Imperial Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alf's_Imperial_Army) devoted to sensational but non-violent warfare and regularly organised battles on campus. He founded the [Imperial British Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_British_Conservative_Party) to provide a counterbalance to international [capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism) and the various forms of [Nazism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazism).[^5448] The Wizard produced an upside-down map using the [Hobo-Dyer projection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobo%E2%80%93Dyer_projection) which placed New Zealand and Australia top-centre.[^5449][^5450]

The Wizard stood unsuccessfully in three Australian federal elections, contesting [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Sydney) in [1969](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_results_for_the_Division_of_Sydney),[^5451] and [Kooyong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Kooyong) in [1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_results_for_the_Division_of_Kooyong)[^5452] and [1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_results_for_the_Division_of_Kooyong).[^5453]

##### New Zealand

In 1974, the Wizard migrated to [Christchurch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch) in New Zealand and began to speak on a ladder in [Cathedral Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_Square,_Christchurch). The city council attempted to have him arrested, but he became so popular that they made the square a [public speaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_speaking) area. Wearing his costume as a [false prophet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_prophet) of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England), or his wizard's pointy hat, he has spoken there at lunchtimes in the summer months.[^5454]

He confronted [Telecom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telecom_New_Zealand) over the colour of public telephone boxes, played for the local rugby team, heckled Christian [evangelist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelism) [Ray Comfort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_Comfort), evaded the compulsory [New Zealand census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_census) and performed [rain dances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rain_dance) in [Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_Region), [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland) and the Australian [outback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outback).

In 1982, the [New Zealand Art Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Art_Gallery_of_New_Zealand) directors association issued a statement that in their opinion the Wizard was an authentic living work of art and the [city council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch_City_Council) appointed him "Wizard of Christchurch". In 1990, the Prime Minister of New Zealand, [Mike Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Moore_%28New_Zealand_politician%29), an old friend, appointed him the official "Wizard of New Zealand".

With the help of the mayor, [Vicki Buck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicki_Buck), the city of Christchurch hosted a wizards' conclave in 1995 when visiting colleagues gathered to help build a wizard's nest on top of the university library tower, to witness the Wizard hatching from a giant egg in the city art gallery, sky diving whilst chanting a spell for a major rugby match and performing various rituals round the city. Soon afterwards, accompanied by 49 assistant wizards, he came down by gondola from the [Port Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Hills) with tablets bearing the address of his new website.[^5455]

He initially provided his services free. In 1998, the Christchurch City Council signed a contract with him to "provide acts of wizardry and other wizard-like-services - as part of promotional work for the city of Christchurch" for an annual fee of \$16,000. The Wizard also received financial support from his partner, Alice Flett.[^5456] In 1998, an autobiography titled *My Life as a Miracle* was published.[^5457]

On 8 September 2003, the Wizard's large wooden house was destroyed by a fire, which Christchurch police treated as arson. The "Wizardmobile", constructed from the front halves of two [VW Beetles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VW_Beetle), was also attacked and damaged.[^5458] The Wizard was awarded the [Queen's Service Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Service_Medal) in the [2009 Queen's Birthday Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Birthday_Honours_%28New_Zealand%29) for service to the community.[^5459]

After the February [2011 Christchurch earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Christchurch_earthquake), the Wizard planned to retire and permanently leave Christchurch, saying that the town he loved had gone and that it was the end of an era.[^5460] After it was announced by the [Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_Earthquake_Recovery_Authority) and the Anglican bishop that the remains of [Christchurch Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch_Cathedral) would be demolished, the Wizard returned to Christchurch to oppose the demolition.[^5461] The Wizard continues to speak on the need to preserve Christchurch's heritage buildings.

Between 2014 and 2021, Ari Freeman was the Wizard's apprentice.[^5462] He distanced himself from the Wizard due to the latter's "divisive politics" and public comments about women and [drag storytime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drag_Queen_Story_Hour) events.[^5463]

In October 2021, the Christchurch City Council ended its contract with the Wizard after twenty-three years of service.[^5464][^5465] The Wizard said he was disappointed but would continue to appear in the city.[^5466] The Wizard stood as a candidate in the [2022 Christchurch mayoral election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Christchurch_mayoral_election),[^5467] receiving 2,474 votes and coming in fifth place.[^5468]

#### Documentaries

*The Wizard of New Zealand QSM*, directed by Grant John Neville[^5469] and [director of photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_photography) Karlos Filipov, includes interviews with the Wizard, [Mike Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Moore_%28New_Zealand_politician%29) and many others.[^5470] Among other topics, the documentary details the Wizard's views that women cause wars through their shopping habits and that governments with monarchies are more stable. It was awarded Best Short Documentary at the [Beijing International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_International_Film_Festival) 2010,[^5471] and Best Film about Real People at the Official Best of Fest 2010.[^5472][^5473]

*The Wizard and the Commodore - Chathams Islands/New Zealand*, directed by Samuel A. Miller,[^5474] follows the subject on a trip to the [Chatham Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham_Islands), about 900 km east of mainland New Zealand. The film premiered on 1 July 2016 in New Zealand.[^5475]

### 1874 Argentine presidential election

Presidential elections were held in Argentina on 12 April 1874. [Nicolás Avellaneda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Avellaneda) was declared the winner of the elections. Supporters of rival candidate [Bartolomé Mitre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolom%C3%A9_Mitre) rebelled.[^5476]

#### Background

President [Domingo Faustino Sarmiento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domingo_Faustino_Sarmiento)'s pragmatic approach to Buenos Aires' demands and his successful control of separatist revolts in the north paved the way to high office for his vice president, Autonomist Party leader [Adolfo Alsina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolfo_Alsina). Alsina gained the support of a sizable faction of Mitre's Nationalist Party, resulting in the formation of the paramount political group in Argentina for the next 42 years: The [National Autonomist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Autonomist_Party) (PAN). Mitre himself did not support Alsina, however, whom he viewed as a veiled Buenos Aires separatist. The elder statesman ran for the presidency again, though the seasoned Alsina outmaneuvered him by fielding [Nicolás Avellaneda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicol%C3%A1s_Avellaneda), a moderate lawyer from remote [Tucumán Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tucum%C3%A1n_Province). The electoral college met on 12 April 1874, and awarded Mitre only three provinces, including Buenos Aires.

As he had repeatedly up to 1861, Mitre took up arms again. Hoping to prevent Avellaneda's 12 October inaugural, he mutineered a [gunboat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gunboat); he was defeated, however, and only President Avellaneda's [commutation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commutation_of_sentence) spared his life.[^5477]

### 2018 Makassar mayoral election

The **2018 Makassar mayoral election** took place on 27 June 2018 as part of the [simultaneous local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Indonesian_local_elections) in [Makassar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makassar), [South Sulawesi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sulawesi), [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia). It was held to elect the mayor of Makassar and the deputy mayor.

[Munafri Arifuddin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munafri_Arifuddin), who was supported by 10 from 11 political parties in the city's Regional People's Representative Council, was the only candidate in an [uncontested election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncontested_election). Incumbent mayor [Mohammad Ramdhan Pomanto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Ramdhan_Pomanto) initially registered to run for a second term as an independent candidate, but his candidacy was later revoked by a [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Indonesia) ruling.

Despite running as a single candidate, Arifuddin, who was the CEO of local football club [PSM Makassar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PSM_Makassar) and nephew of then-Indonesian vice president [Jusuf Kalla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jusuf_Kalla), lost the vote to an [empty ballot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/None_of_the_above) (*kotak kosong*), forcing the election to be repeated in 2020 and for an acting mayor to be appointed by the [Ministry of Home Affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Home_Affairs_%28Indonesia%29).[^5478] Although a lawsuit was brought to the [Constitutional Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Indonesia), the appeal was rejected, making the election the first in Indonesian electoral history in which an empty ballot won.

#### Timeline

The [KPU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komisi_Pemilihan_Umum) set a temporary voter count at 862,731 in March 2018, spread across 15 subdistricts.[^5479] The voters voted at 2,765 polling stations. A budget of Rp 60 billion (US\$4.35 million) was assigned for the election, of which 16.4 billion came from the 2017 budget and the rest from the 2018 fiscal year.[^5480] Registration for party-backed candidates was opened between 8 and 10 January 2018, while independent candidates were required to register between 22 and 26 November 2017.[^5481] The campaign period was from 15 February to 24 June, with a three-day [election silence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_silence) before voting on 27 June.[^5482] The vote itself follows a [first past the post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_past_the_post) system.[^5483]

The candidates were assigned their ballot numbers on 13 February 2018.[^5484]

#### Candidates

| Ballot number[^5484] | Candidate | Position | Running mate | Supporting parties |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| 1 | Munafri Arifuddin | CEO of [PSM Makassar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PSM_Makassar) | Rachmatika Dewi | [Nasdem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasdem_Party) [Golkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golkar) [PDI-P](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PDI-P) [Gerindra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerindra) [Hanura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanura) [PKS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partai_Keadilan_Sejahtera) [PKB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Awakening_Party) [PPP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Development_Party) [PKPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PKPI), [PBB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partai_Bulan_Bintang) Total: 43 seats[^5485] |

Munafri Arifuddin, a member of [Golkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golkar)[^5486] and nephew of the then-Vice President [Jusuf Kalla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jusuf_Kalla),[^5487] was supported by 10 parties.[^5488] Also the CEO of the [PSM Makassar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PSM_Makassar) football club, he had promised to keep this position if elected.[^5489] Arifuddin's running mate Rachmatika Dewi was a deputy speaker of the city council and the chief of [Nasdem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasdem) in Makassar.[^5490]

Although initially supported by some political parties, [Mohammad Ramdhan Pomanto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohammad_Ramdhan_Pomanto) registered with the KPU as an independent candidate, having collected 117,492 valid copies of ID cards out of the ~65,000 required as an independent candidate.[^5491] [Demokrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partai_Demokrat) was the only party represented in the [People's Representative Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Representative_Council) that officially supported him. Other parties declared their initial support to him, but withdrew later.[^5492] His running mate Indira Mulyasari was the deputy speaker of the city council, although she resigned for the election.[^5493]

In February, the Munafri-Dewi pair sued the local KPU in order to cancel Pomanto's candidacy, citing a case in which Pomanto distributed smartphones while serving as the city's mayor.[^5494] The South Sulawesi high court on national administration (*Pengadilan Tinggi Tata Usaha Negara*) on March 21 ordered the KPU to cancel Pomanto's candidacy.[^5495] The election body then brought the case to the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_Indonesia),[^5496] which upheld the PT TUN decision. Pomanto stated that he would continue pressing his case through the legal system.[^5497] However, the electoral commission decided to disqualify him following a closed-door meeting,[^5498] making the election an uncontested one. However, Arifuddin was still required to win a majority of the votes (voters could vote for an [empty ballot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/None_of_the_above)) or the elections would be redone in 2020.[^5499]

#### Aftermath

Following the announcement of the results, the Munafri-Dewi campaign team filed a lawsuit to the [Constitutional Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_Court_of_Indonesia), claiming "structured, systematic and massive cheating", accusing Pomanto of having interfered in favor of the "none of the above option" within his capacity as mayor, and demanding that the "none of the above" option/empty column be cancelled.[^5501] In 10 August, the court ruled against the appeal, hence awarding "victory" for the none of the above option - the first in Indonesian electoral history.[^5478][^5502]

The [repeat election was held in 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Makassar_mayoral_election), with Pomanto and Munafri both contesting the election with two other pairs of candidates. Pomanto would win the 2020 election with 41 percent of votes to secure a second term.[^5503] Munafri would contest the mayoralship again [in 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Makassar_mayoral_election), and was elected.[^5504]

### Dead mall

A **dead mall**,[^5505] also known as a **ghost mall** or **zombie mall**, is a [shopping mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shopping_mall) that has low consumer traffic or is deteriorating in some manner.[^5506]

Many malls in [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America) are considered "dead" when they have no surviving [anchor store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anchor_store) or successor that could attract people to the mall. Without the pedestrian traffic that department stores previously generated, sales volumes decline for almost all stores and rental revenues from those stores can no longer sustain the costly maintenance of the malls.[^5507][^5508]

#### Changes in the retail climate

Structural changes in the department-store industry have also made survival of these malls difficult. These changes have contributed to some areas or suburbs having insufficient traditional department stores to fill all the existing larger-lease-area *anchor spaces*. A few large national chains have replaced many local and regional chains, and some national chains are defunct.

In the [U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States) and [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada), newer "[big box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big-box_store)" chains (also referred to as "category killers") such as [Walmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walmart), [Target](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Target_Corporation) Corporation and [Best Buy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Buy) normally prefer purpose-built free-standing buildings rather than using mall-anchor spaces.[^5509] Twenty-first-century retailing trends favor open air [lifestyle centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lifestyle_center_%28retail%29); these centers resemble elements of [power centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_center_%28retail%29), big box stores, and strip malls; and (most disruptively for storefronts) [online shopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_shopping) over indoor malls.[^5510] The massive change led *[Newsweek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsweek)* to declare the indoor mall format obsolete in 2008.[^5511] The year 2007 marked the first time since the 1950s that no new malls were built in the United States.[^5509] Most Canadian malls still remain indoors after renovations due to the harsh winter climate throughout most of the country; however, the [Don Mills Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Mills_Centre) was turned into an open-air shopping plaza. Attitudes about malls have also been changing. With changing priorities, people have less time to spend driving to and strolling through malls and, during the [Great Recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Recession), specialty stores offered what many shoppers saw as useless luxuries they could no longer afford. In this respect, big box stores and conventional strip malls have a time-saving advantage.[^5512]

##### Demolition by neglect and failed redevelopment

Another cause for dead malls in the U.S. is "[demolition by neglect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demolition_by_neglect)" (DBN) which refers to allowing a mall to sit without any form of maintenance, redevelopment, or filling in vacant spaces until they are forced to sell the mall or if it no longer makes a profit, and such actions can not only lead to vacancies but also significant disrepair like failed [HVAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HVAC), a non-functional [fire sprinkler system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_sprinkler_system), and broken [escalators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Escalator). In severe cases, DBN can justify demolition of a mall, making renovations no longer viable for it (and potentially prohibitively expensive).

Some developers, such as [General Growth Properties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Growth_Properties) and [Simon Property Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Property_Group), are accused of neglecting underperforming malls only to focus on "Class-A" premier malls. Support for this accusation surfaced in 2011, when GGP, recently emerging from bankruptcy, spun off 30 underperforming properties to a new company: [Rouse Properties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rouse_Properties), which gets its name from [The Rouse Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rouse_Company). The new company would not redevelop failing malls, and instead would let them sit until they can no longer make a profit, like [Collin Creek Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collin_Creek_Mall) in [Plano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plano,_Texas).[^5513] Simon also spun off 44 underperforming properties in a new company: Washington Prime Group.[^5514][^5515]

The most notable companies accused of DBN include [Ashkenazy Acquisition Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Ashkenazy) for lack of maintenance and adequate security,[^5516] [Namdar Realty Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namdar_Realty_Group) and [Mason Asset Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mason_Asset_Management) for financial exploitation and letting properties deteriorate,[^5517] [Kohan Retail Investment Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kohan_Retail_Investment_Group) for also allowing properties to deteriorate,[^5518] and Moonbeam Capital Investments for cutting costs by disabling important safety components in their properties, such as [HVAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HVAC), sometimes leading to [fire suppression system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_suppression_system) failures.[^5519] Notable cases of malls that have become dead or defunct due to DBN include [Harborplace Festival Marketplace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harborplace_Festival_Marketplace) in [Baltimore, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore,_Maryland), [Marley Station Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marley_Station_Mall) in [Glen Burnie, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_Burnie,_Maryland), [Burlington Center Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington_Center_Mall) in [Burlington Township, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burlington_Township,_New_Jersey), and [Faneuil Hall Marketplace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faneuil_Hall_Marketplace) in [Boston, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Massachusetts).[^5520]

The number of dead malls has increased significantly because the economic health of malls across the United States has been in decline, with high vacancy rates in many of these malls.[^5521] From 2006 to 2010, the percentage of malls that are considered to be "dying" by real estate experts (have a vacancy rate of at least 40%), unhealthy (20-40%), or in trouble (10-20%) all increased greatly, and these high vacancy rates only partially decreased from 2010 to 2014.[^5521] In 2014, nearly 3% of all malls in the United States were considered to be "dying" (40% or higher vacancy rates) and nearly one-fifth of all malls had vacancy rates considered "troubling" (10% or higher).[^5521]

Some real estate experts say the "fundamental problem" is a glut of malls in many parts of the country creating a market that is "extremely over-retailed".[^5521] Cowen Research reported that the number of malls in the U.S. grew more than twice as fast as the population between 1970 and 2015; Cowen also reported that shopping center "gross leasable area" in the U.S. is 40 percent more shopping space per capita than Canada and five times more than the U.K.[^5522]

Some malls have maintained profitability, particularly in areas with frequent inclement weather (or otherwise weather undesirable for outdoor activities, such as shopping in an open-air shopping/lifestyle center) or large populations of senior citizens who can partake in [mall walking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mall_walking).[^5523] Combined with lower rents, these factors have led to companies like [Simon Malls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Property_Group) enjoying high profits and occupancy averages of 92%.[^5524] Some retailers have also begun to re-evaluate the mall environment, a positive sign for the industry.[^5525]

A [retail apocalypse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retail_apocalypse) that started in the 2010s made the dead mall situation even more noticeable. This is due to the complete closing of several retailers, as well as anchor tenants [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's) and [JCPenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JCPenney) closing many locations and the sharp decline in [Sears Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears_Holdings). The trend was particularly noticeable when [Pittsburgh Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Mills), a mall once worth as much as \$190 million, was sold at a [foreclosure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreclosure) sale for \$100, with the mall itself being purchased by [lien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lien) holder [Wells Fargo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Fargo).[^5526][^5527]

#### Demographic change

It has been suggested that some malls die when the surrounding neighborhoods undergo a [demographic change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographic_change) or [socio-economic decline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socio-economic_mobility_in_the_United_States).[^5509]

#### COVID-19 pandemic

The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated many issues affecting malls.[^5528] During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic), many malls closed temporarily due to [stay-at-home orders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stay-at-home_orders).[^5529][^5530] A number of notable retailers filed for bankruptcy during the pandemic including [Ascena Retail Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascena_Retail_Group), [Brooks Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooks_Brothers), [GNC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GNC_%28store%29), [JCPenney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._C._Penney), [Lord & Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_&_Taylor), and [Neiman Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neiman_Marcus).

North American malls that have permanently closed citing the pandemic as a precipitating factor include [Northgate Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northgate_Mall_%28Durham%29) in Durham, North Carolina, [Cascade Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cascade_Mall) in Burlington, Washington, and the [Metrocenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metrocenter_%28Phoenix,_Arizona%29) in Phoenix, Arizona.

#### Redevelopment

Dead malls are occasionally redeveloped. Leasing or management companies may change the architecture, layout, decor, or other component of a shopping center to attract more renters and draw more profits. Several dead malls have been significantly renovated into open-air shopping centers.[^5531]

Redevelopment can involve a switch from retail usage to office or educational use for a building, such as in the case with [Eastgate Metroplex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastgate_Metroplex) in [Tulsa, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulsa,_Oklahoma),[^5532] [Park Central Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Central_Mall) in [Phoenix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix,_Arizona), [Eastmont Town Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastmont_Town_Center) in [Oakland, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland,_California), [Windsor Park Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor_Park_Mall) in [San Antonio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio) (which became the global headquarters of [Rackspace Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rackspace_Technology)), [Global Mall at the Crossings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Mall_at_the_Crossings) in [Nashville, Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee), and the [Coral Springs Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_Springs_Mall) in Florida. Allegheny Center Mall, a retail mall just north of downtown [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania), closed as a retail mall in the early 1990s. The mall was redeveloped into office space with much of the space taken by telecommunications carriers, [data center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_center) operators, and [Internet service providers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_service_provider), and became a major [carrier hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrier_hotel) serving southwestern Pennsylvania. Another use for a former mall occurred in [Lexington, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexington,_Kentucky), where [Lexington Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lexington_Mall) was partially demolished and converted into a [satellite worship center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-site_church) for a [local megachurch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southland_Christian_Church_%28Lexington,_Kentucky%29).

Conversion from a shopping mall into an open-air, mixed-use area may entail the demolition of parts of or all of the former shopping mall. An example of this came from [Fairfax County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_County,_Virginia), where the former Springfield Mall was converted into [Springfield Town Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springfield_Town_Center), a [mixed-use development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-use_development) that includes a twelve-screen movie theatre, shops, and restaurants with outdoor seating and entrances. When the structures are demolished completely, it is known as a [greyfield site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyfield_land). In jurisdictions such as [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont) (with a strict permitting process) or in major urban areas (where open fields are long gone), this greyfielding can be much easier and cheaper than building on a [greenfield site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenfield_site). An example of this type of redevelopment is [Prestonwood Town Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prestonwood_Town_Center) in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas) and [Voorhees Town Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voorhees_Town_Center) in [Voorhees Township](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voorhees_Township,_New_Jersey), [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey). Also, in [Boardman, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boardman_Township,_Ohio), the [Southern Park Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Park_Mall) demolished the former [Sears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears) building to construct DeBartolo Commons, named after [Edward J. DeBartolo Sr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_J._DeBartolo_Sr.) founder of the [Edward J. DeBartolo Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_J._DeBartolo_Corporation).[^5533]

[Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_%28company%29), [FedEx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FedEx), [DHL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DHL), [UPS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Parcel_Service) and the [United States Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Postal_Service) have acquired the sites of some former malls and converted them to fulfillment centers.[^5534] A proposal called "Re-Habit"[^5535] uses portions of struggling malls, particularly vacated big box space, for homeless housing.[^5536] As an example of this concept, the vacant [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's) in the [Landmark Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landmark_Mall) of [Alexandria, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria,_Virginia), has been converted into a temporary homeless shelter[^5537] for the Carpenter's Shelter.[^5538]

Some major healthcare systems such as Vanderbilt Health and the University of Rochester (UR) Health have converted several dying malls into new "health malls" or "mall to medicine". The large spaces allow for the easy conversion of space-intensive activities such as ambulatory surgical centers, while the multiple storefronts facilitate "one stop shopping" for all of health related needs. Roughly half of [100 Oaks Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/100_Oaks_Mall) in Nashville, Tennessee, became part of [Vanderbilt University Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_University_Medical_Center).[^5539] Following the model, it is expanding to other dead or dying malls throughout its region,[^5540] while [University of Rochester Medical Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Rochester_Medical_Center) has converted roughly one-third of [The Marketplace Mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Marketplace_Mall) in [Henrietta, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrietta,_New_York).[^5541]
