### Money burning

**Money burning** or **burning money** is the purposeful act of destroying [money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money). In the prototypical example, [banknotes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banknote) are destroyed by setting them on [fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire). Burning money decreases the [wealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wealth) of the owner without directly enriching any particular party. It also reduces the [money supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_supply) and (very slightly) slows down the [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation) rate.

Money is usually burned to communicate a message, either for artistic effect, as a form of protest, or as a [signal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signalling_%28economics%29). The burning of money is illegal in some jurisdictions.[^5542]

#### Macroeconomic effect

For the purposes of [macroeconomics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macroeconomics), burning money is equivalent to removing the money from circulation, and locking it away forever; the salient feature is that no one may ever use the money again. Burning money shrinks the [money supply](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Money_supply), and is therefore a special case of [contractionary monetary policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contractionary_monetary_policy) that can be implemented by anyone. In the usual case, the [central bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_bank) withdraws money from circulation by selling government bonds or foreign currency. The difference with money burning is that the central bank does not have to exchange any assets of value for the money burnt. Money burning is thus equivalent to gifting the money back to the central bank (or other money issuing authority). If the economy is at [full employment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Full_employment) equilibrium, shrinking the money supply causes [deflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deflation) (or decreases the rate of [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation)), increasing the real value of the money left in circulation.

Assuming that the burned money is [paper money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paper_money) with negligible intrinsic value, no real [goods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_%28economics%29) are destroyed, so the overall wealth of the world is unaffected. Instead, all surviving money slightly increases in value; everyone gains wealth in proportion to the amount of money they already hold.[^5543] Economist [Steven Landsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Landsburg) proposes in *[The Armchair Economist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Armchair_Economist)* that burning one's fortune (in paper money) is a form of [philanthropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philanthropy) more [egalitarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egalitarianism) than deeding it to the [United States Treasury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Treasury).[^5543] In 1920, [Thomas Nixon Carver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Nixon_Carver) wrote that dumping money into the sea is better for society than spending it wastefully, as the latter wastes the [labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_economics) that it hires.[^5544]

##### Opposites

Central banks routinely collect and destroy worn-out coins and banknotes in exchange for new ones. This does not affect the money supply, and is done to maintain a healthy population of usable currency. The practice raises an interesting possibility. If an individual can steal the money before it is incinerated, the effect is the opposite of burning money; the thief is enriched at the expense of the rest of society. [One such incident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughton_incinerator_thefts) at the [Bank of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_England) inspired the 2001 TV movie *[Hot Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Money)* and the 2008 film *[Mad Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad_Money_%28film%29)*.[^5545]

Another, more common near-opposite is the creation of [counterfeit money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterfeit_money). Undetected counterfeit decreases the value of existing money, one of the reasons why attempting to pass it is illegal in most jurisdictions and is aggressively investigated.[^5546] Another way to analyze the cost of forgery is to consider the effects of a central bank's [monetary policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monetary_policy). Taking the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States) as an example, if the [Federal Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve) decides that the monetary base should be a given amount, then every \$100 bill forged is a bill the Fed cannot print and use to buy [Treasury bonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasury_bonds). The [interest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interest_%28economics%29) earnings (after expenses) on those bonds is turned over to the US Treasury, so any lost interest must be made up by U.S. [taxpayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxpayer), who therefore bear the cost of counterfeiting.[^5547]

#### Rationales

Behaviorally speaking, burning money is usually seen as a purely negative act. The cognitive impact of burning money can even be a useful motivational tool: patients who suffer from [nail biting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nail_biting) may be trained to burn a dollar bill every time they engage in the habit. One study found this form of suppression training by self-punishment to be effective compared to control groups, although not as effective as substitution training.[^5548]

On the other hand, there are some situations where burning money might not be so unreasonable. It is said[^5549] that the ancient Greek philosopher [Aristippus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristippus) was once on a ship at sea when he was threatened by pirates; he took out his money, counted it, and dropped it into the sea, commenting, "Better for the money to perish because of Aristippus than vice versa." [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero) would later cite this episode as an example of a circumstance that must be considered in its full context: "...it is a useless act to throw money into the sea; but not with the design which Aristippus had when he did so."[^5550]

Since around 2015, the UK has experienced a surge of interest in money burning. This has been noted in both the book *The Mysterium* [^5551] and in a *Kindred Spirit* article that is reprinted in [International Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Times).[^5552] An annual Mass Burn Event - where people are invited to burn money - is held at the [Cockpit Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cockpit_Theatre) in London every autumn.[^5553][^5554]

##### Symbolism

Publicly burning money can be an act of protest or a kind of artistic statement. Often the point is to emphasize money's intrinsic worthlessness.[^5543]

In 1984, [Serge Gainsbourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serge_Gainsbourg) burned a 500 [French franc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_franc) note on television to protest against heavy taxation.[^5555]

On 23 August 1994, the [K Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K_Foundation) (an art duo consisting of [Bill Drummond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Drummond) and [Jimmy Cauty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Cauty)) [burned one million pounds sterling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K_Foundation_Burn_a_Million_Quid) in cash on the Scottish island of [Jura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jura,_Scotland). This money represented the bulk of the K Foundation's funds, earned by Drummond and Cauty as [The KLF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_KLF), one of the United Kingdom's most successful pop groups of the early 1990s. The duo have never fully explained their motivations for the burning.[^5556]

In the 1995 film *[Dead Presidents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Presidents)*, the [title sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_sequence) directed by [Kyle Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyle_Cooper) features close shots of burning [U.S. bills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Reserve_Note); it took two days of shooting and experimenting with the paper to get the effect right.[^5557]

In the early 18th century, [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City) courts would publicly burn the *counterfeit* bills they gathered, to show that they were both dangerous and worthless.[^5558]

In traditional [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China) and Vietnamese [ancestor veneration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancestor_veneration), imitation money in the form of [joss paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_paper) are ceremonially burned, with the aspiration that the dead may use the money to finance a more comfortable afterlife.

In 2010, the spokesperson for the Swedish [Feminist Initiative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminist_Initiative_%28Sweden%29), [Gudrun Schyman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudrun_Schyman), burned [SEK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_krona) 100,000 during a speech about the inequality in wages for men and women.[^5559]

In 2018, a collective of artists called Distributed Gallery have created a machine named Chaos Machine which burns banknotes and turns them into cryptocurrencies while playing music.[^5560]

##### Game theory

In [game theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_theory), a threat to burn money can affect the strategies of the players involved; a classic example is the situation described as '[battle of the sexes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_sexes_%28game_theory%29)', where the ability to burn money allows the player to achieve the desired equilibrium without actually having to burn money.[^5561][^5562]

##### For commodity value

[Fiat money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiat_money) can sometimes be destroyed by converting it into [commodity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commodity) form, rather than completely forfeiting the value of the money. Sometimes, currency intended for use as fiat money becomes more valuable as a commodity, usually when [inflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation) causes its [face value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Face_value) to fall below its intrinsic value. For example, in [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India) in 2007, [Rupee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupee) coins disappeared from the market when their face value dropped below the value of the stainless steel from which they were made.[^5563] Similarly, in 1965, the US government had to switch from silver to copper-nickel clad [quarter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarter_%28United_States_coin%29) coins because the silver value of the coins had exceeded their face value and were being melted down by individuals for profit. The same occurred to [5-franc coins of Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_franc_coins), which up to the year 1969 were minted using a [silver alloy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_alloy). At the peak of [hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperinflation_in_the_Weimar_Republic), people burned banknotes for warmth, as their face value had fallen below their value as fuel.[^5547]

#### Legality

The legality of money burning varies with jurisdiction.

##### Australia

Section 16 of the *Crimes (Currency) Act 1981* prohibits deliberate damage and destruction of Australian money without a relevant legal permit. The law covers both current Australian money and historical coins and notes. Breaking this law can lead to detention or a fine.[^5564]

According to this law, even writing words on a banknote can be punished.[^5565]

##### Brazil

In Brazil, whether it is illegal for a person to burn their own money is a controversial topic.[^5566] It is not mentioned explicitly in Brazilian law. João Sidney Figueiredo Filho,[^5567] has affirmed that "when money is inside the Central Bank, then it is the property of the National Treasury. When it leaves, it is not." But the chief of police Jéferson Botelho Pereira has concluded that "whoever rips money is committing a crime against the property of the Union".[^5568]

The production of paper money by the State Bank is under the exclusive authority of the Central Bank, and is issued by the Brazilian Union.[^5569] By that reasoning, the paper on which the money is printed is the property of the State, and its intrinsic value belongs to the person. Articles 98 and 99 of the New Brazilian Civil Code give "money" its own definition. This is because a banknote cannot become a common good, if the owner himself decides to keep it in his possession indefinitely. This makes money different from other state assets such as rivers, seas, streets, roads and piazzas, which are all immobile.

##### Canada

The Currency Act states that "no person shall melt down, break up or use otherwise than as currency any coin that is legal tender in Canada." Similarly, Section 456 of The Criminal Code of Canada says: "Every one who (a) defaces a current coin, or (b) utters a current coin that has been defaced, is guilty of an offence punishable on summary conviction."

However neither the Currency Act nor Criminal Code mention paper currency. It therefore remains legal to completely destroy paper currency.[^5570]

##### Eurozone

According to the [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission)'s Recommendation dated 22 March 2010,[^5571] "[Member states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union) must not prohibit or punish the complete destruction of small quantities of [Euro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro) coins or notes when this happens in private. However they must prohibit the unauthorised destruction of large amounts of Euro coins or notes." Also, "Member states must not encourage the mutilation of Euro notes or coins for artistic purposes, but they are required to tolerate it. Mutilated coins or notes should be considered unfit for circulation."

The [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union) defines "falsifying or fraudulently altering money in any way" as a crime.[^5572] Also, according to the EU ruling 1210/2010, "all money that is unfit for circulation must be delivered to the relevant national authority". EU countries must remove the currency from circulation and reimburse the holder",[^5573] no matter what the country of issue.[^5574]

The [European Central Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank) has established that "Member states may refuse to reimburse Euro money that has been deliberately rendered unfit for circulation, or where it has been caused by a process that would predictably have led to the money becoming unfit. The exception to this is money collected for charitable purposes, such as coins thrown into a fountain".[^5575] The ECB legal department also states "the ECB will refuse to replace money that has been stamped for advertising purposes".[^5576]

The European Union provides an obligation at the community level to retire "neutralized" notes from circulation, or those rendered unfit for security systems.[^5577]

##### New Zealand

Section 154 of the *Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act 2021* makes it an offence to wilfully deface, disfigure, or mutilate any bank note in [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand). The penalty is a fine of up to [NZ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NZD)\$1,000.[^5578]

##### Philippines

By Presidential Decree No. 247, willful mutilation of coins or notes is punishable by a fine of up to [₱](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_peso)20,000, imprisonment up to 5 years, or both.[^5579]

##### Singapore

Singapore's Currency Act states that any person who mutilate, destroy, deface, or causes any change (to diminish value/utility of) currency note or coin is fined up to \$2,000.[^5580]

##### Sri Lanka

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka Act No.16 of 2023 makes mutilation of bank notes an offence punishable by imprisonment, a fine, or both.[^5581]

##### Taiwan

Intentionally damaging coins or notes, and rendering them unusable, is fined up to 5 times the nominal value of such coins or notes.[^5582]

##### Turkey

In [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey), defacement or destruction of banknotes can be punished with fines or with prison sentences.[^5583][^5584]

##### United Kingdom

The [Currency and Bank Notes Act 1928](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Currency_and_Bank_Notes_Act_1928) is an Act of the Parliament of the United Kingdom relating to banknotes. Among other things, it makes it a criminal offence to deface a banknote (but not to destroy one). Under Section 10 of the [Coinage Act 1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coinage_Act_1971) "No person shall, except under the authority of a licence granted by the Treasury, melt down or break up any metal coin which is for the time being current in the United Kingdom or which, having been current there, has at any time after 16th May 1969 ceased to be so." As the process of creating [elongated coins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elongated_coins) does not require them to be melted nor broken up, however, Section 10 does not apply and coin elongation is legal within the UK with penny press machines.

##### United States

In the United States, burning banknotes is prohibited under [18 U.S.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_18_of_the_United_States_Code) [§ 333](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/333): *Mutilation of national bank obligations*, which includes "any other thing" that renders a note "unfit to be reissued".[^5585] In an *[amicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amicus_curiae)* brief for *[Atwater v. City of Lago Vista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atwater_v._City_of_Lago_Vista)*, [Solicitor General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Solicitor_General) [Seth Waxman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seth_P._Waxman) writes that arresting an individual who removes the corner dollar values "may expose a counterfeiting operation".[^5586] It is unclear if the statute has ever been applied in response to the complete destruction of a bill. Certainly people have publicly burned small amounts of money for political protests that were picked up by the media, [Living Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_Things_%28band%29) at [South by Southwest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_by_Southwest),[^5587] [Larry Kudlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Kudlow) on *[The Call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Call_%28CNBC%29)*, both in 2009[^5588], without apparent consequence.

The question of legality has been compared to the much more politically charged issue of [flag desecration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_desecration). It can be argued that the desecration of the flag is comparable to the desecration of a photograph of Legal Tender (provided it was modified as to not violate counterfeiting laws). In 1989, in a [Senate Judiciary Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_the_Judiciary) hearing on the [Flag Protection Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_Protection_Act), [William Barr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Barr) testified that any regulation protecting something purely for its symbolic value would be struck down as unconstitutional. The Senate report recommending passage of the Act argued that Barr's theory would render 18 U.S.C. § 333 unconstitutional as well.[^5589] In a dissent in *[Smith v. Goguen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith_v._Goguen)*, Justice [Rehnquist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Rehnquist) counted 18 U.S.C. § 333 in a group of statutes in which the Government protects its interest in some private property which is "not a traditional property interest".[^5590] On the other hand, the Government's interest in protecting circulating currency might not be purely symbolic; it costs the [Bureau of Engraving and Printing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Engraving_and_Printing) approximately 5 cents to replace a note.[^5585]

*Legal Tender*,[^5591] a 1996 [telerobotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telerobotics) art installation by [Ken Goldberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Goldberg), [Eric Paulos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Paulos), [Judith Donath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Donath), and [Mark Pauline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Pauline), was an experiment to see if the law could instill a sense of physical risk in online interactions. After participants were advised that 18 U.S.C. § 333 threatened them with up to six months in jail, they were given the option of remotely defacing small portions of a pair of "purportedly authentic" \$100 bills over the web. A crime may be occurring, but "only if the bills are real, the web site is authentic, and the experiment actually performed."[^5592] In fact, one bill was real and the other counterfeit.[^5593] Almost all of the participants reported that they believed the experiment and the bills to be faked.[^5594]

The destruction of money is also bound by the same laws that govern the destruction of other personal property. In particular, one cannot empower the [executor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executor) of one's [estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estate_%28law%29) to burn one's money after one dies.[^5595]

### Zero-rupee note

A **zero-rupee note** is a [banknote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banknote) imitation issued in [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India) as a means of helping to fight systemic [political corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_corruption). The notes are "paid" in protest by angry citizens to [government functionaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functionary) who solicit [bribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bribery) in return for services which are supposed to be free. Zero-rupee notes, which are made to resemble the old 50-[rupee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_rupee) [banknote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banknote) of India, are the creation of a [non-governmental organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organization) known as 5th Pillar which has, since their inception in 2007, distributed over 2.5 million notes as of August 2014. The notes remain in current use and thousands of notes are distributed every month.

#### History

##### Corruption in India

Bribery, the offering or solicitation of items of value to influence the actions of a government official, is recognized as a pervasive problem in India, with the 2010 report by anti-corruption watchdog organization [Transparency International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transparency_International) ranking India in 87th place on its [Corruption Perceptions Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corruption_Perceptions_Index).[^5596] A 2005 study published by Transparency International India indicated that as many of 62% of Indian citizens had first-hand experience of having paid a bribe or used an illicit "contact" to get a government job done.[^5597]

The 2005 Transparency International India study was the largest study of the Indian bribery problem ever undertaken, with 14,405 respondents from 20 states contributing.[^5598] The survey focused on [petty corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petty_corruption) experienced by common citizens in daily life, rather than upon the large-scale corruption of the rich and powerful.[^5598]

The 2005 study exposed chronic graft problems, with substantial numbers of survey respondents reporting direct experience in being forced to pay bribes to the police (80%), land administration (48%), and judiciary (47%).[^5599] Majorities of survey respondents characterized the police, judiciary, land administration, municipal government, electricity supply system, government hospital system, ration card system, water supply system, and system of assessing individual income taxes as corrupt.[^5599] Fully 45% of survey respondents believed that there was corruption as well in the primary school system.[^5599]

##### Origin of zero-rupee notes

In 2007, a [non-profit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit_organization) known as 5th Pillar created the zero-rupee note as a means for Indians to register their refusal to participate in bribery. Closely patterned after the nation's fifty-rupee notes, these documents instead included anti-corruption slogans "Eliminate corruption at all levels" and "I promise to neither accept nor give bribe."[^5600]

These zero-rupee notes were designed for use by Indian citizens who have been requested to pay bribes in order to obtain services that are legally free or who are hit with illicit surcharges on such routine government transactions as obtaining a [driver's license](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Driver's_license).[^5601] Such currency devices enable the citizen to register their opposition to the illegal request in a tangible form, "paying" the official with these valueless alternative notes.

"The note is a way for any human being to say no to corruption without the fear of facing an encounter with persons in authority", 5th Pillar said in an official statement.[^5602]

President of 5th Pillar, Vijay Anand, expressed satisfaction with the program's efficacy: "People have already started using them and it is working. One [auto rickshaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auto_rickshaw) driver was pulled over by a policeman in the middle of the night who said he could go if he was "taken care of". The driver gave him the note instead. The policeman was shocked but smiled and let him go. The purpose of this is to instill confidence in people to say no to bribery."[^5600]

In addition to registering the individual's protest, zero-rupee notes provide corrupt officials with a sign that efforts are ongoing to fight systemic government corruption. Use of the notes is intended to shame or scare [bureaucrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureaucrat) into honest behavior by reminding these officials that laws against bribery exist.[^5601]

While the zero-rupee notes appear similar to a genuine Indian fifty-rupee note, they are not issued by the Indian government and are thus not [legal tender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_tender). Only one side of the note is printed to resemble currency so as not to run afoul of [counterfeiting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterfeiting) laws.[^5600]

According to 5th Pillar, Indian citizens pay approximately £3 billion (about \$4.9 billion) in bribes each year, a figure considered to be substantially understated by many government insiders.[^5602]

##### Circulation and legacy

Satindar Mohan Bhagat, an [Indian expatriate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-resident_Indian) who is a [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics) professor at the [University of Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maryland) and the director of Association for India's Development, Inc. US, is credited with originating the concept of the zero-rupee note in 2001.[^5603] Upon returning to India for a visit, Bhagat was frustrated by the petty [extortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extortion) demands of government officials that were part of daily life and conceived of the idea of a zero-rupee note as a polite way of declining participation.[^5603] The charity 5th Pillar put Bhagat's idea into practice.[^5603]

5th Pillar began the campaign in the spring of 2007 with a first printing of 25,000 notes that were distributed in the Indian city of [Chennai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chennai).[^5600] Buoyed by the success of the campaign, additional printings followed and use of the zero-rupee note spread across the nation. From their inception through August 2014, 5th Pillar distributed over 2.5 million zero-rupee notes.[^5601]

Zero-rupee notes have been issued in five of the 22 [scheduled languages of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Languages_with_official_status_in_India): [Tamil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamil_language), [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi), [Kannada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannada), [Malayalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam), and [Telugu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telugu_language).[^5604]

This concept for use in the fight against corruption has recently been adopted from 5th Pillar to few other nations suffering from endemic government bribery problems including [Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemen), [Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana), [Benin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benin), [Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico) and [Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal).[^5601]

As of 2015, 5th Pillar expanded the zero-rupee note concept beyond India to other country currencies, on the website ZeroCurrency.org.

### Commission Regulation (EC) No. 2257/94

**Commission Regulation (EC) No. 2257/94 of 16 September 1994 laying down quality standards for bananas**, sometimes referred to in the media as the **bendy banana law**, is a [European Union regulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union_regulation) specifying classification standards for bananas, which took effect on 1 January 1995.[^5605] It was replaced by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 1333/2011 of 19 December 2011 laying down marketing standards for bananas, rules on the verification of compliance with those marketing standards and requirements for notifications in the banana sector with effect as of 9 January 2012.[^5606]

#### Provisions

The regulation applies to unripened green bananas and thus to growers and wholesalers, rather than retailers.[^5607] The main provisions of the regulation were that bananas sold as unripened, and green bananas, should be green and unripened, firm and intact, fit for human consumption, not "affected by rotting", clean, free of pests and damage from pests, free from deformation or abnormal curvature, free from bruising, free of any foreign smell or taste.[^5605] The minimum size (with tolerances and exceptions) is a length of 14 cm and a thickness (grade) of 2.7 cm. It specifies minimum standards for specific quality classifications of bananas (Extra, Class I, Class II).[^5605] Only Extra bananas have to comply fully with the shape specifications. Class II bananas, for instance are permitted to have "defects of shape", and Class I bananas are permitted only "slight defects of shape".[^5605][^5608] This is not true, however, of the size specifications; sale of bananas below the minimum size is almost always prohibited (with exceptions only for bananas from a few regions where bananas are traditionally smaller).[^5605]

#### Applicability

Regulation No. 2257/94 took effect on 1 January 1995. It applied directly, in its entirety, in all [member states of the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union).[^5605] It was repealed by Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) **No. 1333/2011** of 19 December 2011, laying down marketing standards for bananas, rules on the verification of compliance with those marketing standards and requirements for notifications in the banana sector with effect as of 9 January 2012.[^5606] However, the sections of the regulations concerning quality standards for bananas, which include Minimum Requirements and Classification, were brought forwards unaltered from the earlier regulation, so in the new regulation there was no change to the shape requirements, as summarised above under Provisions.

#### Euromyth

This regulation requires that bananas as a minimum standard must not have "abnormal curvature"[^5609] although no definition or guidance was given about the degree of curvature that would be regarded as "abnormal". That led to various stories about an EU ban on curved bananas.[^5610] It has been frequently repeated by [Europhiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europhile) and [Eurosceptics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurosceptics) alike, the former tending to regard it as an apocryphal or misleading [Euromyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euromyth)[^5610] and the latter regarding it as an example of needless European bureaucracy.[^5611]

On 29 July 2008, the European Commission held a preliminary vote concerning the repeal of certain regulations related to the quality of specific fruit and vegetables that included provisions related to size and shape. According to the Commission's press release, "In this era of high prices and growing demand, it makes no sense to throw these products away or destroy them." The Agriculture Commissioner stated, "This is a concrete example of our drive to cut red tape and I will continue to push until it goes through. \[...\] It shouldn't be the EU's job to regulate these things. It is far better to leave it to market operators".[^5612]

Regulation 1221/2008 took effect as of 1 July 2009. Though neither the press release cited above nor Regulation 1221/2008 made any mention of bananas or Regulation 2257/94, some reports of the changes treated them as including the banana quality standards regulation and contained explicit or apparent references to the regulation by using expressions such as "the infamous 'straight banana' ruling".[^5613][^5614] Some sources have claimed that to be an admission that the original regulations indeed banned "bent bananas".[^5615][^5616]

### Horse theft

**Horse theft** is the [crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime) of stealing [horses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse). A person engaged in stealing horses is known as a **horse thief**. Historically, punishments were often severe for horse theft, with several cultures pronouncing the sentence of death upon actual or presumed thieves. Several societies were formed in the United States to prevent horse theft and apprehend horse thieves. However, horse theft continues to occur throughout the world as horses are stolen for their [meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_meat), for ransom, or in disputes between their owners and other persons. Before the invention of the [automobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car), horses were considered essential as there were few ways to call for help and travel long-distance.

Horse theft today is comparable to [automobile theft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motor_vehicle_theft), a crime punishable by felony jail time in most countries.

#### History

##### Europe

Horse theft was a well-known crime in [medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Europe) and [early modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_Europe) times and was severely prosecuted in many areas. While many crimes were punished through ritualized shaming or banishment, horse theft often brought severe punishment, including [branding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_branding), torture, exile and even death.[^5617] According to one 18th century treatise, the use of death as a punishment for horse theft stretches back as far as the first century AD, when the Germanic [Chauci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chauci) tribe would sentence horse thieves to death, while murderers would be sentenced to a fine. This practice derived from the wealth of the populace being in the form of livestock which ranged over large areas, meaning that the theft of animals could only be prevented through fear of the harsh punishment that would result.[^5618]

Horse theft was harshly punished in the French [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux) region in the 15th-18th centuries. Punishments ranged from [whipping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagellation) to a lifetime sentence of service on a [galley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galley) ship, a severe punishment shared by perpetrators of [incest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incest), homicide and poisoning.[^5619]

In [19th-century Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire), the theft of livestock (including horses) made up approximately 16 percent of thefts of peasant property; however, there were no reported thefts of horses from estate property. The offense of stealing a horse was the most severely punished of any theft on Russian estates, due to the importance of horses in day-to-day living. Flogging was the usual punishment for horse thieves, combined with the shaving of heads and beards, and fines of up to three times the value of the horse if the animal had been sold.[^5620]

Since [Henry VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_VIII)'s reign, horse theft was considered a serious crime in England.[^5621] It was made a [non-clergyable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benefit_of_clergy) crime in 1597-1598 and 1601.[^5622] For the rural English county of [Berkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkshire) in the 18th century, horse theft was considered a major property crime, along with stealing from dwellings or warehouses, sheep theft, [highway robbery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highway_robbery) and other major thefts.[^5623] In [Essex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essex) in the 18th century, some [assize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assize) judges decided to execute every horse thief convicted to deter the crime.[^5621] From around the 1750s until 1818, between 13% and 14% of persons convicted of horse theft in [Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Counties), [Norfolk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norfolk), and Western [circuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circuit_court) were executed.[^5624] The [punishment of death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_the_United_Kingdom) for stealing horses was abolished in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland) in 1832, upon the passage of a bill sponsored by [William Ewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Ewart_%28British_politician%29); the legislation, which passed over the strong objections of [Peel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Peel) in the [Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom) and [Lord Wynford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Best,_1st_Baron_Wynford) in the [Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords), also abolished the death penalty in Britain for the theft of sheep and cattle, and for larceny in a dwelling house; Parliament had abolished the death sentence for most larcenies in a [separate bill the same year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forgery,_Abolition_of_Punishment_of_Death_Act_1832).[^5625] By the time of its abolition, actual executions for horse theft had been rare for 50 years.[^5626]

##### United States

The term horse thief came into great popularity in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States) during the 19th century. During that time the [Great Plains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Plains) states, [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas), and other western states were sparsely populated and largely unpoliced. As farmers tilled the land and [migrants headed west](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manifest_Destiny) through the Great Plains, their horses became subject to theft. Since these farmers and migrants depended on their horses, horse thieves garnered a particularly pernicious reputation because they left their victims helpless or greatly handicapped by the loss of their horses. The victims needed their horses for transportation and farming. Such depredation led to the use of the term horse thief as an [insult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insult), one that conveys the impression of the person who perpetrated the insult as one lacking any shred of [moral decency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_obligation).[^5627]

In Pennsylvania, the "An Act to Increase the Punishments of Horse Stealing" law was passed in 1780 and repealed in 1860, which stated people guilty of such a crime should be [branded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_branding). The law ran as follows; *"the first offense \[the convicted\] shall stand in the pillory for one hour, and shall be publicly whipped on his, her or their \[bare\] backs with thirty-nine lashes, well laid on, and at the same time shall have his, her or their ears cut off and nailed to the pillory, and for the second offense shall be whipped and pilloried in like manner and be branded on the forehead in a plain and visible manner with the letters H. T."*[^5628]

This punishment was referenced in [Cormac McCarthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cormac_McCarthy)'s novel *[Blood Meridian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_Meridian)* as the character Toadvine is branded with the letters H. T. on his forehead. H stands for Horse, T for Thief and F for Felon; *"On his forehead were burned the letters H T and lower and almost between the eyes the letter F and these markings were splayed and garish as if the iron had been left too long. When he turned to look at the kid the kid could see that he had no ears."*[^5629]

In the United States, the [Anti Horse Thief Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti_Horse_Thief_Association), first organized in 1854 in [Clark County, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_County,_Missouri), was an organization developed for the purposes of protecting property, especially horses and other livestock, from theft, and recovering such property if and when it was stolen. Originally conceived by farmers living in the area where [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois) and [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa) intersect, it soon spread, with the first charter organization in [Oklahoma Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_Territory) being created in 1894. By 1916 the associated numbered over 40,000 members in nine central and western US states, and a drop in horse thefts had been noted.

Between 1899 and 1909, members of the Oklahoma branch of the AHTA recovered \$83,000 worth of livestock and saw the conviction of over 250 thieves.[^5630] A similar group, which operated mainly in [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio), was the [Bentonville Anti-Horse Thief Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bentonville_Anti-Horse_Thief_Society). Men suspected of being thieves would be pursued by members of the organization, and often hanged without trial.[^5631] [The Society in Dedham for Apprehending Horse Thieves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Society_in_Dedham_for_Apprehending_Horse_Thieves) was a third such organization that operated in the United States, this one in [Dedham, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedham,_Massachusetts). It is today "the oldest continually existing horse thief apprehending organization in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States), and one of [Dedham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedham,_Massachusetts)’s most venerable social organizations."[^5632] Most of these clubs became defunct or developed into social clubs with the decline of horse theft in the US.[^5633]

#### Present day

Horse theft is still relatively common, with an estimated 40,000 horses a year being taken from their lawful owners by strangers or opponents in civil or legal disputes. [Stolen Horse International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stolen_Horse_International) is one modern-day organization in the US that works to reconnect stolen horses with their owners.[^5634] Horses are sometimes stolen for their [meat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse_meat),[^5635] or sometimes for money.[^5636] Punishment for horse theft can still be severe, as one woman in [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas) was sentenced to 60 years in prison for the 2011 theft of five horses and equestrian equipment; one of the horses was later found dead, while the others were recovered.[^5637] Horse thefts today can in some cases be solved through the use of [microchips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microchip_implant_%28animal%29), which is required in the European Union on horses born after 2009 and also often seen in other countries.[^5635]

#### Stolen racehorses

- [Fanfreluche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanfreluche_%28horse%29) was stolen June 1977 from [Claiborne Farm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claiborne_Farm). The Thoroughbred mare was in foal to [Secretariat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretariat_%28horse%29) at the time. The horse was found about 150 miles away as a stray by a farmer who kept her until December when she was identified and returned to her owners.[^5638]
- [Ocean Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocean_Bay), a Venezuelan racehorse stolen and slaughtered in 2020 for food when the country was in economic chaos. Parts of the butchered stallion's skeleton were found just hours after the horse was discovered missing.[^5639]
- [Shergar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shergar) was stolen for a £2 million ransom on 8 February 1983, allegedly by the [IRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army), and was never recovered.[^5640]

### Not proven

**Not proven** ([Scottish Gaelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Gaelic_language): *gun dearbhadh*[^5641]) was a [verdict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verdict) available to a [court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courts_of_Scotland) of law in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland) until 2026. From 1728, under [Scots law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scots_law), a [criminal trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_procedure) could end in one of three verdicts, one of [conviction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conviction) ("guilty") and two of [acquittal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquittal) ("not proven" and "not guilty").[^5642][^5643]

Between the [Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoration_%28Scotland%29) in the late 17th century and the early 18th century, [jurors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jury) in Scotland were expected only to find whether individual factual allegations were proven or not proven, rather than to rule on an accused's guilt.[^5644] In 1728, the jury in a murder trial asserted "its ancient right" to declare a defendant "not guilty".[^5645] Over time, the "not guilty" verdict regained wide acceptance and use amongst Scots juries, with the encouragement of defence lawyers. It eventually displaced "not proven" as the primary verdict of acquittal. Until 2026, juries could return a verdict of either "not guilty" or "not proven", with the same legal effect of acquittal.[^5646]

Although its effect was the same as a not guilty verdict, research from 2019 using mock juries suggested there was inconsistency in understanding its meaning and confusion about its effect.[^5647] The [Victims, Witnesses, and Justice Reform (Scotland) Act 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victims,_Witnesses,_and_Justice_Reform_%28Scotland%29_Act_2025), passed by the [Scottish Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Parliament) in September 2025, included provisions that removed the verdict.[^5648][^5649] Since 1 January 2026, only guilty and not guilty verdicts are available in new trials.

#### History

By the early 17th century, the standard practice of juries in Scotland was to return a finding of "fylet, culpable and convict" or "clene, innocent and acquit".[^5650] This changed in the late 17th century, at which point the role of the jury became simply to "declare whether or not the facts alleged had been proved", with the judge left to determine, based on that declaration, whether the accused was guilty or not.[^5651]

There is some disagreement between historians as to why this change happened. [David Hume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hume) and [Hugo Arnot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Arnot) argue that it was rooted in religious oppression. The Crown persecuted the [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters) but popular support made it impossible to convict them in a jury trial. To pare the power of the jury, the Scottish judges began restricting the jury's role: no longer would the jury announce whether the accused was "guilty" or "not guilty"; instead it would decide whether specific factual allegations were "proven" or "not proven", and the judge would then decide whether to convict.

##### Reintroduction of "not guilty"

In 1728, in the trial of [Carnegie of Finhaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_of_Finhaven) for the [murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder) of the [Earl of Strathmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Lyon,_6th_Earl_of_Strathmore_and_Kinghorne), the defence lawyer ([Robert Dundas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Dundas,_of_Arniston,_the_elder)) persuaded a jury to reassert its ancient right of acquitting, of finding an accused "not guilty", in spite of the facts being proven. The law required the jury merely to look at the facts and pass a verdict of "proven" or "not proven" depending on whether they believed the evidence proved that the accused had killed the Earl. Carnegie had undoubtedly killed the Earl, but had also clearly not intended to do so. If the jury brought in a "proven" verdict they would in effect constrain the judge to find Carnegie guilty of murder, for which the punishment was [hanging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanging). To avert this outcome, the jury asserted what it believed to be their "ancient right" to judge the whole case and not just the facts, and brought in the verdict of "not guilty".

The reintroduction of the "not guilty" verdict was part of a wider movement during the 17th and 18th century which saw a gradual increase in the power of juries, such as the trial of [William Penn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Penn) in 1670, in which an English jury first gained the right to pass a verdict contrary to the law (known as [jury nullification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jury_nullification)), and the trial of [John Peter Zenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Peter_Zenger) in New York in 1735 in which jury nullification is credited with establishing [freedom of the press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press_in_the_United_States) as a firm right in what became the United States. Legal academic Ian Willock argues that the 1728 case was "of great significance in calling a halt to a process of attrition which might have led to the total extinction of the criminal jury".[^5644]

Although jurors continued to use both "not guilty" and "not proven" after 1728, jurors tended to favour the "not guilty" verdict over the "not proven" and the interpretation changed.

In 1827, [Walter Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Scott), who was sheriff in the court of [Selkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selkirk,_Scottish_Borders), wrote in his journal that "the jury gave that bastard verdict, *Not proven*."[^5652] The case he was referring to was the trial of Mary Elder for the [poisoning of Margaret Warden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisoning_of_Margaret_Warden).[^5653]

##### Debate around the verdict

There have been repeated calls to abolish the "not proven" verdict since the middle of the 20th century.[^5654] In 1975, the Thomson Committee on Criminal Procedure in Scotland (chaired by [Lord Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Thomson,_1st_Baron_Thomson_of_Fleet)) recommended retaining the three-verdict system.[^5655] The [Scottish Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Office) consulted on removing "not proven" in 1994.[^5656] Unsuccessful attempts to scrap the not proven verdict were made in Parliament by [Donald Dewar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Dewar) in 1969, [George Robertson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Robertson,_Baron_Robertson_of_Port_Ellen) in 1993 (prompted by the trial outcome in the [murder of Amanda Duffy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Amanda_Duffy)) and [Lord Macauly of Bragar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Macaulay,_Baron_Macaulay_of_Bragar) in 1995.[^5656] A member's bill to abolish the not proven verdict was debated in the [Scottish Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Parliament) in 2016, but was rejected by 80 votes to 28.[^5657]

Proponents of abolition argued that the verdict was widely regarded as an [acquittal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acquittal) used when the [jury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jury) did not have enough [evidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evidence_%28law%29) to [convict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conviction) but was not sufficiently convinced of the accused person's innocence to bring in a not guilty verdict.[^5646] Conversely, its opponents argued that a two-verdict system would lead to an increase in wrongful convictions.[^5643]

Following a not proven verdict in a criminal trial in 2015, Miss M successfully sued Stephen Coxen in the civil courts, in what was the first civil damages action for rape following an unsuccessful criminal prosecution in almost 100 years.

##### Abolition

In April 2023, the Scottish government published the [Victims, Witnesses, and Justice Reform (Scotland) Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victims,_Witnesses,_and_Justice_Reform_%28Scotland%29_Bill), which included a provision to abolish the not proven verdict.[^5658] The bill passed in the [Scottish Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Parliament) in September 2025.[^5659] Alongside this there were a number of other changes to the Scottish justice system, including; creating a specialist sexual offences court; changing the threshold required for a conviction in a jury trial to a two-thirds majority; and implementing *Suzanne's Law* which will require the parole board to take into account if a killer continues to refuse to reveal where they hid their victim's body. The legislation received [Royal Assent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Assent) on 30 October 2025, and on 11 December a commencement order was laid in the Scottish Parliament that removed the not proven verdict for new trials from 1 January 2026.[^5659]

#### Procedure prior to abolition

In Scotland, a criminal case may be decided either *in solemn procedure* by a jury (instructed by the judge), or *in summary procedure* by the judge alone (with no jury appointed). There are various rules for when the one or the other procedure may or must be employed; in general, juries are employed for the more severe accusations, while petty crimes and offences are treated summarily. A criminal case jury consisted of fifteen jurors, who made their decision by a simple majority vote: eight votes were necessary and sufficient for the verdict *guilty*.[^5642]

As of 1999, approximately one-third of all acquittal verdicts by Scottish juries used the formulation *not proven*; the others used *not guilty*. The verdict *not proven* was also available for judges in the summary procedure, and was employed in about a fifth of such acquittals.[^5642] The proportion of *not proven* acquittals was generally higher in the more severe cases, as was the proportion of acquittals versus convictions. This might have many different reasons, for example that on average it might be more difficult to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt in more serious cases.[^5643]

#### Use in other jurisdictions

In general, the verdict has not been permanently adopted outside Scotland, but it was sometimes used in [British colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_colony), especially in areas where Scottish emigrants had settled.[^5660]

Its most famous uses in the United States came when [Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate) [Arlen Specter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arlen_Specter) tried to vote "not proven" on the two articles of [impeachment of Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impeachment_of_Bill_Clinton)[^5661] (his votes were recorded as "not guilty"[^5643]) and when, at the [O. J. Simpson murder case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O._J._Simpson_murder_case), various reformers, including Fred Goldman, [Ron Goldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Goldman)'s father, pushed for a change to "not proven" because of what they felt was an incorrect [presumption of innocence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presumption_of_innocence) on the part of Simpson.

The verdict is often referenced in US cases where the jury is obliged to find the state has not proved its case beyond a reasonable doubt, but there is widespread feeling that the defendant does not deserve the exoneration of a "not guilty" verdict. A popular saying about the "not proven" verdict is that it means "not guilty, but don't do it again".[^5662]

In 2005, a proposal was made in the *[University of Chicago Law Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago_Law_Review)* to introduce the not proven verdict into the United States.[^5643]

### Tennessee login law

On June 1, 2011, [lawmakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawmaker) in the US state of [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee) passed a bill that makes sharing login information for sites that provide music and movies, such as [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix) and [Napster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napster), illegal.[^5664] The law, pushed for by [recording industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_industry) professionals, is the first of its kind in that it is actually an update for a bill originally existing to punish [cable theft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable_television_piracy) now targeting the [Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet).

While the law punishes people for sharing [passwords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Password), it is really aimed at those sharing and selling their passwords in large quantities - up to \$500 in theft resulting in a misdemeanor, and anything else after that a felony.[^5665]

#### Reaction

Initial reaction to the law was negative from [social network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_network) users. Many see the issue in the same light as with [music piracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_piracy).
