### Jarvis v Swans Tours Ltd

***Jarvis v Swans Tours Ltd*** [\[1972\] EWCA 8](https://www.bailii.org/ew/cases/EWCA/1972/8.html) is an [English contract law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_contract_law) case on the [measure of damages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measure_of_damages_under_English_law) for disappointing breaches of contract.

#### Facts

Mr. Jarvis was a solicitor for [Barking Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barking_and_Dagenham_London_Borough_Council). He chose to go for a Christmas holiday to [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland). The brochure from Swan Tours Ltd advertising a holiday in Mörlialp, [Giswil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giswil) described the attractions as follows:

> [House Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_party) Centre with special resident host. ... Mörlialp is a most wonderful little resort on a sunny plateau ... Up there you will find yourself in the midst of beautiful alpine scenery, which in winter becomes a wonderland of sun, snow and ice, with a wide variety of fine ski-runs, a skating rink and exhilarating [toboggan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toboggan) run ... Why did we choose the Hotel Krone ... mainly and most of all because of the '[Gemütlichkeit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gem%C3%BCtlichkeit)' and friendly welcome you will receive from Herr and Frau Weibel. ... The Hotel Krone has its own Alphütte Bar which will be open several evenings a week. ... No doubt you will be in for a great time, when you book this houseparty holiday ... Mr. Weibel, the charming owner, speaks [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language).

In a yellow highlighted box it added:

> Swans House Party in Mörlialp. All these House Party arrangements are included in the price of your holiday. Welcome party on arrival. Afternoon tea and cake for 7 days. Swiss dinner by candlelight. [Fondue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fondue) party. [Yodeler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yodeler) evening. Chali farewell party in the 'Alphütte Bar'. Service of representative.

It also stated, "Hire of Skis, Sticks and Boots ... Ski Tuition ... 12 days £11.10." Mr Jarvis booked 15 days with a ski pack in August 1969 for £63.45, including a Christmas supplement. He found that the "house party" was only 13 people in the first week and none in the second week. Mr Weibel could not speak English. The judge, [Lord Denning MR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Denning,_Baron_Denning) said:

> So there was Mr. Jarvis, in the second week, in this hotel with no house party at all, and no one could speak English, except himself. He was very disappointed, too, with the ski-ing. It was some distance away at Giswil. There were no ordinary length skis. There were only mini-skis, about 3 ft. long. So he did not get his ski-ing as he wanted to. In the second week he did get some longer skis for a couple of days, but then, because of the boots, his feet got rubbed and he could not continue even with the long skis. So his ski-ing holiday, from his point of view, was pretty well ruined.
>
> There were also no Swiss cakes, just crisps and little dry nut cakes. The "yodeler" was a local man who came in work clothes and sang four or five songs quickly. The "Alphütte Bar" was empty and only open one evening.

Mr Jarvis sued for breach of contract. The trial judge awarded £31.72, as the difference between the value paid and the value of the service received (half of what was paid for). Mr Jarvis appealed for more.

#### Judgment

Lord Denning MR held that Mr Jarvis could recover damages for the cost of his holiday, but also damages for "disappointment, the distress, the upset and frustration caused by the breach." He said old limitations on damages for distress and disappointment are "out of date". Accordingly, £125 was awarded.

> What is the legal position? I think that the statements in the brochure were representations or warranties. The breaches of them give Mr. Jarvis a right to damages. It is not necessary to decide whether they were representations or warranties: because since the [Misrepresentation Act 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misrepresentation_Act_1967), there is a remedy in damages for misrepresentation as well as for breach of warranty.
>
> The one question in the case is: What is the amount of damages? The judge seems to have taken the difference in value between what he paid for and what he got. He said that he intended to give "the difference between the two values and no other damages" under any other head. He thought that Mr. Jarvis had got half of what he paid for. So the judge gave him half the amount which he had paid, namely, £31.72. Mr. Jarvis appeals to this court. He says that the damages ought to have been much more.
>
> There is one point I must mention first. Counsel together made a very good note of the judge's judgment. They agreed it. It is very clear and intelligible. It shows plainly enough the ground of the judge's decision: but, by an oversight, it was not submitted to the judge, as it should have been: see *Bruen v. Bruce* (Practice Note) \[1959\] 1 WLR 684. In some circumstances we should send it back to the judge for his comments. But I do not think we need do so here. The judge received the notice of appeal and made notes for our consideration. I do not think he would have wished to add to them. We will, therefore, decide the case on the material before us.
>
> What is the right way of assessing damages? It has often been said that on a breach of contract damages cannot be given for mental distress. Thus in *Hamlin v. Great Northern Railway Co.* (1856) 1 H.& N 408, 411 Pollock C.B. said that damages cannot be given "for the disappointment of mind occasioned by the breach of contract." and in *Hobbs v. London & South Western Railway Co.* (1875) LR 10 QB 111, 122, Mellor J. said that
>
> > for the mere inconvenience, such as annoyance and loss of temper, or vexation, or for being disappointed in a particular thing which you have set your mind upon, without real physical inconvenience resulting, you cannot recover damages.
>
> The courts in those days only allowed the plaintiff to recover damages if he suffered physical inconvenience, such as having to walk five miles home, as in *Hobbs' case*; or to live in an over-crowded house, *Bailey v. Bullock* \[1950\] 2 All ER 1167.
>
> I think that those limitations are out of date. In a proper case damages for mental distress can be recovered in contract, just as damages for shock can be recovered in tort. One such case is a contract for a holiday, or any other contract to provide entertainment and enjoyment. If the contracting party breaks his contract, damages can be given for the disappointment, the distress, the upset and frustration caused by the breach. I know that it is difficult to assess in terms of money, but it is no more difficult than the assessment which the courts have to make every day in personal injury cases for loss of amenities. Take the present case. Mr. Jarvis has only a fortnight's holiday in the year. He books it far ahead, and looks forward to it all that time. He ought to be compensated for the loss of it.
>
> A good illustration was given by [Edmund Davies L.J.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_Davies) in the course of the argument. He put the case of a man who has taken a ticket for Glyndebourne. It is the only night on which he can get there. He hires a car to take him. The car does not turn up. His damages are not limited to the mere cost of the ticket. He is entitled to general damages for the disappointment he has suffered and the loss of the entertainment which he should have had. Here, Mr. Jarvis's fortnight's winter holiday has been a grave disappointment. It is true that he was conveyed to Switzerland and back and had meals and bed in the hotel. But that is not what he went for. He went to enjoy himself with all the facilities which the defendants said he would have. He is entitled to damages for the lack of those facilities, and for his loss of enjoyment.
>
> A similar case occurred in 1951. It was *Stedman v. Swan's Tours* (1951) 95 SJ 727. A holiday-maker was awarded damages because he did not get the bedroom and the accommodation which he was promised. The county court judge awarded him £13.15. This court increased it to £50.
>
> I think the judge was in error in taking the sum paid for the holiday £63.45 and halving it. The right measure of damages is to compensate him for the loss of entertainment and enjoyment which he was promised, and which he did not get.
>
> Looking at the matter quite broadly, I think the damages in this case should be the sum of £125. I would allow the appeal, accordingly.

Edmund Davies, Baron Edmund-Davies\|Edmund Davies LJ and [Stephenson LJ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Stephenson_%28judge%29) concurred.

#### Commentary

*Jarvis v Swans Tours Ltd* has been called "the *[Donoghue v Stevenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donoghue_v_Stevenson)* of Tourism Law".[^5666]

[^5666]: Atherton, Trudie-Ann; Atherton, Trevor C. ["The Legalities of Overbooking, Overcrowding, Delay and Disappointment: Lessons for the Sydney 2000 Olympics"](http://www.austlii.edu.au/au/journals/UNSWLJ/1999/33.html#fnB37). New South Wales Law Journal.

### Toy Biz, Inc. v. United States

***Toy Biz, Inc. v. United States*** was a 2003 decision in the [United States Court of International Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Court_of_International_Trade) that determined that for purposes of [tariffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariffs), [Toy Biz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toy_Biz)'s [Marvel Comics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvel_Comics) [action figures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Action_figures) were [toys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toy), not [dolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doll), because they represented "nonhuman creatures".[^5667] This decision effectively halved the tariff rate, from 12 percent tax to 6.8 percent.[^5668]

#### Background

The [Harmonized Tariff Schedule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonized_Tariff_Schedule_for_the_United_States) in [US law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_United_States) distinguished between two types of action figures for determining tariffs: dolls, which are defined to include human figures, and toys, which include nonhuman "creatures".[^5669] Because duties on dolls were higher than those on toys, the toy company Toy Biz argued before the [US Court of International Trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Court_of_International_Trade), that their Marvel Comics action figures (including the [X-Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-Men) and [Fantastic Four](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantastic_Four)) represented "nonhuman creatures" and were subject to the lower tariff rates for toys instead of the higher ones for dolls.[^5669] The [US Customs Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Customs_Service) claimed that the "non-human characteristics" were insufficient in transforming the characters into non-humans.[^5670] On January 3, 2003, after examining more than 60 action figures, Judge [Judith Barzilay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Barzilay) ruled in their favor, granting Toy Biz reimbursement for import taxes on previous toys.[^5671]

#### Reaction

Because a common theme in Marvel Comics had been the struggle for [mutants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutant_%28Marvel_Comics%29) like the X-Men to prove their humanity, the ruling was surprising to fans.[^5672] Marvel responded to these concerns by claiming "our heroes are living, breathing human beings - but humans who have extraordinary abilities ... A decision that the X-Men figures indeed do have 'nonhuman' characteristics further proves our characters have special, out-of-this world powers".[^5669] The case has often been cited as one of the strangest legal cases in US history.

In 2007, the Harmonized Tariff Schedule was amended to eliminate the distinction between dolls and other toys, which are now in the same category.[^5673][^5674]

[^5667]: *Toy Biz v. United States* (United States Court of International Trade January 3, 2003), [Text](http://www.cit.uscourts.gov/sites/cit/files/slip-op%2003-2.pdf).

[^5668]: Iglesias, Matthew (December 29, 2011). ["How Trade Policy Cost The X-Men Their Humanity"](https://slate.com/business/2011/12/are-mutants-human.html). *Slate.com*. Retrieved November 22, 2018.

[^5669]: King, Neal (January 20, 2003). ["Fans Howl in Protest as Judge Decides X-Men Aren't Human"](https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB1043013622300562504). *The Wall Street Journal*. Retrieved November 22, 2018.

[^5670]: Maher, Cian (September 12, 2019). ["That time the X-Men's humanity was put on trial in a real court of law"](https://www.polygon.com/comics/2019/9/12/20862474/x-men-series-toys-human-legal-issue-marvel-comics/). *Polygon.com*. Retrieved April 15, 2026.

[^5671]: ["Toy Biz, Inc. v. United States, No. 96-10 (Ct. Int'l Trade 2003)"](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/cit/96-10/96-10-2003-01-03.html). *Justia Law*. Retrieved August 18, 2026.

[^5672]: ["No Time for Mutants"](https://web.archive.org/web/20120226052607/http://www.ojr.org/ojr/spike/1043234172.php). *USC Annenberg Online Journalism Review*. January 22, 2003. Archived from the original on February 26, 2012. Retrieved October 31, 2023.

[^5673]: Daily, James (December 27, 2011). ["Are the X-Men Human? A Federal Court Says No"](https://lawandthemultiverse.com/2011/12/27/are-the-x-men-human-federal-court-says-no/). *Law and the Multiverse*. Retrieved November 22, 2018.

[^5674]: ["Amendments to the Harmonized System Nomenclature effective from 1 January 2007"](https://www.wcoomd.org/-/media/wco/public/global/pdf/topics/nomenclature/instruments-and-tools/hs-nomenclature-older-edition/2007/hs2007_net_eng1.pdf?la=en) (PDF). World Customs Organization.

### Charivari

**Charivari** (/ˌʃɪvəˈriː, ˈʃɪvəriː/, [UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_English) also /ˌʃɑːrɪˈvɑːri/, [US](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_English) also /ʃəˌrɪvəˈriː/,[^5675][^5676] alternatively spelled **shivaree** or **chivaree** and also called a **skimmington**) was a European and North American folk custom designed to shame a member of the community, in which a mock [parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parade) was staged through the settlement accompanied by a discordant mock [serenade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serenade). Since the crowd aimed to make as much noise as possible by beating on pots and pans or anything that came to hand, these parades were often referred to as **rough music**.

Parades were of three types. In the first and generally most violent form, an alleged wrongdoer (or wrongdoers) might be dragged from their home or place of work and paraded by force through a community. In the process, the victim was subject to the derision of the crowd and might be pelted, and was frequently dunked at the end of the proceedings. A safer form involved a neighbour of the wrongdoer impersonating the victim while being carried through the streets. The impersonator was not themselves punished, and often cried out or sang ribald verses mocking the wrongdoer. In the common form, an [effigy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effigy) was employed instead, abused and often burnt at the end of the proceedings.[^5677]

Communities used "rough music" to express their disapproval of different types of violation of community norms. For example, they might target marriages of which they disapproved, such as a union between an older widower and much younger woman, or the premature remarriage of a widow or widower. Villages also used charivari in cases of adulterous relationships, against wife-beaters or unmarried mothers. It was also used as a form of shaming upon husbands who were beaten by their wives and had not stood up for themselves.[^5678] In some cases, the community disapproved of any remarriage by older widows or widowers. *Charivari* is the original French word, and in Canada it is used by both Anglophones and Francophones. *Chivaree* became the common variant in [Ontario, Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario,_Canada). In the United States, the term *shivaree* is more common.[^5679]

As species of popular justice rites, charivaric events were carefully planned and often staged at times of traditional festivity, thereby blending justice and celebration.[^5680]

#### Etymology

The origin of the word *charivari* is likely from the [Vulgar Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgar_Latin) caribaria, plural of *caribarium*, already referring to the custom of rattling kitchenware with an iron rod,[^5681] itself probably from the Greek καρηβαρία (*karēbaría*), literally "heaviness in the head" but also used to mean "headache", from κάρα "head" and βαρύς "heavy". In any case, the tradition has been practised for at least 700 years. A painting in the early 14th-century French manuscript *[Roman de Fauvel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_de_Fauvel)* shows a charivari underway.

#### Regional variations

##### England

So-called "rough music" practices in England were known by many regional or local designations. In the North the most commonly employed term was "**stang riding**", a stang being a long pole carried on the shoulders of two men between which an object or a person could be mounted. In the South, the term **skimmington**, or **skimmington ride**, was most commonly employed, a skimmington being a type of large wooden ladle with which an unruly wife might beat her husband. Other terms include "**lewbelling**", "**tin-panning**", "**ran tanning**", a "**nominey**" or "**wooset**".[^5682] Where effigies of the "wrongdoers" were made they were frequently burned as the climax of the event (as the inscription on the Rampton photograph indicates[^5683]) or "ritually drowned" (thrown into a pond or river).

The very essence of the practice was [public humiliation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_humiliation) of the victim under the eyes of their neighbours [^5684] Rough music practices were irregularly scattered throughout English communities in the nineteenth century. In the twentieth they declined but endured in a few places, such as [Rampton, Nottinghamshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rampton,_Nottinghamshire) (1909),[^5683] [Middleton Cheney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleton_Cheney) (1909) and [Blisworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blisworth) (1920s and 1936), Northamptonshire.[^5685] There were in fact some examples after the Second World War in Sussex, at [West Hoathly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Hoathly) in 1947 and [Copthorne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copthorne,_West_Sussex) around 1951, and an attempt at traditional rough music practice was last documented by the folklorist Theo Brown in a Devonshire village around 1973.[^5686]

In Warwickshire, the custom was known as "loo-belling" or "lewbelling",[^5687] and in northern England as "riding the stang".[^5688] Other names given to this or similar customs were "rough-musicking" and "hussitting" (said to be a reference to the [Hussites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hussites) or followers of [John Huss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Huss)).[^5689]

Noisy, masked processions were held outside the home of the accused wrongdoer, involving the cacophonous rattling of bones and cleavers, the ringing of bells, hooting, blowing bull's horns, the banging of frying pans, saucepans, kettles, or other kitchen or barn implements with the intention of creating long-lasting embarrassment to the alleged perpetrator.[^5690] During a rough music performance, the victim could be displayed upon a pole or donkey (in person or as an effigy), their "crimes" becoming the subject of mime, theatrical performances or [recitatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recitatives), along with a litany of obscenities and insults.[^5690] Alternatively, one of the participants would "ride the stang" (a pole carried between the shoulders of two or more men or youths) while banging an old kettle or pan with a stick and reciting a rhyme (called a "nominy") such as the following:

> With a ran, tan, tan,\
> On my old tin can,\
> Mrs. \_\_\_\_\_\_\_ and her good man.\
> She bang'd him, she bang'd him,\
> For spending a penny when he stood in need.\
> She up with a three-footed stool;\
> She struck him so hard, and she cut so deep,\
> Till the blood run down like a new stuck sheep![^5691]

Rough music processions are well attested in the medieval period as punishments for violations of the assumed gender norms. Men who had allowed themselves to be dominated by their shrewish wives were liable to be targeted and a frieze from [Montacute House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montacute_House), an Elizabethan Manor in Somerset depicts just such an occurrence. However, in the nineteenth century the practice seems to have been somewhat refocused; whilst in the early period rough music was often used against men who had failed to assert their authority over their wives, by the end of the nineteenth century it was mostly targeted against men who had exceeded their authority by beating them.[^5692] Thus, in contrast to the verses above referring to a shrewish wife there were also songs referring to the use of rough music as a protection for wives.

Rough music song originating from [South Stoke, Oxfordshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Stoke,_Oxfordshire):[^5693]

> There is a man in our town\
> Who often beats his wife,\
> So if he does it any more,\
> We'll put his nose right out before.\
> Holler boys, holler boys,\
> Make the bells ring,\
> Holler boys, holler boys.\
> God save the King.

The participants were generally young men temporarily bestowed with the power of rule over the everyday affairs of the community.[^5690] As above, issues of sexuality and domestic hierarchy most often formed the pretexts for rough music,[^5690] including acts of domestic violence or child abuse. However, rough music was also used as a sanction against those who committed certain species of economic crimes such as blocking footpaths, preventing traditional [gleaning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gleaning), or profiteering at times of poor harvests. Occupational groups, such as butchers, employed rough music against others in the same trade who refused to abide by the commonly agreed labour customs.[^5694]

Rough music practices would often be repeated for three or up to seven nights in a row.[^5685] Many victims fled their communities and cases of suicide are not unknown.[^5695] As forms of [vigilantism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vigilantism) that were likely to lead to [public disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riot), ran-tanning and similar activities were banned under the Highways Act of 1882.[^5683]

###### Origins, history and form

Skimmingtons are recorded in England in early medieval times and they are recorded in colonial America from around the 1730s.[^5696][^5697] The term is particularly associated with the [West Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Country) region of England and, although the etymology is not certain, it has been suggested that it derived from the [ladle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ladle_%28spoon%29) used in that region for cheesemaking, which was perceived as a weapon used by a woman to beat a weak or henpecked husband. The rationale for a skimmington varied, but one major theme was disapproval of a man for weakness in his relationship with his wife. A description of the custom in 1856 cites three main targets: a man who is worsted by his wife in a quarrel; a cuckolded man who accepts his wife's [adultery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adultery); and any married person who engages in licentious conduct.[^5698] To "ride such a person skimmington" involved exposing them or their effigy to ridicule on a cart, or on the back of a horse or donkey. Some accounts describe the participants as carrying ladles and spoons with which to beat each other, at least in the case of skimmingtons prompted by marital discord. The noisy parade passed through the neighbourhood, and served as a punishment to the offender and a warning to others to abide by community norms; Roberts suggests that the homes of other potential victims were visited in a pointed manner during a skimmington.[^5698] According to one citation, a skimmington was broken up by the police in a village in Dorset as late as 1917;[^5688] and incidents have been reported from the 1930s, the 1950s and perhaps even the 1970s.[^5689]

The antiquary and lexicographer [Francis Grose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Grose) described a skimmington as: "Saucepans, frying-pans, poker and tongs, marrow-bones and cleavers, bulls horns, etc. beaten upon and sounded in ludicrous processions" *([A Classical Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Classical_Dictionary_of_the_Vulgar_Tongue)*, 1796).

###### Western Rising

During the [Western Rising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Rising) of 1628-1631, which was a rebellion in south-west England against the [enclosure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enclosure) of royal forest lands, the name "Lady Skimmington" was adopted by the leader of the protest movement.[^5699] According to some sources the name was used by a number of men involved with the Western Rising, who dressed in women's clothes not only as a method of disguise, but also in order to symbolise their protest against a breach of the established order.[^5700]

###### Similar customs

Many folk customs around the world have involved making loud noises to scare away evil spirits.[^5701]

Tuneless, cacophonous "rough music", played on horns, bugles, whistles, tin trays and frying pans, was a feature of the custom known as *Teddy Rowe's Band*. This had taken place annually, possibly for several centuries, in the early hours of the morning, to herald the start of [Pack Monday Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pack_Monday_Fair) at [Sherborne, Dorset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherborne,_Dorset), until it was banned by the police in 1964 because of hooliganism the previous year.[^5702] The fair is still held, on the first Monday after Old [Michaelmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michaelmas) Day (10 October)[^5703] - [St Michael's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Michael) Day in the [Old Style calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Style_and_New_Style_dates).

The *Tin Can Band* at [Broughton, Northamptonshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broughton,_Northamptonshire), a seasonal custom, takes place at midnight on the third Sunday in December. The participants march around the village for about an hour, rattling pans, dustbin lids, kettles and anything else that will make a noise.[^5704][^5705] The council once attempted to stop the tin-canning; participants were [summoned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summons) and fined, but a dance was organised to raise money to pay the fines and the custom continues.[^5685][^5705] The village is sufficiently proud of its custom for it to feature on the village sign.[^5706]

##### Mainland Europe

Equivalents include the [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language): *[haberfeldtreiben](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/haberfeldtreiben)* and [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_language): *[katzenmusik](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/katzenmusik)*, [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language): *[scampanate](https://it.wikipedia.org/wiki/scampanate)*, Spanish [cacerolada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cacerolada), (also cacerolazo or cacerolada) and [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language): *[charivari](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/charivari)*.[^5690]

The custom has been documented back to the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages) but it is likely that it was traditional before that. It was first recorded in France, as a regular wedding activity to celebrate the nuptials at some point after the vows had been taken. But charivari achieved its greatest importance as it became transformed into a form of community censure against socially unacceptable marriages; for example, the marriage of [widows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widow) before the end of the customary social period of formal [mourning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourning). In the early 17th century at the [Council of Tours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Tours), the [Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholicism) forbade the ritual of charivari and threatened its practitioners with [excommunication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excommunication).[^5707] It did not want the community taking on the judgment and punishment of parishioners. But the custom continued in rural areas.

The charivari as celebration was a custom initially practised by the upper classes, but as time went on, the lower classes also participated and often looked forward to the next opportunity to join in.[^5708] The two main purposes of the charivari in Europe were to facilitate change in the current social structure and to act as a form of [censure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censure) within the community. The goal was to enforce social standards and to rid the community of socially unacceptable relationships that threatened the stability of the whole.[^5709]

In Europe various types of charivari took place that differed from similar practices in other parts of the world. For example, the community might conduct a stag hunt against adulterers by creating a mock chase of human "stags" by human "hounds". The hounds would pursue the stags (that is, those who were committing the adulterous relationship) and dispense animal blood on their doorsteps. European charivaris were highly provocative, leading to overt public humiliation. The people used them to acknowledge and correct misbehaviour. In other parts of the world, similar public rituals around nuptials were practised mostly for celebration.[^5710]

[Humiliation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humiliation) was the most common consequence of the European charivari. The acts which victims endured were forms of social ostracism often so embarrassing that they would leave the community for places where they were not known.[^5711] Sometimes the charivari resulted in [murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder) or [suicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide). Examples from the south of [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France) include five cases of a charivari victim's firing on his accusers: these incidents resulted in two people being blinded and three killed. Some victims committed suicide, unable to recover from the public humiliation and [social exclusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_exclusion).[^5712]

[Norman Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Lewis_%28author%29) recorded the survival of the custom in 1950s [Ibiza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibiza) "in spite of the energetic disapproval of the [Guardia Civil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardia_Civil)". It was called *cencerrada*, consisted of raucous nocturnal music, and was aimed at widows or widowers who remarried prematurely.[^5713]

It is possible that the blowing of car horns after weddings in France (and indeed in many European countries) today is a holdover from the charivari of the past.[^5714]

##### North America

Charivari has been practiced in much of the United States, but it was most frequent on the frontier, where communities were small and more formal enforcement was lacking. It was documented into the early 20th century, but was thought to have mostly died out by mid century. In [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada), charivaris have occurred in [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario), [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec), and the Atlantic provinces, but not always as an expression of disapproval.

The early French colonists took the custom of charivari to their settlements in Quebec. Some historians believe the custom spread to English-speaking areas of Lower Canada and eventually into the American South, but it was independently common in English society, so was likely to be part of Anglo-American customs. Charivari is well documented in the [Hudson Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Valley) from the earliest days of English settlers through the early 1900s.[^5715] The earliest documented examples of Canadian charivari were in Quebec in the mid-17th century. One of the most notable was on June 28, 1683. After the widow of François Vézier dit Laverdure remarried only three weeks after her husband’s death, people of Quebec City conducted a loud and strident charivari against the newlyweds at their home.[^5716]

As practised in North America, the charivari tended to be less extreme and punitive than the traditional European custom. Each was unique and heavily influenced by the standing of the family involved, as well as who was participating. While embellished with some European traditions, in a North American charivari participants might throw the culprits into horse tanks or force them to buy candy bars for the crowd.

> All in fun - it was just a shiveree, you know, and nobody got mad about it. At least not very mad.

 Johnson (1990), p. 382.

This account from an American charivari in Kansas exemplifies the North American attitude. In contrast to punitive charivari in small villages in Europe, meant to ostracize and isolate the evildoers, North American charivaris were used as "unifying rituals", in which those in the wrong were brought back into the community after what might amount to a minor [hazing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazing).[^5717] In some communities the ritual served as a gentle spoof of the newlyweds, intended to disrupt for a while any sexual activities that might be under way. In parts of the midwest US, such as Kansas, in the mid 1960-1970s, shivaree customs continued as good natured wedding humour along the lines of the musical *[Oklahoma!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma!)*. Rituals included wheeling the bride about in a wheelbarrow or tying cowbells under a wedding bed. This ritual may be the base of the fastening of tin cans to the newlyweds car.[^5718]

In Tampa, Florida, in September 1885, a large chivaree was held on the occasion of local official James T. Magbee's wedding. According to historian Kyle S. Vanlandingham, the party was "the wildest and noisiest of all the chivaree parties in Tampa's history," attended by "several hundred" men and lasting "until near daylight". The music produced during the chivaree was reportedly "hideous and unearthly beyond description".[^5719]

Charivari is believed to have inspired the development of the [Acadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acadia) tradition of [Tintamarre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tintamarre).

#### Importance of noise

The use of excessive noise was a universal practice in association with variations in the custom. Loud singing and chanting were common in Europe, including England, and throughout North America. For an 1860 English charivari against a wife-beater, someone wrote an original chant which the crowd was happy to adopt:

> Has beat his wife!\
> Has beat his wife!\
> It is a very great shame and disgrace\
> To all who live in this place\
> It is indeed, upon my life![^5720]

In Europe the noise, songs, and chants had special meanings for the crowd. When directed against adulterers, the songs represented the community’s disgust. For a too-early remarriage of a widow or widower, the noises symbolized the scream of the late husband or wife in the night.[^5721]

#### Other usages

Perhaps the most common usage of the word today is in relation to circus performances, where a 'charivari' is a type of show opening that sees a raucous tumble of clowns and other performers into the playing space. This is the most common form of entrance used in today's classical [circus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circus), whereas the two- and three-ring circuses of the last century usually preferred a parade, or a 'spec'.

Charivari was sometimes called "riding the 'stang", when the target was a man who had been subject to scolding, beating, or other abuse from his wife. The man was made to "ride the 'stang", which meant that he was placed backwards on a horse, mule or ladder and paraded through town to be mocked, while people banged pots and pans.[^5722] [^5723] [^5724] [^5725]

The charivari was used to belittle those who could not or would not consummate their marriage. In the mid-16th century, historic records attest to a charivari against [Martin Guerre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Guerre) in the small village of [Artigat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artigat) in the French [Pyrenees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenees) for that reason. After he married at the age of 14, his wife did not get pregnant for eight years, so villagers ridiculed him. Later in his life, another man took over Guerre's identity and life. The trial against the impostor was what captured the events for history. In the 20th century, the events formed the basis of a French film, *[Le Retour de Martin Guerre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Retour_de_Martin_Guerre)* (1982), and the history *The Return of Martin Guerre* by the American history professor [Natalie Zemon Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natalie_Zemon_Davis).[^5726]

With the charivari widely practised among rural villagers across Europe,[^5727] the term and practice were part of common culture. Over time, the word was applied to other items. In [Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bavaria), *charivari* was adopted as the name for the silver ornaments worn with [Lederhosen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lederhosen); the items consist of small trophies from game, like teeth from wild boar, or deer, jaws and fangs from foxes and various marters, feathers and claws from jaybirds and birds of prey. A Bavarian Charivari resembles the so-called "[chatelaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatelaine_%28chain%29)", a women's ornament consisting of a silver chain with numerous pendants like a mini silver box of needles, a small pair of scissors, a tiny bottle of perfume, etc.

In the Philippines, Charivari is punishable for being a public disorder under Article 155 of the Revised Penal Code.

#### In music

Charivari would later be taken up by composers of the [French Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Baroque) tradition as a 'rustic' or 'pastoral' character piece. Notable examples are those of the renowned [viola da gamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viola_da_gamba) virtuoso [Marin Marais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marin_Marais) in his five collections of pieces for the *basse de viole* and [continuo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basso_continuo). Some are quite advanced and difficult and subsequently evoke the title's origins.

The British [period instrument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Period_instrument)/[early music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_music) ensemble Charivari Agréable (founded in 1993) states that their name translates as "'pleasant tumult' (from Saint-Lambert’s 1707 treatise on accompaniment)".[^5728]

#### In art and literature

- In the 14th-century political satire *[Roman de Fauvel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_de_Fauvel)*, the evil half-man, half-horse central character Fauvel marries the allegorical figure of Vainglory, and the townspeople hold a charivari in the street as he goes to his marriage bed.
- In [Wallace Stegner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_Stegner)'s 1971 [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize)-winning novel *[Angle of Repose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angle_of_Repose)*, shortly after new bride Susan Burling Ward arrives in 1876 in the California mining town [New Almaden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Almaden), her husband learns with alarm that "\[t\]here was some talk about a charivari" among the miners, some of whom throw snickering glances at Susan.
- [Québécois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qu%C3%A9b%C3%A9cois_people) writer Robert Goulet's 1961 novel *The Violent Season* depicts a charivari that occurs in rural [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec).[^5729]
- *[The Late Lancashire Witches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Late_Lancashire_Witches)*, a play by [Thomas Heywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Heywood) and [Richard Brome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Brome), features a horseback skimmington ride prompted by a woman who seeks greater independence.
- In [Samuel Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Butler_%28poet%29)'s *[Hudibras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudibras)*, the central character encounters a skimmington in a scene notably illustrated by [William Hogarth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Hogarth).
- A skimmington is depicted in a plaster frieze in [Montacute House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montacute_House), which dates from the [Elizabethan era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_era), and shows a man mounted on a pole, carried on the shoulders of others.[^5730]
- A skimmington forms a well-known scene in [Thomas Hardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Hardy)'s 1884 novel *[The Mayor of Casterbridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mayor_of_Casterbridge)*.[^5685] Effigies of the mayor and Lucetta, a former lover, are paraded through the streets on a donkey by a noisy crowd when rumours of their prior relationship surface. Lucetta, now respectably married to Henchard's rival Farfrae, collapses in distress and humiliation, miscarries her baby and dies.

> "They are coming up Corn Street after all! They sit back to back!"\
> \
> "What, two of 'em, are there two figures?"\
> "Yes. Two images on a donkey, back to back, their elbows tied to one another's! She's facing the head, and he's facing the tail."\
> "Is it meant for anybody in particular?"\
> "Well, it mid be. The man has got on a blue coat and kerseymere leggings; he has black whiskers, and a reddish face. 'Tis a stuffed figure, with a falseface." (...)\
> \
> The numerous lights round the two effigies threw them up into lurid distinctness; it was impossible to mistake the pair for other than the intended victims.\
> \
> "Come in, come in," implored Elizabeth; "and let me shut the window!"\
> "She's me, she's me, even to the parasol, my green parasol!" cried Lucetta with a wild laugh as she stepped in. She stood motionless for one second, then fell heavily to the floor.

 Thomas Hardy, *The Mayor of Casterbridge*

- The Skimmity Hitchers are a [Scrumpy and Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrumpy_and_Western) band from the West Country of England. They took their name from the Skimmington (known as Skimmity in Dorset) to reflect their music and stage show, which is a mix of rough music, parody, drunkenness and audience humiliation.

#### In popular culture

- *[Le Charivari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Charivari)* was a French satirical magazine first published in 1832. Its British counterpart, established in 1841, was entitled *[Punch, or The London Charivari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punch_%28magazine%29)*.
- In the film *[The Purchase Price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Purchase_Price)*, members of a [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota) farming community celebrate the marriage of [Barbara Stanwyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Stanwyck)'s and [George Brent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Brent)'s characters by holding a noisy, drunken shivaree a couple days after their nuptials.
- In the television show *[The Waltons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Waltons)*, the episode titled "The Shivaree" focused on a wedding between a city boy and a country girl. The groom almost calls off the marriage after being humiliated by a shivaree thrown by his wife's family and friends.
- In the television show *[The Rifleman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rifleman)*, in the episode titled "Shivaree", two travelers are forced to get married when it is discovered that they are actually a young unmarried couple in disguise.
- The *[Midsomer Murders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midsomer_Murders)* television episode "Four Funerals and a Wedding" prominently features a Skimmington ride.
- In the fantasy novel series *[Discworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discworld)*, [Terry Pratchett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Pratchett) refers to the 'dissonant piping and war-drums of vengeance' sounds of rough music in a scene where a rural town finds out that a local man beat his daughter, causing her miscarriage, and a drunken mob come to kill him for the crime.
- In the television show *[Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Quinn,_Medicine_Woman)*, the episode titled "Return Engagement, Part 1" references a shivaree after an ex-prostitute marries the telegraph operator.
- In the musical *[Oklahoma!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma!)*, Laurey and Curly are given a (lighthearted) shivaree on their wedding night by a group of rowdy cowboys near the end of Act II.
- In the British drama series [*Jamestown*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamestown_%28TV_series%29), season 2, episode 8, the Widow Castell is made to walk a Skimmington in order to shame her for not remarrying soon enough. The men in power want her under the control of a husband to stymie her meddling in colony politics.
- In the 1950 film *[Never A Dull Moment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Never_a_Dull_Moment_%281950_film%29)*, newlyweds Chris and Kay are given a shivaree by local ranchers on Kay’s first night at her husband’s ranch.
- In the American animated sitcom [*Archer*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archer_%282009_TV_series%29), season 5, episode 12, titled "Filibuster", Cyril proposes that the servants conduct a shivaree while he and Julia Calderon consummate their marriage. She declines.
- In the 1966 film [*El Dorado*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Dorado_%281966_film%29), Cole Thorton ([John Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wayne)) tells Mississippi ([James Caan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Caan)) that they were unable to re-enter the saloon they just left because the "shivaree" (i.e., the fight they had with other bar patrons) "wore out our welcome".
- In the television show *[Death Valley Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_Valley_Days)*, season 1, episode 8, "The Chivaree", the couple getting married discuss the expected "chivareeing" to follow their upcoming wedding. The groom opposes, after having already been chided in the town previously, but the scorned ex-lover of the bride insists. The bride and groom sit quietly in the window and endure the ruckus for two days before inviting the crowd in for food and drink.
- In the TV series *[Game of Thrones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Game_of_Thrones)*, Cersei Lannister's hair is cut off and she is paraded naked through the streets of King's Landing, whilst a bell is rung to repeated chants of "Shame!"
- ' Burning Ash ': (1992) - [Charlie Drake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Drake) short film about a neighbourhood dispute, which, in the end credits, cites 1959, not 1951, as the last time the practise at that time had occurred for the same reason.

### Axinomancy

**Axinomancy** is an obscure method of [divination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divination) using an [axe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axe), [hatchet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatchet), or (rarely) a [saw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saw). Most methods involve throwing an axe into the ground, or swinging it into a tree, and interpreting the direction of the handle or the quivering of the blade.[^5731][^5732] A form of this is axiomancy; this is when the quivering of the [blade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade) of an [axe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axe) that has been thrust into a wooden table is interpreted by the [diviner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divination).

Another interesting method is heating an axe-head in a fire until it glows, and then interpreting the colors and shapes.[^5731] A variant, attributed to the ancient Greeks, who held it in good repute, is to balance a spherical piece of [agate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agate) on the edge of the axe (held sharp edge up).[^5733][^5734] The direction in which the agate rolls can be interpreted as needed.[^5735][^5733]

Some sources claim that [Psalm 74](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_74) refers to the use of axinomancy to predict the fall of Jerusalem, although in the text the reference to *upright axes* is not specifically for divination.[^5736]

### Jerusalem syndrome

**Jerusalem syndrome** is a group of mental phenomena involving the presence of religiously themed ideas or experiences that are triggered by a visit to the city of [Jerusalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem). It is not endemic to one single religion or denomination but has affected [Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism), [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity), and [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam) of many different backgrounds.[^5737] It is not listed as a recognised condition in the *[Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagnostic_and_Statistical_Manual_of_Mental_Disorders)* or the *[International Classification of Diseases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Classification_of_Diseases)*.[^5738]

The best known, although not the most prevalent, manifestation of Jerusalem syndrome (classified as Type III) is the phenomenon whereby a person who seems previously balanced and devoid of any signs of [psychopathology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychopathology) becomes [psychotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychosis) after arriving in Jerusalem. The psychosis is characterised by an intense religious theme and typically resolves to full recovery after a few weeks or after being removed from the area. The religious focus of Jerusalem syndrome distinguishes it from the related phenomena of [Stendhal syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stendhal_syndrome) in [Florence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence) or [Paris syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_syndrome) in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris).

In a 2000 article in the *British Journal of Psychiatry*, Bar-El et al. claim to have identified and described a specific syndrome which emerges in tourists with no previous abnormal [psychiatric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatry) history.[^5739] However, this claim has been disputed by M. Kalian and E. Witztum.[^5740][^5741] Kalian and Witztum stressed that nearly all of the tourists who demonstrated the described behaviours were mentally ill prior to their arrival in Jerusalem. They further noted that, of the small proportion of tourists alleged to have exhibited spontaneous [psychosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychosis) after arrival in Jerusalem, Bar-El et al. had presented no evidence that the tourists had been well prior to their arrival in the city.

#### History

Jerusalem syndrome had previously been regarded as a form of [hysteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hysteria), referred to as *fièvre Jérusalemienne* (French, literally 'Jerusalemian fever').[^5742] It was first clinically described in the 1930s by Jerusalem [psychiatrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatrist) Heinz Hermann, one of the founders of modern psychiatric research in [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel).[^5743] Whether or not these behaviors specifically arise from visiting Jerusalem is debated, as similar behaviors have been noted at other places of religious and historical importance, such as [Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca) and [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome) (see [Stendhal syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stendhal_syndrome)). It is known that cases of the syndrome had already been observed during the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages), since it was described in the itinerary of [Felix Fabri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Fabri) and the biography of [Margery Kempe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margery_Kempe).[^5744] Other cases were described in the vast literature of visitors to Jerusalem during the 19th century.

Bar-El et al. suggested that at the approach of the year 2000, large numbers of otherwise normal visitors might be affected by a combination of their presence in Jerusalem and the religious significance of the millennium, causing a massive increase in the numbers of Jerusalem syndrome admissions to hospital. Despite a slight increase in tourist hospitalisations with the rise in total tourism to Jerusalem during the year 2000, the feared epidemic of Jerusalem syndrome never materialised.[^5739]

#### Types

The classic Jerusalem syndrome, where a visit to Jerusalem seems to trigger an intense [religious psychosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_delusion) that resolves quickly after or on departure, has been a subject of debate in the [medical literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_literature).[^5740][^5741][^5745] Most of the discussion has centered on whether this definition of the Jerusalem syndrome is a distinct form of psychosis, or simply a re-expression of a previously existing psychotic illness that was not picked up by the medical authorities in Israel.

In response to this, Bar-El et al. classified the syndrome[^5739] into three major types to reflect the different types of interactions between a visit to Jerusalem and unusual or psychosis-related thought processes. However, Kalian and Witztum have objected, saying that Bar-El et al. presented no evidence to justify the detailed typology and [prognosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prognosis) presented and that the types in fact seem to be unrelated rather than different aspects of a [syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syndrome).

##### Type I

*Jerusalem syndrome imposed on a previous psychotic illness.* This refers to individuals already diagnosed as having a [psychotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychosis) illness before their visit to Jerusalem. They have typically gone to the city because of the influence of religious ideas, often with a goal or mission in mind that they believe needs to be completed on arrival or during their stay. For example, affected persons may believe themselves to be important historical religious figures or may be influenced by important religious ideas or concepts (such as causing the coming of the [Messiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Messiah) or the [second coming of Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Coming)).

##### Type II

*Jerusalem syndrome superimposed on and complicated by [idiosyncratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idiosyncrasy) ideas.* This does not necessarily take the form of mental illness and may simply be a culturally anomalous obsession with the significance of Jerusalem, either as an individual, or as part of a small religious group with idiosyncratic spiritual beliefs.

##### Type III

*Jerusalem syndrome as a discrete form, uncompounded by previous mental illness.* This describes the best-known, if not the most common type, whereby a previously mentally balanced person becomes psychotic after arriving in Jerusalem.[^5738] It can include a paranoid belief that an agency is after the individual, causing their symptoms of psychosis through poisoning and medicating.[^5746]

Bar-El et al. reported 42 such cases over a period of 13 years, but in no case were they able to actually confirm that the condition was temporary.

#### Prevalence

During a period of 13 years (1980-1993) for which admissions to the [Kfar Shaul Mental Health Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kfar_Shaul_Mental_Health_Center) in Jerusalem were analysed, it was reported[^5739] that 1,200 tourists with severe, Jerusalem-themed mental problems were referred to this clinic. Of these, 470 were admitted to the hospital. On average, 100 such tourists have been seen annually, 40 of them requiring admission to the hospital. About three-and-a-half million tourists visit Jerusalem each year. Kalian and Witztum note that, as a proportion of the total number of tourists visiting the city, this is not significantly different from any other city.[^5740][^5747]

#### In popular culture

"The Jerusalem Syndrome", a theater play by [Joshua Sobol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Sobol), deals with the fanaticism that led to the destruction of the Jewish [Second Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Temple).[^5748]

In [*The X-Files* (season 3, episode 11, "Revelations")](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_X-Files_%28season_3%29), released in 1995, the perpetrator is depicted as having "Jerusalem Syndrome" after a visit to the city. He returns to the US and begins to hunt down people with signs of [stigmata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stigmata).

In Robert Stone's 1998 novel *[Damascus Gate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damascus_Gate_%28novel%29)*, several characters are said to be afflicted with Jerusalem Syndrome.

The 2001 song "Jerusalem" was composed by James Raymond on the topic of the Jerusalem Syndrome. It appears on the 2001 record *Just Like Gravity*, by CPR (David Crosby, Jeff Pevar, James Raymond).

A 2006 film by Victor Braun titled *Jerusalem Syndrome* tells the story of a Christian pilgrim with the syndrome.

In *[The Simpsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons)* 2010 episode "[The Greatest Story Ever D'ohed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Greatest_Story_Ever_D'ohed)", [Homer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer_Simpson) develops Jerusalem syndrome while visiting [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel) with his family as part of a tour group from Springfield. The illness and its effects on him become a central element of the episode's plot. Eventually, most members of the tour group are overcome with Jerusalem syndrome, each one proclaiming that he/she is the messiah.[^5749]

In the 2014 [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company) series *[Black Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Box_%28TV_series%29)*, the episode "Jerusalem" (Season 1, Episode 5) features a character diagnosed with Jerusalem syndrome after he becomes suddenly and compulsively religious during a trip to Israel.[^5750]

The 2015 movie *[Jeruzalem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JeruZalem)* features a character that is suspected to have the Jerusalem syndrome.[^5751]

"Jerusalem", the twelfth story in [Neil Gaiman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Gaiman)'s 2015 collection *[Trigger Warning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Gaiman_bibliography)*, centres around a British woman who comes down with the syndrome on holiday. She believes God is speaking to her and eventually flees her home to return to Jerusalem.[^5752]

The catalog of the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art)'s 2016 show about an earlier era of the city's history used the syndrome as the "organizing [metaphor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metaphor)" for the first paragraph of the introduction, per a review.[^5753]

In 2023 the [York Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Theatre) Company produced "The Jerusalem Syndrome,"[^5754] a musical comedy written by Kyle Rosen, Laurence Holzman and Felicia Needleman, and directed by [Don Stephenson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Stephenson). The 14-person cast included [Farah Alvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farah_Alvin) and [Lenny Wolpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenny_Wolpe).

### Religion in Antarctica

**Religion in Antarctica** is largely dominated by [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity), with [churches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_%28building%29) being the only [religious buildings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_building) on the continent. Although used regularly for [Christian worship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_worship), the [Chapel of the Snows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_the_Snows) has also been used for [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism) and [Baháʼí Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bah%C3%A1%CA%BC%C3%AD_Faith) ceremonies. Some of the early religious buildings are now protected as important [historical monuments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_monument).

#### Beginnings

The first [clergyman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clergyman) of any [denomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_denomination) to set foot on Antarctica was [Arnold Spencer-Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Spencer-Smith) (1883-1916), an [Anglican priest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_priest) who was chaplain and photographer for the [Ross Sea Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Sea_Party) of Shackleton's [Imperial Trans Antarctic Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Trans-Antarctic_Expedition).[^5755] Spencer-Smith set up a chapel in Ponting's darkroom in [Scott's Hut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott's_Hut) at [Cape Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Evans). He arranged an altar with a cross and candlesticks and an [aumbry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aumbry) where he reserved the [Blessed Sacrament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blessed_Sacrament); he made a lamp to hang by the aumbry to indicate the [real presence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_presence). In his diary, Spencer-Smith records when he celebrated Eucharist and how many were present. He also records when he heard [confession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confession_%28religion%29) on the continent. Spencer-Smith was the first clergyman to land in Antarctica, the first to celebrate the Eucharist and the first to die and be buried there.[^5755]

A cross on Wind Vane Hill, Cape Evans, was erected by the [Ross Sea Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Sea_Party), led by Captain Aeneas Mackintosh, of Sir [Ernest Shackleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Shackleton)’s [Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Trans-Antarctic_Expedition) of 1914-1917, in memory of three members of the party who died in the vicinity in 1916. The cross has been designated a [Historic Site or Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historic_Sites_and_Monuments_in_Antarctica) (HSM 17), following a proposal by New Zealand and the United Kingdom to the [Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Treaty_System).[^5756]

On 20 February 1946, the first Catholic mass to be held in Antarctica took place at the Stella Maris chapel at the Argentine Orcadas station, led by the Spanish Jesuit Father Felipe Lérida. An 8-metre cross was erected and the pope was contacted by telegram.[^5757]

The first [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic) service in Antarctica was performed in 1947 by [William Menster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Menster) (1913-2007), [Lieutenant Commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Commander) of the [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy) during [Operation Highjump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Highjump).[^5758] During a Catholic service held in a tent set up on land, he [consecrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consecrated) Antarctica. Ministering to approximately 2,000 men from a variety of [Christian denominations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_denomination) gave him experience in leading [ecumenical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecumenical) services.

Although they are used mostly for Christian worship, the [Chapel of the Snows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_the_Snows) has also been used for [Buddhist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhist) and [Baháʼí Faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bah%C3%A1%CA%BC%C3%AD_Faith) ceremonies. Some of the buildings are among historically important sites and under protection, such as the Chilean [Captain Arturo Prat Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Arturo_Prat_Base)'s wooden cross and a Statue of Our Lady of the Carmel.[^5759]

#### History (including the subantarctic islands)

Around 1900, [whaling stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whaling_station) and expedition camps were erected in the larger area. After [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II), some [military expeditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_expedition) explored the region. The [International Geophysical Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Geophysical_Year) (1957-1958) marked the end of a long period during the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War) when scientific interchange between [East and West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East%E2%80%93West_dichotomy) had been seriously interrupted and has since contributed to civil scientific exploration. Since the 1950s, most stations in Antarctica have been constructed exclusively for [scientific research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_research). Extended stays in the region can be an extremely stressful experience for the researchers who often have been separated from their families for months at a time.[^5760] [Jesuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuit), who have had a long tradition of geophysical research in Antarctica, contributed as well to the early Antarctic missions. Notable Jesuit scholars like [Edward A. Bradley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradley_Nunatak), [Henry F. Birkenhauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkenhauer_Island), J. Joseph Lynch and Daniel J. Linehan have been among those.[^5761]

The first churches south of the [Antarctic Convergence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Convergence) and north of 60° S latitude (and thus not part of the [Antarctic Treaty System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Treaty_System)) are [Notre-Dame des Vents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre-Dame_des_Vents) at [Port-aux-Français](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-aux-Fran%C3%A7ais) on the main island of [Kerguelen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerguelen_Islands) and the [Norwegian Lutheran Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Anglican_Church,_Grytviken), a former [Lutheran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Norway) [chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel) in [Grytviken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grytviken), [South Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Georgia_and_the_South_Sandwich_Islands) (since 1913). After years of abandonment and weathering the harsh elements of the region (roof damaged in 1994), the Grytviken church was renovated by the keepers of [South Georgia Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Georgia_Museum) and volunteers in 1996-1998 and now serves for occasional church services and marriage ceremonies.[^5762]

Some churches north of the Antarctic Convergence serve Antarctic territories, such as the [Christ Church Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ_Church_Cathedral_%28Falkland_Islands%29) in [Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley,_Falkland_Islands), which is the southernmost Anglican cathedral in the world. It serves as the parish church not only for the Falkland Islands, but also [South Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Georgia_Island) and the [British Antarctic Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Antarctic_Territory). [Punta Arenas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punta_Arenas), at the southern tip of the South American mainland (just north of Tierra del Fuego), also has a Roman Catholic cathedral, which serves the [Chilean Antarctic Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilean_Antarctic_Territory).

Christians have increasingly turned toward Internet communications for fellowship in the 21st century.[^5763]

#### Notable buildings

Out of nearly 90 stations in Antarctica, half are only used in the summer months. Most [research stations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_station) have a small meeting room dual-purposed for religious assemblies.[^5764] Larger stations and communities use a separate room, often a makeshift steel container for religious purposes.[^5764]

The [Chapel of the Snows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_the_Snows,_Antarctica) was erected in 1956 as a Christian chapel used by several denominations at [McMurdo Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMurdo_Station), [Ross Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Island). The Chapel offers various Protestant and Catholic services, but also allows for meetings of other religions, such as Latter-day Saints, [Baháʼís](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bah%C3%A1%CA%BC%C3%AD_Faith) and [Buddhists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism) and is used as well for secular groups (e.g. [Alcoholics Anonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholics_Anonymous)). The chapel had been rebuilt after a fire in 1978 and was reconsecrated in 1989.

##### Catholic sites

The majority of Catholic Antarctic sites exist due to the Argentine presence on the Continent. The Worldwide Antarctic Program proposes building a Catholic [chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel) at [Mario Zucchelli Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Zucchelli_Station), [Terra Nova Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_Nova_Bay), Antarctica, while the first Catholic chapel (named after [Saint Francis of Assisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Francis_of_Assisi)) was built in 1976 at the Argentine [Esperanza Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esperanza_Base).[^5765] The [Chapel of Our Lady of the Snows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_Our_Lady_of_the_Snows_%28Belgrano_II_Base%29) is at the Argentine [Belgrano II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrano_II) Base at [Coats Land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coats_Land). It is a permanent Catholic chapel made entirely of ice.[^5766]

Further dedicated religious buildings are the [Chapel of Santisima Virgen de Lujan, Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_Santisima_Virgen_de_Lujan,_Antarctica), a Catholic chapel at [Marambio Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marambio_Base), [Seymour Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seymour_Island), San Francisco de Asis Chapel, a [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church) chapel at [Esperanza Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esperanza_Base), [Antarctic Peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Peninsula) and [Santa Maria Reina de la Paz Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapel_of_St._Mary_Queen_of_Peace), a Catholic church at the [Villa Las Estrellas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villa_Las_Estrellas), [South Shetland Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shetland_Islands). Santa María Reina de la Paz is a repurposed container allowing for 36 persons to convene.[^5767]

There is a small Catholic shrine near [McMurdo Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McMurdo_Station) called "Our Lady of the Snows". Popularly known as "Roll Cage Mary", the shrine was dedicated to a United States Navy [Seabee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seabee) who was killed during the construction of the station. It has been maintained by [Carmelite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmelite) nuns in [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand).[^5768]

##### Eastern Orthodox Christian revival

[Religious activities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_activities) were halted during the [Soviet Antarctic Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Antarctic_Expedition). However, this changed with the fall of the Soviet Union and Communism within [Central and Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_and_Eastern_Europe).

The [St. Ivan Rilski Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Ivan_Rilski_Chapel), a [Bulgarian Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Orthodox_Church) chapel at [St. Kliment Ohridski Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Kliment_Ohridski_Base), [South Shetland Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shetland_Islands), was built in 2003 and is the first Eastern Orthodox edifice in Antarctica, and was the southernmost Eastern Orthodox building of worship in the world till 2011 when St Volodymyr ([Vladimir the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_the_Great)) Chapel at Ukrainian [Vernadsky Research Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vernadsky_Research_Base) was erected.

The [Buromskiy Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buromskiy_Island) cemetery belongs among the most important monuments in the region.[^5769] A Russian Orthodox cross has been erected in the meantime to mark the site. The island holds a [cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemetery) for about 60 citizens of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union), [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovakia), the [German Democratic Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Democratic_Republic) and [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland) who died in the performance of their duties while serving as members of Soviet and Russian Antarctic expeditions. It has been designated a [Historic Site or Monument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historic_Sites_and_Monuments_in_Antarctica) (HSM 9) following a proposal by Russia to the [Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_Treaty_System).[^5756]

In 2002, [Patriarch Alexy II of Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriarch_Alexy_II_of_Moscow) asked for a "Temple for Antarctica" (Храм Антарктиде) and initiated the [Trinity Church, Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Church,_Antarctica), a [Russian Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Orthodox_Church) church at [Bellingshausen Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellingshausen_Station), South Shetland Islands.[^5770][^5771] The Church is being positioned as a widely visible landmark[^5764] and is maintained by the Moscow Patriarch.[^5772] It was first maintained by a single priest. In the meanwhile two priests maintain the services, which are being exchanged annually. They both contribute to the maintenance of the overall station.[^5773] 29 January 2007 saw the first church wedding on Antarctica, between a Chilean and a Russian.[^5773][^5774] The first baptism (for adults) also took place there.[^5775]

#### Islam

While the [Pakistani program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan_Antarctic_Programme) at [Jinnah Antarctic Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinnah_Antarctic_Station) brought [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim) to Antarctica in 1991,[^5776] there are no [mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosque) on the continent or on any of the outlying islands, as there is yet no consensus as to observing [Islamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam) religious customs.[^5777]

It would also be impossible to fast for the month of Ramadan for an entire solar day during the summer in the Southern Hemisphere, so alternatives to this problem have been proposed by multiple sources. It has been reported that Muslim scientists on Antarctica use [Mecca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecca) time for Ramadan fasting.[^5778]
