### The All-Joking, All-Drunken Synod of Fools and Jesters

**The All-Joking, All-Drunken Synod of Fools and Jesters**[^5779] (1692[^5780]-1725)[^5781] was a club founded by [Peter I of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_the_Great). The group included many of Peter's closest friends, and its activities centered mostly around drinking and reveling. The group was not without controversies; some of its parodies against the [Russian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Orthodox_Church) in particular were heavily criticized.

#### The Jolly Company

As a teenager and young adult, [Peter I of Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_the_Great) had a large group of friends and followers. Some were childhood friends who had been with him since throughout his stay at [Preobrazhenskoye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preobrazhenskoye_District) or before, such as [Nikita Zotov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Zotov) and [Fyodor Romodanovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyodor_Romodanovsky); others were older patriotic men from respected families, such as Prince Michael Cherkassky, Prince Peter Prozorovsky, and [Fedor Golovin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyodor_Alexeyevich_Golovin); and some others were foreigners, such as [Patrick Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Gordon) and [Franz Lefort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Lefort), whose company Peter enjoyed. Together, the "cohesive group" often wandered the countryside and interrupted noblemen, asking for food and shelter for the night. Known as the "Jolly Company", it had anywhere from 80 to 200 members. In addition to the vast varieties of food, games, and events at the parties the Jolly Company held, there were also substantial amounts of [alcoholic beverages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholic_beverage).[^5782]

In time, the Jolly Company held more and more parties within Moscow itself, often within the home of Franz Lefort. Lefort, however, had limited funds, and he could not often afford to host the Tsar. To assist Lefort, Peter first built Lefort a large dining hall, and when that grew to be too small, he built him a fully furnished stone mansion with a banquet hall that could hold 1,500 men. The hall would become "a kind of [clubhouse](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/clubhouse)" for the Jolly Company, even when Peter or Lefort were absent.[^5783]

#### Transformation into the "Synod"

The Jolly Company slowly "proceeded to more organized buffoonery and masquerades" as Peter gave many of the men titles that they addressed each other by, often for ridiculous reasons. For example, a boyar named Ivan Buturlin was forever known as "The Polish King" because he played the enemy in a mock battle at Preobrazhenskoye, while Fyodor Romodanovsky was first known as "King of Pressburg" and then as "Prince-Caesar". Many years later, Peter would address Romodanovsky as "Your Majesty" and even presented him as the Tsar to defeated military opponents.[^5784]

The Jolly Company eventually formed a group known as The All-Joking, All-Drunken Synod of Fools and Jesters, which had a "Prince-Pope", a college of cardinals, bishops, archimandrites, priests and deacons. Deacon Peter created several rituals, ceremonies, and commandments for the group, which involved primarily heavy drinking requirements,[^5785] and was the leader of the group, despite his lowly title.[^5786] The group ended up including *every* man of power within the Tsar's government,[^5786] and even real clergymen as well.[^5787]

In January 1695, just three years after the election of Nikita Zotov as "Prince-Pope", Peter refused to partake in a traditional Russian Orthodox ceremony of having holy water sprinkled over his head during the [Epiphany Ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epiphany_%28holiday%29).[^5788] Instead, Peter and the Synod celebrated their own version of the Russian folk custom of *sviatki*, with partying, drinking, and even eroticism. Peter even specifically designed Zotov's election and the celebration to conflict with the traditional Church celebration.[^5780]

#### Mocking of the Russian Orthodox Church

Peter's creation of this group was not without controversy, both at the time and in the eyes of historians. Peter formed the Drunken Synod when he was just eighteen and let it continue until the end of his life. The mock-[Synod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synod) angered many [Orthodox Russians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Orthodox_Church); many even believed because of it that Peter was the [Antichrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antichrist).[^5789] [Robert K. Massie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_K._Massie) says that this quickly changed after "Peter quickly steered the parody to a safer mimicry of the [Roman Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church)", which did not bother as many Russians.[^5790] [Robin Milner-Gulland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Milner-Gulland) notes that the Synod has been seen in various lights - as an imitation of [Hellfire Clubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellfire_Club), a physical manifestation of Peter's drive at modernizing Russia or of Peter's partial seizures, or simply as a way for Peter and his friends to enjoy themselves.[^5791]

[^5779]: The group is also known by various similarly-phrased titles.

### Hell house

**Hell houses** are [haunted house](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haunted_house) adaptions by [evangelical Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangelicalism) organizations that depict [sinners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sin) and their horrible fate in [Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell_in_Christianity). Scenes portrayed may include [date rape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Date_rape),[^5792] [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage), [gambling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gambling), [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion), [extramarital sex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extramarital_sex), [raving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rave), [drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_drug), and [alcohol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholic_beverage).[^5793] They were most prominent during the late 1990s and 2000s. Other hell houses focus on the theme of the [seven deadly sins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_deadly_sins).[^5794] Hell houses typically emphasize the belief that those who do not [repent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repentance_%28Christianity%29) of their sins and choose to follow [Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus_in_Christianity) are condemned to Hell.

A Hell house, like a conventional haunted-house attraction, is a space set aside for actors to frighten patrons with gruesome exhibits and scenes, presented as a series of short vignettes with a narrated guide. Unlike haunted houses, Hell houses focus on real-life situations and the effects of sin or the fate of unrepentant sinners in the [afterlife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afterlife) and often feature an [altar call](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altar_call).[^5793] They are most typically operated in the days preceding [Halloween](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloween).

#### History

The first known Hell house was set up by [Jerry Falwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Falwell) in [Lynchburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynchburg,_Virginia), [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia), beginning production in 1972. The attraction, called ScareMare, was backed by Falwell's [Liberty University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_University) and features [culture war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_war) issues appealing to the [Moral Majority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_Majority) of the 1980s and the [new Christian right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Christian_right).[^5795][^5796][^5793] ScareMare continues annually as of 2025.[^5797]

Hell houses and similar attractions such as Judgment houses, [Revelation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Revelation) Walk, [Rapture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapture) Walk, [Tribulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Tribulation) Trail, and stage productions like *Heaven's Gates, Hell's Flames* became more common among conservative evangelical churches in the 1980s and 1990s.[^5793] Trinity Assembly of God in [Cedar Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedar_Hill,_Texas), [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas), is known to have presented a Hell house since 1990.[^5798] Initially popular in the Southern and Western United States, events are now held throughout the United States and in other countries.[^5793]

From 1995, the concept was promoted and adapted by Keenan Roberts, originally of [Roswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell,_New_Mexico), [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico), who started a Hell house in [Arvada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arvada,_Colorado), [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado). Since that time, Hell houses have become a regular fixture of the Halloween season in parts of the United States. Roberts remained active in the Hell house ministry by providing kits and directions to enable churches to perform their own attractions.[^5799] As of 16 January 2017, the "Hell House Kit" was still available. As of 2023, a package of hell house scripts and scenes was being sold for \$479.[^5800]

In October 2000, documentary filmmaker George Ratliff filmed a production of a Hell house in Cedar Hill, Texas, from scripting to the final night of the production.[^5801] The resulting documentary, *[Hell House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hell_House_%28film%29)*,[^5802] has inspired numerous live plays and hell-house performances, including one based on Pastor Roberts' production, which played for a month during the 2006 Halloween season in an off-[Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadway_theatre) production in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_%28state%29), by [Les Freres Corbusier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Freres_Corbusier).[^5803][^5804]

### Saint Guinefort

**Saint Guinefort** (modern French pronunciation: \[ɡinfɔʁ\]) was a legendary 13th-century French [greyhound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyhound) that received local veneration as a [folk saint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_saint).[^5805][^5806][^5807]

#### Legend

Guinefort's story is a variation on the well-travelled "dog defends master's child against animal assailant" motif, as indexed in the international classification system as [B524ff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motif-Index_of_Folk-Literature), similar to the Welsh story of the dog [Gelert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gelert).[^5808]

In one of the earliest versions of the story, described by the [Dominican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominican_Order) friar [Stephen of Bourbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_of_Bourbon) in 1250, Guinefort the [greyhound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyhound) belonged to a Lord who lived in a castle near [Lyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyon).[^5809]

One day, the unnamed Lord and Lady of the castle left their infant son home alone, sleeping in his cradle. When the nurse returned to the house, she found the nursery in chaos - the cradle spattered with blood and Guinefort sat beside it with bloody jaws. Her screams drew first the Lady of the house and then the Lord. He, believing Guinefort to have devoured his son, slew the dog with his sword. Only then did the family approach to find their son sleeping in his cradle, safe and sound, along with the body of a snake killed by dog bites. Guinefort had killed the snake and saved the child. On realizing the mistake the family dropped the dog down a well, covered it with stones and planted trees around it, setting up a [shrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shrine) for Guinefort.[^5806]

Upon learning of the dog's martyrdom, the local peasants venerated the dog as a saint and visited his shrine when they were in need, especially mothers with sick children. They honored the dog as a martyr who could help heal sicknesses and other needs.[^5806][^5807]

As [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism) churches emerged in the [16th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16th_century), they "criticized the [cult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult) of Guinefort seeing in it an example of the abuses and enacted errors of the Catholic Church." The [Catholic hierarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierarchy_of_the_Catholic_Church) adopted the continued critique, and sought to suppress Guinefort belief and practices, and [ostracize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostracism) practitioners.[^5810]

The custom was regarded as harmful and superstitious by the Church, which made efforts to eradicate it and enacted a [fine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_%28penalty%29) for the continued practice.[^5811] Community memory of the practices was still present in the 1970s, with the last known visit by someone to Saint Guinefort Wood to effect a cure for a sick child occurring around the 1940s.[^5806][^5807]

Historian John Bossy used this canine folk saint to explore medieval attitudes to sanctity.[^5812]

### Dinkoism

**Dinkoism** (/ˈdɪnkɔɪzəm/), the **Dinkoist religion**, or **Dinkamatham**[^5813][^5814] is a [parody religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parody_religion) and [social movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_movement) that emerged and evolved on [social networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_network)[^5815] organized by independent welfare groups in the Indian state of [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala). Adherents describe Dinkoism as a genuine religion.

\

#### History

According to a report in *[India Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India_Today)*, Dinkoism[^5815] was established in 2008 in Kerala by a group of [rationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rationalism) with the intention of ridiculing "the absurdity of blind religious faith".[^5816] The community planned to become politically active.[^5817] A report in *[The New Indian Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_Indian_Express)* said Dinkoism is gaining members through Facebook.[^5815] The [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC) described Dinkoism in 2016 as an atheist movement with significant growth on social media.[^5818]

#### Description

The religion purports to worship [Dinkan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinkan), a comic book character.[^5819] Dinkoists celebrate the character, a [superhero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superhero) mouse that appeared in 1983 in defunct [Malayalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam)-language children's magazine *[Balamangalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balamangalam)*, as their God for the purpose of exposing [superstitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superstition_in_India) and fallacies and practices of traditional religions.[^5818][^5820]

#### Events and protests

The concept of Dinkoism has spread through social media but the movement has also organised protest events. On January 30, 2016, a group of Dinkoists, under the banner of *Mooshikasena* (Rat Army) held a mock protest in front of Dhe Puttu restaurant owned by popular actor [Dileep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dileep_%28actor%29) alleging his upcoming film Professor Dinkan hurt their religious sentiments, mocking similar protests happening worldwide.[^5821][^5822]

Earlier Dinkoism was in news when an expatriate Dinkoist living in California obtained a license plate with the inscription DINKAN for his car, out of his devotion for Dinkan.[^5823] In 2016, [J. Devika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._Devika) wrote an article about the concept of Dinkoism and the logic of the market.[^5824]

Dinkan's image have been used in various protests. In 2026, Dinkan posters were spotted in [NEET paper leak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_NEET_controversy) protests.[^5825]

#### Conferences

Dinkoists of Kozhikode organised a conference at the Sports Council Hall, [Mananchira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mananchira) on March 20, 2016. They organised a variety of entertainments with a theme of [tapioca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapioca). E. A. Jabbar, a prominent rationalist, endorsed Dinkoism.[^5819]

In April 2016, 25,000 Dinkoists were expected to gather for a convention called a "Dinkamatha Maha Sammelanam" to "present their rights as a minority community".[^5817] Dinkoists have received threatening messages as well as opposition from believers of other religions.[^5815]

### Dreadnought hoax

The ***Dreadnought* hoax** was a [practical joke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Practical_joke) pulled by [Horace de Vere Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_de_Vere_Cole) in 1910. Cole tricked the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy) into showing their [flagship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagship), the [battleship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship) [HMS *Dreadnought*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Dreadnought_%281906%29), to a fake delegation of [Abyssinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Empire) royals. The hoax drew attention in Britain to the emergence of the [Bloomsbury Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomsbury_Group), among whom some of Cole's collaborators numbered. The hoax was a repeat of a similar impersonation that Cole and [Adrian Stephen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Stephen) had organised while they were students at [Cambridge University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_University) in 1905.

#### Background

##### Hoaxers

[Horace de Vere Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_de_Vere_Cole) was born in Ireland in 1881 to a well-to-do family.[^5826] He was [commissioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_%28armed_forces%29) into the [Yorkshire Hussars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Hussars) and served in the [Second Boer War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Boer_War), where he was seriously wounded and invalided out of service.[^5827][^5828] On his return to Britain, he became an undergraduate at [Trinity College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College,_Cambridge); he studied little and spent his time entertaining and undertaking hoaxes and pranks.[^5829]

One of Cole's closest friends at Trinity was [Adrian Stephen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Stephen), a keen sportsman and actor. Cole's biographer, Martyn Downer, considers that Stephen was a "perfect foil for ... \[Cole\]: someone sympathetic and encouraging yet unafraid to take him on".[^5830] Stephen was the son of [Leslie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leslie_Stephen), the writer and critic, and [Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia_Stephen), the philanthropist and [Pre-Raphaelite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Raphaelite_Brotherhood) model. Adrian Stephen's elder brother, [Thoby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoby_Stephen), was also at Trinity, and their sisters, Vanessa (later [Vanessa Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanessa_Bell)) and Virginia (later [Virginia Woolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Woolf)), would visit.[^5831] After university, the four Stephen siblings became members of the [Bloomsbury Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomsbury_Group), the set of associated writers, intellectuals, philosophers and artists, many of whose members had also been at Trinity College. Cole was on the fringes of the group but never a member.[^5832]

##### Cambridge Zanzibar hoax

In early 1905, while in their second year at [Trinity College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College,_Cambridge), [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge), Cole and Adrian Stephen decided to use a visit to England of [Sayyid Ali bin Hamud Al-Busaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_bin_Hamud_of_Zanzibar), the eighth [Sultan of Zanzibar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Sultans_of_Zanzibar), as the basis for a hoax.[^5833][^5834] A plan was put together to fake a [state visit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_visit) of the sultan to Cambridge, although they realised that as the sultan's picture had recently appeared in the press, there was a risk the visiting sultan would be shown as a fraud. They decided that Cole would impersonate the sultan's uncle rather than the sultan.[^5835] On 2 March, they sent a [telegram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegram) to the [Mayor of Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mayors_of_Cambridge) to ask if he could arrange a suitable reception for the sultan:

> The Sultan of Zanzibar will arrive today at Cambridge at 4.27 for a short visit. Could you arrange to show him buildings of interest and send carriage?\
> Henry Lucas, Hotel Cecil, London[^5836][^5837]

The students obtained robes and turbans from the theatrical costumier [Willy Clarkson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy_Clarkson), applied [blackface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackface) make-up and took the train from London. A carriage met the group at [Cambridge railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_railway_station) and took them to [the guildhall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_Guildhall), where they were met by the mayor and town clerk. After a brief reception they were taken on a tour of the town, including some of the [university's colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colleges_of_the_University_of_Cambridge); the hoaxers were seen by some of their friends and acquaintances, who did not recognise them.[^5838][^5839] After less than an hour they demanded to be returned to the station. As they did not want to return to London, returning from which would have meant them breaking the 10:00 pm college [curfew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curfew), on arrival at the station, they ran out of a side exit and took two [hansom cabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hansom_cab) to a friend's house, where they changed back into their normal attire.[^5840][^5841]

The following day Cole gave an interview to the *[Daily Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_Mail)* about the hoax; the story appeared in the paper on 4 March 1905 and was repeated in local newspapers. The *[St James's Gazette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Gazette)* considered the events "a most audacious practical joke".[^5837][^5842] The Mayor wanted the students involved to be [sent down](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/send%20down) (expelled), but was persuaded by the [Vice-Chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice-Chancellor_of_the_University_of_Cambridge) that this would damage his reputation further.[^5843]

##### Dreadnoughts and the Royal Navy

In the early 20th century, Britain's naval fleet was seen as one of the foundations of its empire, and a reflection of the country's power and wealth.[^5844] As Britain was portrayed in books, plays and popular culture as an island nation, the [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy) was seen as the defender of the island and its first line of defence.[^5845] A [leading article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leading_article) in *[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Observer)* in 1909 described the supremacy of the Royal Navy as "the best security for the world's peace and advancement".[^5846]

[HMS *Dreadnought*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Dreadnought_%281906%29), the first of Britain's "dreadnought" class of [battleship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship), entered into Royal Navy service in 1906.[^5847] *Dreadnought* was the most technologically advanced ship built; it was better armed, faster and stronger than any other vessel afloat.[^5848] According to the historian Jan Rüger, from the time the ship was launched, it took on cultural significance as a symbol and it entered into public consciousness through songs and advertising. When the ship visited London in 1909, part of three [fleet reviews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fleet_review_%28Commonwealth_realms%29) held, a million people were estimated to have watched its arrival, and by 1910 it "had become a cultural icon with undeniable symbolic status".[^5849] Rüger gives examples of advertising for [Oxo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxo_%28food%29) [stock cubes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bouillon_cube): "Drink OXO and dread nought"; a tailoring business that used the slogan "Dreadnought and wear British clothing"; and "Dreadnought [trams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tram)" ran, styled as battleships, and complete with imitation guns.[^5850] The cultural historian Elisa deCourcy describes the *Dreadnought* as having "a near sacrosanct nature" for the [Edwardians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwardian_era).[^5844]

In February 1910 the captain of *Dreadnought* was [Herbert Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_Richmond); [Admiral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Admiral) Sir [William May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_May_%28Royal_Navy_officer%29) was the Commander-in-Chief, [Home Fleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Fleet); as such, *Dreadnought* was his [flagship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagship).[^5851][^5852] Also present on *Dreadnought* was Commander [Willie Fisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wordsworth_Fisher), the Stephens' cousin, who was on the staff of the Admiral.[^5853][^5854]

#### Hoax

In a talk given in 1940 Woolf described how, in 1910, young naval officers enjoyed playing [practical jokes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Practical_joke) on one another:

> the officers of the [Hawke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Hawke_%281891%29) and the Dreadnought had a feud. ... And Cole's friend who was on the Hawke had come to Cole, and said to him, "You're a great hand at hoaxing people; couldn't you do something to pull the leg of the Dreadnought? They want taking down a bit. Couldn't you manage to play off one of your jokes against them?"[^5855]

This involved Cole and five friends, writer Virginia Stephen (later [Virginia Woolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Woolf)), her brother [Adrian Stephen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Stephen), [Guy Ridley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Ridley), [Anthony Buxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Buxton) and the artist [Duncan Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Grant), who had themselves disguised by the theatrical costumier [Willy Clarkson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy_Clarkson)[^5856] with [skin darkeners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackface) and turbans to resemble members of [the Abyssinian royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomonic_dynasty). The main limitation of the disguises was that the "royals" could not eat anything or their make-up would be ruined. Adrian Stephen took the role of "interpreter".

On 7 February 1910 Clarkson's employees visited Woolf's home and applied the stage make-up to Woolf, Grant, Buxton and Ridley, then provided eastern robes. According to the *[Daily Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily_Mirror)*, they were also wearing £500 of jewellery;[^5857][^5858] Martin Downer, in his biography of Cole, doubts the amount, which is not repeated by any of the participants.[^5859]

A friend of Stephen's sent a telegram to the "C-in-C, Home Fleet" ([Commander-in-chief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander-in-chief) of [the vessels defending Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Fleet)) stating that "Prince Makalen of Abbysinia *\[*[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic)*\]* and suite arrive 4.20 today Weymouth. He wishes to see Dreadnought. Kindly arrange meet them on arrival";[^5860] the message was signed "Harding Foreign Office". Cole had found a post office staffed only by women, as he thought they were less likely to ask questions about the message.[^5861] Cole, with his entourage, went to London's [Paddington station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddington_station) where Cole claimed that he was "Herbert Cholmondeley" of the [Foreign Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Foreign_Office) and demanded a special train to [Weymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weymouth,_Dorset); the stationmaster arranged [a VIP coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_railroad_car).

In Weymouth, the navy welcomed the princes with an [honour guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honour_guard). An [Abyssinian flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Ethiopia) was not found, so the navy proceeded to use [that of Zanzibar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Zanzibar) and to play Zanzibar's national anthem.[^5862]

The group inspected the fleet. To show their appreciation, they communicated in a gibberish of words drawn from Latin and Greek; they asked for [prayer mats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prayer_mat) and attempted to bestow fake [military honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_awards_and_decorations) on some of the officers. Commander Fisher failed to recognise either of his cousins.[^5863]

When the prank was uncovered in London, the ringleader [Horace de Vere Cole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace_de_Vere_Cole) contacted the press and sent a photo of the "princes" to the *Daily Mirror*. The group's pacifist views were considered a source of embarrassment, and the Royal Navy briefly became an object of ridicule. The navy later demanded that Cole be arrested. However, Cole and his compatriots had not broken any law. Instead, except for Virginia Woolf, they were subjected to [a symbolic thrashing on the buttocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagellation) by junior Royal Navy officers.[^5864]

#### Aftermath

According to press reports, during the visit to *Dreadnought*, the visitors repeatedly showed amazement or appreciation by exclaiming, "[bunga bunga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunga_bunga)!"[^5865] In 1915 during the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War), HMS *Dreadnought* rammed and sank [a German submarine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SM_U-29_%28Germany%29), the only battleship ever to do so. Among the telegrams of congratulation was one that read "BUNGA BUNGA".[^5866]

A song was heard in [music halls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_hall) that year, sung to the tune of "[The Girl I Left Behind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Girl_I_Left_Behind)":

> When I went on board a Dreadnought ship\
> I looked like a costermonger;\
> They said I was an Abyssinian prince\
> 'Cos I shouted 'Bunga Bunga!'[^5867]

Thirty years later, in 1940, Virginia Woolf gave talks about the *Dreadnought* hoax to the [Rodmell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodmell) [Women's Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Institutes) and also to the [Memoir Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memoir_Club), the latter attended by [E. M. Forster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._M._Forster).[^5868]

### Nebraska Admiral

**Nebraska Admiral** (formally, **Admiral in the Great Navy of the State of Nebraska**) is the state of [Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska)'s highest civic honor, and an [honorary title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_of_honor) bestowed upon individuals by approval of the [Governor of Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Nebraska). It is not a [military rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_rank), requires no specific duties, and carries with it no pay or any other compensation. Admirals have the option of joining the **Nebraska Admirals Association**, a [non-profit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit_organization) that promotes "The Good Life" of Nebraska.

The award certificate describes the honor in a deliberately [tongue-in-cheek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongue-in-cheek) fashion:

> And I \[the Governor of Nebraska\] do strictly charge and require all [officers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_%28armed_forces%29), [seamen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seaman_%28rank%29), [tadpoles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tadpole) and [goldfish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldfish) under your command to be obedient to your orders as Admiral, and you are to observe and follow, from time to time, such directions you shall receive, according to the rules and discipline of the Great Navy of the State of Nebraska.

The use of the title of admiral, instead of some other high-ranking military title, is a humorous reference to the fact that Nebraska has no navy; only 0.68% of the state is water, the fifth-lowest percentage in the nation. Nebraska relies on the [United States Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Armed_Forces) for its defense and has had no active [state defense force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_defense_force) of any sort since 1972. Additionally, Nebraska is the only triple-landlocked state in the nation.

#### History

The Great Navy of the State of Nebraska was created in 1931. The [Lieutenant Governor of Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_Governor_of_Nebraska) at that time, [Theodore W. Metcalfe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_W._Metcalfe), was serving as Acting [Governor of Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Nebraska) while Governor [Charles W. Bryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_W._Bryan) was outside the state. At the urging of some of his friends, he appointed "20 to 25 prominent Nebraskans" as Nebraska Admirals.[^5869]

Commissions in the Nebraska Navy have always been given to prominent citizens both inside and outside of Nebraska. However, anyone who has "contributed in some way to the state, promote the Good Life in Nebraska, and warrant recognition as determined by the Governor" can request or be nominated for an admiralship.

#### Charitable activities

The Nebraska Admirals Association was established in 1986. It is a [501(c)(3)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/501%28c%29) non-profit organization that is devoted to a number of causes, including promoting Nebraska products, educational activities, awarding scholarships, promoting tourism, and providing support for ships and sailors in the [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy) named after Nebraska-related entities.

#### Current guidelines for Admiralships

As of October 2026, Governor [Jim Pillen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Pillen) requires the following criteria for awarding an Admiralship:[^5870]

- The nominator or nominee must be a resident of Nebraska.
- Self-nominations will not be honored.
- Those who are nominating persons for Admiralships will need to send the request by U.S. postal mail or present it to the Governor's Office. E-mail requests will not be accepted. All requests must be in writing.
- If the date for the Admiralship is not specifically requested, the received date will be used on the certificate.
- The Governor retains full discretion for any Admiralship requests.
- The Governor's Office requests notice of two to three weeks to process Admiralships.

#### Controversial admiralships

[Equatorial Guinea President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Presidents_of_Equatorial_Guinea) [Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teodoro_Obiang_Nguema_Mbasogo)[^5880] and former [Gambian President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_The_Gambia) [Yahya Jammeh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahya_Jammeh)[^5881] were both reportedly granted a Nebraska Admiralship. Both Nguema[^5882] and Jammeh[^5883] have been criticized for their dictatorial rule over their respective countries, and the reported granting of the admiralship to Jammeh by [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Nebraska) [Dave Heineman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Heineman) drew the criticism of the state's [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska_Democratic_Party) leader.[^5884]

Governor [Pete Ricketts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pete_Ricketts) revoked admiralship from two women, [Amanda Gailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanda_Gailey) and Courtney Lawton, in January 2018, less than a month after the award. The honor was revoked, according to the governor's spokesman, because the two had protested the appearance of [Turning Point USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turning_Point_USA), a conservative group that maintains a [Professor Watchlist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professor_Watchlist), on the campus of the [University of Nebraska-Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nebraska%E2%80%93Lincoln).[^5885] The governor's office had no enforcement power to retrieve the certificates presented to Gailey and Lawton.[^5886]

### War rug

The **war rug** ([Dari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dari_language): فرش جنگی, romanized: *farš jangi*) tradition of [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan) has its origins in the decade of [Soviet occupation of Afghanistan from 1979](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet%E2%80%93Afghan_War)[^5887] and has continued through the subsequent military, political and social conflicts. Afghan rug-makers began incorporating the apparatus of war into their designs almost immediately after the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union) invaded their country. War rugs continue to be sold, with patterns evolving over time, depicting weaponry such as [drones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_warfare) and events such as the [2021 Fall of Kabul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Kabul_%282021%29).[^5888]

The terms *Baluch* and *war rug* are generalizations given to the genre by rug dealers, commercial galleries, collectors, critics, and commentators. The rugs are characterized as conveying their makers' experiences and interpretations of the circumstances and politics of war and conflict in the region.[^5889]

Professor [Jamal J. Elias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamal_J._Elias) has stated that war rugs are made not to reflect the experiences of their creators, but in response to market demand. Rug brokers and dealers have responded to the market for war rugs, supplying individual creators in bulk with patterns and materials. The rugs are then produced in bulk by individual weavers, including [children](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_labour), working from home. Finished rugs are sold by the brokers, with individual weavers seeing little of the profits.[^5890]

Since the withdrawal of the USSR, the same themes and subjects have been reused and remade. Additionally, after [9/11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks) the events of that day were recorded in carpets, and more recently - since 2015 - [drones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unmanned_aerial_vehicle) have appeared as subject matter.[^5891][^5892]

### Attack on Marstrand

The **attack on Marstrand** was a successful [Dano-Norwegian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark-Norway) [siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege) of the [Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden) town of [Marstrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marstrand) and [Carlsten fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlsten) which took place between 21-27 July 1719 ([N.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar)) during the end of the [Great Northern War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Northern_War).

After a Dano-Norwegian assault on northern [Bohuslän](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohusl%C3%A4n), ships under the command of [Peter Tordenskjold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Tordenskjold) attacked the Swedes at Marstrand harbor and the immobile ships of the Swedish Gothenburg Fleet. The Danes subsequently attacked Carlsten fortress, whose [garrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrison) surrendered swiftly, partly because of [psychological warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_warfare).

The commander of the fortress, [Colonel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel) [Henrich Danckwardt](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrich%20Danckwardt), was later sentenced to death by a Swedish [court-martial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court-martial) for abandoning the fort while it was still deemed defensible.

The surrender of [Carlsten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlsten) fortress in 1719 is still surrounded by myths and legends.

#### Background

After the death of [Charles XII of Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_XII_of_Sweden) on 11 December 1718 (N.S.) at [Fredriksten fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fredriksten) in Norway, the Swedish army marched back across the border to Sweden. [The Great Northern War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Northern_War) which had been fought continuously since 1700, had depleted fighting forces on both sides. As the [Russian Pillage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Pillage_of_1719-1721) of Sweden posed a threat to Sweden's eastern seaboard, a large part of the [Swedish Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Navy) was operating in the [Baltic Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_Sea). Denmark-Norway, seeing this as an opportunity, put plans into motion to retake lost territories on the Swedish west coast. There were also plans for a naval and land invasion of [Bohuslän](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohusl%C3%A4n).[^5895]

The Swedish vessels which had previously been stationed in [Gothenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothenburg), the [Gothenburg Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothenburg_Squadron), had been attacked by [Peter Tordenskjold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Tordenskjold)'s fleet in 1717 and had been ordered by [Charles XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_XII) to remain scattered along the Bohuslän coast. A majority of the squadron was stationed in [Marstrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marstrand) by the Spring of 1719, and a few smaller ships were located near [Strömstad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Str%C3%B6mstad). A couple of smaller vessels escorted transports between Gothenburg and Marstrand on the Nordre River, leaving a single [galley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galley) to defend Gothenburg. The [frigates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frigates) at Marstrand were not operational, due to a lack of sailors and of food and equipment for the crews. Maintenance of the fortresses was handled poorly and in early 1719, local fortification experts complained over not getting paid for a long time. Similar concerns were raised by the naval officers' corps and the carpenters of Gothenburg.[^5896]

##### Blockade and rearmament

At the time, Swedish privateers headquartered in Gothenburg were hijacking foreign vessels. This irritated Dano-Norwegian authorities, so on March 27, a Dano-Norwegian naval force, consisting of four [ships of the line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ships_of_the_line) and a [frigate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frigate), anchored in Rivö Bay outside of Gothenburg, blockading the city. The blockading force was under the command of [Tordenskjold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tordenskjold), who had recently been promoted to the lower admiral rank of [schout-bij-nacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schout-bij-nacht).[^5897] To avoid endangering the peace conference that was to take place in Stockholm in the spring, Tordenskjold was ordered not to assault Gothenburg. In early June, the blockading naval force increased to seven ships of the line, two frigates, four [barges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barge), two floating [batteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artillery_battery), one *bombarderskip*, five galleys and two [Galliots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galliots). The smaller Danish vessels attempted to halt Swedish naval traffic between Nordre river and Marstrand. In mid-June, an additional 26 Danish merchant ships arrived from [Øresund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%98resund) with supplies for the Danish blockading fleet.[^5898]

The stockpiling of supplies in Strömstad in 1718 for [Charles XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_XII_of_Sweden)'s army had resulted in the need for emptying the existing supply caches - which were filled to the brim - as quickly as possible. Many Swedish naval transports with cannons and supplies were moved to Sundsborg and [Svinesund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svinesund) south towards [Uddevalla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uddevalla). The removal of vital supplies caused the defense of northern Bohuslän to falter.[^5899] By the end of May, a convoy of transport vessels had docked at Marstrand for [transshipment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transshipment) to more capable vessels, where the cargo rerouted for further transport through Nordre river. A part of the convoy later returned to Strömstad. On May 23, [Field Marshal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_marshal) [Carl Gustav Rehnskiöld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Gustav_Rehnski%C3%B6ld) took command of Swedish troops in Bohuslän. Following an inspection in May, it was deemed that fortifications needed repair in several locations around the region.[^5900]

The strong Danish blockade outside Gothenburg, with an estimated force of 1,300 soldiers and several special-purpose vessels for bombarding coastal defense positions, implied that the Danes were to attack either Marstrand or [Älvsborg fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%84lvsborg_fortress). Captain Erik Sjöblad of the Gothenburg Squadron was ordered to moor all frigates and galleys to defend the harbor inlets. Rehnskiöld later gave the order to sink all anchored Swedish ships.[^5901]

##### Assault on Strömstad

The peace talks in Stockholm failed, and King [Frederick IV of Denmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_IV_of_Denmark) ordered his troops to attack Sweden. Frederick IV had over 30,000 soldiers available in southern Norway, along with an attack force which would attack Strömstad from the north. A naval force with 8,000 soldiers was to invade [Hisingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hisingen).[^5902] The Swedish transport ships in Strömstad could not vacate Strömstad before Danish Vice Admiral Andreas Rosenpalm blockaded the only way out with a naval force of at least three frigates and four galleys at the end of June. After Rehnskiöld and the commander of the Gothenburg Squadron, Admiral Jonas Fredrik Örnfelt, had assessed the situation and had received intelligence that Norwegian forces were indeed marching towards Strömstad, the order was given to [scuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuttling) the transport fleet.[^5903]

Several Swedish galleys and a smaller vessel attempted to slip out of the area at night through an inner channel but this route was blockaded as well. The Gothenburg squadron's galleys *Kristiania*, *Lovisa* and *Bellona*, along with the [brig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brig) *Pollux*, were all sunk at Tånge Bay and Tångeflo south of Strömstad on July 5.[^5904] The *Strömstad* and *Gå På*, equipped with 20 cannons each, were also sunk, along with fourteen fully loaded cargo ships in Strömstad harbor.[^5905] All remaining caches were opened, so that both civilians and military could take what they could, and the remains were then destroyed. Afterwards, Swedish troops under the command of Rehnskiöld totalling around 5,000 - including the [garrisons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrison) at the [fortifications of Gothenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortifications_of_Gothenburg), Nya Älvsborg and [Carlsten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlsten) - started south towards Uddevalla.[^5906] The first Danish troops arrived in Strömstad between July 6 and July 8. Frederick IV later arrived along with additional soldiers.[^5905]

By the end of June, heavy Danish surveillance of the Gothenburg archipelago had been arranged; a force consisting of eight vessels had been deployed between Klåver island and [Tjuvkil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tjuvkil). Since the vessels were attempting to halt naval traffic between Marstrand and Tjuvkil, and since they were pillaging the archipelago, the Swedes found it highly probable that Tordenskjold was planning to attack Marstrand. The Swedes performed a counter-attack against the Danish blockaders on the night of July 3, when the Swedish galley *Lucretia* and the [brigantines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigantine) *Luren*, *Uppassaren* and *Framfuss* from [Kippholmen](https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kippholmen) in the mouth of Nordre river, managed to creep down [Hisingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hisingen) and get past the Danish reconnaissance fleet without being spotted. The Danish galley *Prins Kristian*, armed with 9 cannons, was attacked and hijacked at Rivö's mouth.[^5907]

#### Battle of Marstrand

##### Friday, July 10

In the first week of July, Tordenskjold scrambled an attack force which he planned to use in his assault on Marstrand. On July 10, the attack began. In the afternoon, the Carlsten fortress garrison reported seeing at least 18 Danish vessels. Tordenskjold had left ships of the line and frigates outside of Gothenburg and the attack force at Marstrand consisted partly of barges armed with cannons and mortars, and galleys with an additional 50 soldiers aboard each ship. Between 600 and 700 soldiers landed at Metsund on the east side of the undefended Koön, east of Marstrand. At the same time, 12 heavy mortars were being transported to the west side of the island. Only the far western part of the island could be bombarded from the fortress. Colonel [Henrich Danckwardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henrich_Danckwardt), commander of Carlsten had on June 27 requested an additional 400-500 men, to prevent an invasion of Koön and Klåverön (south of Marstrand) but the soldiers had not arrived in time to repel Tordenskjold's attack. The Danish tactic of landing on the east side of Koön was virtually the same as the leading General of Norway, [Ulrik Frederik Gyldenløve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulrik_Frederik_Gyldenl%C3%B8ve), had used when he occupied Marstrand and Carlsten at the [Battle of Marstrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marstrand) in July 1677.[^5908]

##### Saturday, July 11

In the morning, heavy barrages were fired from the new Danish artillery stationed at Koön, at Carlsten fortress. Tordenskjold describes in one of his later writings of the new artillery station being heavily fired upon by three Swedish galleys, a barge and three other vessels. He also describes that the Danes were fired upon from Carlsten and its southern outworks. From 6-7 p.m., the cannon fire from Hedvigsholm outwork, which was placed on an island near Koön, consisted of four 36-pounder, two 12-pounder and two 6-pounder cannons. Hedvigsholm was only staffed with twelve men under the command of a [non-commissioned officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-commissioned_officer). When the NCO realized that he would not be able to hold the fortress due to the heavy incoming fire, he sent word to Danckwardt about the situation. Squadron chief Sjöblad decided that the Hedvigsholm battery should be destroyed, to prevent the cannon falling into enemy hands. Danckwardt dispatched Lieutenant Breittenberg to destroy the cannon. Upon his arrival, Breittenberg found that both the Hedvigsholm garrison and the cannon were unharmed, but decided to carry on with his mission. When the Danes noticed that the battery fire from Hedvigsholm had ceased, they started firing upon the Swedish naval vessels in the harbor and managed to sink the vessel which was carrying the crew and ammunition of Hedvigsholm - around seven barrels of gunpowder - to the fortress.[^5909]

After the events in Marstrand, a military hearing was held at the end of July 1719 with commander Danckwardt. Upon being asked why he had not ordered additional manpower to Hedvigsholm, which was considered the strongest and most effective battery to defend the town, which was also being supported by the galley *Prins Fredrik av Hessen*, Danckwardt defended his actions by arguing that if he had not destroyed Hedvigsholm, the outwork would have been captured, regardless of its number of personnel. He also pointed out that the enemy would have been able to wade between Koön and Hedvigsholm, something the hearing officials did not agree with.[^5910]

##### Sunday, July 12

On Saturday night, another Danish cannon battery had been constructed, even closer to Carlsten and the northern river inlet. It was equipped with four 100-pounder mortars and between thirty and forty lighter mortars. Tordenskjold had also planned on using ten 24-pounder cannon but this was prevented by officers responsible for fortifications and the artillery. These officers had been brought on the ships but were not under Tordenskjolds command. They believed that the battery was unsafe, and refused to hand over the cannon. [Fascines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascine) and other supplies necessary to produce the battery were not available, according to army officers. Tordenskjold then ordered a [fahnenjunkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fahnenjunker) and nine gunners under his command, together with additional manpower from the ships, to build the battery. The heavy mortars were carried from the northern side of Koön to the new battery. When it was considered ready, Tordenskjold ordered a barrage against Carlsten, which had little effect on the fortress. Even though Tordenskjold had Swedish naval vessels in his firing range, he avoided firing against them in order to attempt to capture them unharmed.[^5911]

###### Marstrand falls

From 7-8:00 a.m., the first negotiator was dispatched to Marstrand, Danish Captain-Lieutenant Conrad Ployart who was sailing towards the northern outwork Antonetta - which was guarding the northern inlet - in a [sloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sloop) with a clearly visible [white flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_flag). A Swedish sloop carrying a Lieutenant Brännö was sent to meet with the Danish vessel half-way. Ployart demanded access to the fortress but was told that he should speak with the commander, "His excellency" Field Marshal Rehnskiöld, if he wanted anything.[^5912] The Danish officer lamented the fact that he could not meet the commander in person and added that if there were any women present in the fortress, they would immediately be given the chance to leave. Ployart had also received orders to offer the Swedes a deal, the Swedes would have to hand over six naval vessels in exchange for the Danes not firing at Marstrand.[^5913] The Swedes rejected the offer.

After Ployart had returned with the Swedes' rejection, Tordenskjold mounted an assault on the vessels and outworks which were defending the northern harbor inlet. The artillery galiot *Johannes* and the mortar barge *Lange Maren* fired the first rounds. Two barges, the *Hjælperinden* and the *Fredrikshald* were in reserve. The Swedish outworks consisted of Antonetta - equipped with four 6-pounder cannons and a crew of seven - and the Northern Blockhouse, a smaller outwork equipped with two 36-pounder guns. Captain Sjöblad had stationed an additional three cannons close to the Northern Blockhouse, which were served by 15 men. The outworks did not have enough ammunition and were commanded by [NCOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-commissioned_officer). After firing at the outworks, with the help of a galley and eight sloops, 200-300 Danish soldiers were landed on Marstrand island and close to Antonetta.[^5913] After the Swedes had returned fire against the landing force, its guns were spiked and the crews retreated to Carlsten. The Northern Blockhouse suffered the same fate and so the Danes, commanded by Captains Kaas and Kleve, could rapidly enter the city. In the harbor, the Swedish frigate *Kalmar* and the galley *Greve Mörner* continued to defend the northern inlet until the Danish troops eventually entered the city.[^5914]

At the war hearing, Danckwardt was asked why he had not contributed more to the defense of the northern inlet outworks. The two outworks could have defended each other by cross fire and he could have sent one of the seven professional officers from Carlsten to act as a commander. Danckwardt defended himself by saying that he could not afford to send away even more personnel from Carlsten and that the men would have been cut off if the outworks were conquered.[^5915]

###### Sinking of the Swedish fleet

At the same time as the Danes were storming into the city, Danish sloops were sailing towards the Swedish vessels in the harbor. Since the Swedish ship crews were understaffed, they realized that they would not be able to survive the imminent battle; their only way of retreat towards Carlsten was being blockaded and the Swedish ships fired their last [broadsides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadside_%28naval%29). Thereafter, the Swedes fired shots at their own vessels' [strakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strake).

Most of the ships' crews managed to return safely to Carlsten. The vessels which were sunk were the frigates *Halmstad*, *Stettin* and *Kalmar*, all armed with 40 cannon, as well as *Fredricus* (36) and *Charlotta* (30). The galleys *Stå Bra* and *Greve Mörner* with 9 cannons each, the sloop *Diana* (4) along with two [fire ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_ships) were sunk. Tordenskjolds soldiers managed to prevent the sinking of the frigates *Varberg* (40 cannons) and *William Galley* (14), the galiot *Prins Fredrik av Hessen* (9) and the barge *Ge På* (18). *William Galley* was probably a captured British vessel or possibly a privateer.[^5916]

During the hearing, Danckwardt mentioned that a few volunteers from the ship crews and the garrison had left the fortress to "overwhelm the enemy" but could not get any further than the castle hill, since enemy soldiers were deployed around Marstrand cemetery, which was close by. The force of volunteers promptly turned back and re-entered the fortress, according to Danckwardt.[^5917] In the afternoon, firing on Carlsten continued from the mortar batteries on Koön. A shed which was being used as temporary gunpowder storage was hit and exploded. A fire also broke out on the tower roof and on parts of *Fyrkantsbatteriet*, an outwork on the eastern side of the fortress, which were put out by fortress personnel. No deaths were reported as a result of the artillery fire but Swedish morale was depressed because of the Danish conquering of their outworks and the sinking of the Swedish fleet. On the night to Monday, Tordenskjold landed 200 soldiers on Marstrand island, 500 men in total.[^5918]

##### Monday, July 13

During the day, only a few rounds were fired from the fortress and none at all from the Danes. Inside the fortress, the commander ordered artillery officers Captain Josias Mörck and Lieutenant Graan to burn the city down, the officers stated that they did not have any suitable ammunition. At the hearing, Danckwardt was asked why the retreating outwork crews failed to burn the city down, to which he replied that he was not aware that this could have been done any other way except by firing from the fortress. He also argued that the artillery officers unwillingness was because they had their houses inside the city.[^5919]

The Danes transported the captured vessels away from the area, moving up additional mortars and repairing a cannon battery on Koön, which had sustained fire from the *Prins Fredrik av Hessen*. Repairs could be done uninterrupted because Carlsten only had one cannon which could reach the battery and this cannon was damaged.[^5919] The crew of Carlsten consisted of Redväg's company from the [Älvsborg Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%84lvsborg_Regiment) with around 100 men and a company from Zengerlein's Saxon Infantry Regiment which had at least 100 men, both units totalling 227 infantrymen. The artillery, under the command of Captain Mörck, consisted of 54 men. 107 men were acquired from the ship crews as well, the entire crew consisted of a total of 388 men.[^5920]

The fortress had been heavily expanded since the Danish assault in 1677. This rendered Carlsten one of the most heavily defended fortresses in the country. The fortification of the city of Marstrand and the construction of Carlsten fortress was, and still is, one of the largest investments ever in Swedish static defense.[^5921]

##### Tuesday, July 14

Artillery fire against the fortress continued until 11:00 a.m. In the afternoon, Lieutenant Ployart approached the fortress as a negotiator along with an army drummer and asked the Swedes to be let inside. Blindfolded, Ployart was promptly taken to see the Swedish commander. Ployart handed over a sealed letter written by Tordenskjold. The letter, which consisted of flattery and threats, is preserved today in the Danish National Archives.[^5922] While Danckwardt was preparing a proper reply to the letter, one of his captains brought another letter from Tordenskjold to his attention. In it, Tordenskjold offered a sum of 3,000 [ducats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ducats) and the mercy of the Danish king, if the Swedes surrendered. According to Danckwardt, he had replied to the second letter, that even if he had been offered 300,000 ducats, he would rather have blown the fortress up, than abandoning it for money.[^5923] Swedish Captain Jacob von Utfall accompanied Ployart to Tordenskjold later in the day and suggested that an armistice would be appropriate, to which Tordenskjold agreed.[^5924]

When von Utfall had returned to Carlsten, Danckwardt called all officers to a meeting. The protocol of the meeting was later used as an instrument of surrender. The officers explained the situation, the artillery suffered lack of personnel and bad gun carriages. The supply of food was estimated to be able to sustain them for a month but there was a lack of water. The fortress had next to no combat personnel, the naval crews were deemed not of much use in the case of an ambush, due to their lack of combat training, their sole purpose at the fortress was as a fire brigade. Tordenskjold used this time by placing additional light mortars on suitable locations in Marstrand.[^5925]

##### Wednesday, July 15

The Swedish meeting continued during the morning. Tordenskjold was still preparing an assault by relocating the Danish barges, floating batteries and galleys closer to the fortress. Since the Carlsten garrison was deemed too exhausted to sustain an assault, the Swedes agreed to [surrender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrender_%28military%29) before the end of the armistice. All of the Swedish officers signed the instrument of surrender which was handed over to the Danes by Captain von Utfall.[^5926]

> Hwarföre conjunctim resolverades att En formel Capitulation skall giöras genom Capitainen von Uthfall i dhe Puncter och Propositioner som det Jnstrumentet ad acta uthwijsar och aparto underskrifwes. Datum Carlsteen d. 15 Julii 1719

 Quote from the instrument of surrender, Kuylenstierna 1899, pp. 77-78

After two hours, Utfall returned with the document which had been signed by Tordenskjold. All Swedish forces were instructed to leave the fortress by 3:00 p.m., all officers who wished to return to Marstrand were allowed to do so, without being treated as a [prisoner of war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war). The Swedes were granted an additional two hours, properly to vacate the fortress. [^5927]

At four in the afternoon, Tordenskjold arrived at the fortress gate and was promptly let in. Danckwardt met with him and showed him to the commanders quarters, where the other officers had gathered. After a while of conversation, the commander and a number of officers accompanied Tordenskjold to a house in Marstrand, where they all enjoyed red wine. At 9:00 p.m., all men returned to their quarters. The only breach of the peace was when soldiers from the Saxon regiment and a group of artillerymen broke into a storage facility and stole the butter supply. The Saxon soldiers were ordered to vacate the city and to spend the night standing outside the fortress wall surrounded by armed Danish soldiers.[^5928]

##### Thursday, July 16

In the morning, all Swedes marched out of the fortress. At around four in the afternoon, the commander left the fortress for a house in Marstrand. At 9:00 p.m., the remaining Swedish soldiers of the infantry and the artillery vacated the fortress.[^5929]

##### Friday, July 17

The Swedish troops were transported to [Tjuvkil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tjuvkil) on the mainland, except for a few troops from the artillery and the Saxon regiment, which were transferred to Danish service. During the transport, Tordenskjold handed out gifts to the officers such as watches and feather fans, along with other goods that had been taken from captured ships. After arriving at Tjuvkil, Danckwardt sent a letter to Field Marshal Rehnskiöld in Uddevalla explaining the situation. After reading the letter, Rehnskiöld issued an arrest warrant for Danckwardt. Danckwardt was arrested at [Bohus fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohus_Fortress) when he was attempting to travel to Gothenburg.[^5930]

#### Aftermath

Field Marshal Rehnskiöld and his officers were now left with a tough decision: should they stay with the Swedish troops at Uddevalla and protect the roads to [Vänersborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V%C3%A4nersborg) and [Dalsland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalsland) or move south towards Hisingen, to avoid being cut off by the Danish forces which could land north of Gothenburg? Rehnskiöld chose to stay, which turned out to be a good decision since the Danish army at Strömstad later pulled back into Norway at the end of August.[^5931] Tordenskjold used the naval base to attack Nya Älvsborg fortress on July 21 and later [Nya Varvet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nya_Varvet) at Göta river mouth. While under Dano-Norwegian rule, Carlsten fortress was named Kristiansten and Norwegian Major General Hartvig Huitfeldt was assigned to command the fortress garrison. On November 12, 1720, after the signing of the [Treaty of Frederiksborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Frederiksborg), the fortress was returned to Swedish control and was once again renamed Carlsten.[^5932]

On July 22, all officers who had signed the Carlsten instrument of surrender were arrested. After a war hearing with Danckwardt on July 21, a court martial was held on August 27, where he was violently disciplined for his actions.[^5933] [Charles XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_XI)'s war law § 73 states that any fortress commander that surrenders the fortress to the enemy without being under sufficient distress, shall receive the highest degree of punishment.[^5934] On September 5, Danckwardt was sentenced to death by beheading in accordance with these laws. The execution took place on September 16. The executioner, Jonas Wessman, was allegedly late and under the influence of alcohol which resulted in him not performing the beheading correctly and was forced to strike three times in order to completely remove the head from the body. Wessman was brought to court, but was let off with a formal warning.[^5935]

On November 13, 1719, a court martial was held with the arrested Carlsten officers. The officers stated that all documents that they had signed on Carlsten were simply a report on the fortress' defensive capabilities and that the last parts, that documented the official surrendering of the fortress, must have been added after the signing, without their knowledge. Because of this, the officers were not sentenced to death.[^5934]

#### Myths

Carlsten's surrender has been compared to [Siege of Sveaborg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Sveaborg) and its surrender in 1808. Psychological warfare was used in both cases to break down their opponents will to fight.[^5936] Certain events at Marstrand in 1719 have become myths, which can sometimes be confirmed or disproved with the help of documents from the time.

##### Espionage

Peter Tordenskjold (then known as Peter Wessel) was a crewman on a civilian British vessel in the summer of 1710. Bad weather forced the crew to navigate the vessel towards Marstrand. Peter Wessel seized an opportunity to explore the town's surroundings and fortifications without being suspected as a Danish spy. He left afterwards on a Dutch warship and reported his findings in a letter to Frederick IV, which he sent on February 28, 1711.[^5937]

##### Tordenskjold's soldiers

Captain von Utfalls visit to Tordenskjold at Marstrand on July 14, was described in a more detailed way by Danish author Casper Peter Rothe. Rothe claims that Tordenskjold had only between 200 and 300 soldiers present in the city. While the soldiers were being deployed, Utfall was invited into a local tavern. Tordenskjold ordered his men to roam the streets slowly in larger groups so that it would appear to the intoxicated von Utfall that there were at least 1,000 of them.[^5938] The story is most likely untrue, as the number of Danish soldiers in the city was listed as 500 men on the Swedish instrument of surrender, which corresponds with Danish intelligence.[^5924]

##### Reinforcements

In his letter to Danckwardt, Tordenskjold mentions that he was awaiting reinforcements of 2,000 men which were deployed on the [Koster Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koster_Islands). Rothe's version of the same document mentions that the reinforcements consisted of 20,000 men.[^5939] The threat was not unfounded, General Major Hans Jacob von Arnold was in command of a landing force of around 8,000 men, who were embarked on 28 transport ships near [Larkollen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larkollen) but had been forced to return just prior to Tordenskjold's assault due to strong winds. These ships, along with escorts, were supposed to land troops on Hisingen.[^5940][^5941]

##### Defeated and humiliated

Rothe's version of the events at Marstrand, describes Danish soldiers humiliating the captured Swedish officers by verbally abusing them and forcing them to dress up in women's decorative clothing.[^5942] Other reports suggest the opposite, that Tordenskjold and Danckwardt, along with their officers socialised for several hours on the night of July 15.

##### Alleged Saxon betrayal

One of Danckwardt's explanations for his actions was that soldiers with the [Saxon Infantry Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxon_Infantry_Regiment) had allegedly mutinied. The regiment, commanded by Colonel Georg David Zengerlein, was composed of Saxon prisoners of war who had been captured during the battles in Saxony-Poland. They had then been conscripted into the Swedish army and were therefore considered badly motivated mercenaries.[^5943] That these soldiers were merely present at Carlsten, was seen as a weak point by both the Danish and Swedish militaries. Prior to the assault, Field Marshal Rehnskiöld had attempted to dispatch another ship of 150 Swedish soldiers to relieve the 100 Saxon soldiers but owing to a large number of Danish vessels occupying the area, the force had to return to Uddevalla.[^5944] According to Danish reports, the Danish Captain Kleve had sneaked up to the fortress wall at night and overheard how the Saxon sentries were talking about forcing the commander to surrender.[^5945] The discipline inside the fortress was poor and women were granted entry into the fortress at night, which was forbidden. Tordenskjold used this to his advantage by smuggling in letters written in German, which urged the Saxon soldiers to surrender.[^5946] There is nothing relating to a Saxon mutiny stated in the Swedish instrument of surrender. During a war hearing, Captain Palmcrona verified that the Germans were behaving. Colonel Zengerlein of the Saxon Infantry Regiment was the chairman of the war hearing and he would never have been elected to the position if the Swedes had doubted him or his unit.[^5947]
