### Schwerer Gustav

**Schwerer Gustav** (German pronunciation: \[ˈʃveːʁɐ ˈɡʊstaf\]; lit. 'Heavy Gustav') was a German 80-centimetre (31.5 in) [railway gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_gun). It was developed in the late 1930s by [Krupp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krupp) in [Rügenwalde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%BCgenwalde); there are theories of another one being built, but only one was ever actually fired. They were created as [siege artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_siege_artillery) for the explicit purpose of destroying the main forts of the French [Maginot Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maginot_Line), the strongest fortifications in existence at the time. The fully assembled gun weighed nearly 1,350 [tonnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonne) (1,490 [short tons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_ton)) and could fire high-explosive shells weighing 4.8 t (5.3 short tons) to a range of 47 km (29 mi), or armour-piercing shells weighing 7.1 t (7.8 short tons) to a range of 38 km (24 mi).[^6115][^6116]

The gun was designed in preparation for the [Battle of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_France) but was not ready for action when that battle began, and the [Wehrmacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wehrmacht) offensive through Belgium rapidly outflanked and isolated the Maginot Line, which was then besieged with more conventional heavy guns until [French capitulation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_22_June_1940).[^6117] Gustav was later deployed in the Soviet Union during the [Battle of Sevastopol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sevastopol), part of [Operation Barbarossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Barbarossa), where, among other things, it destroyed a munitions depot located roughly 30 m (98 ft) below sea level.[^6118] The gun was moved to [Leningrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leningrad), and may have been intended to be used in the [Warsaw Uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw_Uprising) like other German heavy siege pieces, but the uprising was crushed before it could be prepared to fire. Gustav was destroyed by the Germans near the end of the war in 1945 to avoid capture by the Soviet [Red Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Army).[^6119]

*Schwerer Gustav* was the largest-calibre [rifled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rifling) weapon ever used in combat, and in terms of weight, the heaviest mobile artillery piece ever built. It fired the heaviest shells of any artillery piece.[^6120] It was surpassed in [calibre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caliber) only by the British [Mallet's Mortar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mallet's_Mortar) and the American [Little David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_David) bomb-testing mortar, both at 36 inches (91.5 cm), but was the only one of the three to go into action.

#### Development

In 1934, the German Army High Command ([Oberkommando des Heeres (OKH)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberkommando_des_Heeres)) commissioned [Krupp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krupp) of [Essen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essen) to design a gun to destroy the forts of the French [Maginot Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maginot_Line) that were nearing completion. The gun's shells had to punch through seven metres of [reinforced concrete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforced_concrete) or one full metre of steel armour plate, from beyond the range of French artillery.[^6121] Krupp engineer Erich Müller calculated that the task would require a weapon with a calibre of around 80 centimetres (31 in), firing a projectile weighing seven tonnes (15,000 lb) from a barrel 30 metres (98 ft) long. The weapon would have a weight of over 1,000 tonnes (1,100 short tons). The size and weight meant that to be at all movable it would need to be supported on twin sets of railway tracks. The railway tracks were specifically engineered to accommodate the immense weight and size of *Schwerer Gustav*. Constructed with reinforced steel, these tracks provided a stable foundation for the weapon's movement. Specialized [locomotives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locomotives) and [cranes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crane_%28rail%29) were employed to transport and position the gun with precision.[^6122]

In common with smaller railway guns, the only barrel movement on the mount itself would be elevation, traverse being managed by moving the weapon along a curved section of railway line. Krupp prepared plans for calibres of 70 cm, 80 cm, 85 cm, and 1 m.[^6123]

Nothing further happened until March 1936 when, during a visit to Essen, [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler) inquired as to the giant guns' feasibility. No definite commitment was given by Hitler, but design work began on an 80 cm model. The resulting plans were completed in early 1937 and approved. Fabrication of the gun started in mid-1937. Technical complications in the forging of such massive pieces of steel made it apparent that the original completion date of early 1940 could not be met.[^6124]

Krupp built a test model in late 1939 and sent it to the [Hillersleben](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillersleben) [proving ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proving_ground) for testing. Penetration was tested on this occasion. Firing at high elevation, the 7,100-kilogram (15,700 lb) shell was able to penetrate the specified seven metres of concrete and the one metre armour plate.[^6125] When the tests were completed in mid-1940 the complex carriage was further developed. [Alfried Krupp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfried_Krupp_von_Bohlen_und_Halbach), after whose father the gun was named, personally hosted Hitler at the Rügenwalde (now [Darłowo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dar%C5%82owo), Poland) Proving Ground during the formal acceptance trials of the Gustav Gun in early 1941.

Two guns were ordered. The first round was test-fired from the commissioned gun barrel on 10 September 1941 from a makeshift gun carriage at Hillersleben. In November 1941, the barrel was taken to Rügenwalde, where eight further firing tests were carried out using the 7,100 kilogram armour-piercing (AP) shell out to a range of 37,210 metres (23.12 miles).

In combat, the gun was mounted on a specially designed chassis, supported by eight [bogies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogie) on two parallel railway tracks. Each of the bogies had five axles, giving a total of 40 axles (80 wheels). Krupp named the gun *Schwerer Gustav* (Heavy Gustav) after the senior director of the firm, [Gustav Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustav_Krupp_von_Bohlen_und_Halbach).

The gun could fire a heavy concrete-piercing shell and a lighter high-explosive shell. An extremely-long-range rocket projectile was also planned with a range of 150 kilometres (93 mi), that would require the barrel being extended to 84 metres (276 ft).[^6126]

In keeping with the tradition of the Krupp company, no payment was asked for the first gun.[^6127] They charged seven million [Reichsmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_reichsmark) (approximately 24 million USD in 2015) for the second gun, *Dora*, named after the senior engineer's wife (supposedly).

#### History

##### Schwerer Gustav

In February 1942, Heavy Artillery Unit (E) 672 reorganised and went on the march, and *Schwerer Gustav* began its long ride to [Crimea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimea). The train carrying the gun was of 25 cars, a total length of 1.5 kilometres (0.9 mi). The gun reached the [Perekop Isthmus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isthmus_of_Perekop) in early March 1942, where it was held until early April. The Germans built a special railway [spur line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spur_line) to the [Simferopol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simferopol)-[Sevastopol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevastopol) railway 16 kilometres (9.9 mi) north of the target. At the end of the spur, they built four semi-circular tracks especially for the Gustav to traverse. Outer tracks were required for the cranes that assembled Gustav.

The [siege of Sevastopol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Sevastopol_%281941%E2%80%931942%29) was the gun's first combat test. 4,000 men and five weeks were needed to get the gun into firing position; 500 men were needed to fire it.[^6128] Installation began in early May, and by 5 June the gun was ready to fire.[^6129] The following targets were engaged:

| 5 June | [Coastal guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coastal_artillery) at a range of 25,000 m. Eight shells fired |
|----|----|
| 5 June | Fort *Stalin*. Six shells fired. |
| 6 June | Fort *Molotov*. Seven shells fired. |
| 6 June | "White Cliff" also known as "Ammunition Mountain": an undersea ammunition magazine in Severnaya ("Northern") Bay. The magazine was sited 30 metres under the sea with at least 10 metres of concrete protection. After nine shells were fired, the magazine was ruined and one of the boats in the bay sunk.[^6130] |
| 7 June | Firing in support of an infantry attack on *Südwestspitze*, an outlying fortification. Seven shells fired. |
| 11 June | Fort *Siberia* knocked out of action. Five shells fired. |
| 17 June | [Maxim Gorky Fortresses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxim_Gorky_Fortresses) bombarded. Five shells fired. |

By the end of the siege on 4 July the city of [Sevastopol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sevastopol) lay in ruins, and 30,000 tons of artillery ammunition had been fired. Gustav had fired 47 rounds and worn out its original barrel, which had already fired around 250 rounds during testing and development. The gun was fitted with the spare barrel and the original was sent back to Krupp's factory in Essen for relining.[^6118]

The gun was then dismantled and moved to the northern part of the Eastern Front, where an attack was planned on [Leningrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg). The gun was placed 30 km (18.6 mi) from the city near the railway station of [Taytsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taytsy). The gun was fully operational when the attack was cancelled. The gun then spent the winter of 1942/43 near Leningrad.[^6131]

##### Dora

*Dora* is considered by some to be a secondary gustav. In reality many sources state it as a "Nickname". There is no proof of a second Gustav having been made.

##### Langer Gustav

The Langer Gustav was a long cannon with 52 centimetre (20.5 in) calibre and a 43-metre barrel. It was intended to fire super-long-range rocket projectiles weighing 680 kilograms to a range of 190 kilometres (118 mi). This gave it the range to hit [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London) from [Calais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calais), France. It was never completed after being damaged during construction by one of the many [RAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force) bombing raids on Essen.

\

#### Postwar whereabouts

On 14 April 1945, one day before the arrival of US troops, Schwerer Gustav was destroyed to prevent its capture. On 22 April 1945, its ruins were discovered in a forest 15 kilometres (9.3 mi) north of [Auerbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auerbach_%28Vogtland%29) and about 50 kilometres (31 mi) southwest of [Chemnitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemnitz). In summer 1945 Schwerer Gustav was studied by Soviet specialists and in autumn of the same year was transferred to [Merseburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merseburg), where the Soviets were gathering German material.[^6132]

In March 1945, *Dora* was transferred to [Grafenwöhr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grafenw%C3%B6hr) and was destroyed on 19 April 1945. The debris was discovered by American troops sometime after the discovery of *Schwerer Gustav's* ruins. The debris was scrapped in the 1950s.

Part of the third (52 centimetre) gun was found after the war in the Krupp production facilities in Essen.

The world's largest "Dora ensemble" is located in the [Bundeswehr Military History Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundeswehr_Military_History_Museum) in Dresden.

### Darwin Awards

The **Darwin Awards** are a rhetorical [tongue-in-cheek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tongue-in-cheek) honor that originated in [Usenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usenet) newsgroup discussions around 1985. They recognize individuals who have supposedly [contributed to human evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culling) by [selecting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_selection) themselves out of the [gene pool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_pool) by dying or becoming [sterilized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sterilization_%28medicine%29) by their own actions.

The project became more formalized with the creation of a [website](https://darwinawards.com/) in 1993, followed by a series of books starting in 2000 by Wendy Northcutt. The criterion for the awards states: "In the spirit of [Charles Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin), the Darwin Awards commemorate individuals who protect our gene pool by making the ultimate sacrifice of their own lives. Darwin Award winners eliminate themselves in an extraordinarily idiotic manner, thereby improving our species' chances of long-term survival."[^6134]

Accidental self-sterilization also qualifies, but the site notes: "Of necessity, the award is usually bestowed posthumously." The candidate is disqualified, though, if "innocent bystanders" are killed in the process, as they might have contributed positively to the gene pool. The logical problem presented by award winners who may have had children is not addressed in the selection process owing to the difficulty of ascertaining a candidate's parental status; the Darwin Award rules state that the presence of offspring does not disqualify a nominee.[^6135]

#### History

The origin of the Darwin Awards can be traced back to posts on [Usenet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usenet) group discussions as early as 1985. A post on August 7, 1985, describes the awards as being "given posthumously to people who have made the supreme sacrifice to keep their genes out of our pool. Style counts, not everyone who dies from their own stupidity can win."[^6136] This early post cites an example of a person who tried to break into a [vending machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_by_vending_machine) and was crushed to death when he pulled it over on himself.[^6136] Another widely distributed early story mentioning the Darwin Awards, later determined to be an urban legend by the [Arizona Highway Patrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_Highway_Patrol),[^6137] is the [JATO Rocket Car](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JATO_Rocket_Car), which describes a man who strapped a [jet-assisted take-off](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet-assisted_take-off) unit to his [Chevrolet Impala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chevrolet_Impala) in the [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona) desert and who died on the side of a cliff as his car achieved speeds of 250 to 300 miles per hour (400 to 480 km/h). Wendy Northcutt says the official Darwin Awards website run by Northcutt does its best to confirm all stories submitted, listing them as, "confirmed true by Darwin". Many of the [viral emails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viral_email) circulating the Internet, however, are hoaxes and urban legends.[^6138][^6139][^6140][^6141]

The website and collection of books were started in 1993 by Wendy Northcutt, who studied [molecular biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_biology) at the [University of California, Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley),[^6142] and [neurobiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neurobiology) at [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University), doing research on cancer and [telomerase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telomerase). In her spare time, she organized [chain letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_letter) from family members into the original Darwin Awards website hosted in her personal account space at Stanford. She eventually gave up practical research in 1998, and devoted herself full-time to her website and books in September 1999.[^6143] By 2002, the website received 7 million page hits per month.[^6144]

Northcutt encountered some difficulty in publishing the first book, since most publishers would only offer her a deal if she agreed to remove the stories from the Internet, but she refused: "It was a community! I could not do that. Even though it might have cost me a lot of money, I kept saying no." She eventually found a publisher who agreed to print a book containing only 10% of the material gathered for the website. The first book turned out to be a success, and was listed on *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times)*' best-seller list for 6 months.[^6145]

Not all of the feedback from the stories Northcutt published was positive, and she occasionally received emails from people who knew the deceased. One such person advised: "This is horrible. It has shocked our community to the core. You should remove this." Northcutt demurred: "I can't. It's just too stupid." Northcutt kept the stories on the website and in her books, citing them as a "funny-but-true safety guide", and mentioning that children who read the book are going to be much more careful around explosives.[^6146]

The website also awards Honorable Mentions to individuals who survive their misadventures with their reproductive capacity intact. One example of this is [Larry Walters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Walters), who attached [helium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helium)-filled [weather balloons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_balloon) to a lawn chair and floated far above [Long Beach, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Beach,_California), in July 1982. He reached an altitude of 16,000 feet (4,900 m), but survived, to be later fined for crossing [controlled airspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Controlled_airspace).[^6147] (Walters later fell and [died by suicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawnchair_Larry_flight), the same year Northcutt began the website.) Another notable honorable mention was given to the two men who attempted to burgle the home of footballer [Duncan Ferguson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Ferguson) (who had an infamous reputation for physical aggression on and off the pitch, including four convictions for assault and who had served six months in Glasgow's [Barlinnie Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barlinnie_Prison)) in 2001, with one burglar requiring three days' hospitalisation after being confronted by the player.[^6148]

A 2014 study published in the *[British Medical Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Medical_Journal)* found that between 1995 and 2014, males represented 88.7% of Darwin Award winners (see figure).[^6149]

The comedy film *[The Darwin Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Darwin_Awards_%28film%29)* (2006), written and directed by [Finn Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finn_Taylor), was based on the website and many of the Darwin Awards stories.[^6150]

#### Rules

Northcutt has stated five requirements for a Darwin Award:[^6134][^6142] Two of them are that the event must be verified to have happened, and that the nominee themselves were responsible for the activity. The others are:

##### Nominee must be dead or rendered sterile

This may be subject to dispute. Potential awardees may be out of the gene pool because of age; others have already reproduced before their deaths. To avoid debates about the possibility of [*in vitro* fertilization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-vitro_fertilization), [artificial insemination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_insemination), or [cloning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_cloning), the original Darwin Awards book applied the following "deserted island" test to potential winners: If the person were unable to reproduce when stranded on a deserted island with a fertile member of the opposite sex, they would be considered sterile.[^6151] Winners of the award, in general, either are dead or have become unable to use their [sexual organs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_organs).

##### Astoundingly stupid judgment

The candidate's foolishness must be unique and sensational, likely because the award is intended to be funny. A number of foolish but common activities, such as smoking in bed or refusing [measles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Measles) vaccination, are excluded from consideration. In contrast, [self-immolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-immolation) caused by smoking after being administered a flammable ointment in a hospital and specifically told not to smoke is grounds for nomination.[^6152] One "Honorable Mention" (a man who attempted suicide by swallowing [nitroglycerin pills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyceryl_trinitrate_%28pharmacology%29), and then tried to detonate them by running into a wall) is noted to be in this category, despite being intentional and self-inflicted (i.e. attempted suicide), which would normally disqualify the inductee.[^6153]

##### Capable of sound judgment

In 2011, the awards targeted a 16-year-old boy in Leeds who died stealing copper wiring.[^6154] In 2012, Northcutt made similar light of a 14-year-old girl in Brazil who was killed while leaning out of a school bus window, but she was "disqualified" for the award itself because of the likely public objection owing to the girl's age, which Northcutt asserts is based on "[magical thinking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magical_thinking)".[^6155]

Under this rule, and for reasons of good taste, individuals whose misfortune was caused by mental impairment or disability are not eligible for a Darwin Award, primarily to avoid mocking or making light of disabled people, and to ensure that the awards do not celebrate or trivialize tragedies involving vulnerable individuals. The same rule also disqualifies children under the age of 16 from winning the award.[^6156]

#### Reception

The Darwin Awards have received varying levels of scrutiny from the scientific community. In his book *Encyclopedia of Evolution*, biology professor Stanley A. Rice comments: "Despite the tremendous value of these stories as entertainment, it is unlikely that they represent evolution in action", stating that their stupidity could reflect their upbringing, and is less reflective of intelligence but rather impulsivity. And that impulsivity is a genetic trait in humans that can have evolutionary drawbacks, but remains because it also benefits in avoiding missed opportunities.[^6157] On an essay in the book *The Evolution of Evil*, professor Nathan Hallanger acknowledges that the Darwin Awards are meant as [black humor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_humor), but associates them with the [eugenics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenics) movement of the early 20th century.[^6158] [University of Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford) [biophysicist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biophysicist) Sylvia McLain, writing for *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian)*, says that while the Darwin Awards are "clearly meant to be funny", they do not accurately represent how genetics work, further noting "...that 'smart' people do stupid things all the time."[^6159] [Geologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology) and [science communicator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_communicator) [Sharon A. Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sharon_A._Hill) has criticized the Darwin Awards on both scientific and ethical grounds, claiming that many factors in addition to genetics impact personal intelligence and judgement. She then says the awards exemplify "ignorance" and "heartlessness".[^6160]

#### Notable recipients

- [Garry Hoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garry_Hoy), who fell from the 24th story of the [Toronto-Dominion Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto-Dominion_Centre) whilst attempting to demonstrate to a group of students that the windows were unbreakable. His death has been featured in television programs such as *[1000 Ways to Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1000_Ways_to_Die)* and *[MythBusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MythBusters)*.[^6161]
- [Charles Stephens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Stephens_%28daredevil%29), the first person to die while attempting to go over [Niagara Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls) in a barrel.[^6162]
- [John Allen Chau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Allen_Chau), an American man killed when he attempted to [proselytize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proselytize) to the [Sentinelese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentinelese), an [uncontacted people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncontacted_people) living on [North Sentinel Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sentinel_Island).[^6163]

### The Hands of Che Guevara

***The Hands of Che Guevara*** (Dutch: ***De handen van Che Guevara***; Spanish: ***Las manos de Che Guevara***) is a 2006 documentary film made by Dutch [film director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_director) [Peter de Kock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_de_Kock). The documentary is a search for the severed hands of the Latin American guerrilla fighter [Ernesto Che Guevara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernesto_Che_Guevara).

After Guevara's execution in [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia) in 1967, his hands were severed from his body for purposes of identification. After fingerprints were taken, the hands, and Guevara's body, disappeared. In 1997 the body was found buried under a landing strip in Vallegrande, [Bolivia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolivia).[^6164] Guevara's hands were not found in the grave, and it is not clear what became of them after his death, although some accounts indicate they were sent to Cuba by Antonio Arguedas.[^6165][^6166]

The film attempts to answer the question of their location.

There is also a book of the same title. It is called *Las Manos de Guevara (The Hands of Che Guevara)*, written by Evgenii Dolmatovskii. It was published in 1974 by Planeta.[^6167]

Archived from [the original](http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,876626,00.html) on September 13, 2009. Retrieved 2012-02-10.

### Mordred

**Mordred** or **Modred** (/ˈmɔːrdrɛd, ˈmoʊdrɛd/; Welsh: ***Medraut*** or ***Medrawt***) is a major figure in the legend of [King Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Arthur). The earliest known mention of a possibly historical Medraut is in the Welsh chronicle *[Annales Cambriae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annales_Cambriae)*, wherein he and Arthur are ambiguously associated with the [Battle of Camlann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Camlann) in a brief entry for the year 537. Medraut's figure seemed to have been regarded positively in the early Welsh tradition and may have been related to that of [Arthur's son](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Arthur's_family).

As **Modredus**, Mordred was depicted as Arthur's traitorous nephew and a legitimate son of [King Lot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Lot) in the pseudo-historical work *[Historia Regum Britanniae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historia_Regum_Britanniae)*, which then served as the basis for the subsequent evolution of the legend from the 12th century. Later variants most often characterised Mordred as Arthur's own and villainous bastard son, born of an incestuous relationship with [his half-sister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgause), the queen of [Lothian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lothian) or [Orkney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkney) named either Anna, Orcades, or Morgause. The accounts presented in the *Historia* and most other versions include Mordred's death at Camlann, typically in a final duel, during which he manages to mortally wound his own slayer, Arthur. Mordred is usually a brother or half-brother to [Gawain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gawain); however, his other family relations, as well as his relationships with Arthur's wife [Guinevere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinevere), vary greatly.

In a popular telling, originating from the French chivalric romances of the 13th century and made prominent today through its inclusion in *[Le Morte d'Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Morte_d'Arthur)*, Mordred is a power-hungry son of Arthur from the incest with Morgause, prophesied by [Merlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlin) and destined to bring Britain to ruin. He survives Arthur's attempt to get rid of him soon after his birth and, years later, joins his half-brothers Gawain, [Agravain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agravain), [Gaheris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaheris) and [Gareth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth) in Arthur's fellowship of the [Round Table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Round_Table) as a young and immoral knight. Eventually, Mordred learns of his true parentage and becomes the main actor in Arthur's downfall. He helps Agravain to expose the illicit love affair between Guinevere and [Lancelot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancelot) and then takes advantage of the resulting civil war to make himself the [high king](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_king) of Britain, ultimately leading to both his own and Arthur's deaths in their battle.

Today, he remains an iconic character in many modern adaptations of the [Arthurian legend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthurian_legend). In such works, he usually appears as a villain and the archenemy of Arthur.

#### Name

The name *Mordred*, found as the [Latinised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latinisation_of_names) *Modredus* in [Geoffrey of Monmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_of_Monmouth)'s *[Historia Regum Britanniae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historia_Regum_Britanniae)*, comes from [Old Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Welsh) *Medraut* (comparable to [Old Cornish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Cornish) *Modred* and [Old Breton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Breton) *Modrot*).[^6168] It may be ultimately derived from Latin *Moderātus*, meaning "within bounds, observing moderation, moderate" with some influence from Latin *mors*, "death".[^6169][^6170]

#### Early Welsh sources

The earliest surviving mention of Mordred (referred to as Medraut) is found in an entry for the year 537 in the chronicle *[Annales Cambriae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annales_Cambriae)* (*The Annals of Wales*), which references his name in an association with the [Battle of Camlann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Camlann).[^6171]

> *Gueith Camlann in qua Arthur et Medraut corruerunt.*\
> "The strife of Camlann, in which Arthur and Medraut fell."

This brief entry gives no information as to whether Mordred killed Arthur or was killed by Arthur, if they were fighting against one another at all, if they were fighting on the same side, or even if they died in the battle or were just defeated. As noted by [Leslie Alcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leslie_Alcock), the reader assumes conflict between the two in the light of later tradition.[^6172] The *Annales* themselves were completed between 960 and 970, meaning that (although their authors likely drew from older material[^6173]) they cannot be considered a contemporary source, having been compiled 400 years after the events they describe.[^6174]

[Meilyr Brydydd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meilyr_Brydydd), writing at the same time as Geoffrey of Monmouth, mentions Mordred in his lament for the death of [Gruffudd ap Cynan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gruffudd_ap_Cynan) (d. 1137). He describes Gruffudd as having *eissor Medrawd* ("the nature of Medrawd"), as to have valour in battle. Similarly, [Gwalchmai ap Meilyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwalchmai_ap_Meilyr) praised [Madog ap Maredudd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madog_ap_Maredudd), king of [Powys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powys) (d. 1160) as having *Arthur gerdernyd, menwyd Medrawd* ("Arthur's strength, the good nature of Medrawd").[^6175] This would support the idea that early perceptions of Mordred were largely positive.

However, Mordred's later characterisation as the king's villainous son may had a precedent in the figure of [Amr (or Amhar)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amhar), a son of Arthur's known from only two references. The more important of these, found in an appendix to the 9th-century chronicle *[Historia Brittonum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historia_Brittonum)* (*The History of the Britons*), describes his marvelous grave beside the [Herefordshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herefordshire) spring where he had been slain by his own father in some unchronicled tragedy.[^6176][^6177] What connection exists between the stories of Amr and Mordred, if there is one, has never been satisfactorily explained.

An early 12th-century Italian high relief known as the [Modena Archivolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modena_Archivolt) seems to show a scene of abduction of [Guinevere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinevere) inspired by an original Welsh Arthurian tradition, perhaps as retold by Breton and other continental bards in their otherwise unrecorded oral stories. While often interpreted as that of [Melwas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melwas), a mysterious figure identified as Mardoc may instead represent Mordred.[^6178][^6179][^6180]

#### Depictions in legend

##### Geoffrey and Welsh tradition

In Geoffrey's influential *Historia Regum Britanniae* (*The History of the Kings of Britain*), written around 1136, Modredus (Mordred) is portrayed as the nephew of and traitor to King Arthur. Geoffrey might have based his Modredus on the early 6th-century "[high king](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_king)" of [Gwynedd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwynedd), [Maelgwn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maelgwn_Gwynedd), whom the 6th-century writer [Gildas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gildas) had described as a [usurper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usurper),[^6181] or on [Mandubracius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandubracius), a 1st-century BC king of the [Trinovantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinovantes).[^6182] The unhistorical account presented by Geoffrey narrates Arthur leaving Modredus in charge of his throne as he crosses the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel) to wage war on [Lucius Tiberius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Tiberius) of Rome. During Arthur's absence, Modredus crowns himself as [King of the Britons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_of_the_Britons) and lives in an adulterous union with Arthur's wife, Guenhuvara (Guinevere). Geoffrey does not make it clear how complicit Guenhuvara is with his actions, simply stating that the Queen had "broken her vows" and "about this matter... \[he\] prefers to say nothing."[^6183] Arthur returns to Britain and they fight at the Battle of Camlann, where Modredus is ultimately slain. Arthur, having been gravely wounded in battle, is sent off to be healed by [Morgen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_le_Fay) in [Avalon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalon).

A number of other Welsh sources also refer to Medraut, usually in relation to Camlann. One [Welsh Triad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_Triads), based on Geoffrey's *Historia*, provides an account of his betrayal of Arthur;[^6184] in another, he is described as the author of one of the "Three Unrestrained Ravagings of the Isle of Britain" - he came to Arthur's court at [Kelliwic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelliwic) in [Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall), devoured all of the food and drink, and even dragged Gwenhwyfar (Guinevere) from her throne and beat her.[^6185] In another Triad, however, he is described as one of "men of such gentle, kindly, and fair words that anyone would be sorry to refuse them anything."[^6168] The *[Mabinogion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mabinogion)* also describes him in terms of courtliness, calmness, and purity.[^6186]

##### Life in romances

The 12th-century poems of the emerging [chivalric romance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivalric_romance) genre such as those by [Chrétien de Troyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chr%C3%A9tien_de_Troyes), dealing with the adventures of various knights during Arthur's reign, would typically not mention Mordred at all. This changed through the 13th century, as the [Old French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_French) cyclical prose romance literature greatly expanded on the history of Mordred prior to the war against Arthur.

In the Prose *Merlin* part of the [Vulgate Cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate_Cycle) (in which his name is sometimes written as **Mordret**), Mordred's elder half-brother [Gawain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gawain) saves the infant Mordred and [their mother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgause) from being taken away as prisoners by the [Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxons) king Taurus. In the revision known as the [Post-Vulgate Cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Vulgate_Cycle), and consequently in [Thomas Malory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Malory)'s English compilation *[Le Morte d'Arthur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Morte_d'Arthur)* (*The Death of Arthur*), Arthur is told a cryptic (and, apparently, [self-fulfilling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-fulfilling_prophecy)) prophecy by [Merlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlin) about a newly-born child that is to be his undoing, and so he tries to avert his fate by ordering to get rid of all [May Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_Day) newborns. Whether they were intended to be killed or merely sent off to a distant land (the texts are vague about this), the ship on which the children were placed sinks and they drown. This episode, sometimes dubbed the "May Day massacre",[^6187] leads to a war between Arthur and the furious [King Lot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Lot), acting on his belief that he is the biological father of Mordred. Lot dies in a battle at the hands of Arthur's vassal king [Pellinore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pellinore), beginning a long and deadly blood feud between the two royal families. Meanwhile, however, and unknown to both Lot and Arthur, the baby miraculously survives. It turns out Mordred was found and rescued by a fisherman and his wife, who then raise him as their own son until he is 14.[^6188] In this branch of the legend, following his early life as a commoner, the young Mordred is later reunited with his mother, which happens long after Merlin's downfall caused by the [Lady of the Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_of_the_Lake).

The grown-up Mordred becomes involved in the adventures of his brothers, first as a [squire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squire) and then as a [knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight), as well as others such as [Brunor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunor), eventually joining King Arthur's elite fellowship of the [Knights of the Round Table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knights_of_the_Round_Table). Especially since the Post-Vulgate, Mordred tends to be depicted as murderously violent and known for his un-[chivalrous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chivalry) and lustful habits, including engaging in rape (as in an incident in the Post-Vulgate *Queste*, when he brutally kills a maiden and is injured for his actions by King [Bagdemagus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagdemagus), who is then in turn mortally wounded by Gawain; there is also an attempted rape in the standalone romance *Claris et Laris*).[^6186] Notably, it is Mordred who fatally stabs in the back one of the best Knights of the Round Table, [Lamorak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamorak), in an unfair fight involving most of his brothers ([one of whom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaheris) had even murdered their own mother for being Lamorak's lover). Mordred displays stronger knightly values in the earlier Vulgate Cycle (as does Gawain too in comparison to his later Post-Vulgate portrayal), where he is also shown as womanising and murderous, but to a significantly lesser degree. The Prose *Lancelot* describes Mordred, at the age of 20, as "a large, tall knight; he had curly, blond hair and would have had a very handsome face if his demeanour had not been so wicked."[^6189] He becomes a protege and companion of the eponymous great knight [Lancelot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancelot). The older knight comes to the young Mordred's rescue on multiple occasions, such as helping to save his life at the Castle of the White Thorn (*Castel de la Blanche Espine*), and Mordred in turn treats the much older Lancelot as his personal hero. In this version, his turning point toward villainy happens after they meet an old hermit monk who begins to tell his own prophecy for the two "most unfortunate knights", revealing Mordred's true parentage by Arthur and predicting Mordred's and Lancelot's respective roles in the coming ruin of Arthur's kingdom.[^6190] However, the angry Mordred kills the monk before he can finish. While Lancelot tells his secret lover Guinevere (but not Arthur), she refuses to believe in the story of the prophecy and does not banish Mordred. The young knight, on his part, tries to get himself killed before accepting his destiny. The Prose *Lancelot* indicates Mordred was about 22 years old at the time, as well as just two years into his knighthood.

Eventually, Mordred overthrows Arthur's rule when the latter is engaged in, depending on the version, either the war against Lancelot (as in Malory) or the second Roman War that followed it immediately afterwards. In the Vulgate *Mort Artu*, Mordred achieves his coup with the help of a letter supposedly sent by the dying Arthur but actually forged by Mordred. The *Mort Artu* narration adds that "there was much good in Mordred, and as soon as he made himself elevated to the throne, he made himself well beloved by all," and so they were "ready to die to defend \[his\] honor" once Arthur did return with his army.[^6191] Mordred's few opponents during his brief rule included [Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Kay), who was gravely wounded by Mordred's supporters and died after fleeing to [Brittany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brittany). In the Vulgate *Mort Artu*, Arthur himself proposes him as a regent, while in the French-influenced English poem [Stanzaic *Morte Arthur*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanzaic_Morte_Arthur), the council of Britain's knights first elects Mordred for the position in Arthur's absence as the most worthy candidate. The [Alliterative *Morte Arthure*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliterative_Morte_Arthure) is a unique text in which Mordred is presented as not only a possibly better ruler than Arthur[^6192] but also as reluctant to be left by Arthur in charge of Britain.[^6193] In the later romances, as in the chronicles, the returning Arthur's veteran army is ambushed and nearly destroyed by Mordred's supporters and foreign allies during their sea landing at [Dover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dover), where Gawain is mortally wounded while fighting as Arthur's loyalist. Afterwards, a series of inconclusive engagements follows, until both sides agree to all meet each other at the [one final battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Camlann), in which Mordred typically fights exceptionally well while commanding the loyalty of thousands of men willing to lay down their lives for him against Arthur. In some versions, including [Elis Gruffydd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elis_Gruffydd)'s[^6194] and Malory's, the fighting begins accidentally during the last-minute negotiations between Arthur and Mordred.

##### Death

In [Henry of Huntingdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Huntingdon)'s retelling of Geoffrey's *Historia*, Mordred is beheaded at Camlann in a lone charge against him and his entire host by King Arthur himself, who suffers many injuries in the process. In the alliterative *Morte Arthure*, Mordred first kills Gawain by his own hand in an early battle against Arthur's landing forces and then deeply grieves after him. In the Vulgate *Mort Artu* (and consequently in Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur*), the terrible final battle begins by accident during a last-effort peace meeting between him and Arthur. In the ensuing fighting, Mordred personally slays his cousin [Ywain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ywain) after the latter's rescue of the unhorsed Arthur, and decapitates the already badly wounded [Sagramore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sagramore). He also kills Sagramore in addition to six other Round Table knights loyal to Arthur in the Post-Vulgate depiction of the battle, which presents this as an incredible and unprecedented feat. These and many other versions of the legend feature the motif of Arthur and Mordred striking down each other in a duel after most of the others on both sides have died. Furthermore, the Post-Vulgate says it was only the death of Sagramore, here depicted as Mordred's own foster brother, that finally motivates Arthur to kill his son immediately afterwards.

*Le Morte d'Arthur* features the now-iconic scene where the two meet on foot as Arthur charges Mordred and runs a spear through him. With the last of his strength, Mordred impales himself even further to come within striking distance, and lands a mortal blow with his sword to Arthur's head. Malory's telling is a variant of the original account from the Vulgate *Mort Artu*, in which Arthur and Mordred both charge at each other on horses three times until Arthur drives his lance through Mordred's body, but then fully withdraws it (a ray of sunlight even shines through the hole) before Mordred's sword powerfully strikes his head and they both fall from their saddles.[^6195] The Alliterative *Morte Arthure* has Mordred grievously wound Arthur with the ceremonial sword [Clarent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarent), stolen for him from Arthur by his co-conspirator Guinevere, but then Arthur slashes off Mordred's sword arm and brutally skewers him up on the sword Caliburn ([Excalibur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur)). One copy of the Welsh text *Ymddiddan Arthur a'r Eryr* has the dying Arthur tell Guinevere how he struck Mordred nine times with Caledfwlch (another name variant of Excalibur).[^6196]

The Post-Vulgate retelling of *Mort Artu* deals with the aftermath of Mordred's death in more detail than the earlier works. In it, Arthur says before being taken away: "Mordred, in an evil hour did I beget you. You have ruined me and the kingdom of [Logres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logres), and you have died for it. Cursed be the hour in which you were born."[^6197] One of the few survivors of Arthur's army, [Bleoberis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleoberis), then drags Mordred's corpse behind a horse around the battlefield of [Salisbury Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salisbury_Plain) until it is torn to pieces. Later, as it had been commanded by the dying Arthur, the [Archbishop of Canterbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archbishop_of_Canterbury) constructs the Tower of the Dead tomb memorial, from which Bleoberis hangs Mordred's head as a warning against treason. It remains there for centuries until it is removed by the visiting [Ganelon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganelon). Conversely, [Margam Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margam_Abbey)'s chronicle *Annales de Margan* claims Arthur is buried alongside Mordred, here described as his nephew, in another tomb purportedly exhumed in the "real Avalon" at [Glastonbury Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glastonbury_Abbey).[^6198]

There have also been alternative stories of Mordred's demise. [Thomas Grey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Grey_%28chronicler%29)'s *[Scalacronica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scalacronica)* attributes the killing of Mordred to Ywan (Ywain) at Camlann.[^6199] In *[La Tavola Ritonda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Tavola_Ritonda)*, it is Lancelot who kills Mordred at the castle of Urbano where Mordred has besieged Guinevere after Arthur's death.[^6200] In [Jean d'Outremeuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_d'Outremeuse)'s *Ly Myreur des Histors*, Mordred survives the great battle and rules with the traitorous Guinevere until they are defeated and captured by Lancelot and [King Carados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caradoc) in London; Guinevere is then executed by Lancelot, and Mordred is entombed alive with her body, which he [consumes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_cannibalism) before dying of starvation.[^6201]

#### Family relations

##### Parents and siblings

Traditions vary regarding Mordred's relationship to Arthur. Medraut is never considered Arthur's son in Welsh texts, only his nephew, though *[The Dream of Rhonabwy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dream_of_Rhonabwy)* mentions that the king had been his foster father. In early literature derived from Geoffrey's *Historia*, Mordred was considered the legitimate son of Arthur's sister or half-sister queen named [Anna or Gwyar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgause) and her husband [Lot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Lot), the king of either [Lothian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lothian) or [Orkney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orkney). Today, however, he is best known as Arthur's own illegitimate son by his beautiful half-sister and Lot's wife, known as Morgause (Orcades / Morcades / Morgawse / Margawse), [the Queen of Orkney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgause). This motif was introduced in the Vulgate Cycle, in which their union happens at the time when neither of them have yet known of their blood relation and she was not married yet. Accounts of Mordred's incestuous origin story (including two different variants in just the different parts of the main version of the Vulgate Cycle) present the circumstances of it variably, attributing various degrees of blame or innocence to either party of the teenage (usually aged 15) Arthur's tryst with his much older (mother to children almost his age) half-sister.[^6202]

Her eldest son Gawain has been Mordred's brother already in the *Historia* as well as in [Layamon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Layamon)'s [*Brut*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Layamon's_Brut). Besides him, Mordred's other brothers or half-brothers often appearing in literature include [Agravain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agravain) and [Gaheris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaheris) in the tradition derived from the French romances, beginning with the prose versions of [Robert de Boron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_de_Boron)'s poems *[Merlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlin_%28Robert_de_Boron_poem%29)* and *Perceval*. Another of the brothers, [Gareth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gareth), joined them in the later versions. In the Vulgate *Lancelot*, Mordred is the youngest of the siblings who begins his knightly career as Agravain's own squire, and the two of them later conspire to reveal Lancelot's affair with Guinevere, resulting in Agravain's death and consequently the civil war between Arthur's and Lancelot's factions. In stark contrast to many modern works, Mordred's only interaction with Arthur's other sister [Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_le_Fay) in any medieval text occurs in the Post-Vulgate *Queste*, when all the Orkney brothers visit Morgan's castle and are informed by her about Guinevere's infidelity.

The 14th-century Scottish chronicler [John of Fordun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Fordun) claimed that Mordred was the rightful heir to the throne of Britain, as Arthur was an illegitimate child (in his account, Mordred was the legitimate son of Lot and Anna, who here is [Uther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uther_Pendragon)'s sister). This sentiment was elaborated upon by [Walter Bower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Bower) and by [Hector Boece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hector_Boece), who in his *Historia Gentis Scotorum* goes so far as to say Arthur and Mordred's brother Gawain were traitors and villains, and Arthur usurped the throne from Mordred.[^6203] According to Boece, Arthur agreed to make Mordred his heir, but on the advice of the Britons who did not want Mordred to rule, he later made [Constantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_%28Briton%29) his heir; this led to the war in which Arthur and Mordred died. In [John Mair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Major_%28philosopher%29)'s Scottish *Historia Maioris Britanniae*, Arthurus, Modred and Valvanus (Gawain) were all said to be underage and thus unfit to rule, with Arthur himself described as a bastard. However, Mordred is also not depicted heroically, using mercenaries to seize both the throne and Guanora (Guinevere).[^6204]

##### Spouses and offspring

In Geoffrey's *Historia* and certain other texts (such as the Alliterative *Morte Arthure* reimagination of the *Historia*, where he is portrayed sympathetically), Mordred marries his aunt Guinevere consensually after taking over the throne. However, in later writings like the Vulgate Cycle (*Lancelot-Grail*) and *Le Morte d'Arthur*, Guinevere (now the wife of Mordred's real father) is not treated as a traitor and instead flees Mordred's proposal and hides in the [Tower of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_of_London). Willing adultery is still tied to her role in these later romances, but Mordred has been replaced as her lover by Lancelot. Related to this motif, a version of the Galician-Portuguese Post-Vulgate *Demanda* makes Mordred hate Lancelot due to his own, unrequited love for Guinevere.[^6205]

The 18th-century Welsh antiquarian [Lewis Morris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Morris_%281701%E2%80%931765%29), based on statements made by Boece, suggested that Medrawd had a wife named [Cwyllog](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cwyllog), daughter of Caw.[^6206] Another late Welsh tradition tells of Medrawd's marriage with Guinevere's sister, [Gwenhwy(f)ach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwenhwyfach).[^6206]

Mordred has been often said to be succeeded by his sons. They are always being numbered as two, though they are usually not named, nor is their mother. In Geoffrey's version, after the Battle of Camlann, Constantine is appointed Arthur's successor. However, Mordred's young sons and their Saxon allies rise against him.[^6207] After they are defeated, one of them flees to sanctuary in the Church of [Amphibalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphibalus) in [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester) while the other hides in a London [friary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monastery). Constantine tracks them down and kills them before the altars of their respective hiding places. This act invokes the vengeance of God, and three years later Constantine is killed by his nephew [Aurelius Conanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurelius_Conanus).[^6208] Geoffrey's account of the episode may be based on Constantine's murder of two "royal youths" as mentioned by Gildas.[^6209] In the Alliterative *Morte Arthure*, the dying Arthur personally orders Constantine to kill Mordred's infant sons. Guinevere had been asked by Mordred to flee with them to Ireland, but she instead returns to Arthur's [Caerleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caerleon) without care or concern for the safety of their children[^6210] who are then consequently drowned.

The elder of Mordred's sons is named Melehan or Melian (possibly the same as Melou from Layamon's *Brut*[^6211]), but he is the younger one in the *Lancelot-Grail* and the Post-Vulgate Cycle. In the Vulgate telling, in a battle near [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester) years later (soon after Guinevere's death), Melehan mortally wounds [Lionel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Lionel), brother to [Bors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bors) the Younger and a cousin of Lancelot. Bors then splits Melehan's head, avenging his brother's death, while the angry Lancelot chases after and decapitates the unnamed other brother who tried to escape deep into a forest.[^6212] Spanish chivalric romance *Florambel de Lucea* tells of the surviving Arthur having been saved by his sister Morgaina (i.e. Morgan) in a later battle against the grown-up sons of **Morderec**.[^6213] In the post-medieval Portuguese romance *Memorial das Proezas da Segunda Távola Redonda* (*Memorial of the Deeds of the Second Round Table*), the adult sons of **Morderete**, named Godifert and Dagobert, oppose Arthur's successor King Sagramor Constantino following the almost complete Saxon occupation of Britain. They are described as half-Saxon children of the daughter of the Duke of [Saxony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Saxony), Arnalda, aided by their cousin Briantes.[^6214]

#### Modern portrayals

Mordred is especially prominent in popular modern era Arthurian literature, as well as in other media such as film, television, and comics.[^6215] He has been played on screen by [Leonard Penn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Penn) (*The [Adventures of Sir Galahad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventures_of_Sir_Galahad)*, 1949), [Brian Worth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Worth) (*[The Adventures of Sir Lancelot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Adventures_of_Sir_Lancelot)*, 1956-1957), [David Hemmings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hemmings) (*[Camelot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camelot_%28film%29)*, 1967), [Robert Addie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Addie) (*[Excalibur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_%28film%29)*, 1981), [Nickolas Grace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nickolas_Grace) (*Morte d'Arthur*, 1984), [Simon Templeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Templeman) (voice in *[The Legend of Prince Valiant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Legend_of_Prince_Valiant)*, 1991-1993), [Jason Done](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Done) (*[Merlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlin_%28miniseries%29)*, 1998), [Craig Sheffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Sheffer) (*Merlin: The Return*, 2000), [Hans Matheson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Matheson) (*[The Mists of Avalon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mists_of_Avalon_%28miniseries%29)*, 2001), [Asa Butterfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asa_Butterfield) and [Alexander Vlahos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Vlahos) (*[Merlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merlin_%282008_TV_series%29)*, 2008-2012), [Rob Knighton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Knighton) (*King Arthur: Legend of the Sword*, 2017), and [Miyuki Sawashiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miyuki_Sawashiro) (voice in *[Fate/Apocrypha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fate/Apocrypha)*, 2017), among others. In modern adaptations, the character of Morgause is usually conflated with that of [Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_le_Fay_in_modern_culture), typically cast as Mordred's villainous mother (or alternatively his lover or wife), often manipulative and sometimes abusive. Some modern books and other media even feature Mordred as protagonist.

Virtually everywhere Mordred appears, his name is synonymous with [treason](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treason). In [Dante's *Inferno*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inferno_%28Dante%29), he is found in the first round of the lowest circle of Hell, set apart for traitors: "him who, at one blow, had chest and shadow / shattered by Arthur's hand" (Canto XXXII).[^6216] A few works from the Middle Ages and today, however, portray Mordred as less a traitor and more a conflicted opportunist, or even a victim of fate.[^6217] Even Malory, who depicts Mordred as a villain, notes that the people rallied to him because, "with Arthur was none other life but war and strife, and with Sir Mordred was great joy and bliss."[^6218]

### Carl Tanzler

**Georg Carl Tänzler**, also known as **Count Carl von Cosel** (February 8, 1877 - July, 1952[^6219] ), was a German-born American [radiology technologist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiology_technologist) at the [Marine-Hospital Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Hospital_Service) in [Key West, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_West,_Florida), United States. He developed an [obsession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erotomania) with a young [Cuban-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban-American) [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis) patient, Elena "Helen" Milagro de Hoyos (July 31, 1909 - October 25, 1931), that carried on well after her death.[^6220] In 1933, almost two years after her death, Tanzler removed Hoyos' body from its tomb and lived with the corpse at his home for seven years until its discovery by Hoyos' relatives and authorities in 1940.[^6221]

#### Early life

He was born as Karl Tänzler or Georg Karl Tänzler on February 8, 1877 in [Dresden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dresden), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany).

Tänzler grew up in the [German Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Empire) but, at some point, travelled to [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India) and later to [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia) just before the outbreak of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I). During his stay in Australia, over the course of World War I, Tänzler was kept with other Germans in Australia in [internment camps and prisons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentration_camp), supposedly for his own protection and safety because of his German ethnicity. He attempted and failed to escape by constructing a ship vessel. He was released shortly after the end of World War I, but since he was not allowed to move back to his native [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany), he instead left for the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands). In "The Trial Bay Organ: A Product of Wit and Ingenuity" by "Carl von Cosel", an autobiographical account in the *[Rosicrucian Digest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosicrucian_Digest)*[^6222] of March and April 1939, he gives details about his stay in Australia before his [internment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internment_in_the_United_Kingdom_during_the_First_World_War) during [the Great War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I), as well as his subsequent return to Germany after the War:[^6223][^6219]

> Many years ago, Carl von Cosel travelled from India to Australia with the intention of proceeding to the South Seas Islands. He paused in Australia to collect equipment and suitable boats, and to become acquainted with prevailing weather and sea conditions. However, he became interested in engineering and electrical work there, bought property, boats, an organ, an island in the Pacific, so that he was still in Australia at the end of ten years. He had just begun to build a trans-ocean flyer when the war broke out and the British military authorities placed him in a concentration camp for 'safe-keeping' along with many officers India and China who were prisoners of war. Later he was removed to [Trial Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_Bay) to a castle-like prison on the cliffs, and there the work in this narrative was accomplished. At the end of the war no prisoner was permitted to return to his former residence, but all were shipped to the prisoner's exchange in Holland. When Carl von Cosel was released he set out to find his mother from whom he had not heard since the beginning of the war. Finding her safe, he remained with her for three years, witnessing the chaos that followed in the wake of the war. ... Finally, she suggested that her son return to his sister in the United States ...

Tanzler's account of [Trial Bay Gaol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_Bay_Gaol), his secret building of a [sailboat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sailboat), etc., is confirmed by [Nyanatiloka Mahathera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyanatiloka), who mentions that he planned to escape from the Gaol with "Count Carl von Cosel" in a sailboat, and provides other information about the internment of Germans in Australia during World War I.[^6224]

Around 1920, following his return to Germany, Tanzler married Doris Schäfer (1889-1977). Together they had two children: Ayesha Tanzler (1922-1998), and Clarista Tanzler (1924-1934), who died of [diphtheria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diphtheria).[^6225]

Tanzler [emigrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emigrated) to the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_of_America) from Germany in 1926, sailing from [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam) on February 6, 1926 to [Havana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana), [Cuba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba). From Cuba, he settled in [Zephyrhills, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zephyrhills,_Florida), where his sister had already emigrated, and was later joined by his wife and daughters. Leaving his family behind in Zephyrhills in 1927, he took a job as a [radiology technician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiology_technician) at the [U.S. Marine Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Hospital_Service) in [Key West, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_West,_Florida) under the name Carl von Cosel.

During his childhood in Germany, and later while traveling briefly in [Genoa, Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa,_Italy), Tanzler claimed to have been visited by visions of a dead, purported ancestor, [Countess Anna Constantia von Cosel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Constantia_von_Brockdorff) (1680-1765), who revealed the face of his true love, an exotic dark-haired woman, to him.[^6220] He was convinced these "visions" were messages from Anna Constantia von Brockdorff from the dead. He was infatuated with her physical appearance, dark hair, and beauty. Because Anna Constantia von Brockdorff was also known as "the Countess of Cozel", he adopted the name **Karl Tänzler von Cosel**, which he preferred to be called by.

#### Maria Elena Milagro de Hoyos

On April 22, 1930, while working at the [Marine Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Hospital_Service) in [Key West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_West), Tanzler met Maria Elena Milagro de Hoyos (1909-1931), a local [Cuban-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuban-American) woman who had been brought to the hospital by her mother for an examination. Tanzler immediately believed her to be the beautiful dark-haired woman revealed to him in his earlier "visions."[^6226] By all accounts, Elena was viewed as a local beauty in Key West.[^6220][^6226][^6227]

Elena was the daughter of local cigar maker Francisco "Pancho" Hoyos (1883-1934) and Aurora Milagro (1881-1940). She had two sisters, Florinda "Nana" Milagro Hoyos (1906-1944), who married Mario Medina (c. 1905-1944) and also succumbed to [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis); and Celia Milagro Hoyos (1913-1934).

On February 18, 1926, Elena married Luis Mesa (1908-1974), the son of Caridad and Isaac Mesa. Mesa left Elena shortly after she suffered a [miscarriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miscarriage), and moved to [Miami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami). Elena was legally married to Mesa at the time of her death.

Elena was subsequently diagnosed with [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis), a disease typically fatal at the time and which eventually would claim the lives of almost all of her immediate family. Tanzler attempted to cure Elena with a variety of treatments, remedies, X-rays, and other medical equipment that were brought to the Hoyos' home.[^6220][^6226] Tanzler also showered Elena with gifts of jewelry and clothing, and allegedly professed his love to her, but no evidence has surfaced to show that Elena reciprocated any of his affection.[^6220][^6226]

#### Obsession

Despite Tanzler's best efforts, Elena died of [tuberculosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuberculosis) at her parents' home in Key West on October 25, 1931.[^6220] Tanzler paid for her funeral, and with the permission of her family, he then commissioned the construction of an above-ground [mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum) in the [Key West Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_West_Cemetery), which he visited almost every night.[^6220][^6226]

One evening in April 1933, Tanzler crept through the cemetery where Elena was buried and removed her body from the mausoleum, carting it through the cemetery after dark on a [toy wagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toy_wagon),[^6228] and transported it to his home. He reportedly said that Elena's spirit would come to him when he would sit by her grave and serenade her corpse with a favorite Spanish song. He also said that she would often tell him to take her from the grave.[^6220]

Tanzler attached the corpse's bones with piano wire and fitted the face with [glass eyes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ocular_prosthesis). As the skin of the corpse decomposed, Tanzler replaced it with silk cloth soaked in wax and [plaster of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaster). As the hair fell out of Elena's decomposing scalp, Tanzler fashioned a wig from her hair, which he had previously obtained from her mother.[^6226] Tanzler filled the corpse's [abdominal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdominal) and chest cavity with rags to keep the original form, dressed Elena's remains in stockings, jewelry, and gloves and kept the body in his bed. Tanzler also used copious amounts of perfume, disinfectants, and preserving agents to mask the odor and forestall the effects of the corpse's [decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decomposition).[^6229]

In October 1940, Elena's sister Florinda heard rumors of Tanzler sleeping with the disinterred body of her sister. She confronted Tanzler at his home, where Elena's body was eventually discovered (he was also caught dancing with her corpse in front of an open window). Florinda notified the authorities, and Tanzler was arrested and detained. Tanzler was [psychiatrically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatry) examined and found [mentally competent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Competence_%28law%29) to stand trial on the charge of "wantonly and maliciously destroying a grave and removing a body without authorization."[^6220] After a [preliminary hearing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preliminary_hearing) on October 9, 1940, at the [Monroe County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monroe_County,_Florida) Courthouse in Key West, Tanzler was held to answer on the charge, but the case was eventually dropped. He was released, as the [statute of limitations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_limitations) for the crime had expired.[^6220][^6226]

Shortly after the corpse's discovery by authorities, physicians and [pathologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathologists) examined Elena's body and put it on public display at the Dean-Lopez Funeral Home, where as many as 6,800 people viewed it.[^6227] Elena's body was eventually returned to the [Key West Cemetery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_West_Cemetery) where the remains were buried in an unmarked grave, in a secret location, to prevent further tampering. Her body was said to have been dismembered and placed in a metal box.[^6230][^6220] Portions of the original memorial plaque commissioned by Tanzler and affixed to Elena Hoyos's mausoleum have been reassembled and are on display at the [Martello Gallery-Key West Art and Historical Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martello_Gallery-Key_West_Art_and_Historical_Museum) in Key West.[^6231]

The facts underlying the case and the preliminary hearing drew much interest from the media at the time (most notably, from the *[Key West Citizen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Key_West_Citizen)* and *[Miami Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Herald)*) and created a sensation among the public, both regionally and nationwide. The public mood was generally sympathetic to Tanzler, whom many viewed as an eccentric "romantic."[^6220]

Though not reported contemporaneously, research (most notably by authors Harrison and Swicegood) has revealed evidence of Tanzler's [necrophilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necrophilia) with Elena's corpse.[^6220][^6226] Two physicians (Dr. DePoo and Dr. Foraker) who attended the 1940 [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy) of Elena's remains recalled in 1972 that a paper tube had been inserted in the vaginal area of the corpse that allowed for intercourse.[^6220][^6226] Others contend that since no evidence of necrophilia was presented at the 1940 preliminary hearing and because the physicians' "proof" surfaced in 1972, over 30 years after the case had been dismissed, the necrophilia allegation is questionable. While no existing contemporary photographs of the autopsy or photographs taken at the public display show a tube, the necrophilia claim was repeated by the [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Box_Office) *[Autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy_%28TV_series%29)* program in 1999.[^6229]

#### Later life and death

In 1944, Tanzler moved to [Pasco County, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasco_County,_Florida), close to Zephyrhills, where he wrote an autobiography that appeared in the [pulp publication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulp_magazine) *[Fantastic Adventures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantastic_Adventures)* in 1947. His home was near his wife Doris, who helped to support Tanzler in his later years.[^6220] Tanzler received [United States citizenship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_citizen) in 1950 in [Tampa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampa).

Separated from his [obsession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erotomania), Tanzler used a [death mask](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_mask) to create a life-sized [effigy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effigy) of Elena and lived with it until his death at age 75 on July 3, 1952.[^6229] His body was discovered on the floor of his home three weeks after his death. He died under the name "Carl Tanzler".

It has been recounted that Tanzler was found in the arms of Elena's effigy upon discovery of his corpse. Still, his obituary reported that he died on the floor behind one of his organs. The obituary recounted: "a metal cylinder on a shelf above a table in it wrapped in silken cloth and a robe was a waxen image".

It has been written (most notably by Swicegood) that Tanzler had the bodies switched (or that Elena's remains were secretly returned to him) and that he died with the real body of Elena.[^6220]

The story of Tanzler and Elena would be reproduced in pulp magazines in the years following his death, with various parties adding new details to the case.[^6232][^6233] An article written by Michelfelder in 1982 tells of how renovation workers found a note allegedly written by Tanzler, confessing to have killed Elena by poisoning her:[^6233]

> She died because I gave this to her mercifully. I mixed the root of wolfsbane (monkshood) with aconite diluted. It was palatable and my loved one departed this miserable world on October 25, 1931. Suffer no more sweet Elena. I have sent you to the angels with my golden elixir...

Key West Police Chief Bienvenido Perez also claimed Tanzler had once told him that he "would kill Elena if necessary to fulfil \[his\] destiny".[^6232] The poison confession letter article was also cited by historian David L. Sloan on episode 44 of the *NightMerica* podcast.[^6234]
