#### Asia

##### Armenia

| Name | Region | Description |
|----|----|----|
| Aragatsyan panir | [Aragatsotn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aragatsotn_Province) | A semi-hard cheese made from high-quality sheep's milk or its mixture with cow's or goat's milk. It has a mild nutty flavor, soft texture, and a natural rind. Less salty than brined cheeses, with a fat content of 50% or higher. |
| Chanakh | [Armenian Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_Highlands) | A traditional [brined cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brined_cheese) with a sharp, salty flavor and firm, slightly brittle texture, aged in brine and shaped into blocks or truncated cones. |
| [Chechil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechil) | [Armenian Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_Highlands) | A brined [string cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_cheese) that originated either in [Armenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenia) or in [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_%28country%29), it has a consistency approximating that of [suluguni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suluguni) or [mozzarella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozzarella) and is produced in the form of dense strings, rolled up in a figure eight of thick braid-shaped ropes. |
| Kanach panir | [Shirak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirak_Province) | A [mold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mold)-ripened cheese known for its greenish appearance and crumbly texture. It is aged in clay pots or leather bags, where natural or introduced mold develops, giving the cheese a sharp flavor and soft texture. Commonly consumed in the [Shirak Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirak_Province), it is typically served fresh and not used in cooked dishes. |
| Lori | [Lori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lori_Province) | A semi-soft Armenian cheese made from pasteurized cow's milk. Similar to [halloumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloumi), its curds are boiled during production and the cheese is preserved in brine. |
| [Motal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motal_%28cheese%29) | [Syunik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syunik_Province) and [Artsakh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Artsakh) | A traditional Armenian [brined cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brined_cheese) made primarily from sheep's milk or a mixture of sheep's and goat's milk. It is aged for several months in *tki*, leather containers made from animal hides, and may include herbs such as [wild thyme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_thyme). The cheese has a crumbly texture and a strong, distinctive flavor. |
| Tel panir | [Armenian Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_Highlands) | Tel panir is a traditional Armenian [string cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_cheese) made from strained, fermented milk. A type of [chechil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechil) cheese, it’s known for its distinctive braided or threaded form. |
| Yeghegnadzor | [Vayots Dzor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vayots_Dzor_Province) | A semi-soft, aromatic cheese traditionally aged in clay vessels buried underground. Made from cow's or goat's milk with local herbs and seeds, it develops a sharp, salty flavor and creamy, slightly crumbly texture after at least six months of underground maturation. Also known as *horats panir*. |

##### China

The dominant Han Chinese culture is not dairy-centric, in part due to low rates of [lactase persistence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lactase_persistence). However, some indigenous sociolinguistic groups in regions of the country, such as [Inner Mongolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Mongolia), [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet) and [Yunnan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yunnan), have strong cheese traditions.

| Name | Description |

##### Mongolia

There are two types of Mongolian cheese (бяслаг). They are similar in taste and are like a cross between mozzarella and an unsalted feta cheese.

- түүхий сүүний - this is a creamy version of Mongolian cheese made by boiling the milk and keeping the cream top.
- болсон сүүний - this is similar but is made without the cream.

Its natural rind is yellow-orange in color. |

There is no silage feeding or feeding with fermentation hay. This special, natural feeding makes the milk, and later the cheese, particularly aromatic. The cheese matures for at least 3 months. Staazer has a round loaf shape weighing about 6 kg. The dough is pale yellow, the consistency is compact with few fermentation holes. The taste is aromatic and mildly creamy. In addition to the regular Staazer, there are also the varieties: Staazer with wild garlic - 50% fat (Staazer cheese with wild garlic in the dough) Staazer with hay flowers - 45% fat (Staazer cheese with dried hay flowers on the rind)[^6849] |

In [Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albania), [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria), [Moldova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moldova), [North Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Macedonia), [Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia) and [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania), the term is often used to refer to all yellow cheeses (or even any cheese other than [sirene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirene)). |
| [Sirene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sirene) |  | A type of [brine cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brine_cheese) made in South-Eastern Europe, especially popular in [Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia), [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria), [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania), [Albania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albania), [North Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Macedonia), [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece) and [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel). It is made of [goat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goat) milk, [sheep milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheep_milk), [cow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cow)'s milk or a combination of milks.[^6857] It is slightly crumbly with a fat content of about 30-35%. It is commonly produced in blocks, and has a slightly grainy texture. |

The [whey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whey) used is usually a by-product in the production process of other harder cheeses, commonly that of [halloumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halloumi) or [kefalotyri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kefalotyri) cheese.[^6876] |

##### Denmark

|----|----|----|

The cheese is typically aged between 12 and 52 weeks in rectangular blocks of 6 or 9 kg, coated with a bacterial culture. The culture is washed off at the end of the aging cycle, and the cheese is packaged for retail sales. |
| [Danablu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danish_Blue) | Øverød, [Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealand) | Danablu (Danish Blue) is a strong, blue-veined cheese. This semi-soft creamery cheese is typically drum or block shaped and has a white to yellowish, slightly moist, edible rind. Made from full fat cow's milk and homogenised cream, it has a fat content of 25-30% and is aged for eight to twelve weeks |
| [Esrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esrom) | Esrum, [Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealand) | Esrom, or *Danish Port Salut cheese*, is a Trappist-style pale yellow semi-soft cow's milk cheese with a pungent aroma and a full, sweet flavour. It is a porous cheese, with many small holes throughout, and is slightly elastic and buttery in texture. |
| [Fynbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fynbo) | [Funen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funen) | A semi-hard Danish cheese named after the island of [Fyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyn). It has a flavor of buckwheat and is processed with a combination of mesophilic and thermophilic bacterial cultures. |
| [Havarti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havarti) | Øverød, [Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zealand) | Also known as *cream Havarti*, a semi-soft cow's milk cheese made like most cheeses by introducing rennet to milk to cause curdling. The curds are pressed into cheese molds which are drained, and then the cheese is aged. It is a washed curd cheese, which contributes to the subtle flavor. It is interior-ripened, rindless, smooth and slightly bright-surfaced. It has very small and irregular openings ("eyes") distributed in the mass. Havarti has a buttery aroma and can be somewhat sharp in the stronger varieties, much like Swiss cheese. The taste is buttery, and from somewhat sweet to very sweet, and it is slightly acidic. |
| [Maribo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maribo_cheese) | [Lolland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lolland) | A semi-hard cheese made from cow's milk. It has a firm, dry interior; a creamy texture; and many small, irregular holes. It has a pale tan rind covered in yellow wax. Its flavour is tangy, and it is sometimes seasoned with caraway seeds. |
| [Molbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molbo_cheese) | [Mols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mols) | A semi-hard cow's milk cheese made in the region of [Mols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mols). It is very similar to Edam, with a delicate, light flavour that is slightly tangy and salty. It has small, regular holes and is covered in a red wax coating. |
| [Saga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saga_%28cheese%29) | Tolstrup, [Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutland) | A mix of blue cheese and brie, creamy, blue-veined cheese with a white-mould rind. Saga is a very mild blue-veined cheese. It comes with a delicate blue mold, that may not appear in other varieties of blue cheeses. It is aged for more than 60 days. |
| [Samsø cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sams%C3%B8_cheese) | [Samsø](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sams%C3%B8) | A cow's milk cheese named after the island of [Samsø](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sams%C3%B8). It is similar to Emmentaler, although its flavour is milder: gentle and nutty in young cheeses and pungent with sweet and sour notes in older ones. Samsø's interior has a supple, elastic texture; a yellow colour; and a few large, irregular holes. It is the national cheese of Denmark. |
| [Tybo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tybo_cheese) | [Thy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thy_%28district%29), [Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutland) | A cow's milk cheese, similar to a mild Samsø. It is loaf-shaped, with a cream-colored, holey interior and a yellow rind. It has a slightly salty, smooth, and lactic flavor. |
| Vesterhavsost | Thise, Northwest [Jutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutland) | A semi-soft cow's milk cheese with briny[^6881] and caramelly tasting notes, it is comparable to Gouda. |

Until the early 20th century, ġbejniet made from [unpasteurised milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasteurised) were one of the causes of the spread of [Brucellosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brucellosis) which was so prevalent as to be called "the Maltese fever". |

##### Montenegro

| Name | Description |
|----|----|
| Kolašinski sir[^6886] [^6887] | A type of soft "Leafy" cheese made of [cow milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cow_milk), produced in Northern Montenegro town of Kolašin. This is a cow milk cheese exclusive to the Central North region, more specifically, around Kolašin town. This is due to the specific composition of flora that free-ranging cows feed upon on the [upland pastures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upland_pasture), as well as to the microclimatic conditions of the locality. The attempts to make this cheese elsewhere following the same recipe have failed. The producers from this region are proud of their cheese, and for years have been trying to initialize the procedure for the protection of geographic origin. This cheese is very valued as a delicacy in whole of Montenegro, and it is one of the most expensive fresh cheeses on the national market. The name of this cheese is derived from its specific texture. Thin, sometimes almost transparent, layers create a leafy structure, and make strings when the cheese is pulled apart. It has a pleasant mild fragrance. It does not contain high levels of fat, so its taste is mild and light.All producers make it in a similar manner, although every family has their own small secret that distinguishes their cheese, of which they are rather protective. What is known is that this cheese is made by combining the skimmed and whole cow milk. After adding the rennet, which makes milk curd, the cheese is drained and then frequently turned and folded. It is this manipulation that creates thin layers - leaves - that give it a characteristic texture. |
| Pljevaljski sir[^6888] | A type of best semisoft cheese made of [cow milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cow_milk), produced in Northern Montenegro town of Pljevlja. Cheese from Pljevlja is a ubiquitous part of Montenegrin meal. It is white cheese made from unpasteurized cow milk. The characteristic flavour comes from the maturation process that takes place in special wooden barrel-like containers. The cheese matures for at least three weeks until it achieves its characteristic strong flavour and creamy texture. Currently, there is an ongoing procedure for protection of geographic origin for this cheese. |
| Podgorički sir[^6889] | A salty brined cheese made from cow milk.Also named "Kučki sir", made in Southern Montenegro city of Podgorica. |
| Nikšićki kozji sir | Made from best whole goat milk, produced in Western Montenegro town of Nikšić. |
| Njeguški sir[^6890] | In the Southern Montenegro town of Cetinje surroundings at Njeguši the famous cheese of Njeguši is produced. It is being kept at shaded in airy places up to 3 months before degustation. Dried and rich in cow milk fats - simply exquisite. |

##### Netherlands

The Netherlands is one of the major cheese producing countries of Europe, with a tradition of cheesemaking as shown by the [Dutch cheese markets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_cheese_markets).

In English-language menus "кашкавал" is translated as "yellow cheese" (whereas *sirene* is usually translated as "white cheese" or simply "cheese"). ##### Poland

The history of [cheesemaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheesemaker) in Poland goes back to 5500 BC, when cheese similar to [mozzarella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozzarella) was produced in [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic) times in [Kujawy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kujawy) (north-central Poland).[^6896][^6897]

Poland is the 7th largest cheese producer in the world and has the 18th highest cheese consumption.

Marek Kosmulski described over 600 types of Polish cheeses manufactured between 1948 and 2019.

##### Switzerland

[Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland) is home to over 450 varieties of cheese.[^6921] [Cows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cow) [milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milk) is used in about 99 percent of the cheeses produced. The remaining share is made up of [sheep milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheep_milk) and [goat milk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goat_milk).

It is made by adding [white vinegar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinegar) to cooled down boiled milk and then gathering the curd and stuffing it in a pot or jug and then the pot is buried under the ground where water is sometimes added to the soil. [Salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt) is added daily to thicken the yogurt even more and the outside of the yogurt filled cheesecloth is rinsed with [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water) to allow any remaining [whey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whey) to seep through. | Name | Region | Description |
|----|----|----|
| [Farmer cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmer_cheese) | Various | Varieties of which are made in most cultures with a strong dairy culture |
| [Port wine cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_wine_cheese) |  | An orange- and red-colored cheese that prepared with alcoholic [port wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_wine) as it is made[^6959] |
| [Smoked cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoked_cheese) | Various | A style of preparing any number of hard or semi-hard cheeses, using smoke or smoke flavoring.[^6960][^6961] Pictured is smoked [Gruyère cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gruy%C3%A8re_cheese) |
| [Soy cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soy_cheese) |  | Not a dairy product, but a [cheese analogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheese_analogue) made from soybeans/soy protein.[^6962] Pictured is soy cheese manufactured to the consistency of a cream cheese. |
| [Rice cheese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice_cheese) |  | As with soy cheese, an analogue from rice/rice protein[^6963] |

### List of phobias

The [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language) suffixes **-phobia**, **-phobic**, **-phobe** (from [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek) φόβος *phobos*, 'fear') occur in technical usage in [psychiatry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatry) to construct words that describe irrational, [abnormal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abnormal), unwarranted, persistent, or disabling [fear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear) as a mental disorder (e.g., [agoraphobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agoraphobia)), in [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemistry) to describe chemical aversions (e.g., [hydrophobic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrophobic)), in [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology) to describe organisms that dislike certain conditions (e.g., [acidophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acidophobia)), and in [medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine) to describe hypersensitivity to a stimulus, usually sensory (e.g., [photophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photophobia)). In common usage, they also form words that describe dislike or hatred of a particular thing or subject (e.g., [homophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homophobia)). The suffix is [antonymic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonym) to *-phil-*.

For more information on the psychiatric side, including how psychiatry groups phobias such as agoraphobia, social phobia, or simple phobia, see [phobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phobia). The following lists include words ending in *-phobia*, and include fears that have acquired names. In some cases, the naming of phobias has become a [word game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_game), a notable example being a 1998 humorous article published by [BBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_News).[^6964] In some cases, a word ending in *-phobia* may have an [antonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonym) with the suffix *-phil-*, e.g., [Germanophobe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-German_sentiment)/[Germanophile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanophile).

Many *-phobia* lists circulate on the Internet, with words collected from indiscriminate sources, often copying each other. Also, a number of psychiatric websites exist that at the first glance cover a huge number of phobias, but in fact use a standard text to fit any phobia and reuse it for all unusual phobias by merely changing the name. Sometimes it leads to bizarre results, such as suggestions to cure "prostitute phobia".[^6965] Such practice is known as [content spamming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Content_spamming) and is used to attract [search engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_search_engine).

An article published in 1897 in the *[American Journal of Psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Journal_of_Psychology)* noted, "the absurd tendency to give Greek names to objects feared (which, as [Arndt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudolf_Arndt) says, would give us such terms as klopsophobia - fear of thieves and triakaidekaphobia \[*[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic)*\] - fear of the number 13 ...)".[^6966]

#### Psychological conditions

Specialists may prefer to avoid the suffix *-phobia* and use more descriptive terms such as [personality disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personality_disorder), [anxiety disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anxiety_disorder), and [avoidant personality disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avoidant_personality_disorder). Terms should strictly have a Greek prefix, although many are irregularly formed with Latin or even English prefixes. Many use inaccurate or imprecise prefixes, such as aerophobia (fear of air) for fear of flying.

##### Ethnic/national/religious prejudices and discrimination

The suffix *-phobia* is used to coin terms that denote a particular anti-ethnic or anti-demographic sentiment, such as [Americanophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Americanism), [Europhobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Europeanism), [Francophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francophobia), Hispanophobia, and [Indophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Indian_sentiment). Often a synonym with the prefix "anti-" already exists (e.g. [Polonophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Polish_sentiment) vs. [anti-Polonism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Polish_sentiment)). Anti-religious sentiments are expressed in terms such as [Christianophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-Christian_sentiment) and [Islamophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamophobia).

#### *-phobia* in the natural sciences

In the natural sciences, words with the suffix *-phobia/-phobic* generally describe a predisposition for avoidance or exclusion.

| Phobia | Condition |
|----|----|
| [Acidophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acidophobe) | preference for non-acidic conditions |
| [Heliophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heliophobia) | aversion to [sunlight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunlight) |
| [Hydrophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrophobe) | the property of being repelled by [water](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water) |
| [Lipophobicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lipophobicity) | the property of [fat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat) rejection (sometimes also called *lipophobia*) |
| [Oleophobicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oleophobic) | the property of [oil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil) rejection |
| [Photophobia (biology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photophobia_%28biology%29) | a negative [phototaxis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phototaxis) or [phototropism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phototropism) response, or a tendency to stay out of the [light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light) |
| [Ultrahydrophobicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultrahydrophobicity) | the property given to materials that are extremely difficult to get [wet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moisture) |
| [Thermophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermophobia) | aversion to [heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat) |

#### Jocular and fictional phobias

- Aibohphobia - a humorous term for the fear of [palindromes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palindrome), which is a palindrome itself. The term is a piece of [computer humor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_humor) entered into the 1981 *[The Devil's DP Dictionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Devil's_DP_Dictionary)*.[^7010]
- Anatidaephobia - the fictional fear that one is being watched by a duck. The word comes from the name of the family *[Anatidae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatidae),* and was used in [Gary Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Larson)'s *[The Far Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Far_Side)*.[^7011]
- Anoraknophobia - a [portmanteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portmanteau) of "[anorak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parka)" and "[arachnophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arachnophobia)". It was used in the *[Wallace & Gromit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallace_&_Gromit)* comic book *Anoraknophobia*. Also the title of an [album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anoraknophobia) by [Marillion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marillion).
- Arachibutyrophobia - fear of [peanut butter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanut_butter) sticking to the roof of the mouth, from Latin *[arachis](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/arachis)* "peanut" and *[butyrum](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/butyrum)* "butter".[^7012] The word is used by [Charles M. Schulz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_M._Schulz) in a 1982 installment of his *[Peanuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peanuts)* comic strip,[^7013] and by [Peter O'Donnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_O'Donnell) in his 1985 [Modesty Blaise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modesty_Blaise) [adventure novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adventure_fiction) *[Dead Man's Handle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Man's_Handle)*.
- Charlophobia - the fictional fear of any person named Charlotte or Charlie, mentioned in the comedic book *A Duck is Watching Me: Strange and Unusual Phobias (2014),* by Bernie Hobbs. The phobia was created to mock [name bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bias), a form of discrimination studied by researchers at the [University of California, Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley) and the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago).[^7014]
- [Hippopotomonstrosesquipedaliophobia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippopotomonstrosesquipedaliophobia) - fear of long words,[^7015] from the root word *[sesquipedalophobia](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/sesquipedalophobia#English)* combined with *monstrum* and *[hippopotamus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippopotamus)*. This was mentioned on the first episode of *Brainiac* Series Five as a [Tickle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Tickle)'s Teaser.
- Keanuphobia - fear of [Keanu Reeves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keanu_Reeves), portrayed in the [Dean Koontz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_Koontz) book, *[False Memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_Memory_%28novel%29)*, where a woman has an [irrational fear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irrational_fear_%28phobia%29) of Reeves and has to see her psychiatrist, Mark Ahriman, each week, unaware that she only has the fear in the first place because Ahriman implanted it via [hypnotic suggestion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypnotic_suggestion) to amuse himself. He calls her "*Keanuphobe*" in his head.
- Luposlipaphobia - fear of being pursued by timber wolves around a kitchen table while wearing socks on a newly waxed floor. Coined humorously by cartoonist [Gary Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Larson) for his comic [The Far Side](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Far_Side).
- Nihilophobia - fear of nothingness, from Latin *nihil and* "nothing, none", as described by [the Doctor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doctor_%28Star_Trek%29) in the *Star Trek: Voyager* episode "Night". Voyager's morale officer and chef [Neelix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neelix) has this condition, having [panic attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_attack) while the ship was traversing a dark expanse of space known as the Void. It is also the title of a 2008 album by [Neuronium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuronium).
- Robophobia - irrational fear of robots or androids, also known as "[Grimwade's Syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Grimwade)". It was first used in "[The Robots of Death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Robots_of_Death)",[^7016] the fifth serial of the [14th season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Who_season_14) of the British [science fiction television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_fiction_television) series *[Doctor Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Who).*
- Semaphobia - fear of average web developers to use [Semantic Web](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semantic_Web) technologies.[^7017]
- Venustraphobia - fear of beautiful women, according to a 1998 [humorous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humor) article published by [BBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_News).[^6964]

[^6964]: [The A-Z of Fear](http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/low/entertainment/173250.stm), a 30 October 1998 BBC News unsigned article in the "Entertainment" section

### List of chemical elements

118 [chemical elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_element) have been [identified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_chemical_element_discoveries) and named officially by [IUPAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_of_Pure_and_Applied_Chemistry). A chemical element, often simply called an element, is a type of [atom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom) which has a specific number of [protons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton) in its [atomic nucleus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_nucleus) (i.e., a specific [atomic number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_number), or *Z*).[^7018]

The definitive visualisation of all 118 elements is the [periodic table of the elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_table), whose [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_periodic_table) along the principles of the [periodic law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_law) was one of the founding developments of modern [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemistry). It is a tabular [arrangement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrangement) of the elements by their chemical properties that usually uses abbreviated [chemical symbols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_symbol) in place of full element names, but the linear list format presented here is also useful. Like the periodic table, the list below organizes the elements by the number of protons in their atoms; it can also be organized by other properties, such as [atomic weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_weight), [density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Density), and [electronegativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronegativity). For more detailed information about the origins of element names, see [List of chemical element name etymologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_chemical_element_name_etymologies).

[^7032]: Greek *hḗlios* 'sun'

[^7034]: Greek *líthos* 'stone'

[^7035]: Beryl, mineral (ultimately after Belur, Karnataka, India?)(4)

[^7036]: Borax, mineral (from Arabic: [*bawraq*](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D8%A8%D9%88%D8%B1%D9%82#Arabic), Middle Persian: \**bōrag*)

[^7037]: Latin *carbo* 'coal'

[^7038]: Greek *nítron* + *-gen*, 'niter-forming'

[^7039]: Greek *oxy-* + *-gen*, 'acid-forming'

[^7040]: Latin *fluo* 'to flow'

[^7041]: Greek *néon* 'new'

[^7042]: Coined by Humphry Davy who first isolated it, from English *soda* (specifically caustic soda), via Italian from Arabic *ṣudāʕ* 'headache'

[^7043]: Magnesia region, eastern Thessaly, Greece

[^7044]: Alumina, from Latin *alumen* (gen. *aluminis*) 'bitter salt, alum'

[^7045]: Latin *silex* 'flint' (originally *silicium*)

[^7046]: Greek *phōsphóros* 'light-bearing'

[^7047]: Latin

[^7048]: Greek *chlōrós* 'greenish yellow'

[^7049]: Greek *argós* 'idle' (it is inert)

[^7050]: Neo-Latin *potassa* 'potash', from *pot* + *ash*

[^7051]: Latin *calx* 'lime'

[^7052]: Latin *Scandia* 'Scandinavia'

[^7053]: Titans, children of Gaia and Ouranos

[^7054]: Vanadis, a name for Norse goddess Freyja

[^7055]: Greek *chróma* 'colour'

[^7056]: Corrupted from *[magnesia](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/magnesia#Latin) [negra](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/negra#Latin)*; see magnesium

[^7057]: English, from Proto-Celtic \*īsarnom 'iron', from a root meaning 'blood'

[^7058]: German *[Kobold](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Kobold#German)*, 'goblin'

[^7059]: Nickel, a mischievous sprite in German miner mythology

[^7060]: English, from Latin *[cuprum](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/cuprum#Latin)*, after Cyprus

[^7061]: Most likely German *[Zinke](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Zinke#German)*, 'prong, tooth', but some suggest Persian [*sang*](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D8%B3%D9%86%DA%AF#Persian) 'stone'

### List of largest cities

The [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations) uses three definitions for what constitutes a city, as not all cities in all jurisdictions are classified using the same criteria. Cities may be defined as the [cities proper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_proper), their [metropolitan regions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area), or the extent of their [urban area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_area). A complicating factor is that many large cities in the world have not only homeless or the unhoused, but also vast [slum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slum) communities. This leads to official census data being less accurate in representing the actual number of residents in a given area.

#### Definitions

##### City proper (administrative unit)

A city can be defined by its administrative boundaries, otherwise known as [city proper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_proper). [UNICEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF) defines city proper as, "the population living within the administrative boundaries of a city or controlled directly from the city by a single authority." A city proper is a locality defined according to legal or political boundaries and an administratively recognised urban status that is usually characterised by some form of [local government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Local_government).[^7154][^7155][^7156] Cities proper and their boundaries and population data may not include suburbs.[^7157]

The use of city proper as defined by administrative boundaries may not include suburban areas where an important proportion of the population working or studying in the city lives.[^7157] Because of this definition, the city proper population figure may differ greatly from the urban area population figure, as many cities are amalgamations of smaller municipalities, and conversely, many Chinese cities govern territories that extend well beyond the core urban area into suburban and rural areas.[^7158] The Chinese municipality of [Chongqing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chongqing), which is the largest city proper in the world by population, comprises a huge administrative area of 82,403 km², around the size of [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria). However, around 30% of its 30-million population are agricultural workers living in a [rural setting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_area).[^7159][^7160][^7161]

##### Metropolitan area

A city can be defined by the inhabitants of its [demographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demography) population, as by [metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area), or [labour market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_economics) area. UNICEF defines metropolitan area as follows:

> A formal local government area comprising the urban area as a whole and its primary commuter areas, typically formed around a city with a large concentration of people (i.e., a population of at least 100,000). In addition to the city proper, a metropolitan area includes both the surrounding territory with urban levels of residential [density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_density) and some additional lower-density areas that are adjacent to and linked to the city (e.g., through frequent transport, road linkages or commuting facilities).

In many countries, metropolitan areas are established either as a local administrative organisation or only for statistical purposes. In the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States), [metropolitan statistical area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_statistical_area) (MSA) is defined by the [U.S. Office of Management and Budget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Office_of_Management_and_Budget) (OMB).[^7162] In the [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines), metropolitan areas have an official agency, such as [Metropolitan Manila Development Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Manila_Development_Authority) (MMDA), which manages [Manila metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Manila).[^7163] Similar agencies exist in [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia), such as Jabodetabekjur Development Cooperation Agency for [Jakarta metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jakarta_metropolitan_area).[^7164]

##### Urban area

A city can be defined as a conditionally [contiguous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geographic_contiguity) [urban area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_area), with relatively less regard to territorial or administrative boundaries. [UNICEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF) defines urban area as follows:

> The definition of "urban" varies from country to country, and, with periodic reclassification, can also vary within one country over time, making direct comparisons difficult. An urban area can be defined by one or more of the following: administrative criteria or political boundaries (e.g., area within the jurisdiction of a municipality or town committee), a threshold population size (where the minimum for an urban settlement is typically in the region of 2,000 people, although this varies globally between 200 and 50,000), population density, economic function (e.g., where a significant majority of the population is not primarily engaged in agriculture, or where there is surplus employment) or the presence of urban characteristics (e.g., paved streets, electric lighting, sewerage).

According to [Demographia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographia), an urban area is a continuously built up land mass of urban development that is within a labor market (metropolitan area or metropolitan region) and contains no [rural land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_area).

### List of tallest buildings

This is a list of the tallest [buildings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Building). Tall buildings, such as [skyscrapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyscraper), are intended here as enclosed structures with continuously occupiable floors and a height of at least 350 metres (1,148 ft). Such definition excludes [non-building structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-building_structure), such as [radio towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_tower).

#### History

Historically, the world's tallest man-made structure was the [Great Pyramid of Giza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza) in [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt), which held the position for more than 3,800 years[^7279] until the construction of [Lincoln Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Cathedral) in 1311. The [Strasbourg Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strasbourg_Cathedral) in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France), completed in 1439, was the world's tallest building until 1874.

The first building considered to be a skyscraper was the 138 ft (42.1 m) [Home Insurance Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Insurance_Building), built in Chicago in 1885. The [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States) would remain the location of the world's tallest building throughout the 20th century until 1998, when the [Petronas Towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petronas_Towers) were completed. Since then, two other buildings have gained the title: [Taipei 101](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taipei_101) in 2004 and [Burj Khalifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burj_Khalifa) in 2009.[^7280] Since the beginning of the 21st century, the [Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East), [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China), and [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia) have experienced booms in skyscraper construction.[^7281]

#### Ranking criteria and alternatives

The international non-profit organization [Council on Vertical Urbanism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_on_Vertical_Urbanism) (CVU) was formed in 1969 and announces the title of "The World's Tallest Building" and sets the standards by which buildings are measured. It maintains a list of the 100 tallest completed buildings in the world.[^7282] The organization currently ranks [Burj Khalifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burj_Khalifa) in [Dubai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubai) as the tallest at 828 m (2,717 ft).[^7282] However, the CVU only recognizes buildings that are complete, and some buildings included within the lists in this article are not considered finished by the CVU.

In 1996, as a response to the dispute as to whether the [Petronas Towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petronas_Towers) or the [Sears Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willis_Tower) was taller,[^7283] the council listed and ranked buildings in four categories:[^7284]

- height to structural or architectural top;
- height to highest occupied floor;
- height to top of roof (removed as category in November 2009);[^7285] and
- height to top of any part of the building.

All categories measure the building from the level of the lowest significant open-air pedestrian entrance.[^7286]

[Spires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spire) are considered integral parts of the architectural design of buildings, changes to which would substantially change the appearance and design of the building, whereas antennas may be added or removed without such consequences. The Petronas Towers, with their spires, are thus ranked higher than the Willis Tower (formerly the Sears Tower) with its antennas, despite the Petronas Towers' lower roofs and lower highest point.[^7284]

Until 1996, the world's tallest building was defined by the height to the top of the tallest architectural element, including spires but not antennae.[^7284] In 1930, this definitional argument led to a rivalry between the [Bank of Manhattan Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/40_Wall_Street) and the [Chrysler Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler_Building). The Bank of Manhattan Building (i.e. 40 Wall Street) employed only a short spire, was 282.5 m (927 ft) tall, and had a much higher top occupied floor (the second category in the 1996 criteria for tallest building). In contrast, the Chrysler Building employed a very large 38 m (125 ft) spire secretly assembled inside the building to claim the title of world's tallest building with a total height of 319 m (1046 ft), although it had a lower top occupied floor and a shorter height when both buildings' spires were excluded.

Upset by Chrysler's victory, [Shreve & Lamb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shreve,_Lamb_&_Harmon), the consulting architects of the Bank of Manhattan Building, wrote a newspaper article claiming that their building was actually the tallest, since it contained the world's highest usable floor, at 255 m (837 ft). They pointed out that the observation deck in the Bank of Manhattan Building was nearly 30 m (98 ft) above the top floor in the Chrysler Building, whose surpassing spire was strictly ornamental and inaccessible.[^7287]

The Burj Khalifa currently tops the list regardless of which criterion is applied, though at a much lower margin when measured to highest occupied floor.[^7288][^7289]

#### Tallest buildings in the world

As of 2026, this list includes all 98 buildings (completed and architecturally [topped out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topping_out)) that reach a height of 350 m (1,150 ft) or more, as assessed by their highest architectural feature. The building is considered as architecturally topped out when it is under construction, structurally topped out, fully clad, and the highest finished architectural elements are in place.[^7286]

Of these buildings, almost half are in China. Six of the last seven buildings to have held the record as "[tallest building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyscraper)" are still found in the list, with the exception being [the North Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1_World_Trade_Center_%281970%E2%80%932001%29) of the original [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City) [World Trade Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Center_%281973%E2%80%932001%29) at 417 m (1,368 ft) after its destruction in the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks) of 2001. Had the World Trade Center Twin Towers never been destroyed and [One World Trade Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_World_Trade_Center) never built, they would have ranked 39 and 40 on the list today.

#### Alternative measurements

##### Height to pinnacle (highest point)

This measurement disregards distinctions between architectural and non-architectural extensions, and simply measures to the highest point, irrespective of material or function of the highest element.[^7286]

This measurement is useful for [air traffic obstacle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_traffic_obstacle) determinations, and is also a wholly objective measure. However, this measurement includes extensions that are easily added, removed, and modified from a building and are independent of the overall structure.

This measurement only recently came into use, when the [Petronas Towers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petronas_Towers) passed the Sears Tower (now named [Willis Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willis_Tower)) in height. The former was considered taller because its spires were considered architectural, while the latter's antennae were not. This led to the split of definitions, with the Sears Tower claiming the lead in this and the height-to-roof (now highest occupied floor) categories, and with the Petronas claiming the lead in the architectural height category.

If the original [World Trade Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Center_%281973%E2%80%932001%29) towers were still standing, the [North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1_World_Trade_Center_%281971%E2%80%932001%29) (1,728 feet (526.7 m), including the antenna) and [South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2_World_Trade_Center_%281971%E2%80%932001%29) Towers (1,377 feet (419.7 m)) would fall between numbers 11 and 37 on the current list (as it can be assumed the rebuilt One World Trade Center would have never been built).

##### Height to roof

This **list of tallest buildings by height to roof** ranks completed [skyscrapers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skyscraper) by height to roof which reach a height of 300 metres (984 ft) or more. Only buildings with continuously occupiable floors are included, thus [non-building structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonbuilding_structure), including towers, are not included. Some assessments of the tallest building use 'height to roof' to determine tallest building, as 'architectural feature' is regarded as a subjective and an imprecise comparative measure. However, in November 2009, the [CTBUH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CTBUH) stopped using the roof height as the metric for tall buildings because modern tall buildings rarely have a part of the building that can categorically be deemed the roof.[^7391]

### List of animal sounds

Certain words in the [English language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language) represent **animal sounds**: the noises and [vocalizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speech_production) of particular animals, especially noises used by [animals for communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_communication). The words can be used as [verbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verb) or [interjections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interjection) in addition to [nouns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noun), and many of them are also specifically [onomatopoeic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onomatopoeic).

#### List of animal sounds

| Animal | Description | Audio recording |
|----|----|----|
| [Alligator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alligator) | [bellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellow_%28sound%29), hiss |  |
| [Alpaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpaca) | alarm call, cluck/click, hum, orgle, scream[^7498] |  |
| [American woodcock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_woodcock) | meep, peent ([birders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birdwatching)) |  |
| [Antelope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antelope) | snort[^7499] |  |
| [Australian magpie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_magpie) | quardle-oodle-ardle-wardle-doodle |  |
| [Badger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badger) | growl[^7500] |  |
| [Bat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bat) | screech,[^7501] squeak, eek |  |
| [Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear) | [roar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roar), growl |  |
| [Beaver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaver) | grunting, sighing, gnawing, whining, tooth chattering, hissing[^7502] |  |
| [Bee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee) | buzz |  |
| [Big cat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_cat) ([Tiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiger), [Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion), [Jaguar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaguar), [Leopard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopard)) | [roar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roar),[^7503] growl,[^7504] snarl[^7505] |  |
| [Bison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bison) | [bellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellow_%28sound%29), moo, low |  |
| [Camel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camel) | grunt |  |
| [Capybara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capybara) | squeak,[^7506] chatter, bark |  |
| [Cat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat) | mew, [meow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meow), [purr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purr), hiss, trill, chirp, chatter, caterwaul, growl, mrrp, nya |  |
| [Cattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle) | moo, low |  |
| [Chicken](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicken) | cluck, buck, crow[^7507] cha-caw, bah-gawk (female)[^7508] cock-a-doodle-doo (male) |  |
| [Chinchilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinchilla) | squeak[^7509] |  |
| [Cicada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicada) | chirp[^7510] |  |
| [Coyote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coyote) | yip, [howl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howling), yelp, whine, growl, huff, [bark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bark_%28sound%29)[^7511] |  |
| [Crab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crab) | chirp, click, creak[^7512] |  |
| [Crane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crane_%28bird%29) | trumpet, bugle[^7513] |  |
| [Cricket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket_%28insect%29) | [chirp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stridulation) |  |
| [Crocodile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crocodile) | hiss, growl |  |
| [Crow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crow) | [caw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corvus_%28genus%29), cah[^7514] |  |
| [Curlew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curlew) | pipe[^7515] |  |
| [Deer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deer) | [bellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellow_%28sound%29), [bell](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/bell) (buck), bleat (doe, fawn) |  |
