| *confer* (*[cf.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cf.)*) | compare | The abbreviation *cf.* is used in text to suggest a comparison with something else (cf. [citation signal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citation_signal)). |
| *[Congregatio Sanctissimi Redemptoris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregatio_Sanctissimi_Redemptoris) C.Ss.R* | Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer | Redemptorists |
| *coniunctis viribus* | with connected strength | Or "with united powers". Sometimes rendered *conjunctis viribus*. Motto of [Queen Mary, University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Mary,_University_of_London). |
| [*consensu*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensu_%28law%29) | with consent |  |
| *consuetudo pro lege servatur* | Custom serves for law. | Where there are no specific laws, the matter should be decided by custom;[^7588] established customs have the force of laws.[^7589] Also *consuetudo est altera lex* (custom is another law) and *consuetudo vincit communem legem* (custom overrules the common law); see also: [Consuetudinary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Customary_law). |
| *consummatum est* | It is completed. | The last words of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus) on the [cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crucifixion) in the [Latin translation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate) of [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_of_John) 19:30. |
| *[contemptus mundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemptus_mundi)/saeculi* | scorn for the world/times | Despising the [secular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secularism) world. The [monk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monasticism) or [philosopher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy)'s rejection of a mundane life and worldly values. |
| *contra bonos mores* | against good morals | Offensive to the conscience and to a sense of justice. |
| *contra legem* | against law | Especially in [civil law jurisdictions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_law_%28legal_system%29), said of an understanding of a [statute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute) that directly contradicts its wording and thus is valid neither by interpretation nor by [analogy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analogy). |
| *contra mundum* | against the world | against public opinion; see also [contra mundum injunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contra_mundum_injunction), enforceable against anyone, rather than a named party; [Athanasius Contra Mundum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athanasius_Contra_Mundum), Athanasius of Alexandria, 4th-century Christian patriarch and theologian, exiled five times by four emperors. |
| *[contra proferentem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contra_proferentem)* | against the proferror | In [contract law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contract_law), the doctrine of contractual interpretation which provides that an ambiguous term will be construed against the party that imposed its inclusion in the contract - or, more accurately, against the interests of the party who imposed it. |
| *contra spem spero* | I hope against hope | Title of a poem by [Lesya Ukrainka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesya_Ukrainka); it derives from an expression found in Paul's Letter to the Romans 4:18 (Greek: παρ' ἐλπίδα ἐπ' ἐλπίδι, Latin: contra spem in spe\[m\]) with reference to [Abraham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham) the Patriarch who maintained faith in becoming the father of many nations despite being childless and well-advanced in years. |
| [*contra vim mortis non crescit herba* (or *salvia*) *in hortis*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contra_vim_mortis_non_crescit_herba_in_hortis) | No herb (or [sage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvia)) grows in the gardens against the power of death | there is no medicine against death; from various medieval medicinal texts |
| *contradictio in terminis* | contradiction in terms | Something that would embody a [contradiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contradiction) with the very definition of one of its terms; for example, payment for a gift, or a circle with corners. The [fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacy) of proposing such a thing. |
| *[contra principia negantem non est disputandum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contra_principia_negantem_non_est_disputandum)* | there can be no debate with those who deny the foundations | Debate is fruitless when you don't agree on common rules, facts, presuppositions. |
| *cor ad cor loquitur* | heart speaks to heart | From [Augustine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Hippo)'s *[Confessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confessions_%28St._Augustine%29)*, referring to a prescribed method of prayer: having a "heart to heart" with God. Commonly used in reference to a later quote by Cardinal [John Henry Newman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Henry_Newman). A motto of Newman Clubs. |
| *cor aut mors* | Heart or Death | (Your choice is between) The Heart (Moral Values, Duty, Loyalty) or Death (to no longer matter, no longer to be respected as person of integrity.) |
| *cor meum tibi offero domine prompte et sincere* | my heart I offer to you Lord promptly and sincerely | [John Calvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Calvin)'s personal motto, also adopted by [Calvin College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_College) |
| *cor unum* | one heart | A popular school motto and often used as a name for religious and other organisations such as the [Pontifical Council Cor Unum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontifical_Council_Cor_Unum). |
| *coram* | in the presence of | Used before a list of the names of the judges on a panel hearing a particular case. |
| *coram Deo* | in the presence of God | A phrase from [Christian theology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_theology) which summarizes the idea of [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians) living in the presence of, under the authority of, and to the honor and glory of [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God); see also [coram Deo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coram_Deo_%28disambiguation%29). |
| *coram episcopo* | in the presence of the bishop | Refers to the celebration of Mass in the Roman Catholic Church where the bishop is present but does not preside over the service.[^7590] Cf. *coram Summo Pontifice*, in the presence of the Pope, in similar circumstances.[^7591] |
| *[coram nobis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coram_nobis), coram vobis* | in our presence, in your presence | Two kinds of [writs of error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writ_of_error), calling for the decision to be reviewed by the same court that made it. *Coram nobis* is short for *quae coram nobis resident* (let them, i.e. the matters on the court record, remain before us), and was the form historically used for the [Court of King's Bench](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_King's_Bench_%28England%29); the "[us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_we)" means the King, who was theoretically the head of that court. *Coram vobis* is the analogous version ("let the matters remain before you") for the [Court of Common Pleas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_of_Common_Pleas), where the King did not sit, even notionally. |
| *[coram non judice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coram_non_judice)* | not before a judge | legal proceeding that is outside the presence of a judge, thus a violation of the law and a [nullity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_nullity) |
| *coram populo* | in the presence of the people |  |
| *coram publico* | in view of the public |  |
| [*Corpus Christi*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blessed_Sacrament) | Body of Christ | The name of a [feast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Christi_%28feast%29) in the [Roman Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church) commemorating the [Eucharist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eucharist). It is also the name of a city in Texas, [Corpus Christi, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Christi,_Texas), the name of Colleges at [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Christi_College,_Oxford) and [Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Christi_College,_Cambridge) universities, and [a controversial play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Christi_%28play%29). |
| *[corpus delicti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_delicti)* | body of the offence | The fact that a crime has been committed, a necessary factor in convicting someone of having committed that crime; if there was no crime, there can not have been a criminal. |
| *Corpus Iuris Canonici* | Body of [Canon Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_law) | The official compilation of canon law in the [Roman Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church) (cf. *[Codex Iuris Canonici](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28full%29)*). |
| *[Corpus Juris Civilis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corpus_Juris_Civilis)* | Body of Civil Law | The body of [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_law) or [civil law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_law_%28legal_system%29). |
| *corpus vile* | worthless body | A person or thing fit only to be the object of an experiment, as in the phrase 'Fiat experimentum in corpore vili.' |
| *corrigenda* | things to be corrected |  |
| *corruptio optimi pessima* | the corruption of the best is the worst |  |
| *corruptissima re publica plurimae leges* | When the republic is at its most corrupt the laws are most numerous | [Tacitus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacitus) |
| *corvus oculum corvi non eruit* | a raven does not pick out an eye of another raven |  |
| *corruptus in extremis* | corrupt to the extreme | Motto of the fictional [Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_Quimby)'s office in [The Simpsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons) |
| *cras amet qui nunquam amavit; quique amavit, cras amet* | May he who has never loved before, love tomorrow; And may he who has loved, love tomorrow as well | The refrain from the 'Pervigilium Veneris', a poem which describes a three-day holiday in the cult of Venus, located somewhere in Sicily, involving the whole town in religious festivities joined with a deep sense of nature and Venus as the "procreatrix", the life-giving force behind the natural world. |
| *cras es noster* | Tomorrow, be ours | As "The Future is Ours", motto of [San Jacinto College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jacinto_College), Texas |
| *creatio [ex nihilo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex_nihilo)* | creation out of nothing | A concept about creation, often used in a theological or philosophical context. Also known as the 'First Cause' argument in [philosophy of religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy_of_religion). Contrasted with *creatio ex materia.* |
| *Credo in Unum Deum* | I Believe in One God | The first words of the [Nicene Creed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicene_Creed) and the [Apostles' Creed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apostles'_Creed). |
| *credo quia absurdum est* | I believe it because it is absurd | A very common misquote of [Tertullian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertullian)'s *et mortuus est Dei Filius prorsus credibile quia ineptum est* (and the Son of God is dead: in short, it is credible because it is unfitting), meaning that it is so absurd to say that God's son has died that it would have to be a matter of belief, rather than reason. The misquoted phrase, however, is commonly used to mock the [dogmatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dogmatism) beliefs of the religious (see [fideism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fideism)). This phrase is commonly shortened to *credo quia absurdum*, and is also sometimes rendered *credo quia impossibile est* (I believe it because it is impossible) or, as [Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Darwin) used it in [his autobiography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Autobiography_of_Charles_Darwin), *credo quia incredibile*. |
| *credo ut intelligam* | I believe so that I may understand | A motto of St Anselm, used as the motto of [St. Anselm Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Anselm_Hall), Manchester |
| *crescamus in Illo per omnia* | May we grow in Him through all things | Motto of [Cheverus High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheverus_High_School) |
| *crescat scientia vita excolatur* | let knowledge grow, let life be enriched | Motto of the [University of Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chicago); often rendered in English as an [iambic tetrameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iambic_tetrameter), "Let knowledge grow from more to more, and so be human life enriched". |
| *crescente luce* | Light ever increasing | Motto of [James Cook University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook_University) |
| *[Crescite et multiplicamini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crescite_et_multiplicamini)* | Increase and multiply | Motto of [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland) until 1874 |
| *crescit cum commercio civitas* | Civilization prospers with commerce | Motto of [Claremont McKenna College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claremont_McKenna_College). |
| *crescit eundo* | it grows as it goes | From [Lucretius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucretius)' *[De rerum natura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_rerum_natura)* book VI, where it refers in context to the motion of a [thunderbolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightning) across the sky, which acquires power and momentum as it goes. This metaphor was adapted as the [state motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_and_territory_mottos) of [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico) (adopted in 1887 as the territory's motto, and kept in 1912 when New Mexico received statehood) and is seen on [the seal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_of_New_Mexico). Also the motto of [Rocky Mount, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mount,_Virginia) and [Omega Delta Phi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omega_Delta_Phi). |
| *cruci dum spiro fido* | while I live, I trust in the cross, Whilst I trust in the Cross I have life | Motto of the [Sisters of Loreto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisters_of_Loreto) (IBVM) and its associated schools. |
| *cucullus non facit monachum* | The hood does not make the monk | [William Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare), *[Twelfth Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelfth_Night)*, act 1, scene 5, 53-54[^7592] |
| *[cui bono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cui_bono)* | Good for whom? | "Who benefits?" An [adage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adage) in criminal investigation which suggests that considering who would benefit from an unwelcome event is likely to reveal who is responsible for that event (cf. *cui prodest*). Also the motto of the [Crime Syndicate of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_Syndicate_of_America), a fictional supervillain group. The opposite is *cui malo* (Bad for whom?). |
| *cui multum sit datum, multum ab eo postulabitur* | to whom much is given, much is expected | Motto of The [Brooklyn Latin School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Latin_School). Taken from the Gospel of Luke 12:48. |
| *cui prodest* | for whom it advances | Short for *cui prodest scelus is fecit* (for whom the crime advances, he has done it) in [Seneca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger)'s *Medea*. Thus, the murderer is often the one who gains by the murder (cf. *cui bono*). |
| [*cuique suum*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suum_cuique) | to each his own |  |
| *[cuius est solum, eius est usque ad coelum et ad inferos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuius_est_solum,_eius_est_usque_ad_coelum_et_ad_inferos)* | Whose the land is, all the way to the sky and to the [underworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underworld) is his. | First coined by Accursius of Bologna in the 13th century. A [Roman legal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_law) principle of [property law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property_law) that is no longer observed in most situations today. Less literally, "For whosoever owns the soil, it is theirs up to the sky and down to the depths." |
| *[cuius regio, eius religio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuius_regio,_eius_religio)* | whose region, his religion | The privilege of a ruler to choose the religion of his subjects. A regional prince's ability to choose his people's religion was established at the [Peace of Augsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_Augsburg) in 1555. |
| *cuiusvis hominis est errare, nullius nisi insipientis in errore perseverare.* | Anyone can err, but only the fool persists in his fault | [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero), [Philippica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippicae) [XII, 5](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/la:In%20M.%20Antonium%20Oratio%20-%20Philippica%20XII#%5B5%5D). |
| *culpa* | fault | Also "blame" or "[guilt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guilt_%28emotion%29)". In law, an act of neglect. In general, guilt, sin, or a fault. See also *[mea culpa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mea_culpa)*. |
| *Cum Deo pro Patria et Libertate* | With God for Fatherland and Liberty | Appears on [Francis II Rákóczi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_II_R%C3%A1k%C3%B3czi)'s flag |
| *cum fontibus* | with sources | e.g., *[Woltjer, Jan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Woltjer_%28classical_scholar%29) (1877). *Lucretii philosophia cum fontibus comparata* \[*[Lucretius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucretius)'s philosophy, compared with its sources*\] (Thesis). Groningen: Noordhoff Uitgevers.* |
| *cum gladiis et fustibus* | with swords and clubs | From the Bible. Occurs in [Matthew 26:47](https://bible.oremus.org/?passage=Matthew%2026:47&version=nrsv) and [Luke 22:52](https://bible.oremus.org/?passage=Luke%2022:52&version=nrsv). |
| *cum gladio et sale* | with sword and salt | Motto of a well-paid soldier. See [salary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salary). |
| *cum grano salis* | with a [grain of salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grain_of_salt) | Not to be taken too seriously or as the literal truth. |
| *[cum hoc ergo propter hoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cum_hoc_ergo_propter_hoc)* | with this, therefore on account of this | Fallacy of assuming that [correlation implies causation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation_does_not_imply_causation). |
| *cum laude* | with praise | The standard formula for academic [Latin honors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_honors) in the United States. Greater honors include *magna cum laude* and *summa cum laude*. |
| *cum mortuis in lingua mortua* | with the dead in a dead language | Movement from *[Pictures at an Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pictures_at_an_Exhibition)* by [Modest Mussorgsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modest_Mussorgsky) |
| *cum privilegio ad imprimendum solum* | with the exclusive right to print | [Copyright notice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_notice) used in 16th-century England, used for comic effect in *[The Taming of the Shrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Taming_of_the_Shrew)* by William Shakespeare[^7593] where Lucentio is urged by his servant Biondello to "seize your privilege to declare her \[ [Bianca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bianca_Minola)\] yours alone". |
| *[cum tempore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cum_tempore)* (c.t.) | with time | academic custom to start lectures 15 minutes later than advertised; *sine tempore* (s.t.) indicates lectures start on time. |
| *cuncti adsint meritaeque expectent praemia palmae* | let all come who by merit deserve the most reward | Motto of [University College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_London). |
| *[cupio dissolvi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupio_dissolvi)* | desire to be dissolved | From the Bible, locution indicating a will to death ("I want to die"). |
| *cur Deus Homo* | Why the God-Man | The question attributed to Anselm in his work of by this name, wherein he reflects on why the Christ of Christianity must be both fully Divine and fully Human. Often translated "why did God become Man?" |
| *[cura personalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cura_personalis)* | care for the whole person | Motto of [Georgetown University School of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_University_School_of_Medicine) and [University of Scranton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Scranton) |
| *[cura te ipsum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cura_te_ipsum)* | take care of your own self | Exhortation to [physicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physician), or experts in general, to deal with their own problems before addressing those of others |
| *[curriculum vitae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curriculum_vitae)* | course of life | An overview of a person's life and qualifications, similar to a [résumé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C3%A9sum%C3%A9) |
| *custodi civitatem, Domine* | guard the city, O Lord | Motto of the [City of Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_Westminster) |
| *custos morum* | keeper of morals | A [censor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship) |
| *cygnis insignis* | distinguished by its swans | [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_mottos) of [Western Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Australia) |
| *cygnus inter anates* | swan among ducks |  |

#### D

| Latin | Translation | Notes |
|----|----|----|
| *da Deus fortunae* | O God, give fortune/happiness | A traditional greeting of [Czech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic) [brewers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brewing). |
| *[da mihi factum, dabo tibi ius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Da_mihi_factum,_dabo_tibi_ius)* | Give me the fact, I will give you the law | Also *da mihi facta, dabo tibi ius* (plural "facta" (facts) for the singular "factum"). A legal principle of [Roman law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_law) that parties to a suit should present the facts and the judge will rule on the law that governs them. Related to *[iura novit curia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iura_novit_curia)* (the court knows the law). |
| *damnant quod non intellegunt* | They condemn what they do not understand | Paraphrase of [Quintilianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintilian), *De Institutione Oratoria*, Book 10, chapter 1, 26: "Modesto tamen et circumspecto iudicio de tantis viris pronuntiandum est, ne, quod plerisque accidit, *damnent quae non intellegunt*." \[Yet students must pronounce with diffidence and circumspection on the merits of such illustrious characters, lest, as is the case with many, *they condemn what they do not understand*. (translated by Rev. John Selby Watson) |
| *[damnatio ad bestias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damnatio_ad_bestias)* | condemnation to \[the\] beasts | Colloquially, "thrown to the lions". |
| *[damnatio memoriae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damnatio_memoriae)* | damnation of memory | The ancient Roman custom by which it was pretended that disgraced Romans, especially former emperors, never existed, by eliminating all records and likenesses of them. |
| *damnum absque injuria* | damage without injury | Meaning a loss that results from no one's wrongdoing. In [Roman law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_law), a person is not responsible for unintended, consequential injury to another that results from a lawful act. This protection does not necessarily apply to unintended damage caused by one's negligence or folly. |
| *[damnum fatale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_of_God)* | damage through fate | A loss arising from an inevitable accident where individual persons cannot be held legally liable for damages. |
| *dat deus incrementum*, or, *deus dat incrementum* | God gives growth | Motto of several schools. |
| *data venia* | with due respect / given the excuse | Used before disagreeing with someone. |
| *datum perficiemus munus* | We shall accomplish the mission assigned | Motto of [Batalhão de Operações Policiais Especiais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batalh%C3%A3o_de_Opera%C3%A7%C3%B5es_Policiais_Especiais) (BOPE), [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil). |
| *de bene esse* | as well done | In law, a *de bene esse* deposition is used to preserve the testimony of a witness who is expected not to be available to appear at trial and be cross-examined. |
| *de bonis asportatis* | carrying goods away | In law, trespass *de bonis asportatis* was the traditional name for [larceny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larceny), i.e., the unlawful theft of [chattels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_property) (moveable goods). |
| *de dato* | of the date | Used, e.g., in "as we agreed in the meeting d.d. 26th May 2006". |
| *[de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto)* | by deed | Said of something that is the actual [state of affairs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_affairs_%28sociology%29), in contrast to something's legal or official standing, which is described as *de jure*. *De facto* refers to "the way things really are" rather than what is officially presented as the fact of the matter in question. |
| *de fideli* | with faithfulness | A clerk of a court makes this declaration when he is appointed, by which he promises to perform his duties faithfully as a servant of the court. |
| *de fideli administratione* | of faithful administration | Describes an oath taken to faithfully administer the duties of a job or office, like that taken by a court reporter.[^7594] |
| *de futuro* | regarding the future | Usually used in the context of "at a future time". |
| *[de gustibus non est disputandum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_gustibus_non_est_disputandum)* | Of tastes there is nothing to be disputed | Less literally, "there is no accounting for taste", because they are judged subjectively and not objectively: everyone has their own and none deserve preeminence. The complete phrase is "de gustibus et coloribus non est disputandum" ("when we talk about tastes and colours there is nothing to be disputed"). Probably of [Scholastic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholasticism) origin; see [Wiktionary](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/de%20gustibus%20non%20est%20disputandum). |
| *de integro* | again, a second time |  |
| *[de jure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_jure)* | by law | "Official", in contrast with *de facto*; analogous to "in principle", whereas *de facto* is to "in practice". In other contexts, it can mean "according to law", "by right", and "legally". |
| *de lege ferenda* | of/from law to be passed |  |
| *de lege lata* | of/from law passed / of/from law in force |  |
| *de medietate linguae* | of half-tongue | from \[a person's\] language \[group\]; party jury; the right to a jury disproportionally chosen from the accused's ethnic group;[^7595] see [struck jury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Struck_jury). |
| *[de minimis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_minimis) non curat lex* | The law does not care about the smallest things. | A court does not care about small, trivial things. A case must have some importance in order for a court to hear it. See "de minimis non curat praetor". Also used as an adjective: "The court found that the alleged conduct was *de minimis*." |
| *de minimis non curat praetor* | The commander does not care about the smallest things. | Also, "The [chief magistrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_magistrate) does not concern himself with trifles." Trivial matters are no concern of a high official; cf. *aquila non capit muscas* (the eagle does not catch flies). Sometimes *rex* (king) or *lex* (law) is used in place of *[praetor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praetor)*. |
| *de mortuis aut bene aut nihil* | about the dead, either well or nothing | Less literally, "speak well of the dead or not at all"; cf. *de mortuis nil nisi bonum*. |
| *[de mortuis nil nisi bonum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_mortuis_nil_nisi_bonum)* | about the dead, nothing unless a good thing | From *de mortuis nil nisi bonum dicendum est* ("nothing must be said about the dead except the good"), attributed by [Diogenes Laërtius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogenes_La%C3%ABrtius) to [Chilon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chilon_of_Sparta). In legal contexts, this quotation is used with the opposite meaning: defamation of a deceased person is not a crime. In other contexts, it refers to [taboos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taboo) against criticizing the recently deceased. |
| *de nobis fabula narratur* | About us is the story told | Thus: "their story is our story". Originally it referred to the end of Rome's dominance. Now often used when comparing any current situation to a past story or event. |
| *[de novo](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/de%20novo)* | from the new | "Anew" or "afresh". In law, a [trial *de novo*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_de_novo) is a retrial of the issues as though they had not been tried before. In biology, *de novo* means [newly synthesized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_novo_synthesis), and a [*de novo* mutation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_novo_mutation) is a mutation that neither parent possessed or transmitted. In economics, *de novo* refers to newly founded companies, and *de novo* banks are [state banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_bank_%28United_States%29) that have been in operation for five years or less. (Cf. *[ex novo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex_novo)*) |
| *de omni re scibili et quibusdam aliis* | about every knowable thing, and even certain other things | The Italian scholar [Giovanni Pico della Mirandola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Pico_della_Mirandola) of the 15th century wrote the *De omni re scibili* ("concerning every knowable thing") part, and a wag added *et quibusdam aliis* ("and even certain other things"). |
| *de omnibus dubitandum* | Be suspicious of everything / doubt everything | Attributed to the French philosopher [René Descartes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Descartes). It was also [Karl Marx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Marx)'s favorite motto and a title of one of [Søren Kierkegaard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%B8ren_Kierkegaard)'s works, *[De omnibus dubitandum est](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_omnibus_dubitandum_est)*. |
| *[de oppresso liber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_oppresso_liber)* | free from having been oppressed | Loosely, "to liberate the oppressed". Motto of the [United States Army Special Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Special_Forces).[^7596] |
| *de praescientia Dei* | from/through the foreknowledge of God | Motto of the [Worshipful Company of Barbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worshipful_Company_of_Barbers). |
| *[de profundis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Profundis_%28disambiguation%29)* | from the depths | Meaning from out of the depths of misery or dejection. From the Latin translation of the [Vulgate Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate) of [Psalm 130](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_130), of which it is a traditional title in Roman [Catholic liturgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_liturgy). |
| *[de re](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_re)* | about/regarding the matter | In logic, *[de dicto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_dicto)* statements regarding the truth of a proposition are distinguished from *de re* statements regarding the properties of a thing itself. |
| *decessit sine prole* | died without issue | Used in genealogical records, often abbreviated as *d.s.p.*, to indicate a person who died without having had any children. |
| *decessit sine prole legitima* | died without legitimate issue | Used in genealogical records, often abbreviated as *d.s.p.l.*, to indicate a person who died without having had any children with a spouse. |
| *decessit sine prole mascula legitima* | died without legitimate male issue | Used in genealogical records in cases of nobility or other hereditary titles, often abbreviated as *d.s.p.m.l.* or *d.s.p.m. legit*, to indicate a person who died without having had any legitimate male children (indicating there were illegitimate male children) |
| *decessit sine prole mascula superstite* | died without surviving male issue | Used in genealogical records, often abbreviated as *d.s.p.m.*, to indicate a person who died without having had any male children who survived, i.e. outlived him. |
| *decessit sine prole superstite* | died without surviving issue | Used in genealogical records, often abbreviated as *d.s.p.s.*, to indicate a person who died without having had any children who survived, i.e. outlived him. |
| *decessit vita matris* | died in the lifetime of the mother | Used in genealogical records, often abbreviated as *d.v.m.*, to indicate a person who predeceased his or her mother. |
| *decessit vita patris* | died in the lifetime of the father | Used in genealogical records, often abbreviated as *d.v.p.*, to indicate a person who predeceased his or her father. |
| *decus et tutamen* | an ornament and a safeguard | A phrase from [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil)'s *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)*. Inscription on British [one pound coins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_pound_coin). Originally inscribed on coins of the 17th century, it refers to the inscribed edge of the coin as a protection against the [clipping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coin_clipping) of its precious metal. |
| *defendit numerus* | There is safety in numbers |  |
| *Defensor Fortis* | Defender of the Force | Official motto of the [United States Air Force Security Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force_Security_Forces) (Security Police). |
| *[Dei gratia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dei_gratia)* | By the grace of God | Part of the full style of a monarch historically considered to be ruling by [divine right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_right_of_kings), notably in the style of the English and British monarch since 1521 |
| *[Dei gratia rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dei_gratia_rex)* | By the Grace of God, King | Also *[Dei gratia regina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dei_gratia_regina)* ("By the Grace of God, Queen"). Abbreviated as D G REX on [British](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coins_of_the_pound_sterling) and [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coins_of_the_Canadian_dollar) coins. Also occurs on coins of the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire) such as the [Otto Adelheid Pfennig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Adelheid_Pfennig). |
| *Dei sub numine viget* | Under God's Spirit she flourishes | Motto of [Princeton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University), [Princeton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton,_New_Jersey), [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey), United States. |
| *delectatio morosa* | peevish delight | In Catholic theology, pleasure taken in a sinful thought or imagination, such as brooding on sexual images. As voluntary and complacent erotic fantasizing, without attempt to suppress such thoughts, it is distinct from actual sexual desire. |
| *[delegata potestas non potest delegari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delegata_potestas_non_potest_delegari)* | Delegated powers can not be \[further\] delegated | A legal principle whereby one to whom certain powers were delegated may not ipso facto re-delegate them to another. A distinction may be had between delegated powers and the additional power to re-delegate them. |
| *delirant isti Romani* | They are mad, those Romans\[!\] | A Latin translation of [René Goscinny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Goscinny)'s phrase in French ils sont fous, ces romains! or Italian Sono pazzi questi Romani. Cf. [SPQR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SPQR), which [Obelix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obelix) frequently used in the *[Asterix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asterix)* comics. |
| *Deo ac veritati* | for God and for truth | Motto of [Colgate University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colgate_University). |
| *Deo confidimus* | In God we trust | Motto of [Somerset College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_College). |
| *Deo Dante Dedi* | God having given I gave | Motto of [Charterhouse School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charterhouse_School). |
| *Deo domuique* | For God and for home | Motto of [Methodist Ladies' College, Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist_Ladies'_College,_Melbourne). |
| *Deo et patriae* | For God and country | Motto of [Regis High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regis_High_School_%28New_York_City%29) in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_%28state%29), United States. |
| *[Deo gratias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deo_gratias)* | Thanks \[be\] to God | A frequent phrase in the Roman [Catholic liturgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_liturgy), used especially after the recitation of a lesson, the [Last Gospel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Gospel) at [Mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Mass) or as a response to [Ite, missa est](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ite,_missa_est) / [Benedicamus Domino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedicamus_Domino). |
| *Deo juvante* | with God's help | Motto of [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco) and its [monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monarch), which is inscribed on the [royal arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_Monaco). |
| *Deo non fortuna* | by God, not fortune/luck | Motto of the [Epsom College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epsom_College) in [Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrey), England and Fairham Freemasons Lodge No.8002 in the province of Nottinghamshire. |
| *Deo optimo maximo (DOM)* | To the best and greatest God | Derived from the pagan *Iupiter optimo maximo* ("to the best and greatest [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_%28god%29)"). Printed on bottles of [Bénédictine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9n%C3%A9dictine) liqueur. |
| *Deo patriae litteris* | For God, country, \[and\] learning | motto of [Scotch College, Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotch_College,_Melbourne) |
| *Deo regi vicino* | For God, king and neighbour | motto of [Bromsgrove School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bromsgrove_School) |
| *Deo vindice* | with God as protector / with an avenging God | motto of the defunct [Confederate States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America) |
| *Deo volente* | God willing | This was often used in conjunction with a signature at the end of letters. It was used in order to signify that "God willing" this letter will get to you safely, "God willing" the contents of this letter come true. As an abbreviation (simply "D.V.") it is often found in personal letters (in English) of the early 1900s, employed to generally and piously qualify a given statement about a future planned action, that it will be carried out, so long as God wills it (see [James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistle_of_James) [4:13-15](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bible%20%28Wikisource%29/James#4:13), which encourages this way of speaking); cf. [inshallah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inshallah). Motto of [Southern Illinois University Carbondale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Illinois_University_Carbondale). |
| *descensus in cuniculi cavum* | The descent into the cave of the rabbit | Down the rabbit hole; backtranslation, not a genuine Latin phrase; see [Down the rabbit hole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_the_rabbit_hole). |
| *desiderantes meliorem patriam* | they desired a better land | From [Hebrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistle_to_the_Hebrews) 11:16; the motto of the [Order of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Canada). |
| *Deus adiuta Romanis* | God help the Romans | An inscription minted on Eastern Roman [hexagrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hexagram_%28currency%29) during the [Byzantine-Sasanian War of 602-628](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine%E2%80%93Sasanian_War_of_602%E2%80%93628).[^7597] |
| *[Deus caritas est](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deus_caritas_est)* | God Is Love | Title and first words of the first encyclical of [Pope Benedict XVI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Benedict_XVI). For other meanings see [Deus caritas est (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deus_caritas_est_%28disambiguation%29). |
| *[deus ex machina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deus_ex_machina)* | a god from a machine | From the [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language) ἀπὸ μηχανῆς θεός (*apò mēchanēs theós*). A contrived or artificial solution, usually to a literary plot. Refers to the practice in Greek drama of lowering by crane (the *mechanê*) an actor playing a god or goddess onto the stage to resolve an insuperable conflict in the plot. The device is most commonly associated with [Euripides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euripides). |
| *Deus lux mea est* | God is my light | The motto of [The Catholic University of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Catholic_University_of_America). |
| *Deus meumque jus* | God and my right | The principal motto of [Scottish Rite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Rite) [Freemasonry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freemasonry). See also *[Dieu et mon droit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dieu_et_mon_droit)*. |
| *Deus nobis haec otia fecit* | God has given us these days of leisure | Motto of the city of [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool), England. |
| *Deus nobiscum* | God with us | Motto of [Methodist College Belfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methodist_College_Belfast) |
| *Deus nolens exitus* | Get results, whether God likes it or not | Literally: Results, God unwilling. A modern creation with questionable grammar; used in [James Islington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Islington)'s *[The Will of the Many](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Will_of_the_Many)* (2023) from his *Hierarchy* series; title of an episode of the podcast *The Sheridan Tapes*. |
| *[Deus otiosus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deus_otiosus)* | God at leisure |  |
| *Deus spes nostra* | God is our hope | The motto of Sir Thomas de Boteler, founder of Boteler Grammar School in [Warrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington) in 1526. |
| *[Deus vult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deus_vult)* | God wills it | The principal slogan of the [Crusades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades). Motto of Bergen Catholic High School in [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey), United States. |
| *Dicebamus hesterna die...* | \[As\] we were saying yesterday... | Attributed to Fray [Luis de León](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_de_Le%C3%B3n), the beginning of his first lecture after resuming his professorship at [Salamanca University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salamanca_University) following four years of imprisonment by the Inquisition |
| *dictatum erat (dict)* | as previously stated | A recent academic substitution for the spacious and inconvenient phrase "as previously stated". Literally, *has been stated*. Compare also "dicta prius"; literally, *said previously*. |
| *[dicto simpliciter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dicto_simpliciter)* | \[from\] a maxim, simply | I.e. "from a rule without exception." Short for *a dicto simpliciter*, the *a* is often dropped because it is confused with the English indefinite article. A *dicto simpliciter* occurs when an acceptable exception is ignored or eliminated. For example, the appropriateness of using opiates is contingent on suffering extreme pain. To justify the recreational use of opiates by referring to a cancer patient or to justify arresting said patient by comparing him to the recreational user would be a *dicto simpliciter*. |
| *dictum factum* | what is said is done | Motto of [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy) Fighter Squadron VF-194. |
| *dictum meum pactum* | my word \[is\] my bond | Motto of the [London Stock Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Stock_Exchange). |
| *diem perdidi* | I have lost the day | From the [Roman Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Emperor) [Titus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titus). Recorded in the biography of him by [Suetonius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suetonius) in *[Lives of the Twelve Caesars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lives_of_the_Twelve_Caesars)*. |
| *[dies irae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dies_irae)* | Day of wrath | Reference to the [Judgment Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Judgment) in [Christian eschatology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_eschatology). The title of a famous Medieval Latin hymn by [Tommaso da Celano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommaso_da_Celano) in the 13th century and used in the Requiem [Mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_%28liturgy%29). |
| *[dies non](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle_of_no-work-no-pay_%28dies_non%29) juridicum* | Day without [judiciary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judiciary) | Days under [common law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_law) (traditionally Sunday), during which no legal process can be served and any legal judgment is invalid. The [English Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_England) first codified this precept in the reign of [King Charles II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_II_of_England). |
| *dies tenebrosa sicut nox* | a day as dark as night | First entry in *[Annales Cambriae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annales_Cambriae)*, for the year 447.[^7598] |
| *dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet* | He has half the deed done, who has made a beginning.[^7599] | From the second letter by [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace) in his *[First Book of Letters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistles_%28Horace%29)*: *Dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet; [sapere aude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapere_aude), incipe.* \[... dare to know, begin\].[^7600] |
| *[dirigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirigo)* | I direct | In [Classical Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_Latin), "I arrange". [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_mottos) of the [State of Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine), United States; based on a comparison of the State to the star [Polaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polaris). |
| *dis aliter visum* | It seemed otherwise to the gods | In other words, the gods have ideas different from those of mortals, and so events do not always occur in the way persons wish them to. Cf. [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil), *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)*, 2: 428. Also cf. "Man proposes and God disposes" and "My Thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways", Isaiah 55, 8-9. |
| *dis manibus sacrum (D.M.S.)* | Sacred to the ghost-gods | Refers to the [Manes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manes), i.e. Roman spirits of the dead. Loosely, "to the memory of". A conventional pagan inscription preceding the name of the deceased on their tombstone; often shortened to *dis manibus* (D.M.), "for the ghost-gods". Preceded in some earlier monuments by *hic situs est* (H. S. E.), "he lies here". |
| *[disce aut discede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disce_aut_discede)* | learn or depart / learn or leave | Motto of [Royal College, Colombo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_College,_Colombo) and of [King's School, Rochester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_School,_Rochester). |
| *disce ut semper victurus, vive ut cras moriturus* | Learn as if \[you will\] live forever; live as if \[you will\] die tomorrow. | Attributed to [St. Edmund of Abingdon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Edmund_of_Abingdon); first seen in [Isidoro de Sevilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidoro_de_Sevilla) |
| *discendo discimus* | while learning we learn | See also *[§ docendo discitur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28full%29)* |
| *discere faciendo* | learn by doing | Motto of the three [California Polytechnic State Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Polytechnic_State_University) of [San Luis Obispo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Polytechnic_State_University,_San_Luis_Obispo), [Pomona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Polytechnic_University,_Pomona), and [Humboldt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Polytechnic_University,_Humboldt), United States. |
| *[disiecta membra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disiecta_membra)* | scattered limbs | I.e., "scattered remains". Paraphrased from [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), [*Satires*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satires_%28Horace%29), 1, 4, 62, where it is written "*disiecti membra poetae*" (limbs of a scattered poet). |
| *[ditat Deus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ditat_Deus)* | God enriches | [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_and_territory_mottos) of the [State of Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona), United States, adopted in 1911. Probably derived from the translation of the [Vulgate Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate) of [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Genesis) 14: 23. |
| *divide et impera* | [divide and rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divide_and_rule) / "divide and conquer" | A [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire) maxim adopted by [Roman Dictator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Dictator) [Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar), [King Louis XI of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XI_of_France) and the Italian political author [Niccolò Machiavelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niccol%C3%B2_Machiavelli). |
| *dixi* | I have spoken | A popular, [eloquent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eloquence) expression, usually used in the end of a speech. The implied meaning is that the speaker has said all that had to be said and thus the argument is completed. |
| *\["...", ...\] dixit* | \["...", ...\] said | Used to attribute a statement or opinion to its author, rather than the speaker. |
| *[do ut des](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_ancient_Roman_religion)* | I give that you may give | Often said or written of sacrifices, in which one "gives" and expects a return from the gods. |
| *docendo discitur* | It is learned by teaching / one learns by teaching | Attributed to [Seneca the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger). |
| *docendo disco, scribendo cogito* | I learn by teaching, I think by writing |  |
| *doli capax* | capable of guilt | person's ability to commit a wrongful act with the knowledge that it is wrong; cf. *[doli incapax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doli_incapax)*. |
| *dolus specialis* | special intent | "The ... concept is particular to a few civil law systems and cannot sweepingly be equated with the notions of 'special' or 'specific intent' in common law systems. (Genocide scholar [William A. Schabas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Schabas))[^7601] |
| *Domine dirige nos* | O Lord, guide us | Motto of the [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London), England. |
| *Domine salvum fac Regem* | O Lord, save the king | Psalm 20, 10. |
| *Domine salvam fac Reginam* | O Lord, save the queen | After Psalm 20, 10. |
| *Dominica in albis \[depositis\]* | Sunday in \[Setting Aside the\] White Garments | Latin name of the [Octave of Easter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave_of_Easter) in the Roman [Catholic liturgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_liturgy). |
| *[Dominium maris baltici](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominium_maris_baltici)* | Dominion over the Baltic Sea | The territorial aim of the Danish and Swedish kingdoms during the Late Medieval and Early Modern Period to rule over the Baltic Sea |
| *Dominus fortitudo nostra* | The Lord is our strength | Motto of the [Southland College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southland_College), [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines). Psalm 28, 8. |

After Psalm 23, 1. |

| *ergo* | therefore | Denotes a logical conclusion . |

| *errare humanum est* | to err is human | Sometimes attributed to [Seneca the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger), but not attested: *Errare humanum est, perseverare autem diabolicum, et tertia non datur* (To err is human; to persist \[in committing such errors\] is of the devil, and the third possibility is not given.) Several authors contemplated the idea before Seneca: [Livy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livy), *Venia dignus error is humanus* (*Storie*, VIII, 35) and [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero): *is Cuiusvis errare: insipientis nullius nisi, in errore perseverare* (Anyone can err, but only the fool persists in his fault) (*[Philippicae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippicae)*, XII, 2, 5). Cicero, being well-versed in ancient Greek, may well have been alluding to [Euripides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euripides)' play *Hippolytus* some four centuries earlier.[^7608] 300 years later [Saint Augustine of Hippo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Hippo) recycled the idea in his *Sermones*, 164, 14: *Humanum fuit errare, diabolicum est per animositatem in errore manere.*[^7609] The phrase gained currency in the English language after [Alexander Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Pope)'s *[An Essay on Criticism](https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/An%20Essay%20on%20Criticism)* of 1711: "To err is human, to forgive divine" (line 325). |
| *[erratum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erratum)* | error | I.e., mistake. Lists of errors in a previous edition of a work are often marked with the plural *errata* ("errors"). |

| *esse est percipi* | to be is to be perceived | Motto of [George Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Berkeley) for his [subjective idealist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subjective_idealism) philosophical position that nothing exists independently of its perception by a mind except minds themselves. |
| *[esse quam videri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esse_quam_videri)* | to be, rather than to seem | Truly being a thing, rather than merely seeming to be a thing. The motto of many institutions. Prior to Cicero, [Sallust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sallust) used the phrase in *Bellum Catilinae*, 54, 6, writing that [Cato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cato_the_Elder) *esse quam videri bonus malebat* ("preferred to be good, rather than to seem so"). Earlier still, [Aeschylus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeschylus) used a similar phrase in *[Seven Against Thebes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Against_Thebes)*, line 592: *ou gar dokein aristos, all' enai thelei* ("he wishes not to seem the best, but to be the best"). Motto of the State of North Carolina. |
| *est modus in rebus* | there is measure in things | there is a middle or mean in things, there is a middle way or position; from [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), *[Satires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satires_%28Horace%29)* [1.1.106](https://la.wikipedia.org/wiki/s:Sermones%20%28Horatius%29/Liber%20prior/Sermo%20I%20-%20Qui%20fit,%20Maecenas,%20ut%20nemo,%20quam%20sibi%20sortem#105); see also: [Golden mean (philosophy)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_mean_%28philosophy%29). According to Potempski and Galmarini (*Atmos. Chem. Phys.*, 9, 9471-9489, 2009) the sentence should be translated as: "There is an optimal condition in all things", which in the original text is followed by *sunt certi denique fines quos ultra citraque nequit consistere rectum* ("There are therefore precise boundaries beyond which one cannot find the right thing"). |

[Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_and_territory_mottos) of the U.S. state of [Idaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idaho), adopted in 1867; of [S. Thomas' College, Mount Lavinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S._Thomas'_College,_Mount_Lavinia), Sri Lanka; of [Sigma Phi Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigma_Phi_Society); of Main Street Hall, a dormitory at [Phillips Exeter Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillips_Exeter_Academy). |
| *esto quod es* | be what you are | Motto of [Wells Cathedral School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wells_Cathedral_School) |
| *et adhuc sub iudice lis est* | it is still before the court | From [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), *[Ars Poetica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ars_Poetica_%28Horace%29)* (*The Art of Poetry*) [1.78.](https://la.wikipedia.org/wiki/s:Ars%20poetica) |
| *et alibi (et al.)* | and elsewhere | A less common variant on *et cetera* ("and the rest") used at the end of a list of locations to denote unenumerated/omitted ones. |
| *[et alii](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/et%20alii), [et aliae](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/et%20aliae), [et alia](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/et%20alia) (et al.)* | and others | Used similarly to *et cetera* ("and the rest") to denote names that, usually for the sake of space, are unenumerated/omitted. *Alii* is [masculine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammatical_gender), and therefore it can be used to refer to men, or groups of men and women; the feminine *et aliae* is proper when the "others" are all female, but as with many [loanwords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loanword), interlingual use, such as in reference lists, is often invariable. *Et alia* is neuter plural and thus in Latin text is properly used only for inanimate, genderless objects, but some use it as a gender-neutral alternative.[^7610] [APA style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/APA_style) and [MLA style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_MLA_Style_Manual) uses et al. if the work cited was written by more than three authors; [AMA style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMA_style) lists all authors if ≤6, and 3 + et al. if \>6. AMA style forgoes the period (because it forgoes the period on abbreviations generally) and it forgoes the italic (as it does with other loanwords naturalized into scientific English); many journals that follow AMA style do likewise. |
| *[et cetera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Et_cetera) (etc., &c.)* | and the rest | In modern usage, used to mean "and so on" or "and more". |
| *et cum spiritu tuo* | and with your spirit | The usual response to the phrase *[Dominus vobiscum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominus_vobiscum)* used in Roman [Catholic liturgy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_liturgy), for instance at several points during the [Catholic Mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Mass).[^7611] Also used as a general form of greeting among and towards members of Catholic organisations. |
| *[et facere et pati fortia Romanum est](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Et_facere_et_pati_fortia_Romanum_est)* | Acting and suffering bravely is the attribute of a Roman | The words of [Gaius Mucius Scaevola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Mucius_Scaevola) when [Lars Porsena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lars_Porsena) captured him |
| *et facta est lux* | And light came to be *or* was made | From *[Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Genesis)*, 1:3: "and there was light". | *extra omnes* | outside, all \[of you\] | It is issued by the [Master of the Papal Liturgical Celebrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_for_the_Liturgical_Celebrations_of_the_Supreme_Pontiff) before a session of the [papal conclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_conclave) which will elect a new [pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope). When spoken, all those who are not [cardinals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardinal_%28Catholicism%29), or those otherwise mandated to be present at the conclave, must leave the [Sistine Chapel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistine_Chapel). |
| *extra territorium jus dicenti impune non paretur* | he who administers justice outside of his territory is disobeyed with impunity | Refers to [extraterritorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraterritorial) jurisdiction. | *extrema ratio* | extreme solution | last possibility, last possible course of action |
