Part of a much larger phrase: *Monasterium sine libris, est sicut civitas sine opibus, castrum sine numeris, coquina sine suppellectili, mensa sine cibis, hortus sine herbis, pratum sine floribus, arbor sine foliis*. Translation: A monastery without books is like a city without wealth, a fortress without soldiers, a kitchen without utensils, a table without food, a garden without plants, a meadow without flowers, a tree without leaves. |
| *montani semper liberi* | mountaineers \[are\] always free | [State motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_mottos) of [West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Virginia), adopted in 1872; part of the coat of arms for the Colombian city of [Bucaramanga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucaramanga). |
| *Montis Insignia Calpe* | Badge of the Mons Calpe (Rock of [Gibraltar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gibraltar)) | A self-referential literal identifier below the emblem |
| *morbus virgineus* | Disease of the virgins or Virgin's disease | [Hypochromic anemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypochromic_anemia), an iron deficiency anemia common in young women[^7662] |
| *more ferarum* | like beasts | used to describe any sexual act in the manner of beasts |
| *more suo* | in his/her/its/their usual way |  |
| *morior invictus* | I die unvanquished[^7663] | sometimes also translated as "death before defeat"[^7663] |
| *morituri nolumus mori* | we who are about to die don't want to | From Terry Pratchett's 2001 novel *[The Last Hero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Hero_%28Pratchett_novel%29)*, a parody on *morituri te salutant/salutamus* |
| *morituri te salutant* | those who are about to die salute you | Used once in [Suetonius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suetonius)' *[De Vita Caesarum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twelve_Caesars)* 5, (*Divus [Claudius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudius)*), chapter 21,[^7664] by the condemned prisoners manning galleys about to take part in a mock naval battle on [Lake Fucinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fucine_Lake) in AD 52. Popular misconception ascribes it as a gladiator's salute. See also: [Ave Imperator, morituri te salutant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ave_Imperator,_morituri_te_salutant) and [Naumachia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naumachia). |
| *mors certa, hora incerta* | death is certain, its hour is uncertain |  |
| *mors mihi lucrum* | death to me is reward | A common epitaph, from St Paul's [Epistle to the Philippians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistle_to_the_Philippians), 1:21 (*Mihi enim vivere Christus est et mori lucrum*, translated in the [King James Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_James_Bible) as: "For to me to live is Christ and to die is gain") |
| *mors omnibus* | death to all | Signifies anger and depression. |
| *mors tua vita mea* | your death, my life | From medieval Latin, it indicates that battle for survival, where your defeat is necessary for my victory, survival. |
| *mors vincit omnia* | "death conquers all" or "death always wins" | An axiom often found on headstones; cf. *[amor vincit omnia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28A%29)* |
| *morte magis metuenda senectus* | old age should rather be feared than death | from [Juvenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenal) in his *[Satires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satires_%28Juvenal%29)* |
| *mortui vivos docent* | The dead teach the living | Used to justify dissections of human cadavers in order to understand the cause of death. |
| *mortuum flagellas* | you are flogging a dead (man) | From Gerhard Gerhards' (1466-1536) \[better known as Erasmus\] collection of annotated Adagia (1508). Criticising one who will not be affected in any way by the criticism. |
| *[mos maiorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mos_maiorum)* | the custom of our ancestors | an unwritten code of laws and conduct, of the Romans. It institutionalized cultural traditions, societal mores, and general policies, as distinct from written laws. |
| *[motu proprio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motu_proprio)* | on his own initiative | Or "by his own accord." Identifies a class of papal documents, administrative papal bulls. |
| *mulgere hircum* | to milk a male goat | From Gerhard Gerhards' (1466-1536) \[better known as Erasmus\] collection of annotated Adagia (1508). Attempting the impossible. |
| *mulier est hominis confusio* | woman is man's ruin | "Part of a comic definition of woman" from the Altercatio Hadriani Augusti et Secundi.[^7665] Famously quoted by [Chauntecleer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nun's_Priest's_Tale) in [Geoffrey Chaucer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Chaucer)'s *[Canterbury Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_Tales)*. |
| *multa paucis* | Say much in few words |  |
| *multis e gentibus vires* | from many peoples, strength | [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_mottos) of [Saskatchewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saskatchewan) |
| *multitudo sapientium sanitas orbis* | a multitude of the wise is the health of the world | From the Vulgate, Wisdom of Solomon 6:24. [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mottos) of the [University of Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Victoria). |
| *multum in parvo* | much in little | Conciseness. The term "[mipmap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mipmap)" is formed using the phrase's abbreviation "MIP"; motto of [Rutland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutland), a county in central England. Latin phrases are often *multum in parvo*, conveying much in few words. |
| *mundus senescit* | the world grows old |  |
| *mundus vult decipi* | the world wants to be deceived | Ascribed to Roman satirist [Petronius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petronius). Also in [Augustine of Hippo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Hippo)'s [*De Civitate Dei contra Paganos*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_God_%28book%29) (5th century AD), [Sebastian Franck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastian_Franck)'s *Paradoxa Ducenta Octoginta* (1542), and in [James Branch Cabell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Branch_Cabell)'s 1921 novel *[Figures of Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figures_of_Earth)*.[^7666][^7656][^7667][^7668] |
| *[mundus vult decipi, ergo decipiatur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundus_vult_decipi,_ergo_decipiatur)* | the world wants to be deceived, so let it be deceived | Ascribed to Roman satirist [Petronius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petronius). Also in [Augustine of Hippo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Hippo)'s [*De Civitate Dei contra Paganos*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_God_%28book%29) (5th century AD) as "si mundus vult decipi, decipiatur" ("if the world will be gulled, let it be gulled"), and only the first part, "[mundus vult decipi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28full%29)" ("the world wants to be deceived"), in [Sebastian Franck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastian_Franck)'s *Paradoxa Ducenta Octoginta* (1542) and in [James Branch Cabell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Branch_Cabell)'s *[Figures of Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figures_of_Earth)* (1921).[^7666][^7656][^7667][^7668] |
| *munit haec et altera vincit* | this one defends and the other one conquers | [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_mottos) of [Nova Scotia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nova_Scotia). |
| *murus aeneus conscientia sana* | a wall of brass is a clear conscience | a person with a clear conscience is as strong and impenetrable as a wall made of brass; this phrase is often seen as a family motto, particularly associated with the [Earl of Scarbrough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earl_of_Scarbrough) and [Loder Baronets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loder_Baronets) in England |
| *mutata lex non perit* | the law that evolves does not die | Motto of [Seneca the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger) |
| *[mutatis mutandis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutatis_mutandis)* | after changing what needed to be changed | "with the appropriate changes" |
| *mutato nomine de te fabula narratur* | change but the name, and the story is told of yourself | [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), [*Satires*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satires_%28Horace%29), I. 1. 69. Preceded by *Quid rides?* ("Why do you laugh?"; see [Quid rides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28Q%29)). |

#### N

| Latin | Translation | Notes |
|----|----|----|
| *nanos gigantum humeris insidentes* | Dwarfs [standing on the shoulders of giants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_on_the_shoulders_of_giants) | First recorded by [John of Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Salisbury) in the twelfth century and attributed to [Bernard of Chartres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_of_Chartres). Also commonly known by the letters of [Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton): "If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants". |
| *nascentes morimur finisque ab origine pendet* | As we are born we die, and our end hangs from our beginning |  |
| *[nasciturus pro iam nato habetur, quotiens de commodis eius agitur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasciturus_pro_iam_nato_habetur,_quotiens_de_commodis_eius_agitur)* | The unborn is deemed to have been born to the extent that his own inheritance is concerned | Refers to a situation where an unborn child is deemed to be entitled to certain inheritance rights. |
| *natura abhorret a vacuo* | nature abhors vacuum | Pseudo-explanation for why a liquid will climb up a tube to fill a [vacuum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vacuum), often given before the discovery of [atmospheric pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure). |
| *[natura artis magistra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natura_artis_magistra)* | Nature is the teacher of art | Full name of the zoo [Artis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artis_%28zoo%29) in the centre of [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam) |
| *[natura naturans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natura_naturans)* | nature acting | originally linked to [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle), then to his Arabic commentators |
| *natura naturantis* | nature creating, creative nature | literary motif used by [Bolesław Leśmian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boles%C5%82aw_Le%C5%9Bmian) |
| *[natura naturata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natura_naturata)* | nature created | concept explored by [Baruch Spinoza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baruch_Spinoza) |
| *natura nihil frustra facit* | nature does nothing in vain | Cf. [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle): "οὐθὲν γάρ, ὡς φαμέν, μάτην ἡ φύσις ποιεῖ" (Politics I 2, 1253a9) and [Leucippus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leucippus): "Everything that happens does so for a reason and of necessity." |
| *natura non contristatur* | nature is not saddened | That is, the [natural world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nature) is not sentimental or compassionate. Derived by [Arthur Schopenhauer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Schopenhauer) from an earlier source. |
| *natura non facit saltum ita nec lex* | nature does not make a leap, thus neither does the law | Shortened form of *sicut natura nil facit per saltum ita nec lex* (just as nature does nothing by a leap, so neither does the law), referring to both nature and the legal system moving gradually. |
| *[natura non facit saltus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natura_non_facit_saltus)* | nature makes no leaps | A famous [aphorism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphorism) of [Carl Linnaeus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus) stating that all organisms bear relationships on all sides, their forms changing gradually from one [species](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species) to the next. From *[Philosophia Botanica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophia_Botanica) (1751)*. |
| *natura valde simplex est et sibi consona* | Nature is exceedingly simple and harmonious with itself | Sir [Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton)'s famous quote, defining foundation of all modern sciences. Can be found in his Unpublished Scientific Papers of Isaac Newton: A selection from the Portsmouth Collection in the University Library, Cambridge, 1978 edition[^7669] |
| *naturalia non sunt turpia* | What is natural is not dirty | Based on [Servius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurus_Servius_Honoratus)' commentary on [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil)'s *[Georgics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgics)* (3:96): "turpis non est quia per naturam venit." |
| *naturam expellas furca, tamen usque recurret* | You may drive out Nature with a pitchfork, yet she still will hurry back | You must take the basic nature of something into account. - [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), [*Epistles*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistles_%28Horace%29), Book I, epistle X, line 24. |
| *naturam primum cognoscere rerum* | First to learn the nature of things | Motto of the [Australian National University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_National_University) |
| *navigare necesse est, vivere non est necesse* | to sail is necessary; to live is not necessary | Attributed by [Plutarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutarch) to [Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompey), who, during a severe storm, commanded sailors to bring food from Africa to Rome. Translated from Plutarch's Greek "πλεῖν ἀνάγκη, ζῆν οὐκ ἀνάγκη". |
| *ne plus ultra* | nothing more beyond | Also *nec plus ultra* or *non plus ultra*. A descriptive phrase meaning the most extreme point, or the best form, of something. Most notably the [Pillars of Hercules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillars_of_Hercules) were in the geographic sense the *nec plus ultra* of the ancient Mediterranean world, before the discovery of the Americas. [Holy Roman Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Emperor) [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor)'s heraldic emblem contradicted this postulate, using an amended version of the phrase inscribed on two pillars - as *[plus ultra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plus_ultra)* ("more (lies) beyond"), without the negation, referring to the on-going [Spanish colonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas) of the recently discovered Americas, which lay beyond the Pillars of Hercules. *Non plus ultra* is the motto of the Spanish exclave of [Melilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melilla), situated on a Mediterranean cape 230 km east of the original southern Pillar of Hercules. The [Boston Musical Instrument Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Musical_Instrument_Company) engraved *ne plus ultra* on its instruments from 1869 to 1928 to signify that none were better. |
| *ne puero gladium* | do not give a sword to a boy | Never give dangerous tools to someone who is untrained to use them or too immature to understand the damage they can do. |
| *ne supra crepidam sutor iudicaret* | a shoemaker should not judge beyond the shoe | see [Sutor, ne ultra crepidam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutor,_ne_ultra_crepidam) |
| *ne te quaesiveris extra* | do not seek outside yourself | line from the Roman satirist [Persius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persius) inscribed on the boulder to the right of [Sir John Suckling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Suckling_%28poet%29) in the painting of the aforementioned subject by [Sir Anthony van Dyck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Anthony_van_Dyck) (ca. 1638) and invoked by [Ralph Waldo Emerson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Waldo_Emerson) at the opening of his essay [Self-Reliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-Reliance) (1841) |
| *Nec aspera terrent* | They are not terrified of the rough things | They are not afraid of difficulties. Less literally "Difficulties be damned." Motto for [27th Infantry Regiment (United States)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/27th_Infantry_Regiment_%28United_States%29) and the [Duke of Lancaster's Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duke_of_Lancaster's_Regiment). Nec = not; aspera = rough ones/things; terrent = they terrify / do terrify / are terrifying. |
| *Nec deus intersit, nisi dignus vindice nodus (inciderit)* | That a god not intervene, unless a knot show up that be worthy of such an untangler | "When the miraculous power of God is necessary, let it be resorted to: when it is not necessary, let the ordinary means be used." From Horace's *[Ars Poetica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ars_Poetica_%28Horace%29)* as a caution against *[deus ex machina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deus_ex_machina)*. |
| *nec dextrorsum, nec sinistrorsum* | Neither to the right nor to the left | Do not get distracted. Motto for [Bishop Cotton Boys' School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_Cotton_Boys'_School) and the [Bishop Cotton Girls' School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop_Cotton_Girls'_School), both located in Bangalore, India. |
| *nec spe, nec metu* | without hope, without fear |  |
| *nec tamen consumebatur* | and yet it was not consumed | Refers to the [burning bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burning_bush) of [Exodus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Exodus) 3:2. Motto of many [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism) churches throughout the world. |
| *[nec temere, nec timide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nec_temere,_nec_timide)* | neither reckless nor timid | Motto of the [Dutch 11th Air Manoeuvre Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11_Luchtmobiele_Brigade) and the city of [Gdańsk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gda%C5%84sk), Poland |
| *[nec vi, nec clam, nec precario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nec_vi,_nec_clam,_nec_precario)* | Without permission, without secrecy, without interruption | The law of [adverse possession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adverse_possession) |
| *nec vir fortis, nec fæmina casta* | if the man is not firm, the woman is not chaste | From [Jonathan Swift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Swift)'s 1726 satire *[Gulliver's Travels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulliver's_Travels)* where it is attributed to [Polydore Vergil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydore_Vergil)[^7670] |
| *neca eos omnes, Deus suos agnoscet* | kill them all, God will know his own | alternate rendition of *[Caedite eos. Novit enim Dominus qui sunt eius.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caedite_eos._Novit_enim_Dominus_qui_sunt_eius.)* by [Arnaud Amalric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnaud_Amalric) |
| *necesse est aut imiteris aut oderis* | you must either imitate or loathe the world | [Seneca the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger), *[Epistulae morales ad Lucilium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistulae_morales_ad_Lucilium)*, 7:7 |
| *necesse est credere unam tantum esse potentiam absolutam* | It is necessary to believe that there is only one absolute power |  |
| *necessitas etiam timidos fortes facit* | need makes even the timid brave | [Sallust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sallust), *The Conspiracy of Catiline*, 58:19 |

| *[nemo iudex in causa sua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nemo_iudex_in_causa_sua)* | no man shall be a judge in his own cause | Legal principle that no individual can preside over a hearing in which he holds a specific interest or bias |

Motto of the San Beda College Beta Sigma Fraternity. |
| *nemo mortalium omnibus horis sapit* | No mortal is wise at all times | The wisest may make mistakes. |
| *nemo nisi per amicitiam cognoscitur* | No one learns except by friendship | Used to imply that one must like a subject in order to study it. |
| *nemo propheta in patria (sua)* | no man is a prophet in his own land | Concept present in all four Gospels ([Matthew 13:57; Mark 6:4; Luke 4:24; John 4:44](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+13:57;+Mark+6:4;+Luke+4:24;+John+4:44&version=NRSV)). |
| *nemo saltat sobrius* | Nobody dances sober | The short and more common form of *Nemo enim fere saltat sobrius, nisi forte insanit*, "Nobody dances sober, unless he happens to be insane", a quote from Cicero (from the speech "Pro Murena"). |
| *nemo tenetur se ipsum accusare* | no one is bound to accuse himself (the [right to silence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_silence)) | A maxim banning mandatory [self-incrimination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-incrimination). Near-synonymous with *[accusare nemo se debet nisi coram Deo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28A%29)*. Similar phrases include: *nemo tenetur armare adversarium contra se* (no one is bound to arm an opponent against himself), meaning that a defendant is not obligated to in any way assist the prosecutor to his own detriment; *nemo tenetur edere instrumenta contra se* (no one is bound to produce documents against himself, meaning that a defendant is not obligated to provide materials to be used against himself (this is true in [Roman law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_law) and has survived in modern [criminal law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_law), but no longer applies in modern [civil law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_law_%28legal_system%29)); and *nemo tenere prodere se ipsum* (no one is bound to betray himself), meaning that a defendant is not obligated to testify against himself. |

The same image appears in a fable of [Phaedrus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phaedrus_%28fabulist%29). |
| *[Ne quid nimis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ne_quid_nimis)* | Nothing in excess |  |
| *nervos belli, pecuniam infinitam* | Endless money forms the sinews of war | In war, it is essential to be able to purchase supplies and to pay troops (as [Napoleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_Bonaparte) put it, "An army marches on its stomach"). |
| *nihil ad rem* | nothing to do with the point | That is, in law, irrelevant and/or inconsequential. |
| *nihil boni sine labore* | nothing achieved without hard work | Motto of [Palmerston North Boys' High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmerston_North_Boys'_High_School) |
| *[nihil dicit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihil_dicit)* | he says nothing | In law, a declination by a defendant to answer charges or put in a plea. |
| *nihil difficile amanti puto[^7672]* | I think that nothing is difficult for a lover. | From [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero)'s *[Orator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orator_%28Cicero%29)*. |
| *nihil enim lacrima citius arescit* | nothing dries sooner than a tear | [Pseudo-Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Cicero), *[Rhetorica ad Herennium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhetorica_ad_Herennium)*, **2**/31:50 |
| *nihil humanum mihi alienum* | nothing human is alien to me | Adapted from [Terence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terence)'s *[Heauton Timorumenos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heauton_Timorumenos)* (*The Self-Tormentor*), [homo sum humani a me nihil alienum puto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28H%29) ("I am a human being; nothing human is strange to me"). Sometimes ending in est. |
| *nihil in intellectu nisi prius in sensu* | nothing in the intellect unless first in sense | The guiding principle of [empiricism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empiricism), and accepted in some form by [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle), [Aquinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas), [Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Locke), [Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Berkeley), and [Hume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hume). [Leibniz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottfried_Wilhelm_Leibniz), however, added *nisi intellectus ipse* (except the intellect itself). |
| *nihil nimis* | nothing too | Or nothing to excess. Latin translation of the inscription of the [Temple of Apollo at Delphi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi). |
| *[nihil novi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihil_novi)* | nothing of the new | Or just "nothing new". The phrase exists in two versions: as *nihil novi sub sole* (nothing new under the sun), from the [Vulgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate), and as *nihil novi nisi commune consensu* (nothing new unless by the common consensus), a 1505 law of the [Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish%E2%80%93Lithuanian_Commonwealth) and one of the cornerstones of its [Golden Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Liberty). |
| *[nihil obstat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihil_obstat)* | nothing prevents | A notation, usually on a title page, indicating that a [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church) [censor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship) has reviewed the book and found nothing objectionable to faith or morals in its content. See also *[imprimatur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imprimatur)*. |
| *[nihil sine Deo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihil_sine_Deo)* | nothing without God | Motto of the [Kingdom of Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Romania), while ruled by the [Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen) dynasty (1878-1947). |
| *nihil ultra* | nothing beyond | Motto of [St. Xavier's College, Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Xavier's_College,_Calcutta) |
| [*nil admirari*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nihil_admirari) | be surprised at nothing | Or "nihil admirari". [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero), *[Tusculanae Disputationes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tusculanae_Disputationes)* (3,30), [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), [*Epistulae*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistles_%28Horace%29) (1,6,1), and [Seneca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger), *[Epistulae morales ad Lucilium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistulae_morales_ad_Lucilium)*, (8,5). Motto of the Fitzgibbon family. See [John FitzGibbon, 1st Earl of Clare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_FitzGibbon,_1st_Earl_of_Clare) |
| *nil desperandum* | nothing must be despaired at | "never despair" |
| *nil igitur fieri de nilo posse fatendumst* | nothing, therefore, we must confess, can be made from nothing | From [Lucretius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucretius)' *[De rerum natura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_rerum_natura)* (*On the Nature of Things*), [I.205](https://la.wikipedia.org/wiki/s:De%20rerum%20natura%20%28Titus%20Lucretius%20Carus%29/Liber%20I#205) |
| *nil igitur mors est ad nos* | Death, therefore, is nothing to us | From [Lucretius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucretius)' *[De rerum natura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_rerum_natura)* (*On the Nature of Things*), [III.831](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/De%20rerum%20natura%20%28Titus%20Lucretius%20Carus%29/Liber%20III) |
| *nil mortalibus ardui est* | nothing is impossible for humankind | From [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace)'s *[Odes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odes_%28Horace%29)*. Motto of [Rathkeale College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rathkeale_College), New Zealand and [Brunts School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brunts_School), England. |
| *nil nisi bonum* | (about the dead say) nothing unless (it is) good | Short for *[nil nisi bonum de mortuis dicere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_mortuis_nil_nisi_bonum)*. That is, "Don't speak ill of anyone who has died". Also *Nil magnum nisi bonum* (nothing is great unless good), motto of [St Catherine's School, Toorak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Catherine's_School,_Toorak), [Pennant Hills High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennant_Hills_High_School) and [Petit Seminaire Higher Secondary School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petit_Seminaire_Higher_Secondary_School). |
| *nil nisi malis terrori* | no terror, except to the bad | Motto of [The King's School, Macclesfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_King's_School,_Macclesfield) |
| *[nil per os](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nil_per_os)*, rarely *non per os* (n.p.o.) | nothing through the mouth | [Medical shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_prescription) indicating that oral foods and fluids should be withheld from the patient. |
| *[nil satis nisi optimum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nil_satis_nisi_optimum)* | nothing \[is\] enough unless \[it is\] the best | Motto of [Everton F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everton_F.C.), [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool), and several other organisations |
| *nil sine labore* | nothing without labour | Motto of many schools |
| *nil sine numine* | nothing without the divine will | Or "nothing without [providence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_providence)". [State motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_and_territory_mottos) of [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado), adopted in 1861. Probably derived from [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil)'s *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)*, book 2, line 777, *non haec sine numine divum eveniunt* (these things do not come to pass without the will of Heaven). See also *[numen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numen)*. |
| *[nil volentibus arduum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nil_volentibus_arduum)* | Nothing \[is\] arduous for the willing | Nothing is impossible for the willing |
| *nisi* | unless | A [decree *nisi*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decree_nisi) is a court order (often for divorce) that will come into force on a certain date "unless" cause is shown why it should not. |
| *nisi Dominus frustra* | if not the Lord, \[it is\] in vain | That is, "everything is in vain without [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God)". Summarized from [Psalm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalms) 127 (126 Vulgate), *nisi Dominus aedificaverit domum in vanum laboraverunt qui aedificant eam nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem frustra vigilavit qui custodit* (unless the Lord builds the house, they work on a useless thing who build it; unless the Lord guards the community, he keeps watch in vain who guards it); widely used motto. |
| *nisi paria non pugnant* | Unless there are a pair, they do not fight. | Less literally, "it takes two to make a fight". Irascetur aliquis: tu contra beneficiis prouoca; cadit statim simultas ab altera parte deserta; *nisi paria non pugnant*. (If any one is angry with you, meet his anger by returning benefits for it: a quarrel which is only taken up on one side falls to the ground: *it takes two men to fight*.) [Seneca the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger), *De Ira* (On Anger): Book 2, cap. 34, line 5. |
| *nisi prius* | unless previously | In England, a direction that a case be brought up to [Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster) for trial before a single judge and jury. In the United States, a court where civil actions are tried by a single judge sitting with a jury, as distinguished from an [appellate court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appeal). |
| *nitimur in vetitum* | We strive for the forbidden | From [Ovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid)'s *[Amores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amores_%28Ovid%29)*, [III.4:17](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/la:Amores/3.4). It means that when we are denied of something, we will eagerly pursue the denied thing. Used by [Friedrich Nietzsche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Nietzsche) in his *[Ecce Homo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecce_Homo_%28book%29)* to indicate that his philosophy pursues what is forbidden to other [philosophers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophers). |
| *nobis bene, nemini male* | Good for us, Bad for no one | Inscription on the old Nobistor gatepost that divided [Altona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altona,_Hamburg) and [St. Pauli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Pauli) |
| *nolens volens* | unwilling, willing | That is, "whether unwillingly or willingly". Sometimes rendered *volens nolens*, *aut nolens aut volens* or *nolentis volentis*. Similar to *[willy-nilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy-nilly_%28idiom%29)*, though that word is derived from [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English) *will-he nil-he* (\[whether\] he will or \[whether\] he will not). |
| *[noli me tangere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noli_me_tangere)* | do not touch me | Commonly translated "touch me not". According to the [Gospel of John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_of_John), this was said by [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus) to [Mary Magdalene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Magdalene) after his [resurrection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resurrection_of_Jesus). |
| *[Noli turbare circulos meos!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noli_turbare_circulos_meos!)* | Do not disturb my circles! | That is, "Don't upset my calculations!" Said by [Archimedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedes) to a Roman soldier who, despite having been given orders not to, killed Archimedes at the conquest of [Syracuse, Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse,_Sicily). |
| *nolite timere* | be not afraid | heraldic motto, from [Luke 2:10-12](https://bible.oremus.org/?passage=Luke%202:10%E2%80%9312&version=nrsv) |
| *[nolle prosequi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nolle_prosequi)* | to be unwilling to prosecute | A [legal motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motion_%28legal%29) by a [prosecutor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosecutor) or other [plaintiff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaintiff) to drop legal charges, usually in exchange for a [diversion program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversion_program) or [out-of-court settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlement_%28litigation%29). |
| *[nolo contendere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nolo_contendere)* | I do not wish to contend | That is, "no contest". A plea that can be entered on behalf of a defendant in a court that states that the accused doesn't admit guilt, but will accept punishment for a crime. *Nolo contendere* pleas cannot be used as evidence in another trial. |
| *nomen amicitiae sic, quatenus expedit, haeret* | the name of friendship lasts just so long as it is profitable | [Petronius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petronius), *[Satyricon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satyricon)*, 80. |
| *[nomen dubium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomen_dubium)* | doubtful name | A scientific name of unknown or doubtful application. |
| *nomen est omen* | the name is a sign | Thus, "true to its name". |
| *nomen nescio (N.N.)* | I do not know the name | Thus, the name or person in question is unknown. |
| *nomen mysticum* | mystic name | secret members' name in some organizations[^7673] |
| *[nomen nudum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomen_nudum)* | naked name | A purported scientific name that does not fulfill the proper formal criteria and therefore cannot be used unless it is subsequently proposed correctly. |
| *non Angli sed angeli, si forent Christiani* | They are not Angles, but angels, if they were Christian | A pun, ascribed (in a different wording) by [Bede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bede) to [Pope Gregory I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Gregory_I), said to have been uttered by the latter on seeing pale-skinned [Angle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angles_%28tribe%29) children at a slave market. |
| *non auro, sed ferro, recuperanda est patria* | Not with gold, but with iron must the fatherland be reclaimed | According to some Roman this sentence was said by [Marcus Furius Camillus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Furius_Camillus) to [Brennus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brennus_%284th_century_BC%29), the chief of the [Gauls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaul), after he demanded more gold from the citizens of the recently sacked [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome) in 390 BC. |
| *non bene pro toto libertas venditur auro* | liberty is not well sold for all the gold | Motto of [Republic of Ragusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ragusa), inscribed over the gates of [St. Lawrence Fortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lovrijenac). From [Gualterus Anglicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gualterus_Anglicus)'s version of [Aesop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aesop)'s fable "[The Dog and the Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dog_and_the_Wolf)". |
| *non bis in idem* | not twice in the same thing | A legal principle forbidding [double jeopardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_jeopardy). |
| *non canimus surdis, respondent omnia silvae* | we sing not to the deaf; the trees echo every word | [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil), *[Eclogues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclogues)* **10**:8 |
| *non causa pro causa* | not the cause for the cause | Also known as the "[questionable cause](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Questionable_cause)" or "false cause". Refers to any [logical fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_fallacy) where a cause is incorrectly identified. |
| *[non compos mentis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_compos_mentis)* | not in control of the mind | See *compos mentis*. Also rendered *non compos sui* (not in control of himself). [Samuel Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Johnson) theorized that the word [nincompoop](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/nincompoop) may derive from this phrase. |
| *non constat* | it is not certain | Used to explain [scientific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science) phenomena and religious advocations, for example in [medieval history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages), for rulers to issue a 'Non Constat' decree, banning the worship of a holy figure. In legal context, occasionally a backing for nulling information that was presented by an [attorney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawyer). Without any tangible proof, Non constat information is difficult to argue for. |
| *[non ducor, duco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_ducor,_duco)* | I am not led; I lead | [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_mottos) of [São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Paulo) city, [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil). See also *pro Brasilia fiant eximia*. |
| *[non est factum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_est_factum)* | it is not \[my\] deed | a doctrine in contract law that allows a signing party to escape performance of the agreement. A claim of "non est factum" means that the signature on the contract was signed by mistake, without knowledge of its meaning, but was not done so negligently. A successful plea would make the contract void *ab initio*. |
| *non est princeps super leges, sed leges supra principem* | the prince is not above the laws, but the law is above the prince. | [Pliny the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Younger), *Panegyricus* **65**:1. |
| *non extinguetur* | shall not be extinguished | Motto of the [Society of Antiquaries of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Antiquaries_of_London) accompanying their Lamp of knowledge emblem |
| *non facias malum ut inde fiat bonum* | you should not make evil in order that good may be made from it | More simply, "don't do wrong to do right". The direct opposite of the phrase "[the ends justify the means](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_ends_justify_the_means)". |
| *non hos quaesitum munus in usus* | A gift sought for no such purpose | [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil), *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)*, **4**:647, of the sword with which Dido will commit suicide. "Not for so dire an enterprise design’d." ([Dryden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dryden) trans.; 1697)[^7674] "A gift asked for no use like this." ([Mackail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_William_Mackail) trans.; 1885).[^7675] "Ne'er given for an end so dire." (Taylor trans.; 1907)[^7676] "A gift not asked for use like this!" (Williams trans.; 1910).[^7677] Quoted by Francis Bacon of the civil law, "not made for the countries it governeth". |
| *non impediti ratione cogitationis* | unencumbered by the thought process | motto of radio show *[Car Talk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_Talk)* |
| *non in legendo sed in intelligendo leges consistunt* | the laws depend not on being read, but on being understood |  |
| *non licet omnibus adire Corinthum* | not everyone can go to Corinth | The legendary pleasures of [Corinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Corinth) were also quite expensive. Used to refer to anything that not everyone can afford or have the chance to do. |
| *non liquet* | it is not proven | Also "it is not clear" or "it is not evident". A sometimes controversial decision handed down by a judge when they feel that the law is not complete. |
| *non loqui sed facere* | not talk but action | Motto of the [University of Western Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Western_Australia)'s Engineering faculty student society. |
| *non mihi solum* | not for myself alone | Motto of [Anderson Junior College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anderson_Junior_College), Singapore. |
| *non ministrari sed ministrare* | not to be served, but to serve | Motto of [Wellesley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellesley_College) and [Shimer College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shimer_College) (from [Matthew 20:28](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/la:Biblia%20Sacra%20Vulgata%20%28Stuttgartensia%29/Matthaeus) in the [Vulgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate)). |
| *non multa sed multum* | not quantity but quality | Motto of the [Daniel Pearl Magnet High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Pearl_Magnet_High_School). |
| *non nisi parendo vincitur* | \[Nature\] cannot be conquered except by being obeyed | From [Francis Bacon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Bacon)'s *Cogitata et visa*. |
| *[Non nobis Domine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_nobis_Domine)* | Not to us (oh) Lord | Christian hymn based on [Psalm 115](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bible%20%28King%20James%29/Psalms#Psalm_115). |
| *non nobis nati* | 'Born not for ourselves' | Motto of [St Albans School (Hertfordshire)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Albans_School_%28Hertfordshire%29) |
| *[non nobis solum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_nobis_solum)* | not for ourselves alone | Appears in [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero)'s *[De Officiis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Officiis)* [Book 1:22](https://la.wikipedia.org/wiki/s:De%20officiis/Liber%20I) in the form *non nobis solum nati sumus* (we are not born for ourselves alone). Motto of [Lower Canada College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Canada_College), Montreal and University College, [Durham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_University), [Willamette University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willamette_University), [Gillotts School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gillotts_School) Henley. |
| *non numerantur, sed ponderantur* | they are not counted, but weighed | Old saying. [Paul Erdős](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Erd%C5%91s) (1913-1996), in *[The Man Who Loved Only Numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Man_Who_Loved_Only_Numbers)* by [Paul Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Hoffman_%28science_writer%29)[^7678] |
| *non obstante veredicto* | not standing in the way of a [verdict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verdict) | A [judgment notwithstanding verdict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judgment_notwithstanding_verdict), a legal motion asking the [court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court) to reverse the [jury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jury)'s verdict on the grounds that the jury could not have reached such a verdict reasonably. |
| *non olet* | it doesn't smell | See *[pecunia non olet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pecunia_non_olet)*. |
| *non omnia possumus omnes* | not everyone can do everything | [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil), *[Eclogues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclogues)* **8**:63 (and others). |
| *non omnis moriar* | I shall not all die | [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), [*Carmina*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odes_%28Horace%29) **3**/30:6. "Not all of me will die", a phrase expressing the belief that a part of the speaker will survive beyond death. |
| *non plus ultra* | nothing further beyond | the ultimate. See also 'ne plus ultra' |
| *[non possumus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_possumus)* | we cannot |  |
| *non possunt primi esse omnes omni in tempore* | not everyone can occupy the first rank forever | (It is impossible always to excel) [Decimus Laberius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimus_Laberius). |
| *non progredi est regredi* | to not go forward is to go backward |  |
| *non prosequitur* | he does not proceed | A judgment in favor of a defendant when the plaintiff failed to take the necessary steps in an action within the time allowed. |
| *non qui parum habet, sed qui plus cupit, pauper est* | It is not he who has little, but he who wants more, who is the pauper. | [Seneca the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger), *[Epistulae morales ad Lucilium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistulae_morales_ad_Lucilium)*, 2:6. |
| *non quis sed quid* | not who but what | Used in the sense "what matters is not who says it but what he says" - a warning against [ad hominem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_hominem) arguments; frequently used as motto, including that of [Southwestern University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwestern_University). |
| *non satis scire* | to know is not enough | Motto of [Hampshire College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hampshire_College) |
| *[non scholae sed vitae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_scholae_sed_vitae)* | \[We learn\] not for school but for life | An inversion of *non vitae sed scholae* now used as a school motto |
| [*non sequitur*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_sequitur_%28logic%29) | it does not follow | In general, a comment which is absurd due to not making sense in its context (rather than due to being inherently nonsensical or internally inconsistent), often used in humor. As a [logical fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_fallacy), a conclusion that does not follow from a premise. |
| *[non serviam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_serviam)* | I will not serve | Possibly derived from a [Vulgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate) mistranslation of the [Book of Jeremiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_of_Jeremiah). Commonly used in literature as [Satan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan)'s statement of disobedience to [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God), though in the original context the quote is attributed to [Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel), not Satan. |
| *non sibi* | Not for self | A slogan used by many schools and universities. |
| *non sibi solum* | Not for self alone | A slogan used by many schools and universities. |
| *non sibi, sed patriae* | Not for self, but for country | Engraved on the doors of the United States Naval Academy chapel; motto of the [USS *Halyburton* (FFG-40)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Halyburton). |
| *non sibi, sed suis* | Not for one's self but for one's own | A slogan used by many schools and universities. |
| *non sibi, sed omnibus* | Not for one's self but for all | A slogan used by many schools and universities. |
| *non sic dormit, sed vigilat* | Sleeps not but is awake | [Martin Luther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther) on [mortality of the soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_sleep). |
| *non silba, sed anthar; Deo vindice* | Not for self, but for others; God will vindicate | A slogan used by the [Ku Klux Klan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan). Note that this [is not accurate Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_Latin) but rather a [mixture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macaronic_language) of Latin and [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_language)[^7679] |
| *non sum qualis eram* | I am not such as I was | Or "I am not the kind of person I once was". Expresses a change in the speaker. [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), [*Odes*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odes_%28Horace%29) 4/1:3. |
| *non teneas aurum totum quod splendet ut aurum* | Do not hold as gold all that shines as gold | Also, "[All that glitters is not gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_that_glitters_is_not_gold)." [Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shakespeare) in *[The Merchant of Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Merchant_of_Venice)*. |
| *non [timebo](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/timebo) mala* | I will fear no evil | It is possibly a reference to [Psalm 23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_23). Printed on the Colt in *[Supernatural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supernatural_%28American_TV_series%29)*. |
| *non vestra sed vos* | Not yours but you | Motto of [St Chad's College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Chad's_College), [Durham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Durham). |
| [*non vitae sed scholae*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_scholae_sed_vitae) | \[We learn\] not for life but for schooltime | From a passage of [occupatio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupatio) in [Seneca the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger)'s [moral letters to Lucilius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moral_letters_to_Lucilius),[^7680] wherein Lucilius is given the argument that too much literature fails to prepare students for life |
| *non vi, sed verbo* | Not by force, but by the word \[of God\] | From [Martin Luther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther)'s *Invocavit* sermons preached in March 1522 against the [Zwickau prophets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zwickau_prophets) unrest in [Wittenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wittenberg);[^7681] later echoed in the [Augsburg Confession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augsburg_Confession) as *...sine vi humana, sed Verbo*: [bishops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bishop) should act "without human force, but through [the Word](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_1)".[^7682] |
| *nosce te ipsum* | [know thyself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Know_thyself) | From [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero), based on the [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Greek_phrases) γνῶθι σεαυτόν (*gnothi seauton*), inscribed on the *[pronaos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portico)* of the [Temple of Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi) at [Delphi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delphi), according to the Greek periegetic writer [Pausanias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pausanias_%28geographer%29) (10.24.1). A non-traditional Latin rendering, *temet nosce* (thine own self know), is translated in *[The Matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Matrix)* as "know thyself". |
| *[noscitur a sociis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noscitur_a_sociis)* | a word is known by the company it keeps | In [statutory interpretation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statutory_interpretation), when a word is ambiguous, its meaning may be determined by reference to the rest of the statute. |
| *noster nostri* | Literally "Our ours" | Approximately "Our hearts beat as one." |
| *[nota bene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nota_bene) (n.b.)* | mark well | That is, "please note" or "note it well". |
| *[novus ordo seclorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novus_ordo_seclorum)* | new order of the ages | From [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil). Motto on the [Great Seal of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Seal_of_the_United_States). Similar to *Novus Ordo Mundi* (New World Order). |
| *nulla dies sine linea* | Not a day without a line drawn | [Pliny the Elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Elder) attributes this maxim to [Apelles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apelles), an ancient Greek artist. |
| *nulla dies umquam memori vos eximet aevo* | No day shall erase you from the memory of time | From [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil)'s *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)*, Book IX, line 447, on the episode of [Nisus and Euryalus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nisus_and_Euryalus). |
| *[nulla poena sine lege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nulla_poena_sine_lege)* | no penalty without a law | Refers to the legal principle that one cannot be punished for doing something that is not prohibited by law, and is related to [Nullum crimen, nulla poena sine praevia lege poenali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nullum_crimen,_nulla_poena_sine_praevia_lege_poenali). |
| *nulla quaestio* | there is no question, there is no issue |  |
| *nulla tenaci invia est via* | For the tenacious, no road is impassable | Motto of the Dutch car builder [Spyker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spyker). |
| *nullam rem natam* | no thing born | That is, "nothing". It has been theorized that this expression is the origin of [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language) *nulla*, [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language) *rien*, and [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language) and [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_language) *nada*, all with the same meaning. |
| *nulli secundus* | second to none | Motto of the [Coldstream Guards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coldstream_Guards) and Nine Squadron Royal Australian Corps of Transport and the [Pretoria Armour Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretoria_Armour_Regiment). |
| *[nullius in verba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nullius_in_verba)* | On the word of no man | Motto of the [Royal Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society). |
| *[nullum crimen, nulla poena sine praevia lege poenali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nullum_crimen,_nulla_poena_sine_praevia_lege_poenali)* | no crime, no punishment without a previous penal law | Legal principle meaning that one cannot be penalised for doing something that is not prohibited by law; penal law cannot be enacted retroactively. |
| *nullum magnum ingenium sine mixtura dementiae fuit* | There has been no great wisdom without an element of madness | From *De Tranquillitate Animi*, Seneca the Younger. |
| *numen lumen* | God our light | The motto of the [University of Wisconsin-Madison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Madison). The motto of [Elon University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elon_University). |
| *[numerus clausus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerus_clausus)* | closed number | A method to limit the number of students who may study at a university. |
| *nunc aut nunquam* | now or never | Motto of the [Korps Commandotroepen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korps_Commandotroepen), Dutch elite special forces. |
| *[nunc dimittis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nunc_dimittis)* | now you send | beginning of the Song of [Simeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simeon_%28Gospel_of_Luke%29), from the [Gospel of Luke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_of_Luke). |
| *nunc est bibendum* | now is the time to drink | [Carpe-Diem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpe_diem)-type phrase from the [Odes of Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odes_%28Horace%29), *Nunc est bibendum, nunc pede libero pulsanda tellus* (Now is the time to drink, now the time to dance footloose upon the earth). Used as a slogan by [Michelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelin) and the origin of the [Michelin Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelin_Man)'s name *Bibendum*. |
| *nunc id vides, nunc ne vides* | now you see it, now you don't | The motto of [Unseen University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unseen_University) from the [Discworld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discworld) books by [Terry Pratchett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Pratchett). |
| *[nunc pro tunc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nunc_pro_tunc)* | now for then | Something that has retroactive effect, is effective from an earlier date. |
| *nunc scio quid sit amor* | now I know what love is | From [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil), *[Eclogues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclogues)* VIII. |
| *nunquam minus solus quam cum solus* | never less alone than when alone |  |
| *nunquam non paratus* | never unprepared, ever ready, always ready | frequently used as motto, e.g. for the Scottish [Clan Johnstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Johnstone), where it is anglicized as "Ready, Aye, Ready"[^7683] |
| *nunquam obliviscar* | never forget |  |
| *Nusquam est qui ubique est* | He who is everywhere is nowhere | [Seneca the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger), [second](https://la.wikipedia.org/wiki/s:Epistulae%20morales%20ad%20Lucilium/Liber%20I) *[Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistulae_Morales_ad_Lucilium)* |

Why do I do this, you perhaps ask. / I do not know, but I feel it happening to me and I am burning up.) |

| *omnia omnibus* | all things to all men | 1 Corinthians 9:22 |

| *omnia sponte fluant absit violentia rebus* | everything should flow by itself, force should be absent | "let it go" |
| *[omnia sunt communia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnia_sunt_communia)* | all things shall be held in common | from [Acts of the Apostles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acts_of_the_Apostles) |
| *omnis vir enim sui* | Every man for himself! |  |
| *omnibus idem* | the same to all | motto of [Pieter Corneliszoon Hooft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pieter_Corneliszoon_Hooft), usually accompanied by a sun, which shines for (almost) everyone |

"Pray and work (and read), God is there without delay" (or to keep the rhyme: "Work and pray, and God is there without delay") |

| *orando laborando* | by praying, by working | motto of [Rugby School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_School) |

| *pace ac bello merita* | Service during peace and war | Motto of the US [Federal Emergency Management Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Emergency_Management_Agency) shown on its flag |
| *pace tua* | with your peace | Thus, "with your permission" |
| *[Pacem in terris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacem_in_terris)* | Peace on Earth | 1963 [encyclical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encyclical) by [Pope John XXIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXIII) |
| *[pacta sunt servanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacta_sunt_servanda)* | agreements must be kept | Also "contracts must be honoured". Indicates the binding power of treaties. One of the fundamental rules of [international law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_law). |
| *palma non sine pulvere* | no reward without effort | Also "dare to try"; motto of numerous schools. |
| *palmam qui meruit ferat* | He who has earned the palm, let him bear it. | Loosely, "achievement should be rewarded" (or, "let the symbol of victory go to him who has deserved it"); frequently used motto |
| *[panem et circenses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panem_et_circenses)* | bread and circuses | From Juvenal, [*Satires*, book IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satires_%28Juvenal%29), satire X, line 81.[^7687] Originally described all that was needed for emperors to placate the Roman mob. Today used to describe any entertainment used to distract public attention from more important matters. |
| *par sit fortuna labori* | Let the success be equal to the labor. | This motto is of the families [Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buchanan_%28surname%29), [Lowman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lowman_%28surname%29), and [Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmer_%28surname%29), according to [Burke's Peerage & Baronetage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burke's_Peerage). |
| *parvus pendetur fur, magnus abire videtur* | The petty thief is hanged, the big thief gets away. |  |
| [*para bellum*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Si_vis_pacem,_para_bellum) | prepare for war | From "Si vis pacem para bellum": *if you want peace, prepare for war*, if a country is ready for war, its enemies are less likely to attack. Usually used to support a policy of [peace through strength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_through_strength) (deterrence). In antiquity, however, the Romans viewed peace as the aftermath of successful conquest through war, so in this sense the proverb identifies war as the means through which peace will be achieved. |
| *parare Domino plebem perfectam* | to prepare for God a perfect people | motto of the [St. Jean Baptiste High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Jean_Baptiste_High_School) |
| *parati vero parati* | ready aye ready | The motto of the [Royal Canadian Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Navy). |
| *parce sepulto* | forgive the interred | it is ungenerous to hold resentment toward the dead. Quote from the [Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid), III 13-68. |
| *[parens patriae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parens_patriae)* | parent of the nation | A [public policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_policy_%28law%29) requiring courts to protect the [best interests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_interests) of any child involved in a lawsuit. See also *Pater Patriae*. |
| *[pari passu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pari_passu)* | with equal step | Thus, "moving together", "simultaneously", etc. Also used to abbreviate the principle that in bankruptcy creditors must all get the same proportion of their debt. |
| *parturiunt montes, nascetur ridiculus mus* | The mountains are in labour, a ridiculous mouse will be born. | said of works that promise much at the outset but yield little in the end ([Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), *[Ars poetica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ars_Poetica_%28Horace%29)* [137](https://la.wikipedia.org/wiki/s:Ars%20poetica)) - see also [The Mountain in Labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mountain_in_Labour) |
| *parum luceat* | It does not shine \[being darkened by shade\]. | [Quintilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintilian), *[Institutio Oratoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institutio_Oratoria)*, **1**/6:34 - see also [lucus a nonlucendo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28L%29) |
| *parva sub ingenti* | the small under the huge | Implies that the weak are under the protection of the strong, rather than that they are inferior. [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_mottos) of [Prince Edward Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Edward_Island). |
| *parvis imbutus tentabis grandia tutus* | When you are steeped in little things, you shall safely attempt great things. | Motto of [Barnard Castle School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnard_Castle_School), sometimes translated as "Once you have accomplished small things, you may attempt great ones safely". |
| *[passim](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/passim)* | here and there, everywhere | Less literally, "throughout" or "frequently". Said of a word, fact or notion that occurs several times in a cited text. Also used in [proofreading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proofreading), where it refers to a change that is to be repeated everywhere needed. |
| *[pater familias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pater_familias)* | father of the family | Or "master of the house". The eldest male in a family, who held *patria potestas* ("paternal power"). In [Roman law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_law), a father had enormous power over his children, wife, and slaves, though these rights dwindled over time. Derived from the phrase *pater familias*, an [Old Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Latin) expression preserving the archaic -*as* ending for the [genitive case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genitive_case). |
| *Pater Omnipotens* | Father [Almighty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnipotence) | A more direct translation would be "[omnipotent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omnipotence) father". |
| *[Pater Patriae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pater_Patriae)* | father of the nation | A Latin honorific meaning "Father of the Country", or more literally, "Father of the Fatherland". |
| *pater peccavi* | Father, I have sinned | The traditional beginning of a [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church) [confession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confession_%28religion%29). |
| *pauca sed bona* | few, but good | Similar to "quality over quantity"; though there may be few of something, at least they are of good quality. |
| *pauca sed matura* | few, but ripe | Said to be one of [Carl Gauss's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Friedrich_Gauss) favorite quotations. Used in *[The King and I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_King_and_I)* by Rodgers and Hammerstein. |
| *paulatim ergo certe* | slowly therefore surely | Former motto of [Latymer Upper School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latymer_Upper_School) in London (the text *latim er* is concealed in the words) |
| *paulatim sed firmiter* | slowly but surely | Motto of [University College School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_School) in London |
| *pax aeterna* | eternal peace | A common epitaph |
| *[Pax Americana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Americana)* | American Peace | A euphemism for the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States) of America and its sphere of influence. Adapted from *Pax Romana*. |
| *[Pax Britannica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Britannica)* | British Peace | A euphemism for the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire). Adapted from *Pax Romana* |
| *Pax Christi* | Peace of Christ | Used as a wish before the Holy Communion in the Catholic Mass, also the name of the peace movement [Pax Christi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Christi) |
| *pax Dei* | peace of God | Used in the [Peace and Truce of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_and_Truce_of_God) movement in 10th-century France |
| *Pax Deorum* | Peace of the gods | Like the vast majority of inhabitants of the ancient world, the Romans practiced [pagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paganism) rituals, believing it important to achieve a state of *Pax Deorum* (The Peace of the gods) instead of *Ira Deorum* (The Wrath of the gods). |
| *Pax, Domine* | peace, lord | lord or master; used as a form of address when speaking to clergy or educated professionals |
| *pax et bonum* | peace and the good | Motto of St. [Francis of Assisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_of_Assisi) and, consequently, of his monastery in [Assisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assisi); understood by Catholics to mean 'Peace and Goodness be with you,' as is similar in the Mass; translated in [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_language) as *pace e bene*. |
| *pax et justitia* | peace and justice | Motto of [Saint Vincent and the Grenadines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Vincent_and_the_Grenadines) |
| *pax et lux* | peace and light | Motto of [Tufts University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tufts_University) and various schools |
| *[Pax Europaea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Europaea)* | European Peace | euphemism for [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe) after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II) |
| *[Pax Hispanica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Hispanica)* | Spanish Peace | Euphemism for the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire); specifically can mean the twenty-three years of supreme Spanish dominance in Europe (approximately 1598-1621). Adapted from *Pax Romana*. |
| *pax in terra* | peace on earth | Used to exemplify the desired state of peace on earth |
| *Pax Indica* | Indian Peace | Term for hegemony of [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India) in its sphere of influence; adapted from *[Pax Romana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Romana)*; also [a 2012 book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Indica_%28book%29) by [Shashi Tharoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shashi_Tharoor) |
| *[Pax intrantibus, salus exeuntibus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_intrantibus,_salus_exeuntibus)* | Peace to those who enter, health to those who depart. | Used as an inscription over the entrance of buildings (especially homes, monasteries, inns). Often *benedicto habitantibus* (Blessings on those who abide here) is added. |
| *pax matrum, ergo pax familiarum* | peace of mothers, therefore peace of families | If the mother is peaceful, then the family is peaceful. The [inverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_%28logic%29) of the [Southern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_the_Southern_United_States) saying, "If mama ain't happy, ain't nobody happy." |
| *[Pax Mongolica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Mongolica)* | Mongolian Peace | period of peace and prosperity in Asia during the [Mongol Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_Empire) |
| *pax optima rerum* | peace is the greatest good | [Silius Italicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silius_Italicus), *[Punica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punica_%28poem%29)* (11,595); motto of [Kiel University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiel_University) |
| *[Pax Romana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Romana)* | Roman Peace | period of relative prosperity and lack of conflict in the early [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire) |
| *[Pax Sinica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_Sinica)* | Chinese Peace | period of peace in [East Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asia) during times of strong [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China) [hegemony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hegemony) |
| *Pax tecum* | peace be with you (singular) |  |
| *Pax tibi, Marce, Evangelista meus. Hic requiescet corpus tuum.* | Peace to you, Mark, my Evangelist. Here will rest your body. | Legend states that when the evangelist went to the lagoon where Venice would later be founded, an angel came and said this. [^7688] The first part is depicted as the note in the book shown opened by the lion of St Mark's Basilica , Venice; registered trademark of the Assicurazioni Generali , Trieste. [^7689] |
| [*pax vobiscum*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pax_%28liturgy%29) | peace \[be\] with you | A common farewell. The "[you](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You)" is plural ("you all"), so the phrase must be used when speaking to more than one person; *pax tecum* is the form used when speaking to only one person. |
| *peccavi* | I have sinned | Telegraph message and pun from [Charles Napier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_James_Napier), British general, upon completely subjugating the Indian province of Sindh in 1842 ('I have Sindh'). This is, arguably, the most terse military despatch ever sent. The story is apocryphal. |
| *[pecunia non olet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pecunia_non_olet)* | money doesn't smell | According to [Suetonius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suetonius)' *[De vita Caesarum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twelve_Caesars)*, when Emperor [Vespasian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vespasian) was challenged by his son [Titus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titus) for taxing the public lavatories, the emperor held up a coin before his son and asked whether it smelled or simply said *non olet* ("it doesn't smell"). From this, the phrase was expanded to *pecunia non olet*, or rarely *aes non olet* ("copper doesn't smell"). |
| *pecunia, si uti scis, ancilla est; si nescis, domina* | if you know how to use money, money is your slave; if you don't, money is your master | Written on an old Latin tablet in downtown Verona (Italy). |
| *pede poena claudo* | punishment comes limping | That is, retribution comes slowly but surely. From [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), *Odes*, 3, 2, 32. |
| *pendent opera interrupta* | the works hang interrupted | From the *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)* of [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil), Book IV |
| *per* | By, through, by means of | See specific phrases below |
| *per angusta ad augusta* | through difficulties to greatness | Joining sentence of the conspirators in the drama *[Hernani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hernani_%28drama%29)* by [Victor Hugo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Hugo) (1830). The motto of numerous educational establishments. |
| *per annum (pa.)* | each year | Thus, "yearly", occurring every year |
| *per ardua* | through adversity | Motto of the British [RAF Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Regiment) |
| *per ardua ad alta* | through difficulty to heights | Through hardship, great heights are reached; frequently used motto |
| *[per ardua ad astra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_ardua_ad_astra)* | through adversity to the stars | Motto of the [Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force), [Royal Australian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Australian_Air_Force) and [Royal New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_New_Zealand_Air_Force) Air Forces, the U. S. State of Kansas and of several schools. The phrase is used by Latin Poet Virgil in the Aeneid; also used in [H. Rider Haggard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._Rider_Haggard)'s novel *[The People of the Mist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_People_of_the_Mist)*. |
| [*per aspera ad astra*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad_astra_%28phrase%29) | through hardships to the stars | From [Seneca the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger); frequently used motto, sometimes as *ad astra per aspera* ("to the stars through hardships") |
| *[per capita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita)* | by heads | "Per head", i.e., "per person", a ratio by the number of persons. The singular is *per caput*. |
| *per capsulam* | through the small box | That is, "by letter" |
| *per contra* | through the contrary | Or "on the contrary" (cf. *a contrario*) |
| *per crucem vincemus* | through the cross we shall conquer | Motto of [St John Fisher Catholic High School, Dewsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_John_Fisher_Catholic_High_School,_Dewsbury) |
| *Per Crucem Crescens* | through the cross, growth | Motto of *[Lambda Chi Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambda_Chi_Alpha)* |
| *per curiam* | through the senate | Legal term meaning "by the court", as in a [*per curiam* decision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_curiam_decision) |
| *per definitionem* | through the definition | Thus, "by [definition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Definition)" |
| *[per diem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_diem) (pd.)* | by day | Thus, "per day". A specific amount of money an organization allows an individual to spend per day, typically for travel expenses. |
| *per fas et nefas* | through right or wrong | By fair means or foul |
| *per fidem intrepidus* | fearless through faith |  |
| *per incuriam* | through inadvertence or carelessness | Legal term referring to a decision that was made by a court through a clear mistake or unawareness of something, such as forgetting to take some binding precedent into account |
| *per literas regias per lit. reg. per regias literas per reg. lit. etc.* | by royal letters | by [letters patent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letters_patent); of academic degrees: awarded by letters patent from the King/Queen, rather than by a University[^7690][^7691] |
| *per mare per terram* | by sea and by land | Motto of the [Royal Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Marines) and (with small difference) of [Clan Donald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Donald) and the [Compagnies Franches de la Marine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compagnies_Franches_de_la_Marine) |
| *per mensem (pm.)* | by month | Thus, "per month", or "monthly" |
| *per multum cras, cras, crebro dilabitur aetas* | what can be done today should not be delayed |  |
| *[per os](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_os) (p.o.)* | through the mouth | [Medical shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_prescription) for "by mouth" |
| *per pedes* | by feet | Used of a certain place that can be traversed or reached by foot, or to indicate that one is travelling by foot as opposed to by a vehicle |
| *per procura* (*p.p.* or *per pro*) | through the agency | Also rendered *per procurationem*. Used to indicate that a person is signing a document on behalf of another person. Correctly placed before the name of the person signing, but often placed before the name of the person on whose behalf the document is signed, sometimes through incorrect translation of the alternative abbreviation per pro. as "for and on behalf of". |
| *[per quod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_quod)* | by reason of which | In a UK legal context: "by reason of which" (as opposed to *per se* which requires no reasoning). In American jurisprudence often refers to a spouse's claim for [loss of consortium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loss_of_consortium). |
| *[per rectum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectal_%28medicine%29) (pr)* | through the rectum | [Medical shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_prescription); see also *per os* |
| *per rectum ad astra* | via rectum to the stars | a modern parody of [per aspera ad astra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_aspera_ad_astra), originating and most commonly used in Russia, meaning that the path to success took you through most undesirable and objectionable places or environments; or that a found solution to a complex problem is extremely convoluted. |
| *per risum multum poteris cognoscere stultum* | by excessive laughter one can recognise the fool |  |
| *per scientiam ad salutem* | through science to health | Motto of [The Michener Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Michener_Institute) |
| *[per se](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/per%20se)* | through itself | Also "by itself" or "in itself".
