See also *[malum in se](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malum_in_se)*. |
| *[per stirpes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_stirpes)* | through the roots | Used in [wills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_%28law%29) to indicate that each "branch" of the [testator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Testator)'s family should inherit equally. Contrasted with *per capita*. |
| *per unitatem vis* | through unity, strength | Motto of [Texas A&M University Corps of Cadets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_A&M_University_Corps_of_Cadets) |
| *per veritatem vis* | through truth, strength | Motto of [Washington University in St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_University_in_St._Louis) |
| *per volar sunata^(\[sic\])* | born to soar | Frequently used motto; not from Latin but from Dante's *[Purgatorio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purgatorio)*, [Canto XII, 95](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/it:Divina%20Commedia/Purgatorio/Canto%20XII), the Italian phrase "per volar sù nata". |
| *Perfer et obdura; dolor hic tibi proderit olim* | Be patient and tough; some day this pain will be useful to you. | From [Ovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid), [Amores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amores_%28Ovid%29), Book III, Elegy XI |
| *[periculum in mora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periculum_in_mora)* | danger in delay |  |
| *perinde ac \[si\] cadaver \[essent\]* | \[well-disciplined\] like a corpse | Phrase written by [St. Ignatius of Loyola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignatius_of_Loyola) in his *Constitutiones Societatis Iesu* (1954) |
| *perita manus mens exculta* | skilled hand, cultivated mind | Motto of [RMIT University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RMIT_University) in Melbourne, Australia |
| *perge sequar* | advance, I follow | from [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil)'s *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)* [IV 114](https://la.wikipedia.org/wiki/s:Aeneis/Liber%20IV); in Vergil's context: "proceed with your plan, I will do my part." |
| *Pericula ludus* | Danger is my pleasure | Motto of the [Foreign Legion Detachment in Mayotte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Legion_Detachment_in_Mayotte) |
| *[perpetuum mobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetuum_mobile)* | thing in [perpetual motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perpetual_motion) | A musical term; also used to refer to hypothetical perpetual motion machines |
| *Perseverantia et Fide in Deo* | Perseverance and Faith in God | Motto of [Bombay Scottish School, Mahim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombay_Scottish_School,_Mahim), India |
| *[persona non grata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persona_non_grata)* | person not pleasing | An unwelcome, unwanted or undesirable person. In [diplomatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomacy) contexts, a person rejected by the host government. The reverse, *persona grata* ("pleasing person"), is less common, and refers to a diplomat acceptable to the government of the country to which he is sent. |
| *[Pes meus stetit in directo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pes_meus_stetit_in_directo)* | My foot has stood in the right way (or in uprightness; in integrity) | Motto of the Light Armoured Cavalry Regiment Santiago No 1, Spanish Army;[^7692] [Psalm 26:12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_26) |
| *petitio principii* | request of the beginning | [Begging the question](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Begging_the_question), a logical [fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacy) in which a proposition to be proved is implicitly or explicitly assumed in one of the premises |
| *pia desideria* | pious longings | Or "dutiful desires" |
| *pia fraus* | pious fraud | Or "dutiful deceit". Expression from [Ovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid); used to describe deception which serves Church purposes |
| *[pia mater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pia_mater)* | pious mother | Or "tender mother". The delicate innermost of the three membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord. |
| *Pietate et doctrina tuta libertas* | Freedom is made safe through character and learning | Motto of [Dickinson College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickinson_College) |
| *[pinxit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinxit)* | one painted | Thus, "he painted this" or "she painted this". Formerly used on works of art, next to the artist's name. |
| [*piscem natare doces*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teach_fish_how_to_swim) | \[you\] teach a fish to swim | Latin proverb, attributed by [Erasmus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erasmus) in his *[Adagia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adagia)[^7693]* to Greek origin ([Diogenianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogenianus), Ἰχθὺν νήχεσθαι διδάσκεις); corollary Chinese idiom (班門弄斧) |
| *piscis primum a capite foetet* | the fish stinks first from the head | Found in [Erasmus's *Adages*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Works_of_Erasmus);[^7693] similarly in [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Classical_Greek_phrases) (Ἰχθὺς ἐκ τῆς κεφαλῆς ὄζειν ἄρχεται), fifteenth century CE *Paroemiae* of [Michael Apostolius Paroemiographus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Apostolius_Paroemiographus).[^7694] |
| *placet* | it pleases | expression of assent |
| *plaudite, cives* | applaud, citizens | Said by ancient comic actors to solicit the audience's applause |
| *[plene scriptum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plene_scriptum)* | fully written |  |
| *plenus venter non studet libenter* | A full belly does not like studying | I.e., it is difficult to concentrate on mental tasks after a heavy meal. The following variant is also attested: *plenus si venter renuit studere libenter* (the belly, when full, refuses to study willingly). |
| *plenus venter facile de ieiuniis disputat* | A full belly readily discusses fasting. | [Hieronymus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome), Epistulæ 58,2 |
| *[plurale tantum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurale_tantum)* pl. *pluralia tantum* | [plural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plural) only | nouns that only occur in the plural form |
| *[pluralis majestatis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluralis_majestatis)* | plural of majesty | The first-person plural pronoun when used by an important personage to refer to himself or herself; also known as the "royal *we*" |
| *[pluralis modestiae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluralis_modestiae)* | plural of modesty |  |
| *plus minusve (p.m.v.)* | more or less | Frequently found on Roman funerary inscriptions to denote that the age of a decedent is approximate |
| *[plus ultra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plus_ultra)* | further beyond | National motto of Spain and a number of other institutions |
| *pollice compresso favor iudicabatur* | goodwill decided by compressed thumb | Life was spared with a thumb tucked inside a closed fist, simulating a sheathed weapon. Conversely, a thumb up meant to unsheath your sword. |
| *[pollice verso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollice_verso)* | with a turned thumb | Used by Roman crowds to pass judgment on a defeated gladiator. The type of gesture used is uncertain. Also the name of a famous painting depicting gladiators by [Jean-Léon Gérôme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-L%C3%A9on_G%C3%A9r%C3%B4me). |
| *Polonia Restituta* | Rebirth of [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland) |  |
| *[pons asinorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pons_asinorum)* | bridge of asses | Any obstacle that stupid people find hard to cross. Originally used of [Euclid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid)'s Fifth Proposition in [geometry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometry). |
| *[pontifex maximus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontifex_maximus)* | greatest high priest | Or "supreme pontiff". Originally an office in the [Roman Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic), later a title held by [Roman emperors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_emperor), and later a traditional epithet of the [pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope). The *pontifices* were the most important priestly college of the [religion in ancient Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_ancient_Rome); their name is usually thought to derive from *pons facere* ("to make a bridge"), which in turn is usually linked to their religious authority over the bridges of Rome, especially the [Pons Sublicius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pons_Sublicius). |
| *[posse comitatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Posse_comitatus)* | force of the county[^7695] | Thus, to be able to be made into part of a retinue or force. In common law, a sheriff's right to compel people to assist law enforcement in unusual situations. |
| *possunt quia posse videntur* | They can because they think they can | Inscription on the back of Putney medals, awarded to [boat race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Boat_Race) winning [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University) [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_%28university_sport%29). From Virgil's Aeneid Book V line 231. Also the motto of Foster's School, Sherborne, Dorset (1640-1992). |
| *post aut propter* | after it or by means of it | Causality between two phenomena is not established (cf. *post hoc, ergo propter hoc*) |
| *post cibum (p.c.)* | after food | [Medical shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_prescription) for "after meals" (cf. *ante cibum*) |
| *post coitum* | After sex | After sexual intercourse |
| *post coitum omne animal triste est sive gallus et mulier* | After sexual intercourse every animal is sad, except the cock ([rooster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rooster)) and the woman | Or: *triste est omne animal post coitum, praeter mulierem gallumque*. Attributed to [Galen of Pergamum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galen).[^7696] |
| *post eventum* | after the event | Refers to an action or occurrence that takes place after the event that is being discussed (similar in meaning to *post factum*). More specifically, it may refer to a person who is recounting an event long after it took place, implying that details of the story may have changed over time. (Some sources attribute this expression to [George Eliot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Eliot).) |
| *post factum* | after the fact | Not to be confused with *[ex post facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ex_post_facto)*. |
| *post festum* | after the feast | Too late, or after the fact |
| *[post hoc ergo propter hoc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_hoc_ergo_propter_hoc)* | after this, therefore because of this | A logical [fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacy) where one assumes that one thing happening after another thing means that the first thing caused the second. |
| *post meridiem (p.m.)* | after midday | The period from [noon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noon) to [midnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midnight) (cf. *ante meridiem*) |
| *post mortem (pm)* | after death | Usually rendered *postmortem*. Not to be confused with *post meridiem* |
| *Post mortem auctoris (p.m.a.)* | after the author's death | The phrase is used in legal terminology in the context of [intellectual property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property) rights, especially copyright, which commonly lasts until a certain number of years after the author's death. |
| *post nubila phoebus* | after the clouds, the sun | Motto of the [University of Zulia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Zulia), Venezuela, as well as [Hartford, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford,_Connecticut) |
| *post nubes lux* | out of darkness, light | Motto of [Cranfield University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cranfield_University) |
| *post scriptum (p.s.)* | after what has been written | A [postscript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postscript). Used to mark additions to a letter, after the signature. Can be extended to *post post scriptum* (p.p.s.), etc. |
| *[post tenebras lux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_tenebras_lux)*, or, *post tenebras spero lucem* | after darkness, \[I hope for\] light | from [Vulgata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgata), [Job 17:12](https://la.wikipedia.org/wiki/s:Biblia%20Sacra%20Vulgata%20%28Stuttgartensia%29/Iob); frequently used motto |
| *postera crescam laude* | I am going to grow in the esteem of future generations | Motto of the [University of Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Melbourne) |
| *praemia virtutis honores* | honours are the rewards of virtue | Motto of the [Portsmouth Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_Grammar_School) |
| *praemonitus praemunitus* | forewarned is forearmed | Common catch phrase of the title character of the novel *[Captain Blood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Blood_%28novel%29)* |
| *praesis ut prosis* | Lead in order to serve. | Motto of [Lancaster Royal Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_Royal_Grammar_School) |
| *praestant interna (coronae)* | what is inside is better (than the crown) | Motto emphasizing that a person excels primarily through their inner virtues rather than their physical attributes or social rank, a [topos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_topos) in classical [rhetoric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhetoric), inspired in particular by the biblical figure of [David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David) who, according to the [Old Testament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Testament) ([1 Samuel 17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1_Samuel_17)), triumphed over [Goliath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goliath) through faith, bravery and tactical intelligence, despite a physical disadvantage.[^7697] The theme is also recurrent in [Greco-Roman mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Roman_mythology), for instance in the [Labours of Hercules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labours_of_Hercules) or [Homer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer)'s *[Odyssey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odyssey)*. Historically, [court artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_painter) used this motto as a [propaganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propaganda) tool to reinforce the legitimacy of sovereigns, particularly [absolute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolute_monarchy_in_France) or [divine right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_right_of_kings) monarchs like [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV), by praising their personal merits over mere hereditary claims to the crown, as in *L'Automne* (Autumn)[^7698] by [Charles Le Brun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Le_Brun). The motto was sometimes associated with the symbol of the [pomegranate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pomegranate)[^7699] whose tasty [arils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aril) are hidden inside a tough [epicarp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epicarp) topped by a persistent [calyx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calyx_%28botany%29)[^7700] shaped like a crown or, when viewed from above,[^7701] like the six-pointed [Star of David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_of_David), the pomegranate being, in Judeo-Christian and Masonic iconography and ornamentation, a traditional symbol of biblical royalty. |
| *praeter legem* | after the law | Legal terminology, international law |
| *Praga Caput Regni* | Prague, Head of the Kingdom | Motto of [Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prague) from Middle Ages |
| *Praga Caput Rei publicae* | Prague, Head of the Republic | Motto of Prague from 1991 |
| *Praga mater urbium* | Prague, Mother of Cities | Motto of Prague from 1927 |
| *Praga totius Bohemiae domina* | Prague, the mistress of the whole of Bohemia | Former motto of Prague |

| *[prima facie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prima_facie)* | at first sight | Used to designate [evidence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evidence_%28law%29) in a [trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_%28law%29) which is suggestive, but not conclusive, of something (e.g., a person's guilt) |
| *prima luce* | at dawn | Literally "at first light" |
| *primas sum: primatum nil a me alienum puto* | I am a primate; nothing about primates is foreign to me | A sentence by the American anthropologist [Earnest Hooton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earnest_Hooton) and the slogan of primatologists and lovers of primates. Derived from *[homo sum, humani a me nihil alienum puto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28H%29)*. |
| *primum mobile* | first moving thing | Or "first thing able to be moved"; see *primum movens* |
| *[primum movens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primum_movens)* | [prime mover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_argument) | Or "first moving one". A common [theological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theology) term, such as in the [cosmological argument](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmological_argument), based on the assumption that [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God) was the first entity to "move" or "cause" anything. [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle) was one of the first philosophers to discuss the "uncaused cause", a hypothetical originator, and violator, of [causality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Causality). |
| *[primum non nocere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primum_non_nocere)* | first, to not harm | A medical precept. Often falsely attributed to the [Hippocratic Oath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippocratic_Oath), though its true source is probably a paraphrase from [Hippocrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippocrates)' *Epidemics*, where he wrote, "Declare the past, diagnose the present, foretell the future; practice these acts. As to diseases, make a habit of two things: to help, or at least to do no harm." |
| *[primus inter pares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primus_inter_pares)* | first among equals | Position of the [Ecumenical Patriarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecumenical_Patriarch) in the [Eastern Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church), position of the [President of the Swiss Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Swiss_Confederation) among the members of the [Federal Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_Federal_Council), and a title of the [Roman Emperors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Emperor) (cf. *[princeps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeps)*). |
| *principia probant non probantur* | principles prove; they are not proved | [Fundamental principles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_principle) require no proof; they are assumed *a priori*. |
| *principiis obsta (et respice finem)* | resist the beginnings (and consider the end) | [Ovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid), *[Remedia Amoris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remedia_Amoris)*, 91 |
| *[principium individuationis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principium_individuationis)* | Individuation | psychological term: the self-formation of the personality into a coherent whole |
| *prior tempore potior iure* | earlier in time, stronger in law | “First in time, greater in right.”A maxim meaning that the law favors those who establish their rights earlier rather than later. | *[pro aris et focis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_aris_et_focis)* | For altars and hearths | The motto of the [Royal Queensland Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Queensland_Regiment), and many other regiments. |

Often used of a [lawyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawyer)'s work that is not charged for. |
| *pro Brasilia fiant eximia* | let exceptional things be made for Brazil | [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_mottos) of [São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A3o_Paulo_%28state%29) state, [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil). |
| *pro Deo Domo Patria* | For God, home and country | Motto of the [University of Mary Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Mary_Washington) |
| *pro Deo et Patria* | For God and Country | Frequently used motto |
| *pro domo (sua)* | for (one’s own) home or house | serving the interests of a given perspective or for the benefit of a given group. |
| *pro Ecclesia, pro Texana* | For Church, For Texas | Motto of [Baylor University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baylor_University), a private Christian Baptist university in Waco, Texas. |
| *pro fide et patria* | for faith and fatherland | Motto of the originally Irish [Muldoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muldoon_%28disambiguation%29) family and of several schools, such as the [Diocesan College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocesan_College) (Bishops) in Cape Town, South Africa, and [All Hallows High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Hallows_High_School) in the Bronx, New York. |
| *[pro forma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_forma)* | for form | Or "as a matter of form". Prescribing a set form or procedure, or performed in a set manner. |
| *pro gloria et patria* | for glory and fatherland | Motto of [Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prussia) |
| *pro hac vice* | for this occasion | Request of a state court to allow an out-of-state lawyer to represent a client. |
| *[pro multis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_multis)* | for many | It is part of the Rite of Consecration of the [wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine) in [Western Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Christianity) tradition, as part of the [Mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_%28liturgy%29). |
| *[pro parte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_parte)* | in part | Frequently used in [taxonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxonomy_%28general%29) to refer to part of a [group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxon). |
| *pro patria* | for country | Pro Patria Medal: for operational service (minimum 55 days) in defence of the Republic South Africa or in the prevention or suppression of terrorism; issued for the Border War (counter-insurgency operations in South West Africa 1966-89) and for campaigns in Angola (1975-76 and 1987-88). Motto of [The Royal Canadian Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Royal_Canadian_Regiment), [Royal South Australia Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_South_Australia_Regiment), [Hurlstone Agricultural High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurlstone_Agricultural_High_School). |
| *pro patria vigilans* | watchful for the country | Motto of the [United States Army Signal Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal_Corps_%28United_States_Army%29). |
| *pro populo et gloria* | for the people and glory | Motto of [HMS *Westminster*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Westminster_%28L40%29) |
| *pro per* | for self | to defend oneself in court without counsel; abbreviation of *propria persona*. See also: [pro se](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_se). |
| [*pro rata*](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/pro%20rata) | for the rate | i.e., proportionately. |

Also "concerning a matter having come into being". Used to describe a meeting of a special [Presbytery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbytery_%28church_polity%29) or Assembly called to discuss something new, and which was previously unforeseen (literally: "concerning a matter having been born"). |
| *pro rege et lege* | for king and the law | Found on the [Leeds coat of arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_Leeds). |

| *[pro se](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_se)* | for oneself | to defend oneself in court without counsel. Some jurisdictions prefer, "pro per". |
| *pro scientia atque sapientia* | for knowledge and wisdom | motto of [Stuyvesant High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuyvesant_High_School) in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City) |
| *pro scientia et patria* | for science and nation | motto of the [National University of La Plata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_University_of_La_Plata) |
| *pro studio et labore* | for study and work |  |
| *pro tanto* | for so much | Denotes something that has only been partially fulfilled. A philosophical term indicating the acceptance of a theory or idea without fully accepting the explanation. |
| *pro tanto quid retribuemus* | what shall we give in return for so much | The motto of the city of [Belfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast); taken from the [Vulgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate) translation of [Psalm 116](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_116). |
| *[pro tempore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro_tempore)* | for the time (being) | Denotes a temporary current situation; abbreviated *pro tem*. |
| *[probatio pennae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probatio_pennae)* | testing of the pen | [Medieval Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Latin) term for breaking in a new pen |
| *probis pateo* | I am open for honest people | Traditionally inscribed above a city gate or above the front entrance of a dwelling or place of learning. |
| *procedendo* | to be proceeded with | From *procedendo ad judicium*, "to be proceeded with to judgment." A [prerogative writ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prerogative_writ), by which a superior court requires an inferior one to rule on a matter it has neglected. |
| *prodesse quam conspici* | To Accomplish Rather Than To Be Conspicuous | motto of [Miami University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_University) |
| *prohibito* | I prohibit | A [prerogative writ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prerogative_writ), by which a superior court prohibits an inferior court from hearing a matter outside its jurisdiction; also called a [writ of prohibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writ_of_prohibition). |
| *propria manu (p.m.)* | "by one's own hand" |  |
| *propter vitam vivendi perdere causas* | to destroy the reasons for living for the sake of life | That is, to squander life's purpose just in order to stay alive, and live a meaningless life. From [Juvenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenal), *Satyricon* VIII, verses 83-84. |
| *protectio trahit subjectionem, et subjectio protectionem* | Protection draws allegiance, and allegiance draws protection | Legal maxim, indicating that reciprocity of fealty with protection |
| *provehito in altum* | launch forward into the deep | motto of [Memorial University of Newfoundland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_University_of_Newfoundland) |
| *proxime accessit* | he came next | the runner-up |
| *proximo mense (prox.)* | in the following month | Used in formal correspondence to refer to the next month. Used with ult. ("last month") and inst. ("this month"). |
| *pulchrum est paucorum hominum* | Beauty is for the few | from [Friedrich Nietzsche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Nietzsche)'s 1889 book *[Twilight of the Idols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilight_of_the_Idols)* |
| *pulvis et umbra sumus* | we are dust and shadow | From [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), *Carmina* Book IV, 7, 16.[^7702] |

#### Q

| Latin | Translation | Notes |
|----|----|----|
| *qua definitione* | by virtue of definition | Thus: "by definition"; variant of per definitionem; sometimes used in German-speaking countries. Occasionally misrendered as "qua definitionem". |
| *qua patet orbis* | as far as the world extends | Motto of the Royal [Netherlands Marine Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_Marine_Corps) |
| *quae cum ita sint* | these things being the case | Or, "since these things are the case" or "Since things are this way". [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero). |
| *quae non posuisti, ne tollas* | do not take away what you did not put in place | [Plato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plato), *[Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laws_%28dialogue%29)* |
| *quae non prosunt singula multa iuvant* | what alone is not useful helps when accumulated | [Ovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid), *[Remedia amoris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remedia_amoris)* |
| *quaecumque sunt vera* | whatsoever is true | frequently used as motto; taken from [Philippians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistle_to_the_Philippians) [4:8](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/la:Biblia%20Sacra%20Vulgata%20%28Stuttgartensia%29/ad%20Philippenses#Caput_4) of the Bible |
| *quaecumque vera doce me* | teach me whatsoever is true | motto of [St. Joseph's College, Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Joseph's_College,_Edmonton) at the [University of Alberta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Alberta) |
| *quaere* | to seek | Or "you might ask..." Used to suggest doubt or to ask one to consider whether something is correct. Often introduces rhetorical or tangential questions. |
| *quaerite primum regnum Dei* | seek ye first the kingdom of God | Also *quaerite primo regnum dei*; frequently used as motto (e.g. [Newfoundland and Labrador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newfoundland_and_Labrador)) |
| *qualis artifex pereo* | As what kind of artist do I perish? | Or "What a craftsman dies in me!" Attributed to [Nero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nero) in [Suetonius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suetonius)' *[De vita Caesarum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twelve_Caesars)* |
| *Qualitas potentia nostra* | Quality is our might | motto of [Finnish Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_Air_Force) |
| *quam bene non quantum* | how well, not how much | motto of [Mount Royal University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Royal_University), Calgary, Canada |
| *quam bene vivas referre* (or *refert), non quam diu* | it is how well you live that matters, not how long | [Seneca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger), *[Epistulae morales ad Lucilium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistulae_morales_ad_Lucilium)* [CI (101)](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/la:Epistulae%20morales%20ad%20Lucilium/Liber%20XVII%20-%20XVIII) |
| *quamdiu (se) bene gesserit* | as long as he shall have behaved well (legal Latin) | I.e., "\[while on\] good behavior." So for example the [Act of Settlement 1701](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_of_Settlement_1701) stipulated that judges' commissions are valid *quamdiu se bene gesserint* (during good behaviour). (Notice the different singular, "gesserit", and plural, "gesserint", forms.) It was from this phrase that [Frank Herbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Herbert) extracted the name for the [Bene Gesserit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bene_Gesserit) sisterhood in the *[Dune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dune_%28franchise%29)* novels. |
| *[quantocius](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/quantocius) quantotius* | the sooner, the better | or, as quickly as possible |
| *quantum libet (q.l.)* | as much as pleases | [medical shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_prescription) for "as much as you wish" |
| *quantum sufficit (qs)* | as much as is enough | [medical shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_prescription) for "as much as needed" or "as much as will suffice" |
| *quaque hora (qh)* | every hour | [medical shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_prescription); also *quaque die* (qd), "every day", *quaque mane* (qm), "every morning", and *quaque nocte* (qn), "every night" |
| *quare clausum fregit* | wherefore he broke the close | An action of trespass; thus called, by reason the writ demands the person summoned to answer to *wherefore he broke the close* *(quare clausum fregit)*, i.e. why he committed such a trespass. |
| *quater in die (qid)* | four times a day | [medical shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_prescription) |
| *quem deus vult perdere, dementat prius* | [Whom the gods would destroy, they first make mad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whom_the_gods_would_destroy,_they_first_make_mad) |  |
| *quem di diligunt adulescens moritur* | he whom the gods love dies young | Other translations of *diligunt* include "prize especially" or "esteem". From [Plautus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plautus), *[Bacchides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacchides_%28play%29)*, IV, 7, 18. In this comic play, a sarcastic servant says this to his aging master. The rest of the sentence reads: *dum valet sentit sapit* ("while he is healthy, perceptive and wise"). |
| *questio quid iuris* | I ask what law? | from the Summoner's section of [Chaucer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Chaucer)'s General Prologue to *[The Canterbury Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Canterbury_Tales)*, line 648 |
| *qui audet adipiscitur* | [Who Dares Wins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who_Dares_Wins) | The motto of the SAS, of the British Army |
| *qui bene cantat bis orat* | [He who sings well praises twice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He_who_sings,_prays_twice) | from St. [Augustine of Hippo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Hippo)'s commentary on Psalm 73, verse 1: *Qui enim cantat laudem, non solum laudat, sed etiam hilariter laudat* ("He who sings praises, not only praises, but praises joyfully") |
| *qui bono* | who with good | common misspelling of the Latin phrase *[cui bono](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cui_bono)* ("who benefits?") |
| *qui docet in doctrina* | he that teacheth, on teaching | Motto of the [University of Chester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Chester). A less literal translation is "Let those who teach, teach" or "Let the teacher teach". |
| *qui gladio ferit gladio perit* | He who strikes a sword dies by the sword | Or "[live by the sword, die by the sword](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_by_the_sword,_die_by_the_sword)"; derived from Jesus's words in the garden of [Gethsemane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gethsemane) in the [Gospel of Matthew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_of_Matthew) 26:52, *Omnes enim, qui acceperint gladium, gladio peribunt* (for all who take up the sword shall perish by the sword). |
| *qui habet aures audiendi audiat* | he who has ears to hear, let him hear | "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear"; [Mark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_of_Mark) [Mark 4:9](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bible%20%28King%20James%29/Mark#4:9) |
| *qui me tangit, vocem meam audit* | who touches me, hears my voice | common inscription on bells |
| *[qui tacet consentire videtur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silence_procedure)* | he who is silent is taken to agree | Thus, silence gives consent. Sometimes accompanied by the proviso "*ubi loqui debuit ac potuit*", that is, "when he ought to have spoken and was able to". Pope Boniface VII in *Decretale di Bonifacio VIII, Libro V, Tit. 12, reg. 43* AD 1294 |
| *qui prior est tempore potior est jure* | Who is first in point of time is stronger in right | As set forth in the "Property Law" casebook written by Jesse Dukeminier, which is generally used to teach first year law students. |
| *qui tam pro domino rege quam pro se ipso in hac parte sequitur* | he who brings an action for the king as well as for himself | Generally known as 'qui tam,' it is the technical legal term for the unique mechanism in the federal False Claims Act that allows persons and entities with evidence of fraud against federal programs or contracts to sue the wrongdoer on behalf of the Government. |
| *qui totum vult totum perdit* | he who wants everything loses everything | Attributed to [Publilius Syrus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publilius_Syrus) |
| *qui transtulit sustinet* | he who transplanted still sustains | Or "he who brought us across still supports us", meaning [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God). [State motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_and_territory_mottos) of [Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connecticut). Originally written as *sustinet qui transtulit* in 1639. |
| *quia suam uxorem etiam suspicione vacare vellet* | because he should wish his wife to be free even from any suspicion | Attributed to [Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar) by [Plutarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutarch), *Caesar* 10. Translated loosely as "because even the wife of Caesar may not be suspected". At the feast of [Bona Dea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bona_Dea), a sacred festival for females only, which was being held at the Domus Publica, the home of the [Pontifex Maximus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontifex_Maximus), Caesar, and hosted by his second wife, [Pompeia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompeia_%28wife_of_Julius_Caesar%29), the notorious politician [Clodius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publius_Clodius_Pulcher) arrived in disguise. Caught by the outraged noblewomen, Clodius fled before they could kill him on the spot for sacrilege. In the ensuing trial, allegations arose that Pompeia and Clodius were having an affair, and while Caesar asserted that this was not the case and no substantial evidence arose suggesting otherwise, he nevertheless divorced, with this quotation as explanation. |
| *quibuscum(que) viis* | (and) by whatever ways possible | Used by [Honoré de Balzac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honor%C3%A9_de_Balzac) in several works,[^7703] including *[Illusions perdues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illusions_perdues)* and *[Splendeurs et misères des courtisanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splendeurs_et_mis%C3%A8res_des_courtisanes)*. |
| *quid agis* | What are you doing? | What's happening? What's going on? What's the news? What's up? |
| *quid est veritas* | What is truth? | In the [Vulgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate) translation of [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_of_John) 18:38, [Pilate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontius_Pilate)'s question to [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus) (Greek: Τί ἐστιν ἀλήθεια;). A possible answer is an anagram of the phrase: *est vir qui adest*, "it is the man who is here." |
| *quid novi ex Africa* | What of the new out of Africa? | less literally, "What's new from Africa?"; derived from an [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle) quotation |
| *quid nunc* | What now? | Commonly shortened to *quidnunc*. As a noun, a *quidnunc* is a busybody or a gossip. [Patrick Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Campbell,_3rd_Baron_Glenavy) worked for *[The Irish Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Irish_Times)* under the [pseudonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudonym) "Quidnunc". |
| *quid sit quidditas quidditatis* | What is the [quiddity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiddity) of quiddity? | A philosophical question also raised, in the context of German legal theory, by Wilhelm Scheuerle in his classic 1963 essay *Vom Wesen des Wesens: Studien über das sogenannte Wesensargument im juristischen Begründen*.[^7704] |
| *[quid pro quo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quid_pro_quo)* | what for what | Commonly used in English, it is also translated as "this for that" or "a thing for a thing". Signifies a favor exchanged for a favor. The traditional Latin expression for this meaning was *[do ut des](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_ancient_Roman_religion)* ("I give, so that you may give"). |
| *quid pro tanto retribuamus* | What shall we give back in return for so much? | Exhortation regarding civic duty, cultural inheritance, and the responsibility of the living to honor the sacrifices of the past. Generalised from *Quid retribuam Domino pro omnibus quae retribuit mihi?* ("What shall I render to the Lord for all His benefits toward me?") from [Psalm 116](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psalm_116):12. |
| *Quid rides? Mutato nomine de te fabula narratur.* | Why do you laugh? Change but the name, and the story is told of yourself. | [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), [*Satires*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satires_%28Horace%29), I. 1. 69. |
| *quidquid Latine dictum sit altum videtur* | whatever has been said in Latin seems deep | Or "anything said in Latin sounds profound". A recent ironic Latin phrase to poke fun at people who seem to use Latin phrases and quotations only to make themselves sound more important or "educated". Similar to the less common *omnia dicta fortiora si dicta Latina*. |
| *Quidquid non agnoscit glossa, non agnoscit curia* | Whatever the *[Glossa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossa_ordinaria_%28Accursius%29)* does not recognize, the court does not recognize. |  |
| *quieta non movere* | don't move settled things |  |
| *quilibet potest renunciare juri pro se inducto* | anyone may renounce a law introduced for their own benefit | Used in classical law to differentiate law imposed by the state for the benefit of a person in general, but by the state on behalf of them, and one imposed specifically that that person ought to have a say in whether the law is implemented. |
| *[Quis custodiet ipsos custodes?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quis_custodiet_ipsos_custodes?)* | Who will guard the guards themselves? | Commonly associated with [Plato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plato) who in the *[Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Republic_%28Plato%29)* poses this question; and from [Juvenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenal)'s *[On Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire_VI)*, referring to the practice of having [eunuchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunuch) guard women and beginning with the word *sed* ("but"). Usually translated less literally, as "Who watches the watchmen (or modern, 'watchers')?" This translation is a common [epigraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epigraph_%28literature%29), such as of the [Tower Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_Commission) and [Alan Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Moore)'s *[Watchmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchmen)* comic book series. |
| *quis leget haec?* | Who will read this? |  |
| *quis, quid, ubi, quibus auxiliis, cur, quomodo, quando?* | Who, what, where, by what means, why, how, when? | Compare the [Five Ws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Ws). From [Thomas Aquinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Aquinas)'s *[Summa Theologica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summa_Theologica)*, but ancient authors provide other similar lists. |
| *[quis separabit?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quis_separabit?)* | Who will separate us? | motto of [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland) and of the [Order of St Patrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_St_Patrick) |
| *quis ut Deus* | Who \[is\] as God? | Usually translated "Who is like unto God?" Questions who would have the audacity to compare himself to a Supreme Being. It is a translation of the Hebrew name 'Michael' = Mi cha El Who like God מי/כ/ אל [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language): מִיכָאֵל (right to left). |
| *quo errat demonstrator* | where the prover errs | A pun on "[quod erat demonstrandum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q.E.D.)" |
| *quo fata ferunt* | where the fates bear us to | motto of [Bermuda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bermuda) |
| *quo non ascendam* | to what heights can I not rise? | motto of [Army Burn Hall College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Burn_Hall_College) |
| *quod verum tutum* | what is true is right | motto of [Spier's School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spier's_School) |
| *Quo Vadimus?* | Where are we going? | Title of the [series finale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Sports_Night_episodes) of [Aaron Sorkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Sorkin)'s TV [dramedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dramedy) *[Sports Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Night)* |
| *[quo vadis?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quo_vadis?)* | Where are you going? | According to [Vulgate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgate) translation of [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gospel_of_John) 13:36, [Saint Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Peter) asked [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus) *Domine, quo vadis?* ("Lord, where are you going?"). The [King James Version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authorized_King_James_Version) has the translation "Lord, whither goest thou?" |
| *[Quo warranto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quo_warranto)* | by what warrant? | [Medieval Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Latin) title for a [prerogative writ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prerogative_writ) by which a court requires some person or entity to prove the source of some authority it is exercising. Used for various purposes in different jurisdictions. |
| *quocunque jeceris stabit* | whithersoever you throw it, it will stand | motto of the [Isle of Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Man) |
| *quod abundat non obstat* | what is abundant doesn't hinder | It is no problem to have too much of something. |
| *quod cito fit, cito perit* | what is done quickly, perishes quickly | Things done in a hurry are more likely to fail and fail quicker than those done with care. |
| *quod erat demonstrandum* (*[Q.E.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q.E.D.)*) | what was to be demonstrated | The abbreviation is often written at the bottom of a [mathematical proof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathematical_proof). Sometimes translated loosely into English as "The Five Ws", W.W.W.W.W., which stands for "Which Was What We Wanted". |
| *quod erat faciendum* (*Q.E.F.*) | which was to be done | Or "which was to be constructed". Used in translations of Euclid's *[Elements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid's_Elements)* when there was nothing to prove, but there was something being constructed, for example a triangle with the same size as a given line. |
| *quod est* (*q.e.*) | which is |  |
| *quod est necessarium est licitum* | what is necessary is lawful |  |
| *quod gratis asseritur, gratis negatur* | what is asserted without reason may be denied without reason | If no grounds have been given for an assertion, then there are no grounds needed to reject it. |
| *[quod licet Iovi, non licet bovi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quod_licet_Iovi,_non_licet_bovi)* | what is permitted to [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_%28mythology%29) is not permitted to an ox | If an important person does something, it does not necessarily mean that everyone can do it (cf. [double standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_standard)). *Iovi* (also commonly rendered *Jovi*) is the [dative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dative_case) form of *Iuppiter* ("Jupiter" or "Jove"), the chief god of the Romans. |
| *quod me nutrit me destruit* | what nourishes me destroys me | Cf. [§ quod sapit nutrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28full%29). Thought to have originated with Elizabethan playwright [Christopher Marlowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Marlowe). Generally interpreted to mean that that which motivates or drives a person can consume him or her from within. This phrase has become a popular slogan or motto for [pro-ana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-ana) websites, [anorexics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anorexia_nervosa) and [bulimics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulimia_nervosa). |
| *quod natura non dat Salmantica non praestat* | what nature does not give, [Salamanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salamanca) does not provide | Refers to the Spanish [University of Salamanca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Salamanca), meaning that education cannot substitute the lack of brains. |
| *quod non fecerunt barbari, fecerunt Barberini* | What the barbarians did not do, the Barberinis did | A well-known satirical lampoon left attached to the ancient ["speaking" statue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talking_statues_of_Rome) of [Pasquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasquino) on a corner of the [Piazza Navona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piazza_Navona) in Rome, Italy.[^7705] Through a sharp pun the writer criticizes [Pope Urban VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Urban_VIII), of the [Barberini family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barberini_family), who reused stones and decorations from ancient buildings to build new ones, thus wrecking classical constructions that even the barbarians had not touched. |
| *quod periit, periit* | What is gone is gone | What has happened has happened and it cannot be changed, thus we should look forward into the future instead of being pulled by the past. |
| *quod sapit nutrit* | what tastes good nourishes | Ancient saying, promoted by [Galen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galen);[^7706] cf. [§ quod me nutrit me destruit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28full%29) |
| *[quod scripsi, scripsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quod_scripsi,_scripsi)* | What I have written I have written. | Pilate to the chief priests ([John 19:22](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bible%20%28King%20James%29/John#19:22)) |
| *quod supplantandum, prius bene sciendum* | Whatever is to be supplanted, \[must\] first be understood | A caution against following a doctrine of Naive Analogy when attempting to formulate a scientific hypothesis. |
| *quod vide (q.v.)* | which see | Used after a term, phrase, or topic that should be looked up elsewhere in the current document, book, etc. For more than one term or phrase, the plural is *quae vide* (qq.v.). |
| *quodcumque dixerit vobis, facite* | Whatever He tells you, that you shall do. | More colloquially: "Do whatever He \[Jesus\] tells you to do." Instructions of Mary to the servants at the [Wedding at Cana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedding_at_Cana). ([John 2:5](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bible%20%28King%20James%29/John#2:5)). Also the motto of [East Catholic High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Catholic_High_School). |
| *quomodo vales* | How are you? | Mainly in [Neo-Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Latin), but also in [John Jortin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Jortin) (1758), *The Life of Erasmus*, vol. 1, [p. 196](https://books.google.com/books?id=Lhq2_HDZDv0C&pg=PA196) |
| *[quorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quorum)* | of whom | the number of members whose presence is required under the rules to make any given meeting constitutional |
| *quorum pars minima fui* | of whom I was a small part | Attributed to notorious spy [Kim Philby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Philby) discussing his contribution to the status of [Allen Dulles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_Dulles) as a legendary clandestine officer[^7707] |
| *quos amor verus tenuit tenebit* | Those whom true love has held, it will go on holding | from *[Thyestes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thyestes_%28Seneca%29)*, [Seneca the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger) |
| *quot capita, tot sensus* | as many heads, so many perceptions | "There are as many opinions as there are heads" - [Terence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terence) |
| *quot homines tot sententiae* | as many men, so many opinions | Or "there are as many opinions as there are people", "how many people, so many opinions" |
| [*quousque tandem?*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quousque_tandem_abutere,_Catilina,_patientia_nostra?) | For how much longer? | From [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero)'s [first speech](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/la:Oratio%20in%20Catilinam%20Prima%20in%20Senatu%20Habita) *[In Catilinam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catilinarian_orations)* to the [Roman Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Senate) regarding the conspiracy of [Catiline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catiline): *Quo usque tandem abutere, Catilina, patientia nostra?* ("For how much longer, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?"). Besides being a well-known line in itself, it was often used as a text sample in printing (cf. [lorem ipsum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorem_ipsum)). See also *[O tempora, o mores!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O_tempora,_o_mores!)* (from the same speech). |

#### R

| Latin | Translation | Notes |
|----|----|----|
| *radix malorum est cupiditas* | the root of evils is desire | Or "[greed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greed_%28emotion%29) is the root of all evil". Theme of "[The Pardoner's Tale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pardoner's_Tale)" from *[The Canterbury Tales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Canterbury_Tales)*. |
| *rara avis* (*rarissima avis*) | rare bird (very rare bird) | An extraordinary or unusual thing. From [Juvenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenal)'s *[Satires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satires_%28Juvenal%29) [VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satire_VI)*: *rara avis in terris nigroque simillima cygno* ("a rare bird in the lands, and very like a [black swan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_swan)"). |
| *rari nantes in gurgite vasto* | Rare survivors in the immense sea | [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil), *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)*, [I, 118](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/la:Aeneis/Liber%20I#115) |
| *[ratio decidendi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratio_decidendi)* | reasoning for the decision | The legal, moral, political, and social principles used by a court to compose a judgment's rationale. |
| *ratio legis* | reasoning of law | A law's foundation or basis. |
| *ratione personae* | by reason of his/her person | Also "jurisdiction ratione personae" the personal reach of the courts jurisdiction.[^7708] |
| *[ratione soli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ratione_soli)* | by account of the ground | Or "according to the soil". Assigning property rights to a thing based on its presence on a landowner's property. |
| *[ratum](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/ratus#Latin) et [consummatum](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/consummatus)* | confirmed and completed | in [Canon law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_law), a [consummated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consummation) marriage |
| *ratum [tantum](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/tantum)* | confirmed only | in Canon law, a confirmed but unconsummated marriage (which can be dissolved *super rato*) |
| *re* | \[in\] the matter of | More literally, "by the thing". From the [ablative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ablative_case) of *res* ("thing" or "circumstance"). It is a common misconception that the "Re:" in correspondence is an abbreviation for *regarding* or *reply*; this is not the case for traditional letters. However, when used in an [e-mail subject](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-mail_subject_abbreviations), there is evidence that it functions as an abbreviation of *regarding* rather than the Latin word for *thing*. The use of Latin *re*, in the sense of "about", "concerning", is English usage. |
| *rebus sic stantibus* | with matters standing thus | The doctrine that [treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty) obligations hold only as long as the fundamental conditions and expectations that existed at the time of their creation hold. |
| *recte et fortiter* | Upright and Strong | Motto of [Homebush Boys High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homebush_Boys_High_School) |
| *recte et fideliter* | Upright and Faithful | Also "just and faithful" and "accurately and faithfully". Motto of [Ruyton Girls' School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruyton_Girls'_School) |
| *[redde rationem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redde_rationem)* | to give an account | Taken from the Gospel of Luke 16:2. |
| *[reductio ad absurdum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductio_ad_absurdum)* | leading back to the absurd | A common debate technique, and a method of proof in mathematics and philosophy, that proves the thesis by showing that its opposite is absurd or logically untenable. In general usage outside mathematics and philosophy, a *reductio ad absurdum* is a tactic in which the logic of an argument is challenged by reducing the concept to its most absurd extreme. Translated from [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle)'s "ἡ εις άτοπον απαγωγη" (*hi eis atopon apagogi*, "reduction to the impossible"). |
| *[reductio ad Hitlerum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reductio_ad_Hitlerum)* | leading back to Hitler | A term coined by German-American political philosopher [Leo Strauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Strauss) to humorously describe a fallacious argument that compares an opponent's views to those held by [Adolf Hitler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Hitler) or the [Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party). Derived from *reductio ad absurdum*. |
| *reductio ad infinitum* | leading back to the infinite | An argument that creates an infinite series of causes that does not seem to have a beginning. As a fallacy, it rests upon Aristotle's notion that all things must have a cause, but that all series of causes must have a sufficient cause, that is, an unmoved mover. An argument which does not seem to have such a beginning becomes difficult to imagine. If it can be established, separately, that the chain must have a start, then a reductio ad infinitum is a valid refutation technique. |
| *[reformatio in peius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformatio_in_peius)* | change to worse | A decision from a court of appeal is amended to a worse one. With certain exceptions, this is [prohibited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformatio_in_peius) at the [Boards of Appeal of the European Patent Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boards_of_Appeal_of_the_European_Patent_Office) by [case law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_law). |
| *regem ego comitem me comes regem* | you made me a Count, I will make you a King | Motto of the Forbin family |
| *reginam occidere* | to kill the queen | Written by [John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_%28archbishop_of_Esztergom%29), archbishop of [Esztergom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esztergom), to Hungarian nobles planning the [assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Gertrude_of_Merania) of [Gertrude of Merania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gertrude_of_Merania). The full sentence, *Reginam occidere nolite timere bonum est si omnes consentiunt ego non contradico*, has two contradictory meanings depending on how it is punctuated: either *Reginam occidere nolite timere; bonum est; si omnes consentiunt, ego non contradico* (do not fear to kill the queen, it is right; if everyone agrees, I do not oppose it) or *Reginam occidere nolite; timere bonum est; si omnes consentiunt, ego non; contradico* (do not kill the queen; it is good to fear \[doing so\]; \[even\] if everyone agrees, I do not; I oppose it). The queen was assassinated as the plotters saw the bishop's message as an encouragement. |
| *[regnat populus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regnat_populus)* | the people rule | [State motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_mottos) of [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas), adopted in 1907. Originally rendered in 1864 in the plural, *regnant populi* ("the peoples rule"), but subsequently changed to the singular. |
| *regnet christus* | Christ reigns | motto of [Our Lady of the Sacred Heart College, Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our_Lady_of_the_Sacred_Heart_College,_Sydney) |
| *regnum juris regnum pacis* | rule of law, rule of peace | Motto of the [Henry N.R. Jackman Faculty of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_N.R._Jackman_Faculty_of_Law) at the [University of Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Toronto) |
| *Regnum Mariae Patrona Hungariae* | Kingdom of Mary, the Patron of Hungary | Former motto of [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary) |
| *[regressus ad uterum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regressus_ad_uterum)* | return to the womb | Concept used in psychoanalysis by [Sándor Ferenczi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A1ndor_Ferenczi) and the Budapest School |
| *[rem acu tetigisti](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/rem%20acu%20tango#Latin)* | You have touched the point with a needle | i.e., "You have hit the nail on the head" |
| *rem tene, verba sequentur* | Understand the matter, the words will follow | That is, know the contents of your argument, what you intend to say, and then the way to say it, the precise words, will come easily. |
| *[Renovatio imperii Romanorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renovatio_imperii_Romanorum)* | Renewal of the empire of the Romans | A phrase declaring an intention to restore the Roman Empire. |
| *renovatio urbis* | urban renewal | a period of city planning and architectural updating in Renaissance Italy, i.e. the vast architectural programme begun under Doge [Andrea Gritti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrea_Gritti) in Venice[^7709] |
| *repetita iuvant* | repeating does good | Lit: "Repeated things help". Usually said as a jocular remark to defend the speaker's (or writer's) choice to repeat some important piece of information to ensure reception by the audience. |
| *repetitio est mater studiorum* | repetition is the mother of study/learning |  |
| *requiem aeternam dona ei(s), Domine* | give him/her (them) eternal rest, O Lord | From the Christian prayer [Eternal Rest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eternal_Rest), said for the dead. Source of the term [requiem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem), meaning the Mass for the Dead or a musical setting thereof. |
| *[requiescat in pace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiescat_in_pace) (R.I.P.)* | let him/her rest in peace | Or "may he/she rest in peace". A benediction for the dead. Often inscribed on tombstones or other grave markers. "RIP" is commonly reinterpreted as meaning the English phrase "Rest In Peace", the two meaning essentially the same thing. |
| *rerum cognoscere causas* | to learn the causes of things | Motto of the [University of Sheffield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sheffield), the [University of Guelph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Guelph), and [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics). |
| *[res derelictae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Res_derelictae)* | abandoned thing | Voluntarily abandoned property; a form of *[res nullius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Res_nullius)* that can thereby be acquired principally through *[occupatio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupatio)*, or by other means in their specific contexts. |
| *res firma mitescere nescit* | a firm resolve does not know how to weaken | Used in the 1985 film *[American Flyers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Flyers)* where it is colloquially translated as "once you got it up, keep it up". |
| *[res gestae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Res_gestae)* | things done | A phrase used in law representing the belief that certain statements are made naturally, spontaneously and without deliberation during the course of an event, they leave little room for misunderstanding/misinterpretation upon hearing by someone else (i.e. by the witness who will later repeat the statement to the court). As a result, the courts believe that such statements carry a high degree of credibility, and may admit them as an exception to the rule against [hearsay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearsay). |
| *[res ipsa loquitur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Res_ipsa_loquitur)* | the thing speaks for itself | A phrase from the [common law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_law) of [torts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tort) meaning that negligence can be inferred from the fact that such an accident happened, without proof of exactly how. |
| *[res judicata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Res_judicata)* | judged thing | A matter which has been decided by a court. Often refers to the legal concept that once a matter has been finally decided by the courts, it cannot be litigated again (cf. *non bis in idem* and [double jeopardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_jeopardy)). |
| *res, non verba* | "actions speak louder than words", or "deeds, not words" | From rēs ("things, facts") the plural of rēs ("a thing, a fact") + nōn ("not") + verba ("words") the plural of verbum ("a word"). Literally meaning "things, not words" or "facts instead of words" but referring to that "actions be used instead of words". |
| *[res nullius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Res_nullius)* | nobody's property | Goods without an owner. Used for things or beings which belong to nobody and are up for grabs, e.g., uninhabited and uncolonized lands, wandering wild animals, etc. (cf. *terra nullius*, "no man's land"). |
| *[res publica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Res_publica)* | Pertaining to the state or public | source of the word *[republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic)* |
| *respice adspice prospice* | look behind, look here, look ahead | i.e., "examine the past, the present and future". Motto of [CCNY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_College_of_New_York). |
| *respice finem* | look back at the end | i.e., "have regard for the end" or "consider the end"; part of the [dactylic hexameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dactylic_hexameter) *quidquid agis prudenter agas et respice finem* (whatever you do, do it wisely and consider the end) from *[Gesta Romanorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gesta_Romanorum)*. Generally a *[memento mori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memento_mori)*, a warning to remember one's death. Motto of *[Homerton College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homerton_College,_Cambridge)*, *[Trinity College, Kandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_College,_Kandy)*, [Georgetown College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_College) in Kentucky, [Turnbull High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turnbull_High_School), Glasgow, and the [London Oratory School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Oratory_School). |
| *[respondeat superior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Respondeat_superior)* | let the superior respond | Regarded as a legal maxim in agency law, referring to the legal liability of the principal with respect to an employee. Whereas a hired independent contractor acting tortiously may not cause the principal to be legally liable, a hired employee acting tortiously will cause the principal (the employer) to be legally liable, even if the employer did nothing wrong. |
| [*restitutio ad* (or *in*) *integrum*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restitutio_ad_integrum) | restoration to original condition | Principle behind the awarding of damages in common law negligence claims |
| Restitutor Orbis | Restorer of the world | A title given to Roman Emperor [Aurelian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurelian) after reuniting the Roman Empire in the [Crisis of the Third Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century). |
| *resurgam* | I shall arise | "I shall rise again", expressing Christian faith in resurrection at the Last Day. It appears, among other things, in Charlotte Brontë's *[Jane Eyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Eyre)*, as the epitaph written on Helen Burns's grave; in a poem of [Emily Dickinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Dickinson): *Poems* (1955) I. 56 (" 'Arcturus' is his other name"), I slew a worm the other day - A 'Savant' passing by Murmured 'Resurgam' - 'Centipede'! 'Oh Lord - how frail are we'!; and in a letter of Vincent van Gogh.[^7710] The [OED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OED) gives "1662 [J. Trapp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Trapp_%28writer%29), *Annotations upon the Old and New Testament, in five distinct volumes* (London, 1662), vol. I, p. 142: "Howbeit he had hope in his death, and might write Resurgam on his grave" as its earliest attribution in the English *[corpus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text_corpus)*. |
| *retine vim istam, falsa enim dicam, si coges* | Restrain your strength, for if you compel me I will tell lies | An utterance by the [Delphic oracle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythia) recorded by [Eusebius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eusebius) in *[Praeparatio evangelica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praeparatio_evangelica)*, book VI, ch. 5, translated from the Greek of [Porphyry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porphyry_%28philosopher%29) (cf. [E. H. Gifford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Gifford)'s translation)[^7711] and used by [William Wordsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Wordsworth) as a subtitle for his ballad "[Anecdote for Fathers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anecdote_for_Fathers)". |
| *rex regum fidelum et* | king even of faithful kings | Latin motto that appears on the crest of the [Trinity Broadcasting Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Broadcasting_Network) of [Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Crouch) and [Jan Crouch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Crouch). |
| *[rigor mortis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigor_mortis)* | stiffness of death | The rigidity of corpses when chemical reactions cause the limbs to stiffen about 3-4 hours after death. Other signs of death include drop in body temperature (*[algor mortis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algor_mortis)*, "cold of death") and discoloration (*[livor mortis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livor_mortis)*, "bluish color of death"). |
| *risum teneatis, amici?* | Can you help laughing, friends? | An ironic or rueful commentary, appended following a fanciful or unbelievable tale. |
| *risus abundat in ore stultorum* | laughter is abundant in the mouth of fools | excessive and inappropriate laughter signifies stupidity. |
| *[Roma invicta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roma_invicta)* | Unconquered Rome | Inspirational motto inscribed on the Statue of Rome. |
| *Roma locuta, causa finita* | Rome has spoken, the case is closed | In Roman Catholic ecclesiology, doctrinal matters are ultimately decided by the Vatican. |
| *[Romanes eunt domus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanes_eunt_domus)* | People called Romans they go the house | An intentionally garbled Latin phrase from *[Monty Python's Life of Brian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Python's_Life_of_Brian)*. Its intended meaning is "Romans, go home!", in Latin *Romani ite domum*. |
| *[rorate coeli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rorate_coeli)* | drop down ye heavens | a.k.a. *The Advent Prose*. |
| *rosam quae meruit ferat* | She who has earned the rose may bear it | Motto from [Sweet Briar College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_Briar_College) |
| *rus in urbe* | A countryside in the city | Generally used to refer to a haven of peace and quiet within an urban setting, often a garden, but can refer to interior decoration. |

|----|----|----|

| *[sanctum sanctorum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctum_sanctorum)* | [Holy of Holies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_of_Holies) | referring to a more sacred and/or guarded place, within a lesser guarded, yet also holy location. |
