| *[sede vacante](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sede_vacante)* | with the seat being vacant | The "seat" refers to the [Holy See](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_See); the vacancy refers to the [interregnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interregnum) between two [popes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope). |
| *sedes apostolica* | [apostolic](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/apostolic) chair | Synonymous with *Sancta Sedes*. |
| *sedes incertae* | seat (i.e. location) uncertain | Used in [biological classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_classification) to indicate that there is no agreement as to which higher order grouping a [taxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxon) should be placed into. Abbreviated *sed. incert.* |
| *sedet, aeternumque sedebit* | sit, be seated forever | from [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil)'s *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)* 6:617: when you stop trying, then you lose |
| *semel in anno licet insanire* | once in a year one is allowed to go crazy | Concept expressed by various authors, such as [Seneca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger), [Saint Augustine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Hippo) and [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace). It became proverbial during the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages). |
| *semper ad meliora* | always towards better things | Motto of several institutions |
| *semper anticus* | always forward | Motto of the [45th Infantry Division (United States)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/45th_Infantry_Division_%28United_States%29) and its successor, the [45th Infantry Brigade Combat Team (United States)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/45th_Infantry_Brigade_Combat_Team_%28United_States%29) |
| *semper apertus* | always open | Motto of [University of Heidelberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Heidelberg) |
| *[semper ardens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semper_Ardens)* | always burning | Motto of [Carl Jacobsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Jacobsen) and name of a line of beers by [Danish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denmark) brewery [Carlsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlsberg_Group). |
| *semper eadem* | ever the same | personal motto of [Elizabeth I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I_of_England), appears above her royal coat of arms. Used as motto of Elizabeth College, Guernsey, Channel Islands, which was founded by Elizabeth I, and of [Ipswich School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ipswich_School), to whom Elizabeth granted a royal charter. Also the motto of the [City of Leicester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leicester) and [Prince George's County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_George's_County,_Maryland). |
| *semper excelsius* | always higher | Motto of the [K.A.V. Lovania Leuven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K.A.V._Lovania_Leuven) and the House of Wrigley-Pimley-McKerr[^7717] |
| *[semper fidelis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semper_fidelis)* | always faithful | Motto of several institutions, e.g. [United States Marine Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Marine_Corps) |
| *semper fortis* | always brave | Unofficial motto of the [United States Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy) |
| *semper idem* | always the same | Motto of [Underberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underberg) |
| *semper in excretia sumus solim profundum variat* | We're always in the manure; only the depth varies. | [Lord de Ramsey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron_de_Ramsey), [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords), 21 January 1998[^7718] |
| *semper instans* | always threatening | Motto of 846 NAS [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy) |
| *semper invicta* | always invincible | Motto of [Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw) |
| *semper liber* | always free | Motto of the city of [Victoria, British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria,_British_Columbia) |
| *semper libertas* | always freedom | Motto of [Prince George County, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_George_County,_Virginia) |
| *semper maior* | always more, always greater | Motto of [Ignatius of Loyola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignatius_of_Loyola), founder of the [Jesuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuits) (Society of Jesus) |
| *semper necessitas probandi incumbit ei qui agit* | the necessity of proof always lies with the person who lays charges | Latin [maxim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxim_%28philosophy%29) often associated with the [burden of proof in law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burden_of_proof_%28law%29) or [in philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burden_of_proof_%28philosophy%29) |
| *[semper paratus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semper_paratus)* | always prepared | Motto of several institutions, e.g. [United States Coast Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Coast_Guard); see also *[nunquam non paratus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nunquam_non_paratus)* (never unprepared) |
| *semper primus* | always first | Motto of several US military units |
| *semper progrediens* | always progressing | Motto of the island of [Sint Maarten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sint_Maarten), of [King City Secondary School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_City_Secondary_School) in [King City, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_City,_Ontario), Canada and of [Fairfax High School (Fairfax, Virginia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfax_High_School_%28Fairfax,_Virginia%29) |
| *[semper reformanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecclesia_semper_reformanda_est)* | always in need of being reformed | A phrase deriving from the [Nadere Reformatie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadere_Reformatie) movement in the seventeenth century [Dutch Reformed Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Reformed_Church) and widely but informally used in [Reformed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_churches) and [Presbyterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism) churches today. It refers to the conviction of certain Reformed [Protestant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism) theologians that the church must continually re-examine itself in order to maintain its purity of [doctrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctrine) and practice. The term first appeared in print in [Jodocus van Lodenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jodocus_Van_Lodenstein), *Beschouwinge van Zion* (*Contemplation of Zion*), Amsterdam, 1674.[^7719] |
| *[semper supra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semper_supra)* | always above | Motto of the [United States Space Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Space_Force) |
| *semper sursum* | always aim high | Motto of several institutions |
| *semper vigilans* | always vigilant | Motto of several institutions including the [Civil Air Patrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Air_Patrol) of the [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force), the city of [San Diego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego), California |
| *semper vigilo* | always vigilant | Motto of the Scottish Police Forces, Scotland |
| *[Senatus Populusque Romanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SPQR) (SPQR)* | The [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Senate) and the People of Rome | The official name of the [Roman Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic). "SPQR" was carried on battle standards by the [Roman legions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_legion). In addition to being an [ancient Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome) motto, it remains the motto of the modern city of Rome. |
| *[sensu lato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensu)* | with the broad, or general, meaning | Less literally, "in the wide sense". |
| *[sensu stricto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensu) cf. stricto sensu* | "with the tight meaning" | Less literally, "in the strict sense". |
| *[sensus plenior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensus_plenior)* | in the fuller meaning | In biblical [exegesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exegesis), the deeper meaning intended by God, not intended by the human author. |
| *sequere pecuniam* | [follow the money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Follow_the_money) | In an effort to understand why things may be happening contrary to expectations, or even in alignment with them, this idiom suggests that keeping track of where money is going may show the basis for the observed behavior. Similar in spirit to the phrase *cui bono* (who gains?) or *cui prodest* (who advances?), but outside those phrases' historically legal context. |
| *Sermo Tuus Veritas Est* | Thy Word Is Truth | motto of the [General Theological Seminary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Theological_Seminary), [Cornelius Fontem Esua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_Fontem_Esua) |
| *sero venientes male sedentes* | those who are late are poorly seated |  |
| *sero venientibus ossa* | those who are late get bones |  |
| *servabo fidem* | Keeper of the faith | I will keep the faith. |
| *[serviam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serviam)* | I will serve | The answer of St. [Michael the Archangel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_%28archangel%29) to the *[non serviam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_serviam)*, "I will not serve" of [Satan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan), when the angels were tested by God on whether they will serve an inferior being, a man, [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus), as their Lord. |
| *[servus servorum Dei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Servus_servorum_Dei)* | servant of the servants of God | A title for the [Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope). |
| *sesquipedalia verba* | words a [foot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_%28prosody%29) and a half long | From [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace)'s *[Ars Poetica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ars_Poetica_%28Horace%29)*, "*proicit ampullas et sesquipedalia verba*" ("he throws down his high-flown language and his foot-and-a-half-long words"). A [self-referential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-reference) jab at [long words](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longest_word_in_English) and needlessly elaborate language in general. |
| [*Si comprehendis \[,\] non est Deus*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Si_comprehendis,_non_est_Deus) | if you understand \[something\], it is not God | [Augustine of Hippo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Hippo), *Sermo 117.3.5*; *[PL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrologia_Latina)* 38, 663 |
| *si dormiam capiar* | If I sleep, I may be caught | Motto of [HMS *Wakeful* (H88)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Wakeful_%28H88%29) |
| *Si monumentum requiris circumspice* | If you seek (his) monument, look around you | from the [epitaph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epitaph) on [Christopher Wren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Wren)'s tomb in [St Paul's Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul's_Cathedral). |
| *Si non oscillas, noli tintinnare* | If you can't swing, don't ring | Inscribed on a plaque above the front door of the Playboy mansion in Chicago. |
| [*si omnes... ego non*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etiam_si_omnes,_ego_non) | if all ones... not I |  |
| *si peccasse negamus fallimur et nulla est in nobis veritas* | if we deny having made a mistake, we are deceived, and there's no truth in us | From [Christopher Marlowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Marlowe)'s *[The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Faustus_%28play%29)*, where the phrase is translated "if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and there's no truth in us." (cf. 1 John 1:8 in the New Testament) |
| *[si quaeris peninsulam amoenam circumspice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Si_quaeris_peninsulam_amoenam_circumspice)* | if you seek a delightful peninsula, look around | Said to have been based on the tribute to architect [Christopher Wren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Wren) in [St Paul's Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Paul's_Cathedral), [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London): *si monumentum requiris, circumspice* (see above). [State motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_and_territory_mottos) of [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan), adopted in 1835; the spelling of 'peninsulam' is used in the motto, although the correct ancient spelling is 'paeninsulam'. |
| *si quid novisti rectius istis, candidus imperti; si nil, his utere mecum.* | if you can better these principles, tell me; if not, join me in following them | [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace), [*Epistles* I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistularum_liber_primus) [:6, 67-68](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/la:Epistulae%20%28Horatius%29%20-%20Liber%20I#Epistula_VI) |
| *si tacuisses, philosophus mansisses* | If you had kept your silence, you would have stayed a philosopher | This quote is often attributed to the Latin philosopher Boethius of the late fifth and early sixth centuries. It translates literally as, "If you had been silent, you would have remained a philosopher." The phrase illustrates a common use of the subjunctive verb mood. |
| *si vales valeo (SVV)* | if you are well, I am well (abbr) | A common beginning for ancient Roman letters. An abbreviation of *si vales bene est ego valeo*, alternatively written as SVBEEV. The practice fell out of fashion and into obscurity with the decline in Latin literacy. |
| *si vis amari ama* | If you want to be loved, love | This is often attributed to the Roman philosopher [Seneca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_the_Younger), found in the sixth of [his letters to Lucilius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistulae_morales_ad_Lucilium). |
| *[si vis pacem, para bellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Si_vis_pacem,_para_bellum)* | if you want peace, prepare for war | From [Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publius_Flavius_Vegetius_Renatus), *[De Re Militari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Re_Militari)*. Origin of the name *parabellum* for some [ammunition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammunition) and firearms, such as the [Luger Parabellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luger_P08_pistol). (Similar to *[igitur qui desiderat pacem, praeparet bellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28I%29)* and [*in pace ut sapiens aptarit idonea bello*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28I%29).) |
| *[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic)* | thus | Or "just so". States that the preceding quoted material appears exactly that way in the source, despite any errors of spelling, grammar, usage, or fact that may be present. Used only for previous quoted text; *ita* or similar must be used to mean "thus" when referring to something about to be stated. |
| *sic currite ut comprehendatis* | Run to win | More specifically, So run, that ye may obtain, 1 Corinthians 24. Motto of [Divine Word University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divine_Word_University), [Madang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madang), [Papua New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua_New_Guinea). |
| *sic et non* | thus and not | More simply, "yes and no". |
| *sic gorgiamus allos subjectatos nunc* | we gladly feast on those who would subdue us | [Mock-Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_Latin) motto of [The Addams Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Addams_Family). |
| *sic infit* | so it begins |  |
| *sic itur ad astra* | thus you shall go to the stars | From [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil), *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)* book IX, line 641. Possibly the source of the *ad astra* phrases. Motto of several institutions, including the [Royal Canadian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Air_Force). |
| *sic parvis magna* | greatness from small beginnings | Motto of Sir [Francis Drake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Drake) |
| *sic passim* | Thus here and there | Used when referencing books; see *passim*. |
| *sic semper erat, et sic semper erit* | Thus has it always been, and thus shall it ever be |  |
| *[sic semper tyrannis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic_semper_tyrannis)* | thus always [to](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dative) tyrants | Attributed to [Brutus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Junius_Brutus_the_Younger) at the time of [Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar)'s assassination and to [John Wilkes Booth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wilkes_Booth) at the time of [Abraham Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln)'s assassination; whether it was actually said at either of these events is disputed. [State motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._state_and_territory_mottos) of [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia), adopted in 1776. |
| *[sic transit gloria mundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic_transit_gloria_mundi)* | thus passes the glory of the world | A reminder that all things are fleeting. During [Papal coronations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_coronation), a monk reminds the [Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope) of his mortality by saying this phrase, preceded by *pater sancte* ("holy father") while holding before his eyes a burning paper illustrating the passing nature of earthly glories. This is similar to the tradition of a slave in a [Roman triumphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_triumph) whispering *memento mori* in the ear of the celebrant. |
| *sic utere tuo ut alienum non laedas* | use \[what is\] yours so as not to harm \[what is\] of others | Or "use your property in such a way that you do not damage others'". A legal maxim related to property ownership laws, often shortened to simply *sic utere* ("use it thus"). |
| *sic vita est* | thus is life | Or "such is life". Indicates that a circumstance, whether good or bad, is an inherent aspect of living. |
| *sic vos non vobis mellificates apes* | Thus you not for yourselves make honey, bees. | Part of a verse written by [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil) after the poet Bathyllus plagiarized his work. |
| *sidere mens eadem mutato* | Though the constellations change, the mind is universal | Latin motto of the [University of Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sydney). |
| *signetur* (*sig* or *S/*) | let it be labeled | [Medical shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_abbreviations_used_in_medical_prescriptions) |
| *signum fidei* | Sign of the Faith | Motto of the [Institute of the Brothers of the Christian Schools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_the_Brothers_of_the_Christian_Schools). |
| *silentium est aureum* | silence is golden | Latinization of the English expression "silence is golden". Also Latinized as *silentium est aurum* ("silence is gold"). |
| *similia similibus curantur similia similibus curentur* | similar things are taken care of by similar things let similar things be taken care of by similar things | "like is cured by like" and "let like be cured by like"; the first form ("cur**a**ntur") is indicative, while the second form ("cur**e**ntur") is subjunctive. The indicative form is found in [Paracelsus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paracelsus) (16th century), while the subjunctive form is said by [Samuel Hahnemann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Hahnemann), founder of [homeopathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeopathy), and is known as the [law of similars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_similars). |
| *similia similibus solvuntur* | similar substances will dissolve similar substances | Used as a general rule in [chemistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemistry); "like dissolves like" refers to the ability of polar or non polar solvents to dissolve polar or non polar [solutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solutes) respectively.[^7720] |
| *simplex sigillum veri* | simplicity is the sign of truth | expresses a sentiment akin to [Keep It Simple, Stupid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KISS_principle) |
| *sincere et constanter* | sincere and constant | Motto of the [Order of the Red Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Red_Eagle) |
| *sine anno (s.a.)* | without a year | Used in [bibliographies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibliography) to indicate that the date of publication of a document is unknown. |
| *sine die* | without a day | Originally from old [common law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_law) texts, where it indicates that a final, dispositive order has been made in the case. In modern legal context, it means there is nothing left for the court to do, so no date for further proceedings is set, resulting in an "[adjournment sine die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjournment_sine_die)". |
| *[Sine Cerere et Baccho friget Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_Cerere_et_Baccho_friget_Venus)* | without [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_%28mythology%29) and [Bacchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacchus), [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus_%28mythology%29) remains cold | without food and (alcoholic) drink, love will not ensue; from [Terence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terence)'s comedy *[Eunuchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eunuchus)* (161 BC) |
| *[sine ira et studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_ira_et_studio)* | without anger and fondness | Thus, impartially. From [Tacitus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacitus), *[Annals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annals_%28Tacitus%29)* 1.1. |
| *sine honoris titulo* | without honorary title | Addressing oneself to someone whose title is unknown. |
| *sine labore non erit panis in ore* | without labour there will be no bread in mouth |  |
| *sine loco (s.l.)* | without a place | Used in bibliographies to indicate that the place of publication of a document is unknown. |
| *sine metu* | "without fear" | Motto of [Jameson Irish Whiskey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jameson_Irish_Whiskey) |
| *[sine nomine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_nomine) (s.n.)* | "without a name" | Used in bibliographies to indicate that the publisher of a document is unknown. |
| *sine poena nulla lex* | Without penalty, there is no law | Refers to the ineffectiveness of a law without the means of enforcement |
| *sine prole* | Without offspring | Frequently abbreviated to "s.p." or "d.s.p." (*decessit sine prole* - "died without offspring") in genealogical works. |
| *sine prole superstite* | Without surviving children | Without surviving offspring (even in abstract terms) |
| *sine timore aut favore* | Without Fear or Favor | St.George's School, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada motto |
| *[sine qua non](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sine_qua_non)* | without which not | Used to denote something that is an essential part of the whole. See also *condicio sine qua non*. |
| *sine remediis medicina debilis est* | without remedies medicine is powerless | Inscription on a stained glass in the conference hall of a pharmaceutical mill in [Kaunas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaunas), Lithuania. |
| *sine scientia ars nihil est* | without knowledge, skill is nothing | Motto of The International Diving Society and of the Oxford Medical Students' Society. |
| *sisto activitatem* | I cease the activity | Phrase, used to cease the activities of the [Sejm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sejm_of_the_Republic_of_Poland) upon the *[liberum veto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberum_veto)* principle |
| *sit nomen Domini benedictum* | blessed be the name of the Lord | Phrase used in a [pontifical blessing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pontifical_blessing) imparted by a [Catholic bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_bishop) |
| *sit nomine digna* | may it be worthy of the name | National motto of [Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia), also motto of [Durbanville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durbanville), South Africa |
| *sit pax in valle tamesis* | Let there be peace in the [Thames Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Valley) | Motto of [Thames Valley Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Valley_Police), English territorial police force for [Berkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkshire), [Buckinghamshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckinghamshire) and [Oxfordshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxfordshire). |
| *sit sine labe decus* | let honour stainless be | Motto of the Brisbane Boys' College (Brisbane, Australia). |
| *sit tibi terra levis* | may the earth be light to you | Commonly used on gravestones, often contracted as S.T.T.L., the same way as today's R.I.P. |
| *sit venia verbo* | may there be forgiveness for the word | Similar to the English idiom "pardon my French". |
| *Socratici viri* | "Socrates' men" or "Disciples of Socrates" | Coined by [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero)[^7721][^7722] to refer to any who owe philosophical reasoning and method to [Socrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socrates). |
| *sol iustitiae illustra nos* | sun of justice, shine upon us | Motto of [Utrecht University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utrecht_University). |
| *sol lucet omnibus* | the sun shines on everyone | [Petronius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petronius), *Satyricon Lybri* 100. |
| *sol omnia regit* | the sun rules over everything | Inscription near the entrance to [Frombork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frombork) Museum |
| *[sola fide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sola_fide)* | by faith alone | The [material principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Material_principle) of the [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation) and one of the [five solas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_solas), referring to the Protestant claim that the [Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible) teaches that men are [saved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvation) by [faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith) even without works. |
| *sola dosis facit venenum* | [the dose makes the poison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_dose_makes_the_poison) | It is credited to Paracelsus who expressed the classic toxicology maxim "All things are poison and nothing is without poison; only the dose makes a thing not a poison." |
| *[sola gratia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sola_gratia)* | by grace alone | A motto of the [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation) and one of the [five solas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_solas), referring to the Protestant claim that [salvation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvation) is an unearned gift (cf. *ex gratia*), not a direct result of [merit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merit_%28Catholicism%29). |
| *sola lingua bona est lingua mortua* | the only good language is a dead language | Example of [dog Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dog_Latin) humor. |
| *[sola scriptura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sola_scriptura)* | by scripture alone | The [formal principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formal_principle) of the [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation) and one of the [five solas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_solas), referring to the Protestant idea that the [Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible) alone is the ultimate authority, not the [Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope) or tradition. |
| *sola nobilitat virtus* | virtue alone ennobles | Similar to [*virtus sola nobilitas*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28V%29) |
| *solamen miseris socios habuisse doloris* | misery loves company | From [Christopher Marlowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Marlowe)'s *[The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Faustus_%28play%29)*. |
| *soli Deo gloria (S.D.G.)* | glory to God alone | A motto of the [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation) and one of the [five solas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_solas), referring to the idea that [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God) is the creator of all good things and deserves all the praise for them. [Johann Sebastian Bach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Sebastian_Bach) often signed his manuscripts with the abbreviation S.D.G. to invoke this phrase, as well as with AMDG (*ad maiorem Dei gloriam*). The motto of the [MasterWorks Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masterworks_festival), an annual Christian performing arts festival. |
| *solus Christus* | [Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christ) alone | A motto of the [Protestant Reformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_Reformation) and one of the [five solas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_solas), referring to the Protestant claim that the Bible teaches that [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus) is the only [mediator](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/mediator) between God and mankind. Also rendered *solo Christo* ("by Christ alone"). |
| *solus ipse* | I alone |  |
| *[solvitur ambulando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solvitur_ambulando)* | it is solved by walking | The problem is solved by taking a walk, or by simple experiment. |
| *[sortes biblicae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sortes_biblicae)* | biblical lots | method of [divination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divination) where by the [Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible) is opened randomly and the first words which one sees or points to are interpreted as predictive |
| *Spartam nactus es; hanc exorna* | your lot is cast in Sparta, be a credit to it | from [Euripides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euripides)'s *[Telephus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telephus)*, [Agamemnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agamemnon) to [Menelaus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menelaus).[^7723] |
| *specialia generalibus derogant* | special departs from general |  |
| *[species nova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species_nova)* | new species | Used in [biological taxonomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_taxonomy) |
| *spectemur agendo* | let us be judged by our acts | Motto of [Hawthorn Football Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawthorn_Football_Club) |
| *[Speculum Dinae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_Nemorensis)* | Diana's Mirror | [Lake Nemi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Nemi) as referred to by poets and painters[^7724] |
| *speculum speculorum* | mirror of mirrors |  |
| *spem gregis* | the hope of the flock | from [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil)'s *[Eclogues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eclogues)* |
| *spem reduxit* | he has restored hope | [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motto) of [New Brunswick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Brunswick). |
| *spero meliora* | I aspire to greater things | Also translated "I expect better" and "I hope for better things." |
| *spes bona* | good hope | [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motto) of [University of Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cape_Town). |
| *spes vincit thronum* | hope conquers (overcomes) the throne | Refers to [Revelation 3:21](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bible%20%28King%20James%29/Revelation#3:21), "To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne." On the [John Winthrop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Winthrop) family tombstone, Boston, Massachusetts. |
| *spiritus mundi* | spirit of the world | From [The Second Coming (poem)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Second_Coming_%28poem%29) by [William Butler Yeats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Butler_Yeats). Refers to Yeats' belief that each human mind is linked to a single vast intelligence, and that this intelligence causes certain universal symbols to appear in individual minds. The idea is similar to [Carl Jung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Jung)'s concept of the [collective unconscious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_unconscious). |
| *spiritus ubi vult spirat* | the spirit spreads wherever it wants | Refers to The Gospel of Saint [John 3:8](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Bible%20%28King%20James%29/John#3:8), where he mentions how Jesus told Nicodemus "The wind blows wherever it wants, and even though you can hear its noise, you don't know where it comes from or where it goes. The same thing happens to whomever has been born of the Spirit." It is the motto of [Cayetano Heredia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cayetano_Heredia_University)[^7725] |
| *splendor sine occasu* | brightness without setting | Loosely "splendour without diminishment" or "magnificence without ruin". [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motto) of [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia) and of [Boise State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boise_State_University). |
| *stamus contra malo* | we stand against by evil | The motto of the Jungle Patrol in *[The Phantom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Phantom)*. The phrase actually violates [Latin grammar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_grammar) because of a mistranslation from English, as the preposition *contra* takes the [accusative case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accusative_case). The correct Latin rendering of "we stand against evil" would be "*stamus contra malum*". |
| *stante pede* | with a standing foot | "Immediately". |
| *[stare decisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stare_decisis)* | to stand by the decided things | To uphold previous rulings, recognize [precedent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Precedent). |
| *Stat crux dum volvitur orbis* | The Cross is steady while the world turns | Motto of the [Carthusian Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthusian_Order). |
| *stat rosa pristina nomine, nomina nuda tenemus* | the rose of old remains only in its name; we hold only empty names | An epigraph quoted at the end of [Umberto Eco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Eco)'s *[The Name of the Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Name_of_the_Rose)*. A verse by [Bernard of Cluny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_of_Cluny) (although likely mistranscribed in medieval times from an original *stat Roma pristina nomine...*, "primordial Rome remains only in its name..."). |
| *stat sua cuique dies* | There is a day \[turn\] for everybody | [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil), *Aeneid*, X 467 |
| *statim (stat)* | "immediately" | [Medical shorthand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_abbreviations_used_in_medical_prescriptions) used following an urgent request.[^7726] |
| *statio bene fide carinis* | A safe harbour for ships | Motto of [Cork City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cork_%28city%29), [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ireland). Adapted from [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil)'s *Aeneid* (II, 23: *statio male fida carinis*, "an unsafe harbour") but corrupted for unknown reasons to "fide". |
| *[status aparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Status_aparte)* | separate state | The special status of [Aruba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aruba) between 1986 and 2010 as a constituent country within the [Kingdom of the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_the_Netherlands), separate from the [Netherlands Antilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_Antilles) to which it belonged until 1986. |
| *[status quaestionis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Status_quaestionis)* | the state of investigation | most commonly employed in [scholarly literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarly_literature) to refer in a summary way to the accumulated results, scholarly consensus, and areas remaining to be developed on any given topic. |
| *[status quo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Status_quo)* | the state in which | The current condition or situation. |
| *status quo ante* | the state in which \[things were\] before | The state of affairs prior to some upsetting event. |
| *[status quo ante bellum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Status_quo_ante_bellum)* | the state before the war | A common term in peace treaties. |
| *stet* | let it stand | Marginal mark in [proofreading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proofreading) to indicate that something previously deleted or marked for deletion should be retained. |
| *stet fortuna domus* | let the fortune of the house stand | First part of the motto of [Harrow School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrow_School), England, and inscribed upon Ricketts House, at the [California Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Institute_of_Technology). |
| *stipendium peccati mors est* | the reward of sin is death | From [Christopher Marlowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Marlowe)'s *[The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Faustus_%28play%29)*. (See Rom 6:23, "For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.") |
| *strenuis ardua cedunt* | the heights yield to endeavour | Motto of the [University of Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Southampton). |
| *[stricto sensu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sensu) cf. sensu stricto* | with the tight meaning | Less literally, "in the strict sense". |
| *stupor mundi* | the wonder of the world | A title given to [Frederick II, Holy Roman Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_II,_Holy_Roman_Emperor). More literally translated "the bewilderment of the world", or, in its original, pre-[Medieval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Latin) sense, "the stupidity of the world". |
| *[sua sponte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sua_sponte)* | by its own accord | [Legal term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_legal_Latin_terms) when a court takes up a motion on its own initiative, not because any of the parties to the case has made the motion. The regimental motto of the [75th Ranger Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/75th_Ranger_Regiment_%28United_States%29) of the U.S. Army. |
| *suaviter in modo, fortiter in re* | gently in manner, resolutely in execution | Motto of [Essendon Football Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essendon_Football_Club) |
| *sub anno* | under the year | Commonly abbreviated *s.a.*, it is used to cite events recorded in [chronicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronicle) according to the year under which they are listed. For example, "*ASC* MS A, s.a. 855" means the entry for the year 855 in manuscript A of the *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle*. |
| *sub cruce lumen* | The Light Under the Cross | Motto of the [University of Adelaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Adelaide), Australia. Refers to the figurative "light of learning" and the Southern Cross constellation, [Crux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crux). |
| *sub divo* | under the wide open sky | Also, "under the sky", "in the open air", "out in the open" or "outdoors". Ablative "divo" does not distinguish divus, divi, a god, from divum, divi, the sky. |
| *sub finem* | toward the end | Used in citations to refer to the end of a book, page, etc., and abbreviated 's.f.' Used after the page number or title. E.g., 'p. 20 *s.f.* ' |
| *sub Iove frigido* | under cold Jupiter | At night; from [Horace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horace)'s *[Odes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odes_%28Horace%29)* [1.1:25](https://la.wikipedia.org/wiki/s:Carmina%20%28Horatius%29/Liber%20I/Carmen%20I#25) |
| *[sub judice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub_judice)* | under a judge | Said of a case that cannot be publicly discussed until it is finished. Also *sub iudice*. |
| [*sub poena*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subpoena) | under penalty | Source of the English noun *subpoena*. Said of a request, usually by a court, that must be complied with on pain of punishment. Examples include *[sub poena duces tecum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subpoena_duces_tecum)* ("take with you under penalty"), a court [summons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summons) to appear and produce tangible evidence, and *[sub poena ad testificandum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subpoena_ad_testificandum)* ("under penalty to testify"), a summons to appear and give oral testimony. |
| *[sub rosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub_rosa)* | under the rose | "In secret", "privately", "confidentially", or "covertly". In the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages), a [rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose) was suspended from the ceiling of a council chamber to indicate that what was said in the "under the rose" was not to be repeated outside. This practice originates in [Greek mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mythology), where [Aphrodite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aphrodite) gave a rose to her son [Eros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eros), and he, in turn, gave it to [Harpocrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harpocrates), the god of silence, to ensure that his mother's indiscretions, or those of the gods in general, in other accounts, were kept under wraps. |
| *sub nomine* (sub nom.) | under the name | "in the name of", "under the title of"; used in legal citations to indicate the name under which the litigation continued. |
| *[sub silentio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub_silentio)* | under silence | implied but not expressly stated. |
| *[sub specie aeternitatis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub_specie_aeternitatis)* | under the sight of eternity | Thus, "from eternity's point of view". From [Spinoza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baruch_Spinoza), *Ethics*. |
| *sub specie Dei* | under the sight of God | "from God's point of view or perspective". |
| *[sub tuum praesidium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub_tuum_praesidium)* | Beneath thy compassion | Name of the oldest extant [hymn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymn) to the [Theotokos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theotokos) ([Blessed Virgin Mary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blessed_Virgin_Mary)). Also "under your protection". A popular school motto. |
| *Sub umbra floreo* | Under the shade I flourish | National Motto of [Belize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belize), referring to the shade of the [mahogany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahogany) tree. |
| *sub verbo; sub voce* |  | Under the word or heading; abbreviated *s.v.* Used to cite a work, such as a dictionary, with alphabetically arranged entries, e.g. "*[Oxford English Dictionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_English_Dictionary)*, s.v. 'horse.'"" |
| *sublimis ab unda* | Raised from the waves | Motto of King Edward VII and Queen Mary School, Lytham |
| *subsiste sermonem statim* | stop speaking immediately |  |
| *Succisa virescit* | Cut down, we grow back stronger | Motto of [Delbarton School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delbarton_School) |
| *Sudetia non cantat* | One doesn't sing on the [Sudeten Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudetes) | Saying from [Hanakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han%C3%A1) |
| *[sui generis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sui_generis)* | Of its own kind | In a class of its own; of a unique kind. E.g. "The [City of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_of_London) is a *sui generis* entity, with ancient rights that differ from all other jurisdictions in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom)." |
| *[sui iuris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sui_iuris)* | Of one's own right | Capable of responsibility. Has both legal and ecclesiastical use. Commonly rendered *sui juris*. |
| *sum quod eris* | I am what you will be | A [gravestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headstone) inscription to remind the reader of the inevitability of death (cf. *memento mori*). Also rendered *fui quod sis* ("I have been what you are") and *tu fui ego eris* ("I have been you, you will be I"). |
| *sum quod sum* | I am what I am | from [Augustine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_of_Hippo)'s Sermon No. 76.[^7727] |
| *summa cum laude* | with highest praise |  |
| *summa potestas* | sum or totality of power | It refers to the final authority of power in government. For example, power of the Sovereign. |
| *summa summarum* | all in all | Literally "sum of sums". When a short conclusion is rounded up at the end of some elaboration. |
| *[summum bonum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summum_bonum)* | the supreme good | Literally "highest good". Also *summum malum* ("the supreme evil"). |
| *summum ius, summa iniuria* | supreme law, supreme injustice | From [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero) (De officiis, I, 10, 33). An acritical application of law, without understanding and respect of laws's purposes and without considering the overall circumstances, is often a means of supreme injustice. A similar sentence appears in [Terence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terence) (Heautontimorumenos, IV, 5): *Ius summum saepe summa est malitia* ("supreme justice is often out of supreme malice (or wickedness)"). |
| *sumptibus auctoris* | published \[cost of printing paid\] by author | Found in self-published academic books of the 17th to 19th century. Often preceded by Latin name of city in which the work is published. |
| [*sunt lacrimae rerum*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacrimae_rerum) | there are tears for things | From [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil), *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)*. Followed by *et mentem mortalia tangunt* ("and mortal things touch my mind"). [Aeneas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneas) cries as he sees [Carthaginian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage) temple murals depicting the deaths of the [Trojan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_War). See also *hinc illae lacrimae*. |
| *sunt omnes unum* | they are all one |  |
| *sunt pueri pueri, pueri puerilia tractant* | Children are children, and children do childish things | anonymous proverb |
| *sunt superis sua iura* | the gods have their own laws | From [Ovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid)'s *[Metamorphoses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamorphoses)*, [book IX, line 500](https://la.wikipedia.org/wiki/s:Metamorphoses%20%28Ovidius%29/Liber%20IX); also used by [David Hume](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hume) in *[The Natural History of Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Natural_History_of_Religion)*, chapter [XIII](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The%20Natural%20History%20of%20Religion#Section_XIII._-_Impious_Conceptions_Of_The_Divine_Nature_In_Popular_Religions_Of_Both_Kinds) |
| *[suo jure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suo_jure)* | in one's own right | Used in the context of titles of [nobility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobility), for instance where a wife may hold a title in her own right rather than through her marriage. |
| *suo motu* | upon one's own initiative | Also rendered *suo moto*. Usually used when a court of law, upon its own initiative, (i.e., no petition has been filed) proceeds against a person or authority that it deems has committed an illegal act. It is used chiefly in [South Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Asia). |
| *suos cultores scientia coronat* | Knowledge crowns those who seek her | The motto of [Syracuse University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse_University), New York. |
| *super firmum fundamentum dei* | On the firm foundation of God | The motto of [Ursinus College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ursinus_College), Pennsylvania. |
| *super fornicam* | on the lavatory | Where [Thomas More](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_More) accused the reformer, [Martin Luther](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther), of going to celebrate [Mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_%28liturgy%29). |
| *superbia in proelia* | pride in battle | Motto of [Manchester City F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_City_F.C.) |
| *superbus via inscientiae* | proud of the way of ignorance | Motto of the Alien Research Labs of the fictional [Black Mesa Research Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Mesa_Research_Facility) in the video game [*Half-Life* (1998)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-Life_%28video_game%29) |
| *supero omnia* | I surpass everything | A declaration that one succeeds above all others. |
| *surdo oppedere* | to belch before the deaf | From [Erasmus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desiderius_Erasmus)' collection of annotated Adagia (1508): a useless action. |
| *surgam* | I shall rise | Motto of [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University)'s [Philolexian Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philolexian_Society). |
| *sursum corda* | Lift up your hearts | Motto of [Haileybury College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haileybury_College), Hertfordshire. The opening dialogue to the preface of the Eucharistic Prayer or [Anaphora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaphora_%28liturgy%29) in the liturgies of the Christian Church. [Hymnal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymnal) for the German [diocese of Paderborn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Archdiocese_of_Paderborn) from 1874 to 1975. |
| *[sutor, ne ultra crepidam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sutor,_ne_ultra_crepidam)* | Cobbler, no further than the sandal! | Thus, don't offer your opinion on things that are outside your competence. It is said that the Greek painter [Apelles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apelles) once asked the advice of a cobbler on how to render the sandals of a soldier he was painting. When the cobbler started offering advice on other parts of the painting, Apelles rebuked him with this phrase in Greek. It subsequently became a popular Latin expression and a proverb in several languages: [cobbler, keep to your last](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/cobbler,%20keep%20to%20your%20last), German: [Schuster, bleib bei deinem Leisten](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Schuster,%20bleib%20bei%20deinem%20Leisten). |
| [*suum cuique tribuere*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suum_cuique) | to render to every man his due | One of [Justinian I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I)'s three basic precepts of law. Also shortened to *suum cuique* ("to each his own"). |
| *s.v.* |  | Abbreviation for *sub verbo* or *sub voce* (see [above](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Latin_phrases_%28full%29)). |

#### T

| Latin | Translation | Notes |
|----|----|----|
| *tabula gratulatoria* | congratulatory tablet | A list of congratulations. |
| *[tabula rasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabula_rasa)* | scraped tablet | Thus, "blank slate". Romans used to write on [wax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wax)-covered wooden tablets, which were erased by scraping with the flat end of the [stylus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylus). [John Locke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Locke) used the term to describe the human [mind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mind) at birth, before it had acquired any knowledge. |
| *talis qualis* | just as such | "Such as it is" or "as such". |
| *taliter qualiter* | somewhat |  |

| *tanquam ex ungue leonem* | we know the lion by his claw | Said in 1697 by [Johann Bernoulli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johann_Bernoulli) about [Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton)'s anonymously submitted solution to Bernoulli's [challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Later_life_of_Isaac_Newton) regarding the [Brachistochrone curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brachistochrone_curve). |

| *tantum religio potuit suadere malorum* | to such heights of evil are men driven by religion | [Lucretius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucretius), *[De rerum natura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_rerum_natura)* I.101[^7729] Quoted by [Christopher Hitchens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Hitchens) in ch. 2 of *[God Is Not Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_Is_Not_Great)*. |
| *tarde venientibus ossa* | To the late are left the bones |  |
| *Te occidere possunt sed te edere non possunt nefas est* | They can kill you, but they cannot eat you, it is against the law. | The motto of the fictional Enfield Tennis Academy in the [David Foster Wallace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Foster_Wallace) novel *[Infinite Jest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infinite_Jest)*. Translated in the novel as "They can kill you, but the legalities of eating you are quite a bit dicier". |

Rendered also with *nosce te ipsum*, *temet nosce* ("thine own self know") appears in *[The Matrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Matrix)* translated as "know thyself". |

See [entry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempora_mutantur) for details. |

Also, motto of [Worshipful Company of Clockmakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worshipful_Company_of_Clockmakers). |

| *tempus volat, hora fugit* | time flies, the hour flees |  |
| *tendit in ardua virtus* | virtue strives for what is difficult | Appears in [Ovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid)'s *[Epistulae ex Ponto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistulae_ex_Ponto)* |
| *teneo te Africa* | I hold you, Africa! | [Suetonius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twelve_Caesars) attributes this to [Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar), from when Caesar was on the African coast. |
| *tentanda via* | The way must be tried | motto for [York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_University) |

| *[terminus ante/post quem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminus_post_quem)* | limit before/after which | In archaeology or history, refers to the date before which an artefact or feature must have been deposited. Similarly, *terminus ad quem* (limit to which) may also refer to the latest possible date of a non-punctual event (period, era, etc.), while *terminus a quo* (limit from which) may refer to the earliest such date. |
| *terra australis incognita* | unknown southern land | First name used to refer to the Australian continent |

| *[terra nullius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terra_nullius)* | land of none | That is, [no man's land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_man's_land). A neutral or uninhabited area, or a land not under the sovereignty of any recognized political entity. |
| *terras irradient* | let them illuminate the lands | Or "let them give light to the world". An allusion to [Isaiah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaiah) 6.3: *plena est omnis terra gloria eius* ("the whole earth is full of his glory"). Sometimes mistranslated as "they will illuminate the lands" based on mistaking *irradiare* for a [future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_tense) [indicative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Realis_mood) third-[conjugation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammatical_conjugation) verb, whereas it is actually a [present](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Present_tense) [subjunctive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subjunctive_mood) first-conjugation verb. Motto of [Amherst College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amherst_College); the college's original mission was to educate young men to serve God. |

| *[tertium quid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tertium_quid)* | a third something | 1\. Something that cannot be classified into either of two groups considered exhaustive; an intermediate thing or factor. 2. A third person or thing of indeterminate character. |
| *[testis unus, testis nullus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unus_testis,_nullus_testis)* | one witness is not a witness | A law principle expressing that a single witness is not enough to corroborate a story. |
| *[textus receptus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Textus_receptus)* | received text |  |
| *Tibi cordi immaculato concredimus nos ac consecramus* | We consecrate and entrust ourselves to your Immaculate heart (O Mary). | The inscription found on top of the central door of the Minor Basilica of the Immaculate Conception, otherwise known as the [Manila Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Cathedral) in the Philippines |
| *[timeo Danaos et dona ferentes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeo_Danaos_et_dona_ferentes)* | I fear Greeks even if they bring gifts | *[Danaos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danaus)* being a term for the [Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks). In [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil)'s *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)*, II, 49, the phrase is said by [Laocoön](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laoco%C3%B6n) when warning his fellow Trojans against accepting the [Trojan Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_Horse). The full original quote is *quidquid id est timeo Danaos et dona ferentis*, *quidquid id est* meaning "whatever it is" and *ferentis* being an archaic form of *ferentes*. Commonly mistranslated "Beware of Greeks bearing gifts". |
| *timidi mater non flet* | A coward's mother does not weep | A proverb from [Cornelius Nepos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelius_Nepos)'s *Vita* of Thrasybulus: *praeceptum illud omnium in animis esse debet, nihil in bello oportere contemni, neque sine causa dici matrem timidi flere non solere* (that old precept has to be held by all in our minds: nothing should be condemned in war, and it is for a reason that it is said the mother of a coward does not weep \[for her cowardly son\]). |
| *[timor mortis conturbat me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timor_mortis_conturbat_me)* | the fear of death confounds me | [Refrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refrain) originating in the response to the seventh lesson in the [Office of the Dead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_the_Dead). In the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages), this service was read each day by [clerics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clergy). As a refrain, it appears also in other poems and can frequently be found inscribed on tombs. |
| *[tolle lege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolle_lege)* | take up and read | In late August of 386, at the age of 31, Augustine of Hippo converted to Christianity. As Augustine later told it, his conversion was prompted by hearing a child's voice say "take up and read" ([Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language): *tolle, lege*). Resorting to the *[sortes biblicae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sortes_biblicae)*, he opened a book of St. Paul's writings (*Confessiones* 8.12.29) at random and read [Romans 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romans_13):13-14: "Not in rioting and drunkenness, not in [chambering](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/en:chambering) and wantonness, not in strife and envying, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh to fulfil the lusts thereof."[^7731] |
| *toto cælo* | by whole heaven | as far apart as possible; utterly. |
| *totus tuus* | totally yours | Offering one's life in total commitment to another. The motto was adopted by [Pope John Paul II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_Paul_II) to signify his love and servitude to [Mary the Mother of Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blessed_Virgin_Mary_%28Roman_Catholic%29). |
| *[traditionis custodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditionis_custodes)* | guardians of tradition | [Motu proprio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Motu_proprio) issued by [Pope Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Francis) in 2021 regarding the celebration of the [Tridentine Mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tridentine_Mass). |
| *transire benefaciendo* | to travel along while doing good | Literally "beneficial passage." Mentioned in "The Seamy Side of History" (L'envers de l'histoire contemporaine, 1848), part of *[La Comédie humaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Com%C3%A9die_humaine)*, by [Honoré de Balzac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honor%C3%A9_de_Balzac), and *[Around the World in Eighty Days](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Around_the_World_in_Eighty_Days)* by [Jules Verne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jules_Verne). |
| *[translatio imperii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Translatio_imperii)* | transfer of rule | Used to express the belief in the transfer of imperial authority from the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire) of antiquity to the Medieval [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire). |
| *tres faciunt collegium* | three makes company | It takes three to have a valid group; three is the minimum number of members for an organization or a corporation. |
| *treuga Dei* | Truce of God | A decree by the medieval Church that all feuds should be cancelled during the [Sabbath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabbath_in_Christianity), effectively from Wednesday or Thursday night until Monday. See also *[Peace and Truce of God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_and_Truce_of_God)*. |
| *tria juncta in uno* | Three joined in one | Motto of the [Order of the Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Bath) |
| *Triste est omne animal post coitum, præter mulierem gallumque* | Every animal is sad after coitus except the human female and the rooster |  |
| *tu autem Domine miserere nobis* | But Thou, O Lord, have mercy upon us | Phrase said at the end of biblical readings in the liturgy of the medieval church. Also used in brief, "tu autem", as a *memento mori* [epitaph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epitaph). |
| *tuitio fidei et obsequium pauperum* | Defence of the faith and assistance to the poor | Motto of the Association of Canadian Knights of the Sovereign and Military Order of Malta[^7732] and the [Sovereign Military Order of Malta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_Military_Order_of_Malta). |
| *tu fui ego eris* | I was you; you will be me | Thus, "what you are, I was; what I am, you will be.". A *memento mori* [gravestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravestone) inscription to remind the reader that death is unavoidable (cf. *sum quod eris*). |
| *tu ne cede malis, sed contra audentior ito* | you should not give in to evils, but proceed ever more boldly against them | From [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil), *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)*, 6, 95. "Ne cede malis" is the motto of [The Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bronx). |
| *[tu quoque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tu_quoque)* | you too | The logical [fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallacy) of attempting to defend one's position merely by pointing out the same weakness in one's opponent. |
| *tu stultus es* | you are stupid | *Motto* for the [satirical news](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_satire) organization, *[The Onion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Onion)* |
| *tuebor* | I will protect | Found on the Great Seal on the flag of the state of [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan). |
| *tunica propior est pallio* | A tunic is closer \[to the body\] than a cloak | From Plautus' *Trinummus* 1154. Equivalent to "blood is thicker than water" in modern English. |
| *turba* | lit. 'uproar', 'disturbance', 'crowd'; in music, specifically in the [musical settings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passion_%28music%29) of the [Passion of Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passion_of_Jesus), it refers to any text that is spoken by any group of people, including the [disciples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disciple_%28Christianity%29), the Jews, or the soldiers. |  |
| *turris fortis mihi Deus* | God is my strong tower | Motto of [Clan Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Kelly) |
| *tutum te robore reddam* | I will give you safety by strength | Motto of [Clan Crawford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Crawford) |
| *tuum est* | It's up to you | Motto of the [University of British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_British_Columbia) |

#### U

| Latin | Translation | Notes |
|----|----|----|
| *[uberrima fides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uberrima_fides)* | most abundant faith | Or "utmost good faith" (cf. *bona fide*). A legal maxim of [insurance contracts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance_policy) requiring all parties to deal in [good faith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_faith). |
| *ubertas et fidelitas* | fertility and faithfulness | [Motto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_national_mottos) of [Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasmania). |
| *ubi amor, ibi dolor* | where \[there is\] love, there \[is\] pain |  |
| *ubi bene, ibi patria* | where \[it is\] well, there \[is\] the fatherland | Or "Home is where it's good"; see also *[ubi panis ibi patria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubi_panis_ibi_patria)*. |
| *ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est* | where there is charity and love, God is there |  |
| *ubi dubium, ibi libertas* | where \[there is\] doubt, there \[is\] freedom | Anonymous proverb. |
| *ubi jus, ibi remedium* | Where \[there is\] a right, there \[is\] a remedy |  |
| *ubi maior, minor cessat* | Where \[there is\] the greater, the lesser ceases | When there is something of greater importance or authority, things of lesser importance are not relevant.[^7733] |
| *ubi mel, ibi apes* | where \[there is\] honey, there \[are\] bees | Valuable things are often protected and difficult to obtain. |
| *ubi libertas. ibi patria* | where \[there is\] liberty, there \[is\] the fatherland | Or "where there is liberty, there is my country". [Patriotic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriotism) motto. |
| *ubi nihil vales, ibi nihil velis* | where you are worth nothing, there you will wish for nothing | From the writings of the Flemish philosopher [Arnold Geulincx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Geulincx); also quoted by [Samuel Beckett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Beckett) in his first published novel, *[Murphy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murphy_%28novel%29)*. |
| *ubi non accusator, ibi non iudex* | where \[there is\] no accuser, there \[is\] no judge | Thus, there can be no judgment or case if no one charges a defendant with a crime. The phrase is sometimes parodied as "where there are no police, there is no speed limit". |
| *[ubi panis ibi patria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubi_panis_ibi_patria)* | where there is bread, there is my country |  |
| *[ubi pus, ibi evacua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ubi_pus,_ibi_evacua)* | where there is pus, there evacuate it |  |
| *ubi, re vera* | when, in a true thing | Or "whereas, in reality..." Also rendered *ubi, revera* ("when, in fact" or "when, actually"). |
| *ubi societas, ibi ius* | if there's a society, law will be there | By [Aristotle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle). |
| *ubi solitudinem faciunt pacem appellant* | They make a desert and call it peace | from a speech by [Calgacus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgacus) reported/constructed by [Tacitus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacitus), *[Agricola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricola_%28book%29)*, [ch. 30](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/la:De%20vita%20et%20moribus%20Iulii%20Agricolae%20%28Agricola%29#XXX). |
| *ubi sunt?* | where are they? | Nostalgic theme of poems yearning for days gone by. From the line *ubi sunt, qui ante nos fuerunt?* ("Where are they, those who have gone before us?"). |
| *ubi unus, multi sunt* | where \[there is\] one, \[there\] are many |  |
| *ubique, quo fas et gloria ducunt* | everywhere, where right and glory leads | Motto of the [Royal Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Engineers), [Royal Artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Artillery) and most other Engineer or Artillery corps within the armies of the British Commonwealth (for example, the [Royal Australian Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Australian_Engineers), [Royal Canadian Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Engineers), [Royal New Zealand Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_New_Zealand_Engineers), [Royal Canadian Artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Artillery), [Royal Australian Artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Australian_Artillery), [Royal New Zealand Artillery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_New_Zealand_Artillery)). Interunit rivalry often leads to the sarcastic translation of **ubique** to mean *[all over the place](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/all%20over%20the%20place)* in a derogative sense. Motto of the American [Council on Foreign Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_on_Foreign_Relations), where the translation of **ubique** is often given as *omnipresent*, with the implication of pervasive hidden influence.[^7734] |
| *ultima forsan* | perhaps the last | i.e. "perhaps your last hour." A sundial inscription. |
| *ultima ratio* | last method the final argument the last resort (as force) | The term ultima ratio originates from the Thirty Years' War ; the last resort. Short form for the metaphor "The Last Resort of Kings and Common Men" referring to the act of declaring war. Used in names such as the French sniper rifle PGM Ultima Ratio and the fictional Reason weapon system. Louis XIV of France had Ultima Ratio Regum ("last argument of kings") cast on the cannons of his armies. In 1742, Frederick the Great ordered that all cannons of the Prussian Army be inscribed with the inscription Ultima Ratio Regis, the king’s last resort. Motto of the American 1st Battalion 11th Marines ; the French Fourth Artillery Regiment; Swedish Artilleriregementet . Also, the Third Battery of the French Third Marine Artillery Regiment has the motto Ultima Ratio Tribuni . The term is also borne by the gorget owned by Captain William Cattell, which inspired the crescent worn by the revolutionary militia of South Carolina and in turn the state's flag . [^7735] See also Ultima Ratio Regum (video game) . |
| *ultimo mense (ult.)* | in the last month | Used in formal correspondence to refer to the previous month. Used with inst. ("this month") and prox. ("next month"). |
| *[ultra vires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra_vires)* | beyond powers | "Without authority". Used to describe an action done without proper authority, or acting without the rules. The term will most often be used in connection with appeals and petitions. Can be used as a preposition: "the court found that the law was *ultra vires* Parliament." |
| *ultra posse nemo obligatur* | No one is obligated [beyond what he is able to do](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impossibility_of_performance). | Equivalent to *ad impossibilia nemo tenetur*, *impossibilium nulla obligatio est* and *nemo potest ad impossibile obligari*.[^7736][^7737] |
| *ululas Athenas* | (to send) owls to Athens | From Gerhard Gerhards' (1466-1536) \[better known as Erasmus\] collection of annotated Adagia (1508). Latin translation of a classical Greek proverb. Generally means putting large effort in a necessarily fruitless enterprise. Compare "[selling coal to Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selling_coal_to_Newcastle)". |
| *una hirundo non facit ver* | one swallow does not make summer | A single example of something positive does not necessarily mean that all subsequent similar instances will have the same outcome. |
| *una salus victis nullam sperare salutem* | the only safety for the conquered is to hope for no safety | Less literally, "the only safe bet for the vanquished is to expect no safety". Preceded by *moriamur et in media arma ruamus* ("let us die even as we rush into the midst of battle") in [Virgil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgil)'s *[Aeneid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aeneid)*, book 2, lines 353-354. Used in [Tom Clancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Clancy)'s novel *[Without Remorse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Without_Remorse)*, where character [John Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Clark_%28Tom_Clancy%29) translates it as "the one hope of the doomed is not to hope for safety". It was said several times in "[Andromeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Andromeda_episodes)" as the motto of the SOF units. |
| *unitas, iustitia, spes* | unity, justice, hope | Motto of [Vilnius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilnius). |
| *unitas per servitiam* | unity through service | Motto for the St. Xavier's Institution Board of Librarians. |
| *uniti aedificamus* | united we build | Motto of the Mississippi makerspace community |

| *uno sumus animo* | we are one of soul | Motto of Stedelijk Gymnasium Leiden |
| *unus multorum* | one of many | An average person. |

| *[Unus pro omnibus, omnes pro uno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unus_pro_omnibus,_omnes_pro_uno)* | One for all, all for one | unofficial motto of [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland), popularized by [The Three Musketeers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Three_Musketeers) |
| *[Urbi et Orbi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urbi_et_Orbi)* | to the city and the circle \[of the lands\] | Meaning "To [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome) and the World". A standard opening of Roman proclamations. Also a traditional blessing by the [pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope). |
| *urbs in horto* | city in a garden | Motto of the City of [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago). |
| *usque ad finem* | to the very end | Often used in reference to battle, implying a willingness to keep fighting until you die. |
| *usus est magister optimus* | practice is the best teacher. | In other words, *practice makes perfect*. Also sometimes translated "use makes master." |
| *ut aquila versus coelum* | As an eagle towards the sky | Motto of [Bowdoin College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowdoin_College), Brunswick, Maine |
| *ut biberent quoniam esse nollent* | so that they might drink, since they refused to eat | Also rendered with *quando* ("when") in place of *quoniam*. From a book by [Suetonius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suetonius) (*[Vit. Tib.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Twelve_Caesars)*, 2.2) and [Cicero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cicero) (*De Natura Deorum*, 2.3). The phrase was said by Roman admiral [Publius Claudius Pulcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publius_Claudius_Pulcher_%28consul_249_BC%29) right before the [battle of Drepana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Drepana), as he threw overboard the sacred chickens which had refused to eat the grain offered them, an unwelcome [omen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omen) of bad luck. Thus, the sense is, "if they do not perform as expected, they must suffer the consequences". He lost the battle disastrously. |
| *ut cognoscant te* | so that they may know You. | Motto of [Boston College High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_College_High_School). |
| *ut desint vires, tamen est laudanda voluntas* | though the power be lacking, the will is to be praised all the same | From [Ovid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid), *[Epistulae ex Ponto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistulae_ex_Ponto)* (III, 4, 79). |
| *ut dicitur* | as has been said; as above |  |
